title: BOYS AND GIRLS WHO GO ASTRAY
full_text: BOYS AND GIRLS WHO GO ASTRAY What about our boys and girls who go astray? Certainly it is not christian to lynch and murder them, and yet, thoughtlessness on our part and disinclination to seriously study the problem really conduce to that end. Can we not arrest the tenden- cy in that direction? Is it not pos- sible for Christian men and women to do something to save the boys and girls from perdition? At least we can think on the subject and ser- iously so, But it occurs to us that we need definite information to arouse us to the necessity of doing more than we are for the moral elevation of the young and wayward. The informa- tion can be had along many lines. We are thinking of one special line, and we cheerfully throw out the hint with the hope that good may come out of it, Many of our readers know that there is such a place as 'Cheltenham' a reformatory for incorrigible col- ored boys, and that is about all they do know about this institution. Many of our readers have heard that there is such an institution in Baltimore County, near this city, called the Industrial Home for Col- ored Girls, a reformatory for girls who have gotten beyond the control of their parents, or who have been committed to the institutions on ac- count of their shortcomings. Now what we suggest is, that some one of the largest churches in the city hold a 'special public meet- ing, the church crowded with all in- terested in the improvement of our youth along such lines and that the superintendents of these institutions together with as many of the Board of Managers, of the same who may come, to be invited to address the colored citizens of Baltimore on the respective institutions, giving detail- ed information with respect to the institutions, the inmates, their con- dition and suggest ways of mutual helpfulness. Mr. Dorsey, a few months ago, appointed superinten- dent at Cheltenham, is a most excel- lent man aud is disposed sincerely and honestly to do all that he can along the line of improvement at Cheltenham. The boys already are drawn to him and like him very much. Mr. Dorsey has splendid ideas, and has had much experience; that yet for all this he is disposed to get a valuable hint even from a small child. The colored people want to know and ought to know all about Chel- tenham, and we feel that Mr. Dorsey would gladly respond to such an in- vitationand not only tell what he knows, but kindly invite any criti- cism or suggestion which would have a tendency to improve condi- tions in the interest of the boys at the House of Reformation. By all means let us have such a meet- ing. ! Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: ""THE PUNISHMENTS HAVE BEEN TOO SEVERE.""
full_text: "THE PUNISHMENTS HAVE BEEN TOO SEVERE." "The grand jury committee on the House of Reformation for Col- ored Boys, at Cheltenham, submitt- ed a special report yesterday com- mending the management and condition of that institution, "but stating that the punishments in- flicted on the youthful inmates have been too severe." We regret to say that, in our opinion," the report states, "the punishments have been too severe, better suited for hardened adult criminals than for incorrigible youths. "We are pleased to report that the management have promised to modity this somewhat by doing away with the more severe meth- ods. In this connection one of the great needs of the institution is a strong guard building, where un- controllable inmates may be sately confined under proper police pro- tection. We believe that kind treatment and moral suasion will do more to serve the purposes of the institution than harsh and severe punishments."--Baltimore Sun, Wed. Aug. 24th. The above tells its own story. Here we have an institution exclu- sively for the Reformation of col- ored boys officered entirely by the white race. The Siate and City give thousands of dollars, annually, towards its maintenance, and although Governor Lowndes and Mayor Malster are both re- publicans, voted for by colored cit- izens of this State, yet both of these republican gentlemen appointed white men to act as trustees or directors of this eleemosynary institution for colored boys? Why this? The only plausible and log- ically consistent answer would be, that out of a colored population of more than eighty thousand, not one competent colored person could be found to serve in such a capacity. What other answer could there be to it? So far as Mayor Malster is concerned we can scarcely conceive how that he can justify his position in the mat- ter, for the writer, a tax-payər and a citizen of Baltimore, called upon his Honor and told him how im- portant it was that these poor un- fortunate colored boys, should at least, have one reputable member of their race upon the board of control, and earnestly requested him to appoint some colored man on the board. We left with the impression that the Mayor was so disposed. At the very next meet- ing of the City Council, his first appointee, a white man, declined, and immediately the Mayor sent in the name of a Mr. Doyle, white, a prominent whiskey dealer, so we are informed. We have simply stated the matter to show, that leaving the question of "patron- age" severely alone, and address- ing our attention to charitable and educational institutions, whereby the many are to be benefitted we are no more in it" there than in getting office. ointing of colored men on such boards, in the Southern States, is a very common and ordi- nary thing on the part of demo- cratic Governors and Mayors, and for the life of us, we can not un- derstand why Mayor Malster should thus seek to humiliate the Negro race in Maryland. Will he not explain? Are we Negroes worthy of such attention upon_his part? Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: CHELTENHAM AGAIN.
full_text: CHELTENHAM AGAIN. Some time ago we had occasion to call attention to the treatment accorded to the inmates of the so-called reformatory at Cheltenham, in Prince Georges Co. The matter came to the attention of the State authorities, and at their solicta- tion we sent a member of our staff down there to investigate the conditions. We were told that the cruelties that had been formerly practiced there were done away with and that a new regime had been introduced. Since that time we have heard nothing from the institu- tion until now. In referring to an arti- cle taken from a dispatch to the Even- ing News, it will be seen that if the old time practices were done away with they have been renewed. The dispatch states that a "wee color- ed youth" was found on the streets of Washington with not only a ball and chain to his legs, but hand.cuffs on his wrists. This shows that the ball and chain, which we have called attention to heretofore, has not been done away with, notwithstanding the statements made to the authorities. This Cheltenham is a most degrading institution, and is doing the young Ne- groes of this State more harın, if such a thing is possible, than the Baltimore City Jail. And it would be'a mercy to these boys to commit them to the jail than to such an infernal hole as this Cheltenham. When we published Mrs. Douglass' letter, the city authorities and the au- thorities of Cheltenham were horrified beyond measure, and expressed them- selves so; and now it is shown that the truth was told, notwithstanding their strenuous denials. Of course when the city authorities and the Grand Jury visits that place everything is in good order, but as soon as their backs are turned the same old condition of affairs are taken up again. It is time that sach steps were taken against this institution that will either put it out of basiness or reform it al- together. It can only be reformed ed by turning the whole batch of keepers out of the establishment altogether, They are brutal and the boys of the institu- tion have no reason to remember the institution when they get cut of it. save to curse the day they were incar- cerated within its infamous walls. The idea of putting handcuffs and a ball and chain on such children as the one mentioned is an ontrage, and the society that has the care of this, institu- on should be prosecuted to the full extent of the law for cruelty to chil- dren It has been claimed by the authorities of this institution that the boys cannot be kept from running away unless they are confined in some way, and the ball and chain seems to be their cheadest and best way: Now further down in the same county is a reform school that is worthy of the name "Reform." We speak of the Hart Farm School. To this school the worst boys that cau be found in the District of Columbia are sent, and after a few attempts to get away, which many of them do. they find that it is better to stay, as the treatment received there is so different to what they ex- pected. There boys are treated as if they were human beings. They are well fed and well taken care of, and in the course of time good homes are fonud for them and they get a good chance to have a good start in life. There are no brutal keepers, no whipping, no ball and chain and no fences to keep the boys from running away. The boy is taught the value of good conduct, re- ceive good treatment, and is taught to believe that he is a human being. with all that that implies, The result is that the officials of the District have no hesi- tancy in endorsing the good work that is being done at the Hart Farm School We wish that Cheltenham could be brought under such influences. But right here we will say that nothing can be expected of this demoralizing so-call- ed reformatory until the colored citi. zens of this city shall raise up and take the matter into their own hands and de- mand at the hands of the properly qual- ifed authorities better treatment for the boys committed to this place or that it be abolished entirely. title: A Good Ground of Hope.
full_text: A Good Ground of Hope. In addition to what we have al- ready attained, we have a most reasonable ground for hope, in the way of an increase of the benefits now enjoyed by the race. The natural newness of the Republican party, in coming into power, and the terrible and foul suspicion placed upon it by those of demo- cratic persuasion, with respect to more fully realizing the civil rights and other privileges of the colored race, rendered any great advance, in that direction a thing impossi ble. But in the event of popular indorsement at the coming elec- tion, reinforced by such an auspi- cious attestation of public confi- dence, we have every son to hope for such legislative enactments as will greatly im- prove the moral and material con- dition of the race. The adversary, the Democratic party, has greatly magnified the ignorance, vicious- ness and rowdyism of the colored population, and the Republican party, once more in power, will graciously apply itself to the task of converting this ignorance and viciousness into those excellent virtues which characterize an enlightened and progressive peo- ple. rеа- To accomplish this the leaders of the Republican party are pledged to the establishment of an Agricultu- ral and Industrial College for the Colored youth of the State, the enlargement and re-organization, upon a more satisfactory basis, the Cheltenham Reform School for colored boys, as well as the insti- tution of other means looking to the civic, intellectual and moral advance of the colored race. Now in the face of all this, if we are disposed to vote the Demo- cratic ticket, commonsense would inquire what may we expect, as a substitution, from such a source, to take the place of the present benefits and others reasonably sure? With the situation so clearly and pointedly set forth it is abso- lutely unnecessary to urge colored men to vote the entire Republican ticket, from the top to bottom, as their interests are so obviously and and unmistakeably identified with its success. The few colored men who fail to see the directness and urgency of the situation as above delineated, in all probability, are of that class of the population who are moved only by monetary and other cor- rupting influences. Happily for the race such men are significant- ly few. Let us demonstrate on Tuesday next our capacity of grat- Hitude towards that truly conser- vatism which builds and does not destroy, and we can do this by voting the Republican ticket. While granting the purest mo- tives to those who have charge of it we are forced to the conclusion that it is not so managed as to se- cure the best moral results. full_text: EX-SENATOR WELLINGTON. The Afro-American Ledger records with extreme gratification and pleas- ure the many courtesies and favors bestowed on this office by Ex-Senator Wellington. When Mr. Wellington was active in politics he never called in vain npon the colored voter. The colored voters of Maryland always gave him hearty support. In spite of the fact that there is such a little in results, accomplished by Mr. Wel- lington during his carerer, for the race, we prefer to believe, though we may be mistaken, that at heart he was really friendly disposed to our struggling race. In this conr ection we may be par- doned for saying that so far as the interests of the Negro are concerned we have been sadly disappointed by Senator McComas, and we do sin- cerely trust that 'ere he makes his exit from the Senate he will find it in his heart to do something for the Negro. Ex-Senator Wellington has our sincere wishes for peace, prosperity and blessing. Before many years roll around we hope to see him at work in the party with his old time enthusiasm, supported by the black voters, as in days of yore when he was State Chairman. GEN. SHYROCK AS PRESIDENT OF CHELTENHAM KEFORMATORY We rejoice very greatly indeed over the good news that Gen. Thomas J. Shryock has been elected by the Board of Managers of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, as president of that corporation. We are free to confess that we have but little if any hope for permanent usefulness of such in- stitutions as long as the present pol- icy in this respect obtains. But we have to do with certain conditions, which as long as they remain must be seriously taken into consideration. title: MR, GRASTY'S IMPRESSIONS
full_text: MB, GRASTY'S IMPRESSIONS | Mr. Grasty; the Secretary of the | Board of Supervisors of City Cbari- ties, has been visiting in the South, and incidently, he made a visit to Tuskegee. Through the morning papers he gives some idea of how he was favorably impressed at that great school, He seemed to be im- pressed with the idea that the col- ored boys at Cheltenham should, almost exclusively be taught prac- tical agriculture. We had hoped that the wonderful grip of Booker Washington, as well as his judicious executive developement and hand- ling of that great institution, had impressed Mr. Grasty with the need of putting Cheltenham under the management of a superintendent andinstructors taken from the same race as the pupils of that institution This is the paramount need, and everything else is, in a very great degree, useless until this is accom plished. We appreciate good inten- tions, but what the community wants is results, We make the claim and challenge contradiction, that all the education- al and reformatory institutions in the Southern states that are accom- plishing magnificient results both for the community and the race are officered exclusively by teachers of the same race, or by such white peo ple who, practically, make them- selves such. Reformation must come from with- in. The "Kingdom of God is with- in" people, and no one can reach, arouse and stimulate to higher things unless there is the closest con- tact and oneness. But to banish chair-caning, and other industries from Cheltenham is a great blunder. Possibly, nearly one-half of the boys who go to Cheltenham, go from the city and not from the country, and when they become of age there is no power to make them settle in the country. We must deal with facts. Then again, there are only certain months in the year when it is pos- sible to instruct in agriculture and soils, What industries are to en- gage the hands of these boys during the winter months? Mr. Grasty means well, but he is ignorant of many things with respect to colcred people and colored life. The chair- caning industry in this city is not closed against colored boys. There are quite a number of such estab- lishments operated by colored peo- ple in this city as well as in other cities. It would seem, with a population of nearly one hundred thousand col- ared people that patronage for this as well as other industries are abun- dantly wear at hand. Of one thing we are absolutely sure, and that is, the greatest need Cheltenham has is that of a compe- tent colored man as superintendent of that institution and a faculty drawn from the same race. who would work their very hands off of them in demonstrating that those boys can be reformed, uplifted and made useful citizens. Like Sumner, Garrison and others, we believe in this matter with our whole heart, and shall agitate until our white fellow citizens are lead to see the sweet reasonableness and blessing of our contention. title: THE BOARD OF ESTIMATES AND NEGLECTED COLORED CHILDREN
full_text: THE BOARDOF ESTIMATES AND NE- GLECTED COLORED CHILDREN The board of estimates of our city government is composed of Mayor Hayes, Comptroller J. H. Smith, City Enginesr Fendell and Mr. Henry Williams, president of the Second Branch of the City Council. On last Tuesday, in connection with the Cheltenham appropriation matter, the general subject of caring for ne- glected and homeless colored children was freely discussed, There was one thing that was made absolutely clear and unmistakeable, and that was, that each and every one of this Board were thoroughly, intelligent- ly and keenly interested in the prop- er care of all sorts and conditions of the unfortunate or crimina l'y inclin- ed of the colored youth. No intelli- gent colored person could have been present at the hearing and failed to have been specially impressed with the gracious, intelligent and kind spirit which permeated the inquiry with respect to the peculiarities of the situation. President Brackett of the Board of Supervisors of City Charities was present and, incidently, pointed out one of the greatest needs of the city in this direction. It is a notorious fact that many colored boys are sent either to jail or committed to reformatory insti- tutions, who ought not to be sent to such places. But the question is immediately asked, what shall we do with them? The writer is con- nected officially with at least three institutions of a reformatory char- acter, and has enjoyed splendid facil- ities for ascertaining many of the causes of moral delinquencies on the part of colored children. We do not hesitate to most heartily indorse the idea of Dr. Brackett. The need is not only immediate, but in properly supplying such a need, if wisely con- ducted, we shall contribute a great deal towards minimising and reduc- ing criminal tendencies among the colored youth. There is one point in connection with the whole matter, which un- fortunately, is not sufficiently ap- preciated by those in authority, in institucions already established for the reformation of the colored youth. Disregard of its prime importance explains why our success has not been much greater in the reformation of colored youth. If we are not mis- taken, for the most part, whether Roman Catholic or otherwise, the reformatory institutions are operat- ed by those from a race of people alien to the real and secretive life of colored youth. Hence, the members of one race are trying to reform members of an- other race,. and unable to get into the inner life of this race and there- by initiate at its very source any abiding reform, they can only hope to dress the patient, so to speak, up from the outside, with the carnest hope that it may do good. We grant fully and freely that all these persons of an alien race are actuated by the highest and noblest motive, that they are devotedly yielding their best service. And yet for all this the difficulty remains. These unfortunate boys and girls are capable of loving and being loved, they have social natures just like the rest of mankind; they have hopes and fears; they have aspirations, struggles and dejections. When they go from such reformatories they enter "colored society." Not in any particularly social or limited sense, but in the sense that they are asso- ciatedin business, in church, and so- cially intermingle with people of their own color. But little of their inner and real life will touch the white part of so- ciety. Now, from our point of view the greatest need of reformatories, for colored children, are teachers, while in every other respect fully qualified, yet unqualifiedly of the same race as the pupils themselves. It is simply idle to argue the ques- tion whether properly qualified col- ored teachers and instructors can accomplish better results in a color- ed reformatory than teachers of an- other race in the same reforma- tory. The very fact that colored people when left free to choose their own pastors teachers and physicians, in- variably select them from their own race, is evidence most substantial. In the present case it is so much the more absolutely important for per- manent results in reformation that the teachers and instructors should be of the same ráce, In the case of schools, the pupils are fairly moral and sufficiently in- telligent to accept the educational services of teachers of another race although they preſer their own. In the case of criminals, the very fact that they are "in durance vile," and that, objectively, by the sentence of court officers (white) rendersit highly important that they should be emancipated from their general suspicion and distrust of all white faces. Certainly a man who is a Negro, but despite his being a Negro he is much of a perfect gentleman and of general good qualities as to com- mand the respect and esteem of the white community, by reason of his racial identity and his social active- ity in and among the very people of whom he as well as the criminal youth are a part, could by all means be made to touch effectively the in- ner and real spot of life in that col- ored boy's heart, securely barred for- ever from one of alien blood. President Brackett of the Board of Supervisors of City Charities was present and, incidently, pointed out one of the greatest needs of the city in this direction. It is a notorious fact that many colored boys are sent either to jail or committed to reformatory insti- tutions, who ought not to be sent to such places. But the question is immediately asked, what shall we do with them? The writer is con- nected officially with at least three institutions of a reformatory char- acter, and has enjoyed splendid facil- ities for ascertaining many of the causes of moral delinquencies on the part of colored children. We do not hesitate to most heartily indorse the idea of Dr. Brackett. The need is not only immediate, but in properly supplying such a need, if wisely con- ducted, we shall contribute a great deal towards minimising and reduc- ing criminal tendencies among the colored youth. There is one point in connection with the whole matter, which un- fortunately, is not sufficiently ap- preciated by those in authority, in institucions already established for the reformation of the colored youth. Disregard of its prime importance explains why our success has not been much greater in the reformation of colored youth. If we are not mis- taken, for the most part, whether Roman Catholic or otherwise, the reformatory institutions are operat- ed by those from a race of people alien to the real and secretive life of colored youth. Hence, the members of one race are trying to reform members of an- other race,. and unable to get into the inner life of this race and there- by initiate at its very source any abiding reform, they can only hope to dress the patient, so to speak, up from the outside, with the carnest hope that it may do good. We grant fully and freely that all these persons of an alien race are actuated by the highest and noblest motive, that they are devotedly yielding their best service. And yet for all this the difficulty remains. These unfortunate boys and girls are capable of loving and being loved, they have social natures just like the rest of mankind; they have hopes and fears; they have aspirations, struggles and dejections. When they go from such reformatories they enter "colored society." Not in any particularly social or limited sense, but in the sense that they are asso- ciatedin business, in church, and so- cially intermingle with people of their own color. But little of their inner and real life will touch the white part of so- ciety. Now, from our point of view the greatest need of reformatories, for colored children, are teachers, while in every other respect fully qualified, yet unqualifiedly of the same race as the pupils themselves. It is simply idle to argue the ques- tion whether properly qualified col- ored teachers and instructors can accomplish better results in a color- ed reformatory than teachers of an- other race in the same reforma- tory. The very fact that colored people when left free to choose their own pastors teachers and physicians, in- variably select them from their own race, is evidence most substantial. In the present case it is so much the more absolutely important for per- manent results in reformation that the teachers and instructors should be of the same ráce, In the case of schools, the pupils are fairly moral and sufficiently in- telligent to accept the educational services of teachers of another race although they preſer their own. In the case of criminals, the very fact that they are "in durance vile," and that, objectively, by the sentence of court officers (white) rendersit highly important that they should be emancipated from their general suspicion and distrust of all white faces. Certainly a man who is a Negro, but despite his being a Negro he is much of a perfect gentleman and of general good qualities as to com- mand the respect and esteem of the white community, by reason of his racial identity and his social active- ity in and among the very people of whom he as well as the criminal youth are a part, could by all means be made to touch effectively the in- ner and real spot of life in that col- ored boy's heart, securely barred for- ever from one of alien blood. . .

title: CHELTENHAM AGAIN
full_text: CHELTENHAM AGAIN It is now almost a matter of peri- odical expectation that, once in a while, the Grand Juries will in severe language condemn the irregularities and delinquencies of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham. The late Grand Jury has presented the same old story of dark cells, inhuman treatment and inability of the Reformatory to re- form the boys sent hither. We are not surprised at any of the revela- tions made known. We are, how- ever, surprised that intelligent and thoughtful men of the dominant race continue to persuade themselves of the possibility of accomplishing the very best results on behalf of those boys, as well as in the interest of the `community, by means of a staff of officers and teachers of the white race. There might be some hope of the realization of such blessed results if the very best white men and wo- men, of culture, refinement and influ- ence were ordinarily the teachers and instructors. Only a supreme love for humanity could carry such a class of persons to work among such depraved and unfortunate crea- tures. But as a matter of fact, the small salaries which the managers are compelled to pay almost posi- tively insures the employment only, as a rule, of very ordinary white persons to teach and uplift these de- based Negro youth. Washing- ton and Hon. John H. title: A TRIP TO CHELTENHAM.
full_text: A TRIP TO CHELTENHAM. Mayor Hayes and Other Notables Visit the House of Reformation Eor Colored Boys. Last Saturday, Mayor Hayes, in company with Mr. Joseph Janey, Mr. Orin C. Painter, Rev. George F. Bragg, Jr., directors on the part of the institution; Mr. Harry S. Cum- mings, one of the directors on the part of the city and Mr. Hiram Wat- ty, member of the City Council, paid a visit to Cheltenham and thorough- ly inspected that institution, The Mayor expressed himself as being much pleased with some of the things he saw and was not sparing in his condemnation of some other things which he thought ought not to exist. The company partook of dinner at the institution and afthr dinner, the Mayor addressed the boys in the chapel. The Mayor will endeavor to have the appropriation for the in- stitution increased next year, as their is great need of an increase, if the institution i' to be brought up to a proper standard. Rev. Dr. W. V. Tunnell, warden of King Hall Theological Seminary, Washington; D: C., accompanied the committee and also made an address to the boys. A Costly Thimble. Think of it, a thimble which cost $65,000 in American money! And think of a husband who presents his wife with such a gift! It belongs to the queen of Siam. Thimbles were not in use in Siam until a comparatively recent date. The king, seeing that English and Ameri- can women visiting his court used thimbles, had one made for his wife. The thimble, is of gold, enriched with precious stones. It is shaped like a partially opened lotus flower, each petal bearing the interlaced initials of the sovereign and his wife in ame- thysts. rubies, emeralds and topazes. Around the rim of the thimble can be read the date of the marriage of the royal pair according to the Siamese and European calendars, each number and each, letter being of alternate dia- monds and pearls. Norway, Ireland and Spain have more blind people in proportion to population than any other European countries. Spain has 216 per 100,000, Norway 208 and Ireland 111. title: MAYOR HAYES AND CHELTENHAM.
full_text: MAYOR HAYES AND CHELTENHAM. Largely through the efforts of Councilman Watty, and Mr. Cum- mings and Rev. Mr. Bragg, members of the Board of Managers of the House of Reformation for colored boys located at Cheltenham, Prince Georges County, His Honor the Mayor of Baltimore, in company with the above gentlemen, and others of tlie committee from the Board visited the above institution on Sat- urday of last week. It was the Mayor's first visit and he was much pleased with it, and is determiaed to do all in his power to increase the appropriation from the city to- wards this institution for its proper and creditable support. The Mayor freely expressed himself with regard to many things in connection with the management of the institu- tion, and enthusiastically expressed his very great interest in the boys. In fact, his earnest address to the boys in the chapel demonstrated that he was not only a man of a great head, but also of a warm, kindly and sympathetic heart: Seldom have we been so impressed with a speech from a public official as we were with the utterances of Mayor Hayes He spoke right out from the heart. The principles of the Mayor with respect to that institution are sound and have the ring, not of flunkeyism, but of genuine manliness, Certainly the colored people of Maryland have a warm friend in the present Mayor of Baltimore. It is far better to have a head to lose than not to have any head at at all. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: utter. The defeat of the old Re- publican machine in this state, marked a most decided advance for the race in Maryland. We needed to be emancipated from the servil. ity which has characterised such a large number of colored voters for long time. That has at last been accomplished, and the way is now clear for our entrance into poli- tics. We have never been in politics. Heretofore, we have been used to help win victories for others. The present Governor of Maryland could not have been elected without the aid of colored voters. This assertion even Mr. Golsborough must admit. And, yet, what is he to us, more than Mr. Gorman would have been if he had been elected in spite of our opposi- tion. Judging the younger Mr. Gorman by the practical friendness of his father, the senior Gorman, with respect to helping individuals of the colored race, we would cer- tainly conclude that he could not have been less friendly thad his father. But what of Mr. Golds- borough What has he done to- wards our advancement. Soon after his inauguration, his attention was directed to the educational and charitable needs of the Negro pop- ulation of this state. What move has he made in that direction? His attention was also directed to the Melvale Reformatory, for col- ored girls, and the Cheltenham Re- formatory, for colored boys, and the request made that he appoint a suitable colored man, or woman, on each of the Boards of the insti- tutions mentioned. It is hardly necessary to mention that he has failed to make any such appoint- ments. In the face of all this, we do not hesitate in giving it forth as our deliberate conviction, that were such a man as William Cabel Bruce, or Archibald Taylor or any demo- crat of that type, the occupant of the Gobernatorial chair, that such would not hesitate to appoint well qualified persons to serve on such boards, which institutions being wholly concerned with the needs of the colored race. Yea, more that this, it is to just such men that we must look for larger appropriations for the educational and charitable institutions of the state, designed for our people. This freedom which has begun to dawn upon us will dawn, more and more, and satisfy all our ex- pectations, just in proportion as we cooperate with this class of citizens in securing the best men to go to Annapolis. A new political organization is about to be organized throughout the city, among the men of our race. An oragnization which will control some three or four thous- and votes, pledged to the best in- terests of our people. Here, then, is our opportunity. A certain element of the Democratic party anxiously desires to send to Annap- olis the very best men of brains and character in the state. Is there no way whereby we can help in this matter. What do we vitally need, in this state, in an educa- tional and charitable way? The men among us who have studied the conditions ought to make known, definitely, our needs. And, then, if these good friends, candi- dates for the Legislature, will pledge us their hearty and earnest support, along such lines, ought to vote for them, whether they be Democrats, Progressives, or any thing else. We ought to have enough political sense to vote for the men who will openly pledge themselves to the improvement of such interests as directly concern us. title: MARYLAND INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL FOR BOYS
full_text: MARYLAND INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL FOR BOYS Such is the name and title of an institution which has been proposed by His Honor Judge Williams of the Juvenile Court, of the city of Baltimore. The bill which has already been prepared will be in- troduced in the State Legislature. The measure has the heartiest support of the Ministerial Alliance of this city. Judge Williams ap peared before this body. upon its invitation, at the December meet- ing, and outlined the features of the measure, and the Alliance not only warmly indorsed the project, but appointed a committee, repre- senting the various denominations of colored citizens, to communicate with the Governor about the mat- ter, and to cooperate with the Judge in such ways as he should deem most helpful. The bill provides that the in- stitution shall be located in the country, not more than 15 miles remote from this city; it appropri- ates twenty-five thousand dollars for the acquiring of the plant, and ten thousand dollars annually, from the State of Maryland, and five thousand from the city of Balti- a more, towards its maintainence and support. Colored boys between the ages of 8 and 18 may be com- mitteed to the institution by the Judge of the Juvenile Court, or by other judicial authority through- out the State. It needs no argu- ment whatever to establish the necessity of such an institution. We are devoutly glad that it comes from such man as Judge Williams. Apart from his con- nection with the Juvenile Court, and the splendid opportunities thus afforded to judge of the real necessity of such an institution, Judge Williams is a godly man, and a true type of the Christian gentleman, and so impressed were the colored preachers with his sympathetic personality, that were it in their power they would make him Judge of the Juvenile Court for life. And, while writing on this subject, it comes to our mind, from personal knowledge, that there is a large army of such benevolently disposed white citi- zens who share in the same sincere and devoted feelings towards their colored brethren, as our friend Judge Williams. But, the great trouble is, they do not touch the lives of colored citizens at any point, and colored people, generally speaking, are wholly ignorant of their existence. Now is the oppor- tunity for some of the white states- men, at Annapolis, who have, in so many ways, wrought an impression upon colored people, that they are entirely indifferent to anything which pertains to them, save re- strictive legislation, to vindicate the good and redeeming side of their nature. And so we devoutly hope that they may embrace the present opportunity as an earnest of their good intentions. In con- nection with this same subject, it is most timely that we should note the good work of a white country- man, who has proven a real bene- factor of the colored race in Mary- land. And, this we shall do in the article headed "Cheltenham.". Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: CHELTENHAM Cheltenham is situated in Prince George's county, Md. Located at that place, is an institution for colored boys, known as the House of Reformation. The name of Enoch Pratt is not only connected with the public libraries of our city, but also with this institution for colored boys at Cheltenham. The superintendent of the House of Reformation is Mr. John B. Pyles, a white man, and a native of that county. He is a man of a kind heart, but brave and energetic. His is a great task, but he is perfectly at home in the doing of the work devolving upon him. He is, really, a benefactor of the Negro race. just where such bene- faction is most needed. But, we started this article simply to call attention to the fact, that Chelten- ham, in operation, is more of a great industrial school, than a "Reformatory." Some of the many colored boys who enter the portals of Cheltenham receive for the first time a knowledge of the primary lessons in civilization. Good food, warm clothing, school and work; and all under proper discipline. Very recently, a colored tailor, Mr. J. P. Featherstone, of this city, succeeded the former tailor of the institution who was white. We are pleased to learn that Mr. Featherstone is not only giving satisfaction, but is making a good reputation for himself. In a pri- vate letter to one of the members of the Board of Managers, Mr. Featherstone writes, in part, as follows: "The head of my service seems rather much pleased up to the present. I have already turned out 70 blue pants, 50 blue coats, 65 grey pants, 18 grey coats, 36 top shirts, 45 under drawers, with required repairs for entire school. There are 12 boys in my depart- ment;6 machines and 6 bench boys. Two of good behavior, four in moods of behavior, and the other six very troublesome; but 1 am able to keep them, so far, in thorough subjection, and every authority is given me in the com- plete circle of my charges." Mr. Featherstone seems to be the right man in the right place. We are glad of this, because when other vacancies exists, if colored men, of the proper moral and efficient type can be found, they will have vouchsafed them the same opportunity Mr. Featherstone is so well and wisely using. Two things more. From the above sample, the reading colored com- munity can get some idea of the value and importance of the work at Cheltenham. It is a little sur- prising that so few, almost none, representative colored people ever visit this institution. Such not only have a standing invitation, but they are sure to become en- thusiastic supporters of the insti- tution, if once they visit the place. Finally, the only way to learn how to manage such a great institution is by the race availing itself of such opportunities as, now and then, become open as indicated in the filling of the place of tailor. Let the race have the right kind of men for such openings whenever they shall occur. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

Bragg and Mr. Bernard Taylor, members of the Board of Directors of the House of Reformation in Prince Georges County. Maryland, paid a visit to the institution last Tuesday. full_text: MRS. HOOKER IS FRIEND OF BOYS Intervenes To Save Youngsters From Jail While Enroute To Cheltenham Through the efforts of Mrs. Donald Hooker, Mrs. Hugh.Π. Young and other prominent white women the old custom of detain- ing boys in the City Jail while awaiting transportation to the Colored House of Reformation has been abolished. Instead, the boys are now kept in a room on the second floor of the Northern Police Station while waiting for an official from Cheltenham to come after them. Several were kept in the station this week. "We had heard of the existence of the situation," Mrs. Hooker told the Afro-American Thursday morning," went over to jail to see for ourselves. We were shocked to find that colored boys were kept there with criminals and went to see Police Commissioner Gaither about the matter. When we suggested the Northern Police State he and Judge Wiliams, of the Juvenile Court, gave his ready consent." Mrs. Hooker and a number of ladies are also interested in a movement to have the colorea parental school started. An ap- propriation of $10,000 therefore is now lying idle in the city treasury. C. on legal business last week. He also had letters of introduction from Judge Rose, the United States District Attorney, Marshall Stockham and State's Attorney Leach, but officials in Raleigh did not want to see these. saying the one from the Cardinal was enough. title: CHELTENHAM NOT AN IDEAL SPOT: E.B. TAYLOR, MEMBERS OF BOARD OF MANAGERS, ANSWERS EDITORIAL IN LAST WEEK'S AFRO POOR CONDITIONS ADMITTED BOYS HAVE TO WORK OUT BECAUSE STATE DOES NOT PROVIDE SUFFICIENT FUNDS
full_text: CHELTENHAM NOT AN IDEAL SPOT E. B. Taylor, Members of Board of Managers, An- swers Editorial in Last Week's Afro POOR CONDITIONS ADMITTED Boys Have To Work Out Because State Does Not Provide Sufficient Funds The House of Correction at Chel- tenham is not an ideal institution any more than the Colored High School, declared E. B. Taylor, mem- ber of the Board of Managers in reply to an editorial in last week's AFRO-AMERICAN. The editorial commented on the lack of any useful educational sys- tem at Cheltenham, the convict plan of leasing boys to work on adjoining farms, and ended by declaring: Two colored members are on the Board of Managers of Cheltenham. No part of the criticism appears to have touched them sufficiently to make a public statement. Is their silence an evidence of their satis- faction with conditions at Chelton- ham? HAS NOT KEPT SILENT Denying that he had kept silent or was satisfied with Cheltenham, Mr. Taylor pointed out that he had recently printed an article in the AFRO-AMERICAN concerning condi- tions there and therefore could not be accused of keeping silent. "I admit," Mr. Taylor said "that only two trades are taught at the House of Correction, that the boys are hired out to work on adjacent farms, and that the schooling does not proper them for good citizen- ship when they leave, but the fault lies with the colored people them- selves. They should be behind the members on the Board, and should appeal to the Governor and other State authorities to give Chelten- ham an appropriation large enough to operate them properly. "If we did not hire boys out to work, there would not be sufficient money with which to run the insti- tution. BOARD INVESTIGATED "A letter in the AFRO-AMERICAN by James Ireland declaring that the boys were mistreated by Superin- tendent John B. Pyles, that he lay in the shade neglecting his duties and compelled boys to fan him, and that one of the boys had killed an- other, was investigated by our Board which spent a day on the grounds. The AFRO-AMERICAN was invited to this investigation." When informed that the AFRO- AMERICAN knew nothing of an in- vestigation and was hearing of it for the first time, Mr. Taylor said he understood from President Janney of the Board that the AFRO-AMERICAN had been asked to be present if it wished. Mr. Taylor said that the investiga- tion proved that the murder was committed and the boy was public- ly tried for the offense. No one could be found, however, who would sub- stantiate charges against the super- intendent. "Anyone," he said, "can claim that there is mistreatment of boys and shad food at Cheltenham, but unless he is willing to come before the Board and press his charges, his claims are worthless. UP TO COURTS Asked to comment upon the pres- ent conditions by which white chil- dren may be committed to institu- tions for 20 or 60 days while all colored children are committed to Cheltenham until they become 21 years of age, Mr. Taylor said this matter is beyond the province of the Board. "It is up to the Courts," he said. "If you want these things changed, it is up to the people to ask judges not to send boys to Chel- tenham until conditions are like you would have them." full_text: FORUM "The Cat" and Cheltenham, Two Different Institutions.. To the Editor: January 18th, 1913. I would be obliged if you will cor- rect in your next issue the error which appeared in today's paper naming "Warden Lankford" as "sup- erintendent at Cheltenham in Anne Arundel Co." Mr. Lankford is not a warden a: Cheltenham, which, if you mean the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, is not in Anne Arundel County, and has no warden. The reformatory at Cheltenham has the reputation of being a model: for similar institutions in various other parts of the country, as one of the best and most humanely managed semi-penal institutions in the states, and one of the only two containing colored inmates, which has colored representatives on the board. Each Grand Jury has taken occasion to commend its efficient management. Thanking you in advance for mak- ing this correction of an error which I am sure was an inadvertance on your part. in your otherwise very accurate paper, I am, Very truly yours. Ε. Β. title: JUDGE SCORES PROCEDURE IN JUVENILE COURT: COMMITTING YOUTHFUL OFFENDERS FOR LONG TERMS ON TECHNICAL CHARGES TERMED OUTRAGEOUS BOY FOUND NOT GUILTY RICHARD JENKINS FREED FROM CHELTENHAM BY CRIMINAL COURT JUDGE
full_text: JUDGE SCORES PROCEDURE IN JUVENILE COURT Committing Youthful Of P fenders For Long Terms On Technical Charges Termed Outrageous BOY FOUND NOT GUILTY Richard Jenkins Freed From Cheltenham By a Criminal Court Judge In rendering a decision of not guilty in the case of Richard Jenkins, age 16, charged in the Ju- venile Court of being a minor with- out proper care, committed to Chel- tenham, and brought before him on appeal, Judge Stanton violently1 scored the practice of the Juvenile Court in sending boys to these in-s stitutions for long terms when they have committed trivial offenses. Richard Jenkins and a number of boys engaged in a fight in which one of the boys was cut with a pen knife. He was tried in the Ju- venile Court and committed Cheltenham but through Atty. Roy S. Bond his case was appealed, and when the testinzony was presented Judge Stanton stated that the practice of twisting these charges to fit the jurisdiction of the Ju- venile Court and incarcerating these boys for long terms was an outrage. It was pointed out that the shortest term that a boy could serve when sent to one of these institu- tions was 17 months, and that in many cases they had to stay until they were twenty-one, and coming into the criminal court with past crime records and cominitting much greater offenses got sentences for 30 and 60 days. men There was another case recently in the courts where a man and a boy were charged jointly with lar- cony. The boy was tried in the Juvenile Court and committed to Cheltenham indetinitel while the man was given a 30-day sentence, The fault lies not in the adminis- tration of the Juvenile Court, it is declared, but in the construction of the law governing its power and jurisdiction. The Juvenile Court can only commit boys to these institu- tions on the technical charge of their being minors without proper care. This blanket charge is applied to every kind of charge coming into the court and the general rule is to send offenders up until they are of age, however trivial the charge. The more fortunate boys, however, are sometimes placed in homes or other- wise paroled. ( 1 i 1 1 This law seems to have been made especially in interest of these insti- tutions and without regard to the . best interest of the boy or girl, : The whole question of dealing with juvenile offenders should receive more consideration from leaders in religion, education and general wel- 1, fare, it was pointed out. title: COLORED TEACHERS FOR CHELTENHAM: REV. GEO. F. BRAGG, MEMBER OF BOARD, SAYS THIS CHANGE SHOULD BE MADE EFFORT BEGUN IN 1903 TWO COLORED TEACHERS SENT THERE DID REMARKABLE WORK
full_text: COLORED TEACHERS FOR CHELTENHAM Rev. Geo. F. Bragg, Member of Board, Says This Change Should Be Made EFFORT BEGUN IN 1903 Two Colored Teachers Sent There Did Remarkable Work The first and most important change which should be made at the House of Reformation for Boys at Cheltenham is to give the school colored teachers. Rev. Dr. George F.Bragg, Jr., a member of the Board made this statemem to the Afro-American today. He also declared that a State like Maryland which is com- mitted to the policy of separate colored schools and colored teach- ers should see that the policy is also carried om at Cheltenham. This step might easily be brought about he said providing represen- tative persons make this request of Mayor Jackson and Governor Ritchie. Rev. Dr. Braggs state- ment follows: 20 YEARS ON BOARD I was elected a member of the Board of Managers of the House of Reformation in 1901, and have been re-elected every year since that time. From the very begin- ning I have been under the convic- tion that the several schools there should be taught by colored per- sons. Through my persistency in the matter, 20 years ago, a beginning was made in that direction. Gen. Shryock strongly favored it. I am sending herewith an extract from a personal letter received by me from Mrs. Ance E. Mitchell a col- ored body whom I secured as teacher. Mr. Mitchell, her husband, was placed in charge of the chair caning department. The contents of the letter are most suggestive of the present, notwithstanding the letter was written 20 years ago. The date of the letter is Sept. 5, 1903. NEW SUPERINTENDENT In part it says: "Today's Afro-American states your return: I hope your vacation has been both pleasurable and profitable. Of course, you are aware of the changes. Mr. Pyles is now acting Superintendent. The boys are even now under better control, Gen. Shryock, having been down and one evening called all the boys together and grandly and firmly, announced his intention of running the affairs of Cheltenham, laid down the rules to all officers and boys, and already good results are attained. There are now two schools, with the larger boys, and two with the small boys. Gen. Shryock recommended sort of segregation. I have now the smallest boys, to in number, with the exception of a few retained helpers, so as not to cripple the work. "There had been a noticeable degree of improvement in my school, as a whole. Or within the past two months. Am pleased to undertake the helping of the smallest boys before they become hardened. I find many of them impressionable, and fit months for their intellectual moral and physical advancement. There is a whole chapter of happenings, I will not weary you with detail, but be- ing fully aware of your loyalty and struck for the right preaching of our race being an over-prejudiced people, I wait merely relate to you the parting of Mr. Dorsey had resigned with us. Superintendent. "Extending his hand, and bidding both "good-bye", Mr. Dorsey said: "I wish you in all your future efforts. I must say you have done much for source: you, surely, have raised my estimation of your race, and aroused in me a hope for them that I never had before. I am glad to have known you, and to know that in your care are such people." My reply was "Thank you, Mr. Dorsey, but you probably have been most unfortunate in your con- tact with your race. Among us are many superior to me, farther advanced, in every way, I came here merely do my duty al- ways. CONFESSION OF DISTRUST "Thus ran a conversation that was alike pleasing and sure surprising, with its con- fession of distrust of our race, and appar- ent conversion to behalf and hope. I said to John (her husband) our coming has been worth while: that we have lived to see and hear these words, uninvited, from Mr. Dorsey's lips. God surely is with us, and here is one reward for faith- fulness to His laws. Mr. and Mrs. Dor- sey made us a friendly call before leaving." MAYOR HAYES PLEASED I think the above letter is worthy of re-production at this time. In company with Mayor Hayes, I as well as others, visited Mrs. Mitchell's school, and the Mayor was specially pleased and frankly and heartily expressed himself in favor of colored teach- ers for these boys. From the very first I advocated such a change and all during my membership on the board have never lost an op- portunity to urge the same. That is the one thing in connection with this institution that should be done. As for Mr. Pyles I have nothing but words of praise. I think, un- der all the circumstances, he has bravely striven to do his duty. But it is a situation, and not a theory, which confronts us, and I can con- ceive of no good reason for the re- tention of white teachers in the schools of that institution. Mr. and Mrs. Mitchell did splen- did work, but after some years of service, the isolation was too great for them. Such would not be the case if ALL the teachers were of the same race as the boys of that institution. The boys would be brought into the life of the best of their own race, and, reflecting the same, would be transformed into the same likeness. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: FORUM: ""THE CUT"" AND CHELTENHAM, TWO DIFFERENT
full_text: FORUM "The Cut" and Cheltenham, Two Different Institutions. To the Editor: January 18th, 1919. I would be obliged if you will cor- rect in your next issue the error which appeared in today's paper naming "Warden Lankford" as "sup- erintendent at Cheltenham in Anne Arundel Co." Mr. Lankford is not a warden at Cheltenham, which, if you mean the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, is not in Anne Arundel County, and has n warden. The reformatory at Cheltenham has the reputation of being a'model for similar institutions in various other parts of the country, as one of the best and most humanely managed semi-penal institutions in the states, and one of the only two containing colored inm tes, which has colored representatives on the board. Each Grand Jury has taken occasion to commend its efficient management. Thanking you in advance for mak- ing this correction of an error which I am sure was an inadvertance on your part, in your otherwise very accurate paper, I am, Very truly yours, E. B. TAYLOR Representing the City of Baltimore on the Board of Managers, House of Correction, Cheltenham, Prince George's Co., Md. TAKES SLAP AT MINISTER WHO PROPOSED SLATE 1426 Ward St., Baltimore, Md. Mr. Editor of the Afro-American: I read an article entitled "Minister! Proposes Slate." The said minister is not a member of the Baltimore Conference. Two years ago he trans. ferred to the Philadelphia Confer- ence. He may have his transfer on the road to the Baltimore Conference if so he is not a member of any as yet. He is standing on the outside between the LWO conferences. We resent such an article coming from an outsider. We men who have been in this conference for 25, 30 and 40 years do not want instruction from the Rev. Mr. Armstrong. Let hin: prove himself in our church and con- ference before he undertakes to tell us what to do. I have been traveling in the Baltimore Conference for 28 years, and I would not dare to dic- tate to the Conference who they should elect to the General Confer- ence. I pray if Rev. Mr. Armstrong has his transfer in his pocket, he will wait until he gets back in the Balti- more Conference and received by.the Conference and then prove himself Worthy to remain in it. REYJ. RANELSON, 1426 Ward St., Baltimore

title: NINE YAR OLD BOY SENTENCED TO CHELTENHAM: FRANK ONLEY WHO ESCAPED FROM MANY HOMES IS SAFELY HOUSED AT LAST FOUND THRU AFRO SISTER OF ST. ELIZABETH'S RECOGNIZES NAME OF RUNAWAY HELD AT STATION HOUSE
full_text: NINE YEAR OLD BOY SENTENCED TO CHELTENHAM Frank Onley Who Escaped From Many Homes Is Safely Housed At Last FOUND THRU AFRO Sister Of St. Elizabeth's Re- cognizes Name Of Run- away Held At Station House Nine-year-old Frank Onley is an elusive chap, but he is safe now-in the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham, Judge Williams, of the Juvenile Court, having sen- tenced him to that institution on Tuesday. The little fellow, who is described as a "bad boy with a wanderlust," was taken from St. Eliabeth's Home and adopted by Mr. and Mrs. William Davenport, five months ago. He was given a good homel with two other children adopted by the Davenports and sent to School 109, Fremont avenue and King street. He played truant and cut up other didoes and Mrs. Daven- port sent him back to St. Eliza- beth's Home several weeks ago. He was left in the office of one of the sisters, but escaped when her back was turned. the Descriptions were sent out broad cast, but he cluded poilce. He slept under steps, begged pennies and people gave him food. The police of the West- ern District apprehended him last Friday, and he was taken to the Juvenile Court, were he gave a fic- titious name and told the officials that he had been brought here from te country by his parents and gotten lost from them. He was committed to St. Mary's Home, Presstman and Gilmor street. One of the sisters there picked up a copy of the ARFO-AMERICAN last week and read where a boy called Frank Davenport had es- caped from St. Mary's Home. Despite the fact that the boy de- nied that he was the one, one of the sisters went to the home of the Davenports at 298 N. Arlington avenue and ascertained that their ward was the boy wanted. On his promise to do better the boy was turned over to Mrs. Da- venport's brother, John T. Giles, Monday, and he took him to her home. He was washed up, given a change of clothing and a good meal. He was allowed to sit on the front steps with another boy. Tiring of this, he asked to be al- lowed to go into the yard and ran out of the gate. Mrs. Davenport gave chase, and after running four blocks after the boy the police caught him. He tugged and tried to get away, but was taken back home. He was made to put on girl's clothes and placed in an up- stairs room. At night he was taken 10 the Southwestern Police Station, and on Tuesday his sentence to Cheltenham followed. ! title: Jury Frees Boy Tried For Cellmate's Death
full_text: Jury Frees Boy Tried For Cellmate's Death Upper MarYpro, Aug. 10-Stan- Jey Jackson, an inmate, of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, Prince Georges County, ws acquitted by a jury of the charge of murdering William Jones, another inmate, at the special session of the Circuit Court here today. During a haz- ing party staged in the cell Jack- son was alleged to have struck Jones over the head with a bucket. Robert W. Wells, defending Jackson, contended that the boys had been confined to the cell for about twenty days and that the condition of Jones, owing to lack of proper food, was the cause of his death. title: The FORUM
full_text: The FORUM Is The Democratic Party An En- emy of The Colored Schools? Rev. Geo. F. Bragg Asks This Question And Answers It  Mr. Editor, when you were a small boy, in 1895, we had an important election in this city and State. By the most solid vote of Negroes, and thousands of reputable Democrats, a Republican was elected Governor, and a Republican was elected May- The Legislature was Republi- can, and the City Council was Re- publican. The city School Board was also Republican. The colored group asked of the Republican Legislature the found- ing of a state institution, similar to Tuskegee, for Colored People of Maryland. The bill was introdue- ed, and had a chance of passing: but our Republican governor, and his Board of State Education, de- feated it, on the ground, "there is no pressing necessity" for the same. In the City Council, in 1896, the late Dr. J. Marcus Cargill, intro- duced a measure to "eliminate" white teachers from our colored schools. After a Republican City Council had amended nearly all the life out of the bill it finally passed. In the shape in which it passed, if honestly and fairly enforced, the "elimination" would have been ex- ceedingly slow. But, by actual sub- terfuge, with a Republican Mayor, School Board, and Council, every advantage was taken and the mat- ter of elimination delayed Pressure and threats, were brot to bear upon our white Republicans: and, tawo years after the bill had passed the first beginning in the matter of "elimination" was initi- ated, during the fall of 1898, when Henry Grafton Brown, and Miss Nannie Groomes were put in charge of the East Street School, in East Baltimore. Now, as a contrast with the above. In the fall of 1899, Thomas Gordon Hayes, a Democrat, was elected Mayor over W. T. Malster. Despite his infidelity in the matter, Malster received, practically. the united support of the Colored Poeple. Hay- es was under no political obligation to the Colored Race. But soon after his inauguration the. "New chart- er" went into effect. A new School Board, of nine persons, was ap- pointed by Mr. Hayes, and it was this School Board appointed by the Democratic Mayor which wrought a radical change in the Colored Schools. It was this board that gave us Prof. Hugh Brown, and an entire colored faculty in our High School. Mr. Hooper, as Mayor, had the opportunit to appoint a colored man on the Cheltenham Board: but. did not do it. Mr. Malster had the same opportunity, but appointed two white men; and when his at- tention was called to the matter he promised to do better next time. But one of his appointees declined, and he immediately appointed an- other white man, a Mr. Doyle, a whiskey dealer. Now for the contrast, Thomas G. Hayes, a Democratic Mayor, was the first of the Mayors of Balti- more City to make such an appoint- ment. He appointed Gen. Shry- rock and Harry S. Cummings to represent the city of Baltimore on that Board. Timanus, Republi-1 can Mayor, made no appointments of a colored man on the board of that institution. Preston followed the example of the Democratic Hayes, and re-ap-1 pointed Shryrock and Cummings.( Upon the death of these gentlemen, 1 he appointed as their successors.: former Gov. Goldsborough and E. B. Taylor. The late Republican 1 Mayor, following the examples of his predecessors, made no Negro( appointments. I have simply re-1 cited facts. These facts carry their 1 own comment. George F. Bragg, Jr.

title: Grand Jury Report Hits Celtenliam Reformatory: GRAND JURY URGES CURB ON FLOGGINGS AT CHELTENHAM Body In Report Recommends That Whippings Be Permitted Only in Superintendent's Presence POOR SCHOOLING THERE Boys Said To Be Sent To School Rooms Only When Weather Is Inclement Outside
full_text: Grand Jury Report Hits Cheltenham Reformatory GRAND JURY URGES CURB ON FLOGGINGS AT CHELTENHAM Body In Report Recommends That Whippings Be Per- mitted Only in Super- intendent's Presence POOR SCHOOLING THERE Boys Said To Be Sent To School Rooms Only When Weather Is Inclement Outside Recommendations that would stop indiscriminate flogging of inmates of the House of Reformation at Cheltenham, Prince George's County and would increase the length of the t school term were contained in the report of the Grand Jury submitted to Judge Stein last week. The report urges specifically that in cases where punishment is met ed out, it be done only by the super- intendent, or in his presence. This action followed an investigation in-t to the brutal beating administered Earl Crowdy by one of the guards t at Cheltenham last fall. The boy's knee was injured and he spent over a month in the hospital. Poor educational facilities at Cheltenham are also scored in the report, which makes public the fact that juvenile delinquents sent there from the city and counties, are only f sent to school when the weather in inclement outside. In other state in- stitutions for whites, boys get from two to three hours and more school ing per day. Except in the dead of f winter, no classes at all are held at Cheltenham. The report declares that the institution already has suf- ficient calls rooms and should seek the assistance of the State in secur- ing competent teachers. Tuberculosis Patient Not Isolated i 11 Isolation of a patient at the insti tution who is suffering with tuber- culosis is also recommended by he report, which urges that such pa- tients in the future be segregated that there will be no danger of in-t fecting others or be sent to the hos- pital at Henryton. The use of a com-v mon towel for bathing by the boys whereby skin diseases may le spread is called attention to and individual towels for each boy are urged, Convict System Referred To. The conviet system of hiring out boys committed to Cheltenham to surrounding farmers is mentioned in the report, which states, "the man- agement should be relieved of the necessity of hiring boys out and the handicap of the lack of funds." Su- perintendent Pyles recently declared that he was forced to hire boys out to neighboring farmers because the State did not appropriate enough funds to run the institution without outside aid. Of the 300 boys in Cheltenham at present, 200 of them are from Baltimore City. No Mention of Cruelties. 1 The Grand Jury report declares that buildings and grounds were well kept and the inmates of appear- ent good health, with the exception of one tuberculosis patient. Nol mention was made of the cruel prac tice of compelling Loys in squads of eight and ten under the direction of a larger boy to clean sticks, leaves! and other rubbish from the immense grounds with their bare hands, 1 According to inmates, no rakes are, provided the boys, who go over every! inch of the grounds around the d buildings on hands and knees and f using their fingers as rakes remove every leaf, pebble and stick, which is clawed in a pile and later put in a bag held by the older student. Parents of inmates have asked the question, why boys have the time to rake the lawn, with their fingers, when it could be done in a few hours with rakes and the boys' time be spent in learning to read and write instead. Mental Tests For Melvale The grand jury report on the In- dustrial School for Girls at Melvale, states that the larger portion of the 99 inmates there are employed in the sewing room on power machines. The segregation of inmates who are run down, predisposed toward tuber- culosis, or affected with venereal disease is urged, and the abolish- ment of the community towel for bathing purposes. 1 According to the report, the city! school system should be asked to co- operate with the Institution in mak- ing mental tests of all inmates so that those who attend school might be properly graded, and the large number of mental defectives be placed in classes by themselves. Erection of a portable building for recreation purposes is also recom- mended. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

Ritchie and Mayor Jackson Urged to Abolish Broom Factory Altogether Local authorities are inves- tigating the case of Earl Crow dy, an inmate of the Maryland House of Reformation at Chel- tenham, sald to have been brutally beaten by three guards and sent to the hospital to have his wounds dressed. Charging that the broom factory at the House of Reformation for colored boys at Cheltenham is un- fair competition, exploits boys sent there and keeps them from getting any schooling, and employs them at an occupation they cannot use in after life, leading labor officials in a letter to Mayor Jackson and Governor Ritchie urged that the factory be abolished. The statement is signed by Sam- uel Compers head of the A. F. L... Henry F. Broening, head of the State Federation of Labor, Chas Wiegand, of the City Federation of Labor and Will Boyer, secretary of the International Broommakers Union. These officials interviewed city and State officers some time ago and were advised to submit their petition in writing. Labor officials charge that the institution is exploiting the boys by hiring out 82 of them the entire year to Ripple Brothers for $4.916.50. This firm aiso gets its heat, light, power and rent free! whereby it 1200 brooms a day at a labor cost of 16 cents a dozen while free labor plants in Baltimore pay $1.50 per dozen to workers. This Institution is located on a beautiful farm of 1250 acres of fertile soil, and is housed in several sub- stantial brick structures with a mod- ern barn, and other necessary build- ings for an up-to-date farsa. Some 200 boys are cared for, 200 of which are committed from the city. The majority of these boys are hired; out to various farmers in the neigh- borhood, in order to enhance the re- ceipts to maintain the Institution. About 50 boys are employed by a contractor, manufacturing brooms, and are giving satisfactory service. The buildings and farm are in good Horder, the dormitories, school, hos- pital, etc., being clean, well lighted and ventilated. Nearly all the boys, excepting those 1 at the broom factory, were out at work on the neighboring farms at the time of our visit, but those we saw were apparently healthy, and well satisfied, cheerfully responding to all requirements. The one case of tuberculosis among the inmates is segregated from the dormitories, but not the lavatory, thereby endangering the health of the others. Would suggest that this bet corrected. Owing to the fact that the boys are hired out to work, they only receive] about two mo months schooling in a year, during the winter. full_text: CHELTENHAM DAILY BEEF RATION ONE POUND TO 20 BOYS MEAT DIET MEAGRE AT CHELTENHAM Diet Of Each Boy Limited To 1 1-2 Lbs. Beef. And Five Pounds Pork Monthly CRUELTY CHARGED Cheltenham Boys Committee On Fair Treatment Replies To Dr. Bragg That each of the 200 boys at Cheltenham House of Reforma- tion gets one and one-half pounds of beef and five pounds of pork monthly, is clatined in a letter from a "committee of fair treatment" at that place. The letter, which was written response to a communication ap- pearing in these columns recently from the pen of the Rev. Dr. George F. Bragg, sets out in detail the monthly list of provisions bought for the 200 boys in the institution. According to this list each boy gets one and one-half pounds of beef each month. This is the equiv alent of dividing a one pound steak among 20 boys once each day. To this is added a monthly allowance of five pounds of pork meat, each j month or a total meat ration for each boy of one-fifth of a pound each day. The monthly diet sheet sent by this committee includes 1200 loaves of bread, 75 pans of corn bread, 50 bushels of beans. 18 cart loads of cabbages, 25 bags string beans, 24 cart loads of greens, 225 pounds of cats, 1042 pounds of pork. 300 pounds of beef, 180 gallons of milk. 15 hags of potatoes, 15 bags of tur- nips, 30 bags of sweet potatoes, 15 boxes of prunes, peaches and apples. Wants Race Teachers The letter from the committee is as follows: We, the committee on fair treat- fhent, have read Dr. Bragg's letter about having teachers of our own color here. That would be much better than ex-bartenders and old time topers and some one who can- not read themselves, not capable of ruling themselves, auch less. others. What the manager means by a born disciplinarian must be one of the family who is a dive keeper, NO The can hold his job as county poli- tleian and will be recommended by any old bartender or brandy- wine rum slinger. Have two now at the head. They had to be reformed first before they were elevated. What, the Home wants is bright, intelligent and kind bosses at the head and no county brutes. Last week, Freddy Smith, a small boy, always quiet, and good natured, but the nervous and bysterical woman had him lashed 40 lashes but the big stiffs who can kick up h....... only a few lashes. Runny lashed a little boy in the laundry under Mr. Longfelt's bedroom while he was sick and you could hear the child scream all over the Institution. Why don't you brutes try some of that treatment on us large boys. But what can you expect of the unintelligent coun- try cum-slingers? There are some good officers down here who treat us right. Mr. Longfelt is one of thee best and al- ways gives us good advice. He knows how hard we have to work and sees that we get a plenty of wholesome fond. But if one little boy speaks out In the dining room - knocks out the whole school for one viola- tion. Send us a boss, down here who will not work us from dark to dark or hire us out from 4 in the morning to 9 or 10 at night. They regard us as "only niggers." What the Home needs, as Mr. Bragg says, are two good Balti- more men and white men at the head who should be examined as for qualifications, and character. Mr. The county managers don't care a cuss for us, all they care is to get a job for a man to hold his vote: They never come here to visit. -Written by the State Road Com. And Five Pounds Pork Monthly CRUELTY CHARGED Cheltenham Boys Committee On Fair Treatment Replies To Dr. Bragg That each of the 200 boys at Cheltenham House of Reforma- tion gets one and one-half pounds of beef and five pounds of pork monthly, is clatined in a letter from a "committee of fair treatment" at that place. The letter, which was written response to a communication ap- pearing in these columns recently from the pen of the Rev. Dr. George F. Bragg, sets out in detail the monthly list of provisions bought for the 200 boys in the institution. According to this list each boy gets one and one-half pounds of beef each month. This is the equiv alent of dividing a one pound steak among 20 boys once each day. To this is added a monthly allowance of five pounds of pork meat, each j month or a total meat ration for each boy of one-fifth of a pound each day. The monthly diet sheet sent by this committee includes 1200 loaves of bread, 75 pans of corn bread, 50 bushels of beans. 18 cart loads of cabbages, 25 bags string beans, 24 cart loads of greens, 225 pounds of cats, 1042 pounds of pork. 300 pounds of beef, 180 gallons of milk. 15 hags of potatoes, 15 bags of tur- nips, 30 bags of sweet potatoes, 15 boxes of prunes, peaches and apples. Wants Race Teachers The letter from the committee is as follows: We, the committee on fair treat- fhent, have read Dr. Bragg's letter about having teachers of our own color here. That would be much better than ex-bartenders and old time topers and some one who can- not read themselves, not capable of ruling themselves, auch less. others. What the manager means by a born disciplinarian must be one of the family who is a dive keeper, NO The can hold his job as county poli- tleian and will be recommended by any old bartender or brandy- wine rum slinger. Have two now at the head. They had to be reformed first before they were elevated. What, the Home wants is bright, intelligent and kind bosses at the head and no county brutes. Last week, Freddy Smith, a small boy, always quiet, and good natured, but the nervous and bysterical woman had him lashed 40 lashes but the big stiffs who can kick up h....... only a few lashes. Runny lashed a little boy in the laundry under Mr. Longfelt's bedroom while he was sick and you could hear the child scream all over the Institution. Why don't you brutes try some of that treatment on us large boys. But what can you expect of the unintelligent coun- try cum-slingers? There are some good officers down here who treat us right. Mr. Longfelt is one of thee best and al- ways gives us good advice. He knows how hard we have to work and sees that we get a plenty of wholesome fond. But if one little boy speaks out In the dining room - knocks out the whole school for one viola- tion. Send us a boss, down here who will not work us from dark to dark or hire us out from 4 in the morning to 9 or 10 at night. They regard us as "only niggers." What the Home needs, as Mr. Bragg says, are two good Balti- more men and white men at the head who should be examined as for qualifications, and character. In the case of Miss Mary Jane Smith, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Smith, of 2000 North Charles street, and Mr. William Henry Jones, son of Mr. and Mrs. H. J. Jones, of 1000 West Baltimore street, it proved to be a real thing. They met at a dance in 1937, and it was love at first sight with both of them. The moth is a menace to the watermelon crop. It lays its eggs on the vines, and the larvae eat the melons. The moth is a native of South America, and it was first discovered in this country in 1916. It has spread rapidly since then, and it is now found in all parts of the United States. The moth is a serious pest, and it is difficult to control. The best way to control it is to destroy the vines after the melons have been harvested. The moth is a small, brown insect with a wingspread of about one inch. The larvae are white, with brown heads. It is a city of friendly people. It is a city of great traditions. It is a city that is proud of its past and confident of its future. Baltimore is a city that is worth knowing. It is a city that is worth loving. And so, if you ask a North Carolinian what he thinks of Baltimore, he will probably tell you that it is a dirty, smoky city. But if you ask a Baltimorean what he thinks of Baltimore, he will probably tell you that it is the best city in the world. Much worse is a war between nations than a war between individuals.
