In the latter case, only a few people are made miserable, but in the former case, millions of people are made miserable. In the latter case, only a few people are impoverished, but in the former case, millions of people are impoverished. In the latter case, only a few people are made homeless, but in the former case, millions of people are made homeless. In the latter case, only a few people are made orphans, but in the former case, millions of people are made orphans. In the latter case, only a few people are made widows, but in the former case, millions of people are made widows. In the latter case, only a few people are made cripples, but in the former case, millions of people are made cripples. In the latter case, only a few people are made insane, but in the former case, millions of people are made insane. In the latter case, only a few people are made criminals, but in the former case, millions of people are made criminals. In the latter case, only a few people are made paupers, but in the former case, millions of people are made paupers. In the latter case, only a few people are made suicides, but in the former case, millions of people are made suicides. * * * Watching Our Birth And Death Rates It is always interesting to watch the birth and death rates. They show us how our population is increasing or decreasing. The birth rate in the United States is now about 18 per 1,000 population. The death rate is about 11 per 1,000 population. This means that our population is increasing at the rate of about 7 per 1,000 population per year. This is a very slow rate of increase. In fact, it is so slow that it is causing some concern. Some people are worried that our population will eventually start to decrease. They point to the fact that the birth rate is declining and the death rate is increasing. They also point to the fact that the average age of our population is increasing. This means that there are more old people and fewer young people. This is a serious problem, and it is one that we must face. We must find ways to increase the birth rate and decrease the death rate. We must also find ways to make our population younger. If we do not do these things, our population will eventually start to decrease. And if our population starts to decrease, our country will be in serious trouble.

Investigation Asked The undersigned residents of the State of Maryland, petition your Honorable body to investi- gate the conditions above men- tioned and that the Board of Managers and Superintendents of sald Institution be required to report to your body as to the "matters and facts above charged. 1 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Cheltenham
full_text: Cheltenham  Cheltenham, the house of refor- mation for colored boys in Prince Seorges County is back in the spot. jight again after a short respite. This time it is because its secretary, Mr. W. H. Janney, refuses to per- mit Mrs. Edith Jones, of Philadel- phia, to see or communicate with her brother committed there by or- er of Baltimore City courts several years ago. The solution of this case is simple nough. Mrs. Jones has only to ap- ply for a writ of habeas corpus through any local attorney and Cheltenham authorities will be com- pelled to permit her to see her bro- ther. In every single case in which habeas corpus has been asked courts have also returned these boys to their parents and guardians when requested. The solution of the whole Chel- tenham problem is not so easy. The Institution is dominated by natives of Prince. Georges County who are not experts in reform themselves and did not lister to the Mayor's committee last year which recom- mended certain changes. As the result, boys there are mis- erably treated, trained little, if at all, and farmed out like convicts to work on neighboring plantations. If there is any place worse than Cheltenham for cildren, we do not know of it.. Here is a matter for the Grand Jury to go into again. The city should be requested to withhold its appropriation to Cheltenham, until its trustees reform it. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: LANSEY SCORES CHELTENHAM IN ""JURY"" REPORT: BOYS AT REFORM SCHOOL TAUGHT TRADE THEY CAN'T USE BROOM FACTORY IS CALLED FIRE TRAP HIRING OUT OF BOYS ONLY ANOTHER KIND OF PEONAGE
full_text: LANSEY SCORES CHELTENHAM IN "JURY" REPORT Boys At Reform School Taught Trade They Can't Use BROOM FACTORY IS CALLED FIRE TRAP Hiring Out Of Boys Only Another Kind Of Peon- age In a minority report filed with the annual report of the Grand Jury resulting from their investigations of city and state institu- tions, T. Wallis Lansey, manager of Druid Laundry severely scored existing conditions at the Reform School for Colored youth at Cheltenham, and offered several suggestions for the betterment of the institu- tion. In his report Mr. Lansey suggests ine abolishment of the broom fau- tory, where a large majority of the boys are employed. Very few boys after being dismissed from the in- stitution are able to make a living at this trade, he points out. Money expended in this direction should be used to improve the shoe mak- ing and tailoring shops with compe- tent instructors. If these trades are properly taught it will not only enable the boys to make their own clothes and shoes, thus reducing the expense to the state, but would prepare them to make a living and become useful citizens after their dismissal, he declares. Broom Factory Firetrap -. The broom factory is a veritable firetrap, according to Mr. Lansey. There is but one exit which is very small, and due to the highly in- flamable materials used in the mak- ing of brooms, would result in many deaths before the score or more of boys employed there could make their escape. As long as the broom factory remains, he suggests the building of another stairway lead- ing from the basement where factory is located. Bread Soggy the While the bakery was clean and sanitary, the bread made there was neither wholesome or digestible, he states. A loaf handed to him as he passed through was heavy and soggy. The buildings were well kept. Of the 285 boys only six were employed in the shoe shop at the time of the visit; there was no evidence that the trade was being taught. The equipment was old, scant, and antiquated. Neither were there any signs of instruction in the tailoring shop. The only in- struments were six old sewing ma- chines that revealed little evidence of being used. Calls Farm System Peonage The system of hiring out the boys to neighboring farmers as used by the superintendent is described as being but one step from slavery. The boys get but from $25 to $40 a year for their services it is said. This is collected by the institution and saved until they are dismissed at the age of 21. ex- The management complained of the lack of funds to put the insti- tution on a higher plane, Mr. Lan- cey states, if the boys now hired out to private farmers were em- ployed by the institution, to farm the 754 acres on which it is situ- ated between class hours, they would not only be able to defray a large amount of their own pense but would also be able to hire competent instructors. An as- sistant, who is a specialist in insti- tutional work should be employed who by scientific methods of farm- ing could obtain the desired result. Abolish the Aze Limit The present practice of commit- ting a boy to the institution until he is 21 years of age should be abolished, Mr. Lancey declares, and the judges be empowered to limit the boy's stay in accordance with the misdemeanor committed. Many boys after a year in the reform school realize their error and would come out better citizens. To com- mit a boy of 12 who has made a mistake to such an institution, which does not better his condition, until he reaches his majority is the highest form of injustice. Under present conditions if a boy makes the ten grades through good behavior he is subject to parole. This is optional with th authori- ties, however, and results in very few boys being 'freed. This power should be taken out of the hands of the management and embodied in the judges imposing the sentence, he adds. : Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: GRAND JURY PROBES COMPLAINTS AT CHELTENHAM, MD. CHELTENHAM MAY BE PLACED UNDER STATE CONTROL Grand Jury Probe May Re- sult In Drastic Changes At Boys Reformatory. INMATES TESTIFY Witness Before Body Say Bread And Tea Form Main Articles Of Diet. That the House of Reforma- tion for boys at Cheltenham may undergo drastic changes in control and management as a result of an investigation made this week by the Grand Jury is the belief of those interested in the work. Recommendation for stricter State supervision and possibly complete State control may be the outcome, according to some members of the jury. Witnesses Testify The present investigation being made into the affairs of this institu- fon is the result of numerous let- ters sent by inmates from time to ime complaining of conditions here. In a recent letter to the Grand Jury an inmate complained of cruel and inhuman treatment. Besides ack of proper food, long hours of work the letter charged that inhu- ran punishment was administered. Gets Bread and Tea Another witness before the. body testified that bread and tea formed the main diet for most of the time and that the inmates were rarely en meat except from time to time in soup. These complaints, it was pointed out were in line with former charges made to other grand juries in past years.. title: BOYS CLUBBED IN CHELTENHAM SAY INMATES: FORMER INMATES WRITES AFROAMERICAN-OF BARBARITIES PRACTICED AT REFORM SCHOOL PRISON METHOD USED SOLITARY CELLS, BREAD AND WATER DIET, MADE SKELETONS OF BOYS, IS CHARGE
full_text: BOYS CLUBBED IN CHELTENHAM SAY INMATES Former Inmates Writes Afro- American Of Barbarities Practiced At Reform School PRISON METHOD USED Solitary Cells, Bread And Water Diet, Made Skeletons Of Boys, Is Charge That the worst form of crulety and shameful clubbinig of boys with clubs were practiced at the House of Re- formation at Cheltenham, is the charge made by William M. Creasy, for more than three years an inmate of the institution, to this paper this week. Creasy, who volunteered this infor- Is mation, offers to come here as a wit- ness and testify as to detall happen- dings which took place while he was there. His letter follows: Editor AFRO-AMERICAN: I was reading last week's AFRO, and I noticed your Cheltenham ar- ticle. I was an inmate of the House of Reformation in 1912, and I can frankly say that every word in your article is true. The only thing you have not found out half that goes on on the inside of the place. Bread and tea is certainly the chief diet, and not much of that. Two slices of bread and half a cup of tea to a person at breakfast and supper. At dinner the same bread and tea with a bowl of worm broth which they called soup. Work Without Food When the officers are angry at something they cut the boys out of three and four meals hand running and make them work just the same. They have big straps there which they beat the boys with, and they have handles 2½ feet long and the Ilmber part which boys are hit with is just a little longer. The farm overseer is a big colored man weighing 225 or 250 pounds, and he is the chief beater. Mr. J. B. Pyles, the superintendent, used to give his overseer, whose name is Harry Washington, a quart of whis- key and the strap, and sometimes they would go to all five of the schools and beat all the boys un- mercifully. Dies After Blow Whispering or talking is strictly against the rules, except to an of- ficer or guard. While I was there one boy, John Baker, received a blow over the head with a window stick, and he died a few weeks after getting the blow. E. D. Furgang, the teacher at that time of No. 4 school, was the man who delivered the blow. I was beaten nearly to death be- cause I sobbed too loud when I re- ceived a letter that my mother was.. dead. This was about the third month that I was there. Prison Methods Used When a boy would run away he was confined in a small cell, 8 x 3, from 3 to 6 months. His diet was two thin clices of bread, two cups of water a day, the first thirty days he was confined. The superinten- dent would bring Washington around every day, and the boy who was in confinement would receive a severe beating every day for the first thirty days. By this time these boys would look like walking skeletons. Two School Days In Three Years I was at Cheltenham 3 years, 5 months, and a few days, and I had ' school two afternoons during this time. They would hire the boys out with mean people who hated colored peo- ple and the boys were worked just 3 like slaves: They gave us a fairly good sized piece of meat each Thanksgiving, and this the only time we did get any meat. I was sent to, Cheltenham from this town and the men who sent me are still here. If they are making an investigation of the House of Reformation and need a witness who realy knows the inside of the place I am the man. Very truly yours, WM. M. CREASY.

title: Carol--A Dance or Dance Music
full_text: Carol-A Dance or Dance Music Carol-To Sing in a cheerful or joyous strain to warble, torn dance and sing a dance performed in a circle, also a song accompanying it, a choral dance.- Webster's Dictionary. Yes, if they want to. It is their business and nobody's else. Persons accustomed to regard the Christmas season as a serious and stilled celebration must have gotten a shock from Dr. Hugh Birckhead Sunday when he declared that early Christmas music was written for dance purposes. The rector of Emanuel P. E. Church went further and described German carols as written in waltz time, French in march time, and the Russian carols in polka time. Commenting on the French carols, he added that there was no emphasis on the child Jesus as the son of God, but rather on the Bethlehem Babe as an infant, cunning, beauti- ful and unexpressibly dear. The early church, said Dr. Birckhead, emphasized the dance in connection with Christmas carols. How much danc- ing there was can be seen from the fact that it required three church councils to abolish it. V Today most churches regard the dance as sinful in itself C -a thing to be banished to the stage and the dance hall. St. Mark's Church, New York, advertised a dance interpreting the Scriptures recently, and drew down upon its head the ban of the bishops. How far the church ban goes may be seen also in the fact that no dancing is permitted in the Y. M. C. A.'s and the community houses. Church members dance, members of the pastor's family dance at home or publicly in dance halls, but as for church dancing, the thing simply isn't done any more. Cheltenham Again Grand Juries come and Grand Juries go, but the mis- management of Cheltenham, (House of Reformation for Col- ored Boys) like Tennison's book, goes on forever. Reports of the last three Baltimore City Grand Juries pointed out grave faults in Cheltenham and urged relief. It has been shown that the place is unsanitary, that young boys are given less than three months schooling; that they are hired out like convicts, that they are beaten by guards, and by superintendent. One Grand Jury, of which Mr. Joseph P. Evans was a member, in a special report pointed out these things and in addition, urged that Superintendent Pyles, who is now phy- sically unable to perform his duties, be supplanted. While the institution is privately managed, it receives aid from the City and State and Baltimore delinquents are sent there from the Juvenile Court. Last week witnesses appearing before the Grand Jury testified that the chief diet was bread and tea-seldom meat except in soup. : These are the facts. Certainly Baltimore Judges cannot continue to send delinquents to such institutions as cannot help them to become better citizens. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Cheltenham Worse Than Pen, Relatives Can't See Boys
full_text: Cheltenham Worse Than Pen, Relatives Can't See Boys That Cheltenham is worse than a penitentiary in that relatives are not permitted to see boys sent there, is the complaint of Mrs. Edith James 804 South 48th street, Phildelphia. in a letter to the AFRO-AMERICAN this week. Mrs. James' brother, Paul A. Cook, sent to Cheltenham at his mo- ther's death, doesn't know that his father is dead because authorties there have refused to let his sister see him or write to him. The where abouts of young Cook were discov- ered by relatives through the AFRO. AMERICAN. Mrs. James found out that he was put out to work in October 1917 and will become of age in October of this year. In a letter to the AFRO-AMERI- CAN this week she says that the action of the authorities in keep- ing her from seeing or communi- cating with her brother is an out- rage and asks under what state law the authorities are proceeding. In her letter is enclosed also a communication from W. H. Janney, secretary of the House of Reform- ation at Cheltenham, poorly typed on the official stationery and signed also on the typewriter in which Janney states that young Cook has been hired out on his own request. "We have found that it is bad for boys so placed out to come in contact with their people because these poeple visit them, give them money which they do not need, correspond with them and in gen- eral get the boys, dissatisfied with their surroundings no matter how good they may be, with the result, in every case, that the boys run a- way causing much trouble and ex- pense to recaptare them, and worse than-all, forfeit all the money that has been accumulated in our hands for their benefit. "In the case of Paul Cook we have had considerable trouble along this line. Not that he has run a- way, but I think he was preparing to do so, and I had to send our agent to see him and get him straightened out. This was, I think. caused by some visits to him by a supposed brother, of which visits we knew nothing, but it is evident that there has been some influence brought to bear on the boy to make him believe that he could do much better if he were away from his present home. "Therefore we have declined to tell where the boy is located, be- cause it is always better for them not to be, visited by their people while they are at service, as you will see from the above, and when they become of age, all the infor- mation that we have as to their rel- atives is given them, their money is turned over to them and they are sent to their people." 1 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Smith was removed to his home in Staunton where the funer- al took place. Calls Cheltenham A Real Hell Cheltenham is a real Hell Attor- ney Josiah Henry told the AFRO- AMERICAN this week following a hearing in which he failed by ha- beous corpus to secure the release of Paul Cook, age 20, from the State reformatory. Cook was brought to Baltimore from Cheltenham by order of his sister who lives in Philadelphia. She said her brother was commit. ted at the age of 15 as a minor without proper care, and that she had provided a home for him now and wanted him with her. The boy who is hired out to a white family and is under the charge of a guide while in the city ap- peared frightened and told the court he didn't want to leave. : "Cook." said Attorney Henry, "is hired out under what is really a slave contract. He wanted to come but was afraid to say, so for fear there might be some slip and the guard would take him back and beat him up. title: Mr. Emerson Starts
full_text: Mr. Emerson Starts Can the Baltimore City Council succeed when the Baltimore Grand Jury and the Mayor have failed. That is the question which proposes itself after City Councilman Walter S. Emerson in- troduced this week a resolution requesting the Board of Managers at the House of Reforma- tion at Cheltenham to replace its white super- visors and teachers with colored. Cheltenham with a larger per capita expen- diture than several other state institutions is yet the most grievously mismanaged reform school in the state. Part of this is due to an- cient methods; part to its private management which is not responsible to the state and city which support it, and part is undoubtedly due to its white staff which has no genuine interest in reforming boys except as it brings a monthly pay envelope. The grand jury for the past five years has reported adversely on Cheltenham. Juries have recommended that more essential trades be taught, that common school instruction be in- stituted; that changes be made so that inmates be kept clean and better disciplined. The mayor of the city interested himself in Cheltenham, appointed an advisory committee which investigated and recommended certain changes which were disregarded by the reform school. Now comes Mr. Emerson with his resolution to change the staff from white to colored. The city of course has no control of the privately owried Cheltenham. However it appropriates something like $35,000. a year for the boys it sends there. If Cheltenham continues refuse to listen to advice, and good counsel, we trust Mr. Emerson will introduce still another resolution-namely that Baltimore city will build and equip at Ca- tonsville on the farm which now houses the Md. Home and Parental School, its own reform school. Such a move is not only in the interest of the youth but also in the interest of economy. title: AMERICAN LEGION IN ANNUAL CONVENTION: MARYLAND DEPARTMENT HOLDS NINTB ANNUAL MEET AT EASTON, MD. WALTER GREEN POST HITS SCHOOL SYSTEM RESOLUTIONS TAKE SLAP AT COUNTY EDUCATION AND CHELTENHAM
full_text: AMERICAN LEGION IN ANNUAL CONVENTION Maryland Department Holds Ninth Annual Meet At Eas-. ton, Md. WALTER GREEN POST HITS SCHOOL SYSTEM Resolutions Take Slap At County Education And Cheltenham The Maryland Department of the American Legion now in its ninth annual convention at Eas- ton, Md., is expected to act on two resolutions submitted by the Walter Green Post number 14 this week. The resolutions crawn up by Cap- tain Milton Dorsey and Edward H. Marshall are to the effect that the convention go on record as indorsing a uniform length of school year for all children in the counties, adequate establishment of high schools when the law is satisfied, and a uniform salary scale for all teachers. The following grievances are cited in the resolution: a.-The maximum length of the school year for colored boys and giris In our counties is only eight (8) months. b-These children have no high schools in many of the counties, Bal- timore County, for an example. The law, however, in this case states. That a high school may be established wherever there is a minimum of fifteen (15) elementary graduates: Baltimore County had 89 graduates last semester. c-The maximum salaries for coi- ored county teachers is only $70. HIT CHELTENHAM The second resolution points out the evils at Cheltenham Reform School. According the finding of a committee only 30 days' schooling is given to the boys during the year. There are no trades taught these. boys, except baking, broom-making, and farming. The boys are hired out under the convict-lease system to the surround- ing farmers who act as guards with pay in meny cases. No supervision is given the conduct. instruction, and treatment of these boys. No effort is made to reclaim these boys to citizenship. These boys are released under a poor system, since no notification of the release is sent the parent or guar- dian, the transportation is usually left; in the hands of an agreeable passer- by who drops off the released boys anywhere in the designated vicinity. The instiution is privately owned and controlled with the help of a State appropriation of '$53.310. an- nually. The post asks the convention to draw up a petition favoring state con- trol of this institution and recom- mends that measures be taken to rec- tify existing conditions..

title: PEONAGE AND CHAIN GANG AT CHELTENHAM SCHOOL: PEONAGE AND CHAIN GANG AT CHELTENHAM REFORM SCHOOL BOYS DIRTY, RAGGED AND HIRED OUT TO SLAVE BATHS ONCE WEEK PASTORS ARE TOLD THREE MINISTERS CONFERENCES NAME CONILLITTECS TO SCE MAVOR AND GOVERNOR
full_text: PEONAGE AND CHAIN GANG AT CHELTENHAM SCHOOL PEONAGE AND CHAIN GANG AT CHELTENHAM Reform School Boys Dirty, Ragged And Hired Out To Slave BATHS ONCE WEEK PASTORS ARE TOLD Three Ministers Conferen- ces Name Committees To Sce Mayor And Governor Virtual slavery, peonage and a chain gang exist at the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Chel- tenham, Prince Georges County, Md., Dr. Ernest Lyon told the three local ministers' conferences at their various meetings this week. Dr. Lyon said he paid a visit to the institution without notice and there he found 300 boys from Balti- more city and the state of Maryland ragged. and barerooted despite the cold weather, hair uncombed and the older boys hired out in "this Maryland free state". to work on plantations surrounding. Like a chain gang, he said, they stay out all week and come back home Sat- uraday for a bath. Despite the dirty and laborious work these boys have to do, bath- ing facilities are provided only once a week. "The boys are there from the ages of 10 to 21. I went into a room where there were 75 little boys. The teach- er. poorly educated himself, tried to have one of the youngsters stand up and read. But they couldn't. They have had no educational advantages whatever. "The conditions at the institution are shameful. If I weren't a min- ister I would tell what kind of a shame it is." Rev. Bragg Speaks The Rev. Dr. George F. Bragg, for over 25 years a member of the Chel- tenham board, declared that the board at present consisted of 12 per- sons, two members appointed by the governor, two by the mayor and the remaining eight elected by the board itself. The institution is private and is owned by the board of trustees. Most of the members, he said, reside in Prince Georges County and priv- ate interests and politics have pre- vented any change in the personnel. Dr. Lyon referred to the buildings as old and falling apart. The super- intendent. Mr. Pyles, he said. has only one leg. when the institution should have men with at "least four legs" to keep up with the children committed there to be reformed. The A. M. E. ministers named the following committee to cooperate with ministers' meetings of other de- nominations in asking the governor and mayor to withhold appropria- tions from Cheltenham or replace the present personnel with the prop- er administration: The Rev. R. A. Green, the Rev. John T. Colbert. W. L. Fitzgerald. Carl Murphy. Dr. Ernest Lvon, Thad- deous Copeland, the Rev. W. Н. Ма- nokoo, the Rev. C. H. Stepteau, the Rev. W. H. Thomas. Baptist Ministers The Baptist Ministers' committee includes the following the Rev. W. W. Allen. the Rev. L. J. Reynolds, the Rev. Simon Williamson, the Rev. A. J. Payne, the Rev. N. L. Price, the Rev. A. W. Taylor, the Rev. C. R. But- ler, the Rev. J. J. Taylor, the Rev. Geo. A. Crawlev, the Rev. D. G. Mack, the Rev. C. W. King and the Rev. G. Bryan.

The club, of which W. C. McCart 1 is president, reached nearly 350 youngsters in its programi this year St. Mary's Mome for Cirls, St. Kath- erine's Home For Girls, St. Luke's Orphanage, and the Maryland Home For Boys at Catonsville received the turkey and all the trimmings for their Christmas dinners. six Included in the treat were bushels of potatoes, three dozen large mince pies, two bushels sweet pota- toes, 80 pounds of hominy, 16 quarts of cranberries, 40 loaves of bread, 40 pounds of sugar, 20 dozen large oranges, 100 pounds of candy, and 20 dozen large apples. CLUB IN SIXTH YEAR Remember Cheltenham Boys Others Get Cash Just 208 pounds of turkey was one of the items included in the sixth annual treat of the Big Brothers' Club which dis- tributed its Christmas cheer to 250 children in four institutions for children Friday. The club, of which W. C. McCart 1 is president, reached nearly 350 youngsters in its programi this year St. Mary's Mome for Cirls, St. Kath- erine's Home For Girls, St. Luke's Orphanage, and the Maryland Home For Boys at Catonsville received the turkey and all the trimmings for their Christmas dinners. six Included in the treat were bushels of potatoes, three dozen large mince pies, two bushels sweet pota- toes, 80 pounds of hominy, 16 quarts of cranberries, 40 loaves of bread, 40 pounds of sugar, 20 dozen large oranges, 100 pounds of candy, and 20 dozen large apples. Money To Others The home for the Blind at Overlea received 50 pounds of candy. Twenty- five dollars each went to St. Francis Home For Girls, St. Elizabeth Home, and the Mission Helpers on Biddle street near McCulloh. The boys at Cheltenham received 100 pounds of candy. The treat this year cost more than $300, a sum slightly higher than in past years. Contributions were re- ceived from friends of the club, and the secretary reports that a complete list of their names will be published in January. title: PEONAGE TO END AT CHELTENHAM GRAND JURY TOLD: HIRING OUT OF BOYS WILL BE DISCONTINUED AFTER SEPTEMBER 15 WOULD WITHDRAW FINANCIAL SUPPORT STATE SHOULD EITHER CONTROL INSTITUTION OR LEAVE IT ALONE
full_text: PEONAGE TO END AT CHELTENHAM CRAND JURY TOLD Hiring Out Of Boys Will Be Discontinued After Sep- tember 15 WOULD WITHDRAW FINANCIAL SUPPORT State Should Either Control Institution Or Leave It Alone The State of Maryland and the City of Baltimore were called for a showdown at the Cheltenham Reform school in the report of the grand jury filed last week. A special committee appointed to investigate the conditions there in their recommendations say in part that the state should either ap- propriate funds sufficient for the car- rying on of the institution and then see to it that it is properly done or else withdraw all support and estab- lish a State school which will not be operated by private interests. A lack of keen and intelligent in- terest on the part of the city and Hi state, inefficient management and absolute methods in educational and f-institutional work are given as the short comings of the home at the present. No Justification The committee in referring to the practice of hiring boys out say: The by-laws, rules and regulations of your institutions stress the value ON of sound, practical education, school instruction being esteemed as one of the chief means of reclamation. Since our entry into the World War, this part of the work of the Institution has been lost sight of. VO while a pernicious system of hiring out the inmates to farmers in Prince; George's and neighborhood counties has been enforced. The alleged justi- fication for this is that it was neces- sary to help out the farmers during the war. because of the lack of labor. while from that time on the claim is that the ncessities of that insti- tution have been such that the en- forced labor of these boys, hired out to the farmers at 50c and 60c a day in direct competition with higher paid free labor has continued up to the present time. To Discontinue This committee is thankful to state that it is informed by the Superm- tendent and by the Secretary of the Board of Mangers that after ten years this most objectionable method of benefiting the farmers by furnishing them with cheap Negro labor will cease absolutely on September 15. 1927. These officers have admitted that in very many of these cases the boys let out under this system of practical peonage have not receiv- need proper food or lodging and that some of them have been mal-treated. It is a vicious system and should nev- er have been permitted to exist. All Work Of the 275 boys at the institution on Novmber 30. 1926, 121 are listed as general outside workers (presum- ably those farmed out and over whom the institution could have no real oversight): 4 were employed in the broom factory under contract with an outside manufacturer: 40 were p working on farms: 10 were emploved as in the shoe and tailoring shops; 12 in the laundries, and the remainder were utilized in the general work of the institution. Apparently no industrial training of any value is provided and a boy, on leaving the institution. is almost or quite as unfitted to face the world as he was when commit- ted. No Education At All The broom work is done by ma- chinery, every boy doing only a small part of the complete operation, and the work is crude. The boys, who have been farmed out. have received practically no education and those remaining at the institution have re- ceived no more. Our opinion. from what we were able to see. is that there is no edu- cational system whatever. but that the teaching of even the smallest Obous is irregular, desultory and non- productive. We feel that the great opportunity afforded this institution for the reformation and training of the boys has been neglected. State Anpropriations The institution is a private corpo- ration, managed be a board of 16 members. Since 1922. the state has appropriated annually for the sun- port of the institution $15.000. while Baltimore City's annual contribution has ranged from $30.000 to $37.000. For the year ending November 30, 1926. the total receipts. including the above appropriations, were $08.797.51. of of which $6.924 came from the labor of the hous rented out to the farmers: 67.718 from the broom factory, $7.438 from the sale of carden produce, and 3.000 from the enforced sale of live stock to meet present demands. Should Withdraw Support This committee feels strongly that the state and city should support this work adequately, seeing at the same time that it is efficiently con- ducted. If they are unwilling to do so while the institution is in pri- vate hands, they should establish a proner state reformatory for colored boys and finance it properly with- drawing entirely fom the Chelten- ham institution the half-hearted and insufficient support. Dr. Ernest Lvon was the only col- ored member of the investigating committee.  Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: M. E. PREACHERS FIND CONTRACT LABOR BAD AT CHELTENHAM: MINISTERS ALSO SURPRISED TO FIND ""TOTS"" UNDER EIGHT YEARS PHYSICAL CONDITION' DESCRIBED AS GOOD LACK OF EDUCATIONAL FACILITIES WILL BE POINTED OUT IN REPORT
full_text: M. E. PREACHERS FIND CONTRACT LABOR BAD AT CHELTENHAM Ministers Also Surprised To Find "Tots" Under Eight Years PHYSICAL CONDITION DESCRIBED AS GOOD Lack Of Educational Facili- ties Will Be Pointed Out In Report Good physical condition, but bad conrtact labor sys- tem, presence of little 'tots' under eight and practically nothing being done to train the inmates for useful lives, was the reaction of several ministers in a group which visited the House of Refor- mation at Cheltenham Mon- day. The delegation of ministers, head- ed by the Rev. R. A. Green, will sub- mit a detailed report of their visit to the regular session of the preach- ers meeting next Monday. Convict Labor One of the worst features of the system, declared the Rev. Mr. Green. is the contract labor wherein the boys are farmed out to work for out- siders and during which time they get no training as should be given in an institution of this kind. But the most surprising thing we met was the presence of mere "tots" un- der eight. who had been sent there. The chairman also stated that while they found the physical cons ditions excellent, the educational sys- tem was practically nihil. "I cannot see." he said. "how any one could expect the lastitution to help the hous sent there in so far as it is designed to train them for useful- ness." Lacks Funds The Rev. W. A. Manokoo stated that while he did not care to give out any detailed statement before the committee set forth its findings he thought the institution needed funds with which to inaugurate a better administration. Those there at present are courteous and seem- ingly conscientious, but they lack funds with which to provide proper training for the boys. The whole delegation got a fav orable impression from the care of the plant itself. he said. but they found little being done for the boys in the way of training. Many Away At Work Commenting on conditions there the Rev. C. H. Stepteau said: "Upon going to the institution I found that many of the older boy's were off at work and I could not learn some things in detail. "The favorable thing that I notic- ed was that the beds were clean and well made up and the dormitories in a tidy state. "The superintendent was courteous and expressed a desire that more visitors should come down to see the! exact state of affairs so that their criticism could be made from per- sonal knowledge. "My adverse criticism would be that there are small boys there around the ages of seven, ten and twelve. Several said they were there because they were regarded as bad and there was no other place to send them. "Many of them do not know how long they are to stay there. Some will be kept until they are 21. "Some of the larger boys who are hired out earn money for themselves! by working overtime. One boy told me that he earned $11 last week. He was about 19 years old. "Considered as a whole. the criti- cism that I have is of small matters." Recommendations The committee will make definite recommendations. said the Rev. Mr.n Green, and will make some further co Investigation as to the presence of the very young boys they found at the institution. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: 20 Cent Loot Sends Boy To Cheltenham
full_text: 20 Cent Loot Sends Boy To Cheltenham With three previous records against him, Ernest Thompson, 15, 610 Ma- deria street, was com.mitted to Chel- tenham School of Reformation when arraigned before Judge Williams, in Juvenile Court, Thursday. Thompson, according to testimony. is a member of a gang of young des- peradoes who have committed nu- merous major crimes in the Eastern District. Late Sunday evening, in company with three other older boys he held up George Capper. 126 Pratt street, at the point of pistols and knives while he was standing at the corner of Pratt and Albermarle street. Then the boys took twenty cents and a car check from the man which was all he had on his person at the time. Police attracted to the scene, chased-the youth and cap- tured Thompson. He will remain in the reformatory until he is 21 years of age.  Afro Visitors Luke McCulloh. Greenville, N. C. Mrs. William E. Thrower, Ridgewood, N. J. Dr. Chas. T. Lansford, Rochester, N. Y. K. I shall only indicate the particular incident which first fixed my attention upon that institution. title: Mr. Langfield is Suggested for a Place On the Board of Managers at Cheltenham.
full_text: Mr. Langfield is Suggested for a Place On the Board of Managers at Cheltenham. To the Editor: I just returned from Europe. I see they still have rum brutes at Cheltenham Reform School. After my brother and I wrote to the judges and managers about the brutes and their method of treatment, we had been inmates and had worked on farms down in southern Maryland and know how these officials would go to Smith's sa- loon three and four times a week, fill up and sleep their drunk off at the bar. Yet the Board of Managers think they are good enough to re- form boys. They need reforming themselves. Ninety per cent of the boys now discharged from there go to jail or penitentiary. Boys receive no education and little or no Christian instruc- tion. When I was there we had a priest of the Marl- boro Church, a priest of the Episcopal church and a Methodist preacher to come and preach and give religious teachings and Pyles got rid of the priests and only hired his preacher of the Methodist church so the pay would go to help pay the preacher's salary. I hear he got rid of Mr. Langfield. one of the best men ever there. What I am, and brother also. we credit to Mr. Langfield's good counsel and treatment. But officers were jealous and spiteful toward Mr. Langfield because he was offered the assistant superintendency. What we want on the Board of Managers is men like Mr. Langfield, who has had fifty years' experience and would help to improve the school. We have plenty intelligent colored men capable to run the place as it should be run. What good are the county managers? They come on the place only at election times or to get boys to work their farms. What does am McGruder know about the place and how it is managed. My consin carries a scar on his head where an officer known as "Brandywine," Whiskey, Tar Pot, struck him with a monkey wrench. The fellow never was fit to be an officer at the school. Too fond of his rum. Too much of a brute. Perhaps it will be well to build a new reform school, say, on the Eastern Shore. Let all church- es and sell Cheltenham to the government for a place for bootleggers or for insane people. It is a failure as a reformation for our boys. Fifty and one hundred lashes on a boy only hardens him. That is why so many turn out bad and go to jail or penitentiary. Good men who desire to help boys to lead a better life are not desired under running officials. One who can use brute force is most desirable and praised. We are going to write to every judge in the county in Maryland and tell them the boys can receive better treatment at the penitentiary than at the ouse of Reformation. WILLIAM FREEMAN. TOM FREEMAN. Nelson And Rainey Qualified To Head Up Na- tional Work Of Democratic Campaign Com- .mittee. New Yorkers Should Put Aside Their Hammer. To the Editor:- Just a word for Robert J. Nelson of Wil- mington and Washington and Julian D. Rainey of Boston. I have known both very well, Nel- son for many years, and Rainey ever since he quit Norfolk. From super Harlem has come the usual "squawk" of Presidential years against "outsiders" managing a Presidential campaign from New York headquarters. Hitherto, it has been about Negroes invited to help run Repub- lican campaigns. Now it also is against Nelson and Rainey, Democrats, and "Al Smithites." Mr. Nelson is the only Negro extant who ever ran a campaign from the satrt to defeat a Con- gressman for deliberately offending Negro citi- zens and succeeded in his purpose. A U.S. Sen- ator went down in the crash, as Nelson warned him would be the case. Hence the elevation to the upper Branch of Congress of Thomas F. Bayard of Delaware, second of the Bayards to serve in the Senate, and the end of Congress- men Layton's political career. Shoulder to shoulder has Nelson fought seg- regation in the Government departments here with Neval Thomas and Arch Pinkett. They are the triple-Nemses of Cabinet officers in whose jurisdictions segregation flourished. It was as head of the Elks' Civil liberties Bureau that Nelson put the power of that greatest or- ganization behind the anti-segregation fight. Additionally, he has made a Smith Democrat of Neval Thomas, best asset and "bally-ho" among the forthcoming campaign orators. As for Rainey: In 15 years this boy has come from a dining car through law school and the Great War (which he entered as a private and from which he emerged a lieutenant) to a lucra- tive law practice in Boston-the "William H. Lewis" of his generation. Despite his hankering after public office in law-school days, Rainey could not afford to accept an assistant district attorney-ship from the District Attorney he help- ed elect. He has taken into his office from a dining car a young, graduate lawyer, whom he recently sent into the U. S. Court at Boston to win a deportation case against the Government; in 1926 he managed the colored end of the guber- natorial campaign of the late noble and wealthy William A. Gaston, who was defeated, and of David I. Walsh, who was not As Nelson is "Bob" Nelson to thousands of voters, so Rainey is "Jule," to numberless young voters. The Harlemites contend, nevertheless, that only a New York Afric is entitled to manage a Democratic Presidential campaign, as they are original Tammany Democrats. Carried to logi- cal sequence, ultimately, such a contention would forbid Gov. Smith naming Mr. Raskob, hitherto not a Democrat, as Chairman of the Democratic National Committee. But Mr. Raskob is Chair- man! New Yorkers react to the provinces and pro- vincials in politcs just as they do in professional baseball-14 other big league ball clubs exists only to carry out schedules to fetch the penants and the World's series to New York-so national campaign managers must be New Yorkers, des- pite the fact that they cannot carry their own precints. When Aldermen Moore and Hawkins were elected to the Board of Aldermen as Re- publicans from Harlem the fact automatically eliminated Harlem's Afric Dems from National consideration in the matter of managing political campaigns. A leadership whih cannot elect an Alderman certainly cannot elect a President. RIENZI B. LEMUS. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: ASK LEGISLATURE TO e or may take such action and rec- ommend in his budget such amounts as will be necessary and advisable to put the institution on an efficient PROBE CHELTENHAM working basis. Melvin L. Fine, 4th District Delegate, Introduces Reso- lution In House WANTS STATE. CONTROL Abuses And Inefficiency At Private Reformatory Cited Citing long: nding inefficien- cy, lack of facilities and abuses, and asking that the State take over the control of the institution and conduct it in the interest of the inmates, Delegate Melvin L. Fine, from the Fourth District of Baltimore, introduced a resolu- tion asking a searching investi- gation of the House of Reforma- tion for Colored Coys at Chel- tenham, Tuesday. The resolution which asks that a committee be appointed also asks that it report back to the legislature before March 18, 1919, 'hat the Gov- Cites Abuses In his resolution Mr. Fine cites abuses and bad management of the institution covering a long period as revealed by various Grand Jury re- ports., Special mention is made of the fact that the original object of the institution - that of giving the boys such "school instruction" and education as would fit them to take their rightful place in life - was be- ing sadly neglected. It also called attention to the "pernicious system" of hiring out the boys on farms, and declares that under the past regime the boys have left the institution in worse condition than when they en tered. 4. Although appropriations of $15,000 made by the state and from $30,000 and $37,000 by this city are reported each year, the institution under priv- ate management has been inefficient- lv handled and Mr. Fine's resolution asks that the State take direct charge and supervision in order that a re- sponsive management may be insti- tuted.

title: Say Youth Looted Paper Cash Boxes
full_text: Say Youth Looted Paper Cash Boxes  Police are keeping a watchout for a gang of youths who are said to have tampered with and robbed 90 honor system paper boxes, last week. The youth who are known to police are believed to be working under the direction of older boys.  Authorities of the Cheltenham Re- formatory notified police to appro- hend Bernard Robinson, alias “peaches” and hold him as an escapee from that institution. The youth is described as being 15 years of age, 5 feet one inch tall, 115 pounds in weight, gingercake complexion, brown eyes, and with a scar on his upperlip. At the time of his escape the boy was wearing the customary blue uniform pants with a brown jumper, black shoes and no hat.

title: GRAND JURY RE-VISITS REFORM SCHOOL: BODY WOULD ASK CHANGES AT CHELTENHAM GRAND JURY COMMITTEE FORMULATES REPORT FOLLOWING VISIT. STATE FAVOR COLORED TEACHERS AND OTHER CHANGES.
full_text: GRAND JURY RE-VISITS REFORM SCHOOL BODY WOULD ASK CHANGES AT CHELTENHAM Grand Jury Committee Formulates Report Following Visit. STATE CONTROL' Favor Colored Teachers and Other Changes. Another grand jury report will recommend sweeping changes at the House of Re- formation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, it was indicated in a committee hearing of that body Tuesday evening in the grand jury room. The conference, into which was called a number of citizens to consid- er the matter, was headed by Grand Juryman C. M. Falconer, who headed the special committee which visited the institution on an inspection trip last Wednesday. Some Improvements While a number of improvements were cited by the chairman, including the abolishment of the old practice of farming out boys for work, and the achievement of better physical conditions, it was stated that under the present management it was fail- ing to meet the problems of a reform school and that sweeping changes were needed. The chief criticism brought out at the meeting was to the effect that teaching and industrial activities there were not preparing the boys for citizenship. Statistics show that a large percentage of the boys leaving Cheltenham keep straight on to jail and the penitentiary under the pres- ent regime. It was also brought out that this is the result with boys taken there, not as delinquents, but be- cause their families break up or die and they become wards of the com- munity. Politics was also blamed for failure to get a change of management at the institution. Race Teachers The discussion indicated that the Grand Jury report would recommend among other things, race teachers, state control of the institution, or the shutting off of municipal funds until conditions are remedied. The Grand Jury Cheltenham com- mittee comprises: C. M. Falconer, chairman; James E. Preston, Jr., Herbert A. Gillespie, William H. Crane. Frederick P. Steiff (all white), and W. Emmett Coleman. Called into the conference were Dr. Howard Young, Miss Georgianna Fields. R. Maurice Moss, Probation Officer George Ralph and Willian. N. Jones. 0 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Testifying that her husband, Albert W. Monroe, Brooklyn, deserted her while she lay ill in bed, for the love of another woman, Mrs. Flossie M. Monroe, 2411 Etting Street, was granted an absolute divorce in the circuit cour', Friday. full_text: Same Cheltenham Reports, But No Action, Says the Reverend Mr. Bragg; and He Suggests a Plan. To the Editor: According to the Baltimore Sun of August 24, 1898, adverse criticisms of the management of Cheltenham have been made, dating back to that early period. The Sun of that date, said: 1 The grand jury committee on the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Chel- tenham, submitted a special report yester- day commending the management and con- dition of that institution, but stating that the punishments inflicted on the youthful in- mates ha have been too severe. "We regret to say, that in our opinion," the. report states, "the punishments have been too severe, better suited for hardened adult criminals than for incorrigible youths. We are pleased to report that the management have promised to modify this somewhat by doing away with the more severe methods. "In this connection one of the great needs of the institution is a strong guard build- ing, where_uncontrollable inmates may safe- ly be confined under proper police protec- tion. "We believe that kind treatment and moral suasion will do more to serve the purpose of the institution than harsh and severe pun- ishments." For more than a third of a century these criti- cisms have been made, and yet the whole situa- tion is entirely unsatisfactory. Now, my suggestion is just this: Let our preachers' meetings and other organizations pass resolutions requesting the Hon. Wm. Cabell Bruce, and the Hon. M. A. Soper, to take the leadership in this matter, and direct it in the most effective way of accomplishing results. In a matter of this kind Senator Bruce will do for us gladly what we could not pay him to do for us as an attorney. In a matter of this character we need the lead- ership of men of the class we have named. And that class of men would willingly do more for us if they could only feel that such services would be duly appreciated by the colored race. As a matter of fact, in a recent personal letter received from Senator Bruce, among other things, he said: I am, indeed, eager that full justice should. be done, in every respect, to my colored fel- low citizens, and I can not see how any pub- lic man who has the slightest pretensions to the character of a statesman could be other- wise. I do not have to go outside of my own household to find illustrations of the high level of moral worth on which the lives of some of my colored fellow citizens move. Let our public spirited men and women, in- terested in improved conditions for our delin- quent colored boys and girls, address a line to Senator Bruce and Judge Soper, conscripting them for such public service on behalf of those I of the community who need it most. Baltimore. GEO. F. BRAGG, Jr. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Baltimore Should Protest Against This Nuisance.
authors: HENRY ARNOLDROBERT LABAREEPHILIP RANDOLPHGEORGE BRAGG, Jr
full_text: Baltimore Should Protest Against This Nuisance. To the Editor: Investigation will prove that a nuisance is prevalent in Baltimore, which does not exist in many large cities-North or South. The nuisance is the littering of the streets and vestibules of colored people's homes with hand-bills and all other cheap form of advertisements. In nearly every city, there is a city ordinance against this procedure. Two towns in California have legislated against this nuisance in the past three months. The postman in Northwest Baltimore, in many cases, must move advertisements from our mail boxes in order to deposit our mail. The city council would render invaluable service to the tax-payers if an ordinance were passed which would do away with this nuisance. A community cannot be sanitary if the alleys, gutters, doorways and streets are littered with paper blowing every direction, scattering the filth in gutters. Let's fight the nuisance. HENRY F. ARNOLD, No Booing at Lincoln Debate. Pennsylvania Men Defeated Fisk as Well as West Virginia State. To the Editor: I notice on the front page of this week's AFRO- AMERICAN an account of the debate between teams from the West Virginia State College and Lincoln University, in which it was stated that Lincoln's victory by a two to one decision of the judges was "booed" by the students here. As chairman of the faculty committee on debating, might I be permitted to correct this very erron- eous statement? Our president, a number of the faculty, and a fine representation from the student body were present at the debate, and all of us can testify that there was applause, but no booing (either inside or outside the auditorium) when the de- cision was rendered. On the contrary it seems to be the very general opinion here that the decision should have been unanimous in our favor. I say this only to contradict in the most emphatic manner the false report of your correspondent, whoever he might be. I regret all the more the unfortunate impres- sion which this article will make, because one of the most promising of our debaters is one of your own Baltimore boys, Clarence M. Mitchell. For his sake as well as for the sake of the others on the team, would you be willing to correct the misrepresentation made regarding them and the attitude of their fellow students toward them? Let me also say that two of this same team, Messrs. Chapman and Mitchell, met this week in New York a finely equipped team from Fisk Uni- versity in one of the best debates it has been my pleasure of listening to; and in this case also they won a two to one decision of the judges. ROBERT M. LABAREE. Dept. of Social Science, Lincoln University. Travelling in Jim Crow Dixie Which Promises, But Rarely Gives, Equal Pullman Accommoda- tions. To the Editor: There are many interesting, though annoying paradoxes that confront one in the South to-day. Though I was able to get Pullman accommoda- tions out of New York to Atlanta, where I slept in the same car with white passengers, men and women, I was not permitted to eat in the dining car with white passengers, as though there was some great and fundamental difference involved. It is customary, according to some of the Negro leaders in the South, for Negro passengers to be given Lower 13, which is the drawing room, in order to keep them out of the body of the car, so as to avoid contact with the white passengers. But on this trip, I had Lower 6 which is in the body of the car-going to Atlanta. No regular, invariable rule with respect to accommodations for Negroes seems to prevail. Even coming out of Augusta to Atlanta, while considerable juggling and insistence was re- quired to get a berth, finally Lower 1 was secured. The previous week, Dr. Channing Tobias, na- tional colored Y.M.C.A. secretary, had secured sleeping car accommodations out of Augusta, but was given Lower 13 or the drawing room. It may be interesting to know in this connec- tion, too, that traveling from Augusta to Atlan- ta is intra-state, which renders the securing of sleeping car accommodations more unusual. New York City. A PHILIP RANDOLPH. Judge Waxter is the Grandson of the Late Gen- eral Thomas J. Shryock. To the Editor: Judge Waxter, of the juvenile court, is a young man. His work on behalf of our group should not fail of the highest appreciation upon our part. When others of his kind discern how sincerely such efforts are appreciated by the thoughtful class of colored people, they will more and more be inclined to join in the fight for justice and fair treatment of their colored brethren. The grandfather of the judge, General Thomas J. Shryock, a generation ago, was one of the best and staunchest friends we have ever had I knew him well, and worked with him. Lying be- fore me is a letter of his to me, under date of March 28, 1901, in which he uses the following language: "I can assure you that I have held you in the highest regard since our work together in behalf of the re-election of Governor Lowndes. You are one of those with whom I came in contact whom believe one can tie to." Under the presidency of General Shryock, the first general improvements were made at Chel- tenham. One colored teacher, and two colored men, heads of departments, were appointed dur- ing his administration, and he was minded grad- ually, to extend the same kind of service through- out that institution. He was of old "Abolition stock," and a man that demanded a square deal for all. I am glad that his grandson has interested himself in this work, and I trust that through his efforts other white men of his standing may be interested, and finally, that we may have such institutions for the care and training of colored delinquents as will be a credit to the State of Maryland. GEORGE F. BRAGG, Jr. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: Same Cheltenham Reports, But No Action, Says the Reverend Mr. Bragg; and He Suggests a Plan. To the Editor: According to the Baltimore Sun of August 24, 1898, adverse criticisms of the management of Cheltenham have been made, dating back to that early period. The Sun of that date, said: The grand jury Committee on the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Chel- tenham, submitted a special report yester- day commending the management and con- dition of that institution, but stating that the punishments inflicted on the youthful in- mates have been too severe. "We regret to say, that in our opinion," the report states, "the punishments have been too severe, better suited for hardened adult criminals than for incorrigible youths. We are pleased to report that the management have promised to modify this somewhat what by doing away with the more severe methods. "In this connection one of the great needs of the institution is a strong guard build- ing, where uncontrollable inmates may safe- ly be confined under proper police protec- tion. "We believe that kind treatment and moral suasion will do more to serve the purpose of the institution than harsh and severe pun- ishments." For more than a third of a century these criti- cisms have been made, and yet the whole situa- tion is entirely unsatisfactory. Now, my suggestion is just this: Let our preachers' meetings and other organizations pass resolutions requesting the Hon. Wm. Cabell Bruce, and the Hon. M. A. Soper, to take the leadership in this matter, and direct it in the most effective way of accomplishing results. In a matter of this kind Senator Bruce will do for us gladly what we could not pay him to do for us as an attorney. In a matter of this character we need the lead- ership of men of the class we have named. And that class of men would willingly do more for us if they could only feel that such services would be duly appreciated by the colored race. As a matter of fact, in a recent personal letter received from Senator Bruce, among other things, he said: I am, indeed, eager that full justice should be done, in every respect, to my colored fel- low citizens, and I can not see how any pub- lic man who has the slightest pretensions to the character of a statesman could be other- wise. I do not have to go outside of my own household to find illustrations of the high level of moral worth on which the lives of some of my colored fellow citizens move. Let our public spirited men and women, in- terested in improved conditions for our delin- quent colored boys and girls, address a line to Senator Bruce and Judge Soper, conscripting them for such public service on behalf of those of the community who need it most. Baltimore. GEO. F. BRAGG, Ir. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: URGES SCHOOL FOR FEEBLE-MINDED Probation Officer Points Out Need for Corrective Insti- tution Here. CASES ARE CITED Small Boy Commited to Chel- tenham for Lack of Home The crying need for a home for feeble minded boys was shown again this week, when two small boys, suf- fering from low mentality, appeared in juvenile court and one was cont mitted to Cheltenham for lack of a better institution. : Joseph Thomas, who was brought into juvenile court by his parents, was committed to the reform school after he had run from home for the eighth time. According to juvenile court records, the boy was first picked up on the street, on May 1, 1928, again on October 10, December 5 and De- cember 12, 1928. On February 8, 1929, he again ran away from home, was sent back, but disappeared again on February 21, 1929. On this occasion he was committed to the Cheltenham School for Boys where he stayed but a little while and ran away from it. He was again picked up on January 23. 1930, and again on May 3. According to the boy's parents, he was struck by a truck when a child, and since that time has shown him- self to be of a feeble mind, and his greatest fault is running away from home, although his parents claim that he gets the best of treatment. Mr. George Ralph, probation offi- cer, declares that it is not to the lik- ing of the juvenile court to commit boys of this type to Cheltenham, as there are no facilities there for their Improvement. title: Mayor Is Quizzed On Board Appointment Promise: 3 VACANCIES ON SCHOOL BOARD IN MARCH Broening also Has Yet to Make Jail Board Appointment. MAYOR TALKS New Member for Cheltenham Advised.
full_text: Mayor Is Quizzed On Board Appointment Promise 3 VACANCIES ON SCHOOL BOARD IN MARCH Broening also Has Yet to Make Jail Board Appointment. MAYOR TALKS New Member for Chel- tenham Advised. The terms of three mem- bers of the Board of School Commissioners expire in March. They are, Mrs. John Wesley Brown, Mrs. Louis H. Levin and John H. Duncan. Friends of Dr. B. M. Rhetta, local physician, who have twice placed his name before Mayor Broening-once in his first administration and again last year when Dr. Frank J. Good- now, Theodore E. Straus and War- ren S. Seipp were reappointed-have indicated already that they expect to continue the fight to place a colored representative on the school board. Other Cities Have Colored Advocates of this program point out that under the law, in the Dis- trict of Columbia, three of the nine school board members must be col- ored. Atlantic City and New York are other cities which have had colored school commissioners, and on Janu- ary first, Mrs. A. H. Martin, a for- mer Cleveland (Ohio) school teach- er, was sworn in and took her seat as the first elected colored member of the Cleveland school board. Mayor Gave Promise Politicians point out that the may- or in his pre-election speeches made promise of appointment of colored on city boards. After election, he appointed Dr. Howard E. Young to the Jail Board and Willard Allen up- on the Zoning Commission. To the Board of Education, to which his promise was directed, no appoint- ment was made. The Mayor Talks When asked what was the possi- bility of a colored member on the school board this year, Mayor Broen- ing said: "While I have not yet fully made up my mind and am giving the school board and other matters of this kind my serious consideration, I have had so much pressure brought to bear to retain the old school board in office that I can give no definite answer to this question. There would no doubt be consideration of an ap- plicant should a vacancy arise, but there is an agreement to keep the school board out of politics and not make class appointments. "I am being opportuned to keep the present board in office during the development of the program they are putting over. My greatest de- side is to see that the best is done for both colored and white children." Jail Board Welfare workers have an eye on the Jail Board, upon which there has been a vacancy. Parker Emer- son, white, was appointed by the mayor, but has failed to qualify. Effort will be made to have mayor appoint a colored woman to this board. They point to the effective service now being rendered by Mrs. Grace Hartnett, white, as an indi- cation of what could be done by a colored woman member. Cheltenham Another appointment which the mayor will be asked to make this year is a new city representative up- on the board of the House of Refor- mation at Cheltenham. Bailey Con- way and Joseph P. Evans are the mayor's appointees on this board at present. One of the first moves of the board several months ago was to oust Dr. George F. title: WAXTER WOULD CLOSE MELVALE: WAXTER URGES NEGRO WORKERS AT INSTITUTION COLORED PERSONNEL CAN HANDLE THE PROBLEMS BETTER CLOSE MELVALE INSTITUTION IMPOSSIBLE, JUDGE SAYS
full_text: WAXTER WOULD CLOSE MELVALE WAXTER URGES NEGRO WORKERS AT INSTITUTION Colored Personnel Can Handle the Problems Better CLOSE MELVALE Institution Impossible, Juvenile Judge Says A complete Negro person- nel from top to bottom for Cheltenham, and a proposed institution for delinquent girls were urged by Juvenile Court Judge P. J. Waxter, speaking at the "Y" Anniversary at Bethel A.M.E. Church, Sun- day, May. "And whatever body the legisla- ture might be induced to appoint to map out a program for delinquent and feeble minded Negro boys and girls in the state, should have on it a goodly number of Negro men and women," the judge declared. Cheltenham Speaking of Cheltenham, Judge Waxter declared: "Cheltenham has 12,000 acres of land, a fine substantial building, and the state pays good wages, but there is one thing lacking there that every institution should have, that is, the proper attitude the child has toward the institution. Is he contented? Is he getting something out of that school? At Cheltenham they don't have that. "Give them the elements of educa- tion, take them out of the illiterate class. There should be a colored per- sonnel who come into contact with the children who come into the insti- tution, to give them some background, to teach them to understand why they should be right-show them the reason why they are there and the job of a trade to be able to go out and earn their living. "We should have men who are really going to see their problem, men who are going to see their point of view. After all, it is up to you, be- cause it is primarily your problem. "In the whole state of Maryland, there is not one single institution to which the colored feeble minded and delinquent children may be sent. We of the Juvenile Court feel that we should have an addition to Crowns- ville. Melvale Impossible "The two great problems that are facing us are, first, as to the delin- quent child. We do have reformatory schools in which we can take care of them, but there is no institution in the state where the feebleminded can be sent. "The truant girls are sent to the Melvale Industrial Home, but Melvale is absolutely impossible at the pres- ent time. The reports are to the ef- fect that conditions at that place are impossible-the house is in very bad condition, there is no equipment with which to work, the girls have had no knives and forks, but at the present time have spoons with which to eat. The moral condition is terrible. There is no supervision over the building and the girls are not being properly clothed. It is impossible to do any- thing at that place as it now stands. "We have gotten together about from various sources which we to spend as soon as we have ized a definite plan of proced- "We hope to get the backing of Gov. Ritchie. Of course we can't send all children to institutions. We try to keep them out of the institu- tions. Even the best institution in God's world is a bad place for a child. So we have to find some place other than an institution for as many as we can. We take the child out of the home and we try to find a foster parent. With that thought in mind, we are sending one man throughout the counties this summer to try to find homes for the colored children- persons who will adopt them and give them a decent home, and help them get a decent hold on life. "We feel that if we can get enough colored people who understand and will work-that if we can get that kind of colored people interested - we will be able to work and do more for the colored children and will be able to get something done. "Our problem is not dealing with the 5,000 children. In other words, with the 5,000 children we can do a certain amount of work called re- search work. We can find out first of all, the section of the city the child comes from, and can go into the schools with the consent of the Continued on Page Seventeen  MORE MELVALE (Continued from Page One) school board and find out why that child is delinquent and why the teachers are not trying to keep that child out of the court. "The problem there is that the better things of the city are closed to both the child and the parent, and he is thrown more and more back on himself for his recreation. We should spend more money in recreational facilities. City Should Act "Now we feel that first of all, to do these things, the city of Baltimore should set aside a program or map out a plan whereby the colored chil- dren of Baltimore who are delin- quent and feebleminded could be taken care of. We should build a home for such children, get rid of Melvale and put in its place an insti- tution as good as there is for the same class of white children. Equip the institution, and get the highest type of officers over same, so that the child can get his bearing." Other Speakers Other speakers at the anniversary meeting included Dr. Harry S. Mc- Card: Chairman William Anderson of the Committee of Management; Executive Secretary William C. An- derson and the Rev. John T. Colbert, pastor of Grace Presbyterian Church and chairman of the committee in charge of the anniversary. Music was rendered by the Coppin Normal School quartette and by Har- old Bryant, baritone.

title: Low Mentality Shown by Tests at Cheltenham
full_text: Low Mentality Shown by Tests at Cheltenham BOWIE, Md.-Intelligence test given by Nicholas Orem, white superintendent of pub- lic schools in Prince Georges County, and scores tabulated and graphed by the principal and faculty at Bowie State Normal School indicates that the 172 inmates of the Md. House of Reformation at Chel- tenham are of average low in- telligence. The boys, whose ages range from eight to seventeen years, have an average age of 14.4 years, but an av- average mental age only 9.3. Tests would seem to indicate that 93 boys with ages varying from 11 to 14 have still the mental equipment of a boy of 9. With 100 per cent regarded as nor- mal, the 172 boys showed a median intelligence quotient of 70.2. Only one boy of normal intelligence was found. Church, bequeathed third of his $75,000 estate and a legacy of $300 for a memorial window in the musi- cal conservatory, to Wilberforce University, according to his will which was admitted to probate Monday. Zion Church, Cleveland. UNIVERSITY HEALTH WEEK Mrs. Mary Carterwright of the State department of health and Judge S. C. Wright, of the juvenile court, Xenia, Ohio, telked to student groups of the university, Wednesday, as the features of University Health Week. This event is a swanky affair that draws celebrities from far and near. The Glee Club is directed by J. E. Dorsey, former Tuskegee jubilee singer and now professor of music here.. RECEPTION FOR ATHLETES The Athletic Association of the university will entertain visiting athletes to the annual Lincoln University Track and Field Meet, to an informal reception and dance on May 10, after the track meet. But we cannot deny that we be- long to the great body of the oppressed, and that we are subject to the exploitation of the powers that be. To us it is no question of Nordic superiority, rather it should be a question of reaching a definite millenium, in reaching a greater racial harmony. This does not imply subservience. "Some say that the Negro is not a social animal; that he cannot fit into the social scheme of the superior group. For example, the 1920 U.S. cen- sus showed a population of 80,118 colored women and 72,351 men; total, 152,469. In 1900, New York had 60,666 colored folk; and in 1910, 91,700. If the usual, growth of the city has kept up since 1920, New York today has 210,000 colored people. The New York Tattler "guesses" however that the number should be 254,000. Other New York papers have estimated as high as 275,000 or 300,000. They may be correct; but when the census figures are made public next year and show 210,000 Negroes in New York City, the rest of the country can well marvel how so many Har- lemites succeed every ten years in ducking census enumerators. A Snob University "In some of our most popular universities, un- dergraduates are simply products of stuffing machines, and the degree of A.B. becomes a mere label-a standard bonded label on a bootleg bottle," writes Dean Edward Wilber Berry, white, of the College of Arts and Sciences of Johns Hopkins University in a current magazine. Dean Berry thinks that the average college teaches "simply the accumulated debris of the past three or four hundred years of hit-or-miss instruction." Defenders of the college as it is, may well wonder how much of this opinion can be regarded as an effort to better college teaching and how much is a sneer at colleges in general. Dean Berry was privately educated. He holds no de- grees. Yet neither Dean Berry, who is 55 years old and was born in Newark, N. J., nor Johns Hop- kins University can afford to sneer at many other colleges. Nowhere is snobbishness, prejudice, race hatred and intolerance better taught and better ex- emplified in this Christian(?) land, than at Johns Hopkins. Named for a philanthropist who left his wealth. to heal and educate both black and white, it has been turned into a university of snobs for the white aristocrat only. Dean Berry can well afford to confine his sneers to his own college. Cheltenham's Board Two out of sixteen members of the board of trustees of the Maryland House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham are colored. Of the sixteen members, two are named by Governor Albert C. Rtchie in February and two by Mayor Broening in March, and the board it- self chooses twelve. The mayors of Baltimore have always made a practice of naming one white and one colored member. The governors of Maryland have al- ways named only white persons. It seems to be a strange thing that this pro- cedure has so long continued, yet it has, despite the fact that Maryland and Baltimore have al- ways been committed to a separate school system, Jand Cheltenham has been adversely reported on by grand juries for the past five years. Since all the inmates at Cheltenham are colored, both mayor and governor should have enough courage and sufficient confidence in the colored population to name colored men and women to these boards and entrust to them' the problem of making Cheltenham the kind of reform school the state ought to have. It is not enough for the chief executives of the city and of the state to say that Cheltenham is a private institution and nothing can be done. This can be done-responsible colored persons can be placed by them on the Cheltenham board. Until this is done, neither state nor city has done its duty by the colored people. N. Berman's Record Endorsed! 1425 McCulloh Street, Baltimore, Md., Oct. 7, 1930. Mr. Paul Berman, 217 Court House, City. My dear Mr. Berman: I want to let you know how very highly I appreciate your recent visit with me, and others, to the two schools in Virginia for delinquent colored boys and girls. Visible evidence of your enyojment of every phase of the trip were manifest on every hand. I sincerely trust that you may be elected a mem- ber of the State Senate, not merely because you are, in every sense, capable and competent, (and I have known you from your youth) but because I know. that the members of our group will ever find a sin- cere and devoted friend in you. And, especially, because I am persuaded that you will exert every effort towards improving conditions for the care of colored delinquents. Faithfully yours, GEORGE F. BRAGG, JR.
