title: GRASTY ADMITS MELVALE IS DEPLORABLE: SECRETARY OF CITY SUPERVISORS SAYS FUNDS ARE INSUFFICIENT. WASHES HIS HANDS JANNEY SAYS STATE HAS NO RESPONSIBILITY.
full_text: GRASTY ADMITS MELVALE IS DEPLORABLE Secretary of City Super- visors Says Funds are Insufficient. WASHES HIS HANDS Janney Says State Has No Responsibility. Secretary Nathaniel Grasty, white, of the board of City Supervisors, admitted that de- plorable conditions exist at Melvale, while Stuart S. Janney, white, chairman of the State Department of Wel- fare, washed his hands in a declaration that the state had no control over the place, in interviews with AFRO re- porters this week. Recent criticisms of the place by Judge J. S. Waxter and Mrs. Marie Bauernschmidt had not reached Mr. Janney until called to his attention by articles in the AFRO-AMERICAN, he said. Is Deplorable "I am conversant," said Mr. Grasty, "with the conditions at Melvale re. garding which Judge Waxter and Mrs. Bauernschmidt have spoken. Conditions at the institution are de- plorable." "Baltimore city has no other al- ternative but to send colored girls to the House of the Good Shepherd, which is overtaxed, to Melvale or to turn them loose on the streets. "In answer to your question as to what can be done about the condi- tions existing there, I will say that the appropriations are regulated by the Board of Estimates. The city charities cannot give any more to the institution than is appropriated by the Board of Estimates. $200 Per Capita "The supervisors contract with all reformatory institutions at the rate of $200 per capita per child, with the exception of the Maryland Training School for Girls and the Maryland Training School for Boys. These two schools receive $180 per child. Mel- vale, like other institutions, receives $200 per child. "The charity supervisors are in sympathy with the welfare of the girls at Melvale. We believe that the management is doing the best it can with the money at its disposal. I feel that if the board of management at Melvale is unable to get along on the money it has, some plan should be worked out by which the appropri- ations would be more liberal. "The public does not have enough interest in an instituption like Mel- vale to go into their pockets. Those girls out there have souls, and should have a future before them." Washes Hands In his statement, Mr. Janney prac- tically washed his hands of the con- ditions there. Said he: "The state has nothing at all to do with the management or the Vandling of Melvale. But if condi- tions at the institution are as Judge Waxter and Mrs. Bauernschmidt say. I certainly wish it was under the state. We would clean up the place. "Judge Waxter is a mighty fine man, and if he says Melvale is de- plorable, it must be the truth. "This is the first time that the mat- ter has been brought to my atten- tion. I would like to see something done about, but the state has no ju- risdiction over the institution." Dr. Emil Novak ☐☐ Dr. Emil Novak, a member of the city board, declared that nothing had come to his attention about deplor- Hable conditions at Melvale. The mat- ter will come up at a board meeting this month, he said, at which time it will be given proper consideration. Grand Jury Action Dr. Wm. H. Wright, present mem- ber of the grand jury, declared this week that conditions at both Melvale Jand Cheltenham will be given serious attention by that body. A detailed study is being made by him and recommendations for some definite action will assuredly be made. he said The Urban League committee ap- pointed last week is studying the whole situation and will work out a plan for a practical solution of the problem, it is said. title: The G.O.P. Platform
full_text: The G.O.P. Platform The Maryland Republican State Convention included two admirable planks and one in- definite one in its platform as finally adopted. If victorious, the Maryland G.O.P. pledges self to erect an asylum for feeble-minded colored children. Funds for such an asylum were authorized several years ago by the Democratic legislature but Governor Ritchie vetoed the appropriation. Republicans also pledge much needed reforms at the Cheltenham and Melvale reform schools, where incompetence and immorality have been long uncovered without Democrats or Republi- cans becoming perturbed about these matters heretofore. In these two planks the Republican party speaks openly and directly and no one need mis- understand their meaning. The third plank which favors the "general improvement of school facilities for cclored children throughout the state" is neither direct nor explicit. "Facilities" is a rather general term. Under such a plank, the school bulidings, or the grounds, may be improved and the number of teachers increased, and new types of schools added. Specifically, Maryland is educationally de- ficient in providing college and professional training for Negroes such as it provides out of tax funds for whites at the State University of Maryland. Secondly, Maryland illegally fixes by law the minimum pay for white county teachers at $600 to $1,200 a year and for colored county teachers at $40 to $120 a month. In view of the fact that Maryland Democrats have no Negro plank, the G.O.P. platform rep- represents marked advancement. However, if it means to equalize county teachers' salaries and give Negro boys and girls a chance to attend a state college or medical school, it is unfortunate that explicit language could not have been used. title: Clarence Gluy Best Latin Scholar in History of Media, Pa., School
full_text: Clarence Guy Best Latin Scholar 1 in History of Media, Pa., School MEDIA, Pa. Clarence Guy, a senior in the Media High School, Media, Pa., is the most proficient student of Latin that has ever graced the halls of the school, 2. Such is the statement made by the principal, Dr. W. H. Michaels, white, in a recent address before the Chey- ney Community League, of which, Dr. Leslie P. Hill is president. The Latin papers of the other students are pass-, ed to Guy for examination. As well as being a student of Latin, Guy has proved his ability as an ora- tor, having won first prizes in contests sponsored by the Media Branch of the National Association for the Ad- vancement of Colored People, and the Lodge of Elks, He will enter the state and national contests sponsored by the Elks. He is 19 years of age, and a dependable player on the football and baseball teams of the high school. It might be added that Guy is pro- ficient in all of his other studies as well, only "A" and "A plus" appearing on his report during the year. He plans to enter Harvard University in the fall. PRINCIPAL HEADS SCHOOL 52 YRS, CHATHAM, Va.-Fifty-two years as the principal of the same school is the exceptional rcord held by I. H. Smith, principal of a school in Chat- ham, Virginia, which was visited re- cently by Dr. Ambrose Caliver, spec- ialist for the education of Negroes, Office of Education, U.S. Department of the Interior. This long-term principal was in the first class which graduated from Hampton Normal and Agriculture In- stitute, founded at Hampton, Va., in 1868 for the education of children of ex-slaves. CHICAGO 'EXPELS' TWO BALTO. LADS CHICAGO.-The wicked old city of Chicago is too good for Rudolph Jones and Jasper Johnson, both Baltimore boys. Somewhere between here and ten miles out of that city they are sup- posed to be wending their "back, back, back to Baltimore," for the Windy City will have no more of them. In Crook Clean-up Johnson, who was once an inmate of Cheltenham Reform School and Jones, who "did time' 'at Mays Sta- tion, ran afoul of the law last week when Johnson went over to call on Jones, and finding him away, forced the door of an adjoinig room and took a hat and one dollar. After cutting the hat down to "English" style, Johnson was sporting the newly ac- quired lid when he met Jones. Immediately his one time pal rec- ognized the top piece and demanded that it be given him so he could re- turn it to the owner. To this John- son did not agree, and by the time the police reached the scene, Johnson had divided the suit Jones was wear- ing into several equal parts with a razor. When the two were haled before the Judge his sentence was "beat it." A police car took the youths to the ten- mile limit and dumped them out with another reminder of what the Judge had told them. After cutting the hat down to "English" style, Johnson was sporting the newly ac- quired lid when he met Jones. Immediately his one time pal rec- ognized the top piece and demanded that it be given him so he could re- turn it to the owner. To this John- son did not agree, and by the time the police reached the scene, Johnson had divided the suit Jones was wear- ing into several equal parts with a razor. full_text: 13th Dear, Number or Factional Fight Looms in Local G.O.P. Camp GRAND JURY SCORES CHELTENHAM Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission. URGES COLORED PERSONNEL FOR CHELTENHAM Grand Jury Says White Employees Lack Sym- pathy for Inmates MELVALE LACKING Better Care for Convicts than Children The State of Maryland is more concerned about the wel- fare of hardened criminals confined in the penitentiary and the House of Correction than it is about the guidance and comfort of the unfortu- nate boys and girls placed in its care at Cheltenham and Melvale, a report of the grand jury reveals. The report on the several institu- tions of the state contains the fol- lowing contrasting findings of that body. Cheltenham 1. "At Cheltenham we found one dormitory, housing 50 boys with beds of iron. sadly in need of cleaning and paintng. The building had but one toilet and one washroom. 2. "There were but two kinds of endeavor, farming and the broom factory, which gave the boys no op- portunity for initiative, which leaves them sulky and discontented. The broom factory was crowded without enough space to breathe; the flying chaff in the stuffy quarters hampers the respiration and breeds tubercu- losis. 3. "The food was served by bare- foot boys in a crude manner. (Note- This visit was made in February, a winter month.) 4. "There were no inspiring mot- toes, books or any inducements to aspire to better things and the school- ing was a farce." The Penitentiary 1. "At the Penitentiary we found the living quarters clean, comfortable and an order prevailing that showed the inmates were as contented as it were possible to be under such cir- cumstances. 2. "The inmates seemed interested in their work and many were appre- (Continued on page 3, column 6) MORE CHELTENHAM (Continued from page one) hensive of losing their extra pay when contract labor is discontinued. 3. "The kitchen, bakery and store- rooms were up-to-date and the meals were most bountiful. 4. "The prisoners enjoyed many comforts in their cells. Books and magazines were plentiful and some! had victrolas in their cells." The House of Correction 1. "At the House of Correction we found the inmates had a contented appearance ascribed to the fact that they were not employed at too hard work; in well ventilated and well lighted shops. 2. "The food was plentiful wholesome. and 3. "The inmates are able to save from $30 to $40 per month for work in excess of the minimum require- ment. If no order is given by the judge at the time of the committ- Iment, the money thus earned is not sent home, but is placed to the cred- it of the prisoner and turned over to him when he is dismissed." The Baltimore City Jail "At the Baltimore City Jail food was plentiful and served in a clean sanitary manner. The building was clean and the inmates were apparent- ly contented." Urge Colored Personnel The jury recommended that the state purchase the institution at Cheltenham which is now privately owned and man it with a colored personnel. The conditions now exist- ing, they point out, are deplorable, due to the fact that the white em- ployees are wholly lacking in the un- derstanding and sympathy so neces- sary to the rehabilitation of youth. If colored are employed, racial ties and sympathy would do much to cor- rect the evils now existing and would be a great stride forward for human- ity. At Melvale The committee designated to in- spect Cheltenham was composed of Eli L. M. Fishpaw, chairman, Israel Silverstein, Joseph O. Barger, John Brendel and Dr. William H. H. Wr Wright. The same group visited the Mel- vale school for girls and declared that they found this the poorest of the eleven state institutions visited, and said that the state is sadly falling short of its obligations to colored girls. The Cold Spring Road passes within fifty feet of the door, making the place too public. 0 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: 68-Year-Old Descendant of Tecumseh Passes
full_text: 68-Year-Old Descendant of Tecumseh Passes CHARLOTTE, N.C.-(ANI)- Death claimed John Watt, 68- year-old three-quarter Indian blood, here early Friday a his home, where he had lived with his aged wife, Mrs. Ellen Watt, for nearly thirty years. He was one of the few remain- 'ng 'bloods" left whose paternal ancestry descended from the line of Tecumseh, famed Indian chieftian. The family had one daughter who died six years ago. S. S. BOOKER, JR. HELPS DAD LAY CORNERSTONE YOUNGSTOWN, O.-The corner- stone of the new $200,000 "Y" branch building was laid here last Sunday, December 28, at 4 o'clock by Council- man W. S. Vaughn and Simeon S. Booker, Jr. The address was de- livered by U.S. Congressman John G. Cooper, white, with music by the "Y" branch boys' band of twenty-one pieces. The building was made possible through the great expansion cam- paign of 1929 in which the Y.M.C.A. raised $1,176,000 the opening night, closing the campaign before it of- ficially opened. The growth of this branch has been marvelous. From nothing in 1926 to an organization of six hundred mem- bers, men and boys divided into clubs and welfare groups, covering every section of the city and representing every type of our race life. Four hundred or more people shivered in the cold to witness this epoch-mak- ing feature. Secretary S. S. Booker was for- merly head of the Baltimore Y.M.C.A. Crashing Autos May Prove Fatal for Woman Victim Unconscious Three Days while Husband's Mangled Hand is Amputated COKESBURY, Md. Three per- sons were injured severely and one, Mrs. John Forrester, is expected to die from injuries received when their auto was crashed into by a car con- taining white occupants, Saturday night, on the Swan Road as the trio was en route to Aberdeen. Mrs. Forrester suffered a concus- sion of the brain, internal injuries and a broken jaw bone. She had not regained consciousness on Tues- day at the Harve de Grace Hospital. The right hand of her husband, John Forrester, was so badly mangled from glass that it had to be am- putated. David E. Smith, the third member of the party, received a dis- located shoulder. The white persons occupying the second car were also taken to the hospital, but neither their identity nor the extent of their injuries was known at press time. The machine which collided with the Forresters is said to have been swerving to miss a third machine with Pennsylvania licenses, coming out of a side road, when the acci- dent occurred. The machine causing the collision did not stop, Both autos concerned in the mis- hap were demolished. Man Gets Six Months for Drunken Driving Another Held for Grand Jury in Christmas Day Accident Roy UPPER MARLBORO, Md. Davidson was given a sentence of six months in the House of Correction and a fine of $100 in Prince George County police court Friday when he was convicted of driving while drunk. An added fine of $10 was imposed on a charge of reckless driving. Charles Davis, who was shot in the leg last week when he was fired upon in the pantry of the Cheltenham re- formatory, was held for action of the grand jury, charged with enter- ing with intent to rob.: Gene Allen and Theodore Gordon are being held as a result of a gun battle staged near Huntsville, Md., on Christmas Day, when Thomas Washington and Jesse Allen were slightly wounded. Percy Jones, of Oxon Hill,. Md., who is alleged to have forced off the road a machine driven by Harvey Sharrow, white, of 927 G Street southeast, Washington, Christmas night on the Livingston Road, is held under $1,000 bail for the grand jury for driving recklessly while drunk. title: G.O.P. Platform Pledges Better State Institutions: REPUBLICANS DRAFT PLANKS FOR CAMPAIGN Institution for Feebleminded also Promised by Leaders. REFORM SCHOOLS Would Reorganize Melvale, Cheltenham.
full_text: G.O.P. Platform Pledges Better State Institutions REPUBLICANS DRAFT PLANKS FOR CAMPAIGN Institution for Feeble- minded also Promised by Leaders. REFORM SCHOOLS Would Reorganize Melvale, Cheltenham. By WILLIAM N. JONES General improvement of school facilities for Negroes throughout the State, the es- tablishment of an institution for the feeble-minded, and complete changes in the man- agement of reform schools for girls at Melvale and for boys at Cheltenham, were promised in the platform adopted by the Republican State Convention which con- vened at the Maryland Thea- tre here, Monday. The same convention nominated William F. Broening for governor, David A. Robb for attorney gen- eral, W. Newton Jackson for comp- troller, and Charles S. Warner for clerk of the court of appeals: Equal Opportunity A reference which leaders inter- preted as expressing the view of party leaders on the Negro status in Maryland Republicanism came when former Senator Joseph I. France, closing a general endorsement of all candidates declared that if the Maryland Free State meant any thing it should mean free and equal opportunities for every citizen, white ad colored. Dr. France's speech, in which he warned the delegates that it would be best to boost their own candidates rather than adopt a hammering campaign against Governor Ritchie, the Democratic candidate, was in contrast to practically every other speaker who rapped the present governor for his fourth term pirations and declared that he had usurped the power of government (Continued on Page 17, Col. 5) as- G.O.P. PLATFORM ... Continued from Page One. in the state and created a Ritchie dynasty. Reads Plank The plank which referred to Ne- gro institutions was as follows: We are impressed with the marked advance of the colored race in Mary- land and elsewhere. In Baltimore this has been accomplished in considerable measure by the helpful and sympathetic attitude of Mayor Broening. We com- mend the removal of the notorious "lung block" and the provision of more adequate school facilities for the col- ored race in Baltimore city. We favor the general improvement of school facillites for colored children throughout the State. The present State administration has failed in its duty to erect an asylum for the feeble-minded and other mentally deficient colored children. The Republican party recognizes the State's obligation to provide Imme- diately such an institution. We further pledge ourselves to re- organize the management of the Chel- tenham Institution and the Melvale School, and to terminate the abuses which now exist therein. Varied Opinions Just what the plank means as to the main objective of Negro leaders in equalizing salaries of white and Negro teachers in the state, varied in the opinions of several gathered at the convention Monday. It was known that a much more definite plank had been proposed which would pledge the Republican party to amend the law and equalize the minimum pay for public school teachers in the state. Friends of Mayor Broening, how- ever, pointed to the support he has given the equalization policy in the Baltimore schools and declare that should he become governor, he would without doubt appoint men on the State Board of Education who would favor equal educational opportunities for all citizens, white and colored. Paul Berman Talks Paul Berman, white candidate for State Senate from the Fourth Dis- trict, told an AFRO representative. that he was certain a Broening ad- ministration of state education would bring the system up to the same equal condition of the Baltimore public schools, and that he favored and would work for this if elected to the Senate. Although the prohibition plank took up a large part of the hour and one half session of the resolu- tions committee held after organiza- tion of the convention, it was also known that the wording of the Ne- gro plank came in for serious con- sideration. Many Leaders Present Both Councilmen Warner T. Mc- Guinn and Walter S. Emerson mov- ed freely about the platform group. Dr. Ernest Lyon, Willard W. Allen and the Rev. Richard A. Green, the Rev. C. H. Stepteau, Linwood G. Koger, Dr. James White. George A. Watty. Marse Calloway, Dr. Howard Young. Mrs. Howard Young, were among those observed on the plat- form. Mrs. Eliza Fletcher of Annapolis, City Councilman H. M. St. Clair, of Cambridge and Councilman Charles H. Oliver of Annapolis, were among delegates to the convention.

title: RITCHIE'S BUDGET TO LEGISLATURE: APPROPRIATIONS TO STATE-AIDED INSTITUTIONS, BOWIE, MORGAN, SAME AS 1930
full_text: RITCHIE'S BUDGET TO LEGISLATURE Appropriations to State-Aided Insti- tutions, Bowie, Morgan, Same as 1930 ANNAPOLIS, Md.-Governor Rit- chie's budget for 1932 and 1933 went to the legislature Tuesday. Appropriations were in the main, the same as last year. Previously the governor approved additions to Crownsville Hospital for the Insane, a new school for feebleminded child- ren and a new Melvale Reformatory for Cirls. Provident Hospital was allowed a $2,500 increase. Other items were: A.M.E. Home for Aged, $1,500. | Morgan College was allowed $22,- 000. It had requested $43,500 and the education commission approved an $8,000 increase. | Shelter for Aged and Infirm, $500. Maryland Home for Friendless Colored Children, $500. St. Elizabeth's Home for Colored Children, $12,000. St. Mary's Home for Colored Boys, $1,250, increase of $500; had asked for $2,000. St. Peter Claver's Industrial School, $3,000. St. Katharine's Home for Little Colored Girls, $1,250: increase of $500, had asked for $2,000. Cheltenham Home of Reformation for Colored Boys, $20,000; had re- quested $45,000. Industrial Home for Colored Girls, $10,000. Provident Hospital, $12,000; increase of $2,500; $17,500 had been request- ed. Home of Good Shepherd, $4,000. Gibbons Institute, $2,000; $5,000 had been requested. Johns Hopkins received its first state appropriation. The sum was $15,000. It had asked for $25,000. Maryland School for Blind (Col- ored), $15,000. State Institutions | Crownsville State Hospital for the Insane-$256,200, increase of $57,- 000. New buildings requested. Feeble- minded School, 100 beds, $280,000; Dormitory, T.B., 100 beds, $165,000: addition to Hugh Young Building, 100 beds, $165.000. Henryton T.B. Sanitarium's whole budget included in that of Maryland T.B. Sanitarium, branches. Bowie State Normal School-$26,- 180, increase of $150; salaries, $28,500, operating expenses, decrease of $600. Dr. L. D. Turner, Fisk University professor, in his new book on anti-slavery sentiments quotes Thomas Jefferson under date of January 26, 1789, as follows: Upon my return (from Paris) to America, I will endeavor to import as many Germans as I have grown slaves. I will settle them and my grown slaves on farms of 50 acres each, intermingled. Their children shall be brought up as others are, in habits of probity and foresight and I have no doubt but they will be good citizens. Had Heflin lived 120 years ago he would have been compelled to bolt the party because Jeffer- son, its leader, insisted on mixing the races which according to Hefiin "God meant to be kept separate." Is "Negro" Libelous? Thirty years ago the Times Democrat, white daily of New Orleans, was sued for libel by the Rev. Thomas J. Upton, white, who alleged that the newspaper had referred to him as a Negro. A telegraphic dispatch to the Times Democrat referred to the Rev. Mr. Upton as a "cultured gen- tleman," which through an error in the telegraph office was made to read "colored gentleman." The Christian(?) preacher asked $5,000 damages. The court awarded him $50, declaring that no malice was intended, the mistake was not intentional and there was no damage because the lineage of the plaintiff was well known. In nineteen other cases of similar import, U.S. courts have ruled that it is libelous (i.e., calcu- lated to subject to ridicule or hold in contempt) to refer to a white person as a Negro. Last week the twentieth case was defended in San Francisco by a Scripps-Howard newspaper which was sued for $50,000 by Louis Gomez, whom it referred to as a "Portuguese Negro." This case, however, is different in that the newspaper pleads neither truth nor justification for its mistake, but demurs by claiming that "Negro" is not a term of ridicule and contempt. Reference to Gomez as a Portuguese, Spaniard, Frenchman or Japanese would not have led to a libel suit. The contention of the San Francisco News is that the term is one connoting respect and es- teem rather than ridicule and contempt. Our white people in Dixie are not that civi- lized. Perhaps California may be. The decision of the court will be an index to California's cul- ture. The outcome should interest Negroes everywhere. Reforming the Reform Schools Judge J. S. Waxter's courageous address before the Interdenominational and Interracial Minis- ters Alliance of the city last week in which he exposed conditions at Melvale and Cheltenham, deserves the thanks of the entire city. Despite unfavorable reports of grand juries for the past ten years and the periodic protests of various individuals in these columns, Baltimore has slept contentedly while its semi-public re- form schools for colored girls and boys have de- generated under private management into breed- ing places for criminals and sadists. Judge Waxter's exposures include the follow- ing: 1. Sixty-five out of one hundred girls at Melvale Reform School have some form of social disease, contracted for the most part within the institution. 2. In nearly every case girls are homosexualists. 3. No school, no recreation, no knives and forks at table. 4. Conditions at Cheltenham school for boys, slight- ly improved. Who is to blame for this? First of all, these conditions are to be blamed on those members of the board appointed by the governor, and those by the mayor to guard the state's and the city's interests. Their willingness to assume responsibility may be judged from their reaction to Judge Waxter's expose. City Councilman J. Warren Burgess, white, re- cently appointed, has never been to Melvale. Mr. George M. Griffith, white, two years on the board, has visited the institution twice but has noted none of the conditions referred to. Nine "good and true" members of the Melvale board through negligence and incompetency, have been unable to discover conditions which Mrs. Marie O. Bauernschmidt, after one visit, described as "painfully unsanitary," requiring public intervention at once. Fixing responsibility in this case, however culpable it may be, does not clean up Melvale and Cheltenham, does not reclaim and reform the sadists there soon to be turned back into society to pollute it further. The bi-racial committee has offered its ser- vices. Its success in securing and administering new funds for city recreation under supervision of the Playground Athletic League has already been noted. It should have public support in its effort to effect reforms at these two reform schools. Judge Moss Lectures "If there were any precedent, I would sentence you to hang, despite your youthfulness [14]." "It is not my fault that the supreme penalty [hanging] cannot be imposed." In such wise, according to newspaper reports, did Judge Robert Moss of the Anne Arundel County Court at Annapolis, Md., lecture two criminals accused of murder, and assault with intent to kill. The function of a court is to hear evidence, weigh it, determine what, if any law has been violated, and fix the punishment as provided by law to fit the crime. In brief, a court is a place where justice is administered, justice being interpreted to mean "the strict and judicial rendering of what is due." Justice is blind: Our judges are therefore ex- pected not only to be fair and impartial, but to act from necessity rather than choice. Public expressions of the judge should there- fore represent not what he personally thinks or feels, but what the law inexorably demands. No judge is above the law. None should wish to be. Justice may be tempered with mercy or severity, but personal vindictiveness and personal favor have no place in a court of justice govern- ed by law. title: Reforming the Reform Schools
full_text: Reforming the Reform Schools Judge J. S. Waxter's courageous address before the Interdenominational and Interracial Minis- ters Alliance of the city last week in which he exposed conditions at Melvale and Cheltenham, deserves the thanks of the entire city. Despite unfavorable reports of grand juries for the past ten years and the periodic protests of various individuals in these columns, Baltimore has slept contentedly while its semi-public re- form schools for colored girls and boys have de- generated under private management into breed- ing places for criminals and sadists. Judge Waxter's exposures include the follow- ing: 1. Sixty-five out of one hundred girls at Melvale Reform School have some form of social disease, contracted for the most part within the institution. 2. In nearly every case girls are homosexualists. 3. No school, no recreation, no knives and forks at table. 4. Conditions at Cheltenham school for boys, slight- ly improved. Who is to blame for this? First of all, these conditions are to be blamed on those members of the board appointed by the governor, and those by the mayor to guard the state's and the city's interests. Their willingness to assume responsibility may be judged from their reaction to Judge Waxter's expose. City Councilman J. Warren Burgess, white, re- cently appointed, has never been to Melvale. Mr. George M. Griffith, white, two years on the board, has visited the institution twice but has noted none of the conditions referred to. Nine "good and true" members of the Melvale board through negligence and incompetency, have been unable to discover conditions which Mrs. Marie O. Bauernschmidt, after one visit, described as "painfully unsanitary," requiring public intervention at once. Fixing responsibility in this case, however culpable it may be, does not clean up Melvale and Cheltenham, does not reclaim and reform the sadists there soon to be turned back into society to pollute it further. The bi-racial committee has offered its ser- vices. Its success in securing and administering new funds for city recreation under supervision of the Playground Athletic League has already been noted. It should have public support in its effort to effect reforms at these two reform schools. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: BOYS SET FIRE TO CHELTENHAM
full_text: BOYS SET FIRE TO CHELTENHAM WASHINGTON -Three boys, in mates of the Maryland House of Re- formation at Cheltenham, were ar- rested Monday and charged with having started the $5,000 fire which swept the broom factory at the in- stitution on March 10. Police say the trio have confessed and implicated a fourth lad whose name is withheld pending his arrest. Those held are: Granville Haskill, Granville 15; George Johnson, 17, and Thomas Deshields, 16. The boys are said to have admitted throwing blazing rags through a win- dow into heaps of broom straw. The plant was badly damaged by the fire and a stock of finished brooms and raw material were destroyed. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: BIG BROTHERS SPENT $422 FOR NEEDY Organization Makes Annual Distribution of Baskets Christmas Week.  MANY CONTRIBUTIONS Officials Give Detailed Re- port of Year's Work. The Big Brothers organization of Baltimore distributed $422.20 in ma- terial to needy families last year, ac- cording to a report made public by its officials, this week. This organization, which for a number of years was headed by the late Wm. C. McCard, has become a fixture in the holiday life of the city. Their report follows: In accordance with the custom of our late president, William C. McCard, who was so vitally interested in the orphans and children in the various homes of our city. we are glad to report to the public that the response to our appeal this year (1929) for the above was most generous indeed. We were able to give the following-235 pounds of the finest turkey, 8 bushels of white potatoes, 2½ busheis of sweet pota- toes, 100 pounds of hominy, 22 quarts of cranberries. 60 pounds of sugar, 50 large loaves of bread. 44 large mince pies, 325 large apples 325 large oranges and 140 pounds of candy, to six institutions--the Maryland Home for Friendless Colored Chil- dren, the St. Mary's Home for Little Boys, St. Catherine's Home for Little Girls, St. Luke's Home for Orphans, Industrial Heme for Orphans and the Apostolic Home for Neglected Children. Besides we sent $25 to the St. Frances Home, $25 to the St. Eliza- beth's Home, and $25 to the Mission Help- ers-all large homes for children to help with their Christmas dinner. To the little boys at Cheltenham, we sent 100 pounds of candy, to the girls at Mel- vale, 50 pounds of candy, to the little blind children at Overlea. 50 pounds of candy, and to the sick children at Provident Hos- pital, a large basket of oranges and apples. Finally we sent 1½ tons of coal to the St. Luke's orphanage and 11½ tons of coal to the Apostolic orphanage. title: EMMETT SCOTT DOUBTS GRASTY STATEMENT: ""UNTHINKABLE"" THAT BOOKER T. COULD GIVE SUCH ADVICE. SAY LEADER WAS OFT MISQUOTED GRASTY SAID HE ADVISED AGAINST COLORED.
full_text: A EMMETT SCOTT DOUBTS GRASTY STATEMENT "Unthinkable" that Booker T. Could Give Such Advice. SAY LEADER WAS OFT MISQUOTED Grasty Said He Ad- vised Against Colored. WASHINGTON. That it was un- thinkable that the late Booker T. Washington could have advised against the employment of colored attendants at the Cheltenham re- form school for boys, Dr. Einmett J. Scott told The Afro- American this week. Dr. Scott had been asked his opinion about a statement made by Nathaniel G. Grasty, white, secre- tary for the Supervis- ors of Charities for the city of Baltimore, in which it was stated that the late Tuskegee Dr. Scott principal had advised against the employment of colored qteachers at the institution. In an Interview Grasty was quoted as say- ing that before the war Booker T. Washington had advised against the employment fo such teachers. Contrary to Attitude. "Mr. Grasty's statement," said Dr. Scott, "does not indicate when he received the advice from Mr. Wash- ington, whether by letter, or in per- sonal conversation. It certainly was contrary to his general attitude in matters of this kind. "Particlularly does it sem unthink- able to me that Mr. Washington could have offered such advice as colored instructors' would not teach in isolated schools.' The whole pro- gram of the Rosenwald Fund initi- ally projected by Mr. Rosenwald upon recommendation of Mr. Wash- ington indicates that one of the par- ticular things in his mind always to accept employment in isolated sec- tions where they were and are most needed. Often Misquoted. "Often during his lifetime, Mr. Washington was misquoted by per- sons who themselves, wishing to con- tinue situations excluding colored people from activity in connection with their own schools and institu- tions, quoted him as favoring their notions. I cannot make this state- ment with respect to Mr. Grasty, but I do know that Mr. Washington was constantly writing letters refuting alleged statements of his of a simi- lar character." full_text: LARGE CHURCHES SAP MISSIONS, SAYS MINISTER "The condition of mission churches in Baltimore is worse now than it was 20 years ago," said the Rev. Jos- eph Gwynn, pastor of Shiloh Taber- nacle A.M.E. Church, at the Balti- more Preachers' Meeting here Mon- day. Denouncing the attitude of the larger A.M.E. churches that are "sapping the life out of the smaller missions like Oak Street A.M.Ε. Church, Handy Memorial, and Shiloh A.M.E. Chu:ches," the Rev. Mr. Gwynn told the body of ministers that these missions would continue to go down unless a more sympathetic attitude of constructive help was of- fered to them by the larger churches in the Baltimore area. Lindbergh Baby The ministers denounced the tactics employed by officials in the search for the Lindbergh baby. What sort of religion can we preach to the people if we are going to condone the use of unlawful methods in righting a wrong such as the kidnaping of this child, declared the Rev. Charles Stewart. The minister further declared that the employment of racketeers in the search for the child, showed a break- down in the moral fibre of the forces of law and order in this country. title: ELTON FAX SOON TO RECOVER
full_text: ) ELTON FAX SOON GROUP SENT TO TO RECOVER Elton Fax, Baltimore's promising artist, is still confined in the Johns Hopkins Hospital after three months, suffering with a paralytic condition thought to have been in- duced by an abscessed tooth. According to hospital authorities late Thursday. Mr. Fax was much improved, although it was not said when he would be able to leave the institution. Doctors would not give the exact nature of Mr. Fax's ail- ment but assured the AFRO he was much better. He has been ill more than three months, it was said. Mr. Fax astounded Baltimore this Spring when he exhibited a collec- tion of his paintings and sketches in the AFRO building and was one of the leading contributors to the art exhibit of the Women's Co-opera- tive Civic League, winning its first award. He is a graduate of the Syracuse University School of Art and one of the most promising of local artists. N.C. Man Held Here on Murder Taken into custody by Detective Cornelius Roche, John Hines, 27, 1312 Myrtle Avenue, was held for Elm City, Wilson County, North Carolina authorities on charges of murder, Wednesday. In his statement to local police, Hines declared that he shot Ernest Alexander in June, 1930. He lived in Richmond for a year before being traced here. He was employed at the St. Paul Garage. CHELTENHAM Four boys, including two home- less waifs, were ordered sent to the Cheltenham Reformatory after hearings in the juvenile court, this week. The two orphans, brothers, Win- field, 15, and Bernard Jones, 17, were found by a policeman living in a vacant house. When ques- tioned by Northern district officers the boys stated that their parents were dead and that they had been living as best they could for five months. They were sent to the school to assure a home. The two boys, police say, were in tatters and rags when arraigned in the court and exhibited signs of malnutri- tion. Convicted of misdemeanors, Ver- non Russell, 12, 848 Pierce Street, and Harry Laroy. 1539 Shield Place, were ordered sent to the reform school. Held for Mother Joseph Thomas, 12, 1019 Ash- land Avenue, was arrested on charges of being a runaway from home. He was held for his mother, Mrs. Virginia Thomas. Isaiah Burrell, 12, 119 Hamburg Street, was ordered to the juvenile court to answer charges of assault- ing Martin Rudolph, 1214 S. Charles Street. 0 Stabbing Is Mystery After Samuel Hawkins, 42, 320 Worsley Street, had been stabbed in the neck by some one while at- tending a party at the home of Mrs. Alice Conway, 331 East 21½ Street, Northern District police raided the house and arrested six persons, Sat- urday. title: LOOKING AT THE STARS with RALPH MATTHEWS: PAUL ROBESON Has He a Right to be Sore with the Tabloid Papers?
full_text: LOOKING AT THE STARS with RALPH MATTHEWS PAUL ROBESON Has He a Right to be Sore with the Tabloid Papers? PAUL ROBESON has threatened to sue several New York tabloids for associating his name with that of NANCY CUNARD, the daughter of the late steamship magnate. MISS CUNARD came to Harlem to gather material for her book on "Color," and the matronalitan dailies made much ado over the fact, rushing to print with a lot of im- plications, in which ROBESON'S name was used. All of the facts in the case were carried in THE AFRO last November. MR. ROBESON does not object to being called a "friend" of MISS CUNARD'S because of any person- al objection he has to her. He does, however, object to the inti- mation that their relationship was intimate, because he knows only too well, what effect such a false impression will have on his career in America. He realizes that there is no surer way for a colored artist to sign his own death warrant than to have his name connected with that of a white woman. Paul Robeson The first advice that JESSIE SHIPP, the dean of the Negro the- atre, gave BERT WILLIAMS when he was offered a contract to appear in the Ziegfeld Follies, was to keep clear of all compromising situa- tions with the women in the cast. BERT became a success, and died honored by all. BILL ROBINSON owes his success to following the same code. 1 i MR. ROBESON is right in defending his name against such insin- uations. The connection was nothing short of a bit of subtle propagan- da to undermine the popularity of the artist, which he could not afford to let go unchallenged at this time. ALLEN DREW * *** When the Screen Kills the Stage He Won't Work. He's an elongated sort of fellow with a gift for gab. ALLEN DREW is the type of comedian who depends on a magnetic personality plus a wealth of well selected material, to put his act across. He does not use cork. He was born in Tulsa, Oklahoma, 26 years ago, and started shifting for himself at the age of twelve. He drifted into Chicago when he was 21 and began to try his hand, or feet to be exact, in Charleston contests. Having won several, he was picked up by CRACKSHOT HACKLY and given his first stage break. He made out fairly well under the tutelage of this clever comedian and tried his luck in the night clubs as an entertainer. After a while he tired of Chicago and determined to tackle New York. Upon his arrival in Harlem he found the syndicate so tight that he could not break through and was on the verge of deserting Gotham when who should he bump into again, but CRACKSHOT HACKLY. Hackley introduced him to the powers that be in Harlem and he began to work. They let him try his hand in the Douglass Theatre for four days. He stayed there six weeks. His name was made in Harlem. He later went into the Lenox Club as master of ceremonies. It is his ambition to be a white collar comedian. He prefers to be known as the maestro of comedy. His hobbies are shooting pool and watching other comedians work. He spends most of his spare time in theatres studying other actors. He is the proud papa of one child. When asked if he had ever been discouraged enough to give up the stage, he declared that such a thought had never entered his head. "I want to be a comedian," he said, "and nothing else. When there isn't any more stage, I just won't work." Hen, Ken and Ben Their Parents Wanted Them to be School Teachers. You'll see three little boys at the Royal Theatre this week, about four feet tall, who dance like their very lives depend on it. As a matter of fact their lives do depend on it. These kids have got to prove to their parents that their's was the better judgment when they quit high school to become dancers instead of staying on and cramming their heads full of book learning as their parents intended. Their names are HENRY MATTHEWS, JR., KENNETH MARTIN- DALE and BENJAMIN ROBERTS. That's how they got their names of HEN, KEN and BEN. They all went to the Texal High School in Har- lem, but had no idea of becoming dancing partners. Texal High is a co-educational school and the boys say that if it had not been for this fact, they might have continued, but they were financially unable to dress as they would like to with so many girls passing on their appearance. One night all three were broke and there was a dance contest being staged at a Harlem dance hall, in which good money was being offered. KEN and BEN originated a dance called the "Bugle Blues" and the three went up to try their luck. The result was that they not only came off with flying colors and a pocket full of cash, but also the realization that they had invented a dance that had sales possibilities. The trio got to- gether and perfected their dance and have been clicking ever since. * * From Hollywood * Mr. Muse's Favorite Joke and Good Fortune. David Arlen, a Hollywooder, sends the following info: CLARENCE MUSE tells the story of a minister friend of his who married a young couple. "How much?" asked the groom after the ceremony. "Whatever you think it's worth," said the minister. The young man hesitated, then handed him fifty cents. The minister was a good sport. He counted out twenty cents in change and smiling amiably at the young man, returned it to him. MUSE has also been awarded a featured role in "Is My Face Red?" at the R-K-O studios. He has just completed an appear- ance in "New York Town," for First National, in which he appears as a night club entertainer, singing two songs. Muse has composed a song. "Behind the Cabin Door," which has been purchased by First National for Richard Barthelmess's latest picture, "Cabin in the Cotton." It will be sung by a Negro chorus of fifty voices. Muse has a prominent character role in this picture, also. And while we're on the subject, a Baltimore night club waitress is anxious for MR. MUSE to reimburse her for the money she spent for lawyer's fees to keep his son out of Cheltenham. She can be reached at 1031 McCulloh Street. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: Ran Away from Home, Boys Arrested Here Confessing that they had run way from home, after being arrested on suspicion, two boys, James Pope, 13, 4727 J Street, and Edward Dowd, 17, 906 47th Place, Washington, were held pending return to their homes, Tuesday. The boys were taken into custody when a policeman saw them walk- ing on the Washington Boulevard with hand bags. On being question- ed, the boys told conflicting stories. They finally admitted they had run away with the intent of reaching iNew York where they hoped to find work. The boys expressed a hope of be- coming stage stars. The boys had hitch-hiked from Washington to Bal- timore. Their parents were unaware of their escapade. title: 53-YEAR-OLD AGENT NOT WED TO STUDENT: SAMUEL FREDERICK DENIES REPORTED MARRIAGE TO COPPIN NORMAL SENIOR
full_text: 53-YEAR-OLD AGENT NOT WED TO STUDENT Samuel Frederick Denies Reported Marriage to Coppin Normal Senior A statement that Samuel M. Frederick of the Frederick Em- ployment Agency, 1937 Druid Hill Avenue, had wedded the twenty- three-year-old Corona Whiting. Coppin Normal student, was denied by Mr. Frederick, today. The employment agent told the AFRO-AMERICAN that there was no truth in the report coming to the office by mail, announcing the wedding. Miss Whiting was, until Febru- ary when she dropped out of the teacher training school, a senior in the institution. The report was also denied by her father, John T. Whiting. A letter received by the AFRO stated that Mr. Frederick, who is reported as 53 years of age, had taken as his bride the 23-year-old student, and that though there was difference in their ages "she loved him just the same." The note also stated that the couple would make their home at 1937 Druid Hill Ave- nue. Trio Ordered Sent to Reform School Convicted in the Juvenile Court on charges of committing one or more misdemeanors or felonies, 3 boys. were ordered sent to the Cheltenham Reform School, this week. Arraigned in connection with sec- ond offense misdemeanors the boys were tried by Judge Thomas Wax- ter. Following the hearing they were sent to the school for periods ranging from one to three years. The boys who were sent to the school were George Laprade, 14, 502 Wilson Street: Allen Schaffer. 14. 1112 Parrish Street; and Frank Cooper, 13, 1358 Cleveland Street. Young Husband is Paroled to Support Mate Arraigned in the Southwestern police court on charges of non- support that were preferred by his wife, Mrs. Ruth Chandler, 409 N. Parrish Street, on June 24, past, Francis Chandler, 24, 1064 W. Fay- ette Street, was ordered paroled in- definitely by Judge John Tormol- lan, Tuesday. Finds Wife Dead Police are investigating the death of Mrs: Mary Taylor, 28, who was found dead in her home by her hus- band, William Taylor, 1144 Low Street, Monday.

full_text: Virginia Reform School Got Colored Instructors Through BookerT.-Arnold It is Strange Educator Should Reverse Himself in Re- gards to Cheltenham, Writer Points Out. By HENRY F. ARNOLD An interview which is alleged to have taken place between the late Booker T. Washington and Mr. Nathaniel G. Grasty, white secretary for the Super- visors of City Charities, appear- ed in the AFRO-AMERICAN on April 23 under the caption, "Booker T. Advised Against Col- ored Teachers for Cheltenham" which, if allowed to go unchal- lenged, would be a slap at the honesty, sincerity of purpose, and ideals of the man whose life was spent in placing Ne- groes in every nook and corner of America where it was pos- sible. During the life time of Dr. Book- er T. Washington, both the white and colored enemies of the man brought accusations of every de- scription against him for the pur- pose of stifling and precluding his progress as an educator and build- Such accusations, in most cases, were out of jealousy and per- sonal hate. None has been more damaging than the above charge. er. To my way of thinking, the ac- cusation brought by Mr. Grasty was for the purpose of trying to prove to Negroes in Maryland why there are no Negroes connected with Cheltenham, is because Mr. Washington opposed colored teach- ers, and the white people accept- ed his preachment. In the body of the alleged Grasty interview, we find these words:- "Booker Washington was consulted concerning the placement of col- ored teachers. Washington ad- vised the trustees not to employ colored teachers, saying that the instructors would not teach in iso- lated schools." A Strange Apparition One of the first things Mr. Wash- ington did after starting work on Tuskegee's grounds, was to investi- gate a farm in Alabama where col- ored boys were being held in semi- slavery under white instructors, as it is alleged is the case at Chelten- ham. Mr. Washington immediately took up the matter with the Gover- nor of Alabama and some of the leading white citizens of the state, and a reform school known as Mt. Meigs was built and placed under colored teachers. The school is: still in existence, and colored in- structors are on the job. was During this period, there living in Richmond, Va., a man whose name was Henry W. Smythe, who was running a school for de- linquent colored boys. Mr. Smythe made an enviable reputation among the white people of Virginia as a result of his interest in colored youth, and hence a move was start- ed to have a colored school which would teach the boys trades. Baltimorean Mr. Smythe and Booker Wash- ington became friends. Dr. Smythe. who was born in Baltimore, had had tremendous influence with the late railroad magnate, Robert Cur- tis Ogden, who gave Ogden Hall to Hampton Institute. Dr. Wash- ington and Mr. Smythe induced Mr. Ogden to come to Richmond and meet several of the city's out- standing white and colored men, for the purpose of interesting Mr. Ogden in the turning over of a twenty-five hundred acre tract of land which he owned, to be used for a reformatory for colored boys. This tract of land was situated two and one-half miles from Hanover in Hanover County. Dr. Washington assured Mr. Ogden that the land was idle and that hundreds of colored boys, who were getting into trouble, were victims of circumstances, and that a large number of such boys could be saved if they were sent to school and given proper training under colored instructors. Mr. Og- den agreed with Dr. Washington and Mr. Smythe, so it was decided that Mr. Ogden's attorney and an attorney representing the state of Virginia, draw up an agreement to be signed by both parties. "Said refrom school is to be placed under colored instructors, and one-half of the board of gov- ernorship must be white and the other half colored. The state of Virginia must pay a certain amount pro-rata daily for each boy incar- cerated in the school, and the Bi- enniel Session of each legislature must vote a certain sum of money not to exceed two hundred thousand dollars for new buildings and such things which go to maintain a school above the common prison. "The time limit for each boy in- carcerated must not exceed two years unless it is found that the boy has not improved. A school must be maintained by the state for the purpose of giving each boy, who is uneducated, a fourth grade education. title: IN AND ABOUT BALTIMORE: THE NEW STREET
full_text: IN AND ABOUT BALTIMORE By K. W. THE NEW STREET Coming to this office Friday after- noon two young women hailed me at Druid Hill Avenue and St. Mary's Street and blandly asked me where was Jazzbo Street. At first I thought they had discovered I was from the country and were out to have some fun, but suddenly I thought of Jas- per Street, but a square above. I told them, and that was IT. * WHAT'S THE NUMBER? It was told in Tuesday's edition of the AFRO of Norfolk's num- bers determination from prices dis- played in provision stores, but the Virginia City has nothing on Balti- more when it comes to the playing of lotteries in the Jewish neighbor- hood stores of the Northwestern sec- tion. These merchants collect thousands of dollars weekly from players and pay the bets to the winners. There is no attempt at concealment, for I went into two last week in which I had never been. The wagers were made in rear rooms, but a general conversation was carried on in the stores before me whom they had never seen. I daresay mey have no fear of the law or assume all co' ed people play the digits. title: Held for Stealing 15 Pounds of Beef
full_text: Held for Stealing 15 Pounds of Beef Suspected of stealing a round of beef from a stall in Lexington Mar- ket, a 60-year-old man was com- mitted for the action of the grand jury, Saturday. Arraigned before Magistrate Bauer in Western police court, the man, Charles Colbert, 60, of 2420 Stock- ton Street, pleaded not guilty of the charge. The operator of the stall, Frank Knell, reported to Western district police that the beef had been stol- en from his stall. Colbert was arrested on suspi- cion, and later charged with the theft of the fifteen pounds of meat valued at $5. The lock on the stall had been broken during the night.. title: Three Boys Ordered To Reform School
full_text: Three Boys Ordered To Reform School Facing accusation of violating state felony and misdemeanor laws, three boys were ordered sent to the Cheltenham Reformatory, this week. Arraigned in the Juvenile Court before Judge Waxter, the boys gave their names as: Oscar Allen, 14, 1 Port Deposit, Md.: Ernest Johnson, 14. 1142 N. Carrollton Avenue, and Arthur Clark, 927 McDonough. SIFTING THE NEWS By RALPH MATTHEWS RELIGIOUS RACKETEERS Baltimore readers who have been following the trials and tribula- dons of Father Divine might be interested in knowing that the good prophet did not descend from heaven at all, but was at one time a Baltimore hedge-cutter. It was in his home here in Baltimore that he got the idea that he would like to be "God," it has been revealed by the Rev. St. Bishop, The Vine. In a statement to the press this week by the Rev. St. Bishop, he has the following to say: Not only did I teach Divine. but I taught Steamboat Bill- you know, Joe Worlds, Divine's old running mate. It was I who first pronounced the theory that God was within man. I made that statement in 1912 when I was staying at Divine's house in Baltimore, and Divine-he was only George Baker, a hedge-cut- ter, at that time-grabbed it and started out preaching that it had come to him from Heaven. It ain't right, if you know what I mean. This merely proves that even the business of getting people into heaven has been reduced to a racket and the racketeers are stealing each other's thunder. OKLAHOMA TEACHES BANDITS Bank bandits who attempted to rob the Farmers and Merchants Bank at Boley, Okla., found that the idea some seek to create about the Negro's inability to conduct business, was erroneous. Two of the bandits, one white and one colored, are dead from the bullets of a colored bank teller. Many are afraid to entrust their money to our banks. H. C. McCormick, the fearless teller, who shot It out with the bandits before he let them carry off the bank's money, proved that when it comes to risking one's life, the colored teller is all there. Dr. Harry Emerson Fosdick, who points out that only 5,500 Hebrews were freed in Egypt instead of 600,000; and instead of one set of Ten Commandments, there were two. Dr. Fosdick, after a trip to the Holy Land, observes that a traveler is immediately impressed with the fact that it would have been a physical impossibility for the number of people mentioned in the Biblical narrative to have lived in the land of Goshen. Although well founded, Dr. Fosdick's contradictions will have little effect upon alleged Christians, because few churchgoers of either race take religion or the Bible or anything connected therewith seriously any more, since everyday life as practiced by the world at large is itself a complete contradiction of everything the Bible sets forth. Devout churchgoers whoop it up for brotherly love and champion the cause of segregation, discrimina- tion and Jim Crow. Pious charlatans weep crocodile tears over Pha- raoh's oppression of the Hebrew children, while they squeeze the life blood out of their own employees with long hours, intolerable conditions and low wages. Mealy-mouthed hypocrites mourn and lament over the crucifixion of Christ while they turn a deaf ear to the wails of agony of innocent men and women who are meet- ing similar fates at the hands of modern lynchers. While it is highly probable that the early chroniclers, unassisted by modern tabulating equipment, may have been a little off in their arithmetic, we can imagine what a laugh they would get picking out the contradictions in practices of the supposedly Christian nations after 1933 years in which to evolve some degree of perfection. The laugh is on us, not the Bible. title: Shaking Hands With the Scottsboro Boys
full_text: Shaking Hands With the Scottsboro Boys Ralph Matthews's interview with the Scotts- boro boys published in last week's AFRO-AMERI- CAN, presents a human side of this case that has not been emphasized. They have been represented as nine innocent boys, wrongfully imprisoned for three years and condemned to death. In two trials in lower courts, and in two ap- peals to higher courts, these boys have simply been human types without individuality, rarely referred to by name and usually grouped with others as the "Scottsboro Boys." Mr. Matthews certainly begins the process of Individualization. Haywood Patterson is the lead- er and handles the fan mail. He wants to get out and see his people, to go to work and raise a family. Patterson wants to be a bell-boy; Ossie Powell an office boy: Eugene Williams wants to learn typewriting; Allie Montgomery would be Pull- man porter. Down the list it goes. Each has his own eager- ness to get out of jail and each his own plan how to build a future out of a bad beginning.  Boldly, Honestly and Without Equivocation Harry W. Nice, Republican, who needed less than a hundred votes to defeat Albert C. Ritchie for Governor several years ago, has his hat in the ring again. Item number three in his recent "political. talk" to fellow Republicans, calls upon them "TO MEET ALL ISSUES BOLDLY, HONESTLY AND WITHOUT EQUIVOCATION." If that is good medicine for the party, it is also good medicine for the candidate. So we ask Mr. Nice a few questions: Mr. Nice, if the people elect you Governor of the State, would you: 1. Wipe out the race lines in the State laws governing pay of county school teachers? 2. Pledge your party to erase the Jim Crow car laws off the statute books? 3. Substitute for Cheltenham a State reform school for boys equal in equipment and promise to the new Melvale Girls' Reformatory, built by Governor Ritchie? 4. Pledge your party to provide equal facilities for college and university education for all citi- zens instead of just for whites as at present? 5. Pledge yourself to open every phase of State employment to all citizens and see to it that Negroes are employed in proportion to their party strength? These issues are simple, wise and just, Mr. Nice. Do you dare meet them "boidly, honestly and without equivocation?"  The Tuskegee Murders In all that has been reported in these columns concerning the three recent murders at Tuske- gee Institute, there has been no expressed or im- plied criticism of the administration of Dr. R. R. Moton, the principal, except in one particular. Goodness knows, our college and university heads have enough troubles without burdening them also with gratuitous criticism from a non- educational source. Dr. Moton has done a job which few people thought could be done. He filled the shoes of Booker T. Washington, not only consolidating the gains made by Mr. Washington, but adding eight millions in endowment and improvements in plant, personnel and course of study. Unfortunately, into that happy picture are flung three killings, all of them brutal. In two of the cases, the killer or killers escaped. In the third case he was a crazy man, whom many people knew was demented months before the killing. Unfortunately, also, murder is not a private affair. It is a crime for which our laws provide a definite procedure. Individuals may think that the interests of the schcol, or of a community warrant them in inter- fering with orderly processes of grand jury in- dictment and trial before a court. But no one has a right to think himself beyond the law. If Tuskegee has made any error at all, it seems to have made it in assuming that a murder case could be hushed up. It can't. It is as true today as 6,000 years ago, "Murder will out."  Kidnaping Must Stop Or- Beginning with one kidnaping in 1931, the number increased to seven in 1932 and in the first half of 1933 to twelve. The end of prohibi- tion makes it necessary for bootleggers and rack- eteers to seek a new field. They turned to kid- kidnaping. Ransoms demanded vary from $250,000 asked by the kidnapers of John O'Con- nell in Albany, N.Y., to $30,000 paid for release of Mary McElroy in Kansas City. Except for one case in Atlanta and another In Virginia, all kidnapings have happened in the North. Lynchings are preceded by kidnaping. and the South is especially skilled in all phases of lynchings. If the North has more kidnapings, it is because it has more rich people able to pay ransoms. The United States Department of Justice an- nounces a campaign to wipe out kidnap gangs. It is a little Cate. It would be much further ahead had it acted directly after the stealing of the Lindbergh baby, which, incidentally, was the only kidnap case which has ended in murder. National horror at the outcome of the Lind- bergh case has probably caused quick compromise in all eighteen kidnapings since. Victims have been willing to pay, and the racketeers have avoided killings. We have demonstrated how to violate the Prohibition Law and get away with it; how to avoid income taxes and get away with it; how to lynch Negroes and get away with it, and how to violate all insurance and banking laws and get away with that. Our country today represents the sad spec- tacle of wholesale conspiracies to beat the law. If the kidnaping racket can be added to this roll of national sins, we are that much closer to ruin and decay. If kidnapers can succeed, sooner or later, we are all sunk. Goodness knows, our college and university heads have enough troubles without burdening them also with gratuitous criticism from a non- educational source. Dr. Moton has done a job which few people thought could be done. He filled the shoes of Booker T. Washington, not only consolidating the gains made by Mr. Washington, but adding eight millions in endowment and improvements in plant, personnel and course of study. Unfortunately, into that happy picture are flung three killings, all of them brutal. In two of the cases, the killer or killers escaped. In the third case he was a crazy man, whom many people knew was demented months before the killing. Unfortunately, also, murder is not a private affair. It is a crime for which our laws provide a definite procedure. Individuals may think that the interests of the schcol, or of a community warrant them in inter- fering with orderly processes of grand jury in- dictment and trial before a court. But no one has a right to think himself beyond the law. If Tuskegee has made any error at all, it seems to have made it in assuming that a murder case could be hushed up. It can't. It is as true today as 6,000 years ago, "Murder will out." Kidnaping Must Stop Or- Beginning with one kidnaping in 1931, the number increased to seven in 1932 and in the first half of 1933 to twelve. The end of prohibi- tion makes it necessary for bootleggers and rack- eteers to seek a new field. They turned to kid- kidnaping. Ransoms demanded vary from $250,000 asked by the kidnapers of John O'Con- nell in Albany, N.Y., to $30,000 paid for release of Mary McElroy in Kansas City. Except for one case in Atlanta and another In Virginia, all kidnapings have happened in the North. Lynchings are preceded by kidnaping. and the South is especially skilled in all phases of lynchings. If the North has more kidnapings, it is because it has more rich people able to pay ransoms. The United States Department of Justice an- nounces a campaign to wipe out kidnap gangs. It is a little Cate. It would be much further ahead had it acted directly after the stealing of the Lindbergh baby, which, incidentally, was the only kidnap case which has ended in murder. National horror at the outcome of the Lind- bergh case has probably caused quick compromise in all eighteen kidnapings since. Victims have been willing to pay, and the racketeers have avoided killings. We have demonstrated how to violate the Prohibition Law and get away with it; how to avoid income taxes and get away with it; how to lynch Negroes and get away with it, and how to violate all insurance and banking laws and get away with that. Our country today represents the sad spec- tacle of wholesale conspiracies to beat the law. If the kidnaping racket can be added to this roll of national sins, we are that much closer to ruin and decay. If kidnapers can succeed, sooner or later, we are all sunk. . .

title: SCHOOL ROBBER GANG GOES TO CHELTENHAM: SAY BOYS BURGLARIZED 24 PUBLIC SCHOOLS IN BALTO. SEE INCREASE IN DELINQUENCY MORE JUVENILE ARRESTS THAN IN 1932.
full_text: SCHOOL ROBBER GANG GOES TO CHELTENHAM Say Boys Burglarized 24 Public Schools in Balto. SEE INCREASE IN DELINQUENCY More Juvenile Arrests Than in 1932. Arraigned in the juvenile court to face charges of participation in a series of misdemeanors, or being minors without proper guardian- ship, nine boys were ordered sent to the Cheltenham Reform School by Judge Thomas E. Waxter, this week. Two of the boys, John Dixon, 10, 702 Woodyear Street, and Herman Johnson, 12, 551 Hoffman Street, were accused of entering 24 public schools, in every section of the city, and stealing supplies, money and other articles from teachers' desks, and of tearing down pay telephones in the schools and robbing the boxes. Increase Noted The other boys who were impli- cated in violations were given terms at the school ranging from one to two years. Statistics of the court show that during the first quarter the present year there has been an increase of 21 juvenile arrests in comparison with the same period of 1932. Those sent to the school were: James Hammond, 13, 863 Vine; Samuel Murray, 13, 1425 Brunt; John Perry, 17, Alexandria, Va.; James Floyd, 1105 Madison; Wm. title: RITCHIE ASKS $47,500 TO AID INSTITUTIONS: $8,000 INCREASE FOR THE CHARITY RELIEF WORK IN STATE. PROVIDENT MAY GET $17,000 $5,000 MORE THAN WAS GRANTED IN 1932.
full_text: RITCHIE ASKS $47,500 TO AID INSTITUTIONS $8,000 Increase for the Charity Relief Work in State. PROVIDENT MAY GET $17,000 - $5,000 More than was Granted in 1932. A total of $47,500 for colored in- stitutions has been recommended! to Governor Albert C. Ritchie to be included in the state budget for 1933 by the Board of State Aid and Charities, it was learned this week. This amount carries an increase of $8,000 in the recommendation for the awards this year over the amounts granted last year. Of this amount, $17,000 has been asked for Provident Hospital and if included in the state budget and then passed by the state legisla- ture, the institution will receive the amount recommended. This is an increase of $5,000 over the $12,000 granted by the state to Provident Hospital last year. Cheltenham Gets $20,000 The boys' reform school at Chel- tenham, Md., will receive the highest amount if the recommen- dation of $20,000 stands the test of fitting into the budget. No in- crease for this school has been ask- led. It was recommended to the board in a letter that a colored social worker be placed at Cheltenham. The matter will be discussed in a later meeting, it was said at the offices of the board, Thursday. The Good Shepherd Hospital has been recommended a sum of $1,500 with no increase asked over last year. Asks Three Increases In the two other cases of colored institutions the St. Anthony Or- phanage will receive a total of $4,000, an increase of $1,000 and the James Cardinal Gibbons In- Istitute has been recommended to receive a total of $5,000, with a $2,000 increase. title: Taking A Chief Down
full_text: Taking A Chief Down Chief Tshekedi was deposed as ruler of the Bamangwato tribe last week by order of Vice Admiral E. R. G. R. Evans of the British navy, acting as high commissioner for the Bechunaland, protectorate, The chief's crime was that he had presid- ed over a native court which some time ago sentenced a white man to be flogged for living in adultery with a native woman. British laws forbid trial of a European by native court. The chief, who was edu- cated in England, contended that the white man had become a native by taking a com- mon-law native wife and that no European should be allowed to take advantage of the law to flout morals and outrage decency, even in Africa. Fifteen thousand native subjects stood around and watched the British vice ad. miral depose their chief, whose sole recourse now is an appeal to the British crown. Two hundred fully armed British marines ac- companied the vice admiral to impress upon naked black men that British laws are sacred even in tropical interiors of Africa. From this distance, it appears that che English authorities had determined upon the deposition of Chief Tshekedi in advance. Two admissions support this theory. One, the testimony of the European who was flogged, to the effect that he submitted him- self voluntarily to the native court and did not wish to prosecute the case. The other was the pronouncement of the vice admiral that Chief Tshekedi had pre- viously flouted the British administration. The decision of the court would indicate that the chastity of African women and na- tive laws regarding it need not be respected by Europeans, The New Melvale School for Delinquent Girls With the appointment of Miss Sadie George and thirteen assistants to the new state girls' reform school and announcement that the new $150,000 plant will be ready for occupancy by October, Maryland is in a fair way to start work on the proper hand- ling of delinquent cases. It has been a long way from the inade- quate institution at Melvale to a modern re- form school, and even those who have been impatient at the long delay may rejoice that a new day is at hand. Grand jury after grand jury recommend- ed a new plant for Melvale, but until Juve- nile Court Justice J. S. Waxter, Mrs. Marie O. H. Bauernschmidt, and interested friends sold the plans to Governor Ritchie and the state legislature, nothing was accomplished With the new school in operation and the state engaged in the job of making good citizens out of delinquent girls, it ought not be too difficult a job to convince the Gov- ernor that what he has done for the girls at Melvale ought to be duplicated for the boys at Cheltenham. During Governor Ritchie's administration the state has erected a new tuberculosis hospital at Henryton and a new girls' reform school to take the place of Melvale. All good things go by threes. A new Cheltenham ought certainly to supplement the other two good forward steps. Furthermore, the outgoing grand jury recommended it. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Former Cheltenham Inmate Says It Is True Guards Club Boys There.
full_text: Former Cheltenham Inmate Says It Is True Guards Club Boys There. To the Editor of the AFRO: I noticed in your issue of this week's AFRO, September 22, a picture of boys coming from work at Cheltenham House of Refor- mation, and also noted that John Pyles, white, superintendent, says it is all right for guards to hit boys. In 1925, when I lived in Oak- land, Md., I wrote your paper a letter concerning conditions at the Cheltenham reformatory and at that time, according to your paper and the Baltimore Sun, Pyles was supposed to be fired. It seems as though he is still in charge. I am a former inmate of the institution, and it is true boys are clubbed. When they are not work- ing to suit the guards and in the hottest weather are allowed one- half of cup of water. They are cut out of meals hand running three and four at a time. This is all for this time, but I can give you plenty of informa- tion about Cheltenham. WILLIAM CREASY Pennsylvania.
