title: The Whirling Hub
full_text: The Whirling Hub By HERBERT TUCKER and ELLIOTT FREEMAN BOSTON-There is a pinch-hitter in our midst! Our dear friend Elliott has decided that a much-needed rest is the best thing for him, and that there was no better time than Yuletide, so that he can sit and wait patiently by his fireplace for good old Santa. WHERE TO GO * * * * * The T.I.D.'s are making a stab to come back into prominence by giving a shipwreck party at 65 Munroe Street, December 21. You are supposed to have been on the ship when it was wrecked. Whatever you had on at the time, is what you are supposed to wear to the party. I'll see you there. The Mizpahs, a club formed long before my time and your time, is entertaining the public with a dance at the Ritz Plaza during the Yuletide season. DID YOU KNOW THAT? * * * * John Tyler, one of the presidents of the United States, sold his white daughter into slavery because she fell in love with a slave and eloped with him? The colored population of New York is proportionately a third more intelligent than the white population? A colored man invented the first clock made in America in 1754? The city of Chicago was founded by a colored man in 1779? Jan Matzeliger, a Dutch colored man living in Masachusetts, invented the first machine for sewing the sole of shoes to the uppers? (It was his invention that revolutionized the shoe-manufacturing business.) The characters portrayed in the Bible are largely colored? The fastest bicyclist of the world was a colored man by the name of M. W. Taylor? A lowly Louisiana colored man, posing as Prince Apache of Arizona, became the social lion of the elite of New York and Phila- delphia about twenty years ago? Hair-straightening is not a mod- ern idea? Blacks of Egypt straightened their locks about five thous- and years ago? * * WHAT YOU OUGHT TO KNOW * * Louis Davis, formerly of this city but now of Washington, has returned to her native city for an indefinite stay. Her return may mean the renewal of her childhood romance with Herbert Chelten- ham. Millie Braxton of Everett received a telephone call the other day that sent her reeling. To whom the voice on the other side of the wire belonged. I was not able to learn. Whoever it was, must be a blip to have told her something that made her forget all about the dinner she was eating at the time. Such is love! Eva Moulton is said to be making trips to the Snowden house- hold, now that it is time for the great O. Philip to return. There is nothing like having two on the string, is there, Eva? (Aside to O. Philip: your mother says for you to write to her, telling her your plans for the holidays. Are stationery and stamps so scarce down there?) Curtis McLain has elected himself president of the mythical "Back to Normal Club of Boston." Mac seems to feel that the social standards of Boston have gone down too much. He feels that with four colleagues he can bring Boston's social standards back to normal. The former Jean Bonner of U Street, Cambridge, gave birth to a diminutive baby not long ago. It is an incubator baby weighing less than five pounds. Congratulations to you. Jean. Current news has it that Bus Nurse will middle aisle it shortly with Beauteous Erie.. What's sauce for the goose is often sauce for the gander! Con- grats and rats from the gang. (Who is jealous?) That the Brown Marlene is too lucky in numbers, is an event long to be remembered, since she gives tips only to the femmes. It would be wise to send your gals over sometimes, youse guys. You might get rich quicker than you expect! Through byways and highways it is flashed that a certain cor- respondent has learned that the ex-boy friend still likes her a little bit. Friends in Medford would like to see them reconciled. Gladys Bracy was seen in a new make car with plates bearing Rhode Island registrations. The question is: who was her escort? These Cam- bridge girls certainly get around; don't they? It seems that Gladys Wiggins still has a weak spot for her ex- flame, if one were to judge by the way they were talking together the other night. Gladys must have had a rather nice time at the party on Thanksgiving night. So did tots of others, including Alice Mills. Eva Wiggins is seen making weekly treks across the bridge to West Springfield Street now. Evidently it is too cold for the boy friend to make his way across the Charles. or he isn't that much interested. We are led to believe that Teddy Anderson, member of the junior debs, is giving Jimmy Butler, of Depression Hill, the gate. Joe Grey, who is now in Arizona, is asking a certain Arlington Street lass to act more naturally. Kitty Gaines seems to be having plenty of competition, if we are to believe the latest bulletin. Wags have it that a very sweet brown-skin minister and his wife's best girl friend are that way about each other. The girl friend's hubby has a hot temper, but everything is still O.K. because he is still in the dark. Brother, you had better come out in the light before it is too late. Flash!! Saturday night the owl positively will appear at sev- eral rent parties on the Hill. * WHAT YOU WOULD LIKE TO KNOW * What is the Owl and where can he or she be found? What has happened to E. Brown these days? This is asked especially for the benefit of a certain University City lass. Who is, and who is not, going to receive invitations to the Junior League party during the holidays? Why is it that Elaine Roberts, a girl with more charming grace than most of the girls on the Hill, must consistently attend the movies all by herself? What is Parson Charles Gabriel's story? He has declared a moratorium on women through this column al- most weekly and yet each time he is seen out he has a different girl with him. We all thought the parson was a man of his word. That's what thought does for you. Jean Westmoreland, a school girl from D.C., says that Boston fellows are the silliest she has ever met. Why is it that she continues to go out with them? You can't tell me that that old adage about a bird in the hand being worth two in the bush, has any effect on her. * * * * PERFECT MATCHES A certain correspondent of this burg sent in the following matches. In making these pairs he kept in mind the old universal law that opposites attract and likes repel. Here is hoping that no one takes this to heart and accuses yours truly of foul-play. First, we have the perfect match of the Brown Adonis and that most prominent member of the Little Women, our own Inez Russell, of Sargent fame. Next comes the no less perfect match of Kenneth McLain and that belle of Rhode Island, Josephine Edmonds. While in the family, we must stop to consider little Curtis with the petite and alluring Dibby Wilkins. Wallace Roundtree comes to the front with Eleanor Smith, Ted Gould steps into the limelight with Mar- garet O'Banion. William Johnson takes a liking to a great many, but those in particular are Vera Sport, Virginia Ridley, Clarice Cưr- tis and Dorothy Tell. Edward Hutchins is destined to be with Doro- thea Lindenburger. John Tucker seems to prefer Yvette Keelan. Jesse Williams paired with Olga White, Parson Charles Gabriel shows preference to the buxom and debonair Eva Moulton. clean_text: The Whirling Hub By HERBERT TUCKER and ELLIOTT FREEMAN BOSTON-There is a pinch-hitter in our midst! Our dear friend Elliott has decided that a much-needed rest is the best thing for him, and that there was no better time than Yuletide, so that he can sit and wait patiently by his fireplace for good old Santa. WHERE TO GO * * * * * The T.I.D.'s are making a stab to come back into prominence by giving a shipwreck party at 65 Munroe Street, December 21. You are supposed to have been on the ship when it was wrecked. Whatever you had on at the time, is what you are supposed to wear to the party. I'll see you there. The Mizpahs, a club formed long before my time and your time, is entertaining the public with a dance at the Ritz Plaza during the Yuletide season. DID YOU KNOW THAT? * * * * John Tyler, one of the presidents of the United States, sold his white daughter into slavery because she fell in love with a slave and eloped with him? The colored population of New York is proportionately a third more intelligent than the white population? A colored man invented the first clock made in America in 1754? The city of Chicago was founded by a colored man in 1779? Jan Matzeliger, a Dutch colored man living in Masachusetts, invented the first machine for sewing the sole of shoes to the uppers? (It was his invention that revolutionized the shoe-manufacturing business.) The characters portrayed in the Bible are largely colored? The fastest bicyclist of the world was a colored man by the name of M. W. Taylor? A lowly Louisiana colored man, posing as Prince Apache of Arizona, became the social lion of the elite of New York and Phila- delphia about twenty years ago? Hair-straightening is not a mod- ern idea? Blacks of Egypt straightened their locks about five thous- and years ago? * * WHAT YOU OUGHT TO KNOW * * Louis Davis, formerly of this city but now of Washington, has returned to her native city for an indefinite stay. Her return may mean the renewal of her childhood romance with Herbert Chelten- ham. Millie Braxton of Everett received a telephone call the other day that sent her reeling. To whom the voice on the other side of the wire belonged. I was not able to learn. Whoever it was, must be a blip to have told her something that made her forget all about the dinner she was eating at the time. Such is love! Eva Moulton is said to be making trips to the Snowden house- hold, now that it is time for the great O. Philip to return. There is nothing like having two on the string, is there, Eva? (Aside to O. Philip: your mother says for you to write to her, telling her your plans for the holidays. Are stationery and stamps so scarce down there?) Curtis McLain has elected himself president of the mythical "Back to Normal Club of Boston." Mac seems to feel that the social standards of Boston have gone down too much. He feels that with four colleagues he can bring Boston's social standards back to normal. The former Jean Bonner of U Street, Cambridge, gave birth to a diminutive baby not long ago. It is an incubator baby weighing less than five pounds. Congratulations to you. Jean. Current news has it that Bus Nurse will middle aisle it shortly with Beauteous Erie.. What's sauce for the goose is often sauce for the gander! Con- grats and rats from the gang. (Who is jealous?) That the Brown Marlene is too lucky in numbers, is an event long to be remembered, since she gives tips only to the femmes. It would be wise to send your gals over sometimes, youse guys. You might get rich quicker than you expect! Through byways and highways it is flashed that a certain cor- respondent has learned that the ex-boy friend still likes her a little bit. Friends in Medford would like to see them reconciled. Gladys Bracy was seen in a new make car with plates bearing Rhode Island registrations. The question is: who was her escort? These Cam- bridge girls certainly get around; don't they? It seems that Gladys Wiggins still has a weak spot for her ex- flame, if one were to judge by the way they were talking together the other night. Gladys must have had a rather nice time at the party on Thanksgiving night. So did tots of others, including Alice Mills. Eva Wiggins is seen making weekly treks across the bridge to West Springfield Street now. Evidently it is too cold for the boy friend to make his way across the Charles. or he isn't that much interested. We are led to believe that Teddy Anderson, member of the junior debs, is giving Jimmy Butler, of Depression Hill, the gate. Joe Grey, who is now in Arizona, is asking a certain Arlington Street lass to act more naturally. Kitty Gaines seems to be having plenty of competition, if we are to believe the latest bulletin. Wags have it that a very sweet brown-skin minister and his wife's best girl friend are that way about each other. The girl friend's hubby has a hot temper, but everything is still O.K. because he is still in the dark. Brother, you had better come out in the light before it is too late. Flash!! Saturday night the owl positively will appear at sev- eral rent parties on the Hill. * WHAT YOU WOULD LIKE TO KNOW * What is the Owl and where can he or she be found? What has happened to E. Brown these days? This is asked especially for the benefit of a certain University City lass. Who is, and who is not, going to receive invitations to the Junior League party during the holidays? Why is it that Elaine Roberts, a girl with more charming grace than most of the girls on the Hill, must consistently attend the movies all by herself? What is Parson Charles Gabriel's story? He has declared a moratorium on women through this column al- most weekly and yet each time he is seen out he has a different girl with him. We all thought the parson was a man of his word. That's what thought does for you. Jean Westmoreland, a school girl from D.C., says that Boston fellows are the silliest she has ever met. Why is it that she continues to go out with them? You can't tell me that that old adage about a bird in the hand being worth two in the bush, has any effect on her. * * * * PERFECT MATCHES A certain correspondent of this burg sent in the following matches. title: Note from Inmate Cites Brutality at Cheltenham: Boy Charges That Clothing Is Taken, and Food Is Unfit for Dogs.
full_text: Note from Inmate Cites Brutality af Cheltenham Boy Charges That Clothing Is Taken, and Food Is Unfit for Dogs. (Reprinted from late editions of last week) The charges that clothing is tak- en, brutal beatings administered, and poor food is served were lodged this week against Chelten- ham, the reform school for boys, by an inmate whose name is being withheld by the AFRO. The contents of the letter telling of conditions are: "I am an inmate at the Chelten- ham reformatory. "People of Maryland don't know what the boys go through down here. Last week a boy died after being beaten and another was beaten over the head with a club. "The food that is cooked for us is not fit for dogs, but when high officials come down we can't tell them the real way we get along because we are beaten when they leave if we do. Boys' Suits Taken. "If a boy comes here with a suit that is worth $25, it is taken away from him and the first boy to go home gets it. The same thing is done with shoes. "When the boys are drilling, if one of them drops out he is left under a tree until he comes to. "The officers had a still down here, and some of the boys who found it were beaten with sticks and locked up on bread and water. "A boy was writing a story to your paper and another boy told on him. He was badly beaten. If I get out of here, I'll be good, all- right. Some Fall in Water. "In the winter we cut ice on the water and some fall in, they get beaten but when people come down here they don't see any- thing. "I am not telling who I am or how I got this letter out of here, but I am begging the people of Baltimore and the State of Mary- land to see about the boys in Cheltenham. "We were bad boys at home but thouse of reformation is just as bad." Judge Waxter Speaks. Judge Thomas J. S. Waxter, of the juvenile court, was allowed to read the letter. Some parts of it were unintelligible because of the way in which it was written, but he asserted that conditions were bad at Cheltenham. He declared that a preliminary report on a survey that is being made had disclosed many interest- ing things, and he also stated that the next session of the legislature should make the place a state institution. Judge Waxter believes that the institution should be manned largely by a colored personnel, and he stated that the report so far is "loaded with dynamite." This report is being assembled by a representative of the Child Welfare League of America. Grand Jury Urged Change. In the report of January 4, the grand jury recommended that col- ored officers be placed at the re- formatory, and that the state take over the control of it. It was also pointed out that the officials had a difficult job to per- form in the taking care of boys who are physically unsound, feeble-minded, tubercular, and delinquent. The jurymen declared that the food, at a noon meal which was witnessed, was limited in variety although of a wholesome quality.

title: BLAME LOW WAGES FOR CRIME BOOST: Y. SOCIAL WORKER TELLS CIVIC LEAGUE DEPRESSION HITS KIDS. CHELTENHAM 1S GIVEN RAP FARMING CONTRACTS ALMOST LIKE PEONAGE.
full_text: BLAME LOW WAGES FOR CRIME BOOST N. Y. Social Worker Tells Civic League Depression Hits Kids. CHELTENHAM IS GIVEN RAP Farming Contracts Al- most Like Peonage. BALTIMORE, Md.- That the increasing crime rate could not be ascribed to any one cause, but to several mutually inter- dependent causes, Mrs. Armamita W. Anthony, of the department of crime prevention of New York City, told members of the Co-Operative Women's Civic League, Saturday. Mrs. Anthony spoke from theli subject, "The Work of the Crime Prevention Bureau Among Negroes in Harlem," at the social service conference, held by the league at the Booker T. Washington Junior High School. Poverty Blamed Present day crime is characterized by poverty, low economic status, low wages, lack of work and overcrowd- ing of homes, which form a back ground for the large percentage of criminals she said. "Even in prosperous times colored mothers, more often than others, are employed outside of the home. All of us are familiar with the youngster wearing his door key about his neck. What then is to be expected but that children deprived of this parental supervision should get much of their training from the streets? "Although this lack of parental supervision due to poverty is preca- rious enough, it cannot be mcre se- rious than the poverty brought on by unemployment. "With welfare agencies taxed to their utmost to furnish the bare necessities, there is nothing left for recreations, or other things that children consider necessary to their afe. Need Recreation "Movies, for instance, have be- come almost as necessary to the av- erage child as food, clothes ad shelter. Children will steal in or- der to get what adults may consider pure luxuries. "Large families forced into over- crowded rooms and tenements are obviously a menace. Indiscriminate herding of both sexes lays the foun- dation for future immorality. "Then many children are being. forced to leave school and are thus inadequately prepared to find work. Even when they are prepared, they cannot, at all times, find work. Hence they seek excitement which often proves hazardous. A stolen car, a ride with a stranger, or a questionable dance may be the be- ginning of a criminal career. "Children in poor or crowded sec- tions often fail to get that sympa- thetic understanding necessary to formative years. "The work in crime prevention in Harlem has shown that children's behavior isn't always due to pure cussedness, but is a result of some profound maladjustment, physical or mental handicap or bad inheri- tance. Many times these can be prevented if observed at an early age, thus preventing criminal atti- tudes. "Thus, no single cause can be pointed to as being the factor in any criminal situation. With ten- tacles reaching far into the com- munity, correlated factors wind and rewind themselves into resulting misconduct." In explaining the work of her de- partment, Mrs. Anthony pointed out that the moment cases came under the observance of that department, they ceased to be ploice cases but became individual problems of mal- adjustment. To prevent embar- rassment, no uniformed officer is sent on the case. In many instan- ces, Mrs. Anthony said, children were most co-operative, and in some instances brought friends to the de- partment whom they thought in danger. Mrs. Sarah Collins Fernandis. president of the league, presided at the social conference session. The discussion following the ad- dress by Mrs. Anthony was opened by Edward S. Lewis, executive sec retary of the Urban League, who pointed out the lack of colored so- cial service workers under the muni- cipality of the city of Baltimore. Mr. Lewis urged the league to lend its support to the effort to secure workers, and colored policeman and policewomen. Boys Under Peonage In a report on the Cheltenham School for Boys, Mr. Lewis decried the lack of up-to-date trade train- ing equipment. The broom factory, he said, was tuberculosis breeding because of its lack of air cleaning facilities, and that many of the in- mates were in a state of literal peonage to white farmers. "We must have laboratory studies made by members of our own group for we have problems which no white person can ever reach," Mr. Lewis said. Mr. Lewis also pointed out that the type of supervision at Chelten- ham does not make for betterment of the inmates. The people in charge are not of the fine scientific type, he said, but the kind who de- pend upon the "big stick" for-dis- cipline. A talk on the work of the Child Study Group in the city was given by Clarence Roberts, principal of School No. 128. BALTIMORE, Md.- That the increasing crime rate could not be ascribed to any one cause, but to several mutually inter- dependent causes, Mrs. Armamita W. Anthony, of the department of crime prevention of New York City, told members of the Co-Operative Women's Civic League, Saturday. Mrs. Anthony spoke from theli subject, "The Work of the Crime Prevention Bureau Among Negroes in Harlem," at the social service conference, held by the league at the Booker T. Washington Junior High School. Poverty Blamed Present day crime is characterized by poverty, low economic status, low wages, lack of work and overcrowd- ing of homes, which form a back ground for the large percentage of criminals she said. "Even in prosperous times colored mothers, more often than others, are employed outside of the home. All of us are familiar with the youngster wearing his door key about his neck. What then is to be expected but that children deprived of this parental supervision should get much of their training from the streets? "Although this lack of parental supervision due to poverty is preca- rious enough, it cannot be mcre se- rious than the poverty brought on by unemployment. "With welfare agencies taxed to their utmost to furnish the bare necessities, there is nothing left for recreations, or other things that children consider necessary to their afe. Need Recreation "Movies, for instance, have be- come almost as necessary to the av- erage child as food, clothes ad shelter. Children will steal in or- der to get what adults may consider pure luxuries. "Large families forced into over- crowded rooms and tenements are obviously a menace. Indiscriminate herding of both sexes lays the foun- dation for future immorality. "Then many children are being. forced to leave school and are thus inadequately prepared to find work. Even when they are prepared, they cannot, at all times, find work. Hence they seek excitement which often proves hazardous. title: Arrest Guard in Shooting at Cheltenham: Aubrey Bronson of Baltimore in Freedmen's Hospital Seriously Wounded. BOYS MUST EYES DOWN AS WHITE WOMEN PASS Morale at Low Ebb; Boys Escaping Daily.
full_text: Arrest Guard in Shooting at Cheltenham Aubrey Bronson of Balti- more in Freedmen's Hos- pital Seriously Wounded. BOYS MUST EYES DOWN AS WHITE WOMEN PASS Morale at Low Ebb; Boys Escaping Daily. (Exclusively to the AFRO) CHELTENHAM, Md. Rigid si- lence on the part of officials at the boys' reformatory here causes mystery to surround the shooting of Aubrey Bronson, 19, by a white guard named John Hurley, Sat- urday. Barefooted inmates of the re- formatory would reveal no facts concerning the gun play, and visi- tors are permitted to go about the grounds with understanding that they will not question any of the boys. The state's attorney, Allen Bowie, claims to have made a per- sonal investigation of the matter, and has released the guard from arrest on a bond of $1,000. Mr. Bowie's Version Mr. Bowie's version of the shooting is: "A bunch of the boys were go- ing to be fed and he (Bronson) re- fused to get in line. "Later, Bronson went into a room where the guard (Hurley) was sitting and asked for a note of some kind about the matter. In a resulting argument, the guard attempted to strike him (Bron- son) with a cane. "Other boys started to the aid of Bronson and a guard named Grier came to separate Bronson |Continued on Next Page| Arrest Guard in Shooting at Cheltenham [Continued from Page One] and Hurley, who were struggling for possession of the stick. "In a following scuffle, a bullet was fired from Hurley's gun and Bronson was hit, but I don't know where." Further questioning of the attorney revealed that what had been called a cane was really a small sized club. Mr. Bowie, according to John B. Pyles, superintendent, has left instructions for the authorities of the reform school to keep their mouths shut about the matter. Conditions Getting Worse In the meanwhile, conditions are rapidly going down at the in- stitution, according to the super- intendent, and Saturday's shooting has not helped matters much. Mr. Pyles stated that the ap- pearance of AFRO news stories about the conditions of the insti- tution has helped to foster unrest. All inmates have been instruct- ed to keep their eyes on the ground when any of the women ascend steps on the grounds. These women are said to include the wife of Superintendent Pile. Miss Hattie M., his secretary, and a third who has charge of the din- ing room. Punishment of the boys who fail to keep their eyes lowered is set at fifty lashes on their bare backs. Supt. Pyles denied having any knowledge of whippings adminis- tered to the boys, who are inmates, and displayed anger when ques- tioned about a rule which pro- hibits boys from raising their eyes when women are going up the steps of the institution. "I am trying to make them well mannered," he said, "and I tell them to turn their backs when women up going up stairs because it is impolite to look." Rule Necessary When told that his idea of good manners was not practiced any- where, and persons coming up the steps behind a woman are not necessarily paying attention to her, Mr. Pyles admitted that such was the case but he said that the rule was necessary at Chelten- ham. He also stated that the visiting hours at the institution have been limited because of frequent es- capes. Mr. Pyles stated that four boys escaped last Sunday and have not been apprehended. Autoist Gives Ald One boy, according to Mr. Pyles, was picked up in front of the ad- ministration office by an autoist. The superintendent admitted that the guards and boys have been having frequent clashes of late, and he also declared that the trouble between Bronson and Hurley might have been brewing for a long time. Two Guards Hurt - Two guards were seriously in- jured by those boys no longer than the other day," said Mr. Pyles. "What was the nature of their injuries?" he was asked. "Yes, sir, they were some se- rious," he returned and started to change the subject. "Can you describe those injur- ies?" he was asked. "Well, one of the guards was cut about the face in a close-quar- ter fight." he stated slowly. He failed to find a way to de- scribe how the other guard was hurt. Version of Relatives The version of the shooting given by the relatives is: "Bronson was shot by a guard who was yelling at a group of boys and thought that the victim said something 'smart.' "The guard had attempted to strike Bronson with a club, but the youth succeeded in wresting the cudgel from his assailant. "Another guard seized the man in an attempt to stop him from hurting Bronson, but the latter drew a gun and shot over the shoulder of the would-be peace- maker. "No official notification was given of the shooting, although Bronson was sent to the hospital and it was known that he was suffering from a punctured lung." Office Hadn't Heard The Baltimore office of the House of Reformation, queried by the AFRO on Tuesday morning, had had no report of the shoot- ing and learned of it for the first time from the AFRO. Cheltenham is a private school to which the city and state send male delinquents under 21. Near- ly every Baltimore grand jury since 1918 has condemned the place as unfit and unprepared to give correctional training or make good citizens of the boys who are sent there. State Scored The state has also been scored for sending colored boys to a pri- vate school, conducted and oper- ated by white persons who have only monetary interest in the work, while white boys are sent to well-manned reform schools operated by the state. Cheltenham guards are said to be jittery since three boys escaped from the institution Sunday be- fore last, and four more ran away last Sunday. In one case, a visiting woman is said to have helped the boys flee by hiding them in her car. She was caught at the Hanover Street bridge, Baltimore, and forced to carry them back to the school. So many boys are escaping that Sunday one visitor was told that visiting hours will be restricted to the second Sunday in the month. Visitors Sunday were not per- mitted to walk about the grounds with the boys as usual. Privi- leges were curtailed and boys saw their visitors in the hallway near the superintendent's office. Wear White Coats Boys in white coats and white aprons were pointed out to visi- tors Sunday as special waiters at the tables of the white employees, which included three white wom- en. The boys are barefooted so that they will make no noise at meals.

Bronson Says Guard Threatened to Pine Box Him WASHINGTON.--(AFRO Би- reau)-Aubrey Bronson, 21, of 220 N. Caroline Street, Balti- more, Md., is in Freedmen's Hos- pital, suffering from a bullet wound in his chest, said by him to have been inflicted by a guard at the House of Reformation, Cheltenham, Maryland, Bronson is a ward. where According to Bronson, one of the guards came on duty last Sat- urday, acting as if he were under the influence of liquor and start- ing yelling at the boys, declaring himself not to be feeling good. Shortly after the guard came on duty, Bronson said, it was time for supper, and all the boys [Continued on Next Page] Bronson Says Guard Threatened to Kill Him [Continued from Page Onel got in line-laughing and talking loud. Hurley Pointed Him Out Hurley, the accused guard, ac- cording to Bronson, pointed him out and informed him that unless he stopped laughing he would be going out in a pine box. Hurley also gave Bronson orders to sit at table number five, Bronson said. That table is designated for inmates who, for various offenses, are made to sit without eating. Pine-Box Threat "I don't like your looks." Bron- son said the guard gave as his reason for the order, whom he charged made a second threat to send him out in a "pine box." "You are not tough, just rough, and, like sandpaper, you can be smoothed out," Bronson quoted the guard as remarking. "Because he seemed to be drunk, I didn't take him serious- ly," Bronson said, "and I went on to my table and ate my meal. After supper, Guard Hurley came back to the boys' dining room to see whether I had eaten at table number five, and when he learned that I didn't, informed me that he would see me later." Convinced Bronson said that when he went to the dormitory, he was convinced that Hurley was drunk, and, being afraid that he might hurt him, he asked Hurley to give him a permit to see the superin- tendent, John Pyles. This re- quest was refused after asking Hurley twice, Bronson charged. Fired Over Guard "I then turned to go to the school room," Bronson said, and as I did so, Hurley raised a stick to hit me, and I caught it. At that time, Guard Greer stepped in between us and took the stick away from Hurley. Hurley then said, 'Let me at him,' and, reach- ing over Greer's shoulder. fired one shot into my chest," Bronson told the AFRO. After he was shot, Bronson said, he ran down stairs, refus- ing to come back at the request of the two guards. Later, he said, one of his fellow inmates carried him to the reformatory hospital. Brought to Freedmen's He was given emergency treatment there and then trans- ferred to Freedmen's Hospital in a private car, accompanied by three guards and the reformatory physician. At Freedmen's Hos- pital, Bronson was treated by Dr. J. N. Mason of the hospital stafi, No Operation Performed No operation has been per- formed yet to remove the buiiet, according to Eronson. Hospital authorities, when questioned about that, and the extent of the injuries of Bronson, refused to make any comment. Bronson still has the bullet in him. No guards are stationed around him. He posed for an exclusive AFRO photo. Bronson is serving his third sentence in the House of Refor mation, he told the AFRO. He was sent there in 1924 for stay- ing out late at night, for which he served three years. In 1923, he served a year for playing hookey, and in 1929, he was re- turned to the reformatory on a charge of disorderly conduct. Last February he ran away from the home, he said, and was captured and taken back last June. Bronson said he is 21 years of age, and is due to be released from the reformatory, but the of- ficials, he said, are ignoring his age and refusing to allow him to leave.

title: Why Ritchie Was Defeated
full_text: Reprinted from Late Editions of Last Week Why Ritchie Was Defeated Harry W. Nice, Republican, was elected governor of Maryland by some 5,543 votes over Governor Albert C. Ritchie, Democrat. Had 2,772 of those votes been cast for Mr. Ritchie instead of Mr. Nice, they would have given Mr. Ritchie a fifth term in the state house at Annapolis. Strange, isn't it, that Governor Ritchie, who had been elected to this same office in previous years by majorities of forty to sixty thousand should, in thi sfinal plunge, bite the dust by a mere 2,772 votes? Yet it isn't strange to experienced politicians and for that reason the AFRO, now that the election is over, takes a minute to tell why the 2,772 votes were missing. Here they are: In fifteen years the Democratic party, under Governor Ritchie's leadership, has steadily refused: 1. To appoint a single colored Democrat to a state political office. 2. To name colored policemen for Baltimore. 3. To repeal the jim crow car law. 4. To equalize the salaries of county school teachers. 5. To appoint colored staffs for Crownsville State Hospital for the Insane, or Henryton T. B. Sanitarium. 6. To aid Morgan College adequately or establish a state university. 7. To establish a state school for delinquent boys in- stead of the privately owned House of Reformation at Cheltenham. While Governor Ritchie vacationed in Europe, Mr. Nice visited every hole and cranny in the state making friends and soliciting support. While the Democratic state platform contains no single word of promise or encouragement to the colored voters, the Republican platform, at Mr. Nice's directions, pledges definite reforms in several of the items mentioned above. The Democratic party with a two-to-one registration over the Republicans, has proceeded for fifteen years un- der the assumption that it could win without its 15,000 registered colored voters in the state. So it can in many elections. But the time came Tuesday when it needed 2,772 votes and it could not put its hands on them. That is a lesson for the Democratic party which won every important post on the state ticket except the gover norship. That is a lesson for Herbert O'Conor, who is flying high and wide with a majority of 100,000 in his race for the post of attorney-general of Maryland. It's a lesson for Mayor Jackson of Baltimore, who faces a probable primary next May. Not a single one of the seven reforms mentioned above would have menaced the credit of the state, or alienated white supporters of the party. To the contrary they constitute progressive steps which have been taken in many states further South than Maryland. The election is over. To use another expression, the water is under the bridge. However, we repeat here, the Democratic party can win elections without the col what is today perfectly evident to everybody, namely, that ored Democrats, but there are occasions when 2,772 votes are needed. title: State May Pay Morgan College $100,000 Bill: Nice Favors Payment of Debt Contracted in 1890 for Academy. UNIVERSITY OF MD. BROKE AGREEMENT Two Physicians May Get Appointments.
full_text: Reprinted from late editions of last week State May Pay Morgan College $100,000 Bill Nice Favors Payment of Debt Contracted 1890 for Academy. - UNIVERSITY OF MD. in BROKE AGREEMENT Two Physicians May Get Appointments. Morgan College may collect a debt that has been owed to it since 1890 by the University of Mary- land and is said to now be approxi- mately $10 $100,000, when the next session of the legislature convenes in January, 1935, according to in- formation received from Harry W. Nice, governor-elect, this week. During an interview, Thursday, Mr. Nice stated that he is in favor of paying the money to Morgan at the rate of $25,000 a year. The bill was incurred when the University of Maryland sought to get Federal funds made available by the Morrell Act. The officials learned, however, that they could get no money unless they provided educational opportunities for col- ored citizens as well as white. Three alternatives were offered to the University of Maryland. These were: admittance of col- ored students to the university; founding of a state institution for colored students, or making an agreement with a college within the state boundaries under which colored persons would be edu- cated at state expense. The University of Maryland chose the last of these three, and the Princess Anne Academy at Princess Anne, Md., was turned over for the teaching of agricul- tural and mechanical courses. No Sale Made No actual sale was ever made, but the agreement was considered a gentleman's agreement. In 1919 another agreement was made under which the Univer- sity of Maryland is required to ask the state legislature to buy Prin- cess Anne Academy, whenever Morgan College requests that this be done. In the last three sessions of the legislature Morgan has been trying to get the University of Maryland to live up the the terms of its agreement, but has not been suc- cessful on any occasion. Other Changes Expected .. Other changes are expected to take place in civic circles by the time the legislature is in ses- sion. Among these changes will be the taking over of Cheltenham by the state. The board of this institution, which is devoted to the reform of delinquent colored boys, has strongly objected to state control. It is reported that continued op- position to state control of the in- stitution by the board will cause the legislature to withdraw a con- tribution given each year by the state. Further reports indicate that two colored physicians will be given posts in state institutions under the Republican guberna- torial administration. A shake-up in the personnel of several institutions that serve col- ored citizens is also predicted. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Evangelist Out on $2000 Bail on Girl Charge: Girl's Mother Tells Crowded Court He Abused Her 15-Year-Old Daughter. COURT ROOM FILLED WITH CHURCH MEMBERS ""Pray for Me,"" Evangelist Says, ""I'm Framed.""
full_text: Evangelist Out Fugitive and Why He Escaped on $2000 Bail on Girl Charge Girl's Mother Tells Crowd- ed Court He Abused Her 15-Year-Old Daughter. COURT ROOM FILLED WITH CHURCH MEMBERS "Pray for Me," Evangelist Says, "I'm Framed." Special to the AFRO-AMERICAN BOSTON Charged with hav- ing a love affair with a 15-year-old girl, who is expected to become a mother in November, the Rev. Wilbur W. Henry, 22-year-old pastor of the Holy Trinity Bap- tist Church, and a former mem- ber of the famed Henry Brothers' evangelist team, pleaded not guilty, when arraigned before Judge Timothy Ahearn in the Roxbury Court, Monday. His case was continued until the 19th. The former evangelist was released in $2,000 bail. According to the police, a war- rant was issued for the arrest of the handsome "boy-pastor" when a complaint was made by the mother of the allegedly abused girl. The abuse is said to have occurred on February 19. Followers Fill Court The large corridors of the Rox- bury court-house was filled with loyal members of the accused pas- tor's flock. Female and male parishioners surrounded the deb- onair Rev. Mr. Henry, expressed their confidence in him, and pre- dicted his acquittal. The youthful former evangelist, with tears rolling down his eyes, made the following statement for the AFRO: "I am a victim of a frame-up. This is the second attempt made by my enemies to ruin my suc- cessful, youthful ministerial ca- reer. It is all the result of care- ful plotting of my enemies, who are jealous of my success at the Holy Trinity Baptist Church." "Scarcely Knew Girl" Trembling with uncontrollable emotion, the "boy-pastor" declar- ed that he scarcely knew the girl, and only remembers her as a recent addition to his growing number of parishioners. In the tone of voice which made him famous as an evangelist, the Rev. Mr. Henry calmly added: "Sometime ago, an unidentified informant told me that my enemies were out to get my scalp, and shake me down. This at- tempted shake-down was to be made because it is the consensus of opinion that my family is wealthy, which is not true. But I will fight this case to the highest courts of the land." Prayers Requested Making a request to the "kindly AFRO." the former evangelist said he wanted, "his friends throughout the country to pray for him that he will be able to conquer the devil, who is making a diabolical fight to overthrow him and destroy his youthful ministerial career." "Pray for me," he requested, "that I might be able to stand firm on solid rock with Jesus Christ." The arrest of the Rev. Mr. Henry created a furore in church circles here. Several months ago he ran afoul of the law when he was arrested by Officer Parker A. Coleman of the Roxbury Cross- ing station on a drunkenness charge, but his case was subse- quently placed on file. According to the police, the youthful pastor put up a stiff bat- tle with Officer Coleman and po- lice clubs were brought into ac- tion to subdue him. He was char- acterized by the police as "fighting parson." the Escaped youth from Maryland House of Reformation at Cheltenham, who hailed motorists on Crane highway Tuesday and asked for a lift. He said he wanted to get to Annapolis, his home. The boy declared he was beaten last winter by a white guard and had been trying for several months to get away. He exhibited a broken foot and showed where his teeth had been knocked out as proof of his story. title: His Plight at Cheltenham Is Recalled by Inmate in '84.
authors: CHARLES JACKSONAFRICAN UNDERCOVERGEORGE BRAGG, JrT SMITH
full_text: His Plight at Cheltenham Is Re- called by Inmate in '84. To the Editor of the AFRO: I am in favor of abolishing Maryland's Cheitennam Reform- atory, established in 1872. Its motto was to reform the boys sent there and to make them good citizens. The institution made a bad start, and if conditions are as bad there now as they were in the beginning, it should be cut out. I was sent there from Baltimore on August 1, 1884, when I was 11, and stayed until May 1, 1889. I was sent for running away from home. The guards there used a stick or anything to beat the boys. The average boy sent there did not seem bad, so I feel that many were sent to Cheltenham because their parents did not want them. I wrote a story to the AFRO in 1896, telling about conditions of the place. CHARLES E. JACKSON. 239 Norfolk Street, Newark, N.J. Matthews, Miss Elliot Are Called Traitors to Ethiopia. To the Editor of the AFRO: The letter of Carrie Wilkins Elliot in the July 27 issue of your paper was evidently inspired by the propaganda of Ralph Mat- thews and white chiselers with their declaration, "Ethiopians will look down on colored Americans as their inferiors." She asks: "Does Ethiopia re- gard colored Americans as kin- dred?" Prince Malaku Bayen, nephew of the Ethiopian emperor, has just returned to his royal family with a colored American wife. A prince with a "looked-down- upon" wife? Traitors and Mr. Matthews, please explain. This society desires to warn traitors to Ethiopia that their children will spit on their tomb- stones and curse them for hav- ing aided in selling Africa down the gutter. AFRICAN UNDERCOVER DRAGON SOCIETY. Honor Due Miss Barbour. To the Editor of the AFRO: The 1935 Douglass High School year book is beautifully gotten up, is of historical value, and re- flects great credit on all respon- sibile for its production. Especially, do I want to direct attention to the extreme appro- priateness of its dedication. The community can scarcely realize its indebtedness to Miss Fannie! L. Barbour. At a time when the great mass- es of our people had but faint appreciation of education, and the white people, generally, were indifferent, her wonderful tri- umph, along with that of Joseph H. Lockerman, proving the ability of our people to qualify as teach- ers, paved the way for a com- plete revolution with respect to the educational interest of her race. (The Rev.) GEORGE F. BRAGG, JR. 827 N. Arlington Avenue, Baltimore. Instead of an Interracial Church. To the Editor of the AFRO: During the present series of discussions concerning the or- ganizing of interracial churches it is specifically important that we realize that to possess Christianity, it is not necessary for anyone to go to any church. The true church so far has never been founded, else the de- nominational issues would not arise. We need no more churches, but let those we have put Christianity into practice. What the masses must learn to do is to organize militant organi- zations which will force equality of decent wages for work done, and everything which pertains to the necessities of life, including hap- piness. God put everything here. Man must use his brains to obtain it we must use the ballot. T. E. SMITH. 513 Cherokee St., Bethlehem, Pa. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: THE WHIRLING HUB
full_text: THE WHIRLING HUB By ELLIOTT FREEMAN (O. Phillip Snowden substitutes this week for Elliott Freeman, now on vacation.) It was about this time last year that I substituted for Elliott Freeman. If I remember correctly, I began the column by quoting these beautiful lines from Keats's "Ode to Autumn." As autumn is fast approaching, it would not be inappropriate, it seems to me, to begin in similar wise: Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness, Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun; Conspiring with him how to load and bless With fruit the vines that round the thatch-eves run; To bend with apples the moss'd cottage-trees, And fill all fruit with ripeness to the core; To swell and guard, and plump the hazel shells With a sweet kernel ***** These fair strains of poesy are as true today as yesterday, and will be perennially so. Like the sages, of old, let us reflect for a moment upon this thought and recall that though every- thing seems in a state of flux, though governments may change, though the harmony of world peace is threatened at every turn, and though fortunes are lost over-night, that there are, after all, certain abiding and permanent values which we are apt in un- settled times to overlook. ***** WHAT PEOPLE OUGHT TO KNOW William Dean, prominent on the faculty at Atlanta University. has returned to complete work on his doctor's degree at Harvard University, which he hopes to receive in February. Two of Boston's most prominent sons, Moreland Fort, former stellar Boston University athlete, and Marion Fort, Tech graduate and brilliant chemist, will trek altar-ward before Father Time ushers in September. Erskine G. Roberts, former M.I.T. graduate, who has been serving in the capacity of superintendent of mechanical mainten- ance at Tuskegee Institute, for the past two years, has been appoint- ed to the faculty of the engineering school of Howard University. Elwood McKinney, Harvard University sophomore, having received a grade of "A" in all his courses the past year, is head- ing Phi Beta Kappa-ward. Maybe McClane will have company. In answer to the question of many, as to who is the most outstanding Bostonian at Howard University, Stephen Davis and Marion Martin are successfully supporting Boston on its cultural pedestal. Betty McCree, having attained a scholarly record at Roxbury Memorial High School, intends to enter Fisk on a scholarship awarded by the university. Herbert Wilkins, student instructor for the past three years at Lincoln University, in physics, will continue his education at the graduate school of M.I.T., in September. Edith Brown, teacher at the Roxbury Memorial High School, was delegate from Epsilon chapter at the recent convention of the Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, held in California. W. Thomas Fuller, graduate of Colby College, will enter the insurance business in Atlanta, Ga., this fall. May he be suc- cessful. Edward Dixon, for years connected with the General Electric Company in Lynn as draftsman, is the first non-white to receive an appointment in one of Boston's boys' high school. He will take up his duties at the Boston Trade School. ***** MEMOIRS OF A FADING SUMMER Buster Hopkins, known to the little girls as Uncle Bus, during his brief stay in Boston, "lined" all femmes from nine to ninety at his beck and call. Many a wet handkerchief did he leave, but only with the promise that he'd be back. title: IS WITNESS AT BEER HEARING
full_text: IS WITNESS AT BEER HEARING With the Rev. Ernest Lyon, pas- tor of Ames M.E. Church, acting as the star witness, Clarence Webb, 32, 1235 W. Lafayette Avenue was held for violating the new beer law, Sunday. Webb was arrested by Sergeant Edward Hitzelberger at 1:25 a.m. after the minister had complained to the Northwestern district about the noise in the rear of his home. Officers testified that when the house at 828 Woodyear Street which is operated by Webb, was raided, the man was seen selling beer to number of persons. a Webb, who is well known in the northwestern section, was held on charges of selling intoxicating bev- erages without obtaining a license. The six persons who were arrest- ed in the place and later dismissed were: Clarence Webb, 1235 Lafay- ette: James Luckey, 1619 Mount; John McBride, 647 Calhoun; Frank Hobbs, 1235 Lafayette; Norris Brown, 714 Stockton, and Emma Brown, 714 Stockton. SIX BOYS SENT TO CHELTENHAM Facing the accusations of police that they had committed misde- meanors, six boys were sent to the Cheltenham Reform School after trials in the juvenile court, this week. The boys who were accused and sent to the school were: Frank Johnson, 14, 1650 Woodyear Street; Raymond Cross, 12, 612 Fremont Avenue; Howard Thomas, 14, 1531 Woodyear Street; Sylvester Wil- liams 14. 1636 Bruce Street, and James Boone, 16, 1609 Mulliken Street, and Prince Edward, 17, Flor- ence, S.C. Woman Held by Cops As Shoplifter Charges of shoplifting were made against Mrs. Mildred Sessons 23, 1012 Madison Avenue when she was arraigned in the Western Police Court, Saturday. Mrs. Bertha Jellers, a female de- tective at the May Department store stated that she saw the woman take a pair of garters. When she was searched two dresses, two pairs of socks, two pair of hose, a can of Kleenall and the garters were found in a bag. Mrs. Sessons was held for the action of the grand jury. title: Cheltenham Is Not Fit for Humans, Ex-Inmate Says: George Clark Tells of Beatings and Vermin in Food. AUDIENCE REVOLTED BY MAN'S STORY Abolition of the School Is Sought.
full_text: Cheltenham Is Not Fit for Humans, Ex-Inmate Says - George Clark Tells of Beatings and Vermin in Food. : AUDIENCE REVOLTED BY MAN'S STORY Abolition of the School Is Sought. BALTIMORE-Gasps of amaze- ment rippled through Musicians' Hall, Saturday, as George Clark, 28, unfolded a story of alleged in- human treatment suffered by the inmates of Cheltenham. Clark, who spent the years from 1920 to 1930 in the institution, ex- hibited scars and pointed to bumps on his head which he claimed to have received from the white guards at Cheltenham. He ap- peared before a special meeting of the Abolish Cheltenham, Commit- tee, called by Mrs. Maud Bell. Aubrey Brunson, recently shot by one of the guards, was to have spoken, but did not appear. How- ever, those persons seeking infor- mation as to the reputed abuses which the young boys undergo were not disappointed: was incarcerated. "Cheltenham is a place not fit for a dog," declared the former inmate as he launched into his nar- ration. "A dog can get water when he wants it, but those boys can't get any water until the guard is good and ready. "People are told that the boys have school, but they don't. The men out there tell the people most anything." No School, Is Charge At this point, Clark told of his blasted hopes for an education, which he had hoped to receive at Cheltenham. "All I saw there was work," he said. Speaking of punishment, Clark told of the leather straps, four and one-half feet long, which he said are used to beat the boys. "When they are ready to whip you," he continued, "there are two men; one! has this long strap and the other has a stick or cane. Forced to Stoop "They make you kend over with your hands touching the floor. Then they hit you. If you don't bend over, the men will hit you all over the face, head and any- where. Just for talking or any lit- tle things, the guards send you to No. 5 table," the speaker continued. "You just look at the other boys eat. If you say anything to any- body, you go right back on No. 5 at the next meal. "If you keep it up," Clark said further, "they'll beat you up and throw you in a cell for thirty-five or forty days, on bread and water." The speaker told of a beating he claims to have received in 1926. "When the guard struck me with a stick," he said, "I threw up my hand to defend myself. I was then knocked down, struck in the head, kicked in the ribs-onc being brok- en. I stayed in the hospital for six months." Clark denied statements of the superintendent that the youths are taken to the office when they are whipped. He claimed that when- ever a guard takes a notion to beat up one of the boys, it is done. Vermin in Food A revolting story of the food served the youths was related. "Bugs, dirt and vermin can be found in the food," Clark stated. "The boys in the hospital get the same food as the guards, but they have to be nearly dead before be- ing admitted," Clark charged. The former inmate also told of a tobacco-chewing white cook, who allowed the saliva to drip from his mouth into the soup or other food he happened to be preparing. Ob- jection to the man's filthiness or any other things would only bring about a severe lashing, Clark told those assembled. Editor Pays Visit How officials at Cheltenham in- timidate the boys to prevent them giving out information to visitors was also related by Clark. The speaker recalled visits of the grand juries and how the reputed injus- tices were kept hidden from them and other visitors. He also told of a visit made by Carl Murphy, edi- tor of the AFRO-AMERICAN, 1925. in The speaker told of fear of talk- ing with Mr. Murphy, but stated that he promised to write, which he did, sending six letters. Front- page stories of the charges were carried in the AFRO-AMERICAN. He related how the officials tried to find the person who gave out the information. Clark said that one of his fellow inmates knew that he had written the letters, and that he warned him not to tell about it. The speaker said that he knew if the officials learned that he gave out the information they would just about kill him and that he made up his mind to kill the boy should he tell. Bernard Ades, Miss E. Briscoe, and Michael Gold, all white, of the International Labor Defense, were Mr. Ades suggested as a legal also speakers. remedy that: Interested persons have any of the inmates of Cheltenham brought before a judge in a writ of habeas corpus. He stated that proof of the exist- ing conditions could then be pre- sented. Mr. Ades said that should one judge deny the writ, then the matter could be carried further un- til a sympathetic judge could be found. He visualized that in case of suc- cess of having one or two persons liberated by this method, changes would be made. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Most Projects of State Executive Pass Legislature: Made Friends in Order to Break Down Democratic Opposition, He Says. 5 SENATORS TRIED TO GUM UP WORKS Administration Lists 19 Major Achievements.
full_text: Reprinted from Late Editions of Last Week Most Projects of State Executive Pass Legislature - Made Friends in Order to Break Down Democrat- ic Opposition, He Says. 5 SENATORS TRIED TO GUM UP WORKS Administration Lists 19 Major Achievements. ANNAPOLIS, Md. (Special) - Taking into account that he had a legislature with only 24 Republi- cans and 94 Democrats in the House and 11 Republicans and 17 Democrats in the Senate, Governor Harry W. Nice felt that he had done very well this week, as the legislature adjourned. Twenty-four Republicans in the House voted selidly for his 17 ma- jor bills, he said. But in the Senate five members did everything to defeat the Re- publican program. It was not done maliciously, he said, but it was done. The employment agency bill, carrying an appro- priation of $40,000 which would have been supplemented by a Fed- eral grant, he said, was defeated by Senator Phoebus (Rep. Somer- set County). It would have meant four posi- tions in every county and 25 in Baltimore City. Auto Tax Reduced Despite the $4,000,000 deficit left by ex-Governor Albert C. Ritchie, the governor said he had been able to keep the tax rate at the same level and to reduce the automobile tax from $8.30 to $5,20. The Democratic legislature kill- ed the proposition that would make $2 tags possible. Chauffeurs will not be required to renew their driving licenses every year jas formerly. The governor listed among his 19 objectives obtained the follow- ing: 1. Increased appropriation of $20.000 for Morgan College. 2. Ten thousand dollars to take college and professional courses in or outside the state by persons who are denied attendance at the Uni- versity of Maryland. 3. Six thousand dollars for a commission to study means of making higher education available to all people. Coroner Appointed 4. Appointment of Dr. George S. Allen as coroner in Baltimore, and appointment of several jus- tices of the peace. In the case of Mrs. Lula Powell, white, who was objected to as a justice of the peace, the governor said, he asked that her name be withdrawn and he will give her a recess point- ment this week. The governor also stated: 5. "The bill to equalize teachers' salaries was lost, but I hope for at least a five per cent increase for colored as well as white teachers from the 'Cushion Fund.'" Only 5 Rejected 8. "Of 3,000 appointments only five were rejected." 7. "The bill to take over the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham as a state in- stitution went through. Senator Melvin Fine (Rep., 4th Dist.) certainly worked hard on it." 8. "I got a sum for the repair of the executive mansion." 9. "A sum to make a survey of state institutions; 10. "A law establishing pensions for the aged; 11. "A three-man conservation board; 12. "A fireman accident com- mission. 13. "An engineering department in the State Roads Commission." Other accomplishments were: 14. Recodification of military laws of the state. $100,000 to Morgan 15. A law authorizing the state to purchase Princess Anne Acad- emy from Morgan College at a cost of $100,000, to be paid in annual installments of $25,000. 16. Twenty-four bills recodi- fying the banking laws. 17. "A yellow dog law" for or- ganized labor. 18. Separation of state police from auto commissioner's office. 19. Law establishing the right to appeal de novo and to give ad- ditional testimony in awards by accident commission. Made Friends Asked whether he had expect- ted to get this far with a so-called hostile legislature, Governor Nice said he certainly had, that he had not found it difficult to make friends in the legislature, and through these friends to smooth out difficulties. The governor said that at the end of this term he did not ex- pect to run again. When it was suggested that he was now tired out by day and night conferences ture and might change his mind during the 90 days of the legisla- after he was rested, Governor Nice said: "My mind is made up now. I Jam not going to run again." Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: No operation Yet on Cheltenham Boy Shot Last Week
full_text: No Operation Yet on Cheltenham Boy Shot Last Week WASHINGTON-Aubrey Brun- son, 21-year-old Baltimore boy, who was shot by a guard at the House of Reformation, in Chel- tenham, Md., last week, is still in Freedmen's Hospital recovering from the bullet wound in the up- per abdomen. According to Brunson's state- ment to an AFRO reporter this week, no operation has been per- formed yet to remove the bullet. Attending physicians would not give out any information con- cerning the treatment that had been given. Brunson, appearing to be weak, said that he frequently suffered sharp pains in his abdomen and side. He is being attended by Dr. L. Walberg, of the hospital staff. Issue was taken with reports carried in last week's issue of the AFRO that all whipping was done in the superintendent's of- fice. Brunson declared that any of the guards administered cor- poral punishment whenever and wherever they wanted to, and that the superintendent was not necessarily around when the pun- ishment was being administered. Punishments such as bending over and touching the toes for seven hours a day for a week; solitary confinement; standing on one foot for long hours at a time, were described by Brunson as "only a few of the many hor- rible punishments we get." Since being in Freedmen's Hos- pital, Brunson has been visited by his mother and sister and brother. No officials from the re- formatory are known to have vis- ited him since he was brought here last week under heavy guard. 0 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Brutal Beating Laid to Guards at Cheltenham: Inmates Say Steel Knuckles Were among Weapons Used by Three Guards. SUPT. SAYS IT'S OK FOR GUARDS TO HIT INMATES Disclosure Follows Recent Shooting of Boy.
full_text: Brutal Beating Laid to Guards at Cheltenham Inmates Say Steel Knuckles Were among Weapons Used by Three Guards. SUPT. SAYS IT'S OK FOR GUARDS TO HIT INMATES Disclosure Follows Recent Shooting of Boy. CHELTENHAM, Md. Reports that youthful inmates of the Cheltenham Reformatory were beaten frequently and unmerci- fully by white guards at the in- stitution were denied Tuesday by Superintendent John Pyles, white, following an investigation by representatives of the AFRO. Only last week, news was pub- lished of the serious shooting of Aubrey Brunson, Baltimorei youth, by one of the white guards at the institution, precipitated, according to reports, by an argu- ment over the boy's disobedience of a minor order. The investigation was prompted by written accounts of an alleged beating of Louis Waters of Balti- more, said to have been admin- istered recently by three white guards, in a basement room at the institution after the youth was reported to have disobeyed the orders of one of the guards. Eye-Witnesses Give Account Eye-witnesses, when interview- ed by an AFRO reporter, said that the Waters boy was locked in a cell for punishment, instead of being taken to the superintend- ent's office, after he retaliated when a guard, under whose di- rection he was working in a to- bacco barn, struck the youth. Inmates, in their description of the incident, declared that a schada (whipping implement made with several plies of leather), steel knuckles, a taped stick and fists were used to beat the youth un- til his head was a "mass of blood.' Blinded, Led from Cell They stated that Waters was unable to see, when finally re- leased from the cell, and had to be led to the office before being taken to a hospital. When shown a diagram, drawn by one of the inmates as his ver- sion of the affair, more than a dozen other inmates declared that it was a perfect description of the manner in which the boys are handled. They also stated that the in- struments of punishment are used freely by the guards. Use of Weapons Denied Superintendent Pyles declared that no brass knuckles nor black- jack weapons were used at the institution. as he carefully looked at diagram. He showed reporters the schad and said it was the only thing used in punishing the boys, and it was always used in his presence in the office. He also stated that the law for unruly boys is that they be brought to his office by guards for investigation. If he finds that they deserve punishment, he de- clared, it is administered there. Ο.Κ. to Hit Inmates When reminded that if those were orders, guards apparently were assuming additional respon- sibility when they struck boys, he said it was all right for them to do so when they saw fit. He failed to explain why Waters was carried to the basement before being brought to his office. The superintendent's version of the Waters affair was as follows: Waters disobeyed a guard or did not pile the tobacco in the manner the guard wanted. Angered, the guard slapped Waters and Waters picked up an stick to defend himself. Two guards then took him to the cottage, where he attempted to jump out a window. A guard headed him off from the outside and two of them pulled him back through the window. Waters, according to Superin- tendent Pyles, scratched one of the guards, and in return the guard, who had Waters's head clutched in his arm, used his fist to free Waters's hold. Mr. Pyles said that all the blood came from Waters's nose. Boys Still Look Down A white woman came up the steps behind reporters and, know- ing the rule that boys must look down, the reporters watched her. As she reached the top step, where a boy was sitting with his head down, she inquired: "Are you asleep?" Another Boy Escapes Returning to Baltimore Tues- day, the reporters were stopped along the road by a frantic youth who said he had been beaten up last winter by a guard. He ex- hibited a broken foot and indi- cated where several teeth had been lost, allegedly as a result of his beating. He said he had been bounced against the concrete floor and had been seeking a chance to get away for months. When shown the diagram of the Waters incident, which included the name of one of the guards, the escaping youth said: "That man has got them knuckles in the back of his car." He added: "They drink whiskey, too." The youth revealed that he had been sent to Cheltenham seven years ago and was sup- posed to stay until he was 21. He is only 16 now. He said that he was sent there because he would not stay at home, but would stay now rather than return to the re- formatory. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Nice Renews Pledges Made in Platform
full_text: Reprinted from Late Editions of Last Week Nice Renews Pledges Made in Platform The pledge that he plans to car- ry out all phases of the platform of the Republican was renewed Wednesday by Harry W. Nice, gov- ernor-elect of Maryland, in a state- ment to the AFRO-AMERICAN. Mr. Nice refused to make a com- ment that would refer to any race or individual, but he stated that his chief concern is to devise a program of relief that will prevent suffering in the state. If Mr. Nice carries out the plat- form, as he has promised, how- ever, it will automatically mean that Morgan College will be taken over by the state and made into a university. The reform school for boys at Cheltenham, Md., will also be in- vestigated and manned with a colored staff, according to pre-elec- tion promises of the Republican party. Voting Act to Go An act known as the Declara- tion of Intentions Act, which pre- vents many persons from exercis- ing their right to vote, and which the Republican party officials say hits colored voters hardest, will possibly be repealed. The phase of the platform re- lating to this is: "We advocate the complete re- peal of the Declaration of Inten- tions Act and repeal of the Affi- davit of Removal Act. "These pernicious and un-Ameri- can laws have prevented thousands of citizens from voting which im- pose restrictions on the free exer- cise of suffrage. "They not only hamper and re- strict, but in thousands of cases absolutely prevent voting by per- sons otherwise entitled." Minority Group Recognized Mr. Nice expects to have mi- nority representation on all boards and commissions which he shall appoint during his administration. At one time Mr. Nice publicly declared that he was against the appointment of colored police, be- cause he did not want to do any- thing that would arouse racial an- tagonism in Maryland. It was rumored that this state- ment was an effort on the then candidate's party to curry favor with the Eastern Shore voters. Shoreman Wants Police Harry Phoebus, white, senator from Somerset County, on the Eastern Shore, said that Shoremen are not opposed to the appoint- ment of colored officers. title: Morgan Receives $45,O00 State Aid in Budget
full_text: Reprinted from Late Editions of Last Week Morgan Receives $45,000 State Aid in Budget (By Staff Correspondent) Excitement ANNAPOLIS. burned at a fever heat in this city, Wednesday, following the re- lease of the governor's budget of $60,000,000 that includes an allot- ment of $45,000 for Morgan Col- lege. _ This amount marks an increase of $21,600 in the fund provided for the college, but is $30,000 short of the $75,000 requested. Persons close to the governor assert that the shortage can be explained by agreements that are to be made with Lincoln Univer- sity in Pennsylvania and Howard University in Washington, where- by the tuition of Maryland stu- dents will be paid until a state uni- versity can be set up. $59,000 for Henryton It has also been indicated by the administration that the sum of $59,000 requested for new build- ings at Henryton, for the housing and care of tuberculosis victims, will be taken care of in the pro- posed bond issue of $855,000. The proposed budget includes an appropriation of $20,000 for Cheltenham, but activity is now under way to make this institution entirely under state supervision which will mean a necessary in- crease in the appropriation. On Wednesday a special com- mittee from the Cheltenham board visited the governor here, and its members were told that the insti- tutino must be taken over by the state. Members Dubious The committee presented itself following intimations by some of the board members that the state might not be willing to assume control of the institution-as a number of organizations and civic groups have demanded. The Maryland School for the Blind, which requested an appro- priation of $13,000, was granted its wish, and this amount repre- sents no increase over that given last year. No increase was given the N. M. Carroll Home of the M.E. Church, which receives its customary al- lotment of $5,000. The sum of $500 was allotted to the Shelter for the Aged and In- firm, which failed to ask for and did not receive an increase in its appropriation. A.M.E.'s Get $1500 Another static figure in the bud- get is the sum of $1500 for the A.M.E. Home for the Aged, which did not ask for an increase over the amount that it received last year. St. Elizabeth's Home sought an increase of $500 over its appro priation of $12,000 received last year which was granted. Other institutions failing to ask for or receive increases in their appropriations are St. Mary's Home for Boys, $1250; St. Cath- erine's Home for Girls, $1250; and the House of Good Shepherd, $4,000. Princess Anne Cut Princess Anne Academy and Bowie State Normal School were given upsets. The former asked that its allowance be increased from $15,672 to $17,672, but was given a decreased amount of $15,- 513. The latter sought $44,385 instead of its last year's sum of $38,069, but was given $37,411. Crownsville, seeking $245,000, receives $123,950, but will be re- duced to $115,700 in 1937. The Good Shepherd Hospital, a new institution on the list, will re- ceive $5,000. The Henry Watson Children's Aid Society, seeking $15,000 in- stead of its allotment of $8,000, re- ceived $9,000, while the St. Peter Claver Industrial School, request- ing a $500 increase in its allotment of $3,000. had its wish granted. Asylum Gets Increase St. Vincent's Infant Asylum, seeking a $500 increase in its al- lotment of $14,500, was given that amount, which brings its total to $15,000. Provident Hospital, which faced a huge deficit because of the failure of state funds to meet the amount of money expended on state pa- tients, was refused a request for $16,000. The amount alloted, which was $14,000, is an increase of $2,000 over previous allotments. n Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: New Md. Governor Sworn in New York Gets Colored Marshal▲ “Fire” Mother Faints at Funeral WBAL MD. GOVERNOR'S INAUGURAL "When you think I am right, commend me. title: Judging Religions.
full_text: Judging Religions. To the Editor of the AFRO: If our religions were to be judged by each other. there would be no religions right: if we judged our own, there would be no religions wrong. We differ, but the divine object brings the human family into one accord, God is Supreme. God is all. (Mrs.) GERTRUDE WILLIAMS 228 Fourth Street, Lackawanna, N.Y. Replace Cheltenham. To the Editor of the AFRO: After reading of the treatment afforded our boys at Cheltenham. I have been wondering whether it would be a good plan for us to get together and do something our- selves to alleviate the situation. Why can't we get some of our lawyers, doctors and business men to purchase a building and take care of these boys? Our Governor is a good, just man, and I am sure he will help. Baltimore, Md. Likes De Priest; AAA. To the Editor of the AFRO: Μ. We need a man like Oscar De- Priest; he is a good man and I would like to meet him. I think that he will do good work for us. I am also sorry that the AAA was declared unconstitutional and hope that some day soon something will be found to replace it. The farmer will be lost without it. GEORGE W. WHITAKER Box 351 Tarboro, N.C. Students in Theological Seminary Dorms To the Editor of the AFRO: In a recent report of the Middle Atlantic Seminary Conference car- ried in the AFRO this statement was made: "Students from General Theological Seminary would take no part in the discussion, although colored students there are advised not to live in the dormitories." I, and three other colored stu- dents, live at the seminary. When I applied for admittance there was no mention made of my staying anywhere else. In fact, when I asked about commuting from my home I was advised against it be- cause the distractions involved would be harmful to my life here as a student preparing for priest- hood. I might also say that my life here has been most satisfying and inspiringly pleasant. We all have the feeling that we are preparing for the same work in the Catholic Church, embracing people of many races and countries, which causes the petty feeling and prejudices. that you imply, to sink into the background. CHARLES E. HARRISON. 175 Ninth Ave.. New York City

title: No Menacing Reds.
full_text: No Menacing Reds. To the Editor of the AFRO: Fruit has been borne from the seeds sown by your editorial of some months ago, entitled "No Menacing Reds," which said in part: "In fact, there is more real Christianity among white Com- munists than in the white YMCA, the white Christian Endeavor So- cieties or the white so-called Christian churches." Since this editorial was pub- lished, the Communists have been instrumental in organizing both colored and white share- croppers into a union which now has a membership of ten thous- and and which has helped in bet- tering working conditions and wages. The case of Angelo Herndon, the Scottsboro case, defense of Ethiopia, etc., are just a few of the many undertakings. S. CARMAN 1204 E. Baltimore Street Baltimore, Md. 0 Red Cross Snubs Ethiopia. To the Editor of the AFRO: The International Red Cross has refused to give Ethiopia its ser- vices, and will leave the wound- ed of Abyssinia to rot and die in the jungles of Africa. Non-combatant, neutral, medi- cal, surgical and nursing units are recognized as necessary forces of mercy for soldiers wounded and sick in war zones and are accepted civilized forces. DR. JOSEPH T. THOMAS. 2406 E. 40th Street, Cleveland, Ohio. F. D.'s Alarm Clock. To the Editor of the AFRO: In a letter to the President re- cently, I said: "It seems so inconsiderate for those seventy erstwhile, and pos- sible future, enemies of our land and people to come in here on a visit and then try to make a con- trast of the German-Jewish situ- ation with that of the races in our America. "Just why, too, are Mr. Hitler's seventy hired henchmen-doctors traveling by numbers instead of names? Are you asleep?" MOSES ST. MATTHEW ASHLEY Long Island City N.Y. School to Replace Cheltenham Is Urged. To the Editor of the AFRO: Since white officials have re- fused to allow the State of Mary- land to take over control of the Cheltenham Reformatory, I sug- gest that religious, civic, and fraternal organizations unite in the erection of an institution for delinquent boys. This school could be organized with the proper backing of our leading citizens throughout the State. I have an ideal site, 209 acres, adjoining Crownsville State Hospital. I am willing to have a school and cottages erected here, so that misguided boys may have proper spiritual, educational, and indus- trial training to prepare them for good citizenship. MAUD EDGELL. Waterbury, Md. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Nice Names Five to Reform School Boards
full_text: Reprinted from Late Editions of Last Week Nice Names Five to Reform School Boards Appointments of five persons to the boards of two Maryland cor- rectional Institutions were an- nounced this week by Governor Harry W. Nice. Joseph C. Briscoe, principal of the vocational school, and the Rev. Frederick Douglas, pastor of Cosmopolitan Commur.ity Church, are named to the board of man- agement of the Cheltenham Re- formatory for boys, the other eight members being white. On the board of the Maryland Training School for Girls at Glenburnie, Governor Nice ap- pointed Miss Adeline Green and Mrs. Howard E. Young, both of Baltimore, and Charles Oliver of Annapolis. The positions carry no salary, according to Marse Callaway, Fourth District Republican leader. The appointments of the mem- bers of the Governor's Commis- sion on Higher Education were also confirmed this week. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner.
