title: Governor's Stand Spells Doom to Boys' Reformatory
full_text: Governor's Stand Spells Doom to Boys' Reformatory BALTIMORE take it over." - "I purpose to Thus spoke Gov. Harry W. Nice, Monday, in reiteration of his pre- election promises in regard to al- leviating unsatisfactory conditions at the Cheltenham Reformatory, against which repeated complaints have been registered by numer- ous organizations and individuals. The governor's declaration was made following the announcement that a special committee of the retiring grand jury had recom- mended that the institution be taken over by the state. Hits Farming-Out Systen. "I said in my campaign that I believed the institution should be taken over by the state," he de- clared, "and I purpose to take it over. The boys there are wards of the state, and I do not believe the wards of the state should be farmed out as is done in this case." Nice said he was not prepared to discuss the report of the grand jury committee, but expressed fa- miliarity with ger.eral conditions at the reformatory and mentioned a survey, now in his possession but not yet made public, made through the Board of State Aids and Charities. Gov. Nice called attention, in his statement, to the fact that Cheltenham is "one of the last institutions of its kind." Although a number of institutions for chil- dren were originally private, the State of Maryland has taken over practically all of them except Cheltenham; the Melvale School for Girls having gone under state control in 1931. Want Pyle Replaced The grand jury report, submit- ted to the judges of the criminal court on Friday, complained of overcrowding, inadequate medical facilities, lack of recreational de- velopment and the probable influ- ence of older vicious boys on the younger inmates. It was recommended that Su- perintendent Pyle, white, be re- tired and that he be replaced by a trained executive. Although the report failed to discuss the treat- ment of inmates at the reforma- tory, against which so many com- plaints have been lodged, much emphasis was placed on health conditions. title: Goldsboro S. Griffith.
full_text: Goldsboro S. Griffith. To the Editor of the AFRO: No white man in Maryland for many decades after the Civil War labored more earnestly and faithfully for the colored race's betterment than did Golds- borough S. Griffith, whose slogan was: "It is a luxury to do good." Mr. Griffith was born in Havre de Grace, Md., in 1814. It was through his efforts that the Industrial Home for Colored Girls, and the House of Refor- mation for Colored Boys were established. The Rev. George H. Nock, in his, "The Story of a Great Life." says: "Mr. Griffith's sentiment and feeling could not be more terse- ly expressed than in the follow- ing words quoted from one of his reports: "The man who curses an- other because he is black, curses the God that made his so and challenges the infinitude of his wisdom. "The man who says, I hate the Negro', and calls himself a Christian, should read 1 John 4:20: 'If a man say I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar, for he that loveth not his broth- er, whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen.' "Brethren, the time has come when we as the strong- er race are called upon, not only by the demands of our religion, but by the exigen- cies that exist, to pray that the Spirit of God tear away from our hearts every ves- tige of prejudice that hin- ders our deep and practical and helpful sympathy from entering into the needs of the colored people of this city and state. They ask our help they need it-they must have it." - Mr. Griffith was all that the above sentiment implies. The writer of this article enjoyed an intimate acquaintance and fel- lowship with him. Thirty-five years ago, upon the nomination of Mr. Griffith, this writer was elected a member of the board of managers of the House of Reformation, commonly known as "Cheltenham." (The Rev.) GEORGE F. BRAGG 827 N. Arlington Avenue. Baltimore, Md. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Search for Three Who Escaped from Cheltenham
full_text: Reprinted from Late Editions of Last Week: Search for Three Who Escaped from Cheltenham Three youths who escaped from the Cheltenham reformatory are among the eight persons hunted by police and detectives of the missing persons bureau, this week. The boys escaped from the school during the night and were not missed until several hours later. Officials of the school state that the boys have been missing since Tuesday. Leonard Collins, 18, is described as being 5 feet, 7 inches tall, 150 pounds, light brown skin. Arthur J. Shoeman, 18, is said to be 5 feet, 6 inches tall, 125 pounds and light brown skin. Clarence L. Howard is 14, 5 feet, 2 inches tall, 100 pounds and dark skin. Other persons reported missing are: Carl Weaver, 18, of 911 Arlington Ave- nue, 5 feet, 9 inches, 140 pounds, brown skin; wore grey overcoat, blue pants. black sweater. John Ricks, 33, of 649 Bankard Lane; 5 feet, 10 inches, 170 pounds, light brown Iskin. Howard Dillard, 27, of 1403 Madison Avenue; 5 feet. 10 inches, 180 pounds. light brown skin; wore brown coat, ov- eralls, and cap; has scar over left eye. John Smith. 38, 640 Vine Street; 6 feet, 3 inches. 170 pounds, dark skin, small mustache; wore blue overalls and shirt, brown cap. A letter from Miss Mamie White of 859 Hobson Street. Tallahassee, Fla.. re- quests that a search be made for Hugh McCoy White. who formerly lived on Druid Hill Avenue, and is employed at the Bethlehem Steel Company's plant. title: 4 Cheltenham Inmates Freed for Holidays
full_text: Reprinted from late editions of last week 14 Cheltenham Inmates Freed for Holidays BALTIMORE- A Christmas present in the form of freedom was given to four in- mates of the Cheltenham Reforma- tory, Saturday, according to Mrs. Maud Bell, secretary of the Abolish Cheltenham Committeee, which is besieging city officials with a bar- rage of efforts meant to improve the alleged inhuman treatment of the youths confined in the institu- tion. The hopes of another boy to be free on Christmas Day were blasted when officials could not find his parents, Mrs. Bell said. He was returned to the institution. Those released were: John Thomas Brown, son of a Baptist minister; Otis Dickerson, Robert Nettles, and Fitzhugh Briscoe. The youth whose parents could not be found was Robert Wiggins. title: The League Has Failed.
full_text: The League Has Failed. To the Editor of the AFRO: The League of Nations, pre- dominated by England and France, has proved to the world its utter failure as an arbitrative body in carrying out the program of its responsibility of safeguarding the rights of the weaker nations sub- scribing to its convenant. As a black man I see its failure when Italy is allowed to run riot in Ethiopia in defiance of justice and Christian Good-will, thus violating the sacredness of peace. J. B. HOWARD Charleston, S.C. -о- Advice to Ethiopia. To the Editor of the AFRO: I plead to the Ethiopians again. They are slowly but surely fall- ing. If they don't mend their ways and turn to God, great will be the fall. The Lord is asking that the 10th of April be set aside as a day of worship. It is bettter to chey God before it is too late. title: Maryland Reform School Boys Rioted against Alleged Brutal Guards Until They Fled
full_text: Maryland Reform School Boys Rioted against Alleged Brutal Guards Until They Fled Here is Cheltenham din- ing hall, restored to order after the inmates rioted, hurling tin cups, tin plates and other utensils at guards who handcuffed a boy Fri- day night of last week. The guards fled with minor in- juries. One guard had his forehead split. Windows are used for dense growing ferns which shut out one- third of the light in this room. Ferns are more important than the children. A group of boys on the porch of the main building at Cheltenham, Md., Reform School in Prince Georges County, which is run by private interests. Despite snow, ice and freezing weather, these boys are clad only in cot- ton overalls and cotton underwear. Some are hired out to white farmers. Their wages go to the school and the boys are given 50 cents a week. Christmas, some of these boys, barefooted, were sent to the woods to cut logs. The institution has been condemned by every grand jury for 15 years. Welfare surveys recommended the in- stitution be taken over by the State, but the private board of directors refused the offer of Governor Nice to take it over, preferring to hold on to it because it receives over $100,000 appropriations from the city and State annually and provides political patronage. (See picture on front page.) Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Is New Mrs. Maxey with Cab's Band in Hollywood?: Cab Calloway's Drummer Faces Fireworks Mrs. L. Maxey Calls Hubby's Companion Imposter. PROCESS SERVER SPILLED BEANS Wanted Her to Pay 'Other Woman's' Bill.
full_text: Is New Mrs. Maxey with Cab's Band in Hollywood? Cab Calloway's Drummer Faces Fireworks Mrs. L. Maxey Calls Hubby's Companion Imposter. PROCESS SERVER SPILLED BEANS Wanted Her to Pay 'Other Woman's' Bill. By RALPH MATTHEWS NEW YORK CITY--There will be no hi-de-ho in the soul of dapper Leroy Maxey, drummer in Cab Calloway's band, when he returns to Harlem from Hollywood, if Mrs. Sadie Maxey, a beauti- cian and former entertainer, has her way. Mrs. Maxey, who says that she is indirectly responsible for the creation of the Callo- way orchestra, has filed claims for back alimony, which she says will run into big money. Her husband was ordered some- time ago to pay her $15 per week from his salary of $100 per week. Ever since the organization left the East more than three months ago, and long prior to this date, she says she has been neglected. She did not bother, she said, when her husband sent her a re- ceipt for nearly $600 which he had spent on his teeth. Posed as Wife The straw that broke the cam- el's back, however, was a story she read in a Western paper, an- nouncing the arrival of Mr. and Mrs. Maxey on the Coast, and she investigated and learned that an- (Continued on Next Page) Not a Georgia Prison Cage but the dark cell of the Cheltenham, Md., Reform School, where boys rioted, Friday, over harsh treatment of guards. Here are alleged ring leaders who have been placed, like criminals, in this dark hole for 30 days on bread and water. (Other pictures on inside page.) Cab Calloway's Drummer Faces Fireworks (Continued from Preceding Page) other popular Harlem entertainer was allegedly traveling with her husband, posing as Mrs. Maxey. Given Summons To make matters worse, she states, a process-server called at her home and attempted to serve her. with a summons in connection with unpaid furni- ture bills and household arti- cles purchased in the name of Mrs. Theresa Maxey, who was her rival and not herself. She had to produce witnesses to prove her own identity to avoid appearance in court. Helped Make Band Mrs. Maxey, who was herself an entertainer and the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. George Treadwell, one of the old-line families of Flushing, Long Island, met and was married to her husband in 1923. She met Maxey while playing with Lew Leslie's "Dixie to Broad- way" company, first starring ve- hicle of Florence Mills. Maxey was the member of an orchestra known as Robinson's Syncopators in St. Louis, Mo. Upon returning to New York, the then Miss Tread- well used her influence to have the orchestra placed in the Cotton Club at a salary in- crease of from $40 per week to $100 per week per man. The couple were then married. Went on Strike After some time in the club, the band went on strike for $150 per week, and it was then that Irvin Mills snatched the obscure Duke Ellington and his five-piece band from a smaller club, increased the organization and placed them in the Cotton Club. The St. Louis boys were then without their name of Cotton Club Orchestra, and assumed the name of the Missourians, the name which they carried until Cab Cal- loway was placed in control and finally the name, "Cab Calloway and His Missourians" became just Cab Calloway's Orchestra. In "Africana" Before this transition took place, however, Mrs. Maxey again re- sorted to all of her New York con- tacts to place the band again and had them spotted with "Africana," produced by Earl Dancer, with Ethel Waters as the star. This was in 1927. All of these things Mrs. Maxey did, she said, out of love for her husband, and ev- erything was rosy until her husband outgrew her and wrote on the back of their marriage license. "I do not want my wife, Sadie Tread- well Maxey, any more." $3,000 Drums Even after this, she still played the part of a friend, she said, and it was her father who went on the note when her husband purchased his $3,000 set of trap drums, which is said to be one of the finest rhythm sets in Harlem music cir- cles. When Mrs. Maxey learned that her husband had a traveling com- panion, she immediately burned the wires to California, demanding an explanation. Denies Report She received a wire saying: "Don't believe what you read in jig papers. They don't get anything right." Nevertheless, Mrs. Maxey and all Harlem are waiting the return of the prince of hi-de-ho and his crew, who are scheduled for a date at the 125th Street Apollo Theatre within a few weeks' time. 0-

title: NAACP Fires Opening Gun in Jim-Crow War: Protest to Retail Merchants Marks Local Campaign
full_text: NAACP Fires Opening Gun in Jim-Crow War Protest to Retail Merchants Marks Local Campaign BALTIMORE -The local NAACP fired the opening gun on Sunday in its cam- paign to end bans against colored patrons in certain Baltimore stores by calling the discrimination officially to the attention of the Re- tail Merchants' Association. The drive was launched at the association's mass meeting at ; Sharp Street ME Church, and will continue with increasing vigor, Mrs. Lillie M. Jackson, president of the NAACP unit, said. Governor Harry W. Nice was commended in a telegram sent him by the branch during the NAACP meeting. The governor was praised for his stand on the equalization of salaries for all teachers in Mary- land and also for his interest in Cheltenham School for Boys by seeking the resignation of the present board. He was further asked to make two justices of the peace, George W. McMechen and William I. Gosnell, active. Should Know Facts It was also brought to the gov- ernor's notice that the local liquor ☐☐ board was not protecting the col- ored citizens of Baltimore by per- mitting disorderly taverns to operate in respectable neighbor- hoods near churches, schools, the YMCA and other such centers. A telegram was also directed to Joel Hutzler, president of the Re- tail Merchants' Association of ☐ Baltimore protesting against the un-American policy of those Bal- timore department stores that re- fuse to serve colored people. - Speaks on Law More than 800 people attended the meeting presided over by Carl Murphy, president of the AFRO AMERICAN and heard Judge Rowland K. Adams of the Baltimore Supreme Bench de- clare that men in office who do not respect the law cause much trouble in the community. "When men lose respect for the law, then comes disorder and chaos," he said. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Boy Murders Girl Killer: Tragedy Takes Place in State Reform School.
full_text: Boy Murders Girl Killer Tragedy Takes Place in State Reform School. BALTIMORE. Another chapter in a tragic trail of juvenile delinquency and blighted youth was written Friday when Roland McClellan, himself a girl-killer, died at the Freedmen's Hospital with a fractured skull and concussion of the brain. When admitted to the hospital, it was said, attend- ants were told that he re- ceived the injuries when he fell down a flight of stairs at the Cheltenham school of reformation. Another Version Another version, which came to the AFRO-AMERICAN, was to the effect that young McClellan received his fatal injuries as the result of being hit on the head with a baseball bat by another in- mate, James Tynes. The boys quarrelled, it was said, and Tynes used the bat in the fight that resulted. Tynes is reported to have been committed to the institution last July. He was charged with the theft of an automobile and with running over and fatally wound- ing a girl. Killed His Sweetheart McClellan was committed to Cheltenham in May after he had been convicted of killing 15-year-old Lillie May Cherry on April 21 when she visited his home. Testimony at the trial was to the effect that he and Miss Cherry quarrelled over his atten- tions to a Miss Dorothy Wilson, a friend of the slain girl. Miss Cherry went to his home on her way to work at 7:00 a.m., wit- nesses said. He testified that Miss Cherry approached him with a knife and he grabbed a shot gun and fired. The killing at the time caused considerable interest because of the sordidness of life it revealed. Orphaned since 1929, the Cherry girl had lived a precarious life with relatives, it was said. Testi- mony by police brought out that before she was 15 years of age she was visiting the home of Mc- Clellan as his sweetheart. Relatives fought a court battle over the possession of her body and insurance benefits. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: CHELTENHAM TO GET BUILDING FOLLOWING $15,000 BLAZE BALTIMORE According to the Rev. Frederick Douglas, a mem- ber of the executive board of the Cheltenham School for Boys, a new building will replace the institution's $15,000 hospital building which was destroyed by flames on Sunday. title: Ofay Won't Die for 2 Murders
full_text: Ofay Won't Die for 2 Murders JACKSON, Miss.---The sentence of William Clark Mitchell, 54- year-old white man, scheduled to die on December 17 for the mur- der of Lewis Bryant, farmer, and his son, Coot Bryant, was com- muted to life imprisonment by Governor Hugh White last week. Had Mitchell gone to the gal- lows, he would have been the second white man in Mississippt to die for the murder of a col- ored man. Cheltenham Loses Hospital in Fire UPPER MARLBORO, Md. A $15,000 fire which volunteers of three towns battled in sub-freez. ing weather with ice-caked hose lines, destroyed all but the walls of the two-story hospital at the Cheltenham School for Boys, Monday. Four young patients at the in- stitution were rescued safely and removed to other buildings. The firemen were aided by youthful inmates in confining the blaze to the hospital. 72-YEAR-OLD MAN FACES ASSAULT CHARGE ASBURY PARK. title: Cheltenham's Staff to Be All Colored: Nice Indicates to Delegation Board Faces Change, Too
full_text: Cheltenham's Staff to Be All Colored Nice Indicates to Delegation Board Faces Change, Too BALTIMORE-A colored personnel and ultimate col- ored board of directors were indicated when a delegation of citizens led by Mrs. As- bury Smith, chairman of the Citizens' Committee for Col- ored Boys, called on Gover- nor Harry W. Nice to urge immediate action in adjust- ing affairs at the Chelten- ham School on Monday. So certain was the delegation that immediate board changes are inevitable, that it handed the governor a list of possible ap- pointments. Backs Up Executive In presenting the plea of the delegation, Mrs. Smith stated that in view of the governor's proven interest in action at Cheltenham, the committee had come only to indicate a desire to back him up in the courageous attitude he had taken. Calling attention to possi- ble political pressure on one side, the group wanted to as- sure him that he had the support of the community in his determination to wipe out the disgraceful conditions which existed for such a long perlod at the reform school. Adding to what Mrs. Smith said, Sidney Hollander, a mem- ber of the State Welfare Board, reviewed the long fight which those interested in the institution had made. Turning to Governor Nice, he said: "Until you were elected governor, we were not able to get to first base in the matter." Favor Colored Workers Both Mrs. Smith and Mr. Hol- lander advocated acquiring well- trained colored workers or, some white workers who understand what running such an institution means. When a survey was made some time ago, Mr. Hollander said, "Not one employee at Chelten- ham was qualified to do the joo he was expected to do there. "Now that the institution has been taken over by the State, the next job is to get a proper per- sonnel and the kind of board of management that will back up a trained staff and proper pro- gram." Wants All Colored Governor Nice told the dele- gation that he was thoroughly committed to a policy of a whol- ly colored board as well as whol- ly colored staff at the institution. 1 ( ( 1 ! title: Rev. Douglas Offered to Resign Post
full_text: Rev. Douglas Offered to Resign Post BALTIMORE The Rev. Frederick Douglas told the Cheltenham Board of Management and Gov. Harry W. Nice that he would gladly resign his post as chief parole officer, it was learned this week. In a statement immediately fol- lowing consideration of Commis- sioner Jones's report, the Rev. Mr. Douglas stated, that he ac- cepted the position because he was asked to do so, and in the spirit of being of service to the institution during its reorganiza- tion period. Didn't Seek Appointment He did not seek the appoint- ment, he said, and had no idea at the time that it was in conflict with any State law. The Metropolitan pastor, however, refuted the assertion that the parole office was without proper records. He pointed out that the work of the office had been highly praised and that the status of paroled boys had been great- ly improved. Many citizens discussing the Cheltenham situation, this week, were inclined to feel that the en- tire board shared the responsibil- ity out of which the appointment of its own members as employees developed. Old Guard in Control Those who have analyzed the situation declare that the control of the board is still in the hands of the old faction which had kept a strangle-hold on affairs there. The recently appointed mem- bers, it was said, have had pro- gressive ideas, but have been un- able to put them into execution. It is known that practically all of the new members put on some time before the State took it over, are favorable to an efficient col- ored staff. : It was the old influence on the board which maneuvered the leg- islative provision that would put all present employees under civil service and thereby secure them their jobs until their deaths or re- tirement. t 1 1 ( The members of the board are: Enoch Harlan, Howard C. title: Hall, Echols Missing as Va. State Preps for Opener Against Bluefield
full_text: Hall, Echols Missing as Va. State Preps for Opener Against Bluefield PETERSBURG, Va. "Things are looking brighter," was all that big Harry Jefferson, coach at Vir- ginia State, said this week as he surveyed the nicest crop of fresh- men huskies that has been seen in the Trojan camp during his six years as head football mentor, during which he has produced two championship teams. Last year, State won six games, tied one, and lost none to win the CIAA Conference top honors. It was Bluefield who played State to a 0-0 tie. On October 7, State opens against an unchanged Blue- field team, which last year was manned by sophomores for the most part. Hall, Echols, Missing The grim spectres of gradua- tion, poor scholarship, and finan- cial difficulties have reared their ugly heads to cause havoc in the Trojan camp this season. First se- vere blow came with the an- nouncement that Jumping Joe Echols would not return to har- rass the opposition. Most recent set-back is the rumor not yet confirmed that Joe Hall, speed merchant from Philadelphia, would be among the missing. Of the 44 men reporting, an un- lucking 13 were veterans, while 31 were freshmen Although there undoubtedly will be a steady stream of men reporting through- out the week, it is doubtful that many of these will be veterans. Coach Jefferson has already pre- dicted that the Trojan machine of 1939 will be the greenest that State has put on the playing field in many a year. With few, if any, of the return- ing linemen being anything to write home about, there will be a mad scramble for regular line berths. Already the natural abili- ty of several of the newcomers has attracted the critical eyes of the coaching staff. Three freshmen look particular- ly good in the light drills-Charles Lee, Kenneth Whitlock and Ted McCain. Lee is a Charlottesville boy, who is looked upon as one of the best prospects of the new timber, while Whitlock, a Penn- sylvania boy, was a three-letter man in football, basketball and track while in high school. Both are better than average kickers. McCain, a Boston boy, has all that a good passer needs. To Stress Passes With Coach Jefferson planning to develop an overhead game to offset a shoddy line, passers and kickers will bask in the limelight as keymen this season. It will be Dicky Burr, diminutive quarter- back, who looks like All-Ameri-| can timber this year, who will play the stellar role of kicker par excellence. Dicky's toe will bear the major share of the burden if the Trojans kick their way to another CIAA championship. New Men Shine Other newcomers who looked good in the first drill of the sea- son were: John Jackson, who comes from Youngstown, Ohio, and will be sweating for a back- field berth; James Burton, who starred at end for Braddock High in Pennsylvania; Shirley Jordan, a Norfolk boy who comes well- recommended from Booker T. "Things are looking brighter," was all that big Harry Jefferson, coach at Vir- ginia State, said this week as he surveyed the nicest crop of fresh- men huskies that has been seen in the Trojan camp during his six years as head football mentor, during which he has produced two championship teams. Last year, State won six games, tied one, and lost none to win the CIAA Conference top honors. It was Bluefield who played State to a 0-0 tie. On October 7, State opens against an unchanged Blue- field team, which last year was manned by sophomores for the most part. Hall, Echols, Missing The grim spectres of gradua- tion, poor scholarship, and finan- cial difficulties have reared their ugly heads to cause havoc in the Trojan camp this season. First se- vere blow came with the an- nouncement that Jumping Joe Echols would not return to har- rass the opposition. Most recent set-back is the rumor not yet confirmed that Joe Hall, speed merchant from Philadelphia, would be among the missing. Of the 44 men reporting, an un- lucking 13 were veterans, while 31 were freshmen Although there undoubtedly will be a steady stream of men reporting through- out the week, it is doubtful that many of these will be veterans. Coach Jefferson has already pre- dicted that the Trojan machine of 1939 will be the greenest that State has put on the playing field in many a year. With few, if any, of the return- ing linemen being anything to write home about, there will be a mad scramble for regular line berths. Already the natural abili- ty of several of the newcomers has attracted the critical eyes of the coaching staff. Three freshmen look particular- ly good in the light drills-Charles Lee, Kenneth Whitlock and Ted McCain. Lee is a Charlottesville boy, who is looked upon as one of the best prospects of the new timber, while Whitlock, a Penn- sylvania boy, was a three-letter man in football, basketball and track while in high school. Both are better than average kickers. McCain, a Boston boy, has all that a good passer needs. To Stress Passes With Coach Jefferson planning to develop an overhead game to offset a shoddy line, passers and kickers will bask in the limelight as keymen this season. It will be Dicky Burr, diminutive quarter- back, who looks like All-Ameri-| can timber this year, who will play the stellar role of kicker par excellence. Dicky's toe will bear the major share of the burden if the Trojans kick their way to another CIAA championship. New Men Shine Other newcomers who looked good in the first drill of the sea- son were: John Jackson, who comes from Youngstown, Ohio, and will be sweating for a back- field berth; James Burton, who starred at end for Braddock High in Pennsylvania; Shirley Jordan, a Norfolk boy who comes well- recommended from Booker T. Washington High School; Coppin Cartwright, from Phindelphia's Cheltenham High School; and Earl Holmes, a Hampton boy, who has hopes of landing a backfield post, . .

The baby, who is to be chris- tened Francis Edward Yancey, was born in Woburn, Mass.. where Mrs. Yancey had been vis- iting her aunt, Mrs. Susan Saun- ders. Mrs. Yancey, a member of the Smart Set Social Club, is expect- ed to return to Baltimore in May. The new father is staff artist for the AFRO. title: Turner Gets Cheltenham Cottage Post
full_text: Turner Gets Cheltenham Cottage Post BALTIMORE Another step toward the rehabilitation of the Chel- tenham School for Boys, at Cheltenham, Md., was tak- en this week, when for the first time in the recent his- tory of that institution a colored man was placed on its staff of officials as a cot- tage master. This newly appointed cottage master is Milton Turner, 29, of 2220 Madison Avenue, a 1934 graduate of Morgan College and a former county school teacher. Mr. Turner assumed his new duties at Cheltenham on Monday. Не isresponsible, under direction, for the custody, sa fekeeping, training and Milton Turner well-being of the boys at that institution. The salary range of this position is $600 to $720 a year, with full maintenance. Personnel Revised The appointment of Mr. Tur- ner, who stood third on the list in a State employment service examination last fall, is said to have been achieved as a direct result of Governor Herbert R. O'Conor's recent revision of the personnel of the board of man- agers at the school. While colored cottage masters were not uncommon many years ago, no colored have been ap- pointed since the State took over the institution in 1937. Concerning this new appoint- ment, Edward S. Lewis, execu- tive secretary of the Baltimore Urban League and member of the executive committee of the board of managers at Chelten- ham, had this to say on Wednes- day: In Line with Agreement "We feel that this appointment of Mr. Turner is significant, in that it marks the beginning of a policy agreed upon, that those employees at Cheltenham deal- ing intimately with the personnel should be colored." Prior to his appointment, Mr. Turner, who is unmarried, but said to be engaged to Miss Mary Spriggs, of 2413 McCulloh Street, taught at high schools in Ches- tertown, Rockville and Princess Anne, Md. Other colored board members at Cheltenham include: Joseph C. Briscoe, the Rev. Albert J. Mitch- ell, Mrs. Bertha B. Proctor, Miss Ida R. Cummings and John L. Berry.

full_text: Rev. Geo. Bragg Dies; Served One Church 49 Years BALTIMORE - The Rev. George F. Bragg, Jr., 77, editor, author, civic figure and for the past 49 years rector of St. James P.E. Church, died in his sleep at 7:15 a.m., Tuesday, at Provident Hospital, where he was taken on Saturday. The Rev. Mr. Bragg was taken ill two weeks ago with a cold and was confined to his home. Helfenstein, white, bishop of Maryland, presiding. The body will rest at the home. 827 N. Arlington Avenue, until 10 a.m. Thursday, after which time it will lie in State at the church. Baltimore's Oldest in Service The Rev. Mr. Bragg claimed the honor of being the oldest min- ister in Baltimore, in point of service. He has been in the min- istry fifty-two years, having been ordained in 1888, the twelfth Episcopal clergyman of his race. He was considered an authority on the history of the colored church and on the history of col- ored Americans, Marylanders in particular. One of his best-known works is his "Men of Maryland." which is considered authoritative. Educated in Virginia He was born in Warrenton. N.C., January 25, 1863, the son of George F. and Mary Bragg. who soon after his birth moved to Petersburg, Va. He studied first at the Episco- pal Parochial School, then in the St. Stephen Normal School and in the Bishop Payne Divinity School, all in Petersburg. His education was supplement- ed by private instruction from a master of languages, under whom he studied Latin, Greek. Hebrew and philosophy. In 1881, he was appointed a page in the Virginia Legislature and a little later was promoted to the postmastership of the House of Delegates. Pioneer Publisher In 1882 when just 18 years old. he founded and edited the Vir- ginia Lancet, one of the first col- ored weeklies published in Vir- ginia. He conducted this news- paper for five years and on Janu- агу 12, 1887, in St. Stephen Church, Petersburg, he was or- dained deacon by Bishop Whittle of Virginia. He immediately left for Nor- folk. where he began his min- istry as head of a small Episco- pal mission. He remained there for nearly five years, during which time he formally organized Grace Church, secured the lot. built a new church and rectory and improved the cld school building. He also carried on a day indus- trial school in connection with his work. Was Hampton Trustee During this time, Governor Fitzhugh Lee of Virginia appoint- ed him one of the State's trustees of the Hampton Institute, where he served for four years. In December 1888, he was ad- vanced to the priesthood by Bish- op Whittle in St. Luke Church, Norfolk, and in the fall of 1891, he accepted the call to come to St. James Church, Baltimore. which at that time was located on High Street in East Baltimore and had a congregation "ready to die." Growth Steady The Rev. Mr. Bragg set to work, increased the communicant list from 63 to over 200, and erected a new church building at Park Avenue and Preston Street, in 1901. ! In 1931. the church had prog- ressed to the point where it had over 300 members and was: able to give nearly $1,000 a year to charities, missions and bene- volence. In 1932, the old St. James prop- erty on Park Avenue was pur- chased by the city and the church moved into the edifice formerly occupied by the white Church of Ascension. at Arlington and Lafayette Avenues and has re- mained there ever since. Mr. Bragg founded the Maryland Home for Friendless Colored Children, which is now known as the Friendless Home for Colored Boys and is located in Catons- ville. For three decades, the Rev. title: Dedicate Cheltenham Gymnasium in Oct.
full_text: Dedicate Cheltenham Gymnasium in Oct.  BALTIMORE Dedication of the new $80,-000 gymnasium at the Cheltenham School for Boys, originally scheduled for Sunday afternoon, has been postponed to one day early next month, it was learned on Thursday.  The new brick building is one-story high, with a basement equipped with showers and wash rooms. The main floor is suitable for indoor games and may also be used as an auditorium.  Swimming Pool Held Up Addition of a swimming pool to the building is being held up pending granting of additional funds by the next legislature, it was reported.  While the dedication date has tentatively been set for October 12, it is expected that a definite date will be set at a meeting of the board of managers on next Thursday.  N.C. Holds Guards after Convicts Flee  GOLDSBORO, N.C.—Following the escape of two long-term convicts, James Morgan and Richard Brooks, both 35, from the State Hospital for the insane, last week, J. F. Green and Elmore Morrissey, both white watchmen at the hospital, are being held pending an investigation.  Morgan and Brooks, sentenced for robbery, sawed through bars in a second-story cell block and climbed down a rope made of sheets. The two, recaptured five miles south of this city, had made an attempt to escape three weeks previously.

title: Track Greats, New and Old, Headline Penn Carnival
full_text: Track Greats, New and Old, Headline Penn Carnival By GEORGE LYLE, JR. SATURDAY.-Weather doubt- ful, track heavy, high winds sweeping across the track. The faithful devotees of the cinderpath are up betimes this morning to see the running of the forty-sixth annual Pennsylvania Relay Carnival, the No. 1 sports event of the day, which gets off to a flying start with the heats in the collegiate half-mile relay championship. North Texas Teachers win and there is joy in the stands. Then NYU, with George Hagans doing a fine job, takes a first. Xavier, turning in the best time in the trials, easily takes Rutgers and Columbia. In Full Regalia In the finals it appears that the Nordic quartets have been scared by the dark menace and Texas wins, with Pitt and Xavier elcse behind. Up in the stards, a lanky Texan, completely garbed in ten-gallon hat and cowboy boots (minus spurs) attracts plenty of attention. Lunches are being brought out of bags and boxes now and the hotdog man gets lots of takers as the clock reg- 1sters 11:30 and the next re- lay is still an hour away. Walt Arrington, Michigan State field man, has just completed a try in the broad jump, spanning 23 feet 11 5-8 inches to top the field. His triumph is short- lived though. Don Blount, white, of Dartmouth, nosed him out with a leap that carried him a frac- tion over an inch farther. Photographers appear from ev- erywhere and began getting ac- tion shots of the winner and sec- ond-place man. Nice racket that. Lock at Marshall Wilson, lining up that trio of smartly turned-out women. Wonder whether he got their phone num- bers? I'll ask him when he comes over. They seem anxious to speak to Arrington; what's he got that ch! here comes Wilson. They're his sisters? Oh, you mean Walter's, There's another one around? Gee, lucky guy, isn't he? Oh, well, Threadgill on Hand Who's that over there in front of the high jump pit. Al Thread- gill, guess he's thinking of days when he was the big shot in that event. title: Suspicions of Teacher Aid in Arrest of Seven
full_text: Suspicions of Teacher Aid in Arrest of Seven  BALTIMORE During most of last week, four young boys lavishly treated themselves; their chums, and jingled coins in their pockets while in school until a suspicious teacher reported the matter to Policewoman Violet H. Whyte who solved the mystery of a missing $90.  As a result, four boys, all un- der 15 years of age, were given a hearing on Tuesday in Ju- venile Court. The ringleader was committed to Cheltenham, one of the boys was held for further investigation, while the other two were placed on probation.  3 Face Jury Three persons, Mrs. Mary Richards, 50, her son, Charles, 18, of 1843 N. Gilmor Street, and Nathaniel E. Toyer, 19, of 1026 Lexington Street, who were charged with receiving some of the stolen money, were placed under $250 bail each by Mag- istrate J. H. Stanford for grand jury action.  On Monday, January 13, James Sandy, white, of 1601 Westmin- ster Avenue, told police that while eating in a store near Fulton Av- enue and Baker Street, someone had stolen $90 from a compart- ment in his truck which had been parked nearby. The money rep- resented collections for the bakery for which he worked.  Sandy said he did not discover the loss until after he had re- ported at the bakery office. Returning to the scene, he searched for several small boys he had observed loitering about, but failed to find them.  Teacher Gives Clue A few days later, Policewom- an Whyte was told by a school- teacher of the unusual amount of money several of her pupils had in their possession. Her subsequent investigation led to the roundup of the boys and the persons charged with receiving the money. Sergeant Thomas Joyce aided in the roundup.  In signed statements, the boys admitted stealing the money. They said they gave Mrs. Richards, $1 for allowing them to divide the cash on her kitchen table, and gave some money to her son and young daughter and to Toyer.  Sandy was unable to identify the boys at the hearing. He said they appeared to be of the same size as the ones he had observed when he parked his truck.

title: 8 Cheltenham Boys Get 3 to 9 Months, 1 Freed
full_text: 8 Cheltenham Boys Get 3 to 9 Months, 1 Freed UPPER MARLBORO, Md. One of the nine inmates of the Cheltenham School for Boys, who were tried here on Friday before Magistrate Walter Green on charges of riotous assembly, was freed in the custody of his par- ents, while the others received sentences of from three to nine months in the Maryland house of correction. At their first trial before him on December 5, Magistrate Green found the boys not guilty on the original charges of assault and at- tempting to escape and held them in jail until Friday when the charge was changed to riotous as- sembly so that their conviction and a light sentence might be pos- sible. Jesse Wells, 16, Freed The freed youth is Jesse Wells, 16, of 434 Orchard Street, Bal- timore, who was given a sus- pended sentence of six months in the house of correction and placed on probation for a year in the custody of his mother, Mrs. Martha Wells. He was represented by Ben- jamin Kline, white, attorney of Baltimore, and was the only one of the accused youths with coun- sel. This disposition of the case was predicted in an AFRO story in Friday's paper and was made be- cause B. B. Sunderland, white, acting superintendent, and Jo- seph H. Blandford, president of the board of managers, asked that the boys not be returned to the school because they were too dif- ficult to manage. Boys Spurn Cheltenham The boys, themselves, at the earlier hearing, expressed their desire to remain in the Upper Marlboro jail until their case was disposed of rather than be re- turned to Cheltenham. ☐ George Crawford, 17, of Bal- timore, who was given a three- month sentence in the house of ☐ correction because the where- abouts of his parents was not known, was the only found not guilty of these new charges. However, Magistrate Green stated that he will ask Governor Herbert R. O'Conor to commute Crawford's sentence as soon as the youth's parents are located and he will be released in their custody. Others Sentenced The other inmates who were sentenced to the house of cor- rection and the terms they re- ceived are: Charles Jackson, 18, of Wood- bine, nine months; Charles No- land, 17, of Rockville, nine months; George Johns, 16, of 1128 Whatcoat Street, Baltimore, six months; Benjaminin Hardy, 18, ☐ of 1427 Webb Street, Baltimore, six months; William Brooks, 18, of 1414 Ν. Gilmor Street, Baltimore, six months; Charles Jordan, 17, of 1106 Whatcoat Street, Baltimore, six months, and Christopher Thomspon, 16, of 437 Orchard Street, Baltimore, six months, 2 Years for 3 Others Three other inmates of Chel- tenham, who were arrested on December 5 and charged with as- saulting Owen Strong, white, also a cottage master, pleaded guilty at an earlier trial here, Friday, before Magistrate Alan Bowie, ☐☐ and received sentences of two years each in the Maryland house of correction. ! They are Daniel Brown, 17, of Annapolis; William Gardner, 17, of Towson, and Henry Solomon, 18, of Baltimore, According to the testimony, these youths, who were assigned to another cottage, resented Strong's ordering them out of No. 2 cottage at the institution, and struck him several times with wooden clubs. 31 YEARS AS CANAL ZONE TEACHER CRISTOBAL, Canal Zone (ANP) Completing 31 years of unbroken service with the Canal Zone government as teacher and principal in the colored schools, sT. S. Johnston, prominent West - Indian educator, will be retired yat the end of this month and may Isail soon after to Jamaica, his is- land home, to spend his declining years with his wife and relatives. title: $2,686 Estate Given to Heirs
full_text: $2,686 Estate Given to Heirs  BALTIMORE The $2,686 estate of Mrs. Charity McKee, widow of the late president of Florida A. and M. College was distributed to her heirs here, this week.  Beneficiaries included:  Mrs. Philly Mason of St. Louis, $1,283; Mrs. Eudora Tucker, $1283.  Boys’ Home Gets $150  Home for Friendless Boys, $150, by way the Virgin Council No. 42, Daughters of Elks; $150 from the Neighbors in Training Club; Miss Alice Price, $25.12; Bishop Norman Bishop and Ruth Bishop, $100; Miss Elizabeth Smith, $100; and the Rev. Shel- ton Bishop, Hutchins C. Bishop, Vivian Bishop, and Andrew Bishop, $10.62 each.  Mrs. Augusta Boothe, a niece, was omitted from the list of ben- eficiaries because the widow said she had made a settlement on her before her death.  Jones Fired by Recreation Dept.  BALTIMORE J. Alvin Jones, Jr., supervisor in the recreational department of Baltimore, was recently dis- missed $22 in charges of disorderly conduct and assaulting an officer, was dismissed from his job on Saturday.  At a meeting of the seven-man board of the recreation depart- ment, it was apparent that Mr. Jones, former Lexington Market clerk, was guilty of conduct un- becoming a recreational leader and city employee.  They had reference to the so- licitations at a dance given for the benefit of a Social Club on last February 28.  At that time, Mr. Jones, who lives at 1633 W. Baltimore Street, was involved in a disturb- ance in the Odd Fellows’ Hall, Park and Lanvale Streets, which subsequently resulted by charges of Clara Butler and other officers.  6 Vacancies Now at Cheltenham  BALTIMORE The recent death of Dr. Wil- liam H. Debnam, trustee, of Durham, brings to six the num- ber of vacancies on the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys.  The terms of Enoch Harlan, Edward J. Hall, Dr. J. B. John- son, Alpheus K. Williams and James L. Scrimair, expired last June, but Governor O’Conor has not named anyone to fill the vacancies.  Trial of Shore Suspects Shifted  BALTIMORE Although it is expected that the two men indicted for the murder of Harvey Pritchard, white, Stockton, Md., farmer, will go to trial next week, the case has not been entered on the dock- et of the Baltimore County Cir- cuit Court at Towson, where it was moved last week, the Afro learned on Friday morning October.  The change of venue from Worcester County on the Eastern Shore was granted by a judge of the First Judicial Circuit Court. Charged with the murder of the farmer are Arthur Collick, 28, and Charles Absurd, 17, both of Stockton.

title: Snatch Artist Charges Hold 6 Boys under 13
full_text: Snatch Artist Charges Hold 6 Boys under 13  BALTIMORE Alarmed by the series of six pocketbook snatchings reported in the district over a five-day pe- riod Northwestern district police stepped up their investigation and as a result arrested six boys, all under 13 years of age, over the week-end.  Subsequent investigation linked the boys with two of the cases. Given a hearing in Ju- venile court, on Monday, the al- leged ring leader was committed to the Cheltenham School for Boys; another was dismissed. Jailly future of the other four were held under advisement.  Linked with 2 Snatches The following two cases are the ones in which the sextette were named by police: On Tuesday afternoon, Jan- uary 21, Mrs. Beatrice Banton, of 2007 Madison Avenue, was walking near on Presstman Street when as she approached the corner of Irving Street she was accosted by a young boy who, she said, snatched her pocketbook and fled through a nearby alley. The total value of the purse was estimated at $1.52.  The second case was reported by Mrs. Julia Brown, of 2246 Madison Avenue, who while leaving a group of young boys at Bloom and Brunt Streets Satur- day evening, said her bag was snatched by one of them. Among miscellaneous valuables in the purse was $7 in cash and a $25 watch.  With these two cases cleared up officers on Thursday were re- ported endeavoring to find the guilty parties in four other cases still open on their complaint books. The cases were filed by: Mrs. Hazel Street, of 1811 Ful- ton Street, who, while entering the back yard of her home, Fri- day, reported being yoked by an unidentified man who threw one arm around her neck and snatched her purse with the free hand. A pack of cigarettes and eighteen cents in change was the extent of her loss.  The sure sight Mrs. Winifred Robertson, of 1613 Division Street, became a victim when her purse was snatched while she was walking through the 2100 block of Division Street.  The other two victims were Mrs. Emma Weaver, of 623 Lan- vale Street, whose purse contain- ing $3.50 in cash and a $12 check- book was stolen while she was lea- ving a truck from her home, and Mrs. Nettie Bowling, of 2315 Mc- Culloh Street, whose purse con- taining $23 in cash and a $3 handbag was taken at Harlem and Caroline Avenues, Satur- day.

title: Cheltenham Fight Lost
full_text: Cheltenham Fight Lost BALTIMORE Voting as a bloc, the six white members of the board of management of Chelten- ham School for Boys elect- Led Claude D. Jones, 57- year-old white applicant, educational director for that institution on Thurs- day. The five colored members pres- ent voted for Martin J. Brennan, 37, for seventeen years connected with Hampton Institute, for the post. The action of the board, still dominated by the same group under which Cheltenham won the reputation of being one of the! most shamefully mismanaged re- form institutions in the country, dissipates hope, leaders declared Thursday night, that the O'Conor administration will develop a capable colored staff at the insti- tution. White members who voted for Mr. Jones were Enoch Harlan, Joseph H. Blandford, Hal B. Cla- gett, Blossie K. Miller, James E. i Steuart and J. Amos Davis. i Colored members who voted for Mr. Brennan were John L. Berry, the Rev. Albert J. Mitchell, Miss Ida R. Cummings and Mrs. Ber tha B. Proctor. Not present at the meeting were Dr. Harry C. Byrd, Howard C. Hill, Dr. William H. Gibbons, M. Hampton Magruder, white, and Dr. J. L. Johnson. Effort Blocked The election of Mr. Jones fol- lowed an exhaustive personnel report by Col. Harry C. Jones, State employment commissioner, in which he gave the three appli- cants ratings. These ratings, it was said, placed the applicants in the following order: Jones, Bren- non and Charles Kempton. Superintendent Sunderland, it was believed, favored the selec- tion of Mr. Brennon. The action of the controlling bloc, therefore, led some of the colored members to believe that the selection of the white educa- tional director meant that at some future date he would be elevated to the post of superintendent, now held by Sunderland. Second Battle Pending The white bloc also pegged an effort on the part of the colored members to insure that the physical and recreational direc- tor, yet to be named, would be colored. They voted solidly against a resolution offered by the Rev. Mr. Mitchell to the effect that preference be given a colored applicant for this post. Blame O'Conor Leaders interested in reforms at Cheltenham who commented on the selection of the white edu- cational director on Thursday blamed Governor Herbert O'Con- or for the outcome. They pointed out that his fail- ure to name new members to the board when the terms of five members expired last May left in control the same group under which the institution has been so long mismanaged. Whether or not, they say, this action on the part of the Gover- nor is deliberate, the result has been to block the appointment of colored applicants to posts insur- ing efficient and sympathetic ad- ministration of the institution in the interest of the inmates instead of job-seeking whites. Promise Unfulfilled They also state that this action does not square with the Gover- nor's promise to give colored citi- zens a chance to conduct their own institutions. The members whose terms ex- pired last May were Enoch Har- lan, Howard C. Hill, Dr. J. L. Johnson, Blossie K. Miller, James E. Steuart. Miller, Steuart, Har- lan and Blandford voted for Mr. Jones on Thursday. Howard C. Hill has voted generally with the reform group. : Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Yuletide Made Happy for Boys at Cheltenham
full_text: Yuletide Made Happy for Boys at Cheltenham - CHELTENHAM, Md. The holiday season was a happy. one for the boys at the Cheltenham School because many Baltimore men and women, at the suggestion of the school's auxiliary, made contributions of money and gifts. The auxiliary of the school in- cludes Mrs. Bertha Proctor, Miss Ida Cummings, Miss Vivian Young, Mrs. Rose D. Hill, Mrs. Fannie Tibbs, Policewoman Violet Hill Whyte and Edward S. Lewis. Miss Cummings furnished fifty- two bags of candy and peanuts for the boys and collected $51 which was turned over to the school for the purchase of gifts for those boys who have no fam- ilies. Sorority Gives Money Miss Young, representing the Pi Lambda Psi honorary society of Morgan State College, made a donation of $35 with which games and toys for smaller boys were purchased. Policewoman Whyte secured a contribution of nine dozen fleece- lined gloves from Captain Joseph Wallace and Lieutenant Edward Coughlin of the Northwestern police district, and other mem- bers of the committee made per- sonal donations with which toys. games, clothing and gifts were purchased. On Christmas Day, each of the boys were treated to a turkey dinner given by the school and also received fruits and candy. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Morgan Will Be Host to Bucknell Students
full_text: Hampton Grad New Teacher BALTIMORE An appointment and a resig- nation at the Cheltenham School for Boys were announced during a meeting of the school's Board of Managers on Thursday. Jacob Thomas Stewart, 25, Hampton Institute graduate, has been named instructor in tailor- ing. He began his duties this week. His appointment marks the first time within recent years that a colored person has been named to teach tailoring. The job carries with it a sal- ary of $900 a year. Mr. Stewart is a native of DeWitt, Va., but has been residing in Riverhead, N.Y., most of his life. He grad- uated from Hampton in May, 1940. White Supervisor Quits The resignation was that of O. C. title: Gov. Allows 3 Million for Institutions
full_text: Gov. Allows 3 Million for Institutions BALTIMORE Seven State institutions for colored people and nine State- aided institutions will receive in excess of $3,000,000 during the next two years as a result of the State Legislature's recent ap- proval of Governor Herbert R. O'Conor's budget recommenda- tions, an AFRO survey shows this week. In addition, $350,000 of this amount will go toward equaliza- tion of teachers' salaries in the Maryland counties and $50,000 will provide scholarships for Maryland students who desire to study at institutions of higher learning outside the State. A comparison of the O'Conor appropriations with those during the years 1938-39, when the late Harry W. Nice was Governor, shows that Governor O'Conor has allotted twice as much to our in- stitutions as did his predecessor. Mr. Nice appropriated only $1,392,204 as compared with the present governor's three million. $1,372,434 to Four Schools Largest increases over the Nice administration provided by Gov- ernor O'Conor are for the Chel- tenham School for Boys (which during the Nice administration was in process of becoming a State institution), which during Mr. Nice's term received only $90,000 for that two-year period as compared with the $558,378 provided by Mr. O'Conor for the next two years. Morgan State College (which was not State institution during the Nice regime) will receive a total of $519,800 during the next two years as compared with the $120,000 it received during the previous administration. Princess Anne College, which was denied appropriations for new buildings during the Nice term, which allowed only $51,966, will be able to add at least one new building with the $151,966 allowed by the present governor. The Maryland School for Girls at Glenburnie will receive twice as much ($142,290) during the next two years as it received under Mr. Nice, when it was allowed $77,280. Henryton Figure Lower The remainder of the seven State-supported institutions all get considerably more than they received under the Nice adminis- tration except the Henryton Sanatoruim, whose appropriation during the next two years is slightly less than that awarded by Mr. Nice, [Inasmuch as this institution comes under the general admin- istration of the Maryland Tuber- culosis Sanatoria there might be a slight discrepancy in this figure.] Under the Nice administration,; this institution received $228.110, and during the next two years under Mr. O'Conor it will receive $215,340. Bowie State Teachers' College, which received $100,028 under Mr. Nice, will receive $162,050 under Mr. O'Conor; Crownsville State Hospital, which received $573,820 under Mr. Nice, will get $822,800 under Mr. O'Conor. Other Allotments Maintained Of the State-aided institutions, only one will receive increased appropriations over those granted by Mr. Nice. This is the Home for Friendless Colored Boys at Catonsville, which received total of $4.000 under Nice but will get $5,400 during the next years. a 1 Five of the State-aided insti- tutions will receive the same ap- propriation for the next two years they were allowed under the Nice regime. title: Ex-Cheltenham Inmate Gets Twenty-Year Term
full_text: Ex-Cheltenham Inmate Gets Twenty-Year Term BALTIMORE A 15-year-old former Chelten- ham inmate, convicted in Crim- inal Court Thursday of robbing and criminally assaulting at gun- point two teen-age girls and at- tempting to attack another girl, was sentenced by Judge Row- land K. Adams to twenty years in the house of correction. The youth was actually given a total of fifty-two years, twenty years on each of two rape charges, ten years on the assault to rape charge and a year each ☐on the two robbery charges, but ☐ Judge Adams ruled that the sen- tences would run concurrently. Testimony revealed that the first attack occurred on January 10, when the boy accosted Miss Dorothy Beane, 16, of 2521 Wood- brook Avenue, in the 1800 block Madison Avenue and forced her to accompany him to a yard in the rear of a house in the 1900 block of the same street. The other attack is said to have occurred on January 18, when Miss Dorothy Barney, 18, of 1344 Druid Hill Avenue, was stopped by the 'accused youth at Eutaw Place and Lanvale Street and forced into a nearby yard. With her at the time was Miss Ruth Howell, 17, same address, whom he attempted to attack. Miss Beane accused the boy of taking $3.50 from her at the time of the attack on her and Miss Howell said he took her watch and about $10.60. Gregory Haw- kins represented the boy. title: White Man Wins Honor for 1st Time
full_text: White Man Wins Honor for 1st Time BALTIMORE. Vance E. Thomas, white, su. perintendent of the Cheltenham School for Boys, five women and five men were selected this week for places on the AFRO's 1941 Honor Roll, This year marks the first time a white man has been selected for this honor. Basis of the selec- tion was superlative service to the community during the year 1941. The five women selceted are Miss Janet Green, president of the East Baltimore Residential Pro- tective Association; Mrs. Nellie Moore, Girl Scout field advisor; Mrs. Enolia P. McMillan, presi- dent of the Maryland State NAACP; Mrs. Florence Snowden, president of the Northwest Resi dential Protective Association; and Mrs. Violet Hill White, po- licewoman. Templeton Chosen The men on the honor rol, in addition to Mr. Thomas, are Fur- man L. Templeton, now connect. ed with the Office of Civilian Defense, but selected for his work as industrial secretary of the Ur- ban League; Joseph H. Neal, or- ganizer for the CIO's Steel Work. ers' Organizing Committee; De- tective Patrolman J. Hiram But- ler; Avon B. Collins, housing project manager; and Leroy A. Coles, Sr., Boy Scout leace. Those named on the honor roll were chosen from a list of per- sons suggested by AFRO readers and members of the city depart- ment staff of the AFRO. Another Precedent Broken Another deviation from what has been the case in the past is the fact that the 1941 horroil includes a person, Policewoman Whyte, who has previously been on the honor roll. However, be- cause of the fact that she was the first woman in recent years to be cited for meritorious service with the police department, it was felt that she should be included. She is sharing honors with De- tective Patrolman Butler, who was similarly honored. Honorable Mention Those awarded honorable men- tion are: Mrs. Sayde George, su- perintendent of the Maryland Training School for Girls at Glenburnie, Md., Raymond A. C. Young, postal employce and NAACP worker; The Rev. C. Baker Pearle, pas- tor of Payne AME Church: Father Cedric E. Mills, rector of St. James P.E. Churchn; Miss Anita Williams, senior social worker with the Cathore Chari- ties; Reginald Gardner, pres.dent of the Maryland Association for Promotion of Business; Dr. Maceo Williams, director of the Druid Health Center, and Chales Key, Morgan professor and di..ector of the Baltimore Negro Health Week celebration.

title: 400 at Urban League Dinner Honor Lewis
full_text: 400 at Urban League Dinner Honor Lewis BALTIMORE More than 400 persons of both races joined in paying tribute to Edward S. Lewis at the Baltimore Urban League's twelfth annual dinner meeting Thursday evening at the Cadoa, 118 W. Franklin Street. Mr. Lewis was executive secre- tary of the local branch for eleven year, leaving the first of the month for a similar post in New York.  Optimism Expressed The participating speakers all struck notes of optimism in re- counting the gains for workers ob- tained by the league during 1942, which augur even more work opportunities in the future. Before reviewing his administra- tion, Mr. Lewis asked the guests to join with him in a silent tri- bute to the late Father John T. Gillard, a board member, who made it possible for the dinner to be held in the Cadoa several years ago after Johns Hopkins had refused to open its doors: Credits Staff, Board He also paid special tribute to the members of his staff and board and announced that Dr. Bruce McDonald, white, president of the board, had agreed to serve another year. Mr. Lewis cited the increase in the league's annual budget, dur- ing the past eleven years, from $4,000 to a proposed $14,000 for 1943, and said there still remain the following problems to be solved: (1) department store discrim- ination, (2) uniforms for colored police, and (3) equalization of school facilities which, he esti- mated will cost a million dollars. His insistence that a colored person's appointment to the school board would help solve the latter problem brought sus- tained applause Not Discouraged The New York secretary said, however, that he is not discour- aged by the total picture - not even by the FEPC reversals. "We gathered here tonight to represent one of the elements of a new world society not based on race, but on opportunities, democ- racy, and freedom," he said in closing. "I believe that this really is a people's war and that the gates of hell shall not prevail against the new day now dawning." Allen Sees New Hope A. J. Allen, league industrial secretary, in his annual report, de- clared that the most significant factor in the opening of new em- ployment opportunities for col- ored workers is that their chil- dren, likewise, have a reasonable hope for future employment. He revealed that league efforts have made $750,000 in earnings available to members of the build- ing trades heretofore denied em- ployment. Hepbron Praises Lewis James M. Hepbron, white di- rector of the Criminal Justice Commission and the Community Fund, paid a personal tribute to Mr. Lewis, whom he termed his "friend, counsellor and co- worker.". He discussed the work of the Governor's Commission on Juve- nile Delinquency and indicated that its recommendations would be made quite soon. J. Harvey Kerns of Cincinnati, who succeeds Mr. Lewis as ex- ecutive secretary, was present. He will take up his duties March 1. Mr. and Mrs. Lewis received gifts from the Social Workers' Roundtable, the Book-of-the- Month Club, the Painters' Asso- ciation and the Urban League Women's Auxiliary. Several musical numbers were rendered by the Baltimore Sing- ers, directed by Gerald B. Wilson. Among those present were Congress- man Daniel Ellison; Walter Sondheim, director of U.S. Employment Service in Maryland; Kenneth Douty, War Man- power Commission assistant State direc- tor; Mr. and Mrs. Vance Thomas of Cheltenham School for Boys; G. Laird Ferguson, and Saul Purdue, Glenn L. Martin Company's Canton Di- vision; Harry Cohen, Baltimore Federa- tion of Labor: James Drury, post agent, National Maritime Union; Councilman Jacob Edelman, Bert Hanner, WFBR program manager; Sid- ney Katz, Md. CIO Industrial Council; Harold Buchman, local attorney; and Max Orlov, painters' union representa- tive. Bob McGuinn, lawyer for the carpen- ters' union, which now has more than 500 members; Dallas Nicholas, presi- dent, Monumental Bar Association; Mrs. Violet Hill Whyte, policewoman. ! title: The Week: War Training Week? Separate, Unequal Jobs at Cheltenham Collins a Pioneer
full_text: The Week War Training Week? Separate, Unequal Jobs at Cheltenham Collins a Pioneer By B. M. PHILLIPS This is War Training Week. Emphasis is on increasing enroll- ment in the city's war vocational training schools to prepare for vital jobs in war industries. The campaign is sponsored by the vocational war produc- tion training division of the city's schools, and it ought to be conducted without regard to race, color or creed. But it isn't. title: Drop Charges Against Clarke at Cheltenham: White Superintendent Lifts Suspension of Educational Director
full_text: Drop Charges Against Clarke af Cheltenham White Superintendent Lifts Suspension of Educational Director BALTIMORE Charges of insubordination against Daniel Clarke, education- al supervisor at Cheltenham School for Boys, have been with- drawn and his suspension lifted, it was announced Thursday. Col. Harry C. Jones, head of the State Employment Commis- sion which must pass on suspen- sions and dismissals at State in- stitutions, told the AFRO that his office had received notice of withdrawal of the charges by Vance E. Thomas, white, superin- tendent of the school. Howard C. Hill, white, acting president of the school's board of managers, said that Mr. Clarke returned to work Monday and that he and Mr. Thomas had reached a working agreement. Suspended on May 17 Mr. Clarke, the only colored ad- ministrative employee at the in- stitution, was suspended May 17 by Mr. Thomas for refusing to teach a class. However, those close to the Cheltenham situation saw in the suspension an attempt by the ad- ministration to punish Mr. Clarke for joining with other employees who have insisted upon an end to segregation of colored and white staff members at the school. It is also known that Mr. Clarke and other employees have insist- ed that the administration should carry out the order of the board of managers issued March 25, ending segregation in the cafe- teria and housing facilities and a subsequent order urging replace- ment of white employees with colored. Board in 7-Hour Session The board held a seven-hour meeting last Tuesday at which time some of the difficulties were ironed out, but no statement was made. It is expected that the board will hold another meet- ing this week. Eight colored employees have resigned from the school staff in the past two months on account of what they term "bungling" of the question of equal facilities for staff members by Mr. Thomas.
