title: Cheltenham Head, 5 Women on Honor Roll: New Superintendent of Boys' Institution Is First White Man on AFRO's Honor Roll; Policewoman Whyte and Detective Butler Share Mythical Honors
full_text: Cheltenham Head, 5 Women on Honor Roll New Superintendent of Boys' Institution Is First White Man on AFRO's Honor Roll; Policewoman Whyte and Detective Butler Share Mythical Honors Cheltenham Superintendent Vance E. Thomas, new superintendent of the Cheltenham School for Boys, is the first white person to gain a place on the Baltimore AFRO's honor roll for superior service. When he took over the management of the Prince Georges County school in March, it was VANCE E. THOMAS branded as one of the State's worst correctional institutions. In the nine months he has been there, Mr. Thomas has improved the spirit and morale of the school, done away with severe corporal punishment and substituted, in his own words, "the heaven principle of privileges-hope for reward-rather than the hell principle." In 1941, for the first time in many years, the Baltimore City grand jury report was able to praise the institution and point out the effective and progressive measures of discipline, training and parole. Since March, Mr. Thomas has been able to release at least 300 boys on parole, and under supervision of a parole officer many of them have been able to return to a normal life, taking an active part in the YMCA activities. When he took over, there were only two colored cottage masters; today there are fifteen cottage masters and teachers out of the staff of sixty and every step is being made to include colored persons on the staff of this institution, which is operated for colored youth. Law-Enforcement Officers Mrs. Violet Hill Whyte, policewoman, and Detective Patrolman J. Hiram Butler are sharing a berth on the honor roll this year for their outstanding police work, which won them gold bars for meritorious service and commendation from Governor Herbert R. O'Conor two weeks ago. MRS. VIOLET HILL WHYTE Mrs. Whyte was not only the lone policewoman cited in 1941. but she is also one of the few policewom- en to be so honored in the history of the Batlimore Police Department. She was appointed in 1937 by the late Governor Harry W. Nice and was the first colored person in that city department. Policewoman Whyte divides her time between routine police duties, which are many, rearing four chil- dren, the youngest of whom is in high school, and participating in the acti- vities of numerous civic and welfare organizations. In achieving his second consecu- tive commendation, Detective Butler DETECTIVE BUTLER displayed the same type of persistency that resulted in his appointment with two other officers in 1938. His superior officers have nothing but praise for his outstanding police work and thorough investigations. Butler and Levi Jolley, manager of the Philadelphia AFRO-AMERICAN newspaper, were the first two colored persons to take the examination for probationary patrolmen in 1934. Officer Butler took the examination every year after that until he was appointed. While it is true that Police Commissioner Stanton has failed to appoint any other officers in addition to the four now on the force and has also failed to put any of them in uniform, the high type of efficinecy as demonstrated by Policewoman Whyte and Detective Butler is one of the strongest arguments we have in our fight for uniformed policemen. Boy Scout Leader By winning the coveted Silver Beaver, national Boy Scout council award for noteworthy service of exceptional character to boyhood in his community, during the annual Boy Scout meeting in February, 1941, Leroy A. Coles, Sr., clinched his place on the honor roll. Despite his duties as a mail carrier, Mr. Coles has found time to take an active part in Boy Scout activities during the past twelve years. He helped form the first colored troop in the city, in1928. Troop No. 275, located at the Sharp Street Community House. He then served as its assistant scoutmaster, scoutmaster, and then was elevated to neighborhood commissioner in 1938. Two years later he left this post to serve as Monumental District commissioner, his duties included the supervision of all the troops in Baltimore. His area at the end of the year had a total of 879 boys enrolled in forty-five troops, an increase of nine troops and 157 boys over 1940. On December 31, because of pressing duties and the need for building up his original troop, Mr. Coles resigned this post, but his work during the year, coupled with his winning the coveted scout award, recommended him for a place on the honor roll. Steel Workers' Organizer LEROY A. COLES, Sr. As an organizer for the CIO's Steel Workers' Organizing Committee. Joseph H. Neal was largely responsible for the unionizing of the Bethlehem Steel Company plant at Sparrows Point, and subsequent pay increases which placed about $1,040,000 additional in the pockets JOSEPH H. NEAL of approximately 6,000 colored workers there. Mr. Neal joined forces with the union as one of its first local organizers the early part of 1941, when the SWOC began its intensified drive on the steel plant and imported John Thornton from Pittsburgh and ten white organizers to work under Nicholas Fontecchio of Chicago. The pay increase came in April, when the company, under pressure from the union, granted basic wage increases of from 62½ cents to 72½ cents an hour. Mr. Neal, an employee of the company for about seven years, also enjoys the distinction of being the only colored official in the SWOC's union local No. 224, set up at the plant in July. He is vice-president. His election to this office was unanimous in appreciation and acknowledgement for his work with the union in the early stages of organizing the steel plant. Mr. Neal makes his home at 613 Baker Street. Girl Scout Secretary Increased participation by colored Girl Scouts in city-wide scouting projects, and sub- stantial representation of colored scout leaders on the standing city-wide committees which run Baltimore's scouting affairs are the tangible results of Mrs. Nellie Moore's first term as colored field secretary. MRS. NELLIE MOORE Since her appointment in January, 1941, this nominee for the AFRO's 1941 roll of honor, has invested six Girl Scout troops, bringing the total number of troops to fifteen and putting Balti- more in third place, with Washington and Richmond only a few troops ahead. The new troops are located at the Mt. Washington Baptist Church, Pimlico, Md., Troop 506; Trinity AME Church, Troops 507 and 514; Public School 100, Troop 513; Union Baptist Church, Troop 501, and Metropolitan Baptist Church, Troop 516. Mrs. Moore resigned from a Baltimore parent-education teaching position to take the Girl Scout appointment, although she had worked for five years previously as a volunteer member of the colored district committee. This year, for the first time, Girl Scout leaders have been taught by a colored instructor, and Mrs. Moore's success in obtaining leader co-operation has been outstanding. Housing Project Manager Avon B. Collins wins his place on the honor roll because of his excellent work in set- ting up and maintaining high community standards as a manager of the city's low-rent housing projects. Although he had done similar work at the Langston Project in Washing- ton, his work as resident manager in Baltimore was that of a pioneer, and has won respect and admiration from his tenants and from housing officials of both races. Last week, he repre- sented the local housing authority at the regional conference of the National Association of Housing Officials, which met in Louisville, Ky. Mr. Collins has served as manager at each of the three colored projects now in operation, but is most closely associated with the Edgar Allan Poe Homes, which was the first of seven such projects erected in the city. Under his administration, there has been established at the Pue Homes, a tenants' council, numerous civic clubs, a nursery school, a Boy Scout troop, and an extensive adult and junior recreation program, which is also being developed at the other projects. State Ν.Α.Α.C.P. President AVON B. COLLINS Organized in May. 1941, the Maryland State branch of the NAACP, under the efficient leadership of its president. Mrs. Enolia P. McMillan, now includes nine member branches, and has as its aim an active NAACP unit in each county of the State in which a number of MRS. ENOLIA P. MCMILLAN colored people reside. By virtue of a generous contribution of her time and energies, Mrs. McMillan qualifies for nomination on the 1941 AFRO roll of honor. This quiet-spoken woman keeps up a personal contact with each of the Maryland branches, which include Baltimore, Balnew, Catonsville, Frederick, and the Counties of Prince Georges, Calvert, Charles, Montgomery and Kent. Mrs. McMillan was president of the Maryland Teachers' As- sociation in 1936, when that body joined with the NAACP in the court fight for equalization of teachers' salaries. She is the mother of a 13-month-old son and at present is on leave from the Baltimore school system. Her findings in a Columbia University master's thesis reported to the Teachers' Association on inequalities in teachers' pay, school equipment, length of terms, transportation, and courses of study, were used by that body as a basis of the salary equalization fight. Improvement Group Head Mrs. Florence Snowden was selected for the honor roll because of her persevering, untiring and successful work as president of the Northwest Residential Protective Asso- ciation in its efforts to improve and protect residential neighborhoods. After battling for almost a year, this community group was successful last April in getting the Board of Liquor License Com- missioners to close two taverns at Biddle Street and Druid Hill Avenue, both of which were eyesores and the cause of disorderly conduct and unfavorable influences in the community, where three schools and a church are located. Previous to that, the organization won the support of Mayor Jackson, who vetoed a proposed spot-zoning ordinance which would have changed the 1200 block of McCulloh Street from residential to a first commercial district so that a white grocer could establish his business there. In addition. Mrs. Snowden served as captain of one of the teams in the NAACP campaign and is active in various other civic endeavors. MRS. FLORENCE SNOWDEN Urban League Secretary Taking over the newly created position of industrial secretary of the Baltimore Urban League on January 2, 1941, Furman L. Templeton has led a successful fight this year for jobs for colored skilled workers in various unionized trades formerly closed to them and has broken jim crow barriers in many companies and industries. Mr. Templeton was responsible for the hiring of nine boys as messengers by the local Postal Telegraph Company. He was instrumental in getting the State Plumbing Board to accept the applications of colored plumbers for consideration toward grant- ing them licenses-something never before accomplished here, as there are no colored licensed plumbers in Baltimore and but one in the State. He has helped to break down barriers in local defense industries, was one of the leaders in the fight for jobs at the Glenn L. Martin Aircraft Plant, and has secured the promise of officials at the Bethlehem-Fairfield Shipyard that they will hire and train colored men as soon as a building is completed there within the near future. So outstanding has Mr. Templeton's work been that through- out the year he has reecived job offers from various government agencies, notably the Office of Production Management, and last Monday he resigned his post to be regional racial relations staff advisor with the Office of Civilian Defense at a salary of $4,600. Eastside Civic Worker FURMAN TEMPLETON Miss Janet Green is heralded as East Baltimore's most militant community and civic worker, diligently taking part in all community betterment campaigns, despite the fact that she has to travel fifty-two miles a day to teach school in Hereford, Md. Miss Green is MISS JANET GREEN president of the East Baltimore Residential Protective Associa- tion, which will soon observe its first anniversary. This group appeared before the Legislature last spring and succeeded in having a bill passed for the appointment of an extra policewoman. in East Baltimore. It has also been instrumental in ridding the neighborhood of annoying taverns. As chairman of the NAACP campaign in October, Miss Green induced East Baltimoreans to triple their efforts of co-operation, with the result that to date 6,000 memberships and more than $6,000 has been reported in the campaign. In addition to these activities, she finds time to be active at the First Baptist Church, serving as assistant church clerk and working with the young people's choir. She is a native Balti- morean, the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. John C. Green, and grand- daughter of the late Bishop Alexander Wayman of the AME Church. title: YOUR NEIGHBOR: BRIEF SKETCHES OF FELLOW BALTIMOREANS YOU SHOULD KNOW
full_text: YOUR NEIGHBOR Brief Sketches of Fellow Baltimoreans You Should Know [EDITOR'S NOTE: This is the elev- enth in a series of thumbnail sketches of Baltimoreans of both races, designed to acquaint AFRO readers with each other.] By E. A. HARLESTON BALTIMORE | Joseph C. Briscoe, principal of Carver Vocational School, has a full-time job trying to gear his  JOSEPH C. BRISCOE school's curriculum to meet the war-time interests and needs of his pupils. Fully 55 per cent of his student body is engaged in part-time work after school hours. Working Hours Vary In most cases it's an individual matter. Some go to their jobs immediately after school and work until 1 and 2 a.m. Still oth- ers start work at 2 a.m. and quit at 7 in the morning. Health and recreational prob- lems must be considered, Mr. Bris- coe pointed out, and the task of revamping the school schedule to benefit all concerned is a tremen- dous one. "We have litle time for extra- curricula activities now," the prin- cipal asserted. "Most of our boys and girls feel a serious obligation to their work which precludes ev- en such activities as a victory corps." Mr. Briscoe, with a refined de meanor, fights for what he believes is right. On Cheltenham Board A member of the board of the Cheltenham School for Boys eight years, he has been diligent in ex (ercising his powers, and has main tained that segregation at the school be abolished, unequivo cably. When affairs at Provident Hos pital, of which he has been a board member for many years, were not being managed to meet his standards, he refused to go along "for the sake of peace" and sent in his resignation. In adidtion the Vocational prin cipal is an active board member of the Druid Hill YMCA, is on the Boy Scout district committee, and still finds time to continue ſteaching Sunday school at St. Katherine PE Church after thirty years' service. Mr. Briscoe is married to the former Mrs. Virginia Hall. a di rector in the Department of Pub- lic Welfare. They live at 1301 Madison Avenue. More Fowl, Seafood The war hasn't seriously affect- ed his personal life to any extent although Mr. Briscoe admits that he is eating more fowl and sea. food than formerly. He'll still be able to see his favorite teams play baseball, a sport about which he is quite enthusiastic. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: The Week: Official Spring Without a Vest ""Nice"" Medals End of Jim Crow Cars
full_text: The Week Official Spring Without a Vest "Nice" Medals End of Jim Crow Cars By CARL MURPHY Forsythia and crocuses are in bloom, barberry and bush honey- suckles have put out baby leaves, green has come back into lawns, and last week I heard the first mocking bird. It's official-spring is here. Ollie Stewart has promised to send me the words of the new N. African soldiers' song called "Dirty Gertie of Bizerte." That is, the words that may be printed. Without a Vest Vincent Tubbs, second member of the AFRO's editorial depart- ment to leave the U.S. to go abroad as a war correspondent, couldn't get released from his Norfolk draft board until P. B. Young, Sr. (Journal and Guide), put in a good word for him. Up to the time I saw Vincent in uniform with his coat open, I didn't realize that U.S. Army officers wear no vests. But they have on long underwear. The church has no rules for keeping Lent, says Archdeacon Bravrid Harris of Norfolk. All forms of self-denial-giving up amusements, smoking, or even fasting are not in themselves right or wrong. But you commit a sin if you set up for yourself any form of self-denial and then fail to carry it out. - Maryland's reform school for boys at Cheltenham is having a tempest in a teapot because some colored and white staff members want to sleep and eat together. Some twenty white members of the staff are con- scientious objectors to whom race hate is as bad as war. Seems funny that anything like this could happen in a colored State school. But it isn't funny to those who believe in white supremacy. Charming Jimmy Readers from all over the U.S. wrote to smiling Sgt. Jimmy Stewart in Hawaii after his pic appeared in the AFRO the week of January 19. Says Jimmie, whose sinile is indeed charming: "My morale is above 100 per cent. For my social aspirations, the fu- ture looks quite bright." If you rent out a room in your home and haven't registered with the OPA rent bureau, you may still do so without being penal- ized. "Nice" Medals Citations to seven members of 41st Singing Engineers for their fine work in building airfields, roads and bridges in Liberia are printed in detail in this week's AFRO. According to President Bar- clay, two of the Americans were honored because they were "nice to Liberians." This may not be the first time soldiers were decorated for being "nice," (Continued on Page 2, Col. 3) The Week (Continued from Page 1) 7 but it is certainly the first time we have seen anybody quite so frank about it as the Liberian President. Bill Jones, 41st band leader and the man most responsible for the kind of music that makes everybody want to sing, impressed the Africans too. Naive Mr. Barclay pinned a medal on Bill for "recreational services rendered." Until the going got tough in the Civil War, Union soldiers of the 100th Indiana Volunteers declared, "This is a white man's war." How does it feel to win $1,000? Mrs. Ethel H. Grubbs of Wash- ington, that much richer by rea- son of the AFRO's post office game, said three days afterwards that she still was as in a dream up in the clouds. Quiet as It's Kept The 76th Coast Artillery, which was organized at Fort Bragg, N.C., fought with the Marines at Guad- alcanal and was withdrawn when the army later took over. With these men were George Cox of Durham and Leroy Haynes of Chicago, both Morehouse College athletes. Colored troops in the South Pacific are now located in the New Hebrides, New Caledonia, the Solomons, and New Guinea. Copies of Monsignor Ryan's ad- dress at Howard U. distributed to the press contained the epithet nr. President Mordecai Johnson says the Catholic U. professor did not read that part of his speech. ■Congressman Will Rogers, Jr., of the 16th District, California, and son of the great humorist, writes me: "One reason for my coming to Congress was my great concern over race prejudice. When there is an opportunity on the House floor to fight against race discrimination I will cer- tainly be there doing it." End of J.C. Cars Seen Speaker Conlon of the Mary- land Legislature is fumbling with the jim-crow repeal bill. That happens every session. A How- ard U. law school professor named Hart personally had the courts abolish jim crow on inter-State traffic arteries, but not on trans- port facilities within the State. He fought his case through the lower court to the court of ap- peals and won. If we had more lawyers like the late Professor Hart, jim crow on all inter-State railroads would soon end. As the war lasts two years more (and I predict it will), jim crow on trains will be dealt its heaviest blow by car riders themselves. car. Smoking by law is restricted to smoking cars on trains, but so many people disobey the law that virtually every car is a smoking The trains will continue to be crowded with soldiers. Civilians will be glad to ride anywhere, and conductors won't be able to keep whites out of the jim-crow cars when there are seats there. We have already arrived at that point. E. A. Gannon, passenger agent for the Baltimore and An- napolis Electric R.R. (B. & Ο. owned), told the Legislature last week that war-time travel makes enforcement of the separate car law in Maryland impossible. He asked that it be abolished. Sergeant William S. Medley of the 377th Engineers, was taken from a bus between Clover and Camp Pickett, Va., because he sat with a white sailor. The sailor didn't object; the conductor did. When white soldiers and sailors join colored comrades in insisting on throwing jim crow out of the window, bus conductors will not be such smart elecks. Pop Summers Dr. H. H. (Pop) Summers, Wil- berforce U. professor of Greek and theology, who was buried last week in Harrisburg, Pa., was a remarkable man. Thirty-six years ago we attended Howard Uni- versity together. Most of us were 18 then; Pop was 43. He had been a teacher and principal of a pub- lic school in Steelton, Pa., for seventeen years, and with the late Dr. Numa P. G. Adams, decided he wanted a college education. Being twice as old as the rest of us didn't bother Pop, neither did he mind the nickname we gave him. He was hungry for knowledge and went on to finish college, theological school, and to earn two master's degrees final- ly at the age of 65. He thus spent some twenty- two years in college-teaching in the winter and studying in the summer. At the age when most men are retiring from ac- tive life, Pop Summers was just getting ready to do his best work as a teacher at Wil- berforce University. They don't come any more dur- able and gentlemanly than Pop. He was a credit to his profession.

title: Jim Crow Foe Gets 4 Years
full_text: 17 Teach Plane Care at N.C. Field GOLDSBORO, N. C. (ANP) - Seventeen colored civilian avia- tion instructors and now on duty at Seymour Johnson Field here, teaching engine repairing, pro- pelller care and other phases of airplane maintenance. Their classes, usually contain- ing from five to ten persons, in- clue both soldiers and civilians. All supervisors are white but the instructors say their treatment has been excellent. All received their original train- ing at Chanute Field, Ill., Jim Crow Foe Gets 4 Years | BALTIMORE. -- Charles Butcher, 26, white, ousted em- ployee of the Cheltenham School for Boys, on Monday received a four-year sentence in the Federal Court for refusing to obey an or- der to report to a conscientious objectors' camp. A Harvard graduate, Butcher began working at Cheltenham in November. He was released from the institution in January on three charges, one of them being his insistence on eating in a din- ing hall reserved for colored em- ployees. Butcher stated that he had been offered several jobs since his dis- missal from Cheltenham, but de- clined them because he wanted to do what he could in straighten- ing out the racial situation at the institution. He said that the case is a "test" for clarification of Selective Serv- ice regulations concerning con- scientious objectors and would be carried to the United States Su- preme Court, if necessary. Judge Coleman refused to grant Butcher bail, pending a ruling on his appeal. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

West Street, has been set for August 16. Mr. Walker died on July 19 as the result of burns received from a gasoline explosion in Lemon's! cellar the night before. title: Girls Riot at School in Md.: President of Board, Police Restore Quiet 18 GIRLS INVOLVED Ringleader Returned to Home of Parents
full_text: Girls Riot at School in Md. President of Board, Police Restore Quiet 18 GIRLS INVOLVED Ringleader Returned to Home of Parents BALTIMORE-A riot at the Maryland Training School for Girls at Glenburnie on Saturday was quelled only when police and the board president put in an ap- pearance. Before their arrival, however, the girls had broken window panes and furniture, doing damage amounting to over $200. Cause for the rampage, it is re- ported, was an order that they "turn in"-go to bed at 8 p.m. Too Early to Go to Bed The girls said that 8 p.m. was too early and, since it was still light, they would not obey. When attempts were made to get them to retire, some of them fled the school grounds. Others went to the room of Miss Mae Rideout, the matron who had given the order, and pro- ceeded to damage her clothing, the furniture, and break out win- dow panes. About eighteen girls were in- volved in the disturbance, which was finally brought under control when nearby Ferndale police and H. H. Murphy, president of the board of managers, were sum- moned. Mr. Murphy reported that the ringleader, a 17-year-old, who is too old for the type of training at the school, has been returned to her parents. School Problems Cited He indicated that the school is faced with the same problem which obtains at Cheltenham School for Boys: namely, that the Institution is given all types of girls to care for when in reality it can only accommodate those who are amenable to training. He pointed out that the rioting was led by girls with mental de- ficiences and incorrigibles for which it has no provision, adding that members of his board are meeting with the State Depart- ment of Public Welfare with a view towards discovering some method of segregating them. Extra Work" for Rioters Restrictions and extra work have been ordered for all the par- ticipants in Saturday's disturbance, Mr. Murphy declared. Mrs. Sadye P. George, superin- tendent of the institution, said that the attack on Miss Rideout's property occurred the following morning while she (Mrs. George) was bringing the leader of the disturbance into town, and was apparently an attempt to "get even" with Miss Rideout for fore- ing the girl to leave the school. Mrs. George reported that most of the damage was done in the music room, but that the trouble had subsided by Monday. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Citizens Tell How They're Paying Their 1942 Taxes
full_text: Citizens Tell How They're Paying Their 1942 Taxes By RUTH JENKINS BALTIMORE Despite the fact that the largest crowds in many years paid income taxes daily at the Custom House, inquiries last week revealed that hundreds of taxpayers were likely to be caught in the last-minute rush on the March 15 deadline. The Custom House at Gay and Lombard Streets has been kept open until 9 p.m. to meet the de- mands of the thousands paying their taxes in person. But in order to accommodate the deadline crowd, it remained open until midnight on Saturday and Monday. Taxes were also paid by check or by money order, through the mails. With the government still con- sidering phases of the pay-as-you- go and collection-at-the-souce systems of taxation, the major- ity of wage-earners have adopted the quarterly installment plan for the payments now due. Must Meet Deadline Custom House officials warned this week that where the quar- ly payment plan is used, the first installment or one-fourth of the tax due must be paid in full by March 15. Otherwise, a notice will be sent the taxpayer, demanding full pay- ment of the total tax within ten days, plus a 6 per cent interest charge. Taxpayers questioned last week in regard to their taxes made the following replies: MRS. VIRGIE WATERS, presi- dent, Master Beauticians' As- sociation, 527 umberland Street: "My hus- band and I filed our returns to- gether and have already paid the first install- ment." To Pay Quarterly ROBERT SAMPLE, foreman at the Maryland Drydock, Fairfield, Md., 1209 Wilmer Court: "I just got my return worked out on Wednesday. I'm paying my taxes in installments." FURMAN TEMPLETON, OCD racial relations adviser: "I'm going to use the installment plan, But I wish the government would adopt that pay-as-you- go system be- cause people usually get caught short when the install- ments are due anyway." JOHN W. SMITH, carpenter at Port Deposit, Md., 1318 Мс- Culloh Street: "Since I suf- fered dent which kept: me out ill for five months last. year, my tax is going to be very small. I'm still an acci- waiting for my salary statement from my employer. If I collect compensation from the State In- dustrial Accident Commission in a lump sum, I'll be able to pay the tax in full." "Foolish" to Pay All MRS. VIRGINIA H. BRISCOE, director of the Samuel Cole- ridge-Taylor re- ception center: "With the state of affairs now existing in Con gress in regard to taxation, it would seem foolish to pay 1942 taxes oth- erwise than in quarterly installments." J. EDGAR STANLEY, cottage master at Cheltenham School for Boys: "My income was relatively small last year since my main- tenance was included at the school and since I have a young daughter as a dependant." WILLIAM I. GOSNELL, attor ney, 1151 Myrtle Avenue: "I will most likely get caught in the deadline rush. And as broke as I am, my pay- ments will cer- tainly be made in install- ments." title: For Christian Fellowship
full_text: For Christian Fellowship By KATHERINE OCCUPANCY in the early summer of its recently purchased headquarters at 14 West Madison street will establish another milepost in the work of the Maryland-Dela- ware Council of Churches and Christian Education. This organization, made up of sixteen Prot- estant denominations, is the official Protestant agency for interdenominational work in the two states. Through it Episcopalians and Bap- tists, Lutherans and Presbyterians, Meth- odists and members of various other com- munions disregard their differences and work together on what the Rev. Willis R. Ford, executive secretary of the council, calls "the level of total agreement" in projects of mutual concern. The activities of the council radiate into more than 39 different areas of religious and social work. Its objective is the establishment of Christian fellowship throughout the world. Roots Go Back To 1842 Although the council was organized just ten years ago with the merger, in the Spring of 1937, of the Maryland-Delaware Council of Religious Education, the Baltimore Council of Religious Education and the Baltimore Fed- eration of Churches, its roots go down through more than a century to the forma- tion, in 1842, of the Baltimore Sunday-School Union for co-operative, interdenominational Sunday-school work in Baltimore. In a short time its work reached out into the counties, resulting in the incorporation, 1846, of the Maryland Sunday-School Unton as an aux- iliary of the American Sunday-School Union. Accomplishments of this organization were modest but consistent until the Civil War, when churches as well as lay institutions and families were split by differences. In 1863 the outlook seemed so bleak that the union was about to disband. It was resuscitated by the election as its president of Goldsborough S. Grifmth, who had a wide reputation as Sunday. school worker and organizer. During his 41 years in office, ferminated by his death in 1904, Mr, Griffith not only succeeded in "saving the union" but, with the coworkers he recruited among clergy and laiety, was influential in the organization o six social agencies in the State. These were the Henry Watson Children's Aid Society, the Maryland Prisoners Aid Society, Cheltenham School for Colored Boys and Melvale-now Glen Burnie-School for Colored Girls; the Society for the Protection of Children fron Cruelty and Immorality, and the Children's Fresh Air Society. Helped Prostrate Virginia In 1864, while the Civil War was still rag. Ing, 170 Sunday-schools were organized in the Valley of Virginia, extending as far as Win. chester, Charles Town and Martinsburg. Nu merous churches which had been closed and used as hospitals during the war were as sisted financially, after Appomattox, to re open. Missionaries, or field workers employed by the union, drove horses and buggies over roads on which 20 miles was a day's journey traveled by train and on foot to organize : total of nearly 1,000 Sunday-schools in Balti more and Maryland, besides a total of 452 ir Virginia before 1891. In the early years of the present century one of the outstanding accomplishment among the churches in Baltimore was the growth and development of a local church SCARBOROUGH program of religious education whiep received nation-wide and international recognition. The program originated with Preston Fiddis. then superintendent of the Harlem Avenue Christian Church School and successor to Mr. Griffith as president of the Maryland Sunday- School Union. Through its department of Christian minis- try to service men during World War II. the council gave free week-end lodging in eight- een church dormitories to 163,560 men anl women; served 150,000 free meals. In addi- tion, it sponsored five denominational church clubs in the city for service men and women. Women Furnished Company Houses Sixty-five company houses in five camps were furnished by church women. Presents and cards were distributed by the thousands at the Christmases of 1944 and 1945; 500 planos and record-players, with 15,000 rec- ords, were given camps and ships. Equally challenging to the council was the concentration in and around Baltimore of the army of migrant defense workers and their families. Practically every shade of religious opinion was represented among them, and there were few or no churches in the vicinity of the mushrooming war-housing areas to serve them. To provide these people with a religious ministry, the denominations composing the council took areas in which to work-Luther- ans in one place, Methodists in another, and so on. This system succesfully is being continued among the 50,000 people or so still living in these areas, Salvaging Delinquent Children Working co-operatively with the Juvenile Court and the appropriate denominational agencies, the council's department of Chris. tian social relations endeavors to provide cach Protestant child who appears in court, charged with delinquency, with a religious and social ministry. Boys and girls are given opportunity to participate in such group ac tivities as scouting, dramatics and youth choirs. Two trained case workers are em- ployed by the council to assist the clergy in counseling these children, who are helped to overcome their fears and their sense of in- security, and to assist in stabilizing the emo- tional pattern of the homes in order that parents may know better how to rear their children. Of the 804 Protestant children who appeared in the Juvenile Court in 1946, only 24 were there a second time. Ten weekday schools of religious educa- tion are being conducted for children in four counties of the State and efforts are being made to establish similar schools at Hagers- town and Cumberland. Other educational work on the council's agenda includes vaca- tion Bible schools, audio-visual education, re- ligious broadcasts and training for religious leaders. Looking toward the future, the Council of Churches and Religious Education is work- ing out an "agreement of comity" for the de nominations and churches in the Maryland Delaware area. Under it, efforts will be made to locate new churches in accordance with population trends, providing each commu nity with adequate facilities for worship and avoiding the crection of three or fous churches of different denominations within a block or so of each other.

title: The Cheltenham Plan Is Still A Valid One
full_text: The Cheltenham Plan Is Still A Valid One in the miast of so muen new planning for the expansion of Maryland's institutional care, one old plan should not be overlooked. The old (1943) plan concerns the building of a new Cheltenham School for Boys at a site closer to Baltimore and the use of the exist. ing institution for mental cases, For years it has been known that the present Cheltenham school is in the wrong location to attract a competent staff and to provide the sort of training calculated to re- store young delinquents as useful members of society. The situation came to a head in 1943, following a particularly critical report by the Maryland Commission on Juvenile De- linquency, and resulted in a definite postwar construction program to (1) build a com pletely new institution for normal delin quent Negro boys closer to Baltimore, and (2) utilize the present Cheltenham for the custody and training of defective Negro hoys. The double-purpose Cheltenham plan was a settled State policy, approved by the Legis. lature. But when Governor Lane came into office the plan was quietly dropped and the lunds earmarked for the new school were used for general budget purposes. Since then there has been the usual run of reports on shocking conditions at Cheltenham, in- cluding one by the Governor himself, but nothing has been done to implement the established plan for the institution. Probably the Cheltenham plan now needs, revision to fit the use of the existing institu- tion into the larger plans to reorganize the mental institutions. But the great virtue of the original Cheltenham plan still remains: Maryland could get two badly needed in stitutions for the price of one new one. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: An Anne Arundel Assessment That Is Worse Than Inequitable
full_text: An Anne Arundel Assessment That Is Worse Than Inequitable The fantastic property assessments in Anne Arundel county have now been brought officially to the attention of the Board of Public Works, the State govern- ment's top-ranking administrative agency. The board was offered a 74-acre tract in the Curtis Bay section for $93,000. The board considered the offer at its meeting Wednes- day. Board members were told that the prop- erty was assessed at $6.865, or about seven per cent of the proposed sales price. That is the worst assessment case to be reported out of Anne Arundel county. Prop- erties are assessed for the purpose of im- posing taxes to support the State and local governments. They are supposed by law to be assessed at market value without looking to forced sales. Properties in Anne Arundel county have been grossly underassessed. That is another way of saying that property owners in Anne Arundel county have been escaping their proper share in financing the cost of the State government. And recent assessment cases have shown that there are great inequities among assess- ments within Anne Arundel county. That is another way of saying that the cost of financing the county government has been falling unfairly on the shoulders of the prop- erty owners-some have been paying far less than they should have paid. In regard to the unbelievably inequitable assessment case brought to the attention of the members of the Board of Public Works, it is worth noting that the board members took no action, formal or otherwise, about the assessment. It is true that they rejected the property offer; but they did so because they did not think the property would be a proper site for a new Cheltenham School for Boys. The failure to take action here can be excused only on one ground. Efforts are being made to give Anne Arundel county a sound assessment roll. Those efforts are pro- ducing results. Apparently the members of the board believe that conditions in Anne Arundel county will be corrected in full. If that be true, it is good news. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: REV. NATHAN THOMPSON DEAD Widely Known Congregational Minister And Educator. Laurel, Md.. July 3.-The Rev. Na- than Thompson, 79 years old, died yes- terday at the Lindens, his home here, after a 9-day illness of cerebral hem- orrhage. Пе was Π native of New Braintree, Mass.. and graduated from Williston Seminary in 1851. Amherst College in 1861, and Andover Theologi- cal Seminary in 1865. For 10 years he was pastor of the First Congregational Church, in Boul- der, Colo.. during which time he was a member of the board of trustees of Colorado State University and was last president of the board under territorial government. Later he was minister in Boxboro, Mass., and principal of Lawrence Academy, Groton, Mass., and Elgin Academy. Elgin, Ill. He was also superintendent of the House of Re- formation, Cheltenham, Md. He was a member of the Classical Club of Baltimore and the Phi Beta Kappa Association of the District of Columbia. For the last 15 years be has made him home in Laurel, Md. He leaves a widow and two daughters. The funeral will be held tomorrow morn- ing. The body will be cremated at Loudon Park and the ashes buried in New Braintree. Mass. title: ANDERSON THE STAR: MAKES THE BEST LEAP IN TEST HELD AT DUNHAM LATIN SCHOOL CITY WILL HOLD MEET TODAY CENTRAL Y. M. C. A. GYM WILL BE USED BY THE ATHLETES----PREPARING FOR THE TRACK SEASON
full_text: ANDERSON THE STAR Makes The Best Leap In Test Held At Dunham Latin School. CITY WILL HOLD MEET TODAY Central Y. M. C. A. Gym Will Be Used By The Athletes-Preparing For The Track Season. By JESSE A. LINTHICUM. Jack Anderson, a member of the sixth period, was the star in the weekly test held yesterday afternoon by the Dunham Latin Schoolin the gymnasium, on Brevard street. Professor Buerlein sent his athletes through the standing higa jump event and Anderson made the longest leap, which was 4 feet 10 inches. Anderson's showing puts him in a position to win the trophy offered to the athlete scoring the greatest number of points. He had nine previous to yes- terday and was awarded five more. Somerset Fitchett still holds the lead, although he broke his fine winning streak yesterday. Previous to the stand- ing high jump test, Fitchett had gained five points in every event. Yesterday he finished third and was awarded three points. In six meets held so far he has scored 28 points out of a pos- sible 30. Some fine marks were made in res- terday's test. The boys are doing bet- ter each week, and Professor Buerlein declares more school records are liable to go when they are called together Jan- uary 15 for the second monthly meet. R. Diggs captured first place in the third period, L. Gwyn led the athletes in the fourth, F. Primrose in the fifth, P. Dallom in the eighth and R. Scar- lett in the ninth. The summary: Third Period-R. Diggs. 5 points; Wil- liam Thomsen, 4; G. Hodel, 3: E. Din- ning. 2, and S. Shriver. 1. Fourth Period-L. Gwyn, 5 points; J. Paca, 4; S. Fitchett, 3; J. Kirwan, 2, and E. King, 1. Fifth Period-F. Primrose, 5 points; R. Anderson, 4; W. Shackleford, 3; R. Ohrenshall, 2, and L. Hodel, 1. Sixth Period-J. Anderson, 5 points; P. Beal, 4; E. Mowbray, 3: A. Owens, 2, and S. Gibson, 1. Eighth Period-P. Dallom, 5 points: T. Cockey, 4; F. Ohrenshall, 3; W. Per- kins, 2, and P. Williams, 1. Ninth Period-R. Scarlett, 5 points: E. Bennett, 4; G. Hamill, 3; A. Hund- ley, 2, and A. Wehr, 1. City College will stage its first weekly meet this afternoon in the Central Young Men's Christian Association gym- nasium. It has been decided to have some of the events held every Thursday in Cen- tral's gym and the remaining ones in the schoolyard on North Howard street. Professor Lorett has announced the fol- lowing events for today: 25-yard dash, 1,000-yard run and 880-vard walk. To- morrow the lung test and pole climb for freshmen will be held. The committee in charge of the week- ly meets consists of Manager Lumpkin, Captain Taylor and Donald Cronin. City is looking for one of the most successful seasons experienced at the North Howard street institution for sev- eral years. The squad numbers 30 men. Donald Cronin, of last year's stars, has joined the squad. Cronin did not report at the beginning of the season. He won first place last season and was award- ed a fine trophy. Although the Christmas holidays in- terfered with the training, Professor Lo- rett has the team in pretty good trim. They were sent through a stiff practice Tuesday, and some fast time is expect- ed in the events carded for today. The squad is made up of boys between the ages of 13 and 19 years and of all weights. from the 90-pounders to those around the 165-pound mark. Manager Lumpkin announced yester- day that he has completed arrangements with the Central Young Men's Christian Association officials for a dual track and field meet in Central's gymnasium Feb- ruary 5. This will get the Orange and Black in shape for the important meets scheduled to be held next month. City expects to enter all of the big events. The relay team will meet Poly- technic at the Fifth Regiment-Johns Hopkins games at the armory February 20 and City has decided to send its share to the George Washington games in Washington February 13. Much inter- est is being taken in the big interscho- lastic track meet planned by the Tome School officials at Port Deposit. The collegians will have their full strength in that event. Points will be awarded in the weekly track meets. Ten prizes will be given at the end of the season, the highest man getting a gold medal, the second a silver and each of the next eight a bronze. An athlete who will bear watch- ing is Long, the Philadelphia boy, who starred at Cheltenham High School. Among last season's men who are looked upon as likely contenders for first place are Waples, Taylor, Lumpkin, Cronin, Cohn and Lyons. Waples is a high jumper, Lumpkin runs in the 440 and also is a distance man, Taylor and Lyons are distance runners and Cronin performs in the dashes. City College's basketball team will play the Loyola High School five to- morrow afternoon in the former's gym- nasium. City was put through a hard workout yesterday and Capt. Dick Tall is looking for a victory. These teams appear evenly matched and basketball fans anticipate a close contest. Both teams have had a long rest and the game is the first to be played by each team this season. City's quintet displayed fine form before the holidays, Park School falling easy prey by a comfortable score. One of the best games of the season is expected tomorrow afternoon at the Friends School gymnasium, when the Quakers meet the Polytechnic basket- ball team. The Quakers have a strong squad, having defeated every team played this season. While Polv has not been so fortunate, Manager Broadbelt has rounded out a well-balanced quint and declares his team will make a better showing in the remaining contests. title: MORE ROOM NEEDED FOR DELINQUENTS: STATE BOARD TO OBTAIN ADDITIONAL FACILITIES FOR FEEBLE MINDED
full_text: MORE ROOM NEEDED FOR DELINQUENTS State Board To Obtain Additional Facilities For Feeble Minded Immediate steps to obtain additional facilities for feeble- minded juvenile delinquents are to be taken by the advisory committee of the State Board of Mental Hygiene, it was announced yester- day by Dr. George H. title: COUNCIL HEARS OF CHILD NEEDS: WAXTER: ASKS EARLY BUILDING AT SOCIAL AGENCIES MEETING
full_text: COUNCIL HEARS OF CHILD NEEDS Waxter Asks Early Building At Social Agencies Meeting Maryland should put into effect "as soon as possible" an act of the 1943 General Assembly directing the construction of new institutions for defective children, and the es- tablishment of a new training school for delinquent Negro boys now sent to Cheltenham, Thomas J. S. Waxter, head of the Municipal Department of Welfare, told the Council of Social Agencies yester- day. The recommendation followed a similar demand made Tuesday by the advisory committee of the State Board of Mental Hygiene, which is studying the problem of adequate care for feeble-minded and delin- quent children. Council Of Social Agencies Mr. Waxter, addressing. the eighth annual meeting of the Coun- cil of Social Agencies at the Lords Baltimore Hotel, added that Chel-- tenham should be given a com- pletely Negro staff and should be "programed to. rehabilitate chil- dren and not simply to provide custody for certain children who represent a problem to the public peace." The director went on to state that there are practically no insti- tutional facilities for the dependent Negro child, although there are numerous such establishments for the white child. Additional Facilities Needed "The Community Fund might well consider expanding the facili- ties at the small Negro institution known as the Bragg House," he de- clared, "Consideration should also be given to the need for convales- cent care of Negro children to parallel the care now given white children in Happy Hills. Additional facilities are urgently needed also for feeble-minded children." The speaker suggested that the next Legislature "might well con- sider the establishment of a 'Youth Authority' to provide for young people between the ages of 16 and 10." Mr. Waxter linked the problem of juvenile delinquency with that of housing, declaring, "many chil- dren, both white and Negro, in Baltimore, live under conditions which almost inevitably will affect adversely the growth of a whole- some adult personality. Protection Of Values "It has been pointed out time and again that the city must erad- icate its slum areas so as to pro- tect property values. Human values demand the same action. The effort must be made to insure decent housing to all citizens so that chil- dren may be raised to be normal, happy, industrious adults." Maintaining the national income at a high level will be the "most vexing problem of the post-war period," Mr. Waxter said. "This means work for the able-bodied at compensatory wages. The burden of this will fall predominantly upon private enterprise.... Be- hind private enterprise, the nation may, again, have to assume the re- sponsibility of a works program. Hopes For No More WPA "It is to be hoped that if such a necessity arises such devices as the WPA, with the so-called 'sub- sistence wage' will not be resorted to, and that employment will be given on work which is socially de- sirable and at accepted rates of pay. "Following financial security in importance may be an adjustment of the difficulties which are so dy- namic at the present time between the dominant white majority of the people who live in the city and the 20 per cent. minority who are Negroes. The solution of this prob- lem rests in the future. It will, how- ever, require the best that the lead- ers in both groups have in the way of understanding and tolerance. "There is no royal road to its solution, nor any master plan. It will have to be worked out by an innumerable series of adjustments spread over a long period of years. This problem should be faced frankly with the facts placed before us on the table without in any way minimizing its inherent diffi- culties." Reports For 1943 Read Reports of the work of 1943 were read to the Council by Miss Esther Stamats, of the Education and Recreation Division; the Rev. F. R. Isaac, of the Family and Child Care Division, and Miss Anna D. Ward, speaking for the council as a whole.. L.. Edwin Goldman was reelected president, along with the entire of- ficial staff. These include Roszel C. Thomsen, first vice-president; Rob- ert O. Bonnell, second vice-presi- dent; Dr. Merrell L. Stout, third vice-president, and George B. Sim- mons, treasurer. Mrs. Henry E. Cor- ner, Jr., Lester Levy, and J. Cook- man Boyd, Jr., were added to the board of directors.

The Mansfield champion base ball club of the State of Connecticut was defeated at the Newington grounds yesterday by the Lord Baltimore nine by a score of 13 to 6. The attendance was not near so large as on some of the other championship games previously, though it is estimated that about 1,500 persons were present.

full_text: THAT AX IS STILL ALOOF Department Heads Rest Easily; Not So Subordinates. WORRIED FACES AT CITY HALL "Hold-Overs" Fear Changes will Come Soon-Probation Period Of Six Months Over. Now Sure Of Their Place. City Engineer H. Kent McCay. City Solicitor S. S. Field. Health Commissioner James Bosley. Building Inspector Clarence E. Stubbs. City Librarian William F. Coyle. City Collector Jacob W. Hook. Superintendent of P'ublic Buildings George T. Ames. Lighting Superintendent Robert J. MeCuen. Collector of Water Rents and Li- censes Daniel J. Loden. Water Engineer Ezra B. Whitman. Harbor Engineer Oscar F. Lackey. Commissioner of Street Cleaning Williato A. Larkins. President Richard H. Johns, Col. Israel Rosenfeld and Sydney T. Manning, of the Fire Board. The members of the Water Board, Harbor Board and Jail Board. The Commissioners of Finance. Public Bath Commission. All other unpaid commissions. No nominations were sent to the Second Branch of the City Council by Mayor Pres- ton yesterday afternoon, and department heads who have been on probation for six months rested easy, so far as their post- tlons were concerned, for the first time since October 21 last, when they received their commissions. Several had heard rumors of changes, and as the six months' probationship of the charter expires today fear was felt that the Mayor would send in the names of their Buccessors yesterday. All department heads and commissioners appointed last fall are now secure in their positions, as the Council has adjourned until Monday afternoon, April 15. They cannot be removed, except for cause and after public trial before the Mayor. Not So For Subordinates. Bat the comfortable feeling does not ex- tend to subordinates who have been "hold- Ing over" since the beginning of the Pres- ton administration. These men expect the ax, and if Democratic Councilmen are to get what has been promised them the ax will fall before May 1. It was stated yes- terday that changes would be made about the middle of April, now that the Legisla- ture has adjourned. j ] 1 1 1 : 1 Land Commissioner John J. Hanson and State's Attorney William F. Broening were among Mayor Preston's callers at the City Hall yesterday morning. As Mr. Hanson is the chairman of the Republican City Com- mittee it was suspected that the visit had something to do with several minority places the Mayor will have to fill on im- portant municipal boards within the next two weeks, including the late William W. Melutire's position as a Republican ineni- her of the Sewerage Commission and the Republican vacancy on the Board of Com- missioners for Opening Streets. 1 Secrecy was maintained as to the cause of the presence of the two Republican offi- cials at the City Hall. After leaving the Mayor's olice Mr. Hanson called on Collec- tor of Water Rents and Licenses Loden. To Succeed Mr. McIntire. It is believed that Mr. A. title: CHELTENHAM IS PRAISED
full_text: CHELTENHAM IS PRAISED Russell Sage Inspectors Call It Among The Best. "One of the best in the country," was the opinion after the investigation of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, Md., yesterday by inspectors of the Russell Sage Foundation, New York. The inspectors are Miss Florence L. Latti- more and Miss Ralph, of New York, and they made the trip with Lieut. Joseph J. Janney, secretary of the foundation for Baltimore, and several members of the board of managers of the institution. This institution, which is said to rank with the best in the country and far above many others in the State, had 30T colored boys when the inspectors arrived. The superintendent and the entire force of teachers, foremen and assistant superin- tendents are white, except two colored men who have minor positions. Superin- tendent J. B. Tyles conducted the visitors through the five schools and over the farms of the institution. Gen. Thomas J. Shryock is president of the board of managers. CARDS FOR COLLEGE. About 200 players took part Monday night in a card party held under the aus- pices of the alumne of Mount St. Agnes' College, Mount Washington, at the Cath- olic Club, 408 North Charles street. The proceeds of the affair will be added to a fund being collected to establish a per- petual scholarship at the college. Those who directed the arrangements for the party were: Mrs.- Frank P. Scrivener, Robert L. Porter, N. Charles Burke, John J. Roach, Misses- Alma Thomas, Hammond J. Dugan, Daniel J. Leonard, Thomas H. Hooper. Mary Regina Possy. Oral Hygiene Work Begun. The work of the Oral Hygiene Council of Maryland in the public schools began yesterday at School No. 1, Greene and Fayette streets, when Dr. B. Holly Smith and Dr. T. O. Heatwole completed the in- stallation of a dental clinic. From 1.30 o'clock to 3.30 o'clock each day there will be two volunteer dentists on hand to ex- amine the mouths of the children. The work will not interfere with the regular practice of dentistry, as the work of the clinic will be chictly advisory. Spoke Before Florists. Mr. Wallace Pierson, a well-known for- ist of Cromwell, Conn., gave an interesting talk on roses Monday night before a large- ly attended meeting of the Florists' Club, of Baltimore. He brought with him for distribution among the florists 200 samples of a new variety of rose raised on his place this season. The Baltimore florists were very much Interested in the description given by Mr. Pierson of his extensive business. He has 1,000,000 square feet of glass and his es- tablishment covers about 18 acres.

title: Is A Convict Of 26 A Juvenile Delinquent?
full_text: Is A Convict Of 26 A Juvenile Delinquent? Most people agree that there is a bad gap in the State correctional system. Adult offenders go to the Penitentiary or the House of Correction. Juvenile of- fenders go to the Maryland Training School or to Cheltenham. But there exists an in-between group of offenders who properly belong neither in a school for juvenile delinquents nor in an adult prison. These difficult cases have a dis- ruptive influence in juvenile institu- tions; yet, obviously, throwing them with adult convicts is very bad practice. | Judge Emory Niles put his finger on 'this weakness last January when he convicted two boys, aged 14 and 15, of safebreaking. At the time he described as a "disgraceful thing the tragic lack of proper facilities in Maryland for taking care of boys who are not suited for commitment to the Maryland Train- ing School." ... An in-between institution of the needed kind was authorized by the Gen- eral Assembly in 1943. And now Gover- nor O'Conor has come forward with a suggestion that the present State penal farm at Roxbury be made over for the .purpose. The penal farm is well suited to the purpose; and, so far as the institution itself is concerned, the Governor's sug. gestion is a good one. But there seems to be a good deal of confusion about the age composition of the in-between group. ... The legal authorization is for an in- stitution "for incorrigible offenders between the ages of 16 and 20." Yet the case on which Judge Niles made his pro- nouncement dealt with two boys áged 14 and 15. Clearly, these two boys be- long in the group. But the law appar- ently excludes them. Just to complicate things further, the Governor in his statement now speaks of offenders "between the ages of 16 and 26." Thus the Governor has ven. tured to enlarge the age group---but in the wrong direction. A convicted crimi- nal aged 26 is no "in-between." He is an adult criminal, and the place for him is not in an in-between group but with other adult criminals. Before we go much further, the Gen- eral Assembly may well reconsider the enlargement of the in-between age group-but with a view to enlarging it downward, not upward. A 14-year-old safecracker clearly belongs in it. But not a safecracker of 26. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: A SUPPOSED CLUE TO CHARLEY ROSS
full_text: A SurrOSED CLUE TO CHARLEY ROSS.- A man giving the name of Sam Benners was ar- rested in Ilarrisburg. Pa., a few days since, and taken to Philadelphia, supposed to have been engaged with the Mosher gang in the abduction of Charley Ross. He said at first that he knew nothing of the case, but afterwards admitted that he had known Mosher, but denied having any knowledge of the missing boy. At another heering Beuners said Charley Ross was in Pean- sylvaja and had never been out of it. That he was not many miles from Philadelphia, and that he had seen him not longer than three weeks ago. Where the boy is Benuers will not say, but the officers who made the arrest and those who have been on the lookout for the last forty days think that the boy is probably in Wrights- ville or in the neighborhood of Lancaster or Columbia, as in going to and fro between Har- risburg and Philadelphia Benners always stopped at these places. - Philadelphia Timis. JAY COOKE'S DESERTED MANSION.-The valn- able property known as Ogontz, late the resi- dence of Jay Cooke, in Cheltenhsin township, Montgomery county, Pa., comprising 214 acres, is still offered for sale by the assignees. Tne mansion house and other buildings are in good condition, and a millionsire might make lum- self almost as happy there as if he were a poor mau. The property would be cheap enough at $150,000 to a man who could afford to live in it. The number of men in Philadelphia who could pay for it and keep it running can be couuted on one's fingers. The estate is more beautiful now than when Mr. Cooke left it, for it is older, more mellow, and riper than it was. The air of newness is worn off, the trees are better grown, the chestnuts are in the prime of their glory at this season, and with every fitful breeze the nuts rain down upon the grass beneath. SUCCESS OF THE BLASTING AT HELL GATE.- The survey of the new bottom at Hell Gate, which bas been in progress since the blast, was completed on Saturday. The survey shows a depth of not less than ten feet below mean low water in any one spot, save one near the shore, at a point where the reef before the blast used to project two and one-half feet above low water. Even that is probably buta small heap of stones, which will easily be removed by dredging. The Bridgeport stes steamer Americus on Saturday after- noon rau close in shore over the site of the old cofterdam. Work on the Flood rock is progress- ing finely, though only a small force of men is employed there as yet. On Wednesday last a large portion of the roof of the main heading fell in, but fortunately nobody was standing be- neath it. Conductors on a Boston street railroad stole a barrel of punched tickets and turned them in for cash fares, thus stealing several thousand | dollars.

full_text: CHELTENHAM POST ELIGIBLES NAMED Former Sing Sing Official One Of 3 Seeking Office Of Education Supervisor The name of a former educational director at Sing Sing prison, New York, was included yesterday in the list of eligibles for appointment as supervisor of education at the Chel- tenham School for Boys, a State in- stitution for Negroes. The list was announced by Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commis- sioner, and was transmitted to Joseph Blanford, Cheltenham superintendent. Y., director of education at Sing Sing until July of this year, when the post was eliminated. CLAUDE D. JONES, 56, of Washington, former superintendent of the Na- tional Training School for Boys at Washington. MARTIN J. BRENNAN, 39, head of the industrial arts department at Hampton Institute, Hampton, Va. The position of supervisor.of educa- tion, recently created at the suggestion of an advisory board studying condi- tions at the school, pays $2,400 a year and maintenance. 400 Boys At School Approximately 400 boys are quar- tered at the school, and the new super- visor will have charge of the entire educational program, assisted by two elementary teachers. title: LOCAL MATTERS
full_text: LOCAL MATTERS. Prisoner's Aid and Relief of Extreme Destitution-A Work Based on Faith. The executive committee of the Maryland Prisoner s Aid Association, Joseph Merreſteld chairman, and Chas L Oudesluys secretary, have ac- cepted the resignations of Rev. Penfield Doll and Mrs Doil, agents of the society. The com- mittee to whom the matter was referred at the late annual meeting of the aid association acted on the resignations yesterday and clected from among a number of applicants Rev.J. B. Shontz and wife, of Wilkesbarre, Pa.,as the future agents of the society. It was represented that Mr. and Mrs. Shontz had had much experience in the pe- culiar work required of them in the visitation of jails, almshouses, &c. Mr. Shontz speaks Ger- man as well as Euglish, and graduated from the Theological Seminary at Mercersburg, Pa. Tney have no family. Mrs. Doll will continue as ma- tron at the Baltimore city jail. Mr. and Mrs. Doll have engaged engaged in other home work considered of an important nature, and other home missionary wholly disconnected with prison labor Mr. Doil and his wife, as agents, received to- gether $800 a year from the association, and in addition to their visitation and other required duties as agents gave temporary shelter and ministration for an hour or a day, or longer, dur- ing the past seven years, in their own house, to 1,008 released male prisoners and 104 females. They are anxious to gi give all their time and at- tention to the relief of all extreme cases of des- titution which come to them. Of nem. Of this class 108 persons, comprising men, women and chi dren, have been cared for within the past three years in their house, Independent of released prisoners. The names of the this and de- tails of every contribution and individual bene- fited are recorded, and a journal accurately kept by the unttiing workers, who say they find pressing upon them the duty of relieving many extreme cases every month. The Railroad and State Negotiations -Going for the Judiciary-Orphans' Court Practices-Appeal Tax Court and Property Assessments - Mine Inspector's Report-The Railroad Case-Miscellaneous Matters, &c. [Correspondence of the Baltimore Sun.) ANNAPOLIS, MD., Jan. 28, 1878. Only the House of Delcrates was in session to-day, the Senate having held over until to- morrow from Friday last. Speaker Hohlitzell cleared his desk of all work. The House passed nineteen hills, and read sixteen a second time and four the first time, Dr. Wm. II. Cole acting both as reading and chief clerk in the absence (from sickness) of Mr. Kidd. THE FALTIMORE AND OHIO RAILROAD CASE. In the hearing which is to be riven of the Baltimore and Ohio railroad case before the Anance and ways and means committees of the Legislature on Wednesday next. Mr. John King. Jr., first vice-president, will represent the rail- road company, the present effort to adjust the company's mattere with the State having been pretty much left in that officer's hands. The purpose is, if possible, to arrive at a settlement on such a basis as will govern and keep affairs etraight in all the future, and it is believed it will be successful, though of course there have been, and may be yet, scrious difficulties in the way. A good spirit, however, prevails on both sides. CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS. Four or five proposed constitutional amend. ments have come to the surface this session in one shape or another. Those of Judge Pinkney, for corporations to be created under a general law and to take away entirely from the counties and city of Baltimore the power to contract debts for internal improvements, have becu men- tioned. A needed amendment is heard of out- side as yet, so that the Legislature could pass a general law in regard to extending the bounda- ries of cities and growing towns. Only the or- ganizations of counties is provided for, and Wi- comico and Garrett have been created since 1867. It is evident that the extension of the bounds of municipalities was overlooked in the organic law which gives the Legislature power to create municipalities. Another important amendment is being pre- pared, aud, it is said. is likely to go to the pop- ular vote, viz., to remodel the judiciary, to re- turn to the one-judge, ten-year term system for circuits, and permanent Court of Appeals of five members, and some changes in the city beucb.- Many reasous are supplied for tius change, be- sides the cost of the present elaborate system. bat the bill for the purpose has not been pre- pared yet and the provisions are not matured. It is very evident, however, that the judiciary will not be withont assailants in this Legisla- ture, and the disposition to attack it was one of the very first things that began to crop out after the General Assemoly met. The latest proposed amendment is to reach the Orphans' Court judges of Baltimore city. This measure comes from a very prominent legal practitioner, who has probably been kept wait. ing. He proposes to substitute one properly qualified judge for the three now comprising the court, to sit five hours on each of three days of the weck. In his preamble the author of this amendment says of the present Orphans' Court: "In order to reach this learned tribunal it is ne- cessary first to have your name inscribed in a book and procure of a clerk a ticket of admis- sion, and then to place yourself at the end of a qucue as at a French theatre, guarded by a bal- lift, and wait your turn to enter a closed box in front of the tribunal," which the writer thinks 13 ridiculous. Being paid only a per diem, the court, it is charged, for that reason remains only in session one to two hours a day, whereas the whole business could be done by one mau, who need be on duty only three days in each week, without the formality attending the brief daily sessions of the present court. The paper has not been presented to the Legislature, and is men- tioned here only as the latest idea for a consti- tional amendment. PROPERTY ASSESSMENTS. The most important thing done in the House was the passage of Mr. McCosker's bill giving the Appeal Tax Court of Baltimore city power to lessen as well as increase assessments of real, Jeasehold and personal property for taxation "on satisfactory cause being shown;" also to make transfers and correct accounts of assess- able property charged to taxpayers. Appeals may be taken from the Appeal Tax Court to the Superior Court of Baltimore city, and the sher- iff shall then he directed to summon a jury of twelve taxpayers, who shall meet on the prem- ises and make a final and conclusive assess- ment, the costs to be paid by the party appealing. The bill now goes to the Senate. It was intended by Mr. Rayner, who is an active member of the judiciary com- mittee. to make the law mandatory on the Ap- peal Tax Court to reopen assessments on the petition of the owner of property assessed, but that will be done in the Seunte. This law has been asked by a number of taxpayers of the city, the Appeal Tax Court having at present the power to increase but not to lower assess- ments returned by the boaras of control and re- view. MINE INSPECTOR'S REPORT. The second annual report of Peter Cain, mine inspector for Allegany and Garrett counties, Md, for the year 1877. has been sent to the Leg- islature through the Governor. The report re- fers to the canal, railroad and mining strikes, and the freshet, as well as other circumstances tending to lessen the production of coal for the year and to lower prices and afford opportunity for under-cutting by the Clearfield (Pa.) mining companies. A number of contracts were di- verted from Maryland to Pennsylvania inines under these circumstances. The inspector de- tails his visits to the different mines, and be- lieves his inspections have had good effect. There are about thirty mines in operation in the Maryland coal region, nearly ali of them in Alle- gany county. In some lew instances attention was called to the existence of "black damp" in mines, which was remedied by fresh air at once on the sug- gestion of the inspector. The Allegany delega- tion manifested considerable interest in the re- port, which, however, contained very little or no information not before well known. BUSINESS MISSTATEMENTS, The bill by Mr. Burt, of Baltimore, in regard to making a penal offense of false businese state- ments by corporations, is based on the Pennsyl- vania law. The bill 18 now betore the judiciary committee and nas received the commendation of the press. It punishes with a fine of not more than $10.000 and imprisonment six months to two years in jail of all directors or other officers of any corporation who shall sien or publish, either generally or for private circulation among stocknolders, estoer knowingly or by neglect of duty, any oficial statement of the affairs of the corporation tending to give a fictitions value, more or less, to the shares of stock of such cor- poration. The law is designed to stop lying re- ports trom business corporations, and the pen- alty is considered not too severe for a misde- meanor, which it is proposed to make such false reports. BUSQUEHANNA AND TIDEWATER CANAL. The treasurer of the Susquehanna and Tide- water canal has asked an early interview with the ways and means committee of the House in regard to the default of that corporation to pay the state the interest, $60.000, due on mortgage to the State. The canal is controlled by the Reading railroad. A proposition was published last week in the Financial Chronicle to the effect that the Reading railroad desired to pay the debt in scrip fundable in income bonds for five years. This proposition, however, will hardly meet with favor. A committee of gentlemen Interested in the canal and railroad is expected to meet the ways and means committee this week. COLORED HOUSE OF REFUGE, The Speaker presented the petition of Enoch Pratt in behalf of the House of Reforma- tiou and Instruction for Colored Children, and asking an appropriation 01 $15,000 to build and furnish another family buliding, in addition to the yearly appropriation of $10,000 usually given. The petition sets forth that it is now five years since the institution was commenced at Cheltenham, and says: "We first built one- half the main building, then the other half. fol- lowed by a family building. The commitments have been so rapid we have not been able to furnish accommodations fast enough. We have now the main building, with the three family buildings. and we have over two hundred boys, and proper room for one only hunored and fifty: and to-day we say we have the most noble and efficient institution in the State., except the In- stitution for the Deafaud Dumb." LEGISLATIVE NOTES. It is understood the committee on federal re- lations will report favorably on the Maryland and Delaware ship canal by the Sassafras river route.
