[Correspondence of the Baltimore Sun.) ANNAPOLIS, MD., Jan. 28, 1878. Only the House of Delcrates was in session to-day, the Senate having held over until to- morrow from Friday last. Speaker Hohlitzell cleared his desk of all work. The House passed nineteen hills, and read sixteen a second time and four the first time, Dr. Wm. II. Cole acting both as reading and chief clerk in the absence (from sickness) of Mr. Kidd. THE FALTIMORE AND OHIO RAILROAD CASE. In the hearing which is to be riven of the Baltimore and Ohio railroad case before the Anance and ways and means committees of the Legislature on Wednesday next. Mr. John King. Jr., first vice-president, will represent the rail- road company, the present effort to adjust the company's mattere with the State having been pretty much left in that officer's hands. The purpose is, if possible, to arrive at a settlement on such a basis as will govern and keep affairs etraight in all the future, and it is believed it will be successful, though of course there have been, and may be yet, scrious difficulties in the way. A good spirit, however, prevails on both sides. CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENTS. Four or five proposed constitutional amend. ments have come to the surface this session in one shape or another. Those of Judge Pinkney, for corporations to be created under a general law and to take away entirely from the counties and city of Baltimore the power to contract debts for internal improvements, have becu men- tioned. A needed amendment is heard of out- side as yet, so that the Legislature could pass a general law in regard to extending the bounda- ries of cities and growing towns. Only the or- ganizations of counties is provided for, and Wi- comico and Garrett have been created since 1867. It is evident that the extension of the bounds of municipalities was overlooked in the organic law which gives the Legislature power to create municipalities. Another important amendment is being pre- pared, aud, it is said. is likely to go to the pop- ular vote, viz., to remodel the judiciary, to re- turn to the one-judge, ten-year term system for circuits, and permanent Court of Appeals of five members, and some changes in the city beucb.- Many reasous are supplied for tius change, be- sides the cost of the present elaborate system. bat the bill for the purpose has not been pre- pared yet and the provisions are not matured. It is very evident, however, that the judiciary will not be withont assailants in this Legisla- ture, and the disposition to attack it was one of the very first things that began to crop out after the General Assemoly met. The latest proposed amendment is to reach the Orphans' Court judges of Baltimore city. This measure comes from a very prominent legal practitioner, who has probably been kept wait. ing. He proposes to substitute one properly qualified judge for the three now comprising the court, to sit five hours on each of three days of the weck. In his preamble the author of this amendment says of the present Orphans' Court: "In order to reach this learned tribunal it is ne- cessary first to have your name inscribed in a book and procure of a clerk a ticket of admis- sion, and then to place yourself at the end of a qucue as at a French theatre, guarded by a bal- lift, and wait your turn to enter a closed box in front of the tribunal," which the writer thinks 13 ridiculous. Being paid only a per diem, the court, it is charged, for that reason remains only in session one to two hours a day, whereas the whole business could be done by one mau, who need be on duty only three days in each week, without the formality attending the brief daily sessions of the present court. The paper has not been presented to the Legislature, and is men- tioned here only as the latest idea for a consti- tional amendment. PROPERTY ASSESSMENTS. The most important thing done in the House was the passage of Mr. McCosker's bill giving the Appeal Tax Court of Baltimore city power to lessen as well as increase assessments of real, Jeasehold and personal property for taxation "on satisfactory cause being shown;" also to make transfers and correct accounts of assess- able property charged to taxpayers. Appeals may be taken from the Appeal Tax Court to the Superior Court of Baltimore city, and the sher- iff shall then he directed to summon a jury of twelve taxpayers, who shall meet on the prem- ises and make a final and conclusive assess- ment, the costs to be paid by the party appealing. The bill now goes to the Senate. It was intended by Mr. Rayner, who is an active member of the judiciary com- mittee. to make the law mandatory on the Ap- peal Tax Court to reopen assessments on the petition of the owner of property assessed, but that will be done in the Seunte. This law has been asked by a number of taxpayers of the city, the Appeal Tax Court having at present the power to increase but not to lower assess- ments returned by the boaras of control and re- view. MINE INSPECTOR'S REPORT. The second annual report of Peter Cain, mine inspector for Allegany and Garrett counties, Md, for the year 1877. has been sent to the Leg- islature through the Governor. The report re- fers to the canal, railroad and mining strikes, and the freshet, as well as other circumstances tending to lessen the production of coal for the year and to lower prices and afford opportunity for under-cutting by the Clearfield (Pa.) mining companies. A number of contracts were di- verted from Maryland to Pennsylvania inines under these circumstances. The inspector de- tails his visits to the different mines, and be- lieves his inspections have had good effect. There are about thirty mines in operation in the Maryland coal region, nearly ali of them in Alle- gany county. In some lew instances attention was called to the existence of "black damp" in mines, which was remedied by fresh air at once on the sug- gestion of the inspector. The Allegany delega- tion manifested considerable interest in the re- port, which, however, contained very little or no information not before well known. BUSINESS MISSTATEMENTS, The bill by Mr. Burt, of Baltimore, in regard to making a penal offense of false businese state- ments by corporations, is based on the Pennsyl- vania law. The bill 18 now betore the judiciary committee and nas received the commendation of the press. It punishes with a fine of not more than $10.000 and imprisonment six months to two years in jail of all directors or other officers of any corporation who shall sien or publish, either generally or for private circulation among stocknolders, estoer knowingly or by neglect of duty, any oficial statement of the affairs of the corporation tending to give a fictitions value, more or less, to the shares of stock of such cor- poration. The law is designed to stop lying re- ports trom business corporations, and the pen- alty is considered not too severe for a misde- meanor, which it is proposed to make such false reports. The treasurer of the Susquehanna and Tide- water canal has asked an early interview with the ways and means committee of the House in regard to the default of that corporation to pay the state the interest, $60.000, due on mortgage to the State. The canal is controlled by the Reading railroad. A proposition was published last week in the Financial Chronicle to the effect that the Reading railroad desired to pay the debt in scrip fundable in income bonds for five years. This proposition, however, will hardly meet with favor. A committee of gentlemen Interested in the canal and railroad is expected to meet the ways and means committee this week. title: THE DECLINE IN BRITISH INDUSTRIES
full_text: THE DECLINE IN BRITISH INDUSTRIES At the late session of the British Social Science Congress, at Cheltenham, Mr. David Chadwick, a well-known member of Parliament, delivered an interesting discourse on the causes of the present depression and stagnant condition of industrial enterprise, and what are the best remedies. Heshowed that while British imports had increased in the course of the deccunial period in the sum of 145 millions of pounds sterling, the exports of British products had only increased 108% millions. In the four years from 1878 to 1876 there had been a decrease of 564 millons in the exports of British products, accompanied with an increase of 23 millions in the imports in the same period. These figures afford a striking instance of consumption ont- running production. Mr. Chadwick attributes the inflation of business in 1872-173 to the extra- ordinary stimuins given to foreign and colonial trade by the numerous government loans to which British capitalists contributed so largely, and the money realized from which was used in the construction of railroads and public works by the many foreign benefi- ciaries of British largesse. The greater part of these loans have been entirely sunk. and there is httle chance now of either interest or principal being realized. This enormous bankruptcy of the debtors to Great Britam was one cause of the depression of trade which began in 1873 and which, in Mr. Chadwick's forcible language, has culminated in the paralysis of 1878. Other causes which he enumerated for the depression: of trade were the three bad harvests since 1871, which, according to the figures of Mr. Caird, bad involved a loss of eighty-seven and a-half millions sterling, together with the famine in India and China and the consequent loss of trade with these countries. The successful competition of foreign countries, and especially of the United States, aided by protective dutics in those countries, was also a cause, and Mr. Chadwick did not forget to mention that India, now manufacturing its own cotton goods, has ceased to buy them of Manchester. great deal of capital previously active had been locked up in opening new and unproductive coal pits and iron mines: the Turkish war and the fear of war with Russia, and finally the re- currence of the decennial cycle of bad trade, which had had its regular period for one hun- dred and fifty years, aided in intensifying the general depression. With regard to the effects of American competition, a Birmingham cor- respondent of the New York Times, writing under date of October 25, furnishes some pointed instances. Birmingham still does an enormous business, as the letter referred to shows, but Belgium, France and the United States have all three greatly interfered with her special industries. This has been par- ticularly the case in the manufacture of arms, of which Birmingham at one time had the monopo- ly. During the late Russo-Turkish war Rhode Island and Connecticut almost entirely took this profitable business to themselves, and many others of the special industnes of the busy city are feeling the effects of the competition forced upon them by our manufacturers. The correspondent of the Times says that all the Birmingham inanufac- turers with whom he has conversed look for- ward to a continuous decline in their city's trade. A member of the Chamber of Com- merce said to him: "Our export trade with America is dead." An ironmonger, who represented as having once had a large market in this country, no longer sends out a single article, bat, instead, sells in Birmingham a good deal of imported American merchandise. These wares and notions" be pronounced "ex- cellent." "They are a clever people," he said, "and best ns on our own ground, but the tarifts kili us. There was once a famous form here, Van Wort, relatives of the great Washington: they did an extensive trade in exports to the States; they closed up their business some time ago; the truth is, the American trade is over, and what a trade it was when I was a boy! Why, sir, the Americans are actually sending us clectro-plated goods.". 18 The last report of the Birmingham Chamber of Commerce is full of gloomy forebodings. In regard to trade with this country it says: "To the United States, formerly our most valuable enstomer, the exports are constantly diminish- ing, and to such a serious extent that in a few years, unless a change takes place, the Ameri- cau trade in this district will be aitogether ex- tinguished." This general withdrawal of trade has made British manufacturers so anxious that in Birmingham and elsewhere many of them are disposed to abandon their free trade princi- ples and look to a revision of the tauft for pro- tection." I am a free trader," said a Birming ham buttonmaker to the Times correspondent, but really I think we might try a little pro- tection on countries which trouble us most. 1 don't know about America, but Spain is abom- inable; they have made a dead set against us there; 25 per cent. worse than any other coun- try they think a fair thing for John Bull." The doctrine of reciprocity treaties seems to be gaining ground, and a leading manufacturer is reported as saying that he had a knowledge of Birmingham trade extending over forty years, and was satisfied that it could not stand alone against the active competition and the discriminating legislation of all the world. Mr. Chadwick, however, in the address adverted to, attributing the trade depression to natural and temporary causes, looked to natural instead of artificial remedies for relief. He wanted greater economy in national and local expenditures, and in private expenditure on intoxicating Jiquors, which latter, he said, annually cost the British people 155,000,000 pounds sterling (or $775,000,000.) He wanted reduction in the cost of production both in agriculture and manufac- tures, removal of the restrictions upon trade everywhere as far as practicable, the restora- tion of peace amongst belligerent nations and the subjection of joint stock companies to re- strictions which would secure the limiting of their operations to valid enterprises and pro- tect the subscribers to their stock from being defrauded by speculating managers. title: English Anniversary--St George's Day and Dinner in Baltimore
full_text: English Anniversary-St George's Day and Dinner in in Baltimore. St George's day was celebrated by me du George's society (English) last night by a dinner at Rennert's Hotel, at which about eighty gentlemen sat down to a bill of fare that included not only the typical roast beef of Old Eugland, but the deli- cacies of Maryland The Stars and Stripes, Union Jack and a portrait of Queen Victoria were among the decorations JS. Brancker, preal- dent of the association occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Mayor F. C La- trobe, Revs Wm Kirkus aud Jas Chipchare, S. Eccles. E. G Lind, Professors Gilman, Martin, Morris and Farlay, of Johns Hopkins Univer- sity. Dr. Morrison, John HB Latrobe, Capi Pfeifer, of the steamship Leipzig, O H Hough- ton, Stewart Darrell, Dr. T Clay Maddux, W. W Spence, D Donnelly. F. WN Crouch. an- thor of Kathleen Mavourneen," Wm Good- win, of Liverpool, England, and others After full justice had been done to the dinner Mr J S. Brancker, the president, made a state- ment as to the condition of the society, showing the good which it had effected since its organi- zation. After the toasts of "The Queen" and The President of the United States" had been given- Rev. Mr Kirkus, in replying to the toast of "St George's Day," apoke of the freedom allow- ed to Englishmen in this country on political and social subjects, although he did not think that they ever showed as much candor on that subject as Americans Englishmen were never heard to say that the government was made up of unmitigated and unprincipled scoundrels, avd yet the press, not only of the country, but also of Baltimore, daily furnishes this news, which, if not refreshing, is at least valuable. With all the kindness extended to Englishmen by Amer- icans, they still continued to look upon the old country as their nome. There was something' which they could not find elsewhere-in fact, some one whom they could look up to. He him self was not pledged ecclesiastically to Saint George, as there were some things about him. that would not bear looking into-in fact, a sort of hazy theology not exactly suited for to-day.. And yet he thought it was better for a people to have a saint better than themselves, and not. be so constituted that they did not think they were so good that they ought to be mayor of a city or President of the United States. Не thought, however, that there should be some- thing which ought to be lasting and should not merely be voted for, and therefore he respondea heartily to the toast of "St. George's Day " The toast of "Old England" was responded to, by Professor Martin, of Johns Hopkins Univer- sity, and that of "The Engrishman" by Mr. Mil- ler, who sang the song from the opera of "Pina- fore" "For he is an Englishman." "The Colo- nies" was responded to by Mr. Stewart Darrell, and "Our Sister Societies by Mr. W. W. Spence, of the St. Andrew's, and Mr Dantel Donnelly, of the Hibernian Society. Mr. Donnelly said that he looked upon Irishmen and Englishmen as one, and every Irishman in the city henored the St. George's Society The toast, "The City of Baltimore," was re- sponded to by Mayor Latrobe, who said that when he came into office he had prepared a speech to deliver at every banquet, but, iuding: it would not suit the St. George's society, had been compelled to leave it at home Maryland- ers showed by the names which they had given to their cities and counties that they were proud of their English ancestry and recollec- tions, and he hoped oficially that during this, season there would be a large emigration of Euglishmen to Baltimore President D. C. Guшан, гевропJag το το toast of the "Johns Hopkins University," said he was grateful for the explanation of the char- acter of St George which had been so lacidly given by Rev Mr. Kirkus He knew that St. Michael and All Angels was in the reverend gentleman's location, but he did not know that St George also resided in his parish. He had been looking around the audience, but could not find the typical John Bull. His own ancestors left their country (perhaps for their country's good) 200 years ago, and he was therefore a. member of the society in posse, if not in esse. It was remarkable to see how, since the days of the colonies. English science and letters had exercised their inquence in this country. He instanced Cambridge, Yale, William and Mary Colleges, and many others And so what! could have been done better in Baltimore? Wherever the cross of St George waved he felt that there would be those who loved liberty next to learning, and engaged in the study of science and letters "The Ladies" was responded to very happily by Mr W Y. Perot, and The Founders of the Society" by Mr W H. Perot. Songs, duets and quartertes made up the programme, and early morning was reached before the company separated. John Merryman, Mrs. Merryman,and; Misses Nannie and Bettie Merryman bave re- turned home from their European tour. They reached New York on Saturday, in the steamer Germanic, Capt Kennedy, from Liverpool. Mr. Merrymau and family sailed from New York on 31st October They spent some time in London, and visited the principal points of interestin England. Paris and Rome were visited, and considerable time devoted to Southern Italy. They returned to London early in April. Two Hereforde, purchased for himself and for Mr. Frank Brown, of Sykesville, and a Devon bull, from the Queen's Norfolk farm, on account of the prohibition, cannot now be shipped to this country. Two Southdown rams for the Druid Hill Park flock, which he also bought, willi arrive in the steamer Nova Scotian, due here on. next Saturday. Mr Merryman goes to Wash- ington to-day to confer with the President and! to give his views relative to the inexpediency of coutinuing a prohibition of English cattle. Colored House of Reformation. -The House of Reformation and Instruction for Col- ored Children, at Cheltenham, Prince George's county, has 210 inmates, while the three build- ings are intended to accommodate only 50, voye in cach. The bo trd of managers hope to get an appropriation from the neat State Legislature to erect a fourth building. For the past 18 months justices of the peace have been request- ed to refrain from committing children to the, institution except in extreme cases. Forty boys now there would be bound out to good homes it such could be found, but in these times it is difficult to make that disposition of them. Those farmers and others who take boys are required to pay wages, which the managers put in a sav- ings bank until the boys are of age. Badly Burned -Annie Kaschupe, 6 years of age, was seriously burned yesterday by her clothing catching fire white she she was picking coke from a pite of cinders at the chemical works. in Canton. She is the daughter of Mi- chael Kaschupe, No & Potomac street. Cauton, who is an invalid. The girl's legs, arms and face were burned. Painful Acordent. -Charles Enright, a work- man at Chipman & Son's chair factory, Canton. was severely wounded in the face yesterday by a splinter thrown off from a circular saw. The splinter, which was five inches long and half an inch thick, struck Enright below the right eye, The point coming out back of the cheek-bone. Roller Kinks. The Baltimore and Washing-' ton roller rinks closed last night. The season In Baltimore was most successful. The director of the Baltimore rink goes to Saratoga to open an establishment there. An interesting game of polo was played last night. Arrivals at Pimilico. The stable of E. A. Clabaugh, consisting of Westminster, Odep, Achsah, Dart, Lucia, Cloverbrook, Rochester and Vigilant, arrived at Pimlico on Tuesday. Yesterday the stable of M. Donahue, of New York. arrived. title: The Soldiers' Home At Pikesville
full_text: The Soldiers' Home At Pikesville. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: Having noticed in your paper, of which I have been a constant reader for years, the article about the Soldiers' Home in Pikesville, I am wondering how patriotic Baltimore can stand by and let such sad happenings occur unheeded. Of course, the residents of this place are now too old to be soldiers, but they were soldiers who faced death and horrors worse than death in a losing cause, the cause as they then saw it, and they can still lose their home and grin and bear it. The war is over now. What do we need with soldiers?. By the time we have an- other war we will have more boys grown to manhood to carry a rifle so the country is safe. Why not take up a collection for the purpose of building a shot tower where the Soldiers' Home now stands at Pikesville? Or another good idea would be to buy the Shot Tower and give the old Civil War veterans the privilege of standing on the sidewalk on Fayette street, explaining to a gaping visitor what shot and shell are made for. Then build a park around the old Shot Tower and have benches in it for the unfor- tunate war veterans to sleep on. I ask you Baltimoreans, who also claim to be Southerners, to look to the welfare of these old men and try to give them some happiness in their old age. A READER AND SISTER OF A WORLD WAR VETERAN. ■ Forest Park, Md., Feb. 25. Hopes He Will Pray For Repent- ance And Be Forgiven, TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: I noticed a brief letter in THE SUN of the 24th inst., signed "Republican." Well, from the tone of his letter, he seems to be very sorry and heart-broken that he voted for Senator France. Не says he voted for Mr. France because David J. Lewis was a Socialist. Now he asks God to forgive him for casting his vote for Mr. France. Then he knows that he committed a' double sin-first, by voting for Mr. France; second, by charging the Hon. David J. Lewis with. something of which he is not guilty. If the writer would have had any fore- sight he could have seen the weakness in Senator France's policy before he voted. for him. I hope he will pray for re- pentance and he will be blessed. C. N. STEM. Sabillasville, Md., Feb. 24. ३ Most Of Us Will Compromise On Taking It Sitting Down. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: The eminent physician, Dr. Reynold Webb Wilcox, president of the American College of Physicians, in this morning's SUN says: "Drinking sitting down will promote temperance." "He doubts effi- cacy of prohibition and assails blue laws." And says, "The Ten Command- ments themselves say nothing about Sun- day observance, except that we shall not work."' He surely has forgotten the Ten Com- mandments, or maybe, he never knew them. I ask him to read carefully the Fourth Commandment. The first clause, Exodus, xx, 8: "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy." : G. M. SCAGGS.: Cheltenham, Md., Feb. 23. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Remarkable Longevity
full_text: Kemarkable Longevity.-Easter Prestby, colored, living with her daughter, Maria Barnes, at the house of Elizabeth Anderson, No. 11 Grove street, presents a very remarkable evi- dence of longevity, and is, from all accounts, considerably over one hundred years old.- Though presenting every indication of extreme old age, her hair being white as snow, she re- tains her faculties and is able to converse in. telligently. She says that her age is 110 years, but has no record of it except by her memory. The daughter is reported to be over eighty, and is still able to walk about and to do light work. Easter remembers and relates many incidents of old times, though relating to matters of no special importance. Unlike most centenarians, she says that she never saw Gon. Washington, but that she heard enough about him when he was living. She was born in Harford county and lived there most of her life. When the emancipation proclamation was issued by President Lincoln she was owned by Mr. David Strectt, now living at Hillon and Forrest streets, who offered her a home for life, and desired her to remain with him. Her daughter Marta was owned by Mr. Jehu Gorsuch, of this city, who also offered to provide for her, but the two old women refused, and, taking advantage of the proclamation, went away from their homes and have since lived together at various places in the city. Mr. Streett says that his grandfather, also named David Streett, bought Easter from Mr. Hall, of Long Green, Harford county, in 1794, and that she remained in the family until emanci- pated. She was married and had several chil- dren before 1794. Her husband died many years ago. According to his reckoning, Easter is much older than she claims to be. He says that his father, who died in 1861, stated to him that Easter was one hundred and four years old that year, which would make her one hundred and twenty-three now. Mr. Streett saya Easter was always highly esteemed in the family, and was an excellent nurse, house-servant and cook, When, by his record, Easter was one hundred years old, his father brought a beefsteak to her, saying that he wished her to cook it for him, as no one else could do so as well. She replied that she thought she could make it eatable and soon afterwards brought it in, cooked to perfection. With a quiet smile she requested her master "If it met with his appro- bation" to prosent her with a quarter in token thereof. When over ninety her sight was very defective, but afterwards she got her "second sight," and was for a long time able to see as well as any young woman. Since they have been free the old women have frequently been assisted by their former masters, but havo re- cently been in destitute circumstances. Both of them have always borne good characters, and much sympathy is expressed for their con- dition by the colored familles who surround them. Produce and Prices-Strawberries and Peas. The wholesale produce market of Bal- timore has been fairly active this week in the usual winter vegetables and other articles. On Wednesday 96 quarts of Charleston strawber- ries, grown in the open air, were sold to market- men at 40 conts a quart. They were well ripened and fairly good. About thirty boxes of Florida green peas sold at $2 a bushel box. New rad- ishes have been recoived from Charleston and Norfolk and sold at $2 50 per 100 bunches. Pro- duce dealers are anxious about the remarkably forward condition of vegetation in the South, which is fully a month ahead of the proper season. They hope the southern section and the Norfolk truckers will get enough cold weather yet to keep back their crops, and save them from a freezing out that might come later on in the spring. A Charleston grower has written to his comunission house here that from the outlook at the time he wrote straw- berries would be plentiful soon. Fish are be- coming more abundant, although the cold snap interfered with Chesapeake fishermen. Prices are still rather stiff for some varieties, but in a few days there will be a full supply of all kinds. The prices at the city retail markets yesterday were as follows: Turkeys 16 to 18 cts. per pound, dressed chickens 25 to 40 cents each, ducks 35 to 50 cents, geese 75 cents to $1 25, Irish pota- toes 20 cents per peck; sweet potatoes 30 to 40 cents, turnips 12 to 15 cents, cabbages 2 to 12 conts a head, kale 20 to 25 cents peck, broccoli 25 to 30 cents peck, sprouts 25 to 30 cents peck, onions 40 to 50 cents peck, parsnips 5 to 8 cents buuch, apples 25 to 40 cents peck, dried apples 8 to 10 cents quart, poaches 10 cents, peeled do. 15 to 18 cents quart, eggs 15a16 cents dozen, roll butter 30 to 35 cents, print butter 35 to 40 cents and Delaware print butter 40 to 45 cents pound, rockfish, perch und pike 50 to 60c. bunch, boiling rock $1 to $1 50 each, haddock 5 cents pound, shad $1 to $1 50 pair, herring 50 cents, dozen. Legislative Visit to a State Institution.- The House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children was visited yesterday by the legislative committee on public institutions. The committee, consisting of Delegates Doun- vin, Rose, Ridgely and Owen, and Senator Far- row, accompanied by Senator Welflcy, of Gar- rett county, Delegate Touchstone, of Cecil coun- ty, and others, arrived at Cheltenham Station,. on the Baltimore and Potomac railroad, on a special train, which had been placed at their disposal by Mr. Geo. C. Wilkins, superinten- dent, about ten o'clock A. M. Gen. John W. Horu, superintendent of the house, mot the committee and escorted them to the insti- tution, where they were received by Mr. Enoch Pratt, president of the board of man- agers. A thorough tour of inspection was made of the main building, also of the four family buildings, erected some distance from and to the rear of the main building. The committee were much pleased with all that they saw, especially the cleanliness and order observable in the departments. The inmates exhibit aptness to learn, and are taught rudi- mentary lessons in the school-room and how to work in tailor and shoe shops and on the farm. The managers explained to the committee the practical working of the institution, and said they needed an appropriation of $10,000 in order to make areaways around the building to prevent dampness, also to renew flooring, etc., which had been injured in consequence of dampness. A band, composed of boys of the House, entertained the committee with music, and others of the children sang a number of popular songs. Mr. Pratt returned to the city with the committee. Acquitted of Cruelty to Animals.-Rob- ort Stewart and John Bankard, garbage cart men, were tried in the Criminal Court yester- day for cruelty to animals. Mr. Charles P. Montague, president of the Society for the Pre- vention of Cruelty to Animals, conducted the prosecution in lieu of the prosecuting attorney for the State, the law organizing the society requiring the prosecution to be conducted in that manuer. The accused were proved to have beaten the horse soverely, but the horso was shown to have a very bad temper, and to have been very unruly and obstinate. Mr. Montague said he had believed the men guilty, but in view of the testimony he did not feel that it would be right to ask for their convic- tion. His society proposed to pursue the guilty to punishment, but did not want any innocont person punished. Stewart and Bankard were accordingly declared not guilty. Punishment of False Pretenses.-Ernest alias "Doc" Schaar pleaded guilty in the Criminal Court to false pretenses on oue in- dictment, three others being stetted. The records of the court showed that the accused had been before the court a number of times on similar charges in the past ten years, and had been sentenced in several cases. Judge Pinkney sentenced him to four years in the pen- Itentiary. He had obtained numerous sums of a dollar or so from small shopkeepers and others, mostly women, as part payment in advance for groceries and other articles, which he pretonded to be authorized to sell under market prices. title: Brutal Outrage on a Child--The Perpetrator in Jail
full_text: Brutal Outrage on a Child-The Per- petrator in Jail. [Correspondenco of the Baltimore Sun.] BRYANTOWN, CHARLES CO., MD., July 1. This community was thrown into a state of inteuse excitement and indignation, on Sunday evening last, by the news of an outrage com- mitted by a colored boy named Henry Johnson, agod 17 years, on a little daughter of Mr. Henry L. Mudd, farmer, residing about two miles from this place. Mr. Mudd and his wife were seated on the verandah of their house when their little daughter, aged two years and ten mouths, camo up and complained of what the boy had done. The child had been playing through the rooms and on the porches of the first flor of the house in company with a little sister just learning to walk, and was most of the tine in sight of the parents. The boy had avalled himself of their presence on the back porch to accomplish his purpose. The child was in no way injured beyond the base indignity inflicted upon her. The father at once started to avenge the outrage, but the boy had fled. He had been in the employ of Mr. Mudd for two years, and came from the colored House of Reformation, at Cheltenham, about six miles from Upper Marlboro'. The alarm was given and the whole county turned out to hunt the criminal. The search contin- ned all night, and on Monday morning he was found by two colored men and brought to Mr. Mudd. The enraged father, it is stated, drew a knife and would have killed him, but was prevented by his wife and a number of others. Some of the mon present went for a constable in the immediate neighborhood, and the boy was taken to Port Tobacco and lodged in jail. Ham- ilton and Mayor Latrobe, at the invitation of Mr. Enoch Pratt, president, visited the House of Reformation and Instruction for Colored Children, located at Cheltenham, Prince George's county, about 42 miles from Balti- more, on the Pope's Creek Branch of the Balti- more and Potomac ralkroad. A special train left Calvert Station at 9.30 A. M., having on board Mr. Enoth Pratt, president of the board of managers; E. Stabler, Jr., secretary; W. E. Woodyear, treasurer; Cyrus Blackburn, Alex. P. Hill, B. F. Deford, Charles Markoll, Wm. S. Whiteley and Charles T. Boehm, of the board of managers; Messrs. Samuel M. Price, of Bal- timore county; C. C. Magruder, Jr., of Prince George's county; Edwin Blackburn and W. F. Weber, of Baltimore city. Gov. Hamilton joined the party at Marlboro' Station, he having taken an early train from Annapolis. The visitors were met at the station by Gen. John W. Horn, superintendent, who had provided vehicles to transport them up to the house, which is dis- tant about threo-quarters of a mile. On ac- count of the visit the inmates had been given a holiday, and they were apparently enjoying the bright sunshino in strolling about the spa- cious grounds. Shortly after entering the build- ing Mr. Pratt conducted the Governor, Mayor and others to the chapel, in the upper story, where a brass band, consisting of 13 inmatos, en- tertained the visitors with martial music and popular airs. The main building, as well as the four family buildings, were thoroughly in- spected, Governor Hamilton and Mayor Latrobe expressing gratification at the constantly recur- ring evidences of strict discipline, neatness and order everywhere observable. The kitchen, laundry and workshops were all visited, and called forth the unanimous verdict that the inmates were better cared for than nine-tenths of their fellows outside of the institution. At pres- ent there are 211 boys in the House, their ages ranging from 8 to 20 years. There is plenty of work found for them on the farm, (of 700 acres,) in the workshops and domestic employment about the House. Everything consumed by the boys, except meats, is raised upon the place. This year 70,000 heads of cabbage and 2,500 bushels of potatoes were parts of the crop. Shoes and clothing, including caps worn by the inmates, are manufactured by them, while a large number are employed in caning chairs for an establishment in Baltimore. Some of the boys have made considerable progress in studying in the schools, where the rudimentary branches are taught by faithful teachers. Specimens of writing were exhibited that would do credit to white boys of similar age. Governor Hamilton was much interested in the farming operations, and in company with Mr. Pratt and others inspected the cows, calves, lambs and swine. At noon the bell sounded the dinner call, when the boys occupying the family buildings formed in companies and marched in columns of twos to the main build- ing and into the dining-hall, keeping step to the cry of "hep, hep," from one of the larger boys in each squad. Filing in, each boy took his place at the table, and when all the tables were surrounded heads were reverently bowed while grace was said by all in unison, At a signal all seated and began the meal, which consisted of stewed meat and potatoes and large slices of wholesome bread. In less than two minutes scores of plates were emptied and raised above the head of each voracious con- sumer, signifying that, like Oliver Twist, they wanted more. And more they received, some of them getting as many as four large plate- fuls of the eavory food. Mr. W. F. Weber, architect of the buildings, procured photographic views of them, also a group picture of the visitors standing on the front steps of the main building. After this the company dined at the expense of the man- agers of the institution. The special train re- turned to the city shortly after 6 o'clock, bring- ing all back safely. Gov. title: The Bryantown Outrage--Confession of the Culprit and Threats of Lynching
authors: Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun
full_text: [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.! The Bryantoivn Outrage-Confession of the Culprit and Threats of Lynch- ing. PORT TOBACCO, CHARLES COUNTY, MD., July 2.-Henry Johnson, colored, the youth who, on Sunday last, committed an outrage on a three- year-old child of Mr. Henry L. Mudd, at Bryan- town, is still in jail. He acknowledged his guilt to Justico Dent, and has not since dented it, but has given willingly to all who asked it a rull description and accountof the whole affair. On the committal of Johnson by Justice Dent, the constable started off with his prisoner to lodge him in jall here, but sald on locking him up that he had no idea on starting that he should be permitted to proceed with him un- molested. A number of colored men in the vicinity of Bryantown, it is said, expressed their willingness to lynch him. The prisoner states that he was born in Bal- timore, and that his parents live in that city, in Bethel row, on Saratoga street, near Gay street. Whou 8 years of age he was sent to the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham, Prince George's county, where he stayed five years, and was taught to read and write. title: Factory At Cheltenham Destroyed By Flames: Broom Storage House Also Wrecked By Early Morning Blaze Of Unknown Origin
full_text: Factory At Cheltenham Destroyed By Flames Broom Storage House Also Wrecked By Early Morning Blaze Of Unknown Origin, Fire of unknown origin destroyed the broom factory and the broom storage house of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, Prince George's county, carly Sunday, it was learned in Baltimore yesterday. title: NURSES' DANCE AT SOUTHERN
full_text: NURSES' DANCE AT SOUTHERN Ten. Members Of Staff From Over- seas Are Guests. Five hundred persons attended the dance given last night in the Southern Hotel' by the graduate nurses of Mercy Hospital in honor of the pupil nurses. Among the guests there were 25 over- seas men, among them Lieut. Noah Wal- ker, who was wounded at Chateau- Thierry and Lieut. William Heathy- both of Baltimore and ten returned oversea nurses, all from Mercy Hospital. One of the features of the evening was a violin solo by Miss Woytyck, of New York. Dr. A. G. Rytina, chairman of the dance committee, estimated that the profits would be about $700. This money is to be utilized in building a home for the student nurses at the institution. Mercy Hospital was one of the first to answer the call for nurses during the influenza epidemic at Camp Meade and maintains one of the largest charity wards in the city. : FIVE IN WHISKY ROUND-UP -Two Boys Sent To Reformatories, Two Men To Jail And One Fined. Two boys were among four alleged bootleggers who pleaded guilty in the United States Court yesterday of fur- nishing whisky to soldiers. They were Lloyd Kirkland, who was sent to the Reform School at Cheshire, Conn., for 11 months, and James Jefferson, colored, who was committed to the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham for the same period. The other two were James Casey and Robert R. Henchey, who went to jail for four months and two months, re- spectively. Robert E. Wisdom, colored, belied his name when he undertook to take four and a half quarts of whisky with him upon his return to Chattanooga, Tenn., the other day. He was caught at the railroad station and pleaded guilty of attempting to take intoxicating liquor into dry territory. He was fined $25, and his whisky was added to the confis- cated lot in the custody of Marshal Stockham. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: RELAYS ARE CLASSIFIED Poly Placed In Division 1 By The Penn Management. NORTHERNERS FEEL STING Tech And Washington Central Fin- ished One, Two In Big Race Last Year. Polytechnic has been placed in Class 1 by the Penn authorities for the twenty- fifth relay carnival to be held on Frank- lin Field April 25 and 26. In this divi- sion are De Witt Clinton, Harrisburg Technical, McKinley Manual Training High of Washigton, Washington Cen- tral, Philadelphia Central, West Phila- delphia, Worcester Classical, Lynn Classical, Lynn English and Crane Tech- nical of Chicago. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: I must think that any man who has any State pride would blush for shame after reading the proceedings in Annapolis which took place Thursday evening last during the hearing before the Judiciary Committee, of the House in relation to the bill to prohibit State aid to privately owned institutions, The spectacle of an outside, irresponsible interloper presum- ing to tell the people of Maryland how they should govern themselves should meet with the most vehement rebuke. The bill in question has undoubtedly for its purpose the crippling of certain insti- tutions allied to the Catholic Church, but, like all such mischievous measures, cuts both ways. As Dr. Lewis, president of Western Maryland College, forcibly stated before the committee February 20. it would not only cripple his col- lege, but likewise other institutions, among which are Washington College. Johns Hopkins University, St. Mary's School. Maryland School for Boys, Jewish Hospital for Consumptives, School for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, a similar school for girls in Baltimore county. Home of the Friendless and others, insti- tutions in no way allied with the Cath- olic Church. Ex-Senator Perkins told the committee that the passage of the bill would end the State tax rate sky- high. Will it? Let us see? ..It is proposed to withhold the aid now given by the State to these various reformatory institutions for boys and girls, many of whom, the majority prob- ably, are incorrigible, some three or four tiousand of them. What is it proposed to do with them? Close up the institu- tions, put them out of business-what are you going to do with these thousands of boy's and girls? Turn them out in the world to become a prey to wicked and depraved influence, to become candi- dates for our penal institutions, and in the last analysis become a charge upon the State in another and more expensive form? God forbid. What are you going to do for the poor boy and girl whose parents are, unable to give them the higher education which the present State aid enables them to acquire? One member, in answer to this query, replied: "Let the State own these insti- tutions." So be it; let's do a little figur- ing. To build or construct an institu- tion like the Western Maryland College, the Country School for Boys and St. Mary's Industrial School would cost,' at a low estimate, $200.000. There are some 20 such in the State. There you have $4,000,000, the equipment. Teach- ing staff and upkeep would cost three times as much, so, to "let the State own these institutions" would cost the snug little sum of $12,000,000. Would there be a surplus in the Treasury to meet that expense? Surely not.. Then what follows? A bond issue of at least $10,- 000,000. With the present rate of inter- est--6 per cent.- we will have the beau- tiful sum of $600,000 overhead interest charge. How high will your State tax go? I think when our, farmer friends in the counties realize this they will "sit up and take notice." Now, a word with reference to St. Mary's Industrial School for Boys. I have been honored as a director on the part of the State for a number of years. I have taken great interest in the work done there. Being a frequent vis- itor, I do not hesitate to say that no in- stitution in the State is more efficiently and economically managed Boys are sent there from the city and various counties of the State by the courts, most of whom are incorrigible; others for minor offenses from environments calcu- lated to breed vicious characters. They are taken in hand by Brother Paul and his corps of assistants, are taught trades of various kinds and an elementary edu- cation that fits them to become self- supporting and self-respecting units of our citizenship. I take great pride in the work of the school. It may perhaps be unnecessary for me to state that I am not a member of the Catholic Church. I hold membership in the Brown Me- morial Presbyterian Church. So that my attitude in this matter may not be misunderstood. Now a few words relative to this man Waldron, who seems to have the lead- ing strings to certain members of the Legislature, and who claims all the credit of electing a majority of the members of the lower house, as I believe he claims the credit of electing the pres- ent pro-German pacifist Mayor of Chi- cago. That I may not be misunder- stood, let me say that 56 years ago, as a boy of 17 years, I marched out of Wash- ington county as a soldier and gave three of the best years of my life to my country in the Sixth Maryland Regi- ment, and will carry to my grave the scars of three serious wounds as a result of that service. In my political affilia- tions I am an uncompromising Republi- can. I have spent a lifetime in the serv- ice of my party, have sat around the council board of my party long before some of the gentlemen who will decide the fate of this bill were born. If there are any men of my party who hold seats in this Legislature, and who are there in virtue of any pledge of subservient obedience to the will of this man Wal- dron, to vote and act as he directs, then all I have to say is that they have sold their birthright for a mess of pottage, and have no right to place their party in such an unenvłable position. At this particular time, when our blessed coun- try is engaged in a life-and-death strug- gle to make the world safe for democ- racy, it is treasonable for this outside interloper to come in our midst to foment religious. discord, and he should be drummed out of the State! Is this war to be won by non-Catholics alone? If so, why are not Waldron and his co-conspirators under the colors to- day? Oh, bless you, no! They think too much of their precious slacker hides, but, like cowardly curs, bark at the heels of the more than 540 St. Mary's Indus- trial School boys now under the colors? JOHN R. KING, Director on the part of the State in St. Mary's Industrial. School. Baltimore, March 1./. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: SOME COUNTY INSTITUTIONS: MR. G. S. GRIFFITH'S OBSERVATIONS IN PRINCE GEORGE'S AND HOWARD COUNTIES HOWARD COUNTY HOUSE OF REFORMATION FOR COLORED BOYS
full_text: SOME COUNTY INSTITUTIONS. Mr. G. S. Griffith's Observations in Prince George's and Howard Counties. [Reported for the Baltimore Sun.] G. S. Griffith, president of the Maryland Prisoners' Aid Association, visited on October 3 and 4 the jails and almshouses of Prince George's and Howard counties, also the House of Reforination and Instruction for Colored Boys at Cheltenham. He writes to THE SUN, giving his observations, as follows "The jail at Upper Marlboro' is a two-story brick building with ten cells, containing at this time 12 prisoners, one a white man, charged with stealing two mules and a wagon, the others colored; two are women, one insane, the other for drunkenness and dis- orderly conduct. Two were boys between thirteen and fifteen years of age, one of these on charge of felonious assault. Six were for larceny, and the others for minor offenses. Since the 1st of January 47 prison- ers have been committed to this jail. The sanitary condition was by no means good, and when I spoke to the prisoners about keeping things clean and neat, they said they would willingly to do so it plenty of soap and water were given them. Bedsteads and mattresses are also greatly needed, as the floors, being of brick and cement, are very cold, especially in damp weather. The scanty amount of bedding with which they were supplied is, msutheient and very dirty. I spoke very freely to the keeper in regard to the condition of the building and the necessity of applying to the county com- missioners for the needed articles. All of the prisoners were awaiting trial, and as every man should be regarded as innocent until proved guilty. he should be treated with more consideration. Indeed, cominon humanity demands that no prisoner should have his health injured by confining him in a cold. damp cell, without even a sufficient amount of bedding. Only a day or two pre- vious to my visit a man who had been incar- cerated for three months sunply on sus- picion was released without uial by order of the judge, as there was no evidence against him. I earnestly trust that the county commissioners will give this jail their immediate attention. The prisoners seemed to appreciate my visit very highly, also the books and advice I gave them, thanking me again and again, and saying that I was the onty one who ever thought to come and give them any religious instruction or encourage- ment to lead a better life. The churches both in this and other counties very rightly and coinmendably take up collections to send the gospel to the heathen, but should they neglect these worse than heathen in their very midst. Shall it be said of us. "Sick and in prison, and ye visited me not?" me "The almshouse is a two-story, substantial brick buiging on a farin of 90 acres, bout eight mites from Upper Marlboro", very dif- ficult of access; indeed, its location is so very obscure that the driver of our carriage lost his way twice before he could find the place. An institution of this kind should be within two or three miles of the county town, so that a physician and others who would take an interest in this unfortunate class might have free access to the place. The main building is occupied by the faintly of the superintendent and the white paupers, and was ina tolerably good sanitary condition. The frame building, containing two rooms 14 by 11 feet, one for male the other for female inmates, and de- voted to the use of the colored, is a disgrace and reproach to the county. The institution contains at this time 15 paupers, during the winter the average number is 20. Six of these were white, nine colored and str insane or imbecile. Into these two small rooins all the colored paupers are crowded, the old, blind, sick and heipress with the insane. One of the men was suffering from a very offer.- sive disease, which rendered the air of the 100m not only unpleasant and impure, but very unhealthy for the others. The inmates ate obliged to eat their food holding itin their hands, as the rooms do not contain a table; indeed they are not even supplied with benches or chairs, a few old boxes serv- ingas beats, and this seems very hard when we take into consideration that the majority of these inmates are either blind or very old and feeble. Even when one ales they are compelled to keep the body in the same room with the living until it can be buried. They complained bitterly of their neglected condition, also of the food given them, which. from what I saw of it and their manner of serving, was not very ap- petizing. An eficient matron would greatly improve the condition of things. Anadditional building is absolutely necessary, for the superintendent himself informed that at times he had been compelled to put as many as ten paupers in one of these small rooms. A suitable building, where one of the rooms could be used asa hospital and another devoted exclusively to the insane, could be erected at a cost of from $800 to $1,000, and I sincerely trust that the county commissioners will give this matter their favorable consid- eration. I met Mr. Duvali, one of the board of trustees, and spoke to him about the insti- tution. He acknowledred its bad condition, and said that he had gone before the county commissioners with a petition for a new building, but had not been successful. I wrote to the county commissioners, and earnestly trust that the needed building will be erected. A prohibitory law was passed in Prince George's county, but I regret to say that it is not rigidly enforced, but stands upon their statute-books a dead letter. I even learned in this visit that the jail-keeper is also bartender for the hotel. HOWARD COUNTY. "I visited the Howard county jail, accom- panied by Rev. Louis F. Zinkhan. We found only two prisoners; the one, a negro, will be tried for murder; the other, a tramp, for an assault on a lady. The case of the former will be removed to Baltimore; the latter will have to wait for his trial until the spring term of court in March. The grand jury meets and the court sits but twice a year, so that a pris- oner must wait from one to six months be- fore he can have his trial and his guilt or in- nocence be established. The number of pris- oners committed to the jail since the first of January is 132. Many of these were sent to the House of Correction. The fact is that Ellicott City sends a much larger proportion of prisoners to the Correction than any other city or town in the State. This indicates that the police and magistrates are wide awake- possibly too much so. We have known sev- eral instances within the year of persons being committed of whom other disposition should have been made. A man's liberty is too dear that he should be deprived of it without just cause; and the State taxes are sufficiently high without supporting many prisoners in the Correction, whose only otrense was sickness and poverty. The police recoive about 40 cents for every arrest, and $550 additional if he takes the prisoner to to the Correction. The inagistrate gets his fee; the jailer gots $100 for turning the key on a man, and the State must pay handsomely for the term of imprisonment. The Howard county jail is not a safe building; besides it has no chimney, and is not properly con- structed to be thoroughly ventilated.. HOUSE OF REFORMATION FOR COLORED BOYS. "The members of the school cominittee, Mr. Wm. L. Lincoln, Mr. J. H. Lee and myself went to the House of Reformation and In- struction for Colored Boss at Cheltenham, and examined the four schools. We found that the boys were making satisfactory prog- ress in their studies. The institution con- tains 227 boys, all actively engaged in work, some in the tailor and shoe departments, and others in caning chairs. The sanitary coudi- tion was excellent, under the efficient super- intendence of Mr. Josiah Wagener, and the general health of the inmates good. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: TRIALS AND TRIBULATIONS. - Suit for Divorce-The B. and M. Tele- graph Company-Visit to Cheltenham, 「Reported for the Baltimore Sun.l The grand jury of the United States Dis- trict Court yesterday found presentments against Peter Smith and John F. Garrett for presenting fraudulent claims against the United States government. SUIT FOR DIVORCE. The hearing was begun before Judge Fisher, but not concluded, in the case of Abraham Podrobirrick vs. Sheba Leah Po ro- birrick, bill for divorce a vinculo matrimonii. The complainant states in bis bill that they were married in Russia, thirteen years ago. He alleges that on account of her cruel treat- ment he left her three years ago and came to this country, with a view of procuring a divorce on the ground of abandonment for more than three years. Martin Lehmayer is solicitor for defendant and John W. Simpson for complainant. BANKERS AND MERCHANTS' TELEGRAPH со. After brief argument in the City Circuit Court, Judge Fisher signed an order in the case of Francis P. Stevens vs. the Bankers and Merchants' Telegraph Company, rat- ifying the auditor's account and directing the United Lines Telegraph Company to bring into court the sum of $10,653 94, so that that amount, with interest from yesterday, with costs, be paid over to Wm. A. Dunn for services rendered and money advanced the- company. The exceptions filed in the case were overruled. Other claims against the company to the amount of $4,200 were allowed. DEED OF ASSIGNMENT. In the Superior Court was filed a deed of assignment from Alfred R. McAlba to John W. H. Frey, for the benefit of creditors. Also the bond of the trustee for $3.000, with Wm. S. Tavlor and Geo. B. Creamer sureties. THE CONTESTED WILL CASE. In the contested will case of August Elias Herwig, deceased, on trial in the City Court before Judge Brown and a jury, the tes- timony for the caveator, August Emil Her- wig, son of the testator, was concluded, and nine witnesses examined for the defendant executrix Mrs. Mary E. Keller. The tes- timony will be resumed today. BEFORE COMMISSIONER ROGERS. John Perry, arrested a few days ago by the police authorities for having in his posses- sion United States stamps and offering them for sale, was taken before Commis- sioner Rogers, who committed him for a hearing tomorrow at noon, on a charge of breaking into and robbing the postoffice at Ilchester. Howard county. VISIT TO CHELTENHAM. The grand jury visited the Colored House! of Reformation, at Cheltenham, yesterday.! A special car was tendered by the Baltimore and Potomac Railroad. The Rev. L. F. Zink- han and Rev. W. P. Ryder and three of the managers of the institution, Mr. G. S. Grif- fith, George J. Zimmerman and C. Boehm accompanied the jurymen. They were re- ceived by the superintendent. Isaiah Wagner, and shown through the institution, which the jurymen say is conducted in a very satisfac- tory manner as to industry, comfort and cleanliness. The boys are engaged in farm- ing, shoemaking, tailoring and chair-caning. All the clothing used is made by the boys. Speeches were made at the repast by Gen. R. H. Carr, George R. Coffroth, Assistant Fore- man Grand Jury G. W. Lester, Geo. J. Zim- merman, L. M. Hamline, Rev. W. P. Ryder and Rev. L. F. Zinkhan. Major Dryden and The boys sang songs. SEEKING DAMAGES FOR ASSAULT. The jury of the Court of Common Pleas before whom was tried the case of S. E. title: MINISTERS FAVOR DRAFT
full_text: MINISTERS FAVOR DRAFT Dr. Miller Declares For System In Address To Presbytery. A tribute to mothers who give their sons to their country's cause was paid by the Rev. Dr. Henry W. Miller, mod- erator, last night at the opening of the three hundred and twenty-eighth stated meeting of the Presbytery of Baltimore. The meeting is being held at Faith Presbyterian Church and will be brought to a close tonight. The following offi- cers were elected at the opening session: Stated clerk. the Rev. Dr. Henry Branch: permanent clerk, the Rev. T. L. Spring- er. and temporary clerk. the Rev. A. B. Caldwell, assistant minister of the First Presbyterian Church. In his address Dr. Miller said that the mothers who sent their sons to the front were heroines, who made the great- est of all contributions to their country. Dr. Miller said he was heartily in fa- vor of the selective draft, as he believed in an "equitable sharing in responsibility and an efficient distribution of ability." He said that society should see that jus- tice placed a heavy hand upon the "slacker." For the pacifist, who was conscientiously opposed to war, thespeak- er declared, he had sympathy, but for the one who was a pacifist through coward- ice he had only scorn. At a meeting yesterday morning of the Presbyterian Ministers' Association many of the members spoke in favor of the selective draft. Among the speak- ers were the Revs. Dr. Alfred H. Barr, Dr. DeWitt M. Benham, J. S. Conning and Edward II. Kestler. Training Negro Boys For Service. One hundred negro boys from the House of Reformation at Cheltenham. Prince George's county. are being trained for service in the army or navy, in re- sponse to the President's call for vol- unteers. Also 120 acres of land have been given over to the raising of vege- tables for the sustenance of Uncle Sam's warriors. Gen. Thomas J. Shry- ock is president of the institution and John B. Pyles the superintendent. Cardinal Visits Ill Pastor. The condition of the Rev. Francis P. Doory, pastor of St. Michael's Catholic Church, who was taken to Merey Hos- pital Sunday, remained unchanged last night. There is only slight hope now for his recovery. Cardinal Gibbons and the priests of St. Martin's household all visited him. Many other priests and Catholic laymen stopped at the hospital to learn his condition and to leave mes- sages of sympathy. Dr. Frank Reeves Released. Dr. Frank Reeves, graduate of Johns Hopkins University. was released yes- terday from the custody of the West Virginia authorities, by whom he was arrested last week in Charleston. A dispatch to THE SUN from that city says that although complete maps were in his possession showing the Kanawha oil field. no evidence that he had any illegal purpose in view was obtainable.

title: CITIZENS PROTEST HOLD-UPS
full_text: CITIZENS PROTEST HOLD-UPS Resolutions Are Adopted And Mar- shal Carter Speaks. Twenty-five mon gathered at Clag- gett's Hall, 614 North Fremont avenue, last night, to protest against the many bold-ups in the city within the past few weeks. Among those present were men whose families had been victims of the robbers, or who had merely seen hold- ups/take place. Marshal Carter was there and spoke. A resolution was passed asking the city authorities to call upon the citizens of Baltimore to help preserve order; urging that the various city depart- ments, particularly the Department of Lamps and Lighting, co-operate with the Police Department; demanding that criminals convicted convicted of "crimes against the person" be compelled to serve full sentences and not be paroled; urging the increase of the police force, and call- ing for a committee to go before the Board of Estimates to ask for money enough to increase it George H.-Sohl, president of the Harlem Improvement Association, which called the mecting, asked for volunteers to compose this committee, and about a half-dozen responded. William Nord- hoff, whose wife was shot by a negro in front of her home several weeks ago, was the first to volunteer. Marshal Carter repeated much of the talk he made to the City Club last Sat- urday, adding that the police force was much handicapped by having to do out- side work for the Health Department and other departments. CAUGHT BREAKING INTO HOME Calligan Pulled Out Of Window And Held Until Ponceman Arrives, Caught breaking into the home of George A. Schlund. 2600 Fleet street, Dennis Calligan. 41 years old, was overpowered by two citizens last night and held a prisoner until Patrolman Brady, of the Eastern district, arrived. Joseph Maxwell, 529 South Luzerne avenue, saw Calligan disappear in an alley alongside the Schlund home. Maxwell waited a few minutes and walked across the alley, He saw Callı- gan halfway in a side window. Running to the man, Maxwell caught him by one leg and pulled him out. Crics of "Po- lice!" brought other citizens, and Calli- gan, was hustled to the light of a street lamp. According to Lieutenant Lastner, of the Eastern Police Station, Calligan has a police record, He will have a hearing today before Justice Gerecht on the charge of felonious entry. Negro Boys Committed For Hold-Ups Adolph Byrd, colored, 15 years old, 253 North Bruce street. who held up Harry Volkmar, a little white boy, last Saturday and robbed him of some but- ter, was sent to the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham yesterday by Judge Williams, in the Juvenile Court. The boy will remain in the institution until he is 21 jears old, unless released sooner for good behavior. The "hold- up" occurred on Fayette near Gilmore street. Charles Kennard, colored, 13 years old, who held up two colored girls at the point of a pistol, was also sent to Chel- tenham by Judge Williams until he is 21 years old. The "hold-up" occurred Sunday at the corner of Gilmor and Lan- vale streets. Stole Automobile Tire. A bold thief entered the hardware store of John A. Goeppner. 101-103 North Potomac street, yesterday moru- ing and when clerks were busy waiting on customers the thief picked up a new automobile tire valued at $15 and walked out. Helf an hour later Goepp- mer discovered his loss and telephoned to the Northeastern Police Station. The police have 110 clue to the thief's identity. title: ALLEGED ROBBER 6 YEARS OLD
full_text: ALLEGED ROBBER 6 YEARS OLD Judge Williams Sends Accused Housebreaker Home. Because of his extreme youth, Domi- nick Skirman, 6 years old, 1534 Green- mount avenue, was dismissed yesterday by Judge Williams, in the Juvenile Court, when arraigned on the charge of housebreaking. The boy was the small- est and youngest alleged robber ever in the court. His extreme youth placed him beyond the jurisdiction of the court. Otis Jones and William Rice. both colored and 11 years old, 436 and 446 Federal street. charged with the same offense, were sent to the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham until September 3. The three boys, it was alleged, entered the unoccupied dwell- ing 209 East Preston street last Satur- day and stole window screens and other articles worth $11.50. ASKS $20,000 FOR INJURIES Mrs. Mary Busilik Lifted Into Air By Pavement Doors. For injuries alleged to have been re- ceived on July 15. when she was sud- denly hoisted into the air and thrown to the pavement by the cellar doors in front of the store of Dowell, Helm & Co.. wholesale millinery and cloak dealers, 117 and 119 West Baltimore street, opening under her, Mrs. Mary Busilik sued the firm for $20.000 dam- ages in the Superior Court yesterday, through Isaac Lobe Straus. attorney. It was the sidewalk elevator in the cellar that opened the doors as Mrs. Busilik was passing over them. It is alleged that she was thrown violently to the pavement. JURY RAPS CAR SERVICE Exonerates Motorman Of Blame For Death Of W. H. Cheesman. A jury summoned by Coroner Grem- pler at the Southern Police Station last evening to investigate the death of Wil- liam H. Cheesman, Jr., who was killed in front of his home, 1703 Light street, Saturday by a Light street car, exon- erated the motorman, Frederick Shelby, from all blame. The jury addressed a letter to the United Railways and Elec- tric Company making several recom- mendations regarding the service on the Light street line. The letter, which was signed by the jury, read as follows: "We, the un- dersigned, recommend better service on the Light and Orleans street car line. As regards the cars on that line, we know they are unfit for service. We also desire that some care be exercised in running between Cross and Wells streets, especially when passengers are standing on the footboards, as we regard this section as dangerous to the general public because of the narrow space be- tween the tracks and the curb." title: GRAND JURY REPORT Increase of Perjury and Other Matters: Protest Against the Increase of Perjury and Other Matters
full_text: GRAND JURY REPORT-Protest Against the Increase of Perjury and Other Matters.- The grand jury for the January, term, Mr. R. Q. Taylor, foreman, made its report to Judge Duffy, in the Criminal Court, on Satur- day, and was discharged with the thanks of the court. The new grand jury, of which Mr. David L. Bartlett is foreman, will be swora In today. The report states that it has been in session 68 days, has examined 2,620 wit- nesses, made 470 presentments and 435 Indiat- ments, dismissed 532 and continued seven cases, and has ignored three indictinents, After reviewing the reports of the various committees, the report says: "This grand jury, in full accord with its predecessors, presents as disgraceful to the city, and inimical to justice. the accommodations provided for witnesses summoned before it. The rooms are entirely Inadequate in space, are filthy in appearance, offensive in odor, and such that decent men and women cannot with self-respect wait in until called before the grand jury. The grand jury suggests that a great deal of per- jury might be prevented if the witnesses be- fore it were sworn by the foreman or assist- ant foreman in the presence of the body. Many of the witnesses appear to be not at all impressed by any sense of obligation of an oath taken in a perfunctory way in the office of the clerk of the court. The possibly necessary charge for the clerk's fees could be arranged by order of the court. "While the grand jury recognizes that the reporting by the police of the names of per sons entering or leaving on Sunday places where liquor is sold has done much to pre- vent free traffle in liquor on Sunday, and prevents much public intoxication and dis- order, it must express its opinion that other means are needed to break up this Sunday trade and provide proof for convictions, and at the same time stein the alarming flood of perjury that confronts each successive grand jury when investigating violations of the Sunday law. The dotective force of the city police should be authorized and instructed frequently to visit on Sunday the business places of the more noto- rious violators of the law, and thus get proof sumelent for conviction. Many of these, Sunday cases presented to the grand jury excito reasonable suspicion that the names of persons visiting the saloons and restaurants who do not drink are given by interested parties to the police, so as to keep up the appearance of police inspection and yet escape punishment. Out of 387 Sunday cases presented by the police during this term, with 1,307 witnesses, only 59 present- ments could be found and 328 cases had to bo dismissed. It is said with regret that in the bellef of the grand jury the majority of the witnesses were guilty of perjury. "The grand jury is convinced that the cre- ation of one or more police courts having jurisdiction in all cases of petty larceny and simple assault would insure more certain and speedy justice and save areat,expense. Many offenses against person and property go un- punished because of the time and trouble en- tailed upon the parties aggrieved by attend- ing at the station-house, grand jury and Criminal Court. "The grand jury regrets that so few of the many rumored open violations of the lottory and gambling Inws have been presented to its body for consideration. "The propriety of restoring to the statuto law of Maryland a just enactment providing tor the punishment of conspiracies to Injura the business or to intertere with the em- ployes of persons or corporations is strongly urged. "There is good reason to believe that many witnesses are tampered with both before and after their appearance before the grand jury, by or with the connivance or advice of attor- neys practicing in the Criminal Court, though as yet no such suflicient proof has been pre sented as would warrant indictinent. "The city of Baltimore is to be congratu- lated on the condition and character of its police force and marshal, as shown in the good order and peaco preserved during the excitement attending the car-drivers' strike, and also evidenced by apparent honesty and intelligence manifested by those who have appeared before the grand jury as witnesses."" The committee on the penitentiary, Messrs. John A. Meeth, Chas. Ogle, Martin Emerich, Alexander Barber and J. Thornton Hall, commend the management of the institution, and express its approbation of convict labor. The action of the Legislature iu refusing to abolish shoemaking in the penitentiary is commended. The committee on Spring Grove Asylum for the Insane found there 214 men and 173 women, 78 of whom are from Baltimore city. They commend the treatment of inmates, but say the female department is crowded. The committee on the House of Correction report 209 inmates, of whoin 122 are white males, 54 black males, 19 white females and 14 black females. The committee on the Col- ored House of Reformation at Cheltenham re- port 210 boys, well fed, clothed and apparently contented in the institution. The committee on the House of the Good Shepherd report very favorably on its condition. There are at present 83 Inmates, who sustain the insti- tution by their labor. The erection of addi- tional buildings for the accommodation of Inmates is in contemplation. The city con- tributes nothing to the institution, although fuily two-thirds of the commitments aro from Baltimore. The committee on Bayview Asylum found the institution in first-class order, but recommend an annex to the in- sane department to accommodate Idlotte and imbecile children. Of the 953 inmates 257 aro insano, 98 being white males, 100 white fe- malos, 21 colored males and 29 colored females. The committee on the House of Refuge re- port the institution in good order. title: CARAVAN ON LAST LAP: WILL LEAVE UPPER MARLBORO TODAY FOR WASHINGTON
full_text: CARAVAN ON LAST LAP Will Leave Upper Marlboro Today For Washington. Weary from a toilsome journey over steep, dusty roads, four sunburned suf- fragists arrived in Upper Marlboro last night in their travel-stained prairie schooner. So steep had been the hills over which they had come, the women had found it necessary to keep two of their members at the brake in order to keep the wagon from tumbling on top of the trusty horses Margaret B. and Susan B. Twelve miles were covered by the suf- fragists yesterday. They left Brandy- wine early in the morning and arrived at Cheltenham a little after noon. Here they were entertained at dinner by John Pyle, superintendent of the Cheltenham Reformatory for Colored Boys. After dinner about 60 people came over from the town to attend a meeting, which was held on the grounds of the school. The 300 boys of the school were all in dress uniforms in recognition of the event and a special speakers' stand was ar- ranged. Wilfred H. Townsend, a resi- dent of the town, who is a warm suf- fragist, made one of the addresses. The letter of introduction given them by Mayor Preston was formally pre- sented to John H. Traband, Mayor of Upper Marlboro, by the caravaners Inst night, preceding an open-air meeting held in front of the Courthouse. Today the caravan will move on to Washington on the last lap of their journey before the one that brings them back to Balti- more. An elaborate welcome is being planned for them by the Washington suf- fragists, who will go out in decorated automobiles to greet the cavavan in that city this afternoon. The suffragists ex- pect to make their triumphant entry at 5 o'clock. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: BURNT KNEE THREATENS LIFE
full_text: BURNT KNEE THREATENS LIFE Thomas Robinson, 56 Years Old, Is In Serious Condition. From a burn he received December 18, Thomas Robinson, 56 years old, 2208 Ashton street, is in a critical con- dition at Franklin Square Hospital. Robinson, who lived with his sister, Mrs. Mary F. Lentz, was asleep on a chair in the kitchen and fell from it against a stove. He sustained a burn on his knee which he did not at first consider serious. After treating it him- self for some time he found that it was rapidly becoming worse and called in Dr. Walter A. Cox, 54 South Fulton avenue. The physician found that blood poisoning had developed from the burn and immediately ordered Robinson to go to the hospital. An operation was performed in an effort to save his life, but the infection, it is feared, has ob- tained too strong a hold on him. SMOKER STARTS A FIRE Excelsior In Flames At Pratt And Charles Street. Fire was discovered early last night in the shop of Philip Lindemeyer, prin- ter and stationer, on the fourth floor of the Bass Building, Pratt and Charles streets. The blaze was in a mass of ex- celsior, and supposedly originated_from a spark of a cigarette or pipe. Little damage was done. A passerby saw smoke pouring from the window and ran in and notified Samuel Bass, owner of the building, and, while a third man sounded the alarm, Bass and his employes helped put out the fire. SUNDERLAND AUTO HITS BOY Cheltenham Home Agent Victim To Hospital. Takes Struck by an automobile belonging to Benjamin B. Sunderland, visiting agent of the Cheltenham Home for Colored Boys. Michael E. Sadler, 7 years old, who lives with a brother at 315 South Fulton avenue, was thrown to the ground late yesterday afternoon and sustained lacerations of his side and scalp. The accident occurred at Balti- more street and Carrollton avenue. Mr. Sunderland, who has an office with the E. Stabler, Jr., Coal Company, Eutaw and Madison streets, was going to his home, Frederick and Seminole ave- nues, when the child ran across the street directly in the path of the ma- chine. He was picked up by Mr. Sun- derland and taken to Franklin Square Hospital. BAD FOR CURTIS BAY CHANNEL Senate Subcommittee Decides To Exclude Amendments. This action, if adhered to by the Sen- ate, destroys all hope of amending the House bill so that the Curtis Bay im- provement can be taken care of at this session should Congress finally pass an omnibus waterway appropriations bill.
