title: THE GRAND JURY REPORT: OBSERVATIONS AS TO SUNDAY LIQUOR AND ELECTION LAW VIOLATIONS
full_text: THE GRAND JURY REPORT, Observations as to Sunday Liquor and Election Law Violations [Reported for the Baltimore Sun.1 The grand jury for the January term mado its final report in the Criminal Court on Sat day and was, finally discharged, with the thanks of the court. The new grand jury will be called today. The report is as follows: Hon. Edward Duffy, Judge of the Criminal Court: The grand jury of the State of Mary- land for the body of the city of Baltimore for the January term, 1887, having arrived at the close of their term, make respectful report of the nature and extent of their labors: They have held sessions 91 days and disposed of 1,280 cases; found 686 present- ments and dismissed 594; 3,635 witnesses woro examined. They have been mindful of the charge of your honor, at the beginning of the term, to give attention to certain statutes which come under the head of criminal offenses. They have met with no charge of selling or advertising medicines or medical instruments for the purpose of procuring abortion, and draw, therefore, the happy in- ferenco that such crimes are of less frequency than might possibly have been apprehended. It is also gratifying to state that there has not been a single charge of default of public moneys, and but one accusation of prevent- ing free egress and ingress from and to public buildings. The jury, as required by law, have visited in a body the penitentiary and jail, and found those institutions in a cleanly and orderly condition, and managed in an able and systematic manner, as will appear by the reports of the committees submitted herewith. The managers have also visited the House of Correction, Bayview and Spring Grove Asylums, the House of Refuge, the House of Correction for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, the House of the Good Shep- herd and St. Mary's Industrial School. All appeared in the main satisfactory at theso institutions, as will be shown by the reports of the several committees. The jury investigated a large number of chargos of violation of the Sunday liquor law, but the presentments were compara- tively fow because of the lack of evidence. The police were directed to report the names of persons who may have visited saloons on Sunday, as far as they could be ascertained, but the character of the witnesses sum- moned, for good or evil, precluded, in many instances, the presentment of the proprie- tors, whether the truth was or was not elic- ited. Many claimed that they went habit- ually to saloons or restaurants for meals on Sunday, and neither partook themselves nor did they see others partake of intoxicating drink; others paid social visits to the proprie- tors' families to take their children to Sun- day-school, or for other innocent or praise- worthy purposes, whilst the character and condition of others indicated that their visits were not so innocuous, although they assev- erated they knew nothing of the infraction of the law. It is the opinion of the jury that if it be possible to secure witnesses other than the several classes mentioned the balo- ful trafhe could be much abated if not en- tirely suppressed. In connection with the cases of selling liquor on Sunday, the penalty for the second offense being greater, the jury found it could only be indicated on a pre- sontment after considerable time and labor employed in searching the records of the court, until they were furnished with an alphabetical list of the convictions covering several years past. They would recommend the preservation of this important list, either for the use of future grand juries or for easy and speedy reference in court. The jury, in common with all citizens who value their birthright, deem the preserva- tion of the inviolability of the ballot-box unequivocally essential to prevent their boasted freedom from becoming a mockery, a delusion, "a tale told by an idiot." In approaching, therefore, cases of violation of the election laws (brought invariably by prı- vate citizens) they, representing perhaps every degree of political opinion in the community, not only determined to investigate such cases entirely freed from partisan bias, but did so. They found a number of presentiments, and from the testimony before them, both oral and written, they feel constrained to agree with their immediato predecessors that some of the election ofhcers displayed either ignor- ance of their high duties, or what the jury rezard as its equivalents-treachery and cor- ruption. It is earnestly hoped that the statutes may be so remodeled as to better accomplish the prevention as well as the detection and punishment of fraud. Strict attention and earnest investigation have been given to alleged violations of the law regarding gaming and lotteries, espe- cially policy-writing, resulting in a number of presentments, which were promptly made whenever it was possible to secure proper evidence. With continued and increased vigilance on the part of the police, it is be- lieved these serious evils may be effectually stamped out. Various complaints were made of infrac- tions of the insurance laws, which are said to prevail. In some cases presentments were found, and in others manifest evasions of the law were exhibited. The Legislature is urged to make such modification of the stat- utes as will prevent these evasions, in justico to the many citizens legitimately engaged in this important and honorable business. The attention of the court is respectfully called to the inadequate accommodation for witnesses awaiting their calls for examina- tion. The space in the ante-room is too con- tracted for the large numbers sometimes summoned, and the offices for the male and female witnesses are separated only by a thin partition, the top to which is several feet below the ceiling. It is recommended that this may be corrected in the near future. The grand jury take occasion to tender their sincere thanks for the able, kind and courteous assistance in the work received from the court, the State's attorney, the clerk and their assistants and deputies. Re- spectfully submitted. HENRY C. WAGNER, Foreman. Baltimore, May 7, 1887. The committee on the House of the Good Shepherd found the institution in excellent condition, and they feel that it is impossible to say too much in commendation of its useful- ness or the efficiency of its management. The number of inmates is about 270, many of them reclaimed waifs of tender age. The total number of inmates received since the open- ing, August 6, 1864, is 1,398 Of these 883 were returned to their friends, 231 left of their own accord, 86 died, and 193 remain at present. The number committed was 338; released, 209; at present committed, 69. None committed are ever refused, although the meawre ap- propriation of the State is soon exhausted. It is recommended that the appropriation, for rially increased. the sake of justice and humanity, be mate- The committee on the penitentiary report that it is remarkably cleanly and boro ovi- dences of discipline and general good gov- ernment. The contract for shoes having ex- pired, it has necessarily thrown some 150 of the convicts out of employment, but your committee have no doubt that Warden Horu will soon find employment for those men. The committee on the jail report that it is in good order, and has 414 prisoners well cared for. The reports of the various committees highly commend the management of the House of Refuge, Bayview Asylum, Spring Grove Asylum, the Colored House of Refor- mation at Cheltenham, the House of Correc- tion and St. Mary's Industrial School. The names of the retiring grand jurors are as follows: Henry C. Wagner, T. Burling Hull, Robert W. Hays, John Meeth, Thomas K. Turner, William Brown, John T. Bishop, Asa Needham, George R. Callis, Elias Rosen- baum, Jr., James S. Allison, Sr., Christopher C. Speed, Alexander R. Barrow, George A. Reed, William J. Gray, Jesso V. Ely, Bonja- nmin F. Clark, John P. Merritt, Jacob H. Timanus, William F. C. Gerhardt, Frank H. Kampe, Jas. R. Seager, Delaware C. Thomas. Just before the final adjournment Mr. Henry C. Wagner, the foreman, was presented by the grand jury with a beautiful silver water service, consisting of a swinging pitcher, goblets and slop bowl. Mr. George A. Reed made the presentation speech, and Mr. Wagner responded gracefully, although taken completely by surprise. Mr. Wm. F. U. Gerhardt, secretary, was presented on be- half of the grand jury with a gold-headed cane, and Mr. George A. Reed, presentment clerk, with a gold pen and pencil case. The grand jury found the following indict- monts: Geo Sullens, John Caton and Thomas Derwin, judges of election of the second precinct of the second ward; Jacob Stern- hoim, Martin J. Clark, Henry Gado, judges, and Hezekiah S. Best and John W. McMahon, clerks of election of the second precinct of the thirteenth ward: John C. Cavano and John J. Wilson, clerks, and Chas. Schultz, Jas. B. Yeakle and Frank Guildner, judges of election of the ninth precinct of the tenth ward, violation of the election laws. They also indicted William Armstrong for em- bezzlement of $200 from the Firemen's Insurance Company November 8, 1886; $7,000 on February 1, 1887, and $4,350 January 1, 1887. John D. Lisle was indicted for embezzling $80,000 from the First National Bank of Balti- more. The following indictments were drawn by the State's attorney and sent in to the grand inquest, but were returned to the court by that body unacted on: Charles Innes, lottery; Jacob Castelberg, perjury; Joseph Castelberg and Jacob Castelberg, conspiracy to defraud; Patrick J. Kenny, Patrick Wallace, Tilgh- man H. Blakeley, Thomas J. Nolan and John R. Delaney, judges and clerks of election of the second precinct of the tonth ward, con- spiracy to defraud at the municipal election. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Many claimed that they went habit- ually to saloons or restaurants for meals on Sunday, and neither partook themselves nor did they see others partake of intoxicating drink; others paid social visits to the proprie- tors' families to take their children to Sun- day-school, or for other innocent or praise- worthy purposes, whilst the character and condition of others indicated that their visits were not so innocuous, although they assev- erated they knew nothing of the infraction of the law. title: GRAND JURY REPORTS: SUGGESTIONS FOR IMPROVEMENTS IN LAWS--HIGH LICENSE FAVORED--OTHER MATTERS
full_text: GRAND JURY REPORTS, Suggestions for Improvements in Laws- High License Favored-Other Matters, [Reported for the Baltimore Sun.I The grand jury for the May term of the Criminal Court at the end of their sessions, Saturday, made the following report of their proceedings: "During their sessions seventy days 1,227 cases came before them, of which 474 were presented and 753 dis- missed; 2,746 witnesses were examined. A number of the cases which were disposed of were of a very unimportant character, and it is to be regretted that there is no court before which such cases could be taken and finally disposed of without involving so much loss of time both to grand juries and courts, as well as heavy expenses to the city. Another class of cases were those for vio- lation of the Sunday liquor law. Of these a large majority were dismissed for lack of legal evidence to convict, although from the reports of the officers on their respective beats, the character of the saloon presented and of the various witnesses examined, the grand jury are satisfied that the law is being constantly violated. Somewhat simi- lar difficulties apply to cases involving viola- tions of the lottery laws, and to abate these evils some changes in the existing laws or practices are necessary. The grand jury are of opinion that an effective measure to at least abate the evil of the violation of the liquor law would be the enactment of a high license law, with a proviso that not more than one place for the sale of liquor should be allowed in any one block. "The grand jury made the customary official visits to the various public institutions in the city and counties, penitentiary, Bayview, jail, Spring Grove, House of Retuge, St. Mary's Industrial School, House of Correc- tion, House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, House of the Good Shepherd. All of these, with the exception of one, were found to be in a very satisfactory condition, cleanly and well managed, as far as we could judge. The one exception was the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Chelten- ham. That institution was not in a satisfac- tory condition, but it was explained that this was a temporary and unusual state of things, and that arrangements were being made to put the institution in its usual efficient condi- tion. "In the jail were found a number of boys from 13 to 17 years of age among adult pris- oners. If it be necessary to send such youths to jali, arrangements should be made to keep them apart from the older prisoners, but when practicable it would be advisable to send them to some reformatory. In regard to Bayview Asylum, the accommodation for the insane inmates is undoubtedly insufi- cient, and the grand jury are of opinion that it would be a wise thing for the city council to make such an appropriation as may be nec- essary for additional accommodation, so that the male and female patients may be kept in separate buildings, and this unfortunate class in our community be made more comfortable. At Spring Grove Asylum the accommodation is also inadequate for the large number of patients, particularly in the kitchen and do- Emestic portions. These were originally erected to suffice for a household of 300 patients and attendants, whereas now the number is about 500. The State has always made liberal appropriations for this noble charity, and the addition now required would add to its efficiency and would not be a costly improvement. The House of Refuge has been in existence about 40 years, and has done a grand work for the city and State in reclaiming thousands of erring boys and making them into good citizens. The age of the buildings of course necessitates a considerable outlay to keep them in good condition, but while everytning has been done by the board of managers as efficiently as practicable with the means at their command, a moderate appropriation from both city and State is very desirable at this time. "St. Mary's Industrial School for Boys was found to be a beehive of industry. The boys were found employed in the manufacture of cigars, iron moldings, clothing and shoes. From these a handsome annual revenue is obtained, and the boys are being more or less fitted to earn a living when they leave the institution. "The grand jury would call attention, as previous grand juries have done, to the un- seemly accommodations provided for the wit- nesses attending upon the jury. It is only needed to visit the wretched place where they are herded together to see that it is utterly unfitted for such a purpose. The room to which the witnesses repair after being sworn should not be open to the public, for it is notorious that persons interested in the evi- dence that may be given visit and tamper with the witnesses, and thus defeat justice not unfrequently." The report closes with thanks to the court, State's attorney, clerks and other court officials for courteous assist- ance. Signed W. W. Spence, foreman. The committee on the penitentiary ap- pointed by the court reported that they "made frequent visits to that institution, aud were strongly impressed with the excellent order and system prevailing therein. The discipline is fürım but kind, the food good and wholesome and the prisoners well clad. The reduction of sentence offered for uniform good behavior is one of the strongest lucen- tives to good order, and is one of the greatest triumphs of modern penal science. The sani- tary regulations are of the best, and coupled with the employment of the inmates, are productive of their very good health, appar- ent satisfaction and contentment, Of the 600 prisoners 361 are employed under contract, 60 detailed in performing duties pertaining to tue institution, 12 insane, 3 sick, 17 un- fit for any employment, 116 are unem- ployed and 31 are females. The large number unemployed is due to the loss of the shoe contraor, the result of labor agitation, and your committee would strongly urge upon the law-makers of our State in dealing with the question of prison labor to consider well how important a factor occu- pation is in maintaining the order, discipline and health of a prison. Signed J. B. H. Jeffer- son, Charles C. Homor, George T. Sadler, James St. La Perry, Mayer Stein, Charles Kettlewe Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: YEAR FOR PAPER THIEVES: NEGRO BOYS SENTENCED TO CHELTENHAM FOR STEALING SUNDAY SUNS
full_text: YEAR FOR PAPER THIEVES Negro Boys Sentenced To Chelten- ham For Stealing Sun- day Suns. A year each in Cheltenham was the sen- tence given two newspaper thieves by Judge Elliott, and in passing sentence he declared that the business of stealing newspapers from the doors of subscribers had to be broken up and that he would deal severely with any offenders con- victed before him. State's Attorney Broen- ing has instructed his department to push all such cases vigorously, and Marshal Farnan has been making a special ef- fort through the Police Department to check the widespread evil. Eugene Hall and Oliver Strand, both colored and each 18 years of age, were the boys in this case. They were caught stealing Sunday Suss on the route owned by D. W. Snyder in West Baltimore and held for court by Justice Henry, Police- man N. J. Carr appearing as the officer in the case. They, with others, had been systematically taking papers after de- Hvery by the carrier. Mr. Snyder set five sub-carriers and as many private detec- tives to catch them, and when seen at work the negroes gave their pursuers a hot chase. Strand escaped for the time. Hall. cornered in an alley, drew a knife and threatened to use it, but was over- powered. Juveniles have generally been paroled and older thieves given nominal sentences or paroled in cases of newspaper steal- ing, the small money value of a newspa- paper having an influence on the action. But recently in East Baltimore a negro thief drew a revolver and threatened to kill a carrier, and this boldness has add- ed a new importance to the petty crime. In every part of Baltimore recently news- paper thieves have been persistently op- erating, and one carrier recently made the - statement that "a race of criminals is growing up from the larceny of papers and milk bottles." State's Attorney Broening has recently had Detective Werner working on the problem of breaking up newspaper steal- ing, and citizens' clothes men of the va- rious districts several times have been assigned at points frequented by them. Now that severe sentences will follow arrest and conviction there is a prospect of less boldness. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Cheltenham A Model Institution, He Says
full_text: Cheltenham A Model Institution, He Says. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: "E. J. K.'s" remarks about the Cheltenham Reforniatory for Colored Boys are from hearsay, not from personal observation. Anyone acquainted with the institution and its superintendent knows full well that the boys get plenty to eat, are taken care of and have medical attention when slek. Boys are sent to the institution in poor health. but leave it healthy and strong. I am not connected in any way with this school, CHARLES H. SEGUIN, Baltimore, March 24. Rev. Mr. Zeigler Approves The Idea Of Agricultural High Schools. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUS-Sir: I wish to give most unqualified indorsement to the suggestion of Mr. S. M. Engle in to- day's Sunpaper that the State estab'ish county agricultural high schools instead of running on in a half-hearted effort to build a second-rate agricultural university. This larger question the State is not yet ready for, either from a financial polut of view or the further point of view of public sen- timent. Meanwhile, the agricultural high school is needed, can be readily financed and can find its proper and particular use- fulness in this larger scheme. To my mind, any plan to State universitize, according to the present talk, is to make a growing tumor of what-is-now but an excrescence. Oscar WOODWARD ZEIGLER. title: CADETS HELD ON MURDER CHARGE: WILLIAM R. BOWLUS DIES FROM WOUND RECEIVED IN ALLEGED HAZING PRANK INVESTIGATION IS BEGUN BOARD OF VISITORS HOLDS HEATED SESSION AT ST. JOHN'S FACULTY IS UNDER FIRE THREE OF THE ACCUSED FRESHMEN ARRESTED AND RELEASED ON $5,000 BALL--OTHER TWO MAY SURRENDER TODAY--BODY OF DEAD JUNIOR WILL BE TAKEN TO HOME AT MIDDLETOWN, MD., TODAY
full_text: CADETS HELD ON MURDER CHARGE William R. Bowlus Dies From Wound Received In Alleged Hazing Prank. T INVESTIGATION IS BEGUN Board Of Visitors Holds Heated Session At St. John's FACULTY IS UNDER FIRE 1, Three Of The Accused Freshmen Arrested And Released On $5,000 Bail-Other Two May Surrender Today - Body Of Dead Junior Will Be Taken To Home At Mid- dletown, Md., Today. [From a Staff Correspondent.]. Annapolis, Md., May 28. An inves tigation of the shooting of Cadet Wil- liam R. Bowlus, of the junior class of St. John's College, last Monday night by a member of the freshman class, re- sulting in Bowlus' death today, was made by the board of visitors of the college tonight. The investigation resulted in some rather sharp passages between members of the faculty, who were called before the board, and the visitors. It seems that the faculty has rather limited powers over the discipline of the school, and their recommendations, par- ticularly those relating to the dismissal of students' for hazing, are seldom re- garded by the board. At the same time the visitors seem to desire to hold the faculty responsible for discipline, not- withstanding that body is not given authority to enforce it. The rather potent effort of the visitors tonight to hold the faculty responsible for the events which led up to the death of Cadet Bowlus was the cause of much of the heat of tonight's investigation. MAY REORGANIZE FACULTY. After a prolonged discussion the board appointed a committee of five to consider- the question of reorganization of the faculty of the college while another com. mittee was appointed to investigate every phase of the hazing situation. In the meantime, 12 members of the junior class were ordered suspended indefinitely. There was much discussion as to whether the other eight junfors should share a similar fate, but it was finally agreed to retain them on the rolls, inasmuch as there is no evidence that they participated in any hazing. James M. Munroe, of Annapolis, made the motion providing for a reorganization of the college. The committee to handle this subject are the following: Chairman Moss, Mr. Munroe, Judge Walter I. Dawkins, of Baltimore; State's Attorney Nicholas H. Green, of Annapolis, and former State Senator Joseph II. Bellis, of Annapolis. I TWELVE JUNIORS SUSPENDED. The committee appointed to investigate hazing and report as to the best methods of eradicating it is composed of John Ia Chew, Philemon II. Tuck, of Baltimore; Nevitt Steele, Daniel R. Randall and State Comptroller Harrington. The 12 juniors suspended are: Oliver P. Winslow, son of Dr. Randolph Winslow, and J. S. Bowen, of Baltimore; Herbert Jump, Easton, Md.; J. T. Sadler, Cockeys- ville, Md.; Daniel E. Walsh, Westminster, Md.; C. W. Mowbray, Frederick, Md.; R. R. Ritchie, Lonaconing, Md.; J. E. Selby, Cheltenham, Md.; A. W. Williams, Prince Frederick, Md.; W. R. Nelson, Hebron, Md.; L. D. Fields, Pikesville, Md., and A. L. Fowler, West Annapolis, Md. The board directed its secretary, L. Dor sey Gassaway, to prepare a letter of reso- lutions to be forwarded to the family of Cadet Bowlus and a suitable floral design will also be sent for the funeral tomorrow afternoon. PALL OF SORROW OVER COLLEGE. After lingering for two and a half days Cadet Bowlus dled at 2 o'clock this after- noon at Emergency Hospital, where he had been a patlent since the affray. With his death a pall, fell over historic St. John's. The sympathy for the relatives of the dead lad was general. Nothing so tragic has ever been visited upon the old college. By the death of Bowlus the five fresh- men now out on bail on a charge of assault with intent to kill are held on the charge of murder. The warrants were changed ac- cordingly. Two of the boys, R. Valdez, a Cuban, and George H. Weaver, of New York, were taken late this afternoon and for a time were lodged in the county jail. YOUNG MARBURY SURRENDERS. A third member of the party, Fendall Marbury, son of William L. Marbury, was in Baltimore at the time. Accompanied by his father he came to Annapolis later and the three were released under $5,000 ball. The security was furnished by Mr. Mar- bury, Charles E. Martin, Charles C. Feld- meyer and Nevett Steele. The other two boys, J. W. Noble and Reginald Jones, are at their homes on the Eastern Shore. They will return here to- morrow and it is expected they will be similarly released. MEETING A SECRET ONE. . The meeting of the board tonight was one of the longest that has been held for a long time. Those who attended it were Robert Moss, chairman; Comptroller Harrington, Dr. George Wells, Frank H. Stockett, Harry J. Hopkins, Nicholas H. Green, State's Attorney for Anne Arundel; Bruner, R. Anderson, Philemon H. Tuck, Joseph H. Bellis, L. D. Gassaway, Dr. W. G. Ridout, Judge James R. Brashears, Charles G. Feldmeyer, Judge Walter I. Dawkins, Nevitt Steele, James M. Munroe, ex-Judge D. R. Magruder, John L. Chew and Daniel R. Randall. Prior to the meeting of the board, Chair- man Moss was asked whether the meeting would be an open one. He replied that he thought not, that the meetings of the board were always: private. "But do you think, in view of the gravity of the present case, which is to be, the only matter considered, and in view of the great public interest in it, that the meeting should be open? "No, I do not see it in that light," he replied. "We do not desire to shield anyone, he contſuued, "but I see no reason for an open meeting. After the meeting we will give a statement of what occurs. The board did take the matter up and decided that the meeting should be private. DR. FELL UNABLE TO APPEAR. The first business was the reading of the report on the shooting, which was made by Dr. Fell. In this report he gave a detailed account of the events leading up to the -shooting and the shooting itself, as re- ported to him by the faculty. The board was anxious to have Dr. Fell appear before it personally, but he was so overwrought by the tragedy that he was unable to ap- pear, although he was on the college cam- pus about 11 o'clock at night. The first witness before the board was Lieut. C. S. McNeill, U. S. A., the com- mandant of cadets. Lieutenant McNeill intimated pretty strongly that the system under which the school is run was respon- sible for the hazing that has been going on and he emphatically objected to any assumption that the faculty was responsi- ble. He intimated that the methods and policies of the visitors themselves were to blame. According to his story, it seems that four of the five freshmen who were in the room from which the shot was fired had been playing a game of tennis while a ball game in which the St. John's team was playing was in progress. A party of jun- fors notified the "freshies" that they were not showing the proper college spirit and that they ought to be out rooting for their college nine. The "freshies" were ad- monished not to let such a thing occur again. FOUR FRESHMEN "SLATED." A few days later, when the St. John's team was playing the Franklin-Marshal! College team, the same quartet of freshmen were engaged in a game of tennis. Whether they did this as a matter of bravado and defiance of the juniors or just because they liked tennis was not disclosed. However, the juniors were incensed, and that night the four freshmen were visited in their rooms and "slatted." This means that they were laid across a chair, face down- ward and paddled very entrusiastically with a bed slat, so they were unable to sit down for a couple of days. This occurrence was discovered by mem- bers of the faculty and the juniors responsi- ble for the slatting were reprimanded. This reprimand resulted in a class meet- Ing of the juniors on Monday night. It was announced at that meeting that one of the freshmen had "squealed"; that everything the juniors had done this year was known, and it was time that the divulging of in- formation was stopped. The investigation resulted in some rather sharp passages between members of the faculty, who were called before the board, and the visitors. It seems that the faculty has rather limited powers over the discipline of the school, and their recommendations, par- ticularly those relating to the dismissal of students' for hazing, are seldom re- garded by the board. At the same time the visitors seem to desire to hold the faculty responsible for discipline, not- withstanding that body is not given authority to enforce it. The rather potent effort of the visitors tonight to hold the faculty responsible for the events which led up to the death of Cadet Bowlus was the cause of much of the heat of tonight's investigation. After a prolonged discussion the board appointed a committee of five to consider- the question of reorganization of the faculty of the college while another com. mittee was appointed to investigate every phase of the hazing situation. In the meantime, 12 members of the junior class were ordered suspended indefinitely. There was much discussion as to whether the other eight junfors should share a similar fate, but it was finally agreed to retain them on the rolls, inasmuch as there is no evidence that they participated in any hazing. James M. Munroe, of Annapolis, made the motion providing for a reorganization of the college. The committee to handle this subject are the following: Chairman Moss, Mr. Munroe, Judge Walter I. Dawkins, of Baltimore; State's Attorney Nicholas H. Green, of Annapolis, and former State Senator Joseph II. Bellis, of Annapolis. I TWELVE JUNIORS SUSPENDED. The committee appointed to investigate hazing and report as to the best methods of eradicating it is composed of John Ia Chew, Philemon II. Tuck, of Baltimore; Nevitt Steele, Daniel R. Randall and State Comptroller Harrington. The 12 juniors suspended are: Oliver P. Winslow, son of Dr. Randolph Winslow, and J. S. Bowen, of Baltimore; Herbert Jump, Easton, Md.; J. T. Sadler, Cockeys- ville, Md.; Daniel E. Walsh, Westminster, Md.; C. W. Mowbray, Frederick, Md.; R. R. Ritchie, Lonaconing, Md.; J. E. Selby, Cheltenham, Md.; A. W. Williams, Prince Frederick, Md.; W. title: MAGISTRATES AT CHELTENHAM
full_text: MAGISTRATES AT CHELTENHAM Police Justices Pleased With Negro School Management. Eight police magistrates went to Chel- tenham, Prince George's county, on a tour of inspection of the House of Refuge for Colored Boys yesterday and, although they had two automobiles and the magis- trates were in a hurry to get back to their suppers, there was no one arrested for speeding. 1 The tourists were Justices IHenry, Say-) ler, Dean, Golden, McFaul, Levinson, Ul- rich and Supplee. They were greatly im pressed with the management, location and results of the colored school, which they are convinced is worthy of the support of the community. An exhibition drill was given for the visitors and they inspected the hospital, six dormitories and admin- istration buildings thoroughly. The honor system, they say, is a great success. In spite of the fact that there are no walls about the buildings, it is rare for a boy to break his word and try to escape. 2 Ernest Schwerdscharf Wanted. Marshal Farnan is trying to find Ernest Schwerdscharf, 32 years old, a gardener, formerly of Kolomea, Europe, whose par- ènts are ill there. He is believed to be in Baltimore and the Marshal is anxious to inform him of the illness of his parents in order that he may communicate with them. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Indorses The Maryland Agricultural College Appropriation
full_text: Indorses The Maryland Agricultural College Appropriatlon. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: Apro- pos the recent discussion-in your paper re garding the million-dollar appropriation for the Maryland Agricultural College, the writer desires to add his indorsement to the bill in question. No investment the present Legislature can make will yield better returns than one fostering agriculture and horticulture. The college, although it has suffered much from lack of facilities, has yet to turn out a graduate unable to successfully pursue his life's work. The legislators should meet the issue squarely. Do they want an agricultural college commensurate with the needs of the State of Maryland, or do they want to go on record to their constituents as neglectful of the two impot- tant interests of agriculture and education? JOHN P. MUDD. Philadelphia, March 20. Minister Pleased With The Way The Cheltenham Howe For Col- ored Boys Is Conducted. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: Kind- ly give me space to tell of my recent visit to the Cheltenham House of Refor- mation for Colored Bors. I was very pleased and surprised to find such a clean, well-kept place. There is no sign of real imprisonment there and the en- tire institution is not only well cared for, but is in fine physical condition. The energetic superintendent. John B. Pyles, and his staff are bringing great things to pass. The boys are well trained and are under fine discipline. Colored parents and guardians need not hesitate to send there their boys, who by force of environment cannot be controlled at home. Nor should they be afraid of their boys contracting any con- tagious disease for, under the attending physician, I am convinced that all cases are given the best attention. In looking over the doctor's report to the board of managers. I note that only three deaths have occurred in two years. and that there has been less sick- ness among the boys than formerly. A. ANGOLD BROWN, B.D. Croom, Md., March 27. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Arraigns Reformatory Institutions: In Which Prisoners Contract The Seed Of Disease
full_text: Arraigns Reformatory Institutions In Which Prisoners Contract The Seed Of Disease. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: Are people interested to know that our "re- form" institutions have just claimed two more victims from our country district? Cheltenham has just sent home to us a colored boy, weak and ill from tubercu- losis. A year ago he went away. appar- ently a sturdy boy. The penalty for his boyish wrong doing will probably be his life, and possibly the lives of his family from the infection. At about the same time word came from the House of Correction that a man from Crapo (12 miles away) had just died of tuberculosis. We have locked up these poor creatures and laid down the conditions under which they must live or dic. Therefore, we are all every citizen of Maryland - blood guilty for the health-breaking and death of our imprisoned awbreakers. There is plenty of money to spend for worthy pur- poses and some unworthy ones but not a cent to house and train and care for our prisoners in decency and kindness. To have in Maryland prison institutions where prisoners have enough care, out- door work and receation to give them bet- ter health-to give each man useful training and discipline according to his physical condition-to send them away from the present life, with a short experience at least in decent, healthful living-with the feeling that their State has helped them. while under restraint will this make them worse or more dangerous? Does anyone really think you "reform" people by robbing them of health or even E. J. K. Golden Hill, Md., March 18. life? Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Charles Washington Acquitted of Cutting the Throats of the Layton Children, [Correspondence of the Baltimore sun.j ELLICOTT CmY, MD., Sept. 12-The un- usual interest that was manifested in the trial of the colored boy, Charles Washington, which commenced here yesterday, for the murder of little Beulah Layton, and the at- tempted murder of her sister Sadie, at the home of their parents, in the fourth district of Howard county, in June last, had not sub- sided today. As soon as Judges Miller, Jones and Smith had taken their seats, the prisoner was led to the seat in front of the jury which he had occupied yesterday. Baker Bowie, the colored man who was in the employ of Mr. Layton, and at work in the field with him at the time the crime was com- mitted, was the first witness this morning. His testimony differed from that of Mr. Lay- ton in several material points. He said he accused the boy of the deed, but the boy de- aled it, and said a big white man did it, and ran soross the Beld away from the house. Bowie aaid he measured the track of the supposed murderer. He found a blanket in Layton's kitchen with evidences that it had been used to wipe up blood. to Mr. Mortimer Crapster, a prominent farmer of the neighborhood, was the next witness called. He testified that the boy said he saw a man leaving the house while he was re- turning from the spring, and said he resem- bled Baker Bowie, Mary Washington, mother of the prisoner, testified as to his age. She said he was ten. After the evidence of Mrs. Davis, a neigh- bor of Mr.Layton, Justice Owings, Sherif Day, Dr. S. A. Keene, Warden Lilly of the jail, and Deputy Sheriff Vausant, the State closed its testimony. The defense offered no evidence and stated its willingness to here rest the case. State's Attorney McGuire opened on the part of the State, and made a strong argument to prove the responsibility and guilt of the boy. Mr., Hammond opened for the defense, and was followed by Mr. Wootton, his colleague. Their line of argument was the doubtful tes- timous on the part of the state and the irre- sponsibility of the prisoner. The case was given to the jury at balf-past 2 o'clock, and a verdict of "not guilty" was returned in about baif an hour. After the verdict of the jury, which was a great surprise, was returned, the State's attorney, the boy's mother and bis grandmother went before Justice Cooke and made the necessary atidavits to commit the prisoner to the Colored Reformatory School, at Cheltenham, Prince George's county. title: EVIDENCES OF PROGRESS: THE COLORED STATE FAIR MUCH TASTE AND SKILL DISPLAYED EXCELLENT SPECIMENS OF WORK IN AGRICULTURAL, MECHANICAL, ARTISTIC AND HOUSEKEEPING DEPARTMENTS
full_text: EVIDENCES OF PROGRESS. THE COLORED STATE FAIR. MUCH TASTE AND SKILL DISPLAYED. Excellent Specimens of Work in Agrl- cultural, Mechanical, Artistic and Housekeeping Departments. [Reported for the Baltimore Sun.] The Maryland Colored Industrial Fair, now in progress at the Monumental Assembly Rooms, corner of Centre and St. Paul streets, is one of the strongest evidences of the prog- ress that race has made since they were emancipated, when the problem of freedom and citizenship was solved for them by their white brethren, but it was left to themselves to say whether they would keep step in the maron towards a higher civilization. Whether they could successfully compete with the other race in business, farming, mechanical skiller in the finer arts of life were questions that none could answer. In the Monumental Hallare gathered speci- mens of their handiwork that furnish the most gratifying evidence of their skill and thought. While the agricultural exhibit 18 not very large or varied, yet this is a depart- ment of labor in which their ability cannot be doubted. The products of the farm cou- tributed by the boys from the House of Reformation at Cheltenham are the clearest proof of the colored man's ability to produce the best crops when conditions are favorable. These youth also display stout, serviceable shoes, made by boys of fifteen to nineteen; cane bottoms for chairs by boys of ten, and caps and clothes by boys of fifteen. Going up higher in the industrial scale the mechanical skill is shown both in design and execution. No elaborate machinery is ex- hibited, but the combination tables and ora- dies, the design for an improved shell- thrower, the plow intended to level the earth at the same time as it throws up the furrow, all show an inventive talent in the race that may some day, with better opportunities. evolve something original and peculiar to themselves. In the smaller, nicer details of life one sees work there as skillfully done as anywhere. The cooking is so well done that a loaf of corn bread is often mistaken for a nice cake. The fruit canned by the Maryland cooks makes a fine display arranged on a loug table at one side of the room, and some of the jars of pears are especially fine and white. One jar in particular cannot be surpassed for pure whiteness of the fruit. Some of the most creditable specimens of work in this line are those offered by the children, of ten to fitteen, of the Melvale Industrial School. In needlework, plain and fancy, desigo and productions are tasteful and good. In some of the plain sewing by children of six or eight the stitches are small and regular. Handsomely made dresses are shown, and the fancy needlework in crazy quilts and pillows, plush fire screens, and other articles of adornment, all exhibit a taste that is culti- vated and refined. The war work, the arti- ficial paper flowers and the numerous fancy articles all show something more than mere One piece of work Just exhibited yesterday shows the mechani- cal skill of the race in small things at least. A very handy fellow, Isaac Jones, seat in a log hain about twelve or fifteen feet in length, composed of thirty or forty large links, all cut from one piece of wood, with not a break in any link. He also had two buckets, one hung at either end of a beam, and all from a single block of wood. Some of the chaire, sofas and other articles of fur- niture are neatly finished. A sulky, with barness, is also shown, and artificial teeth in handsome cases with glass covers. Imitation. But it is in the production of the higher works of art, the bower of idealization, that the capacity of a race 18 most severely tested. In the fair, the exhibition of such works is not very large, but those that are there give the strongest grounds for hope of something greater. The specimens are mainly limited to the work of the pencil and brush, there being no specimens of sculpture at all. In the crayon portraits of prominent men, by J. J. Dungee and M. B. Grinage, one sees good, clear execution, with faithful copy of the orig- inal. The likenesses of Dant. A. Payne, Isaac Morris. Fred. Douglass and Mayor Latrobe sre specially faithful. On either side of Douglass's portrait hangs the work of W. D. Henderson, one being an angry child done in crayon, and the other a scene of the wavesand a vessel done in water colors. They are small, but both well done. Among the most hand- some articles in the room are the placques, panels and decorated china. A placque by Emma Mitchell, another by Laura Stith, and a panel by Mary J. Ross, and several pieces of decorated china by L. T. Reaker are spe- cially tasteful in design, and the execution is also good. The whole exhibit throughout the building is one of the most hopeful signs of the ad- vancement of the race. Mr. J. H. B. Latrobe visited the fair yester- day, and was shown through the building anu expressed his admiration of the work. Large numbers of persons have visited the fair. It is to be regretted that no specimens of the musical talent of the colored people are offered, further than the music by the band. In this direction more than any other they differ from the white race, and evidence of such difference might have been exhibited. : Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: Suit for Three-Quarters of a Million, NEW YORK, Nov. 13.-John_H. Smalt, as assignee of a claim held by N. Corwith & Co., lead dealers in this city and Chicago, has brought suit in the Supreme Court against Gurden Corwith, a metal broker and member of the Metal Exchange, to recover $750,009 damages. Corwith for several years bas been the broker in this city for N. Corwith & Co. for the purchase and sale of metals. Assuch he has taken charge of metals purchased or sold for them. It is charged that be has fraudulently misapplied assets and property of Corwith & Co., made false state- ments as to his dealings, and collected and received large sums of money for which he refused to render accounts. Since January, 1887, he received more than 400 carloads of lead belonging to Corwith & Co., it is alleged, of the value of at least $500,000. wních he has not accounted for. In addition to this, plaint- iff alleges the broker bas embezzled the pro- ceeds of this, and has never accounted for it or for other moneys amounting to $750 000. JACKSONVILLE, FLA., Nov. 13. -The board of health today reports seven new cases of yellow fever, only one white. There were two deaths-H. Edmondson, a colored boy. and A. Veneraze, an Italian, at St Luke's Hospital Total cases to date, 4,518; total deaths, 390. The situation is regarded as very hopeful by leading physicians here. The weather is mild and showery. full_text: THE RELIEF VALVE CASE. DECISION BY JUDGE PHELPS. HIS OPINION OF THE TRANSACTIONS. Other News from the Courts Charged With Voting Illegally at the Presi- dential Election-A Murder Trial. Judge Phelps filed yesterday an elaborate opinion in the case of John E. Prunty against Thomas C. Basshor and W. Stebbins, which he heard in Circuit Court No. 2 some weeks ago. The three parties to the controversy were in partnership for the sale of the Prunty relief valve, the suit originating in a disa- greement as to the division of the profits. The opinion says that "an order remanding the cause for further testimony will be signed on application of either side, and if no such application is made within twenty days both the bill and cross-bill will be dismissed, cach side to pay their own costs." Among other things, the opinion says: "For more than twelve years these parties were associated in a manufacturing enter- prise in this city, and their multifarious and complicated dealings extended over a large part of the United States. During all that time there was never a balance sheet nor a statement. As a natural consequence for neurly four years they have had on their bands this costly and so far fruitless litiga- tion. Eighteen hundred pages of testimony, a wagon load of exhibits and a $1,750 audi- tor's report (not objected to as excessive by either side) compose the monument they have raised over their own imprudence. Among other moral lessons it well illustrates the homely maxim of common life, 'Short settlements make long friends. The leading principle involved in the case is one of public policy, and it is also one of grave moment, infinitely transcending in its interests to society any individual rights at stake. "The case comes up on Mr. Prunty's exсер- tions to an auditor's account. The account is credited with $63,233 92 by sales of Prunty relief valves, &c. On the debit side appears, among other items, one of $4,704 76 for com- missions. There is nothing whatever in the pleadings to explain these charges. From the exhibits and correspondence in evidence it appears that in order to make sales of the machines at the prices charged for them to the municipal corporations of various States for the use of their fire departments, the usage of the parties, to which both the plain- tiff and defendants were privy, was to effect an understanding with the chief engineers of those departments by which said officials were to receive contingent compensation in the event of the machine being accepted, generally fixed at the rate of 20 per cent, on the price of each machine sold through their influence. There are exceptional cases in which the sales appear to havebeen legitimate. The dealings with the city of Baltimore on ac- count of its fire department, so far as the evidence goes, were, with one disputed ex- ception, of this character. Prunty had been an employe in the Baltimore fire department. He and his invention were well known to its officials. He himself naively testifies that there was 'no occasion' for commissions here. "There was one transaction of $100 with Spillman in the early part of 1876 about which the testimony is conflicting. Spill- man was chieť ef engineer of the Baltimore city fire department until the close of that year. He swears positively that the $100 was a 'personal loan' from his friend Basshor. It never happened to be repaid by Spillman. It never happened to be deinanded by Basshor. It appears as one of the charges against Prunty as a payment made on account of the concern. That is the view of it to which both defendants stand committed as a busi- ness operation. Basshor, who paid the money, is more explicit. He swears that the $100 was paid 'as commissions for the sale of valves made to the Baltimore fire depart- ment. These are his exact words as taken down by the auditor. He further says that another $50 had been previously paid Spill- man on Prunty's order. Prunty admits the payment of the $50, but swears it was for Spillman's 'services in New York,' and not as commissions on any machines sold in Balti- more. He positively denies any knowledge whatever of the $100 payment, and it is in this connection that he observes there was 'no occasion' for commissions here. He says the $50 charge is correct, but objects to pay his half of the $100. "It is not the least of the evils incident to crooked transactions that they impair the credibility of all parties concerned in them. There is nothing for the court to do here but to believe the two witnesses, who swear to the innocence of all three, or else the one who swears to his own guilt and the guilt of the other two. The solution of this problem may be reserved until it is settled whether this and other issues are not merged in a greater question behind them." The court says that the first question to be considered is whether Prunty can enforce payment of salary for sales made by the inethod indicated, and answers it thus: "Ser- vices, a material part whereof consists in the corrupt solicitation o of public officials, cannot be recognized by any court as a lawful sub- ject for compensation." A large number of authorities are cited. "Take the traditional case," say's the Judge, "of the highwaymen reported in 2, Pothin on Oblig. (Evans) 3, under the name of Everet vs. Williams, one of whom filed a bill on the equity side of the Court of Exchequer against his 'pal' for an account of the proceeds of sundry watches, purses, horses, saddles, bridles, rings, swords, canes and other com- modities acquired by their joint 'dealings' with divers parties on Hounslow Heath, Bag- shot and elsewhere. The bill was dismissed for impertinence, the solicitor fined for con- tempt, all traces of the proceedings were expunged from the records of the court, and both parties were afterward executed." Judge Phelps concludes by declaring that the legitimate and illegitimate sales are so involved that no apportionment is practi- cable until the accounts are sifted and win- nowed, when an entirely new aspect will be placed on the controversy. The evidence showed that the accused was regis- tered in the first precinct of the fifteenth ward, his residence being given as 523 Han- over street, and his age 34 years. In the ninth precinct of the same ward the father of the accused, also named Charles Getzen- danner, was registered. The father's resi- dence was given at 105 Montgomery street. and his age 53 years. After voting in the first precinct the son went to the ninth precinct and voted on the name of his father. His vote was at first re- fused because he gave a wrong number and because the judges did not believe he was 53 years old, as he claimed. Afterward, how- ever, when he returned with the right num- ber his vote was received. The evidence for the defense was that the accused had been drinking heavily for some weeks before elec- tion and was intoxicated on election day. The accused testified that he was at the large fire on Sharp street Sunday, the 2d of Sep- tember, and got wet. May 30.----The an- Dual inspection of the House of Reforma- tion, located at Cheltenham, Prince George's county, took place today and was attended by about 50 Baltimoreans, who came down on a special train early this morning, and an equal number from the county. Warden Lee. of the Baltimore City Jall, was among the visitors from' Baltimore. The inspection was made by a commit- tee of the board of managers. The com- petitive drill between the various compa- nies of the school was won by Company 1, Capt. E. A. Loveless. Baseball and other games were played by the boys. A tug of war between the teams selected from the visitors was won by the team managed hy Mr. Frank Boltou, of Baltimore. Luncheon was served on the campus and brief addresses were made by N. C. Grasty, secretary. Baltimore City Charities, and Rev. George M. Bragg, of Baltimore. AGED VETERAN SHOOTS SELF J. A. McClary Commits Suicide At Tolchester Beach. Chestertown. Md.. May 30. Joshua A McClary shot and killed himself last night at his home. near Toicbester. He was the proprietor of the riding track there. He took his double-barrel gun, went into his yard and fired two shots. One shot took effect Just below his chin in his breast. He was a Union veteran, 72 years Told. May 30.--Samuel Butts, of this city, formerly of West Vir- ginia, employed in Angle's quarries, called today with his wife and three children at the police station and asked Justice Doun for a warrant for Harry Gaze, who he claimed hypnotized him. The warrant was refused. Butts said that on March 31, while em- ployed in the Western Maryland Railway yards here, Gaze hypnotized him. He said a spell was put upon him. Since then, Butts declared, he had been unable to sleep and can scarcely work. He says he is constantly chased by gruesome figures. from which he is unable to escape. He said he asked Gaze to revoke the spell, but Gaze refused. Gaze has mitigated his torture. Butts said, by singing the incanta- tion backward. full_text: WHAT HE THINKS OF US. MUTILATED BY MARYLANDERS. APPLETON'S LETTER TO GEN.MACFEELY Another Original Flag-The Strange Story Told by Widow McPherson- Miscellaneous News of the Exposition. Acting Secretary of War, General Mac- fecly, yesterday received from Mr. Eben Ap- pleton, of New York, the following letter: "I am in receipt of your valued favor of the 20th inst. urging me on behalf of a commit- tee of gentlemen from Baltimore to lend the star-spangled banner to that city next month. It is needless for me to say how gladly I would comply with your request could 1 do so consistently with my duty toward the preservation of that flag, and in order to ac- quaint you with the state of the flag at pres- est permit me to say that some years since the late Rear-Admiral Preble, U. S. Ν., who was deeply interested in the relic, had it taken to the navy-yard he then commanded, and in order to keep the banner from falling to picces had it heavily ba backed with canvas. In its present state it weighs probably 50 pounds. It is very unwieldy and about 30 fect square. It was badly torn by shot and shell during the bombardment of Fort Mc- Henry, and if it were flung to the breeze would be rendered absolutely valueless in a very short time. There is another danger to which this flag has been exposed and from which it has suffered greatly, namely, relic hunters. Incredible as it may seem it has been badly mutilated by these marauders. Add to all this the danger from transportation and that arising from fire and it seems to ine that I should bo greatly to blame were I to allow this precious relic to pass out of my hands. The people who have called on me at the request of the exposition committee to urge the claims of the committee to to the flag on this occasion have gone away assuring me that the stand I have taken was a pertectly proper one." Secretary of War Proctor, who was in Washington, said to a representative of THE SUN that he did not know whether the department would take any further ac- tion in the matter or not. The The closing sen- tence of Mr. Appleton's letter seemed to indi- cate to him that the Baltimore committeo was satistied with the stand Mr. Appleton had taken. Mr. Fraucis P. Stevens and Mr. Andrew D. Greentree, special agent in charge of the relies at Pimlico of the historical committee, con returned last night from New York, where they held several interviews with Mr. Apple- ton. They met Mr. Appleton at his resi- dence Thursday night and at the Astor House yesterday moring. In the course of the latter imterview Mr. Appleton became angry, Mr. Stevens says, and declare with forcible gesticulation, "I'll be d if you get that flag." Mr. Stevens will go to Wash- ington today to report the result of the inter- views and to request secretary Proctor to act in the matter. Mr. Appleton's flag was last seen in Balti- more on Wednesday, October 13, 1880, during. the sesqui-centennial, when it was carried by Mr. Wm. W. Carter, in an open barouche, and was immediately in the rear of the Old Defenders, who were able to participate in the parade. The Old Defenders who were in advance of the flag on that occasion were John J. Daneker, Nathaniel Watts, Wm. Batchelor, Samuel Jenings, Elijah Stans- bury, Asbury Jarrett, Wm. Stites, George Boss and Henry Lightner. All are dead now. ANOTHER "ORIGINAL" FLAG. Mrs. McPherson, living at 1630 East Fayette street, widow of Captain William McPher- son, one of the Old Detenders of Baltimore, claims that the flag which floated over Fort McHenry during its bombardment' by the British fleet is not in the possession of Mr, Eben Appleton, of New York, but is wrapped around the body of her husband and buried with him in Greenmount Cemetery. Sne Bays her husband cominanded a company which was stationed at the fort during the war, and at its close the star-spangled banner which inspired Francis Scott Key was given to him. It was originally sixty feet long, and during Captain McPherson's life was brought out and festooned about the front of his house on every national holiday. He died June 25, 1878, and shortly before his death asked as his dying request that the flag be buried with him, and Mrs. McPherson obeyed. WILL RECALL WAR SCENES. There is not an idle moment for any of the committees or clerks engaged in preparing for the exposition. As the date of the big event is approached the work increases, and thousands of details will be arranged be- tween now and September 9. General Clinton P. Paine, chairman of the military committee, and General Rob- ert Ober, chairman of the transpor- tation committee, have returned from Philadelphia after completing arrangements for the transportation of Pennsylvania troops to Baltimore over the Philadelphia and Reading and the Pennsylvania Rail- roads. All troops will arrive in Baltimore in time to reach Pimlico by 11 o'clock on the morning of the sham battle. The route for the parade of troops on September 13 will be determined upon next week. Col. L. L. Livingston promised some days ago to "make night hideous" by the dis- charge of big guns from Fort McHenry on September 14, and the warships will swell the noise to a wonderful volume. While these iron guns are thundering forth Mr. William Bona will add to the confusion by the explosion of 300 paper shells, some of them 36 inches in circumference, which will be tossed high into the air from mortars made for for the occasion. The smoke from the guns will at the same time be pierced by trashes of light from 3,000 rockets, none of them weighing less than a pound. One hun- dred rockets will be tired simultaneously from the ramparts and from seven floats Mr. Bond will have anchored in the river. Mr. Bond was authorized to take part in the battle at North Point, and will set off there 100 reporting shells. Copls. M. F. Jamar and E. H. Wardwell are working out all the details of the fight at Pinglico, and these, when completed, will be furnished the cominander of each battalion. Every movement of each command will be mapped out and given the proper officer. Gen. H. G. Gibson has been furnished the plans for the American army. Col. C. D. Gaither will in general outline follow the approach of the British army, under Col. Brooke, toward the American troops. Gen. Paine has issued the following order: "Mem- bers of the staff and aids of the provisional American army will notify Col. Jamar, inspector-general, of their acceptance of the position tendered. On this notice of accept- ance they will receive their commissions and be assigned to duty." MISCELLANEOUS NOTES. Among other notable exhibits at Pimlico will be those of the colored citizens of the State. They will occupy three sections. The first will be a display of the State institu- tions, the Cheltenham House of Reforma- tion for Colored Boys, the House of Refor- mation for Colored Girls at Melvale, the Insti- tution for Colored Blind and Deaf Mutes of Maryland and the Orphanage of the Oblate Sisters of Providence. The second will con- tain specimens of drawing, painting and other art work. The third will be devoted to an individual exhibit of various goods. Isaac Myers is chairman of the department of col- ored exhibits, and the committee consists of J. L. H. Smith, Joseph Warren, N. C. н. Groome, and and Malachi Gibson, secretary: Owing to lack of room, many exhibits from Southern States were refused. The railway lines of Virginia, North Cаго- points in those States half-rate tickets will lina and Tennessee announce that from all be sold to the exposition from September to 9. From points Juclusive, and good until September 21. and other extreme southern States the rate is two cents per mile or four cents for the round trip. The committee, R. W. Cator, Lloyd L. Jackson and Jno. R. Bland, are working to have these rates reduced. Mr. Charles H. Latrobe, engineer of the parks, has been directed by the Mayor to use the park rollers and watering-carts on the centre.g avenue, from North street to Cathedral, every morning from 6 to 12 o'clock until the 12th of September, in order to get the avenue in first-class condi- tion. The main exposition building at Pimlico will be ready for the reception of exhibits Monday. Col. J. Thomas Scharf, who has full charge of the exposition buildings, will be on the grounds each day to assist exhib- itors in the placing and arranging of their exhibits. Few marshals are more more occupied with the arrangements for the civic and trades dis- play than Major J. G. Pangborn. For the past month he has devoted his entire timo to the labor, and his whole office force has been employed in exposition work. The New York Life Insurance Compary has permitted him to make this use of his time and efforts, and it displays much interest in the progress of of his preparations. When the annex and the grand stand build- ings are ready it will be announced through the press, which will be about the middle of next week. Exhibitors are expected to get their stands, railings, etc., in position at once so as to have everything in readiness for exhibition by Saturday, September 7. All decorations and signs must be submitted to Col. Scharf before being put into position. Five pupils will be selected from the eighth grade in each of the male grammar and English-German schools to participate in the parade on September 9. They will wear dark clothes, and will met at the City College Tuesday next at two o'clock for organization into companies. The Veteran Corps of the Fifth Regiment has chartered the steamer Wenonah, of the Weems Line, for the bombardment of Fort McHenry. The capacity of the boat is 1,000, but only 300 tickets will be issued to the corps and its friends, thus insuring comfort and safety. A good concert will be furnished during the evening by a fine band. The potters employed by Brown, McNulty & Co., President street, are preparing for the exposition and expect to place 175 uniformed men and a drum corps in the parade. They will also constru construct a large float exhibiting their wa wares for the occasion. Frederick Smith will be marshal. John Murphy, George Lefevre and others have charge of the ar- rangements. Turf journals all over the country are referring to the Pimlico meeting in complimentary terms, and believe the race races will be the most notable of their class ever held. held in the South. She also has his old red silk silk sash, worn by him at the dam the battle of North Point. Jr., conducted a joint rehearsal he exposition chorus at the Calumet Club last night. title: The House Of Reformation For Colored Boys
full_text: The House Of Reformation For Col- ored Boys. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: I visited the other day the House of Refor- mation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, Prince George's county. The institution is situated near Croom, some 10 miles be- low Upper Marlboro and by rail 47 miles from Baltimore. I was impressed with the schools and its methods. The boys seem to be happy, well treated and well fed. The teachers told me that punishment is seldom required, but the discipline seems to be excellent. The boys are taught les- sons in school, how to take care of them selves. how to keep clean and how to work. The school education does not go higher than arithmetic. The work in which they are employed is farm work, broom-making and the manufacture of all the clothing and shoes used in the institution. The boys also do the housework, cleaning and scrubbing, cooking, washing and ironing. They produce the greater part of the food used and have fine gardens. The boys thus trained are in great demand by farmers throughout the State. I was struck with the perfect cleanliness of the whole place. There is nothing to offend either sight or smell. The buildings are fine, a central admin- istration building and six cottages, all of brick. They are arranged in a beautiful campus, shaded by fine trees and orna- mented with flowers. There are the usual farm buildings, all in perfect order. On the farm there is a station of the United States Government for scientific observa- tion. The water supply is pure and abundant, providing the buildings and bathhouses. The water is pumped from a covered reser- voir which collects from a number of near- by springs. The farm contains 1,250 acres and is three miles long, 500 acres being in good timber. The original tract of some 750 acres was given by the late Enoch Pratt and an adjacent farm of 500 acres was purchased. The Institution is governed by a board, of which Gen. Thomas J. clean_text: The House Of Reformation For Col- ored Boys. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: I visited the other day the House of Refor- mation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, Prince George's county. The institution is situated near Croom, some 10 miles be- low Upper Marlboro and by rail 47 miles from Baltimore. I was impressed with the schools and its methods. The boys seem to be happy, well treated and well fed. The teachers told me that punishment is seldom required, but the discipline seems to be excellent. The boys are taught les- sons in school, how to take care of them selves. how to keep clean and how to work. The school education does not go higher than arithmetic. The work in which they are employed is farm work, broom-making and the manufacture of all the clothing and shoes used in the institution. The boys also do the housework, cleaning and scrubbing, cooking, washing and ironing. They produce the greater part of the food used and have fine gardens. The boys thus trained are in great demand by farmers throughout the State. I was struck with the perfect cleanliness of the whole place. There is nothing to offend either sight or smell. The buildings are fine, a central admin- istration building and six cottages, all of brick. They are arranged in a beautiful campus, shaded by fine trees and orna- mented with flowers. There are the usual farm buildings, all in perfect order. On the farm there is a station of the United States Government for scientific observa- tion. The water supply is pure and abundant, providing the buildings and bathhouses. The water is pumped from a covered reser- voir which collects from a number of near- by springs. The farm contains 1,250 acres and is three miles long, 500 acres being in good timber. The original tract of some 750 acres was given by the late Enoch Pratt and an adjacent farm of 500 acres was purchased. The Institution is governed by a board, of which Gen. Thomas J. Shry- ock is president. He and one other rep- resent Baltimore city on the board, ap- pointed by the Mayor, and one manager is appointed by the Governor. Mr. Joseph J. OPPOSES $165,000 AWARD Contractor Alleges Mistake In Bid For Sewer Work By Rival. A protest against the award of a $165.- 000 sewerage contract to B. F. Sweeten & Son because the firm's name was not writ- ten in the proper place on the proposal sheet was filed with the Board of Awards yesterday by James Ferry & Sons, the next lowest bidders. The Sewerage Commission recommended that the contract be given to Sweeten & Son because of a statement that while the general superintendent signed the name in the wrong place, the bid was in proper form and the contract would be carried out. Sweeten & Son were represented by coun- sel. Mr. Ferry appeared in his own behalf and asked that the award be withheld until he could appear before the board with counsel. title: THE CITY COURTS: BITTERS SHIPPED AS MINERAL WATER--MRS. MALLOY'S ESTATE--NOTES
full_text: THE CITY COURTS. Bitters Shippedas Mineral Water-Mrs. Malloy's Estate-Notes. Willoughby M. McCormick, a manufactur- ing chemist at 308 West German street, was tried in the United States District Court yes- terday on the charge of violating the inter- state commerce act. The allegation was that on the 30th of last August Mr. McCormick shipped sixty cases of proprietary bitters to Columbia, S. C., but violated the law by marking the shipment as mineral water. The evidence showed that bitters are classed as first-class freight, and the rate is 89 cents a hundred pounds: mineral waters are fourth- class, and the rate is 53 cents. The weight of the shipment in question was 3.000 pounds, and the saving in freight by the alleged wrong marking was $10 80. W. T. Martin, of Columbia, S. C.. testified that he ordered the goods. lie paid the freight on min- eral water, but paid Mr. McCormick for bit- ters. Gilbert J. Badger,the clerk who shipped the goods, testified that the order was re- ceived from a traveling saleman, whose letter directed that the shipntent be made as min- eral water and not as bitters in order to secure the lower rates. He had done the sume thing at other times. Mr. McCormick did not testity, but the defense was that there was no evidence to show he had knowledge of the occurrence. The jury had not agreed when court adjourned, and they were given leave to bring in a sealed verdict. The penalty for the offense upon conviction is a fine up to $5,000 or imprisonment up to three years. A. G. Safford, of Washington, who represented the interstate commerce commission, assisted District Attorney Ensor in prosecuting the case. James Pollard conducted the defense. The judges of the Orphans' Court heard argument in the controversy between Mrs. Frances Boucher and her stepfather, James Malloy, both of hom claim the right to ad- minister upon the estate of Mrs. Eliza C. Malloy, mother of the one and wife of the other. Mrs. Malloy died early the present month, leaving an estate valued at about $20,000. Mrs. Boucher, who is the only child, claims the entire estate by virtue of a deed executed by Mr. and Mrs. Malloy in 1800, In which each renounced all claim to the other's property. Mr. Malloy contends that the deed in question was only a temporary surrender during his wife's life. The case was argued by Thomas R. Clendinen for Mrs. Boucher and George R. Gaither. Jr., for Mr. Malloy. The court held the matter under advisement. In the case of George Whitelock and Danl. B. Dorsey, trustees. against Sarah E. Westwood and others, Judge Dennis, of the Circuit Court, decided that the defendants, = who were the reversioners under a ninety- nine years' lease, must bear the costs of chancery proceedings to extinguish the rent under a covenant of redemption. The rent is paid by the trustees out of a lot of ground and improvements at the corner of Greene and Saratoga streets. It was devised in 1879 so that it could not be extinguished by a mere conveyance, but only under a decree of court after regular proceedings in equity, which were taken by Schmucker & White- lock, solicitors for the trustees. A formal deed of separation was recorded by Henry Bruuing and his wife, Christina L. Bruning. The deed recites that differences have arisen between theim, in consequence of which they have separated and intend for the future to live apart. All marital rights are renounced by both parties to the deed, and each also renounces any claim he or she may have to the property of the other. Neither waives any cause he or she may have for divorce now or hereafter. The husband's signature is in German and the wife's in English. The deed was sworn to before Jus- tice of the Peace Benzinser. Joseph Ratber, restaurant-keeper, applied In the Court of Common Pleas for the benefit of the insolvent laws. J. Fred. Requardt was appointed preliminary trustee. Accord- ing to the schedule filed in the case there are no assets, and the liabilities aggregate about $2,500. George Thomas, the colored boy convicted in the United States District Court of rifling a mail pouch, was sentenced by Judge Mor- ris to two years in the Colored House of Ref- ormation at Cheltenham. Thomas robbed the mall while mail-carrier between Easton and Matthews, Tulbot county, Md. The Rye Valley Mining Company was in- corporated by Miller R. Creighton, Lewis Cassard, Jr., Wesley M. Oler, Jesse L. Cus- sard and Wm. C. Carman. The incorpora- tion is for general mining purposes. It has a capital stock of $500,000, divided into $10 shares. Alonzo E. Thomas, of 1603 West Franklin street, the United States Express Company's imessenger under indictmerit in Washington on the charge of grand larceny, was released on $2500 ball by United States Commissioner Rogers.
