full_text: A BLOW FOR STALLINGS Defeat Of Yesterday Shows How Incorrect His Dope Was. ORIOLES ARE SOME HITTERS Sam Frock Is Slated To Pitch To- day, And Addie And Vickers To- morrow-Other Baseball Gossip. Well! well! that Oriole team certainly is going some. The way the boys hit yesterday must have made poor old George Stallings, who dropped.from the New York Yankees to the Buffalo Bisons, feel pretty grouchy. When the birds were in Buffalo on their long trip around the circuit, Stallings uon- chalantly remarked that when Baltimore reached the pretty little city in which he now is residing that the Bisous would be looking down at the Birds. That remark came when Jack Dunn wanted him to play a double-header. Now George, it's up to you, old chap, eat those words. Of course a victory is a victory, whether won by one run or 10, but it is gratifying to see the Orioles gather 14 hits in a game. Then, just think, two of those bingles were for two bases and one was for three. Egan got the longest hit of the game and Schmidt was on the job twice with doubles which cleaned up the bases. The Flying Dutchman also foudn a single in his bat bag and uncorked it at the right time. Jimmy Dygert shared the batting honors with Schmidt. He got three singles and each helped boost the score. As a matter of fact James is showing the fans his real hitting class. It will be remembered that he got three hits out of four times up in the last game he worked in Baltimore. Then to repeat yesterday simply means that his batting average will take a big jump this week. Incidentally, that young Dygert is pitch- ing some ball. Ilis last game in Baltimore would have been a shut-out had not Walsh lost a fly ball in the sun, and Jim would have whitewashed the Bisons yesterday had he not made a wild throw to first to catch a runner off the base. Just previous to these games he twirled two shut-outs. When Jimmy is right there is no better pitcher in the league, and it seems that L is just about right now. Sam Frock, another young clouting pitcher, is to work for the Orioles this aft- ernoon. It surely behoores Samuel to de- liver the goods both ways, as Dygert did. Your Uncle Reuben dropped into Buffalo with his gripsack in hand and found all his teammates at the Cheltenham Hotel. Everyone welcomed the Rube and he says he is ready to work. Jack Dunn declares he will work Vickers and Adkins tomorrow in the double-header. The Bisons will have ■ to travel some to beat that pair of pitchers. Mickey Corcoran had a great day yes- terday. He was in his home town, Buffalo, and every time he visits that city some of the fans yell and hoot at him. Mickey does not mind and the crowd must have had a pretty bad heartache yesterday when Mickey got in his two timely singles. Some player, that boy! He is as earnest as the day is long and works every minute he Is on the field. Murray, the outfielder Stallings picked up from St. Louis, was in the Eastern = League some time ago, but neither Dygert nor Egan knew him. In consequence Mur- ray got three hits. But the last time up Dygert went after him in the real style and made the newcomer fan. Bill Byers' hand is mending rapidly and the big catcher soon will join the team. Bill saw the game as played on the para- gon board and he rooted like sin. It is believed that Manager Stallings will send in Stroud to pitch against the Birds this afternoon. Stroud is considered the best pitcher on the Bisons' staff, but Mer- ritt was always regarded with suspicion too. Unless the indignation of the Boston fans prevents it, or some unforeseen ob- struction arises, Buck Herzog, the star shortstop of the Boston National League baseball club and one of the league's lead. ers, will be traded to Pittsburg for. Vin- cent Campbell, who has of late been show- ing considerable class. The story leaked out yesterday from one who is close to the National League lead- ers, and if Messrs. Clarke and Russell can get together, the deal will be put through. Herzog would be glad to get away from Boston, as he does not consider that be has been getting near as much as he is worth. The small-sized rebellion which he stirred up a few days ago has not died out entirely, and Russell's disciplinary measures did not cause him to warm up any to the boss. Campbell played in the game there yes- terday and he raced around the sacks like a greyhound. While he is new in the big league, it is predicted that he will fill Her. zog's shoes capably. While it is never considered good taste to say "I told you so," that Herzog mat- ter up in Boston turned out pretty much as predicted in The Sun. It was remarked in this colunin that it seemed strange for Herzog to be accused of loafing. One of the Boston papers recently published a version of the suspension which seems to bear out The Sun's belief. The story from the Boston paper follows: "Several of the members of the Rustler team are greatly perturbed over that fine which was slipped to Herzog and which caused him to quit the club. Some of them i even appear to see some of that 'Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin' stuff in it for themselves. "A couple of them were discussing the mix-up last evening in a South End drug store. Said one: "'I see where my money. for the winter eats goes glimmering if I don't heave them over to first between the knees and the skyline.' "'You've got that cased out correctly,' replied the other, 'and some time you'll slip over a low one which will rap the man- ager on the ankle and your job will be gone. I'd sure hate to be an infielder." "And then they talked a lot more-uot for publication, but just among themselves. 'Indifferent playing," the charge upon which Herzog was fined, appeared to be a great jokė with all but the infielder. "'I've played on several baseball clubs since I first broke into the minors from the backwoods,' said one, but this is the first time I ever knew that a first base. mán's inability to protect his shins was classed as indifferent playing on the part of the man who barked the shins with a baseball.' "'Herzog's offense was that Tenney couldn't stand the kidding of the New 1 York players. Herzog made a couple of throws that a first baseman would have smothered. but they salled past first and went to the grandstand. Then came the kidding froin the New York bench, and 1 1 that night Herzog was fined. Oh, that in- different playing stuff is great.' "Then they all started down to Revere 1 to spend the evening throwing balls at an African Dodger, just for practice." Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: WIRELESS HERO'S FIRST TRIP

Philadelphia, Aug. 30.-"Jack" Sheetz, the 16-year-old wireless operator whose heroism saved the lives of the passengers and crew of the Lexington, is a Philadel- phia boy This was "Jack's" first trip on the Lex- ington, though he had made journeys on other vessels equipped with wireless. His spirit of adventure Inspired in him a de- sire to visit every port on the coast. For some time past he has been an en- thusiastic amateur, operating a plant of his own at his home in Wyncote, a suburb. Recently he passed an unusually good ex- amination at the Philadelphia Navy Yard, Accordingly he applied to a wireless school here after his school days were over for the summer, and he was soon given a berth on a steamer, making trips on the Indian and other liners before being as- signed to the Lexington on August 22 for his first trip. "Jack's" father, who is a well-to-do business man, was delighted to hear that his boy is a hero. He says he will quit after this experience, however, as he was only working during his vacation period to improve his knowledge of wireless teleg raphy. Early in September "Jack" will return to his studies at the Cheltenham High School, Elkins Park, near Phila- delphia. PHOSPHATE SCHOONER SINKS Malcolm B. Seavey, Bound For Bal- timore, Lost Off Carolina Coast. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] New York, Aug. 30.-According to a wireless dispatch received here today from Captain Kemble, of the Clyde lines Mo- hawk, the schooner Malcolm B. Seavey, bound for Baltimore from Port Tampa with phosphate rock, has been sunk off Georgetown, S. C. A seaman is reported missing, but the remainder of the crew were saved. The Malcolm B. Seavey was commanded by Capt. Henry Dodge, and her cargo was consigned to the Piedmont-Mount Airy Company, of Baltimore. The schooner was consigned to Gray, Irelan & Co., ship- builders. She was a four-master, built at Bath, Maine, in 1901, by the Gardiner G. Deer. ing Company, managing owners of the vessel. The Seavey was 204 feet long. 40 feet beam and 21 feet 5 inches molded depth and registeed 1,247 tons gross. Cap. tain Dodge was part owner of the vessel. For many years the schooner had been visiting Baltimore, bringing in phosphate rock and returning to the South with ore. For some time she had been under a time contract with the Piedmont-Mount Airy Company. Crew At Pumps Two Days. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.) Southport, N. C., Aug. 30.-Stripped of her head sails and leaking badly, the schooner Florence M. Pinley, disabled off Cape Hatteras by the hurricane that swept the Carolina coast. pas picked up yes- terday by the tug Thermometer and towed to this port for repairs. The schooner was in a sorry plight, and the crew was obliged to man the pumpא. from early Monday morning until the tug came to the rescue the following day.

[Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] Laurel, Md., June 28.-The first spring. meeting given by the Laurel Four-County Fair Association began at the Laurel course' today. The entry list promised good rác, ing and the first day's sport proved that it was not a false promise. The first event was for the 2.15 class of pacers. Six started. Every heat was a horse race from start to finish. The first two beats were closely contested. Andy N. J., a horse from Reading, Pa.. proved to be the gamer and won out. He was forced to pace the ürst mile in 2.144 by Clinton M., another Pennsylvania' en- try. title: Baltimoreans At Spring Resorts: On The Boardwalk
full_text: Baltimoreans At Spring Resorts On The Boardwalk ATLANTIC CITY, April 8. None sense three days of rain short- ened the week and in another sense lengthened it. Still, to those fortu- nate enough to be quartered in the tur- reted and pinnacled towers that border the beach front, the downpour made little dif. ference.  While it was not possible on those days to parade the boardwalk in a motor coat, still the great parlors, reception halls and exchanges in the hotels offered a fine promenade. Last Sunday was delightful, and if the promise of the last day or two is kept, tomorrow will be another wonderful day. So few, if any, of the visitors in the crowds that now are here have any reason to complain. As has been the custom for some years the premier Mask and Wig performance is set for the night before Easter in one of the boardwalk playhouses. Nothing could show more vividly how easy it is to lose one's self here than the discovery that the 13-year-old boy, Bernard Rogers, missing from Philadelphia, has been tending ponies on the beach front opposite the IHotel Chalfonte for 10 days, while the police of every city in the land hunted for him in vain. Thousands saw the boy every day; he wore the silver spectacles be had always worn and went under his own name, and yet nobody rec- ognized him in that week and a half. Edward McLean, of Washington; Miss Amy I. Dupont, of Wilmington; Miss Clara Belle Welsh and George Rohlig are among those who have made early box reserva- tion for the Horse Show, to be held on the Million-Dollar Pier April 19, 20, 21 and 22. There are many visitors from Baltimore, some in almost all of the hotels. Mrs. Henry Warfield Ransom has taken a Ventnor cottage. Her daughter is to be married in the fall, it will be recalled, to Benson Mann, Jr., of Philadelphia. Another new cottager in the Chelsea dis- trict is the daughter of the late Senator Elkins, of West Virginia, Mrs. Oliphant. Mrs. Harry Lee Taft, of Chicago, who married a nephew of the President, has apartments at the Marlborough-Blenheim and is to remain until after Easter. Mrs. Taft has been entertained in Baltimore. Mr. and Mrs. Frank II. Callaway have been much around the exchange in Hotel Chalfonte during the rainy days. Mrs. Cal- laway wore once an attractive house gown of wistaria silk. Mrs. John W. Marshall is in the Balti- more colony at the Hotel Chelsea. Mr. and Mrs. Parker Cook arrived in the rainy weather, but are to remain for the Easter parade. Mr. and Mrs. D. H. Emory and Miss Sarah S. Emory are at the Hotel Dennis. Mr. and Mrs. Henry Clay Matthews are among the recent arrivals at the resort. Mrs. Leonard Reeder and Miss Edith Reeder were on the Boardwalk in a rolling chair one of the clear days following the rainy spell. Mr. and Mrs. Thomas A. Whelan have arrived. Mrs. Whelan says it, is their in- tention to remain over Easter. Mr. and Mrs. D. H. Wheatley are now at the Ponce de Leon. Mr. and Mrs. Augustin M. Hopper were in the rolling-chair procession together. Mrs. Hopper has been ill and is here to get the benefit of the sea air. George Pleggemeyer is also conveles- cing. Mrs. Pleggemeyer is here with her husband. -Mrs. Joseph W. Jenkins, Jr., and Mrs. Edmund Plowden Jenkins have attended the band.concerts at the Million-Dollar Pler. Miss Marie Ragsdale has told her friends that she enjoys tlie resort and will remain after the Easter holidays. - Mrs. Charles R. Spence was on the Boardwalk in a single chair, her son Charles Walking beside her. Mrs. Andrew Melville Reid has decided to remain at the resort for Easter. Among the Baltimore people at the Royal Palace are Mr. and Mrs. S. S. Weiss. Mrs. Charles II. Wier and Miss Poe seem to enjoy particularly the musical events on the piers. Miss A. P. Reed and Miss B. Porter are registered at the Beechwood. Mr. and Mrs. J. S. Dew are at the Ra- leigh. Mrs. Isaac Wimbert Mohler and Miss Mohler will remain until after Easter. Among the Baltimore arrivals at the Grand Atlantic are Mr. and Mrs. S. S. Norris. E. G. Rittenhouse, Mrs. J. Rittenhouse and D. M. Rittenhouse are at the Shore- ham. Mr. and Mrs. W. M. Branch are at the Rudolf. Miss E. N. Short is registered at the Muncaster. In the Chalfoute are Mr. and Mrs. C. W. Jones. At the Roxborough are Mrs. J. W. Me- Lean, Mrs. M. R. Johnston, M. R. Johuston and Master W. Johnston. Mrs. A. W. Palmer is registered at the New England. Dr. Fannie E. Hoopes is still at the Chalfonte. Mrs. H. A. Stump is registered at the Cheltenham-Revere.. full_text: PHILADELPHIA AFFAIRS. Reading Railroad Company to Build a Great Abattoir.  HOT WEATHER CLOSES FACTORIES. Many Cases of Sunstroke Reported at the Hospitals-Value of the City's Tax- able Property-The Iron Hall Funds- Architects and the Bourse Contract. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.) PHILADELPHIA, Aug. 10.-The Philadel- phia and Reading Railrond has completed its plans for a great abattoir to be built on the river front at Port Richmond, and work will be at once commenced. The buildings will cover six acres, it is stated, and will have all modern improvements. It is expected that they will cost in the neighborhood of half a million dollars. They will immediately adjoin the great coal wharves of the Reading, which they may in time equal in importance, as far as trade is concerned, for the connection of the Read- ing with the Lehigh Valley will provide an excellent feeder for a trade, and the river furnishes a magnificent opportunity for the export trade. At this point the river is deep enough to float the largest steamships, and the channel is now being further improved by the government. The work on the Reading terminal is now going on very rapidly. It is expected that it wilt be in active operation in a few months.. A charter has been granted to the PPhita- delphia, Cheltenham and Jenkentown Rail- way, which is to be a trolley electric road, and is to connect the lines of the traction company with these two important suburbs. CONTINUED HOT WEATHER. The weather today was, if anything, even more oppressive than yesterday, the ther mometer reaching 94 on the street and the general humidity being very high. Scarcely any wind was stirring, and the little breeze that did exist seemed to have little, if any, cooling effect. Numerous cases of sunstroko are again reported at the hospitals and sev- eral manufactories were compelled to shut down.  THE CITY'S WEALTH. It is expected that the proceed- ings will at once be commenced in tho Dauphin county courts..  SUGAR IN FLORIDA. Mr. Hamilton Disston, of Philadelphia, and other capitalists bought up in Florida Vast tructs of swamps and overflowed lands and decided that they would attempt the cultivation of sugar cane. Altogether they acquired about 6,000,000 acres, or 9,375 squaro miles, paying the State 25 cents an acre. "We would never have dared to venture on this enterprise had it not been for the sugar bounty clause in the McKinley bill," said Mr. Disston. "This year we will make 6,000,000 pounds of sugar and draw a bounty of 51:20,000. Next year we will increase this output, and in a few years Florida will be a rival of Louisiana in the production of cano sugar."  PHILADELPILIA ASSESSMENT. title: SALISBURY'S DEATH: VERDICT OF LACK OF ATTENTION GIVEN BY A JURY OF INQUEST
full_text: SALISBURY'S DEATH. Verdict of Lack of Attention Given by a Jury of Inquest. The jury of inquest convened last night at the western police station by Coroner Davis rendered the following verdict: "Charles Salisbury came to his death March 6, 1893, at the Maryland University Hospital, from the effects of blood poisoning, caused by frosted feet contracted whilean Inmate of the Colored House of Reformation, at Cheltenham, Prince George's county, Md., through a lack of attention on the part of the officers of the institution." Salisbury and Hall, both col- ored, were brought to the Maryland Univer- sity Hospital from the Cheltenham House of Reformation February 8 suffering from gan- grene of the feet, caused by frost. The feet of both boys were nipputated February 10, and Salisbury died March 6. Hall was brought into the jury-room at the inquest in the arms of a policeman, and after giving his evidence he was returned to the hospital in the patrol wagon. He said: "My feet were affected with chilblains. I bad no stockings and my feet hurt me so I could not wear one of my shoes. I lost the shoe, and without stockings and wearing only one shoe I carried clothes from the hot laundry to a line in the House of Reformation yard and hung them up. As a punishment for losing my shoe I was put in a co'd cell, destitute of furniture, and remained there a week. I told an officer of the institution on a Sat- urday that my feet were frosted and the officer said he would see about it. On Mon- day I was released. I lived on bread and water while in the cell. I had no stockings and only the one shoe, so I wrapped myself, feet and all, in two light single blankets to keep warm. I was without stockings three weeks. I was taken to the sick-room Monday after I was let out of the coll. The doctor came to see me there Wednesday and dressed my feet." After being treated by the physician at Cheltenham Salisbury and Halt were sent to the hospital in Baltimore. Gen. John W. Horn, superintendent of the House of Reformation, said: "Both Hall and Salisbury were crazy boys, Hall being only eilly. It was not uncommon for the boys to take off their shoes while at work in the laundry, but they were punished when caught going out without them. There is a stocking factory in the house, and the boys could have all the stockings they wanted to wear. The institution is so comfortable that two boys discharged last winter returned and begged to be taken back. Salisbury and Hall were put in cells more to protect them from running out in the snow barefoot than for punishment. Hall had on two pairs of stockings and one shoo when bo caine to my office after being released from the cell." 4 Dr. C. C. Spruill, resident physician at the Maryland University Hospital, said: "It is possible that Salisbury's feet might have been frozen during the time he was said to have been in the cell." Others who testiſled were Charles N. Wood, colored, an inmate, Dr. J. Latimer, physician, and Nicholas Langenfledt, baker, all con- nected with the House of Reformation. Robert R. Scannel was foreman of the jury I of inquest. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: A Baltimorean Drowned in Texas
full_text: A. Baltimorean Drowned in Texas,-- Information was received in Baltimore yes- terday that Mr. T. Herbert Parlett was drowned June 11 while crossing the Canadian river, in Texas. Mr. Parlett was a son of the late Thomas E. Parlett, who was for many years an auctioneer in this city. About four years ago Mr. T. Herbert Parlott went to Texas, and bad since been manuging a cattle ranch in that State. On the da day of the acci. dent he had forded the Canadian river and gone some distance into the country on busi- ness. Returning he found the stream swollen with a strong current running. Neverthe- less he forced his horse into the water and into the current. The animal's strength was not sufficient to breast the rush of water, and both the horse and rider were carried down the stream and drowned, Mr. Parlett was not married. His remains will be brought to Baltimore for burial. Bequests to Clergymen Made by Miss Emma Jones, -The will of Miss Emma Jones, who died in Washington, D. C., June 18, was Aled for probate in the Baltimore Orphans Court yesterday. Ground rents aggregating $282 are bequeathed by the testatrix for the support of the rector of St. John's Protestant Episcopal Church at Beltsville, Md., and the Income from the money she has on deposit i the Contral Savings Bank is to be used to keep in repair her family lot in the cemetery of that church. Rev. Peregrino Wroth, rector of the Church of the Messiah, Baltimore, and Rev. A. J. Smith, assistant rector of the Church of the Ascension, Washington, are each left $500. E. Allen Jones and Stanley M. Jones, nephews of the testatrix, are left $3,000 each and Miss Jones's personal effects with the exception of ber wardrobe. They are also the residuary legatecs. The Late William Mackessy. He leaves a wife, ive sons and two unmarried daughters. The sons are William, Jeremiah and Joseph Mackessy, who are all in business in Washington: Michael and John, the last mentioned being an engineer in the employ of THE SDN. Reinhardt died yesterday at bis bome, 12 North Gay street of consump- tion. He was twenty-four years old and was a son of Mr. Wm. H. Reinbardt and a nephew of Police Sergeant Reinhardt, of the central district. He was employed as bookkeeper His Leg Broken, William Young, col- ored, aged fourteen years, was brought to Baltimore last night from Snow Hill, Md.. with his right leg broken. He was employed in a pox factory and had his leg broken by being caught in a belt. The boy was taken to the Maryland General Hospital. Mrs. Cochran was represented by Henry J. Broening, of Balti more, and the petitioners by Robert C. Coombs and Joseph F. Morgan, of the St. Mary's bar. The court heard only the at tachment case, and dismissed it upon the payment of costa. The habeas corpus anse will be heard July 23. The writ was sworn out by Isabella Wortb, mother of the girl, Rev Father Nicolage and Sister Ann Paquet, of Victoria, B. C., where the girl was obtained by Mrs. Cochran from an orphan- age. It is alleged that Mrs. Cochran has not compiled with the terms of the agreement under which she was allowed to have the girl. Before the Police Justices Yesterday.- Joseph Opperman, charged with obtaining 85 and a watch by false representations from Walter C. Crockett, was committed for court by Justice Hamilton. Amos Cole, colored, whose age is about thirteen years, was committed by Justice Anderson to the Colored House of Reforma- tion at Cheltenham, on the charge of being a vagabond and destitute minor. Walter Franklin, colored, was committed for court by Justice Anderson, charged with picking the pocket of Mollie Gibson, colored, of 713 Dolphin street. Mr. Chas. W. Barker, who for several years has been associsted with Harris, Brit- ton & Dean as treasurer, since the incorpora- tion of the Drm into a company has resigned his position and will go into mercantile busi- nees on his own account in September. Mesars. Richard M. Duvall and J. S. Rawi- ings will sail for Europe next Saturday on the steamer Mobila. They will be absent until September. Postmaster Warfield went to New York yesterday to visit Postmaster Dayton of that city, and to examine lato the workings of by the Bartholomay Brewing Company. A widow aud one child survive him. The axle of the carriage Fourteenth Ward Democrats.--The Four- teenth Ward Democratic Pleasure Associa- tion was organized at the hall corner of Lombard street and Arlington avenue, with John Joyce as president. Mr. Hoffman was road super- visor of the thirteenth district of Baltimore county. Condemning Milk. The milk inspectors yesterday tested the milk in fourteen deliv- ery wagons and condemned the contents of tive wagons. title: A PRISON FOR YOUTHS: PETITIONS FOR ITS ERECTION TO BE SENT TO THE COUNCIL CORDIAL APPROVAL OF THE PLAN DR. JOHN MORRIS, JUDGE HARLAN AND WARDENS WEYLER AND CONSTANTINE RECOMMEND THE SEPARATION OF YOUNG OFFENDERS FROM OLDER CRIMINALS
full_text: A PRISON FOR YOUTHS. Petitions for Its Erection to Be Sent to the Council. CORDIAL APPROVAL OF THE PLAN. Dr. John Morris, Judge Harlan and Wardens Weyler and Constantine Rec- ommend the Separation of Young Of- fenders from Older Criminals, The committce appointed Tuesday night by the Prisoners' Aid Association to secure the separation of young and old prisoners in the city jail bas gone actively to work. "We are going before the next meeting of the City Council with petitions," yesterday said Dr. John Morris, who was the author of the motion which led to the appoint- iment of the committee. "Our idea," he continued, "is to secure a separate place of confinement for boys under sixteen years old who are in jail awaiting action on their cases by the Criminal Court or the grand Jury. There are rarely more than eight or ten of them in jail at one time, and the cost of a corrugated iron annex to the prison, th about a dozen cells in it, would not be over $1,000. "This trouble has existed for years in Mary- Jand. Crowded six or eight in a cell, old of- fenders with young offenders, there is a great opportunity for debauching the moral feelings of these boys. When they leave prison they come out corrupted and bar- dened, almost sure to return to vicious ways and become confirmed criminals. Some of the youths in the city jail have been sent there three or four times or oftener. "If magistrates would use the power vested in them, they would in many cases commit these youths to the House of Refuge, to St. Mary's Industrial School, or to the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham, thus Saving a large amount of trouble and ex. pense to the city and obviating some of the evils complained of. "It is not my judgment that the right sort of a place could be found in the jail building at present for the isolation of these youths. That is why we want a cheap annex con- structed. "A reformatory for 'first offenders' is not what we are now contemplating, though such an institution as the Elmira Reforma- tory would be in every way desirable. But it is in vain to hope for its establishment in Maryland at this time on account of the great necessary expense. "The power given to judges of criminal cases by the last Legislature, allowing them to give first offenders a probationary period by a suspension of their sentences, has so far worked well and will no doubt prove a great blessing." Said Chief Judge Harlan: "The separa- tion of young and old prisoners is a reform of which I cordialty approve. That children accused or convicted of crime, often mere acts of mischief, should be associated in con- finement with hardened criminals is most demoralizing. Cases frequently come before our magistrates and the judge of the Crimi- nal Court where, for the sake of the public example, it is necessary that some punish- ments be inflicted. Even where there is a discretion to fine or imprison, the mposition of fine does not ac- complish the desired result. If the line is sufliciently large to have any deterent effect, it either cannot be paid at ali or will fall on the parents, who are pun- ished in place of the children, and yet the alternative is to put the child in an environ- ment that will likely make him a criminal. I trust that the committee of the Prisoners' Aid Association may be able to accomplish the object they have in view, and I should be glad to aid them in any way in my power." a Warden Constantine, of the city jail, said in his last annual report: "We are continu- nily receiving children as prisoners for tri- fling offenses, and children committed to the House of Reformation are also sent here when first committed, to be held until such time as the authorities are prepared to re- ceive them at Cheltenham. It is safe to say that when the boy comunitted for court and the one committed for the House of Refor- imation have had their cases disposed of they have learned considerable more vice than they knew when first committed. There is no remedy for it in this prison. It is impos- sible to entirely separate the children from the older prisoners. A place where all youth- ful first offenders could be sent, and no others, would be a great addition to the already great reformatories of the State." Warden Weyier, of the State penitentiary, says he believes thoroughly in a State re- formatory for first offenders between the ages of sixteen and thirty, such as the insti- tutions at Elmira, N. Y, at Huntington, l'a, and Pontine. III. "The young fellows sent to the penitentiary from the counties regard the older and most hardened criminals as reai heroes," said Mr. Weyler. "The amount of danger which a brains, active criminal can do to younger associates is very great." Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: KILLED BY A BRICK. Death of a Colored Youth at the Chel- tenham Reformatory. (Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.1 UPPER MARLBORO', MD., Sept. 5.-Last night Robert Matthews, one of the colored boss from the House of Reformation, at Cheltenham, was brought to Marlboro' jail, charged with causing the death of John T. Dick, a fellow inmate of the institution. Dr. O. B. Stone delivered the accused youth to the sheriff. It was stated that Dick was struck on the head with a brick August 3 and died September 2. The brick was covered with carpet and had been used to keep a door open. It is said that Dick had been tak- ing things belonging to Matthews, whien angered him and he picked up the brick and -threw it, knocking Dick down. The brick struck bim in the forehead and the fall in- jured the back of his head also. The injured boy seemed to be getting well until ten days ago, when a change for the worse took place and he died Monday last. Drs. Duvall and Stone, who made a post-mortem exam- ination, said that the wound from either the brick or the fall was sufficient to cause the death. Crabbing and Oystering. title: A BOY'S GRATITUDE
full_text: A BOY'S GRATITUDE, As Expressed to General Horn, of the Colored House of Reformation, Mr. Enoch Pratt has received from Gen. John W. Horn, superintendent of the Col- ored House of Reformation at Cheltenham, a letter which was received by General Horn from Frank C. Brown, a former inmate of the school, asking for some photographs and information about the school, to be used in an article which he said he was preparing for one of the Chicago newspapers. In his letter Brown said: "I have traveled much since leaving the school, having been to Europe, South Amer- ica and Mexico and all over the United States, always traveling alone and on my earnings, and have lectured, taught school and run stores and restaurants. I cannot be too grateful for the kind providence that made it possible for me to enjoy the benetits of such a school. I was a waif, having run away from Staunton, Va, a year before I was sent there. "Every State should have a school of the kind. They owe it to unfortunate humanity as well as to the progress of civilization." A New Cable Train. One of the new grip cars designed for use on the Calvert and Charles street Blue line of the City Passenger Company, was put in use yesterday on the White line, running on Baltimore street and Madison avenue. The train of cars, composed of closed grip and open smoker, created a little sensation ac first as it looked like one of the ordinars trains running backward. The usual order of cable trains is reversed, the closed grip car being in front and the open car a trailer. The new grip consists of a wheel device at the end of the grip car in- stead of levers in the middle of the car as have been used by this company. The wheels are horizontal, like the brake wheels on a railroad coach, one controlling the grip mechanism to grasp the cable and - the other operating the ear brake. The Council of Jewish Women, "Jewish Physicians and the Contributions of Jews to the Selence of Medicine" was the subject of a paper read last night before the Baltimore Council of Jewish Women by Dr. Aaron Friedenwald. The meeting was held at the Madison Avenue Temple, with Miss Rose Sommerfeld presiding. title: Entertainment by Schoolboys
full_text: Entertainment by Schoolboys. An enjosable musical and literary enter- tainment, concluding with "The Naval In- spector," a comic operetta in one act, was riven last evening by the small boys of Cal- vert Hall College in the concert hall of the institution, Mulberry and Cathedral streets. Recitations, essaye, vocal violin and cluri- net solos were given by Masters William J. Ostondort, Charles O'Donnell Lee, James J. MeDonogh, George S. Nicholas, Richard Mc- Sherry, Jr., Edward H. Burke, Clarence Mil- holland, Eddie Considine, George Yeakel, Harry Stallo, Eugene J. Cronin, Edward L. Flanagan, Frank II. Gunther, John M. Deven, James I. Fation, Charles E. McCusker, Wal- ter M. Farber, Frank H. Stallo, Samuel J. McCormick, Ferd. A. Muth and Harry A. Murphy. Choruses by the Juniors' choir and selections by the orchestra were also given. The cast for "The Naval Inspector" in- cluded Masters T. Reginald Wise, B. A. Hart- well, Ferd. A. Muth, William J. Storck, E. J. Katzenberger, William J. Portner and Wil- liam J. Carroll. Prof. A. J. Shenuit's Or- chestra furnished the music. Begging on the Street, Charles Benson, colored, aged twelve years, was committed to the reformatory at Cheltenham, yesterday, by Justice Schoen, for begging on the street. He was arrested on the complaint of Miss Laura J. Amos, an agent of the Charity Organization Society. The boy has but one leg, but he is an expert bicyclist, and was often scen riding a wheel. His parents live at 512 Preston street. Brune Hotapps and Emil Henkefent were also arrested for begging on the street. The men stated that they were farm hands and out of work. full_text: DEATH OF ENOCH PRATT He Passed Away Peacefully Last Night at Tivoli, His Country Residence. SICK OVER TWO MONTHS. One of Maryland's Widest Known and Most Prominent Men. Merchant, Banker and Founder of Bal- timore's Public Libraries-An Inter- esting Sketch of His Career of In- dustry and Thrift-Personal Charac- teristics which Give a Clear Concep- tion of the Man and His Methods, Mr. Enoch Pratt, founder of the great pub- lie library which bears his name, died a fow minutes before 9 o'clock last night at his country home, "Tivoli," on Woodbourne ave.. near Govanstown, in the eighty-ninth year of his age. His last birthday occurred September 10. Mr. Pratt had been sick over two months with kidney trouble. His death removes one of the most inter- esting of Baltimoreans. Active always, with but few days of sickness until the last fatal Illness came, Mr. Pratt was to be seen every day on the business streets in the centre of the city with a bit of sage advice for this one who asked it and a cheery or brusque remark for each of his thousands of friends. He was the most democratic of men, car- ing but little for the cut of the clothes worn by himself or any other man, and much pre- ferring to walk with a trusty cane alone on foot than to ride in his carriage. And yet, in spite of his years, he easily accomplished much more in this easy-going way thau many men of more nervous, hurried tem- peraments. Personal Characteristics, His build was slight, and this was made more noticeable in recent years by a de cided stoop of his shoulders. To a young man who helped him across South strect at the corner of Baltimore, not long ago, Mr. Pratt commented on his size by remarking that "These rapid-transit fellows don't seem to be able to see us little men." His mouth expressed great determination, but the most prominent characteristic of his face was a pair of deep blue eyes that never lost their keenness nor their lustre. When their owner was giving utterance to some witticism-and this was often these sharp oyes twinkled merrily. His Business Judgment, As a business man Mr. Pratt was charao- terized by sound judginent and by scrupu- lous care. He always lived up to the lotter of his obligations, and he was equally quick to insist that those who dealt with him should do the same. His common senso was large, his application to business apparently tireless and his habits unexceptionable. One of his most marked characteristios was the complete and thorough manner in which he scrutinized and examined the minutest details of every bit of busines that came before him. He much preferred to do this than to rely for success upon the efforts of his subordinutes. He dominated everything and knew everything, although always considerate of those whom he em. ployed. In Early Life, He started business in Baltimore sixty-five years ago with a capital of $150. This was on January 1, 1831, and Mr. Pratt was then twenty-two years old, having been born at North Middleborough. Plymouth couuty. Mass., September 10, 1805. IIis little capital had been accumulated as a clerk in Bostou, where he had obtained a position when ho graduated from an academy at Bridgewater at the age of fifteen. Two weeks before he closed his school days he had written a letter to an intimato friend of his family in Boston and asked him to obtain for him as soon as possible a good place in a wholesale dry goods house. "I suspect I am old enough to do business," he said in this letter. "The preceptor thinks I am. My school will be out in a fortnight and I do not want to stay at home long after it is out." "E. Pratt & Brother." Mr. Pratt's business in Baltimore was at first that of a commission hardware mer chant and later a wholesalo dealer in Iron, For some years he was in business by him- self, but later he took his cousin, Martin Ketth, into the firm. This partnership lasted for about ten years, at the end of which time Mr. Pratt took a younger brother into business with him, the stylo of the firm being E. Pratt & Brother. This brother was named David Pratt. The firm name is still to be read on the weather-beaten sigu over the Coorway of the warehouse at 23 and 23 South Charles street. After the death of his brother, his brother-in-law, the lato Henry Janes, became associated with him. The busi- ness is now carried on by a son of Mr. Janes, Mr. Henry Pratt Janes. As a Bank President, Mr. Pratt became president of the Farm ers and Planters' Bank in 1860. He had been one of its directors for many years be- fore that. This made him at the time of his death the oldest bank official in Baltimore, both in years and in point of servico. Ho worked untiringly in its interest, and made it one of the most stable of Baltimore's Unancial institutions. His fellow-bankers have on several occa- Hons honored him as their donn. They inade aim president of the Baltimoro Clearing- House Association several years ago, and when the Maryland State Bankers' Associa- tion was formed this last April Mr. Pratt was made president. In a speech which he made accepting the presidency he said he felt that there was only one position higher than to be its executive head, and that was to be President of the United States, a posi- tion which he did not want. Among Baltimore bankers Mr. Pratt was a leading advocate of the single gold stand- ard. When this gathering of bankers in April put itself on record with a clear-ring- Ing sound-money declaration Mr. Pratt led in three cheers for the resolution as a more emphatio declaration than a mere formal vote. Finance Commissioner, As one of the finance commissioners of Baltimore city for many yours Mr. Pratt's foresight and prudence in its monetary curities. He was one of the best-posted men affairs enhanced the value of the city's so on municipal finances in this country, and his prestige as a financier made his opinions much sought after and followed. It was in 1877 that he was first chosen a finance commissioner by a unanimous vote of the City Council! This was all the more complimentary to him personally because of the fact that the Council was democratic and Mr. Pratt a life-long republican. Pressuro of private interests compelled him to with- draw after a time, but in 1883, when the late James Hodges became Mayor, he Induced Mr. Pratt to return to the post, and there he remained unth April, 1894. Mr. Hodges had been a fellow-member of the finance com- mission during Mr. Pratt's first incumbency. In 1880 he was nominated for Con- gress by the republicans of the fourth dis trict, but this was declined. He was fre quently mentioned for the governorship. An noute observer of men and events, he took a great interest in politics and legislation. His influence was constantly felt in the City Councils and at Annapolis in procuring action upon important measures. At the time of his death he was a director in the Seaboard and Roanoke and Wilmington, Columbia and Au- gusta Railroad Companies, in the Bay Line -Steamboat Company, the Savings Bank of Baltimore and the Maryland and Peabody Fire Insurance Companies. title: THE GRAND DURY: REPORT FOR THE SEPTEMBER TERM PRESENTED AND THE JURORS DISCHARGED CRITICISMS AND SUGGESTIONS NEED OF BUILDINGS FOR CHILDREN AND WITNESSES IN THE JAIL THE TWO FEMALE MEMBERS OF THE BAYVIEW BOARD PRAISED FOR THE REFORMS THEY HAVE INTRODUCED--FILTRATION OF THE WATER SUPPLY AND EXTENSION OF SEWERS ADVOCATED
full_text: THE GRAND JURY Report for the September Term Presented and the Jurors Discharged CRITICISMS AND SUGGESTIONS. Need of Buildings for Children and Witnesses in the Jail. The Two Female Members of the Bay-. view Board Praised for the Reforms They Have Introduced-Filtration of the Water Supply and Extension of Sèwers Advocated, The grand jury for the September term of the Criminal Court, Mr. William Reed fore- man, was finally discharged yesterday, with the thanks of the court. Its report states that the jury considered 1,991 cases, of which 868 were presented and 1,123 dismissed. Sum- monses were issued for 6,769 witnesses to ap- pear beforo' the jury, and it examined and signed 1,208 election certificates, a greater number than sent before any previous grand jury. The report then continues: "We wish to call special attention to the report on the city jail. The necessity for a separate building for children, who are now Incarcerated with the older prisoners, and also a place for people detained as witnesses is imperative. We commend this to the earnest attention of the Mayor and City Council. The grand jury were much im- pressed with Warden Balley's kindness to the prisoners and the strict discipline which prevails in the institution. "We also desire to call the attention of the court to the report on the penitentiary, which shows an increased revenue to the State. Too much credit cannot be given to Warden Weyler and his deputtes for the per- fect discipline and the healthy condition of the inmates. "In the report on the Bayview Asylum we would call attention to the improvements instituted by the trustees. The two ladies appointed on the board have given much time and shown much practical knowledge in remedying the defects in the Institution. The establishment of the department.of trained nurses marks a great advance in the treatment of inmates. The grand jury recommend that a sufficient appropriation should be made to enable the trustees and Captain Lewis, the superintendent, to carry out the plans for improved ventilation and sanitary conditions, absolutely necessary for the health of the inmates. "The grand fury are unanimous in their appreciation of the devotion to duty, dis- cipline and zeal displayed by the police force. "We desire to tender our thanks to the clerks of the Criminal Court for courtesies extended during our official term." Accompanying the report were the usual reports of the grand jury committees. An Important one of these is the report of the sanitary committee, which, in part, is as follows: Sanitary Condition. "The sanitary committee reports that the general sanitary condition of the city, while not entirely satisfactory, is as good as can be expected under existing ciroumstances; that is, without any filtration of the water supply and without any adequate system of sewers for such a large city. It is inevitable that the contamination of the soil by pollut- ing matters, which ought to go directly into sewers instead of cesspools, bas much to do with the prevalence of typhoid fever and kindred diseases and it is a matter of sur- prise that the health of the city, all things considered, is as good as it is. Still, the con- dition calls for serious consideration. "The powers of the health department shall be amplified by the enactment of proper statutes or ordinances in order to render it more effective and to extend its work and usefulness. Sewers Needed. "The sanitary committee would report that it has visited and inspected several re- ported nuisances, notably one in the section of East Baltimore bounded by Patterson Park, Lombard street, East avenue, Fayette and Luzerne streets. It is a noteworthy fact that during the past summer but few fami lies in the neighborhood escaped malarial fever or some kindred disease occasioned by the foul and stagnant water in this section. This nuisance, as testified to by the city and health commissioners, can only be abated by the bullaing of sewers to properly drain these low lands. The matter has been pushed so far as to have two ordinances drawn by the city commissioner and presented to the City Council for an appropriation sufficient to bulld two sewers, and the committee cannot too strongly urge upon the City Council the necessity for prompt and immediate action. By this improvement a vast area of marshy land will be reclaimed, tax receipts will be augmented and the health of thousands of people materially improved." Building for Young Prisoners. The committee on the jail in their report commend Warden Bailey and Dr. James C. Clarke, jail physician, for the excellent con- dition of the institution. "We heartily indorse the recommendations of former juries and others in regard to the isolation of juvenile offenders," the report continues, "There is an average of fifteen to twenty boys there, whose ages range from seven to sixteen years, committed by mazis- trates mostly on trivial charges because of their parents' unwillingness or inability to pay their fines. It is a terrible object lesson to them, to say the least, to be condned in sight and hearing of criminals of all kinds and conditions, though the warden does all in his power to counteract this by placing them on a separate tler and not letting them come into contact with the other criminals at any time, as they eat at a special table for themselves. "By all means there snould be a separate building for these, and also for the detention of witnesses, who often suffer great hard- ship by being confined with criminals for no other reason than that they witnessed some crime and cannot prove to the satisfaction of the authorities that they will be on band to testify at the trial." Bayview Asylum. The committee on Bayview Asylum found the institution in excellent condition, but overcrowded. They recommend the pur- chase of at least fifty acres of land adjoin- ing the asylum grounds' on the east and a liberal appropriation for a large additional building for the insane. A separate ward or building for tən idiotic children in the ass- lum and the employment of skilled female nurses in the infirmaries are also recom- mended. House of Correction Overcrowded. The committee on the House of Correction reported that the institution is as well con- ducted as possible in its overcrowded condi tiou. They found the institution wholly in- adequate to the number of prisoners, there being but 230 cells and 465 prisoners, of a hom 28 were females. Colored House of Reformation. According to the report of the committee of the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham, the condition of that institu- tion is much worse than that of the others. In the report on that institution the commit- tee say: "The building designated as the hospital is a smail, one-story frame structure, sitting about one foot from the ground, on brick piers. There were six boys confined there the day of our visit, two of whom were far gone with consumption. The room was des- situte of comfort except the cots. There was not a seat of any kind in the room, and the slok boys presented a pitiable sight as they sat on the edges of their cots. The management of this branch of the institution is extremely bad, and demands immediate and radical reform. The sewerage is primative in char- acter, though there were no bad effects ap- parent therefrom. Several of the buildings aro in bad condition and suffering for needed repairs. There were several other less im- portant evidences of neglect, and on the whole the committee were not favorably im- pressed with the management." For the January Term. The grand jury for the January term were not sworn in yesterday, as two of those se- lected were excused. They were Messrs. Gaun M. Hutton and Henry Williams. At a meeting of the Supreme Bench Messrs. Ed- win F. Baker, 211 East Mount Royal avenue. aud Horace Noble, 8 West North avenue, were selected to fill the vacancies. The new grand jurors were then summoned for this morning. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

It is a noteworthy fact that during the past summer but few fami lies in the neighborhood escaped malarial fever or some kindred disease occasioned by the foul and stagnant water in this section. This nuisance, as testified to by the city and health commissioners, can only be abated by the bullaing of sewers to properly drain these low lands. The matter has been pushed so far as to have two ordinances drawn by the city commissioner and presented to the City Council for an appropriation sufficient to bulld two sewers, and the committee cannot too strongly urge upon the City Council the necessity for prompt and immediate action. By this improvement a vast area of marshy land will be reclaimed, tax receipts will be augmented and the health of thousands of people materially improved." Building for Young Prisoners. The committee on the jail in their report commend Warden Bailey and Dr. James C. Clarke, jail physician, for the excellent con- dition of the institution. "We heartily indorse the recommendations of former juries and others in regard to the isolation of juvenile offenders," the report continues, "There is an average of fifteen to twenty boys there, whose ages range from seven to sixteen years, committed by mazis- trates mostly on trivial charges because of their parents' unwillingness or inability to pay their fines. It is a terrible object lesson to them, to say the least, to be condned in sight and hearing of criminals of all kinds and conditions, though the warden does all in his power to counteract this by placing them on a separate tler and not letting them come into contact with the other criminals at any time, as they eat at a special table for themselves. "By all means there snould be a separate building for these, and also for the detention of witnesses, who often suffer great hard- ship by being confined with criminals for no other reason than that they witnessed some crime and cannot prove to the satisfaction of the authorities that they will be on band to testify at the trial." Bayview Asylum. The committee on Bayview Asylum found the institution in excellent condition, but overcrowded. They recommend the pur- chase of at least fifty acres of land adjoin- ing the asylum grounds' on the east and a liberal appropriation for a large additional building for the insane. A separate ward or building for tən idiotic children in the ass- lum and the employment of skilled female nurses in the infirmaries are also recom- mended. House of Correction Overcrowded. The committee on the House of Correction reported that the institution is as well con- ducted as possible in its overcrowded condi tiou. They found the institution wholly in- adequate to the number of prisoners, there being but 230 cells and 465 prisoners, of a hom 28 were females. Colored House of Reformation. According to the report of the committee of the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham, the condition of that institu- tion is much worse than that of the others. In the report on that institution the commit- tee say: "The building designated as the hospital is a smail, one-story frame structure, sitting about one foot from the ground, on brick piers. There were six boys confined there the day of our visit, two of whom were far gone with consumption. The room was des- situte of comfort except the cots. There was not a seat of any kind in the room, and the slok boys presented a pitiable sight as they sat on the edges of their cots. The management of this branch of the institution is extremely bad, and demands immediate and radical reform. The sewerage is primative in char- acter, though there were no bad effects ap- parent therefrom. Several of the buildings aro in bad condition and suffering for needed repairs. There were several other less im- portant evidences of neglect, and on the whole the committee were not favorably im- pressed with the management." For the January Term. The grand jury for the January term were not sworn in yesterday, as two of those se- lected were excused. They were Messrs. Gaun M. Hutton and Henry Williams. At a meeting of the Supreme Bench Messrs. Ed- win F. Baker, 211 East Mount Royal avenue. aud Horace Noble, 8 West North avenue, were selected to fill the vacancies. The new grand jurors were then summoned for this morning. . .

title: PLANS FOR A NEW HOUSE: THE COLORED HOUSE OF REFORMATION AT CHELTENHAM PREPARING TO ERECT A MODERN BUILDING
full_text: PLANS FOR A NEW HOUSE. The Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham Preparing to Erect a Modern Building. Messrs. Ghequier & May, architects, have completed plans for a new building at the Colored House of Reformation, at Cheltenham, to replace the building which was burned several months ago. The new structure will cost about $8,000. It will be built of Baltimore sand brick and will be three stories high, with a double pitch roof, covered with tin. It will have a front of 57 feet 6 inches, and a depth of 34 feet. A wing will be 31 feet 3 inches by 34 feet, also three stories high. The first story will be 9 feet high, while the others will be 13 feet high. On the first floor will be located a play- room, bathrooms, a cellroom and a work- room. The second floor will have a sit- ting room, a bedroom and a schoolroom. In the wing will be located a workroom and a storeroom, and also closets for the storage of the clothing of the boys. The third floor will have two bedrooms and two dormitories. The building, together with the old buildings, will be equipped with modern plumbing arrangements. Running water will be supplied from a large tank. Bath rooms and lavatories will be placed in a circular building, to be erected in the corner created by the wingand main build- Ing. They will be equipped with iron bath tubs and stationary wash stands. An additional building will be erected for a plant for heating the buildings by steam through coils of pipe. The con- tract for the work will be awarded in a - few days. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: THE LATE GENERAL HORN: PROMINENT UNION VETERANS TO ACT AS PALLBEARERS AT HIS FUNERAL TODAY
full_text: THE LATE GENERAL HORN Prominent Union Veterans To Act As Pallbearers At His Funeral Today. The funeral of Gen. John W. Horn, for- merly warden of the Maryland peniten- tiary and superintendent of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Chelten- ham, who died at his farm at Mitchell- ville, Prince George's county, on Monday, will take place this afternoon at 2 o'clock from the residence of his sister, Mrs. Mar- garet Ferguson, 1128 McCulloh street. The funeral will be in accordance with the service of the Grand Army of the Re- public, of which General Horn was past commander of the Grand Army of the De- partment of Maryland. Religious exercises will be conducted at the home by the Rev. Dr. X. Z. Wilson on the part of the fam- ily and the Rev. Jacob L. Grimm, pastor of Otterbein Church, on the part of the Grand Army, of which Mr. Grimm is chap- lain. The service at Loudon Park will be in charge of Department Commander Geo. W. Johnson, Gen. D. L. Stanton, Lieut. M. A. Brian, Col. John E. Hough and Capt. A. S. Cooper. The active pallbearers on the part of the G. A. R. will be Gen. David L. Stanton and Capt. Frank M. Smith; on the part of the Loyal Legion, Col. George W. F. Vernon and Capt. John R. King; from the Union Veterans, Capt. Robert M. Cameron and George C. Irelan; from the Sixth Maryland Infantry, Dr. Hugh A. Maugh- lin and Capt. O. H. P. Mathias. The honorary pallbearers will be: From the G. A. R., Col. Theodore F. Lang, Dr. George R. Graham, Capt. Frank Nolan, Col. M. J. Rose, Capt. E. T. Daneker, Capt. Louis W. Zimmerman; from Mary- land regiments, Col. Wm. A. MeKillup, of the Sixth Infantry; George R. M. Bow- erman, of the Fourth Infantry; Gen. Jas. M. Deems, of the First Infantry; Col. Henry A. Cole, of Cole's Cavalry; Judge Charles E. Phelps, Seventh Infantry; Col. William Louis Schley, of the Fifth In. fantry; Col. B. F. Taylor, of the Second Infantry; Col. Joseph M. Seidsberg, of the Third Infantry, and Capt. William Gib- son, of the Purnell Legion; from the Loyal Legion, Lieut. Noble H. Creager and Capt. Peter Leary; from the Union Veteran Le- giou, Charles L. Marbury and Henry Streib; from the Sixth Maryland Infantry, Louis Rosenberg and Ebenezer Harman. Mr. Henry Eppers will be bugler. The various pallbearers will meet at the G. A. R. headquarters at 1.30 o'clock and go in carriages to the McCulloh street house. Other members of the various com- manderies will asseinble at the entrance to Loudon Park and be in line under their re- spective different commanders at 2.30 o'clock. A simple service wil be performed at the grave. Instead of the former salute of cannon,taps and the bugle will be sounded. The members of the Loyal Legion met at the Carrollton yesterday and passed resolutions of condolence on the death of General Horn.

title: MISS DAMMANN IN A CONVENT
full_text: MISS DAMMANN IN A CONVENT Enters The Order Of The Sacred Heart At The Provincial House In Albany, N. Y. Miss Grace Dammann, daughter of Mr. J. Frank Datamaan, 731 Wont Lanyule street, has joined the order of the Ladies of the Sacred Heart, entering the provin- cial house of the order at Albany, N. Y. The members of this religious commn- nity devote their lives to the Christian education of youth. Boarding schools, parochial schools and orphan anylums for girls are conducted by them. The order was introduced in the United States in 1818 by Madame Philipine Duchesne, who founded a convent at St. Charles, Mo. The Society of the Sacred Heart was founde at Amiens in the year 1840 by Made- moiselle Sophie Barat. It was approved by Pope Plus the Seventh in 1926. The community is semi-clofstered and follows the rule of the Jesuits. One of the most prominent schools con- ducted by the Society of the Sacred Heart Is the famous Eden Hall, at Torrendale, Pa., on the main line of the Pennsylvania Kallroad to New York, about twenty miles from Philadelphia. This institution has been Itherally endowed by the Drexels and other wealthy people.  Now Homestead Methodist Church. Rev. Dr. Sharky. of the Minnesota Methodist Episcopal Conference, deliv- ered a mission address yesterday after- noon to the Foreign Missionary Society of Homestead Methodist Episcopal Church, of which Rev. J. T. Hart is pastor. During his address Dr. Sharky referred to the necessity of a new church at Home- stead. The present building is much too small and the congregation have already decided to build Plans have been pre- pared for a stone edifice to cost about $10,000. Sites are being examined, and it is expected to build this year. The present church is the outgrowth of a mission of Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church. In 1879 the present church was built. It is a frame structure, one story high. The congregation numbers sixty- five, with a Sunday-school of one hundred and eighty pupils.  An Address By A Woman Lawyer. Miss Diana Hirschler, of Philadelphia, Pa., lectured last night before the Balti- more Branch of the Council of Jewish Women, at the Eutaw Place Temple, upon "The Home and Its Relation to the Moral Life of the Community." Miss Hirschler stated in part that the mission of the home was to develop love and sympathy, and that the great truths preached by religion and humanity were Included In the idea of the brotherhood of man. She dwelt long upon the necessity of carrying love and sympathy into the business life and avoiding the terrific strife and struggle engendered there. She is a lawyer, being a member of the Boston bar, and recently admitted to the bar in Philadelphia. She is prominent in the Philadelphia Branch of the Council of Jewish Women.  Colored House Of Reformation. The twenty-fifth report of the board of managers of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Cheltenham, has been issued in neat pamphlet, covering the two years ended November 30, 1897. During the twenty-four years' existence of the institution it has cared for 2,120 boys, all of whom have been discharged except the present 296 inmates. The aver- age number of commitments is 150. An appropriation is asked of $17.000 in addition to the regular appropriation for current expenses. This sum is to be used for improving the sanitary arrangements of the central and family buildings, to extend the water supply and steam-heat- ing system, the construction of bathing arrangements, improvement of the hos- pital, for an ice plant and for a building for temporary detention of uncontrollable inmates. Frank Datamaan, 731 Wont Lanyule street, has joined the order of the Ladies of the Sacred Heart, entering the provin- cial house of the order at Albany, N. Y. The members of this religious commn- nity devote their lives to the Christian education of youth. Boarding schools, parochial schools and orphan anylums for girls are conducted by them. The order was introduced in the United States in 1818 by Madame Philipine Duchesne, who founded a convent at St. Charles, Mo. The Society of the Sacred Heart was founde at Amiens in the year 1840 by Made- moiselle Sophie Barat. It was approved by Pope Plus the Seventh in 1926. The community is semi-clofstered and follows the rule of the Jesuits. One of the most prominent schools con- ducted by the Society of the Sacred Heart Is the famous Eden Hall, at Torrendale, Pa., on the main line of the Pennsylvania Kallroad to New York, about twenty miles from Philadelphia. This institution has been Itherally endowed by the Drexels and other wealthy people. Now Homestead Methodist Church. Rev. Dr. Sharky. of the Minnesota Methodist Episcopal Conference, deliv- ered a mission address yesterday after- noon to the Foreign Missionary Society of Homestead Methodist Episcopal Church, of which Rev. J. T. Hart is pastor. During his address Dr. Sharky referred to the necessity of a new church at Home- stead. The present building is much too small and the congregation have already decided to build Plans have been pre- pared for a stone edifice to cost about $10,000. Sites are being examined, and it is expected to build this year. The present church is the outgrowth of a mission of Waverly Methodist Episcopal Church. In 1879 the present church was built. It is a frame structure, one story high. The congregation numbers sixty- five, with a Sunday-school of one hundred and eighty pupils. An Address By A Woman Lawyer. Miss Diana Hirschler, of Philadelphia, Pa., lectured last night before the Balti- more Branch of the Council of Jewish Women, at the Eutaw Place Temple, upon "The Home and Its Relation to the Moral Life of the Community." Miss Hirschler stated in part that the mission of the home was to develop love and sympathy, and that the great truths preached by religion and humanity were Included In the idea of the brotherhood of man. She dwelt long upon the necessity of carrying love and sympathy into the business life and avoiding the terrific strife and struggle engendered there. She is a lawyer, being a member of the Boston bar, and recently admitted to the bar in Philadelphia. She is prominent in the Philadelphia Branch of the Council of Jewish Women. Colored House Of Reformation. The twenty-fifth report of the board of managers of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Cheltenham, has been issued in neat pamphlet, covering the two years ended November 30, 1897. During the twenty-four years' existence of the institution it has cared for 2,120 boys, all of whom have been discharged except the present 296 inmates. The aver- age number of commitments is 150. An appropriation is asked of $17.000 in addition to the regular appropriation for current expenses. This sum is to be used for improving the sanitary arrangements of the central and family buildings, to extend the water supply and steam-heat- ing system, the construction of bathing arrangements, improvement of the hos- pital, for an ice plant and for a building for temporary detention of uncontrollable inmates. . .

title: TO REFORM BAD BOYS: COLORED HOUSE OF REFORMATION AT CHELTENHAM VISITED BY GRAND JURORS THOROUGH INSPECTION MADE EVERYTHING ON THE PLACE WAS IN EXCELLENT CONDITION VISITORS HEARTY IN THEIR PRAISE OF THE MANAGEMENT OF THE INSTITUTION--HOW ESCAPES ARE PREVENTED--SPECIAL APPROPRIATION OF $17,000 TO BE ASKED OF THE STATE THIS YEAR
full_text: TO REFORM BAD BOYS 4 Colored House Of Reformation At Cheltenham Visited By Grand Jurors. THOROUGH INSPECTION MADE Everything On The Place Was In Excellent Condition. Visitors Hearty In Their Praise Of The Management Of The Institution-How Escapes Are Prevented-Special Appro- priation Of $17,000 To Be Asked Of The State This Year. Members of the grand jury for the Janu- ary term of the Criminal Court, who spent yesterday at the Colored House of Ref- ormation at Cheltenham, were loud in their praises of the management of that Institution and of the apparent health- fulness and contentment of the Inmates. It is doubtful if the visit afforded less pleasure to the grand jurymen than to the colored boys, to whom it came as a great treat by affording them a temporary re- spite from the daily routine of study and work. Under the guidance of Mr. Nathan Thompson, superintendent of the institu- tion, the visitors thoroughly inspected every building on the grounds, examined the dormitories, schoolrooms, workshops and hospital, and questioned the boys to ascertain if they had any complaints to make. Everything was found in a cleanly condition. and in order. In some of the dormitories the beds were found neatly spread, while in others the mattresses were exposed for the purpose, as was ex- plained, of giving them a thorough airing. The boys were found in the schoolrooms, or workshops, according to the routine of the institution. All of them wore clean, neat clothes and all looked to be in good condition. They showed a propensity for begging from the visitors, but were very sly about it, so that no one should hear them except the one addressed. Not one of those questioned said he did not get enough to eat, but one or two said some of the boys did not get all the food they wanted. All the schoolrooms were well heated. There are seven principal buildings on the grounds, the administration and six family buildings. The superintendent lives in the administration building, which also contains the boys' dining room and chapel. The schoolrooms, dormitories, bathhouses and workshops are in the fam- ily buildings. One of the teachers also has his sitting room and sleeping room in each of these buildings. The teachers' bed- rooms are so arranged that they can look through wickets in their doors into the dormitories, so as to have constant super- vision over the boys. are The boys are free to move about the grounds at certain hours and they have abundant opportunity of escape, but the system is such that the absence of any who leave in this way is soon detected. The teachers and superintendents alert and watchful, and there are constant roll-calls. Besides, there is a standing reward of $4 for the return of every run- away, and this has proven a successful means of frustrating escapes. For the punishment of the boys each family build- ing is provided with a cell, but this was found in every case well lighted and clean. In the workshops the boys make and repair all the clothing and shoes worn by them and cane about 82,000 chairs a year. They also do their own laundry work, the cooking and baking, raise the crops, shoe the horses and clean the premises. The institution has about 750 acres of land. Last year there were produced on the premises 420 barrels of corn, 934 bushels of wheat, 27 bushels of rye, 80 tons of hay, besides large quantities of vegetables and fruits. An admirable opportunity to inspect the three hundred boys was afforded when the bell rang to summon them to dinner. From all parts of the grounds the boys of each class rushed to their respective family buildings. Then each class, in charge of its teacher, marched in an orderly manner to the dining room, where plates heaped with potatoes and turnips, with a huge slice of bread and piece of meat beside each, awaited demolition. All the boys re mained standing until they had chanted grace in unison and were given the signal to be seated. Then ensued such a clatter of spoons and such a rapid disappearance of food as to amaze the visitors. After the boys had emptied their plates each one was served bountifully with bean soup. After dinner the boys assembled in the chapel, where they sang hymns for the vis- itors, a number of whom made addresses. Not a boy could be seen in the chapel who did not have a smiling face, and the ap- plause was something tremendous. The institution has been receiving $12,- 000 a year from the city and $10,000 a year from the State. This year a special appro- priation of $17,000 is asked from the State, in addition to the regular appropriation, for introducing sanitary bathing arrange. ments for the boys, constructing an ele- vated reservoir as a precaution against fire and making other improvements which were explained to the visitors. A power house with a 75-horse-power boller bas recently been erected, affording all the steam necessary for use were the funds on hand for making the improvements. The members of the grand jury among the visitors were Messrs. Henry C. Mat- thews, Owen T Johnson, Joseph A. Mc- Kellip and Charles M. Waters, of the committee on the institution; Mr. Henry C. Reed, assistant foreman, who is also one of the institution's board of managers, and Messrs. Andrew J. Miller, M. Howard Mettee, John A. Robb and Andrew H. Turner. Mr. Walter J. Hayward was also present. Messrs. Frank Woods, president, Joseph J. Janney, secretary, and T. Erskine Carson, members of the executive committee of the institution, assisted in entertaining the visitors, who dined with Superintendent Thompson.
