full_text: BETTER SCHOOLHOUSES Grand Jury Report Urges The Expenditure Of More Of The City's Money. DANGER IN RENTED BUILDINGS Narrow Exits And Small, III- Ventilated Rooms. The Issue Of Bonds To Get More Suit- able Edifices Recommended-Criticisms Of The Colored House Of Reformation At Cheltenham Suggestions About Other Institutions. Reports of more than usual Interest were submitted by the grand jury for the September term of the Criminal Court when they were finally discharged Satur- day. The committee on exits of public build- Ings urge in their report the necessity of better publie school buildings and recom- mend the issue of bonds by the elty for the purpose. The report in full is as fol- lows: "In common with many of our citizens, the attention of the grand jury has been drawn to our pubile school buildings, The new structures, where completed, are ad- mirable in every respect, but many of the old and practically all the rented build- ings are a disgrace to our public school system. Children are crowded into small, badly lighted and ventilated rooms, to the constant menace of the health of teachers and children alike. It is impossible to maintain under such conditions proper discipline or attain the best results in any particular, Dangerous School Exits. "The exits from many of these buildings are entirely inadequate. In some of the rented properties, which were formerly private dwellings, there is only one single narrow stairway in the centre of the building. In case of fire or pante arising from any cause the lives of many of the children would be sacrificed in the en- deavor to escape. In the event of such a disaster, which is constantly confronting us, the city would, in all probability, have costly damages to pay. The lives of the children in care of the city, so far as it is possible to do so, should be made abso- lutely sufe, and proper fire-escapes should be erected on afl such buildings at once. In "The school board is not responsible for this state of affairs. They do the best they can with the funds and facilities atforded them. They are confronted by many difficulties by this lack of adequate facilities. To illustrate in one case: one of our best new schools all the rooms are not completed. By reason of this one reacher in one grade, which should be divided into two classes, has nearly sev- enty children under her charge. It is im- possible for her to give or the children to receive proper attention. The result is the teacher and the school are liable to unjust criticism. The trouble is not there, but is owing to lack of a suflicient appro- priation to properly cotaplete and equip sufficient of the building to supply the needs and the demands of the school. Opposed To Rented Buildings. "In the judgment of the grand jury a bill should be passed by the present Legis- lature authorizing the issuing by the city of bonds to an amount suflicient to build and equip modern school buildings to take the place of all rented and badly adapted edifices now being used for school pur- poses in this city." Messrs John S. Chandlee, John L... Blake. Lawrence N. Frederick. Wm. H. Grafflin and David Hutzler composed the committee which made the report. Criticisms Of Cheltenham, The report of the committee on the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham. Prince George's county, con- tains some sharp criticisms on the man- agement of that institution. When the committee visited the institution, on De- comber 18, there were 300 boys confined there. It was 11 o'clock in the morning when the committee arrived, but they found that not a room had been cleaned or a bed made at that hour. While in the administration and some of the family buildings there was a general condition of leanliness, the committee found that in family building No. 2 the walls needed whitewash and the plastering had fallen from the ceiling in several places, exposing the laths and giving a general forlorn ap- pearance to the interior. 100 In the opinion of the committee the fail- ure to have the rooms cleaned and the beds made did not show good management, as there were such a large number of bors to do the work. The committee also found that neither the school nor sleeping room of the boys is heated, and that the bedding in the sleeping room was insutli- cient. The report states that the manage- ment of the institution admitted that the bedding was insufficient, but claimed pov- erty as the reason. The reason assigned for not having heat in the school or bed- toom, the report also s States, was the fea of accident by tire. "Leaving out the question of humanity," the report contin- ues, "the committee consider this condi- tion of affairs detrimental to health, as the colored race is especially subject to throat and lung troubles." The workshop wis found to be well heated, but there is no Sanitary system in the buildings occupied by the boys. The report also states that very little food is raised on the farm of several hun- dred acres attached to the institution, so that nearly all the food has to be shipped from Baltimore at high freight rates. This featume, the committee state, does not compare favorably with that used at the House of Correction, where the produce of the farm largely supplies the institution. The committee recommend the establish- ment of a manual training school at Chel- tenham, so the boys may be taught trades. They found something to praise in the bakehouse and kitchen, which were in a Jeanly condition, and the character of the bread and other food was excellent. The committee, in conclusion, "regret that but few of the directors on the part of the city or State tind time to visit the institu- tion and keep in actual touch with this Important work of reformation among col- ored boys," The committee was composed of Mrs. Arthur Boehm, Joseph Devlin, William II. Rogers, William T. Dillehunt and Alfred II. Pitts. Penitentiary And Jail. The report of the committee on the peni- tentiary praises the management of War- den John F. Weyler, and recommends the the completion of the new penitentiary itminedinte appropriation of $300,000 for buildings in order that their occupancy may not be indennitely postponed. The excess of receipts over expenditures last year was $27.871.84, an increase of $10,- 007.30 over 1896. "If such excellent and judicious management is continued," the report states, "the surplus profits will take care of an interest of 3% per cent. on $800,- 000." The large increase of 58 per cent, in colored prisoners shows, in the opinion of the committee, that crime is more preva- lent among that class and should receive the attention of the court. The general management of the jail was found to be good by the committee on that Institution. Houses Of Correction And Refuge. In their report on the House of Cor- rection the committee express their "full and entire satisfaction as to the able man- ner the affairs are administered, and com- pliment W. D. Slack and his assistants upon their success so far during their term of otuce. The committee recommend the erection of an additional building to meet the demand for more cell space, and also of a building to be used as a workshop. An electric-light plant is also much needed, the report states, and telephone connection with the city is suggested. An electric-light plant for the House of Refuge is also recommended in the report of the committee on that institution. title: No Room For A Boy At Cheltenham
full_text: No Room For A Boy At Cheltenham William Evans, an eight-year-old col- ored boy, was committed to the House of Reformation for Colored Children, at Chel- tenham, Prince George's county, yester- day, by Justice Wamsley at the central police station, and when taken there those in charge of the institution refused to ad- mit him, claiming they had no room for the boy. He was brought back and will probably be sent to some other institu- tion. The boy was charged with grabbing a pocketbook containing $1.50 from Mrs. Cath- arine Kramer, No. 1309 Holbrook street, in Belair market Saturday night. On account of his age this charge was dropped, with the understanding that he be sent to a re- formatory institution. He Has No Authority To Collect Money. A well-dressed young man called at the home of Mrs. John M. Adams, No. 2112 Maryland avenue, Saturday morning, and represented himself as authorized to make collections for Rev. William E. Bartlett, pastor of St. Ann's Catholic Church, York road. He asked for a small sum of money, but was not given it. The man is sup- posed to be the one who called at ex- Mayor Hooper's home, No. 2201 Maryland avenue, recently, as reported in THE SUN Saturday last. Father Bartlett vis- ited police headquarters last week and said no person had authority to make collec- tions in his name or that of the church. Injured In A Runaway. A horse attached to a buggy belonging to Dr. D. Z. Dunnott, resident physician of the Union Protestant Infirmary, Divi- sion and Mosher streets, became unman- ageable Saturday on Lafayette avenue and ran away. William Bradford, who was in the buggy with Dr. Dunnott, tried to get out the back and fell to the ground. He was cut deeply over the left eye and at- tended by Dr. J. G. Huck, 647 West La- fayette avenue. The horse was stopped near McCulloh street. Dr. Dunnott was not hurt. Business Troub'es. Wolf & Strauss, manufacturers of men's clothing at 24 West Baltimore street, made an assignment for the benefit of creditors Saturday to Louis N. Frank, trustee. The bond was for $15.000. Samuel Wolf and Isaac Strauss are the members of the firm. George S. Kirkley, trading as the Union Hardware Company at 1405 North Charles street, also made an assignment for the benefit of creditors. Meredith Jauvier, trustee, bonded for $6.000. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: HOUSE OF REFORMATION: GRAND JURY VISITS THE INSTITUTION FOR COLORED BOYS AT CHELTENHAM, PRINCE GEORGE'S COUNTY
full_text: HOUSE OF REFORMATION Grand Jury Visits The Institution For Colored Boys At Cheltenham, Prince George's County. The grand jury of Baltimore spent the day yesterday inspecting the buildings and grounds of the Colored House of Reforma- tion, at Cheltenham, Prince George's coun- ty, Md., and studying the working of that Institution. They left Union Station at 7 o'clock in the morning and returned in the evening. In consequence of the trip no business session of the jury was held. A larger number of grand jurors made the trip than on any similar occasion pre- viously. The grand jurors present were Thomas B. Gambel, assistant foreman; Henry C. Royston, Dr. Francis G. Con- nolly, Leon Seliger, Thomas W. Morse, Ernst Schmeisser, John R. Young, colored, Michael P. Caughey, Wm. Grecht, Wm. Klingelhofer, Thomas S. Clark, Frank Nolen, Wm. H. Ferris, Reuben Jandorf, Frederick W. Decker, Jr., Charles W. Stockett, Marion H. Ould and Ambrose M. Emory. They were accompanied by Mr. Henry J. Broening, clerk of the Criminal Court, and Messrs. Edward Stabler and Joseph J. Janney, of the board of managers of the Institution. A thorough inspection was made of the buildings and grounds. Since the visit of the last grand jury the power house has been completed, and the boys have been organized into a fire brigade. An exhibi- tion of the brigade showed that only two minutes and a quarter is required to have a large stream of water playing on any of the buildings. The boys were assembled on the lawn, where they sang a number of hymns and were addressed by the visitors. Mr. Nathan Thompson, superintendent of the institution, entertained the visitors at din- ner. Everything was found in excellent condition and the grand jurors praised the management of the institution. John R. Young, the colored member of the grand jury, addressed the boys, and said they have advantages not enjoyed by him when he was a boy, and he had no idea before his visit that such an excellent in- stitution for his race existed in Maryland. title: TYPHOID AT CHELTENHAM: DR. FULTON INVESTIGATES THE EPIDEMIC, WHICH HE SAYS HAS NOT BEEN CHECKED
full_text: TYPHOID AT CHELTENHAM Dr. Fulton Investigates The Epidemic, Which He Says Has Not Been, Checked. At the request of Dr. W. H. Gibbons, health officer for Prince George's county, Dr. John S. Fulton visited the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Chelten- ham, yesterday. Several weeks ago ty- phoid fever appeared among the prisoners, and examinations of the various water sup- plies were made by Prof. W. B. D. Pen- niman, analyst to the State board of health. As a result of these examinations the managers were advised to take their drinking water only from one spring which was found to be pure. Four condemned pumps were disman- tled, but the boys continued to drink from all of the three remaining supplies. The progress of the disease has not been checked. There are now a dozen boys in the hos- pital, eight of whom have typhoid fever, two of them being dangerously ill. Sam- ples of blood were brought to Baltimore for examination by Dr. Stokes. No deaths have so far occurred, nor has any sick- ness appeared among the officers or their families. When asked about the unnecessary se- vere punishments criticised by the grand jury Dr. Fulton said that the disci- pline was, so far as he could see, human. One boy he saw carrying a fence post back and forth in one of the paths. This was said to be the ordinary penalty for disturbing the peace in the dining room. The other punishments are said to be loss of supper for small offenses, and for other sins penalties ranging from confinement in a cell up to carrying the ball and chain. The last is the penalty for persistent at- tempts to escape. Dr. Fulton indorses the recommenda- tions of the grand jury. He says that the chief needs of the institution at present seem to be a better system of sewage disposal and a better hospital. Most of the buildings are furnished with dry box closets, which are cleaned daily. The administration building has water car- riage of the cheapest and most Inadequate sort. The water-carriage system should, Dr. Fulton thinks, be applied to all the buildings and all the sewage disposed of by sub-surface irrigation. There are bathing facilities in all the buildings and the boys are obliged to bathe at regular intervals. If the tubs were replaced by rain baths the bathing could be managed much more economie- ally and the bathrooms would be much cleaner, he said. The present hospital is a small one- story aftair and is now full. There is one tuberculous patient now in the hospital and his presence among convalescents from typhoid exposes them to considerable danger of infection. Dr. Fulton thinks that a hospital is needed having a сарас- ity of twenty-five beds, and that part of it should be fitted up for the isolation of Infectious cases. Gibbons, health officer for Prince George's county, Dr. John S. Fulton visited the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Chelten- ham, yesterday. Several weeks ago ty- phoid fever appeared among the prisoners, and examinations of the various water sup- plies were made by Prof. W. B. D. Pen- niman, analyst to the State board of health. As a result of these examinations the managers were advised to take their drinking water only from one spring which was found to be pure. Four condemned pumps were disman- tled, but the boys continued to drink from all of the three remaining supplies. The progress of the disease has not been checked. There are now a dozen boys in the hos- pital, eight of whom have typhoid fever, two of them being dangerously ill. Sam- ples of blood were brought to Baltimore for examination by Dr. Stokes. No deaths have so far occurred, nor has any sick- ness appeared among the officers or their families. When asked about the unnecessary se- vere punishments criticised by the grand jury Dr. Fulton said that the disci- pline was, so far as he could see, human. One boy he saw carrying a fence post back and forth in one of the paths. This was said to be the ordinary penalty for disturbing the peace in the dining room. The other punishments are said to be loss of supper for small offenses, and for other sins penalties ranging from confinement in a cell up to carrying the ball and chain. The last is the penalty for persistent at- tempts to escape. Dr. Fulton indorses the recommenda- tions of the grand jury. He says that the chief needs of the institution at present seem to be a better system of sewage disposal and a better hospital. Most of the buildings are furnished with dry box closets, which are cleaned daily. The administration building has water car- riage of the cheapest and most Inadequate sort. The water-carriage system should, Dr. Fulton thinks, be applied to all the buildings and all the sewage disposed of by sub-surface irrigation. There are bathing facilities in all the buildings and the boys are obliged to bathe at regular intervals. If the tubs were replaced by rain baths the bathing could be managed much more economie- ally and the bathrooms would be much cleaner, he said. The present hospital is a small one- story aftair and is now full. There is one tuberculous patient now in the hospital and his presence among convalescents from typhoid exposes them to considerable danger of infection. Dr. Fulton thinks that a hospital is needed having a сарас- ity of twenty-five beds, and that part of it should be fitted up for the isolation of Infectious cases. . .

title: PUNISHMENT TOO SEVERE: GRAND JURY CRITICISES CHELTENHAM HOUSE OF REFORMATION--MANAGEMENT PROMISES TO MODIFY IT
full_text: PUNISHMENT TOO SEVERE Grand Jury Criticises Cheltenham House Of Reformation-Management Promises To Modify It. The grand jury committee on the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Chel- tenham, submitted a special report yester- day commending the management and condition of that institution, but stating that the punishments inflicted on the youthful inmates have been too severe. "We regret to say that, in our opinion," the report states, "the punishments have been too severe, better suited for hard- ened adult criminals than for incorrigible youths. "We are pleased to report that the man- agement have promised to modify this somewhat by doing away with the more severe methods. In this connection one of the great needs of the institution is a strong guard building, where uncontrol- lable inmates may be safely confined under proper police protection. We believe that kind treatment and moral suasion will do more to serve the purposes of the institu- tion than harsh and severe punishments." On June 27 the committee visited the in- stitution with other members of the grand jury. The report states that they found "the management able and efficient, and thoroughly devoted to their work, the buildings and grounds clean and in good condition, the food wholesome and abund- ant, and the dormitories clean, well lighted and ventilated." The report heartily Indorses the recom- mendation of the last grand jury for an appropriation of $17,000 to make necessary improvements. An adequate water supply, with fire plugs and hose to be attached to the steam pumps to promptly extinguish a fire, is especially urged. Appropriations of $15,000 from the city, and $12,000 from the State are recommended. Messrs. Frank Nolen, Thomas W. Morse, John R. Young, R. Jandorf and Wm. H. Ferris are the members of the committee, and all signed the report. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: A Nurse For Miss Clark
full_text: A Nurse For Miss Clark. Rev. John M. Giraud, S. J., assistant pastor of Sacred Heart Catholic Church, White Marsh, Prince George's county, visited Loyola College, in Baltimore, yes- terday. He is the priest who accompanied John Berry, the young mulatto who mur- dered Miss Amanda Clark and attempted the life of her sister. Father Giraud returned to Prince George's county yesterday afternoon with one of the Sisters of Bon Secours, who will nurse Miss Annie Clark. He said Berry called for him at 11.25 o'clock Saturday night, and he was brought back to the priesthouse by Joseph Clark, a nephew of the victims. The Prisoner In Jail. Berry was more composed yesterday at the city jail, where he was brought for safe keeping, and did not seem to be great- ly worried about his probable fate. Father Boone, of Loyola College, visited him in the morning and administered spiritual consolation, remaining some time. He promised to get a prayerbook for Berry, which he asked for. One of the directors of Cheltenham Reformatory School for Colored Boys, while at the fall on other business, stopped in Berry's cell and talked with him about his statement that the in- stitution is not a fit place for boys. Mem- bers of the grand jury also took a look at Berry while at the jail. Berry was very much tickled with a picture of himself, sent him by an artist, and which was taken Monday, and he took pride in show- ing it to other prisoners. title: Boy Starved And Frozen
full_text: Boy Starved And Frozen. The Catonsville police station was crowded Saturday afternoon by indignant colored people to hear evidence in the case of Lewis Gray and Annie Marie Elizabeth Henson, both colored, charged with stary- ing and cruelly punishing Gray's eight- year-old boy, Arthur. The boy, a mere skeleton, with both feet so badly frozen that he could not walk, was wrapped in a blanket and carried from his uncle's home to the station house. His condition caused a decided sensation. Capt. George W. Par- ker, of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, who was interested in the case, said he had rarely seen any one in a more pitiful condition. March 20 the boy was committed to the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Cheltenham, by Justice J. T. Brooks, of Irvington, on the charge of incorrigibility, preferred by his father. Constable Harry McAleer started for the institution with the prisoner Friday, but upon reaching Baltimore found that he had missed the train, and took the child to the home of Arthur Stewart, his uncle, at Catonsville. The boy was so weak from starvation that when taken from the car he fell to the ground exhausted. Dr. C. L. Mattfeldt was called to attend the child, and the arrest of his father and the Henson woman, who lived with Gray, followed. It was shown at the hearing that the child, during the recent cold weather, when the mercury was near zero, was compelled το stay outdoors all day as punishment, and when brought in at night was put to bed without food. His feet were badly frost- bitten, and were exhibited Saturday. All flesh of the right heel was eaten away, showing the bone, while large holes were in the soles of his feet. His left foot was also badly frozen, the bone being visible. The accused were held for the May term of court under $1,000 bail. They were un- able to secure bail, and will be taken to Towson jall today by Patrolman Doyle. After the hearing the skeleton youth was put on exhibition at the station house, and those who were unable to gain admittance to the room during the trial were allowed to pass in and view the spectacle. title: KILLED BY A BOAR
full_text: KILLED BY A BOAR A Boy At Cheltenham House Of Re- formation Meets With A Violent Death. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] CHELTENHAM, MD., Dec. 5.-Last Thurs- day a boy committed to the House of Re- formation for Colored Youth was at- tacked and almost instantly killed by a vicious boar. The boy had gone into the pen where the animal was kept to get a shovel, and the boar made a lunge at him and bit him in the thigh. Its sharp teeth made a fearful wound, lacerating the muscles and severing the femoral vein and artery. The boy's screams were heard by employes of the Institution, but he died from loss of blood before he could be car- ried to the hospital. The boy was com- mitted to the House of Reformation from Somerset county. He was about sixteen years old. The remains were buried at the institution. Superintendent Pyles said that the boy's duty was to carry slops to the hogs, and It was while he was engaged in this duty that he entered the pen. Assistant Farmer Curtin was nearby at the time, but could not reach the boy in time to save him. Dr. Hester, the physician of the in- stitution, said that the boy's life could not have been saved, as both the femoral artery and femoral vein were severed. full_text: VISITORS AT CHELTENHAM For The House Of Reformation Colored Boys Inspected By A Party From The City. The managers of the House of Reforma- tion for Colored Boys, located at Chelten- ham, H'rince George's county, gave an ex- cursion to that place yesterday for the pur- pose of inspecting the institution and affording a number of the citizens of Bal- timore an opportunity of seeing the meth- ods by which its reformatory and philan- thropic work was conducted. A special car, bearing the managers and Invited guests, besides a number of ladies, left Union Station at 7.31 o'clock in the morning and a quick trip was made to Cheltenham. In the party were Messrs. Skipwith Wilmer and B. M. Watts, repre- senting the First and Second Branches of the City Council; William Stinson, James E. Hughes, Elisha H. Walker, ex-Mayor Alcaeus Hooper, Judge J. J. Dobler, Mr. Henry Duffy, Morris Soper, Lester H. Latham, Warden Hall, of the city jall; Dr. Brown, of the House of Refuge for Col- ored Girls; Mr. Wright and Colonel Wil- son, of Marlboro', Md. The members of the board of managers who were on the trip were Messrs. Frank Woods, president; Edward Stabler, Jr., G. S. Griffith, T. Erskine Carson, Joseph J. Janney, William E. Walton, F. Snowden HIII, C. C. Magruder, Henry Reese and Charles E. Coffin. Messrs. J. Harry Lee, Charles Markell, James Doyle and Herbert M. Brune, of the board, did not accompany the party. Some of the ladies present were Mrs. Frank Woods, Mrs. James E. Hughes, Mrs. Edward Stabler, Jr., Misses Eliza- beth and Bertha Janney, Mrs. Henry Reese, Miss Holt, Mrs. B. M. Watts, Mrs. T. Erskine Carson and a number of young ladies from the Woman's College. ! Carriages met the party at the station and took them to the institution, where they were welcomed by Superintendent Nathan Thompson. The boys, 275 in num- ber, were gathered in the chapel and were addressed by Mr. Wilmer, Mr. Hughes, Mr. Hooper and Dr. Brown. Led by War- den Hall and Mr. Latham, the boys sang several hymns, and Miss Holt gave a reci- tation. Then followed an inspection of the buildings and the grounds, and a lunch and the return to the city. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. The Opinion Is Expressed That The Police Have The Power To Bring Sunday Liquor Law Violators To Justice-Warden Weyler's Admin- istration Highly Commended. The grand jurors for the January term completed their labors yesterday and after submitting the customary reports, were discharged with the thanks of the court. Mr. Wm. H. Lytle, foreman, was presented by his fellow-jurors a silver- mounted gavel and complimentary resolu- tions. The gavel is the one used by Mr. Lytle during the term. It was handsomely ornamented and appropriately inscribed for presentation. The grand jurors for the May term have been summoned for Monday, when the term begins. The retiring grand jury heard 1,556 cases, of which 1,068 were presented and 488 dismissed. There were 413 larceny cases heard, of which 302 were presented. Foreman Lytle in his report calls atten- tion to the large proportion of larceny cases, and states that this grade of crime is "undoubtedly encouraged by the facili- ties afforded rogues in disposing of stolen property at second-hand stores." It is suggested in the report "that stores of this kind be required by law to furnish to the police every morning a description of the articles bought by them during the preceding twenty-four hours, together with the names and descriptions of the persons from whom they received the goods. This would not only facilitate the recovery of stolen goods, but lead to the speedy apprehension of thieves." The Liquor Law. The experience of the grand jury with regard to Sunday liquor selling was the same as that of previous grand juries. At the request of the grand jury raids were made on the most notorious places by offl- cers in citizen's clothes. "That this pro- ceeding had a salutary effect," the report states, "is shown by the fact that the re- ported violations during the latter part of our term, after the raids had been made, greatly decreased, indicating a dis- position on the part of saloon-keepers to obey the law, and establishing the fact that a vigorous prosecution is the most effective means of securing obedience. It must, however, in justice. be stated that a majority of the licensed dealers con- form to the law regulating the sale of liquor, and deprecate the acts of those who are unmindful of and persistently violate its provisions. cus- "The defects in the law regulating the sale of liquor doubtless make it difficult to detect and punish offenders, yet the grand jury is convinced that the todians of the public safety have the power to bring every violator of this par- ticular law to the bar of justice. A short time ago, by earnest and persistent efforts, they succeeded in measurably breaking up the policy shops and gambling dens of the city. The same degree of zeal and earnestness, we believe, would insure a stricter observance of the Sunday liquor law." Reformatory Recommended. Continuing. the report is as follows: "The grand jury have been seriously impressed with the Increasing number of youthful criminals, the most of whom are colored. This increase may be accounted for by heredity, but more by environment. Many of these youths are the children of dissolute or idle parents, and have never been subjected to the slightest restraint at home-indeed, they are often without even the semblance of a home. In some cases they are required and expected by their parents to aid by theft in support- ing the family. With such surroundings it could scarcely be expected that any- thing but a criminal product would be evolved. An increase of larceny by minors is the ultimate result. near The Institutions suitable for the incar- ceration of juvenile offenders convicted of crimes punishable by imprisonment are over-crowded, and it would be manifestly detrimental to mingle them with older prisohers. Many of these youths. under more favorable environment and with proper moral and physical training, might be reclaimed. We, therefore, recommend the establishment of a Manual Training Reformatory, located the city, where the inmates could be taught use- ful trades or occupations that would enable them to earn an honest livelihood when discharged. Such an institution should have around it sufficient good land, where the youths could be in- structed in agriculture and other employ- ments. Under proper management it could be made nearly, if not altogether, self-supporting. The youths might re- ceive not only a plain education, but be taught habits of industry and morality calculated to fit them for lives of future usefulness." Warden Weyler Commended. The report commends the management of Warden John F. Weyler, of the peniten- tiary, and praises the police and detective departments. In conclusion a cumulative sentence is recommended for habitual of- fenders. Accompanying the report were the usual reports of the committees appointed to visit the various reformatory and penal in- stitutions. These institutions were all found to be well conducted. Warden John F. Weyler, of the peniten- tiary, is firm and unyielding in dealing with the convicts, the committee on the penitentlary state in their report, but from the day of entrance the prisoners are treated as fellow creatures who, though erring, are capable of reformation. The admirable discipline in the prison is shown by the fact that only one or two guards are necessary to preserve order and secure diligence in the large workshops, in each of which a hundred or more men are em- ployed. The unselfish and philanthropic efforts of the Prisoners' Aid Association, of which Mr. Goldsborough S. Griffith is president, has had an ameliorating and beneficent influence upon the prisoners, the committee states.. It is regretted by the committee that facilities for educating the prisoners are wanting. This will be reme- died when the new penitentiary is occu- pled, about September 1, this year. The excess of revenue over expenditures was $29.180.71 for the year ended December 31, 1898. The number of prisoners on the 30th of last April was 894, comprising 370 white men, 475 colored men, & white women and 44 colored women. For the new penitentiary $1,083,724.47 has been re- ceived and $1.007.116.47 expended, leaving a balance of $76,608. The committee unqualifiedly commend the excellent management of Warden Wey- ler. "The penitentiary under his manage- ment," the report states, "has become the best in the United States, and this is due to his energy, tact and wisdom, seconded by an able and efficient board of direc- tors." L. Messrs. F. W. Baker, Emanuel Green- baum, Alexander H. Price, Edwin Turnbull and Horace Noble composed the committee. The City Jail. The committee on the jail commend War- den Hall for his excellent management and Dr. James C. Clark for the faithful performance of his duties as jail physl- cian. Improvements suggested by the com- mittee are better closets, ventilating equip- ment in the towers at the north end of the jail, an additional story over the present hospital, and separate accommodations for boys committed to jail. Female House Of Refuge. The sale of the present buildings on Female House of Refuge is recommended children committed to the institution to get rid of a burden, or are incompetent to raise them in a proper manner. The mere fact that out of a total of 210 boys 60 are between the ages of six and thir- teen ought to convince the public of this fact, and also that the boys cannot be so very bad." The committee recommends the establishment of trade schools at the institution and a fire escape for the junior department. "Two recent fires at the in- stitution," the report states in conclusion, "established the fact that there are not sufficient water or fire plugs to protect the buildings and lives of the inmates." Cheltenham Reformatory. Appropriations of $500 for improving the bathing facilities, and $4,000 for an exten- sion of the steam heating at the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham are recommended in the report of the com- mittee on that institution. Bayview Asylum.' The committee on Bayview reported that under the present management the insti- tution is kept in splendid condition. The thanks of the community, the report states, are due the ladies' society of which Mrs. George C. Wilkins is president for their interest in the female inmates. New boil- ers, a new laundry, cylinder fire escapes and additional space for the storage of coal are recommended for the institution. Spring Grove And Mount Hope. Spring Grove was reported by the com- mittee to be a model insane asylum. "Its management reflects credit upon those in charge," the report states, "and it wel! deserves the fostering care of the State." Of the 898 Mount Hope inmates last year 256 were found by the committee to be dependent upon the public care. St. Mary's Industrial School. St. Mary's Industrial School is com- mended by the committee as an ideal home for boys. The committee suggests that members of the City Council and State government visit the institution from time to time, to become acquainted with its workings and how necessary liberal ap- propriations are for its support. Public Accounts. The committee on public accounts state in their report that they visited the offices of the city commissioner, comptroller and register and clerks of the various courts. Although the committee had free access to the books and were extended every cour- tesy, they found it Impossible to make a proper examination. They recommend that the Legislature empower the Gov- ernor to appoint a State auditor, with assistants, to examine into and report each year upon the workings and condi- tion of all public offices. Exits From Buildings. The committee on exits of public build- Ings recommended in their report that more stringent laws on the subject be passed. They examined many of the pub- lic buildings in the city and found the pro- visions made for exit to be fairly good. The fire escape recently erected at the General German Orphan Asylum, on Ais- quith street, Is commended. Carey and Baker streets occupied by the by the committee on that institution. title: DAMAGE AT CHELTENHAM: BUILDINGS UNROOFED AND CROPS INJURED BY THE STORM
full_text: DAMAGE AT CHELTENHAM Buildings Unroofed And Crops In- jured By The Storm. Mr. Joseph J. Janner, secretary of the Board of Managers of the House of Ref- ormation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, has received a letter and a telegram from the superintendent giving particulars of the damage caused by the recent storm. The letter says that nearly all of the buildings were more or less damaged, and that at least $6,000 will have to be ex- pended to restore them to their former condition. The main building, which stands in the centre of the group, had nearly all of the windows blown out, but was not other- wise seriously damaged. Family Building No. 1 had a part of the gable end blown out, and the remaining five buildings were either wholly or partly unroofed. Family Building No. 5 had the gable wall blown out down to the second floor. The tin roof of the factory building. 40 by 60 feet, was entirely torn off and carried a considerable distance from the building. The straw barrack was blown over, and the large building used as a stable and a place for the storage of fertilizers and farm ma- chinery was badly damaged. A large number of ornamental and shade trees were uprooted, and much damage was done to the growing crops. Three hundred acres were planted in corn and potatoes, and both crops were so badly damaged by wind and hall that the yield will be very small. Tin roofs, slates and debris of all kinds litter the place, and much time and labor will be required to restore the place to its former condition. A dispatch received yesterday morning says that four of the dormitories are ex- posed to the weather. The plant at Cheltenham consists of a main building, in which are located the offices, dining rooms, kitchen, storage rooms, etc., six family buildings, each of two stories and a basement, a two-story factory, boller house, farmers' dwelling, large barn, frame hospital and several out- houses and sheds. Nearly all of the build- ings are of brick. The reformatory has about 250 boys at present. The farm con- tains 750 acres. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: JOHN BERRY ON TRIAL Miss Annie Clark Testifies To The Killing Of Her Sis- ter Near Bowie. THE CONFESSION ADMITTED Admissions Of Guilt Detailed By Several Witnesses. The State Concludes Its Testimony And Asks For A Verdict Of Murder In The First Degree-The Defense Will Endeavor Today To Show A Good Character For The Accused. John Berry, colored, was Identified by Miss Annie Clark in the Criminal Court yesterday as the person who killed her sis- ter and attempted to kill ber on Saturday evening, March 18, 1899. The crime was commitied at the home of the Misses Clark, near Bowie, Prince George's county, MC., where Berry was employed as a ser vant. Miss Clark was the last witness for the State in Berry's trial on the charge of murder. A number of the witnesses who proceded her testified that they heard Berry confess he had committed the crime. There were, besides, mute but strong wit- nesses in two sticks of firewood, a blood- stained suit of old clothes and an open- faced brass watch which were shown to the jury. The sticks of wood were used in the brutal attack on the two ladies. They were dyed red with blood in some places and had a number of long hairs adhering to them. The clothes, it was testified, were worn by Berry while making the murderous assault. Berry also owned the watch, which ich was found under Miss Amanda Clark's body. Miss Clark's Testimony. Miss Annie Clark was dressed in deep mourning. A heavy black vell, which she did not raise in court, covered her face and concealed the wounds inflicted in the brutal attack upon her. There was a care- ful avoidance during ber examination of any reference to the alleged attempted felonius assault upon her. Until called to testify Miss Clark was seated in the private office of Mr. Henry J. Broening, clerk of the court. When wanted as a witness she was escorted into the courtroom by her brother, Mr. Crittenton C. C. Clark, and Mrs. Ma lone, matron. She was given a chair close to the jury and within arm's length of Berry, but she spoke in so low a tone that what she said was heard with difficulty by those closest to her. When asked if she saw Berry in the courtroom, she looked across the table and pointed him out. "John Berry did it. There he is," she said. "My sister and I were sitting at the table a few minutes after 7 o'clock," Miss Clark said, "and were nearly through sup- per, when Berry came in as usual. First he struck me on the top of the head with a heavy plece of oak wood, and then he struck my sister. We had no power to help ourselves. I held my hands over my sister and she held her hands over me to keep him from hitting us. We were begging him not to hurt us and screaming all the time. When my sister was struck the last blow she said, 'I'm gonel Meroy, Jesus!" My sister never spoke another word after that. The Prisoner's Appearance. Berry is a mulatto of a light yellow color, of medium height and about nine- teen years old, He was born in Frederick city and was sent to the House of Refor mation at Cheltenham by his grand- mother, who charged him with being in- corrigible and stealing money from her. He had been at Cheltenham six years when taken out by Miss Amanda Clark, who wanted a boy to work about the house. At the time of the murder be had been with the Misses Clark about two years. In court yesterday he was poorly dressed, but appeared to have been well fed. He wore an old sult of dark clothes and canvas shoes without stockings. He is apparently of a sullen disposition. His black eyes gleamed through partly closed lids, while he listened with pouting lips to the testimony against him. "Berry was brought before me after- ward and I identified him. After his at- tack on us I heard him go through all the rooms in the house. I called to him when he was in the next room to where we were and asked him to go for a doctor, I also asked him to put pillows under our heads and throw something over me, as I was cold. I swore to him I wouldn't teil on him. He compelled me to make the sign of the cross, and said he would go for a doctor after he had changed his clothes. That was the best way out, he said, as they would soon get him if he went away. I told him to stop at my brother's while he was out." The Indictment against Berry was found by the grand jury of Prince George's county. He was taken to Upper Marl- boro' to be tried on April 10, but made affidavit that he could not secure a fair and impartial trial in Prince George's county. His case was then removed to Baltimore for trial, C. C. Magruder and Charles H. Stanley being assigned by the court to defend him. Miss Clark was on the witness stand only ifteen minutes. She was not cross-exam- ined by the defense. When Berry was arraigned yesterday he pleaded not guilty and sald he had em- ployed two colored sttorneys to defend him. One, he said, was a man named Johnson, of Washington, and the other Harry S. Cummings, of Baltimore. Messrs, Magruder and Stanley said they were willing to retire from the case if Berry had employed counsel. Berry's Confession Admitted. A strong effort was made to exclude as evidence the confession made by Berry, but it falled. The witnesses to whom the confession was made were examined to ascertain if the confession had been made under threats or promises of reward. All said the confession was made voluntarily, and Judge Wright ruled that it was ad- missible. During this preliminary exami- nation Berry was called to the stand. "Constable Porter," he said, "took me to Thomas Wells' saloon at Bowie. While there a man I don't know asked me if I did it. I told him no. He put his hand in the constable's pocket and said if I didn't say I did it he would shoot me. The man was stout and red-faced. I made a state- ment before the coroner's jury because I was afraid they would kill me. The man in Wells' saloon was the only one who made threats. I told the colored man Fair- fax that I did it and that's all." "If counsel would come in and say they would try the ease you could withdraw," Judge Wright said to the attorneys for the defense. "The interests of the ac- cused shall be protected. It does not put you in a bad position." Berry said he would recognize the man he referred to if he saw him. He was al- lowed to walk about the courtroom for the purpose of picking him out, but said he could not find him. His statement was de- nied by Constable Porter. The Jury. The trial then proceeded. Mr. Cum- mings came into court later and said he had no connection with the case and had not been employed to defend Berry. At half-past one o'clock the jury had been selected and Deputy State's Attor- ney William C. Smith began the opening statement for the prosecution. Others en- gaged in the prosecution are State's Attor- ney Duffy and State's Attorney Roger Bel- lis, of Prince George's county. Mr. Smith made it plain that the State would ask a verdict of murder in the first degree. No opening statement was made by the de- fense. What Berry Told The Doctors. Dr. Nelson A. Ryon, of Bowie, who was called to attend the Misses Clark on the night of March 18, was the first witness. Dr. Ryon was summoned by Berry, who said somebody had entered the house and nearly killed the two ladies. Miss Aman- da Clark had been dead about an hour when Dr. Ryon reached the house, at 11 P. M. She had three frightful wounds on her head, her skull being fractured at the base and crushed on the left side. The Doctor thought at the time that Miss An- nie Clark was in a critical condition. She had eight or ten wounds. Her upper lip was cut open, some of her teeth were knocked out and her face was scratched. This made the courtroom more comfortable than would otherwise have been the case. Dr. Ryon found the ladies lying on the kitchen floor with pillows under their heads and a sheet thrown over them. At that time Berry was absent, having gone after a priest. The sticks of firewood pro- duced in court were also found by Dr. Ryon. On Sunday, March 19, Miss Annie Clark told Berry in Dr. Ryan's presence that be had committed the crime. Berry made no remark at that time. "Berry said at the inquest," continued Dr. Ryan, "that be committed the crime and had planned it for three or four days. He said he wanted money to go away. He sald he attacked Miss Annie first and then Miss Amanda, using a number of pieces of stovewood. They knocked some of the wood out of his hand. When he thought he had killed them, he said, he searched the house and found 93 cents. He changed bis bloody clothes, he said, before going out. Miss Anule swore she would not tell and he had every confidence in her, but as it had been found out, he said, he would tell all about it." Admissions To The Coroner. Rufus Belt, a justice of the pence, living near Bowie, acted as coroner and held an Inquest over Miss Amanda Clark on Sun day, March 19, at her home. Berry was at the inquest and before the jury. He was told that he need not say anything, but he said he would make a statement. He com- menced by saying, "They did not treat me right. They treated be badly." Mr. Belt asked him in what way the Misses Clark had treated him badly and he replied: ""They quarreled with me about spilling water on the floor and last summer about breaking a culcken's legs." Mr. Belt then inquired what was Berry's motive, asking if be intended to felonious- ly assault Miss Annie and burn the house. An objection was made to this question, but Judge Wright sald the evidence was very clearly admissible. "Berry said," continued Mr. Belt, "that his first inten- tion was to assault Miss Annie, but he changed that, and that his chief motive was to obtain money to go away with. He belleved there was money in the house," Berry confessed the crime to him without Constable Norman Porter testified that any inducements being offered or threats being made. Mr. Perter also heard the confession before the coroner's jury and went upstairs with Berry in the Clark house to get the 93 cents and the bloods clothes. Sheriff Benjamin F. Roby, of Prince George's county, took charge of Berry on Sunday, March 10, and locked him up in the jail at Upper Mariboro'. Smith, foreman of the coro- ner's jury, testified that he warned Berry before he made the confession. He said he attempted to assault Miss Annie after going upstairs for money, but did not ac complish his purpose, because she begged him so hard not to." He says he was fifteen years old in February, though he appears five years older. He was born in Frederick, Md., and says his parents are dead and he does not know if he has any relatives living. He spent six years in Cheltenham Reforma- tory School for Colored Boys, where he was sent by his grandmother, who charged him with being incorrigible and stealing money from her. In color he is light yellow. He is about five feet six inches tall and weighs about 125 pounds. He has straight black hair, mustache and side whiskers, light in growth, but black in color. He confessed to everything con- nected with the awful crime without any effort to conceal the slightest particular, and in a manner as though he was only dis- cussing Idle country gossip. He said: His Story Of The Crime. "Next month will be two years since the Misses Clark took me out of Chelten- ham. They told me I was only to do odd jobs about the house and would be raised, fed and clothed, but soon they had me do- ing work on the farm the same as men were doing. I never had any money to go away with to have fun with other boys. Nearly all the time I had to stay on the farm, where there are 138 acres, no near neighbors and no playthings to amuse me when not working. Often I walked out in the woods to amuse myself. "Sometimes they scolded me for doing things they did not want me to do and not doing things they told me to do which I had forgotten. This made me mad for a while, but I soon got over it. "Last Saturday morning I took some water Into the house and spilled same on the floor. Miss Amanda scolded me for it, and also for bringing mud in on my shoes. For some time I had thought of hurting them for scolding me, but I never thought of killing them. It was between 7 and 8 o'clock that night, when I was sitting back: in a corner In the kitchen beside the stove, that the thought come to me again to hurt them and get even. They had finished their supper and were getting mine ready. Miss Annie was seated at the table, with her back toward me, and Miss Amanda was facing me. A piece of wood I had brought in was too long for the stove and was lying on the floor near me. I picked ir up, went to the table and hit Miss Annie on the head first. She jumped up and both screamed. I struck her several more times and she fell on the floor. Miss Amanda came at me, screaming, and tried to get the club away from me. I commenced on her and she put her arm on her head, when I struck it and she yelled. I had broken it. I struck her until she fell, and then beat her until I crushed her head in. Both were lying on the floor, senseless. "Then I went into their bedroom, next to the kitchen, found a jewelry box under the bed. In it were some bracelets, ear- rings and other jewelry and 93 cents in money. I took the money and left the Jewelry. "Then I was so worked up I did not know what I was doing. I went back to the kitchen, and, as Miss Annie attempted to get up, I started to beat her again. She begged me to stop. Then I started to outrage her, and she was so weak I could easily have done it, but she asked me to stop, at the same tiine trying to push me away, so I gave that up. "She said she would give me $100 if I would go for a doctor, and promised she would never give me away. I made her swear she would not say anything. "I went to my room, on the second floor, took off iny clothes, that were full of blood, aud piled them together. I put on all clean clothes, not my best. as I was in a hurry, and went on a horse after Dr. M. A.Ryon. I met Everett and James Clark, nephews of the ladies, and told them to go to the house quick, as some one had nearly killed the ladies. When I left Miss Amanda was breathing very hard, and when I got back they told me she was dead. I then went to White Marsh Catholic Church, about three miles, and brought the priest back with me. "All the time I said some one else must have beat the ladies. When I got back a lor of people were at the house, and, know- ing I had done the thing, I became badly scared and was afraid to talk. title: UNPARALLELED CRIME: DOUBLE MURDER ATTEMPTED BY A YOUNG NEGRO IN PRINCE GEORGE'S COUNTY TWO LADIES THE VICTIMS ONE KILLED WITH A BILLET OF WOOD, THE OTHER FATALLY WOUNDED BLOODY WORK OF JOHN BERRY, A SERVANT TAKEN FROM CHELTENHAM REFORMATORY AND EMPLOYED BY THE MISSES CLARK--ASSAULTED AT THEIR SUPPER TABLE--LIFE OF THE PRISONER SAVED BY CONVEYING HIM TO BALTIMORE JAIL
full_text: UNPARALLELED CRIME Double Murder Attempted By A Young Negro In Prince George's County. TWO LADIES THE VICTIMS One Killed With A Billet Of Wood, The Other Fatally Wounded. Bloody Work Of John Berry, A Servant Taken From Cheltenham Reformatory And Employed By The Misses Clark-Assaulted At Their Supper Table-Life Of The Prisoner Saved By Conveying Him To Baltimore Jail. [Special from a Staff Correspondent.] BOWIE, MD., March 19.-John Berry, a young negro, aged about nineteen years, killed Miss Amanda Clark near Bowie, in Prince George's county, Saturday night, and at the same time beat into insensibil- Ity and attempted to outrage Miss Annie Clark, a younger sister of the lady he killed. He also planned to set fire to the house when the murder was committed, but changed his mind, and went for as- sistance, and subsequently confessed to all the details of the shocking crime. Scene Of The Murder. The scene of the murder is about two and a half miles south of Bowie, and a more lonesome spot could not well be imagined. The Misses Clark lived alone on a farm on the road from Bowie to White Marsh Church. Berry was secured by Miss Amanda Clark about two years ago from Cheltenham Reformatory School for Colored Boys and was employed to as- sist the two ladies about their house- work. No one can tell just at what hour the young negro commenced the assault, but circumstances and events place the hour at about 7 o'clock on Saturday even- ing. While he has confessed the crime, there are other evidences to corroborate the story, which, in all its details, stamp it as one of the most notable in the crim- inal annals of Prince George's county and its perpetrator to be one of the coolest creatures in existence. There were no witnesses to tell of what took place in the little home, but there are many surround- ings which spoke volumes in testimony to the bloody and heartless nature of the crime. In the kitchen, where the mur- der took place, was found a little table, on which had been placed the evening meal, showing that the murderer made his assault as the two ladies were at their supper. Killed At Supper. Miss Annie, the younger woman, sat at the head of the table with her back to a kitchen door leading from the room into a sunımer kitchen. It was through this door that Berry entered the room and dealt the first biow. He struck Miss Annie on the top of the head with a billet of wood two and a half feet long which had been cut for the stove. The blow knocked her from her chair to the floor. Miss Amanda, the elder, was sitting with her side to the door and did not see the blow delivered, but when she raised her eyes they fell upon Berry standing near her side with the murderous club raised to strike her. Then began a battle of life and death, to save her sister and herself. In her efforts she lost her own life, but was probably instru- mental in saving the life of her sister. Fighting For Life. Berry attempted to strike Miss Amanda, but she warded off the blow with her left arm. The negro backed off and made a second rush at the brave woman, who stood between the brute and her fallen sister. Again he raised the club, and as it desconded she tried to parry the blow. The brute exerted all his strength, and as the bludgeon fell she attempted to shield her head, and the blow fell with full force on her left arın, breaking it at the wrist and causing her to sink to the floor in terror and pain. The brute then beat her over the head, crushing in her skull and scat- tering her brains and blood over the walls of the little kitchen. Preparing For Flight. Daring all this time Miss Annie was ly- ing in an unconscious condition on the floor, and Berry thought she was dead. He then ransacked the house and secured 95 cents in money, which had been re- ceived by the ladies from the sale of eggs. The murderer then went to his room, over the kitchen, and packed his clothing in a satchel, evidently preparing himself for flight. He also went to one of the bed- rooms in the front part of the house, and, taking a straw mattress from a bed, dragged it down stairs and struck match, supposedly to set fire to the house to cover up his crime. Renewed Assault. a At this juncture Miss Annie revived, and hearing the boy in the adjoining room made outery, upon which Berry quickly returned to the kitchen and began to finish Miss Anule. He struck her a blow in the face with a billet of firewood, cut- ting through the end of her nose, through both lips, through her chin and knocking out her front teeth. He then set out to compiete his devilish work by commit- ting in outrage on the prostrate woman. She, however, fought him off, but only after he had torn her clothing from her body. After fighting until her strength was ex- hausted, Miss Annie began to beg for her life. She promised to give him a hundred dollars and never to mention his name if he would spare her. These offers seemed to have some effect on him and he began to question the woman as to the sincerity of her promise to shield him. Swearing On A Crucifix. He left her and went upstairs for a small crucifix which was used by the ladies in their devotions. While she was lying by the side of her dead sister, and almost in death's throes herself, the brute placed the crucifix on her blood-stained lips and said. "You swear you will never tell who did this?" The answer was, "I do." Not satisfied altogether with this form of oath, the negro ran his hand into the bosom of the lady's dress and, tearing a scapula which she wore around her neck from its cord, he placed it on her lips and made her repeat the promise. Going For The Doctor. He then asked if she wanted anything; if he should go for a doctor. She asked him to do so, and he left the room, went to the stable, where he procured a horse and saddle, and started for Bowle. On the way he stopped at the house of Mr. J. W. Clark, a brother of the two victims. He was met by Everett and James Clark, nephews of the Misses Clark, to whom Berry said: "You had better go over to the house, as some one has gotten in there and almost killed both the ladies." The negro then rode off to Bowie, arriv- ing at the home of Dr. M. A. Ryon, to whom he told the same story and said: "You are wanted at once and had better go on horseback, as the roads are bad." The negro himself rode back to the house and put up his horse. When he reached the house he was met by Everett and James Clark, who had gone over from their homes. Going For The Priest. They went into the house with the negro, and Miss Annie said: "Some one go for the priest." "I will go for one," said Berry, and again he went to the stable and rode off to White Marsh Church, where he informed one of the clergymen, and came back with him. When he reached the house this time Dr. Ryon had arrived and said Miss Amanda had been dead about one and a half hours, and that Miss Annie's condi- tion was critical. What The Nephews Saw. Everett Clark and James Clark were the first to arrive at the house after the mur- der. They said: "When we entered the kitchen we found our aunts lying on the right side of the stove, from the door, and covered with a quilt and sheet. Under the head of each was a blood-soaked pil- low. We were terrified at the sight. The walls of the room looked like some one had been killing hogs. Aunt Amanda was nearest the stove and lying on her right side, with her head doubled up under her. Aunt Annie was lying on her back. The furniture in the room was not upset, and there was some fire in the stove. When we heard Berry come back from Bowie we met him and he repented the same story of some one having come into the house during his absence and killing the ladies." Dr. Ryen soon came and they took Miss. Annie into an adjoining rooin. What The Doctor Said. Dr. Ryan said: "As soon as I saw Miss Amanda I knew she was dead. On exam- ining her I found that her skull had been fractured. She had at least eight or nine distinct wounds in her head and left hand and arım. One particularly shocking wound was made on the left temple, which cracked the skull. This wound probably caused her death. As soon as I had ex- amined Miss Annie I asked her who did the job. She did not answer. I then told her that I knew. She asked, 'Who is it?" I said that negro here. She answered 'Yes; I am glad you have found out.'" Preparing To Lynch. By this time the news had spread. Many persens came from miles around. All this time Berry was taking a deep interest in all that was going on. He said to those present: "I wish I knew who did this work. I would kill him." He never seemed to think that suspicion and evidence had fastened on himself. The crowd, as soon as they were in- formed of the part Berry had played, want- ed to kill him on the spot. He was sent three times from the house to a spring near by for the purpose of lynching him, but this was prevented by some of the cooler heads. Fixing The Crime On Berry. Capt. George W. Smith, Martin Keough and Harry Keough, of Bowie, arrived at the house about midnight. They at once set to work to get at the bottom of the crime and began to ply Berry with ques- tions. They soon had him tangled up, and Constable Norman Porter placed him un- der arrest. They took him to the bedside of Miss Annie Clark and asked her if she identified him. She waved her hand and said. "I certainly do. Take him away." Jury Of Inquest. Sheriff Charles Roby was sent for, and he reached the scene about 11 o'clock Sun- day morning. He took charge of Berry, while Justice Rufus Belt summoned the following jury of inquest: George M. Smith, foreman; Martin Keough, Edward Bell, Harry Keough, Joseph Nicholson, Richard Hardesty, Joseph W. Ryan, Charles Seitz, M. E. Brady, Clifton C. Jones, W. W. Phelps and F. B. Lueres. Berry was called. He showed not the slightest fear. Foreman Smith told him that he was not compelled to tell anything, but if he wanted to make any statement he could do so. The prisoner was sullen and not in- clined to talk. He was taken to the kitchen and shown the face of his victim. He looked with a steady gaze upon the face of Miss Clark without showing a sin- gle sign of remorse or fear. Sheriff Roby took the prisoner to Bowie. Just as they were leaving the house a pair of bright handcuffs were slipped over his wrists. Effect Of Cold Steel. At the sound of the click of the cuff locks and the touch of the cold steel Berry cringed, and he then wanted to talk. Lie said he was not at the house, but had gone to a store for some quinine and found the women on his return. He added: "When I saw them all bloody I fainted and took a dose of quinine to brace me up." He denied having changed his clothing, but Martin Keough made a search for the cast-off suit and found the blood-soaked garments in a wooden chest in a summer kitchen. When shown the clothes Berry shut up like a clam. A Teltale Watch. While the hunt for the clothes was be- ing made Mr. Harry Keough lifted up one of the pillows which had been under the lady's head and found a small brass open-face watch, which was handed to Berry, who claimed it. The face of the watch was covered with blood, and at the suggestion of some one the face was cleaned off, and the watch had stopped at 7.30 o'clock. This is about the hour Berry is supposed to have completed his work of slaughter. A Full Confession. At Bowle the prisoner was further ques- tioned and said: "I will tell a colored man about it." Bayliss Fairfax, colored, was asked to talk with him. To Fairfax Berry said: "I did it. I have Intended to do it for several days, but could not get at them right until Saturday. They scolded me about coming into the house with muddy boots, and they did not treat me right, so I killed them." This statement was heard by the officers, and Berry was told to tell all he knew. He said: "The ladies were at the sup- per table and I was bringing stove wood In the kitchen. I had an armful of wood, and as I dropped it into the wood box one of the pieces fell out of the box. I picked it up, and as I did so I thought: "This is my time, and this is the thing to do it with." I turned around and struck Miss Annie on the head. I supposed I had killed her, as she fell stiff. Miss Amanda jumped up from the table and grabbed the stick be- fore I could strike her. She got it out of my hand. I stooped down and got another stick and made at her. Every time I would strike at her she would ward off the blow. This made me mad, and I got a chance and I struck with all my might. She gave a groan and fell by the side of Miss Annie. I struck her sereral times in the head until I sup- posed she was dead. I then went through the house and got 95 cents, which I put in a purse in my room. When I came back I started to outrage Miss Annie and would have done so if I had not taken another thought, which said to me 'You have done enough today.' Miss Annie swore on the cross that she would not tell and would give me $100 to go for a doctor. I got pil- lows for them and suppose that my watch fell out while I was putting their heads on the pillows. After I covered them up I got the horse and went for the doctor and told the Clark boys." Trouble Brewing. While telling the story the negro never changed countenance, but seemed to be re- lating some every-day gossip. But the crowd thought differently and Sheriff Roby saw a storm coming. He telegraphed for a special train, and started for Upper Marlboro', and by this act saved the wretch's neck, as preparations were being made to Iynch him. The Victims. The Misses Clark were maiden ladies and daughters of the late Joshua T. Clark, who at one time was county commissioner from Bowie district and had also served as a justice of the peace. Miss Amanda Clark was fifty-six years of age, while Miss An- nie is forty years old. Both ladies are highly spoken of in the community. The Murderer. John Berry gives his age as fifteen, but he is at least four years older.
