clean_text: UNPARALLELED CRIME Double Murder Attempted By A Young Negro In Prince George's County. TWO LADIES THE VICTIMS One Killed With A Billet Of Wood, The Other Fatally Wounded. Bloody Work Of John Berry, A Servant Taken From Cheltenham Reformatory And Employed By The Misses Clark-Assaulted At Their Supper Table-Life Of The Prisoner Saved By Conveying Him To Baltimore Jail. [Special from a Staff Correspondent.] BOWIE, MD., March 19.-John Berry, a young negro, aged about nineteen years, killed Miss Amanda Clark near Bowie, in Prince George's county, Saturday night, and at the same time beat into insensibil- Ity and attempted to outrage Miss Annie Clark, a younger sister of the lady he killed. He also planned to set fire to the house when the murder was committed, but changed his mind, and went for as- sistance, and subsequently confessed to all the details of the shocking crime. Scene Of The Murder. The scene of the murder is about two and a half miles south of Bowie, and a more lonesome spot could not well be imagined. The Misses Clark lived alone on a farm on the road from Bowie to White Marsh Church. Berry was secured by Miss Amanda Clark about two years ago from Cheltenham Reformatory School for Colored Boys and was employed to as- sist the two ladies about their house- work. No one can tell just at what hour the young negro commenced the assault, but circumstances and events place the hour at about 7 o'clock on Saturday even- ing. While he has confessed the crime, there are other evidences to corroborate the story, which, in all its details, stamp it as one of the most notable in the crim- inal annals of Prince George's county and its perpetrator to be one of the coolest creatures in existence. There were no witnesses to tell of what took place in the little home, but there are many surround- ings which spoke volumes in testimony to the bloody and heartless nature of the crime. In the kitchen, where the mur- der took place, was found a little table, on which had been placed the evening meal, showing that the murderer made his assault as the two ladies were at their supper. Killed At Supper. Miss Annie, the younger woman, sat at the head of the table with her back to a kitchen door leading from the room into a sunımer kitchen. It was through this door that Berry entered the room and dealt the first biow. He struck Miss Annie on the top of the head with a billet of wood two and a half feet long which had been cut for the stove. The blow knocked her from her chair to the floor. Miss Amanda, the elder, was sitting with her side to the door and did not see the blow delivered, but when she raised her eyes they fell upon Berry standing near her side with the murderous club raised to strike her. Then began a battle of life and death, to save her sister and herself. In her efforts she lost her own life, but was probably instru- mental in saving the life of her sister. Fighting For Life. Berry attempted to strike Miss Amanda, but she warded off the blow with her left arm. The negro backed off and made a second rush at the brave woman, who stood between the brute and her fallen sister. Again he raised the club, and as it desconded she tried to parry the blow. The brute exerted all his strength, and as the bludgeon fell she attempted to shield her head, and the blow fell with full force on her left arın, breaking it at the wrist and causing her to sink to the floor in terror and pain. The brute then beat her over the head, crushing in her skull and scat- tering her brains and blood over the walls of the little kitchen. Preparing For Flight. Daring all this time Miss Annie was ly- ing in an unconscious condition on the floor, and Berry thought she was dead. He then ransacked the house and secured 95 cents in money, which had been re- ceived by the ladies from the sale of eggs. The murderer then went to his room, over the kitchen, and packed his clothing in a satchel, evidently preparing himself for flight. He also went to one of the bed- rooms in the front part of the house, and, taking a straw mattress from a bed, dragged it down stairs and struck match, supposedly to set fire to the house to cover up his crime. Renewed Assault. a At this juncture Miss Annie revived, and hearing the boy in the adjoining room made outery, upon which Berry quickly returned to the kitchen and began to finish Miss Anule. He struck her a blow in the face with a billet of firewood, cut- ting through the end of her nose, through both lips, through her chin and knocking out her front teeth. He then set out to compiete his devilish work by commit- ting in outrage on the prostrate woman. She, however, fought him off, but only after he had torn her clothing from her body. After fighting until her strength was ex- hausted, Miss Annie began to beg for her life. She promised to give him a hundred dollars and never to mention his name if he would spare her. These offers seemed to have some effect on him and he began to question the woman as to the sincerity of her promise to shield him. Swearing On A Crucifix. He left her and went upstairs for a small crucifix which was used by the ladies in their devotions. While she was lying by the side of her dead sister, and almost in death's throes herself, the brute placed the crucifix on her blood-stained lips and said. "You swear you will never tell who did this?" The answer was, "I do." Not satisfied altogether with this form of oath, the negro ran his hand into the bosom of the lady's dress and, tearing a scapula which she wore around her neck from its cord, he placed it on her lips and made her repeat the promise. Going For The Doctor. He then asked if she wanted anything; if he should go for a doctor. She asked him to do so, and he left the room, went to the stable, where he procured a horse and saddle, and started for Bowle. On the way he stopped at the house of Mr. J. W. Clark, a brother of the two victims. He was met by Everett and James Clark, nephews of the Misses Clark, to whom Berry said: "You had better go over to the house, as some one has gotten in there and almost killed both the ladies." The negro then rode off to Bowie, arriv- ing at the home of Dr. M. A. Ryon, to whom he told the same story and said: "You are wanted at once and had better go on horseback, as the roads are bad." The negro himself rode back to the house and put up his horse. When he reached the house he was met by Everett and James Clark, who had gone over from their homes. Going For The Priest. They went into the house with the negro, and Miss Annie said: "Some one go for the priest." "I will go for one," said Berry, and again he went to the stable and rode off to White Marsh Church, where he informed one of the clergymen, and came back with him. When he reached the house this time Dr. Ryon had arrived and said Miss Amanda had been dead about one and a half hours, and that Miss Annie's condi- tion was critical. What The Nephews Saw. Everett Clark and James Clark were the first to arrive at the house after the mur- der. They said: "When we entered the kitchen we found our aunts lying on the right side of the stove, from the door, and covered with a quilt and sheet. Under the head of each was a blood-soaked pil- low. We were terrified at the sight. The walls of the room looked like some one had been killing hogs. Aunt Amanda was nearest the stove and lying on her right side, with her head doubled up under her. Aunt Annie was lying on her back. The furniture in the room was not upset, and there was some fire in the stove. When we heard Berry come back from Bowie we met him and he repented the same story of some one having come into the house during his absence and killing the ladies." Dr. Ryen soon came and they took Miss. Annie into an adjoining rooin. What The Doctor Said. Dr. Ryan said: "As soon as I saw Miss Amanda I knew she was dead. On exam- ining her I found that her skull had been fractured. She had at least eight or nine distinct wounds in her head and left hand and arım. One particularly shocking wound was made on the left temple, which cracked the skull. This wound probably caused her death. As soon as I had ex- amined Miss Annie I asked her who did the job. She did not answer. I then told her that I knew. She asked, 'Who is it?" I said that negro here. She answered 'Yes; I am glad you have found out.'" Preparing To Lynch. By this time the news had spread. Many persens came from miles around. All this time Berry was taking a deep interest in all that was going on. He said to those present: "I wish I knew who did this work. I would kill him." He never seemed to think that suspicion and evidence had fastened on himself. The crowd, as soon as they were in- formed of the part Berry had played, want- ed to kill him on the spot. He was sent three times from the house to a spring near by for the purpose of lynching him, but this was prevented by some of the cooler heads. Fixing The Crime On Berry. Capt. George W. Smith, Martin Keough and Harry Keough, of Bowie, arrived at the house about midnight. They at once set to work to get at the bottom of the crime and began to ply Berry with ques- tions. They soon had him tangled up, and Constable Norman Porter placed him un- der arrest. They took him to the bedside of Miss Annie Clark and asked her if she identified him. She waved her hand and said. "I certainly do. Take him away." Jury Of Inquest. Sheriff Charles Roby was sent for, and he reached the scene about 11 o'clock Sun- day morning. He took charge of Berry, while Justice Rufus Belt summoned the following jury of inquest: George M. Smith, foreman; Martin Keough, Edward Bell, Harry Keough, Joseph Nicholson, Richard Hardesty, Joseph W. Ryan, Charles Seitz, M. E. Brady, Clifton C. Jones, W. W. Phelps and F. B. Lueres. Berry was called. He showed not the slightest fear. Foreman Smith told him that he was not compelled to tell anything, but if he wanted to make any statement he could do so. The prisoner was sullen and not in- clined to talk. He was taken to the kitchen and shown the face of his victim. He looked with a steady gaze upon the face of Miss Clark without showing a sin- gle sign of remorse or fear. Sheriff Roby took the prisoner to Bowie. Just as they were leaving the house a pair of bright handcuffs were slipped over his wrists. Effect Of Cold Steel. At the sound of the click of the cuff locks and the touch of the cold steel Berry cringed, and he then wanted to talk. Lie said he was not at the house, but had gone to a store for some quinine and found the women on his return. He added: "When I saw them all bloody I fainted and took a dose of quinine to brace me up." He denied having changed his clothing, but Martin Keough made a search for the cast-off suit and found the blood-soaked garments in a wooden chest in a summer kitchen. When shown the clothes Berry shut up like a clam. A Teltale Watch. While the hunt for the clothes was be- ing made Mr. Harry Keough lifted up one of the pillows which had been under the lady's head and found a small brass open-face watch, which was handed to Berry, who claimed it. The face of the watch was covered with blood, and at the suggestion of some one the face was cleaned off, and the watch had stopped at 7.30 o'clock. This is about the hour Berry is supposed to have completed his work of slaughter. A Full Confession. At Bowle the prisoner was further ques- tioned and said: "I will tell a colored man about it." Bayliss Fairfax, colored, was asked to talk with him. To Fairfax Berry said: "I did it. I have Intended to do it for several days, but could not get at them right until Saturday. They scolded me about coming into the house with muddy boots, and they did not treat me right, so I killed them." This statement was heard by the officers, and Berry was told to tell all he knew. He said: "The ladies were at the sup- per table and I was bringing stove wood In the kitchen. I had an armful of wood, and as I dropped it into the wood box one of the pieces fell out of the box. I picked it up, and as I did so I thought: "This is my time, and this is the thing to do it with." I turned around and struck Miss Annie on the head. I supposed I had killed her, as she fell stiff. Miss Amanda jumped up from the table and grabbed the stick be- fore I could strike her. She got it out of my hand. I stooped down and got another stick and made at her. Every time I would strike at her she would ward off the blow. This made me mad, and I got a chance and I struck with all my might. She gave a groan and fell by the side of Miss Annie. I struck her sereral times in the head until I sup- posed she was dead. I then went through the house and got 95 cents, which I put in a purse in my room. When I came back I started to outrage Miss Annie and would have done so if I had not taken another thought, which said to me 'You have done enough today.' Miss Annie swore on the cross that she would not tell and would give me $100 to go for a doctor. I got pil- lows for them and suppose that my watch fell out while I was putting their heads on the pillows. After I covered them up I got the horse and went for the doctor and told the Clark boys." Trouble Brewing. While telling the story the negro never changed countenance, but seemed to be re- lating some every-day gossip. But the crowd thought differently and Sheriff Roby saw a storm coming. He telegraphed for a special train, and started for Upper Marlboro', and by this act saved the wretch's neck, as preparations were being made to Iynch him. The Victims. title: FALSE EXPECTATIONS: REV. W. M. ALEXANDER, COLORED, PREACHES ON DUTY OF HIS RACE
full_text: "FALSE EXPECTATIONS" Rev. W. M. Alexander, Colored, Preaches On Duty Of His Race. Rev. W. M. Alexander, pastor of Sharon Baptist Church (colored), Presstman and Carey streets, in his Sunday morning ser- mon spoke plainly to his congregation on the folly of false expectations. In part The said: "As a race of people we have spent too much of our time and energy building on sandy foundations. As citizens, as a rule, we have voted, expecting the party for whom we voted to make us more than it is possible for the National or State Gov- ernment to make a dependent people, the masses of whom do not think for them- selves. We must learn that the people make parties and statesmen and that nei- ther can do for any class of people what the law of self help requires them to do for themselves. "The thing for the negio to do is to make the most of opportunities at hand. If em- ployed as laborer, fill your place so faith- fully that your services cannot well be dispensed with. "Teach the youth by word and example in the home how to work for their bread Send them to the publhe schools and keep them in attendance every day during the term, if possible, because the day is near at hand when persons who cannot read and write will find it hard to get employ- ment. "As to the element of the race which has educational advantages and strength enough to help our weaker brethren, we must reach out our hands to them and bring them into our Christian and civic cncles. "We must also work with the white peo- ple who are giving their time, money and thought to help us to help ourselves. I have been reading the reports of the Mary- land Sunday-School Union, the charity or- ganization society, House of Reformation at Cheltenham, for colored boys in this State, and am gratified to know so many agencies are at work for the good of our people. This boys' home is doing a good work, and we ought to ask the Legislature to increase its appropriation so the Board of Managers can make needed improvements." title: THE HOUSE: NO LOCAL OPTION FOR MONTGOMERY--TRUST COMPANIES
full_text: THE HOUSE No Local Option For Montgomery- Trust Companies. ANNAPOLIS, MD., March 29.-The follow- ing bills were reported unfavorably and the unfavorable reports adopted: The local option bill for Montgomery county; to pay to Samuel R. Owens, of Montgomery coun- ty, money erroneously paid into the treas-- ury; to provide for the appointment of a commission to examine into the work of institutions receiving State aid (Senate); to require oath that contracting parties to mortgages make no secret agreement; to authorize Caroline County Commission- ers to borrow money to rebuild - Dover bridge; to regulate the manufacture and sale of lager beer; to provide for the ap- pointment of a board of visitors to the An- napolis jall; to permit officers to enter premises wherein gaming is suspected; to amend the laws relative to contracts with telegraph and telephone companies; to reg- ulate the charge for rental of telephones. Among the House bills which were fa- vorably reported were those to incorporate the Western Maryland Trust Company; to incorporate the City Real Estate Trust Company; to incorporate the Southern Mu- tual Life Insurance Company, and to incor- porate the Investment Trust Company of Baltimore City. Among the Senate bills reported favor- ably were the following, which were ad- vanced to the third-reading file: To incor- porate the Eastern Shore Trust Company; the American Trust and Investment Com- pany; the United Deposit and Fidelity Company of Maryland; the Anne Arundel and Baltimore Electric Railway Company; the Farmers' Banking and Trust Company of Montgomery County; the Consolidated Trust and Finance Company; the Balti- more Elks' Exposition and Social Session Association; the Calvert Banking and De- posit Company: the Southern Trust and Deposit Company of Baltimore. The following House bills were passed: | To incorporate the Tidewater Fire Insur- ance Company of Cambridge; to provide for the election of a Treasurer of Talbot county; to amend the charter of the Great Falls Power Company; to incorporate the Maryland Sanitary Refrigerating, Venti- lating and Heating Company; to incorpo- rate the Baltimore Annual Conference of the Colored Methodist Protestant Church; to direct the Appeal Tax Court of Balti- more not to issue building permits until taxes on land have been paid; to incorpo- rate the Patapsco Investment, Guarantee Title and Trust Company; to amend the game laws of Frederick; to sanction be- quests of Willie F. Hooper, of Wicomico county; to authorize the Police Commis- sioners of Baltimore to pension Herman Heimiller, William J. Lowdenslager, John Davis, John F. Kelly, Ambrose A. Ryan, Joseph S. Townsend, Louis F. Norris, George W. Bailey, Manus A. Behrens, for- merly policemen of Baltimore city; to pro- vide for the incarceration of youthful con- victs in city jail instead of the peniten- tiary, in the discretion of the sentencing judge: to incorporate the Dorchester Elec- tric Light and Power Company; to appro- priate $1,000 for the expenses of the com- mission to establish boundary line between Maryland and Virginia; to prohibit the sale of liquor within 1% miles of Bethel Church of God, in Carroll county; to pro- vide for the payment of appearance fees for attorneys at law in Baltimore county in habeas corpus cases; to provide for the election of Caroline County Commission- ers; to permit wives to enter into business copartnership with their husbands; to pro- vide for tax levy and collection of taxes in Rockville; to amend the Talbot fish laws relative to crabs and terrapin; to amend the charter of La Plata. Charles county; to amend the charter of the Continental Trust Company; to permit Mayor and City Council of Baltimore to appeal from the decisions of Tax Commissioners to State Comptroller and Treasurer; to provide for a special fund for pensions by the Police Commissioners of Baltimore city: to re- fund to Calvin Satterfield $109.78 erro- neously paid to treasury; to amend the fish laws of Frederick county; to make it a misdemeanor for any person other than an attorney to accept fees as such; to permit Easton to exchange land for an alley; to amend the laws relative to sales in bulk; to incorporate the Baltimore City and County Railway, Electric Light and Im- provement Company; to authorize Harford County Commissioners to pension James Bennington; to create a Board of Health for Baltimore county; to refund to the Emmitsburg Railway Company money erroneously paid into the treasury. At the afternoon session the following House bills were passed: To appropriate $1,000 to the Veteran Firemen's Associa- tion; to authorize Harford County Commis- sioners to pension Samuel John Wesley; to prohibit the sale of liquor at Ruxton Station, Baltimore county; to give County Commissioners of Garrett county author- ity to appoint a jail warden: to incorporate the Baltimore Elks' Exposition and Social Session Association; to authorize the State's Attorney of Frederick county to file criminal information; to secure to the Mercantile Library of Talbot a set of the archives of Maryland; to prohibit the shooting of wild fowl on the Great Chop- tank river in Talbot county between May 1 and October 10; to lower the property qualification of members of the Second Branch of the City Council of Baltimore; to provide for a peddler's license for Elk- ton, Cecil county: to refund to William Wood Cook, of Dorchester, money paid for unused packer's license; to authorize Ha- gerstown to extend Prospect street; to amend the road laws of Wicomico; to amend the charter and change the name of the Potomac and Severn Electric Railway Company; to amend the charter of the Na- tional Park, Sandy Spring and Hyattsville Railroad Company; to provide for a police justice for Williamsport; to provide for a bounty for the killing of wild animals In Frederick county; to amend the game laws of Caroline county; to encourage manu- amend the game laws of Frederick county; facturing industries at Hagerstown; to to empower the Druid Ridge Cemetery Company to acquire additional land; to ap- propriate $8,000 for the improvement of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham; to require life and health insurance companies to have a surplus of $100,000, which must be invested in safe securities; to require all releases of mort- gages to be preserved; to provide for the issuance of a license to sell Intoxicating liquors at the Cabin John Bridge Hotel, Montgomery county; to make it a misde- meanor for a person to gun upon the prem- ises of another without permission. The bill to authorize the attachment of one-half of the wages of the debtor was de- feated-20 to 40. The bill to regulate the payment of wages of employes of corporations was upon mo- tion.of Mr. Waller laid upon the table. title: DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA: AN ADDITION TO THE CITY'S NOISES--A POLICEMAN IN POLITICS
authors: Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun
full_text: DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA An Addition To The City's Noises- A Policeman In Politics. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] WASHINGTON. July 20. - To add to the other noises of a big city, the collectors of coal ashes here are to sound a gong wher- ever they go. At present the trolley cars and hucksters do very well as noise pro- ducers, with occasional obligatos on long tin horns from the garbage collectors. The milkmen formerly contributed gong num- bers, but the residents rose up in wrath and had them restrained. Now the gong is to come into its own again, and many are making ready for another agitation against "unnecessary and nerve-racking disturbances before our doors."" While ill with malarial fever Mrs. Grant A. McNutt, 32 years old, and the wife of a clerk in the War Department, leaped from the second-story window of her home, 1801 Oregon avenue. A friend who was in the sick room caught her dress, but the gar- ment parted and Mrs. McNutt fell 15 feet to the pavement. When taken to the Emergency Hospital it was learned she had suffered no apparent injury except the fracture of her wrist and several con- tusions. Mr. McNutt was persuaded to have her placed at St. Elizabeth's until the dan- ger of further delirium shall have passed. During the convention at Kansas City the anti-Norris men presented in behalf of their position an affidavit from Lieut. John C. Daley, of the local police force. Because of the deponent's official position this paper is said to have carried great weight. At any rate one of the Norris men was suficiently moved by it to complain to the Chief of Police. It is against the police regulations for any patrolman or officer to take part in any political meeting. So the Chief of Police has called on Lieut. Daley for an explanation and an Investiga- tion is almost certain to follow. A parade through the business portion of the city Saturday marked the return to Washington of the District National Guard. For about 10 days the organization had been encamped on the farm of John B. Diamond, near Gaithersburg. The expe rience is regarded as having been of great practical value to the brigade, and a most successful outing. Citizens of Gaithers- burg have already Invited the men to re- turn next year. Mr. Diamond has prof- fered the use of his farm a second time, and a committee has been formed to keep the movement alive during the winter. William Smith, George W. Bond, Wi- liam Greenstreet and William Robinson, all colored, are at the Fifth Precinct Station on charges of having escaped from the Cheltenham Reformatory. Word was re- ceived here Saturday the boys had broken loose Friday. They were captured near Anacostin, walking about aimlessly. Rev. Jullus E. Grammer, D. D., rector of - Trinity Episcopal Church, Baltimore, preached today at St. John's Church In this city. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: REFORMING COLORED BOYS: MANAGERS OF THE CHELTENHAM INSTITUTION ELECTED
full_text: REFORMING COLORED BOYS Managers Of The Cheltenham Insti- tution Elected. The annual meeting of the members and subscribers of the House of Reformation for Colored Bors for the election of 12 members of the board of managers was hold yesterday afternoon at the office of Mr. Edward Stabler, Jr., 6 South street. The managers elected are as follows: Goldsborough S. Griffith, Edward Stabler, Jr., J. Erskine Carson, Joseph J. Jannes, Frank Woods, Edward Markell. Nathaniel G. Grasty. Edward Stinson, Baltimore; F. Snowden Hill, ex-Congressman Charles E. Collin and C. C. Magruder, Prince George's county. The Governor of the State and Mayor of Baltimore each appoint twomem- bers of the board to look after the inter- ests of the State and city respectively. The Institution is located at Cheltenham, Prince George's county. It was opened February 4, 1873, when the first two coi- ored boys were cornumitted to the institu- tion. By the end of the year the inmates had Increased to 72. Since then the his- tory of the institution has been one of steady growth, until now it consists of a. farm of 750 acres and all necessary build- Ings and modern equipment, the whole costing about $150,000. The institution has had a total of 2,204 boys under its eare. The total number of Inmates at the end of 1800 was 263. The board still claims that the appropriations made by the State for the support of the Institution are inad- equate. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. BAREFOOT WOMEN IN JAIL Mr. Fait Favors Shoes On Moral Grounds, But Board Said Not. An effort was made last night at the meeting of the Jall Board, held at the in- stitution, to enforce the wearing of shoes by the female inmates of the jail so long as they remained in the Institution. Mr. William Fait, who advocated the measure, made a motion to have the matter investi- gated. bat as there was no second to the motion it was dropped. Mr. Fait enthusiastically favored having ail women in the jail shod in some manner or other. He thought it was really dis- gusting to see the white and the colored won.en going around in their bare feet and believed the wearing of shoes would have a moral erect upon them. He did not think runch, he said. of the refinement of any woman whom he saw on the streets in her bare feer, and thought it would add to the refinement of those in the jail. George W. Mowen said he believed the jail was a place of punishment and hardly thought it wonid do to treat the inmates as if they were saints and angels. He thought the inmates would return to the jail as soon as they were discharged sim- ply to get the shoes. Mr. Fait appealed to Warden Doyle, who thought it a good plan, but would add greatly to the ex- penses, as the shoemakers in the jail had more than they could do to provide shoes for the inen, who had to have them be- cause of the work they did. "Most of the women who come here," said Mr. Doyle, "wear no shoes when they enter, and others might as well be bare- footed." Mr. Kernan suggested in jest that the women be made to wear tights. Mr. Thomas F. McNulty, who presided in the absence of President Tippett, said that If the plan were adopted the fall would have to be enlarged to accommodate the patrons. title: Boys In Serious Trouble
full_text: Boys In Serious Trouble. Joseph Alban, Jesse Fleury, William Lehnert and Harry Jones, bors, were be- fore Justice Poe yesterday, charged with entering the establishment of Jacob Ep- stein, 216 West Baltimore street, and steal- ing a brass clock, four dozen belts and a pair of gloves, valued in all at $8.40. All were released on bail for court, with the exception of Alban, who was held at the station house antil he can get the secur- ity. Frank Jirsa, 16 years old, was re- leased for court by the magistrate, charged with entering the same place and stealing three dozen ladies' belts and two pairs of gloves, valued at $7.75. A short time ago the establishment was much damaged by fire, and it is alleged that the boys were rummaging among the debris and stealing articles of value which they might find. Two boys were caught in the cellar Tues- day night and they implicated the others. Held Up By Negroes. Andrew Polinsky, 38 years old, reported to Patrolman Miller, of the Western dis- trict, yesterday that he was attacked by three negroes while walking on the Balti- more and Ohio railroad, near Mount Airy, about 2 o'clock yesterday morning. Two revolvers were pointed in his face by the negroes, who ordered him to hold up his hands. He did so, and they went through his pockets and took 25 cents, which was all the money he had. As he started to walk away one of the negroes, he says, shot at him three times. One of the bul- lets hit him in the right leg below the knee. He told some train hands of his in- jury and he was brought to Baltimore on a train. Afterward he was removed to the Maryland University Hospital, where he had the wound dressed. Musicians' Dressing Room Robbed. David Politzer and Wiliam Lessner, 17 and 18 years old, respectively, were com- mitted to jail yesterday for a hearing on January 26, by Justice Poe, charged with stealing a silver cigarette case and a sil- ver matchbox, valued at $30, from Signor Emerico Morreale, leader of the orches- tra of the Francis Wilson opera troupe, and also with stealing a gold hunting case watch from Joseph Radcliffe, one of the musicians in the orchestra. The articles are alleged to have been stolen on Satur- day from a dressing room at the Academy of Music. i The young men admitted the charges. The case could not be sent to court yes- terday, because of the fact that the Fran- cis Wilson Opera Company is now playing at Syracuse, N. Y., and the two musicians who lost the articles are with the com- pany. Says He Bought $0 Worth of Candy. Harrison Waters, colored, 12 years old, was taken before Justice Goldman, of the Northwestern Police Station, yesterday. charged with stealing, $0 from Mrs. Mary Ward, 1013 West Lanvale street, iast Tues- day. The boy admitted having stolen the money, which he said he had spent on candy. The prisoner would have been com- mitted for court, but the boy's 'father, James Waters, colored, 247 Campbell street, filed a charge against his son of incorrigi- bility; so Justice Goldman committed him to the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, Prince George's coun- ty, dismissing the charge of larceny. title: North Carolina Legislature
full_text: North Carolina Legislature. [Special Dispatch to the Baltiinore Sun.] RALEIGH, N. C., Jan. 14.-There was a lengthy discussion in the State Senate to- day on the bill to grant a blanket charter to the Whitney Reduction Company, with power to increase its capital stock to $10,- 000,000. A substitute was offered by the com- mittee. The original bill gave the right to condemn lands in towns or anywhere for railways of any kind. The substitute passed by a vote of 35 to 3. Nearly all the long session of the House was consumed in the discussion of a bill increasing the Governor's salary from $8,000 to $4,000. It passed by the close vote of 55 to 52 and was ratified soon after. It increases the salary of Governor Aycock, who takes office tomorrow. Newcastle Visits Philadelphia. PHILADELPHIA, Jan. 14.-Henry Pelham Archibald Pelham-Clinton, Duke of New- castle, arrived here today en route to Flor- ida, where he owns considerable property. With the Duke came Editor Kelway, of the Church Review, and Rev. Harry Wil- son, rector of St. Augustin's Episcopal Church, Stepney, England. The Duke pre- sided at a public meeting tonight, at which Editor Kelway spoke of the progress of the Catholic party in England and the Rev. Mr. Wilson explained the object of the"Red House," an institution established by the Catholic party to redeem the deni- zens of London's slums. The three visitors are looking into the question of establish- ing an American edition of the Church Re- view. Another Clue In Riegel Case. PHILADELPHIA, Jan. 14. - The police to- day recovered broken pieces of the bottle which is believed to have contained the. poison administered to Rev. Father Riegel, rector of the Church of the Presentation, Cheltenham, who is alleged to have been murdered and robbed here about 10 days ago. 1 Among several persons under arrest is a 16-year-old boy known as "Kid" Hartman. He Informed Coroner Dugan that after the phial had been shattered he buried it In the yard in the rear of the Eighth street house. It was discovered, hidden beneath a brick.

Nearly all the long session of the House was consumed in the discussion of a bill increasing the Governor's salary from $8,000 to $4,000. It passed by the close vote of 55 to 52 and was ratified soon after. It increases the salary of Governor Aycock, who takes office tomorrow. Newcastle Visits Philadelphia. PHILADELPHIA, Jan. 14.-Henry Pelham Archibald Pelham-Clinton, Duke of New- castle, arrived here today en route to Flor- ida, where he owns considerable property. With the Duke came Editor Kelway, of the Church Review, and Rev. Harry Wil- son, rector of St. Augustin's Episcopal Church, Stepney, England. The Duke pre- sided at a public meeting tonight, at which Editor Kelway spoke of the progress of the Catholic party in England and the Rev. Mr. Wilson explained the object of the"Red House," an institution established by the Catholic party to redeem the deni- zens of London's slums. PHILADELPHIA, Jan. 14. - The police to- day recovered broken pieces of the bottle which is believed to have contained the. poison administered to Rev. Father Riegel, rector of the Church of the Presentation, Cheltenham, who is alleged to have been murdered and robbed here about 10 days ago. 1 Among several persons under arrest is a 16-year-old boy known as "Kid" Hartman. title: MAYOR IS DETERMINED: WILL APPOINT COLORED DIRECTOR REGARDLESS OF OBJECTIONS WANTS RACE REPRESENTED TO HAVE WHOLE BOARD OF NEGROES WOULDN'T BE ADVISABLE--HARRY S. CUMMINGS ROCOMMENDED
full_text: MAYOR IS DETERMINED Will Appoint Colored Director Regardless Of Objections. WANTS RACE REPRESENTED To Have Whole Board Of Negroes Wouldn't Be Advisable-Harry S. Cummings Recommended. "I don't care who objects; a colored man Is going to be appointed as a member of the board of directors of the Colored House of Reformation!" Such was the reply of Mayor Hayes yes- terday to a Sus reporter's query as to whether he thought any of the members of the board would remonstrate against serving on It with a colored man. "Do you think a colored man could look after the interests of the inmates better than a white man?" the Mayor was asked. "I think that there should be a colored man on that board," said the Mayor. "The colored boys will talk more freely to one of their own race than to a white man, and will acquaint him with their needs. The principle is the same as in the schools. here should be colored teachers for col- cred pupils. It would be impracticable to have the Cheltenham board composed wholly of colored men, because they would probably lack the business and executive ability which the white men possess, but I certainly think that the race should be rep- resented." A petition in favor of the appointment of James W. Highes, 519 St. Paui street, was drawn up and signed by the members of the grand jury yesterday. He is the col- ored member of the grand jury. Messrs. George B. Skinner and William L. Wilcox, of that body, cailed on Mayor Hayes yes- terday morning to present the petition. The Mayor declined to give any hint as to whom he would appoint, saying that he would send the nomination up to the City Council on Monday evening. City Couneliman Hiram Watty, whom the Mayor asked to recommend some one for the position, stated last night that he Tad recommended Harry S. Cummings, a well-known colored lawyer, who was fer- merly a member of the City Council. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: DIRECTORS FOR CHELTENHAM: COUNCIL COMMITTEE INDORSES THE MAYOR'S NOMINEES
full_text: DIRECTORS FOR CHELTENHAM Council Committee Indorses The Mayor's Nominees. The City Council Committee on Police and Jail met yesterday afternoon, and aft- er a lengthy discussion decided to report favorably on Mayor Hayes' ordinance to appoint Gen. Felix Agnus and Hariy S. Cummings, colored, City Directors of the House of Refuge for Colored Boys at Chel- tenham. A contention arose in the committee over the nomination of Cummings, and Mr. Howser vigorously opposed him, wanting to substitute the name of R. M. Hall, col- ored, who is now on the grand jury. Mr. Guyton favored the ordinance as intro- duced. Mr. Howser's was the only vote against a favorable report. The ordinance will come up in the Second Branch next Monday night, and a fight is anticipated, as Major Venable and several other members have declared their inten- tion of voting against Cummings. Building Inspector Preston's ordinance to provide for municipal inspection and super- vision over all electrical wiring will also be reported favorably with several changes. The annual salary of the two inspectors is fixed at $2,500 and $1,500, respectively, and it is provided that for minor electrical work a permit is not necessary. Wiring that is never exposed to view is also ex- empt from inspection. Two other ordinances known as the frame extension ordinances were also passed upon favorably. One of these gives the Building Inspector power to compel all frame extensions hereafter built to be as nearly fireproof as possible. The other authorizes the Building Inspector to make as nearly fireproof as possible without tear- ing them down all frame extensions here- tofore erected. The Building Inspector is given discretionary powers in both these ordinances. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: BOYS BEHAVE WELL: NO DANGER OF SHOTGUN POLICY AT CHELTENHAM NEEDS OF THE INSTITUTION PLANS OF SUPERINTENDENT DORSEY FOR THE COMING YEAR -- PREPARATIONS FOR CHRISTMAS FESTIVITIES
full_text: BOYS BEHAVE WELL No Danger Of Shotgun Policy At Cheltenham. NEEDS OF THE INSTITUTION Plans Of Superintendent Dorsey For The Coming Year-Preparations For Christmas Festivities. A number of reports have reached THE SUN to the effect that residents of the neighborhood of the Colored House of Re- formation, at Cheltenham, Prince George's county, were in constant fear of intrusion from the boys of the institution, and that a "shotgun policy" might be necessary to protect the property of the farmers from the depredations of the boys. A thorough investigation yesterday by a reporter of THE SUN, who visited more than a score of residents near the institution, disclosed no such alarming state of affairs. On the contrary, a number of residents of the section stated that there was now little or no cause of complaint against the boys, with the exception of the stealing of a lit- tle fruit in the season. Two or three years ago, say the neighbors, the nuisance was almost intolerable, but under the superin- tendent who recently resigned, Mr. Nathan Thompson, the boys were brought under good control, and now give no trouble. Should the boys take it into their heads to become troublesome or even dangerous, however, they might very easily do so, for it would be hard to imagine a corrective in- stitution with less evidence of restraint. Escapes have been very frequent, for they have been easy of accomplishment. An instance of this occurred on December 2, just before Mr. John E. Dorsey, the new superintendent, took charge of the institu- tion. James E. Goldsborough and John Williams, allas John J. Gordon, struck and knocked down Mr J. H. Forbes, a teacher, as he unlocked the door of their dormitory in the morning. The thing had been pre- arranged, and the two, with two others in the dormitory, made their escape. All four were soon recaptured, however. Superintendent Dorsey's Force. There are now 237 boys in the institution and to exercise supervision over them there are a superintendent, an assistant superin. tendent and four teachers. There are em- ployed about the place a farmer, an en- gineer, a baker and one or two other as- sistants, but they are not charged with the direct care of the boys. There are sup- posed to be five teachers, but the place of one of them is now vacant. There is not a wall and not even a fence, except a barbed wire one, about the place, and there is not a guard about the institution, so that it is not at all difficult for a boy to slip out of line and disappear. Mr. Dorsey, the superintendent, Is op- posed to corporal punishment and is going to try to control the boys by kindness. He has devised a plan, which is to be put into practice at the first of the year, by which good conduct, tidiness and attention to les- sons will sooner or later secure a boy his parole or even discharge from the institu- tion. The boys are to be graded, from the sixth up to the first, and above that there are to be two "honor grades." The teachers will report cach boy's conduct and atten- tion to lessons to the superintendent every morning, and the boys' standing will be made up every month. They must reach a certain standard in order to be advanced from one grade to another. For bad conduct or for trying to escape they may be reduced one or two grades. When a boy holds his place in the second "honor grade" for a whole month by per- fect conduct he will be eligible to be paroled for a time under the supervision of the Board of Trustees. The "roll of honor boys" will have a special dining room and will enjoy a somewhat choicer grade of food. They wil lalso be allowed to talk with each other at meal times. Agricultural Plans. The agricultural feature of the institu- tion is to be further developed during the coming year, and the cultivation of small fruits, such as strawberries, raspberries, currants, etc., will be taken up on a much larger scale than heretofore. There are now about 325 acres of land under cultiva- tion by the boys, and various farm crops are raised, including wheat, rye, grass, etc. The land is being improved by the cultiva- tion of peas, manuring and feeding. Last year 375 bushels of black and mixed peas were grown and gathered before the vines were turned under to enrich the ground. More The crying need of the institution, say those connected with it, is funds. men are needed to take care of the boys. An additional boiler is required to heat the dormitories and to provide for baths in them, since now the water has to be turned off in cold weather to prevent it from freezing. A system of drainage is badly needed, as well as sufficient stock and im- plements to work the farm. The city this year cut down its appro- priation from $12,000 to $6,000, greatly to the dismay of the Cheltenham officials, and one of the six schools had to be closed for want of money to pay the teacher. Preparing For Christmas. The boys are now busily preparing for Christmas, and all of the buildings are be- ing trimmed with holly and greens. The boys of one of the schools are rehearsing a minstrel show and cakewalk, with which they will entertain the inmates. There will be a Christmas tree for all the boys of the institution and an extra turkey dinner. Dr. Walter G. Cady, chief of the geodetic survey station at Cheltenham, is taking a great deal of Interest in the boys, and has arranged with friends in his Providence (R. I.) home to send a Christmas present to each boy in the institution. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

Representatives of the various charity or ganizations of the city, the police magis- trates and Commissioners, the judges of the Supreme Bench and the State's Attorney's office gathered in McCoy Hall, at the Johns Hopkins University, yesterday to discuss a bill which had been prepared to regulate the control of lawbreakers under the age of 16 years. Bonaparte .suggested a number of improvements and amendments to the law to enable it the better to with- stand criticism in the courts, and he offered two substitutes which covered practically all the essential parts of the bill. Mr. Soper made a sug- tried in the Criminal Court the Supreme gestion that as some cases will have to be the cases and have them all at one time, Bench appoint one of its members to try so that the juvenile defendants may be re- moved as much as possible from ordinary court scenes. Good Result In Chicago. Mr. Levering was instructed on motion to appoint a committee of seven to carry the bill, when it is completed, to the Legis- lature and to do all in its power to see that it is passed. Mr. Levering was asked to take the chairmanship of the committee, but declined. title: MONEY FOR REFORMATORIES: APPROPRIATIONS FROM CITY ARE SUBJECTED TO SEVERE PRUNING
full_text: MONEY FOR REFORMATORIES Appropriations From City Are Sub- jected To Severe Pruning. The manual training department of the House of Refuge will be discontinued after May 1 because of lack of funds. This was determined upon Thursday, when the su- perintendent of the institution, Capt. Charles A. Hancock, resigned. He was ali- pointed January 1 last. President Joshua Levering, of the House of Refuge, said yesterday: "The manual training department, in which 156 boys are employed, will have to be closed because, without our knowing the reason therefor, the appropriation for this year has been cut down from $23,000 to $13,000. The appropriation for the manual training department was formerly $6,000, but is now only $1,500, too small a sum to keep it up." The manual training department has been In existence since 1889. Mr. Joseph J. Janney, secretary, general agent and manager on the part of the city of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Cheltenham, explained last night. why the managers announced that they would not receive any more boys for the present. "We took that action," he said, "because our finances will not allow us to take care of those we have, much less receive others. There are at the institution at present 277 boys and 25 employes. To support them we have an income of $16,000, which is cer- tainly not enough for a place of the kind, and we are busily engaged at present in trying to decide how to continue operations without running into debt. "Up to the present year our income was $10,000 from the State and $12,000 from the city. The subcommittee of the Jall Board visited Cheltenham and was loud in its praises of the way in which the reformatory Is conducted, but apparently this report had no influence upon the Board of Estimates, for, without consulting a single one of the board of managers or asking for any fur- ther information, our appropriation was cut down to $6,000 after we had run three months into this year, without any intima- tion of the reduction. "It is not generally known that this is the only reformatory of the kind in the United States, and we get prisoners from all over the country, committed by the United States courts for violations of United States laws. Of such prisoners there are now about 28, but the average is about 25. We are accomplishing splendid results and are glad that public attention has been drawn to the way in which we are handi- capped." President Richard B. Tippett, of the Jail Board, which has supervision over re- formatory institutions for which the city makes appropriations, said that the amounts for each reformatory institution under the care of the Jall Board were fixed by the Municipal Board of Estimates, and that it would be impossible to make any changes this year. "Forty-eight thousand dollars is the sum total for all reformatory Institutions for this year," said Mr. Tippett yesterday aft- ernoon. "The Board of Estimates fixed the amount of each Institution, and the distribution is being made in strict con- formity to their action. The amount for each Institution for the current year was fixed as follows: House of Refuge, $13,- 000;.. St. Mary's Industrial School, $20,000; Colored House of. Reformation, $6,000; House of Good Shepherd for Colored Girls, $2,500; Industrial Home for Colored Girls, $1,500, and Female House of Refuge, $5,000, making a total of $48,000. "In those institutions where manual training is a part of the course no extra amount has been appropriated for that purpose. At the last report of the House of Refuge for 1900 the Institution had 148 boys committed by the city. St. Mary's Industrial School got $20,000. At the last report for 1900 the Institution had 371 boys committed by the city. The Colored House of Reformation for 1900 bad 144 boys. The appropriation was $12,000, a per capita of $7.50. There was a balance of $406.43. No appropriation was made for manual training nor for repairs. The House of the Good Shepherd for Colored Girls got $2,500, a per capita of $4.75. The Female House of Refuge had an appropriation of $5,000, being a per capita of $6.66 2-3. The ap- propriation for the Industrial Home for Colored Girls was $3,000, being a per cap- Ita of $3.50. From the talks I have had with Mr. Levering and General Riggs I thought they thoroughly understood the method by which the amounts for the ser- eral institutions were appropriated." title: DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA: THOUGHT TO BE "WILLIE" MCCORMICK, HIGH SCHOOL CADETS DRILL
authors: Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun
full_text: DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA Thought To Be "Willie" McCormick. High School Cadets Drill. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] WASHINGTON, May 2. - A strange boy, sald to have been wandering about Glen Echo, Md., for the past few days, has been reported to the police by residents of that locality as possibly "Willie". McCormick, the boy kidnapped from Highbridge, N. Y. In all his intercourse with other persons the boy is said to have been extremely reti- cent. He is described as answering the descriptionsent out by the McCormick family. Youthful Prisoners. Washington's House of Detention last night entertained three boys who were passing through the city under the escort of a United States marshal from North Carolina. They are Fletcher Evans, col- ored, aged 12 years, under sentence of one year's imprisonment at Cheltenham, Md., for the theft of 50 cents; Bennett Holl- man and Luther Hollman, convicted of dis- tilling whisky without a license and un- der sentence to serve a year in the local Reform School. High School Cadets Drill. A great throng gathered about the White House ellipse this afternoon to view the annual review of the High School Cadet Corps. For about two hours the regiment marched in review, executed the manual of arms and conducted dress parade, the music being furnished by the Marine Band. Gen. George H. Harries, commanding the District militia, reviewed the command. At the close of the drill the regiment was divided into two battalions and a sham battle was fought. Col. C. E. Boesch, of the Central High School, commanded the corps. An Extensive Improvement. Messrs. (Woodward & Lothrop, proprie- tors of the Boston House, are about to. begin the construction of a large addition to their present stores. On the site of the old St. Vincent's Orphan Asylum is to be erected a building about 200 feet long and 100 feet deep, which is to adjoin the pres- ent stores. It is estimated the cost of the alterations and construction will be about $500,000. Death Of Mrs. O'Neil. Mrs. O'Neil, wife of Rear-Admiral Charles O'Neil, chief of the Bureau of Ordnance, died at 12.30 o'clock this morning of ano- plexy. She had been in ill health, but had lately Improved greatly. Mrs. O'Neil leaves one son, Dr. O'Neil, of Boston. Funeral services will be held Saturday afternoon and the interiment will be in Arlington Cemetery. Before her marriage Mrs. O'Nell. was Miss Frothingham, of Boston. To Contest Mrs. Sailer's Will. A caveat against the will of the late Eliz- abeth Barber Sailer, which is dated No- vember 10, 1896, and was submitted re- cently for probate, has been filed by 11 heirs-at-law, most of whom live in Ger- many. By the terms of the instrument the testatrix bequeathed her entire estate to the Washington Home for Incurables. It is contended the paper filed is not the decedent's last will, and that if she exe- cuted it she was not of sound mind at the time. She Slipped On A Fish. A verdict for $1,000 damages was found in the suit of Emma L. Clagett and Maur- ice J. Clagett, her husband, against the Washington Market Company and Freder- ick L. Grunewald, surviving partner of M. Moreland & Co. The plaintiffs con- tended that Mrs. Clagett slipped on a fish while walking through the market and sustained serious injury. Arbor Day At Congress Heights. Congress Heights celebrated today as Ar- bor Day and planted about 30 trees. Over 300 persons were present. Among those for whom trees were named were Senator Hanna, Gifford Pinchot, forester of the Agricultural Department; the late Gen. Henry W. Lawton, Secretary Long, Vice- President Roosevelt and Senator Clark, of Montana. Marriage Licenses. Archie M. Nichols and May D. Hardisty, of Montgomery county, Maryland, obtained a marriage license in this city today. Li- censes were issued also to James Stewart and Annie S. Fortune; Edward E. Miner and Mary E. Johnson; Charles Williams and Ruth Matthews. Rev. Buckey Assigned. Rev. Edward Buckey, at one time rector of St. John's Protestant Episcopal Church, Newport, R. I., and who was ordained a priest in the Roman Catholic Church in Baltimore yesterday, is sald to have been assigned as assistant pastor at St. Mat- thew's Catholic Church in this city, vice Rev. Father C. M. Bart, now pastor of St. Teresa's Catholic Church, Anacostia. Fa- ther Buckey is a son of the late Justice M. V. Buckey, of Georgetown. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Boy Confesses Stealing Letter
full_text: Boy Confesses Stealing Letter. James Scott, colored, 15 years old, pleaded guilty in the United States Dis- trict Court yesterday of the larceny of a letter containing $6 from postal sub-sta- tion No. 11, corner Gilmor street and Fred- erick avenue, on February 10 last. He was sentenced to two years in the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham. The boy was employed about the station at the time of the larceny. Charge Against Mr. Hanna Dismissed The United States grand jury yesterday dismissed the case of Robert B. Hanna, charged with assaulting George C. Flory on the Naval Academy grounds at Anuapo- lis on January 4 last. Flory, it was al- leged, was knocked down and had a leg broken. Rachel Brooks' Estate. The estate of the late Rachel Brooks is appraised at $30,304 in inventories filed in the Orphans' Court yesterday. The total is made up of $32,257 in real and $7,047 in personal property. Notes From The Courts. Clara C. De Bols, 1112 East Monument street, was granted an absolute divorce yesterday from George J. De Bois and the custody of their child, Elsle May, aged 7' years. They were married November 16, 1894, and lived together about a month, The divorce was granted on the ground of abandonment. Mrs. De Bols testified that her husband went to New York to look for work, but he never came back. Frank C. Rhodes, a storekeeper at Wil- liamsport, Md., applied for the benefit of the bankruptcy law yesterday by Lewis D. Syester, attorney. His liabilities are $811.07 and assets $175. title: KAFFIRS IN THE WAR: BOER COMMANDANT DECLARES HE WILL SHOOT THEM DOWN BRITISH ARE USING THEM KITCHENER CITES A CASE WHERE NO MERCY WAS SHOWN--CONFLICT COST BRITAIN $6,250,000 WEEKLY IN JULY
full_text: KAFFIRS IN THE WAR Boer Commandant Declares He Will Shoot Them Down. BRITISH ARE USING THEM Kitchener Cites A Case Where No Mercy Was Shown-Conflict Cost Britain $6,250,000 Weekly In July. LONDON, Aug. 1.-A dispatch from Lord Kitchener, dated at Pretoria today, says: "French reports that he has received a letter from Kritzinger announcing an in- tention to shoot all natives in British em- ploy, whether armed or unarmed. Many cases of cold-blooded murder of natives in Cape Colony have recently occurred." Another dispatch from Lord Kitchener says: "On July 28 an officer's patrol of 20 yeo- maury and some native scouts followed two carts and a few Boers 15 miles from the railway at Doorn river, Orange River Colony, where they were cut off by 200 Boers, and after defending themselves in a small building, surrendered when their am- munition was exhausted. Three yeomen were wounded. After the surrender the Boers made the native scouts throw up their hands and shot them In cold blood. They afterward shot a wounded yeoman. The remainder were released. The Boers gave as a reason for shooting the yeoman that they thought he was a 'Cape boy.' Evi- dence on oath has been taken of the mur- ders." A Lorenzo Marquez dispatch says: "A Boer commando with two guns has entered Portuguese territory, camping at Guanetz. Five hundred Portuguese troops are already at Guanetz, and artillery left here for that place this morning. Three hundred troops in addition are in readiness to proceed un- less the Boers surrender." In the House of Commons Lord Stanley, Financial Secretary of the War Ofice, re- plying to a question, said the cost of the war in South Africa from April 1 to July 31 was £35,750,000 ($178,750,000), partly chargeable against the deficit of last year. The actual cost in July was £1,250,000 ($6,- 250,000) weekly. The statement was greeted with Ironical Irish cheers. The Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, sald if the war continued at the same cost for the next three months it would necesst- tate spending the whole of the reserve he had provided for financing the third quar- ter of 1901; but he had reason to hope that this would not be necessary. The House of Lords unanimously voted the grant of £100,000 ($500,000) for Lord Roberts, recommended by King Edward, as a token of appreciation of the Field Mar- shal's services in South Africa. Martial law has been proclaimed on Tucker's and Morgan's Islands, Bermuda, where Boer prisoners are confined. The British transport Manila, Captain Haddock, from Port Natal, July 4, and Table Bay. July 8, has arrived at Bermuda with more prisoners. "Mr. Kruger's American tour," says the Brussels correspondent of the Dail Mail. "will include visits to New York, Philadet. phia, Boston, Washington and Chicago. Negotiations are about to begin for his re- ception by President McKinley." The president of the Royal College of Surgeons, Sir William MacCormac, read a paper before the British Medical Associa- tion, now in session at Cheltenham, stating that the character of gunshot wounds ha'd completely changed since his experiences in the Franco-Prussian War, when he was surgeon-in-chief to the Anglo-American am bulance. Not only was the severity of the wounds diminished, he sald, but they were less frequent. So the improvements made in weapons did not render the prosecution of war worse, as contended in some quar- tera. Only 6 per cent. of the wounded died. With reference to the charges made against the army hospital service in South Africa by Win. Ashmend Bartlett-Burdett- Coutts, Sir William said Mr. Coutts had no idear of the perspective and exaggerated ev- erything.

title: THE JUVENILE COURT BILL: MR. GLENN CLAIMS IT IS NOT OPEN TO OBJECTIONS STATED
full_text: ; THE JUVENILE COURT BILL Mr. Glenn Claims It Is Not Open To Objections Stated. Messrs. Editors: Will you allow me space for a few words in reference to the letter of Mr. Goldsborough S. Griffith about the juvenile court?! It is agreeable to find that on the main principle, which is the foundation of our desire for a juvenile court, Mr. Griffith and the advocates of the court are agreed. He says "family ties are regarded as very sa- cred things." The main object of the pro- posed law is to preserve family ties. The object of having probation officers is to keep children in their own homes and to compel unwilling parents to take care of their own children in cases where, under our present system, the children would have to be sent to reformatories or to jail. This can be done only by means of proba- tion officers.. It is a system which is in force in many other cities and has proved satisfactory. Experience elsewhere has shown that the adoption of the 'probation system lessens the number of children brought up for commitment. The powers of investigation and supervision given to the probation officers are precisely similar to those now exercised by the pald agents of the Society for the Protection of Chil- dren and the Prisoners' Aid Association. Incidentally, the number of charges for which the city and State must pay will be reduced in proportion to the number of chil- dren kept at home instead of going to re- formatories. Mr. Griffith seems unwilling to leave the committing power to a magistrate. What he says as to the ability of a magistrate to deal with these cases of children would apply, if true, to all our magistrates. My experience is that our police station jus- tices are as capable of dealing with such cases as the judges of our courts. It is not necessary that one should be deeply learned in the law in order to decide whether a child is vicious, or neglected, or destitute, or is a subject for commitment by the grand jury. The chief requirements are sympathy (not sentimentalism), com- mon sense and experience. All of these qualities our police justices possess equally with our judges. In the matter of expe- rience they are more used to dealing with this class of cases. There is no reason to fear the dangers which Mr. Griffith suggests as likely to follow the placing of the jurisdiction over children in a single justice. There are cases which come before magistrates in which it is conceivable that politics may have an influence, but there is little oppor- tunity for this in the cases of children and they appeal to the best that is in every man. I believe that any man would find it hard, for political or corrupt reasons, to deal injudiciously with children. On the other hand, the submission of all the cases of children to a single justice will concen- trate public attention on his work and lia- bility to public criticism will require a high standard. If the argument against the capacity of magistrates to deal with these cases is a good one, it seems very im- portant that the power to commit, now vested in civil magistrates who are not un- der the public eye and before whom com- paratively few such cases come, should be discontinued. In speaking of the powers of courts under our present laws, Mr. Grif- fith seems to forget that the chancery pow. ers under a habeas corpus cannot be called into play until after a child has been com- mitted to an institution. There certainly is no hardship in requir- ing children and parents to come to one central place in these days of rapid transit. If the spirit of the law is carried out chil- dren will not be conveyed to the court as "prisoners." At present, whatever the pro- visions of the law may be, minors are not tried separate from adults in the police courts, nor is it easy to see how this sepa- ration could be managed practically. The law does not require that negro boys must be sent to Cheltenham pending action by the grand jury and trial. It merely gives the justice power to send children, pending trial or commitment, to some other place than jail or station-house. If he thinks it best he may proceed as he can now.. The bill before the Legislature was pre- pared by a committee consisting of Mr. Joseph Packard, Gen. Lawrason Riggs, Messrs. Morris A. Soper, Moses R. Walter, Leon E. Greenbaum, William Reynolds and John M. Glenn. It was then submitted to a conference, Invitations to which were sent to representatives of all societies and institutions in the city dealing with chil- dren, the Judges of the Supreme Bench, the State's Attorney and the Police Com- missioners. The meeting was largely at- tended, among those present being three of the police justices. At the conference the law was fully discussed and amended in Important particulars. Unfortunately the invitation was not accepted by any repre- sentatives of the two societies which Mr. Griffith represents. The conference was presided over by Mr. Eugene Levering, president of the Association for the Im- provement of the Condition of the Poor, and a committee was appointed to present, the bill to the Legislature, consisting of Mr. Joseph Packard, Mr. John R. Cary, Dr. William Bullock Clark, Messrs. Frederick D. Morrison, Morris A. Soper, William F. Wheatley and James R. Wheeler. It is hardly correct to characterize such gentle- men as "ill-guided regulators of morals and manners." JOHN M. GLENN. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: CHEVY CHASE LAND SUIT
full_text: CHEVY CHASE LAND SUIT Interesting Decision By The Court In Montgomery. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.) ROCKVILLE, MD., April 19. The close of Mary Hodges against the Chevy Chase Land Company was decided in the Circuit Court for Montgomery County this morning, Judges McSherry and Henderson dismiss- Ing the suit. It was an action of eject- ment to determine the title to about 90 acres of land of the holdings of the Chevy Chase Land Company in the lower section of the county which had been devised by the late Dr. Benjamin B. Hodges to the plaintiff's father for life and then to his children. Shortly after the testator's death a bill was filed in the Equity Court here for the sale of the land for partition. All of the living children of the life tenant were parties to this suit. A decree was passed, a trustee appointed and the land sold. After the sale the plaintiff was born. Her contention was that she was not bound by the decree and sale and is therefore stili entitled to her interest in the land, and this suit was brought to settle that question. The court decided that the plaintiff was bound, under the provisions of an act of 1862, by representation. All the parties being interested in the property being par- ties to the equity suit, as required by that act, hence the decision against the plaintiff. Messrs. Ridout & Bright, of Washington, appeared for Miss Hodges, and Messrs. Ar- thur Peter and Rallston & Siddons, of Wash- ington, and Edward C. Peter, of Rockville, represented the land company. SHOT IN A SALOON - Edward Straton Killed In Frederick By William Johnson. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] FREDERICK, MD., April 19. Edward Straton, 24 years old, was shot and almost instantly killed by his friend, William Johnson, in Dudley Strasberger's saloon, on West All Saints street, this evening. The two men, who had been working on the Baltimore and Ohio Improvements near Mount Airy, had been good friends and came to Frederick this evening to get some beer. They went to Strasberger's saloon, a noted place on All Saints street, and soon formed friends with several negro women. A quarrel soon occurred between the two men, and Johnson pulled his revolver and üred three shots at Straton. The latter reeled and fell on the porch. Some of his friends picked him up and started for a doctor, but when he got as far as Brewers alley he sank to the pavement and ex- pired. The shooting created a consternation among the negroes, and they all fied from the place, no effort being made to appre- hend the murderer. Johnson escaped in the excitement. He is described as a mulatto, about 5 feet 10 inches and weighing 150 pounds. Penitentiary Sentences. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] UPPER MARLBORO, MD., April 19.-In the Circuit Court for Prince George's County, which adjourned the April term today, John Green was sentenced to the penitentiary for five years for assault with intent to rape. James E. Goldborough and John Gordon, colored, both boys from the House of Ref- ormation, at Cheltenham, were sentenced to three years in the penitentiary for assault- ing one of the guards of that institution. Thomas Davage wassentenced to four years in the penitentiary for larceny. Blue Ridge Tunnel. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] HAGERSTOWN, MD., April 19.-Twelve sur- veyors, under Chief Engineer C. H. Bratt, are making the third survey for the pro- posed tunnel for the Western, Maryland rallroad under the Blue Ridge Mountains. The tunnel will be 400 feet below Blue Ridge Summit and run directly under the Monterey Hotel. The surveys will not be finished for several weeks. As soon as the work is completed the cost of tunneling the mountain will be calculated. It is pre- dicted that work will begin in the fall, especially if the railroad is sold. title: NO DANGER OF STARVING: ECONOMY AT CHELTENHAM HAS NOT ATTACKED THE COMMISSARIAT
full_text: NO DANGER OF STARVING Economy At Cheltenham Has Not Attacked The Commissariat. Messrs. Editors: Fearing that the state- ment in regard to the House of Reforma- tion, that the point of starvation is al- most reached, may be misleading and give concern to some parents who have boys there, I wish to assure the public that there is no danger of this. It is true the cutting down of our appropriation by the elty is causing us no little concern, and we feel the necessity of the closest economy in order to avoid a deficiency in our finances; yet there is no intention of shortening the allowance of food either for the boys or for the officers. Economy will be made to affect every other department before it will - be permitted to attack the commissariat. The cut of 50 per cent. in our allowance from the city and the decrease in the ap- propriations to other reformatories is a se- rious mistake, but we feel hopeful that the year 1002 will see us restored at least to the old basis of financial support by the city; if so this temporary embarrassment can in time be overcome. As far as the House of Reformation is concerned, we feel certain that those who were instrumental in cutting down our appropriation never paid us a visit and informed themselves of the needs of the institution. But we will in our own defense say this: That the Jail - Board, through its own subcommittee, must have known that we were worthy of support, for this language is used in a let- ter to me by a member of that subcommit- tee: "I am proud to have been one of a committee to visit such an admirable insti- tution. Would there were more like it!" Whoever is responsible for the cutting down of the appropriation for the House of Reformation-and no one seems willing to shoulder it-it is certain they could not have realized the good work that is being done there. Those in whom is vested the authority to fix the amount of the people's money that may be properly employed in the support of reformatories should be re- quired to visit them personally, and if they are found to be worthy of support, appro- priate the amount that may be needed to maintain them adequately. May 13, 1901. JOSEPH J. JANNEY, Secretary of Board of Managers. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: CHILDRN AND CRIME: CHARITIES AND CORRECTIONS CONFERENCE TAKES UP SUBJECT WANT MARRIAGE RESTRICTED TWO PHYSICIANS URGE LEGISLATION WITH A VIEW TO PREVENTING THE UNION OF THE MENTALLY DEFICIENT
authors: Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun
full_text: CHILDREN AND CRIME Charities And Corrections Con- ference. Takes Up Subject. WANT MARRIAGE RESTRICTED Two Physicians Urge Legislation With A View To Preventing The Union Of The Mentally Deficient. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] WASHINGTON, May 14.-The care of the feeble-minded and epileptics occupied the attention of the general session of the Con- ference of Charities and Corrections this morning. Dr. William A. Polglase, super- intendent of the Michigan Home for the Feeble-Minded and Epileptics, made the re- port of the committee. Miss Margaret Ban- croft, superintendent of the Training School for Feeble-Minded at Haddonfield, N. J., rend a paper on the classification of the mentally deficient. She said this class learns more rapidly when associated with those who are not in the same condition. Dr. Polglase took the opposite view. A paper on "Legal Restrictions on the Marriage of the Unfit" was read by A. C. Rogers, superintendent of the Minnesota School for the Feeble-Minded, at Fairbault, Minn. He reviewed bills which had been considered by State Legislatures with the Intention of putting a stop to the marriage of the mentally deficient or those afflicted with diseases or vicious habits which would be transmitted to their children. None of them had ever passed. The opposition to legal restraints upon marriage was based, he said, upon the lack of public sentiment, upon the theory that they would be an inter- ference with personal liberty, and that it would result in a tendency to increase im- morality. He advised that legislation upon such points should be applied only so far as absolute knowledge of the facts could be obtained. Dr. W. J. Spratling, of New York, held that restricting marriages was the only, way to prevent the increase of this unfor- tunate class, already too large. Destitute and neglected children were con- sidered at a section meeting, where C. D. Randall, of Coldwater, Mich.; Thomas E. Ellison, Joseph P. Byers, secretary of the Ohio State Board of Charities, and others spoke. Meetings were held to discuss the care of the insane and on juvenile reformatories. At the evening session Lyman D. Drake read a paper on "The Origin and Develop- ment of the Juvenile Reformatory," pre- pared by E. P. Wentworth, superintendent of the State Reform School, Portland, Maine. "During the nineteenth century prison life was vastly improved," he said. "At the beginning of the century prisoners were treated more like brutes than men and women, but the public conscience was awakened and conditions began to improve rapidly. The public began to realize that with childish offenders herded with hard- ened criminals the children could not fall to grow up steeped in crime. Today the 58 juvenile reform schools in the United States cost about $3,500,000 a year, and have property valued at $20,000,000." "Girls' Reformatories and Their Inherent Characteristics" was discussed by W. G. Fairbank, superintendent of the State In- dustrial School for Girls, Middletown, Conn. He thought the reformatories for girls received less attention than those for boys. The girls, however, are more valu- able to modern society, in his opinion. Mr. Fairbanks favored the cottage or family plan. In the reformatories, he said, the girls should be taught housework and homemaking first, although typewriting may be taught later. The following officers were elected on a report of the committee on organization: President, Timothy Nicholson, of Richmond; vice- presidents, B. T. Janney, of Washington, D. C.; Franklin MacVeagh, of Chicago, III.: Thomas Muley, of New York; Jose M. Berriz, Havana, Cuba, and Mr. Jose F. Godoy, Washington, D. C.; general secretary, Homer Folks, of New York city: treasurer, A. O. Crozier, of Grand Rapids, Mich.; official reporter, Mrs. Isabel G. Borrows, of New York city. James Hunter, visitor-in-chief, supervisor city charities, Baltimore; Miss Rebecca P. Laughlin, Evening Dis- pensary for Working Women and Girls, Baltimore; Herbert W. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] WASHINGTON, May 14.-The care of the feeble-minded and epileptics occupied the attention of the general session of the Con- ference of Charities and Corrections this morning. Dr. William A. Polglase, super- intendent of the Michigan Home for the Feeble-Minded and Epileptics, made the re- port of the committee. Miss Margaret Ban- croft, superintendent of the Training School for Feeble-Minded at Haddonfield, N. J., rend a paper on the classification of the mentally deficient. She said this class learns more rapidly when associated with those who are not in the same condition. Dr. Polglase took the opposite view. A paper on "Legal Restrictions on the Marriage of the Unfit" was read by A. C. Rogers, superintendent of the Minnesota School for the Feeble-Minded, at Fairbault, Minn. He reviewed bills which had been considered by State Legislatures with the Intention of putting a stop to the marriage of the mentally deficient or those afflicted with diseases or vicious habits which would be transmitted to their children. None of them had ever passed. The opposition to legal restraints upon marriage was based, he said, upon the lack of public sentiment, upon the theory that they would be an inter- ference with personal liberty, and that it would result in a tendency to increase im- morality. He advised that legislation upon such points should be applied only so far as absolute knowledge of the facts could be obtained. Dr. W. J. Spratling, of New York, held that restricting marriages was the only, way to prevent the increase of this unfor- tunate class, already too large. Destitute and neglected children were con- sidered at a section meeting, where C. D. Randall, of Coldwater, Mich.; Thomas E. Ellison, Joseph P. Byers, secretary of the Ohio State Board of Charities, and others spoke. Meetings were held to discuss the care of the insane and on juvenile reformatories. At the evening session Lyman D. Drake read a paper on "The Origin and Develop- ment of the Juvenile Reformatory," pre- pared by E. P. Wentworth, superintendent of the State Reform School, Portland, Maine. "During the nineteenth century prison life was vastly improved," he said. "At the beginning of the century prisoners were treated more like brutes than men and women, but the public conscience was awakened and conditions began to improve rapidly.
