title: CHELTENHAM BOYS IN JAIL
full_text: CHELTENHAM BOYS IN JAIL Charged With An Assault Upon A Keeper, With Intent To Kill. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] MARLEORO, MD.. Dec. 7.-Deputy Sheriff P. E. Hall brought to the county jail James Goldbraugh and John Gordon, charged with committing an assault with intent to kill J. H. Forbes, teacher at the House of Reformation at Cheltenham. These boys were inmates of the institu- tion and hailed from Easton and Freder- ick, Md., and have been more than six years at the home. On Monday last the prisoners were placed in the guard-house for Immoral conduct, and the charge is that they planned a scheme to kill Mr. Forbes and make their escape. When supper was served them they made a rush on the keeper, felled him to the ground with blows and then kicked him until he became unconscious. At once they left the cell and were well on their way to Washington, when arrested at Anacostia, D. C. Mr. Forbes was found by some of the guards and is not confined to his bed un- der the treatment of the institution's physi- clan. Magistrate Squires committed the boys to jail for the action of the grand jury. A FATAL FALL Horris Sutton Accidentally Killed In Harford County. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] BELAIR, MD., Dec. T. - Horris Sutton, aged about 28. a san of Luther Sutton, near Taylor, Harford county, died las evening as the result of injuries received Thursday night by falling from the second- story room of Houch's mill, a distance of 20 feet. Young Sutton was returning to his home from Baltimore, when he stopped at the will to play a game of cards with several, of his friends. The game was played in the office on the second floor, and shortly after 8 o'clock Sutton left the room for the purpose of continuing his journey home. It was not until some time after- ward that the young man was found by This friends on the ground beneath an open door on the second floor and in a uncon- scious condition. He was carried to his home and everything done to save his life. The only injury noticed on his body was a slight wound on the head back of his right car, which, it is thought, caused concus- sion of the brain, resulting in death. title: MAYOR VISITS CHELTENHAM: EXPRESSES REGRET THAT CITY'S APPROPRIATION WAS CUT
full_text: MAYOR VISITS CHELTENHAM Expresses Regret That City's Appro- priation Was Cut. Mayor Hayes paid a long visit to the Colored House of Reformation, at Chel- tenham, Prince George's county, yesterday on invitation from the board of managers, who desired the Mayor to see what is be- ing done to reform the colored boys sent there by the magistrates of the city and counties and with what insufficient means the work is being carried on. In the party accompanying the Mayor were Messrs. Joseph J. Janney, secretary of the board; Harry S. Cummings, Rev. George F. Bragg, Jr., Orrin C. Painter, City Councilman Hiram Watty and Rev. W. V. Tunnell, warden of King Theolog- ical Hall, Washington. The party left on the early morning train and did not get back to the city until late in the evening. The visitors inspected the various school- rooms and dormitories under the guidance of Mr. John E. Dorsey, the superintendent, who entertained the guests at dinner. Aft- erward the boys assembled in the chapel and the Mayor made them an address. His Honor was informed that the insti- tution is considerably in debt, owing to the decreased appropriations by State and city and that the number of inmates has been as high as 300, but of late, compulsory dismissals have been made to such an ex tent as to close one of the schools. Cur- tailments have been effected in many of the departments and the salaries of the teachers have been reduced. Mayor Hayes expressed his sympathy with the work of the institution and said he realized the un- fortunate condition of the reformatory and would bring its needs before those in authority. After his return to the city the Mayor said he was delighted with his trip. "They are doing a noble work down there," he added, "and Mr. Dorsey, the superintend- ent, is a splendid man for the place. The boys seem to like and trust him, and he makes them feel that the institution is a home for them and not a penal institution. It is unfortunate that the city cut its ap- propriation down from $12,000 to $10,000, and had I known the conditions there, I would not have agreed to it." title: GRAND JURY AT CHELTENHAM: FINDS INSTITUTION BELOW STANDARD OF OTHER PLACES
full_text: GRAND JURY AT CHELTENHAM Finds Institution Below Standard Of Other Places. A committee of the grand jury, of which Mr. James King is chairman, visited the Colored House of Reformation at Chelten- ham yesterday and made a thorough in- spection of the place. Besides Mr. King there were present Mark O. Shriver, Leon- ard M. Levering, James L. Reese, John Aftung, William H. Scott, Dr. Charles H. Cockey, Emil Caye, John W. King, James Owens, Joseph J. Janney, James A. Har- ris (colored) and George C. Morrison. Mr. Henry Broening, Clerk of the Criminal Court, was also in the party. The special committee on the institution will report to the grand jury that the in- stitution is in "fairly good condition;" that the sanitary arrangement and drainage are bad; that there is an insufficient number of officers; that more work should be given to the boys, as not over 50 are employed at a time, and that the appropriation for the Institution is not large enough to meet re- quirements. Larger appropriations and a general overhauling of the buildings will be recommended. Mr. James King said last night: "We found about 50 boys of the 250 at work. The kitchen and schoolroom were in fairly good condition. There ought to be more workshops, and with more officers more boys could work on the farm. The appro- priation is too small and will have to be Increased if the school is to be placed on the same standard with other institutions of the kind." Mr. Mark O. Shriver, foreman, was seen at his house, 607 St. Paul street, last night and said: "We were not at all satisfied with the management of the Institution, which seems to be faulty in a number of respects. Still, we think that much allowance should be made for the new superintendent, who has been there only a few months. The school officials claim that they are handi- capped by a lack of money and to this scarcity of funds they attribute many of the conditions we observed. "The place is not kept very clean and the sanitary arrangements are poor. We were told that the superintendent has al- ready achieved considerable improvement with the amount of money at his disposal, and he said that with sufficient funds he could make the institution a model of its kind." full_text: $10,000 FOR CHELTENHAM But Mayor And Comptroller May Di- vert It If They See Fit. The recent discussion over the manage-1 ment of the House of Reformation for Col- ored Boys, at Cheltenham, Prince George's county, and the question as to whether the moral tone of the place was all that it ought to be, prompted the Board of Estimates yesterday to refrain from making a direct appropriation for the institution this year, as has been the custom in the past, but to set aside $10,000 as a fund for "the main- tenance and care of colored youth and chil- dren." The disposal of this fund will be in the hands of the Mayor and City Comp- troller, who are authorized to make a con- tract with the Colored House of Reforma- tion, and that institution can thus be kept under closer supervision by the city au- thorities. 1 1 The institution will, it is supposed, get nearly all, if not all, of the fund, since the other colored homes usually appropriated for have already been taken care of for next year. The officials designated can, however, divert any part of it to another colored asylum if they see fit. If the Col- ored House of Reformation should get the whole $10,000, however, it would still fall short by $5,000 of the sum asked for by the board of managers. This year's appropria- tion was $0,000. I'resident Jeffrey R Brackett and Mr. John M. Gleen, of the Board of Supervisors of City Charities, were before the Board of Estimates, and on behalf of their own board respectfully declined the proposition previously made that they take charge of the fund to be appropriated for the Colored House of Reformation. authors: Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun
full_text: RIVER VIEW TILTING Tournament Of Brave Knights On The Banks Of The Potomac. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.) WASHINGTON, Aug. 20.- Many of the best familles of Maryland and Virginia were represented in the throng of 4,000 persons which witnessed the sixteenth annual tour- nament at River View, Md., on the Poto- mac river, this afternoon. Two thousand five hundred residents of the District of Columbia went to the tilting grounds on the steamer Samuel J. Pentz. full_text: MAY JURY DISMISSED Makes A Number Of Recommen- dations In Its Report. WOULD LASH WIFE BEATERS Says Perjury Is Commited In Shield- ing Saloonkeepers And Urges Re- moval Of Screens And Blinds. Judge Phelps, in the Criminal Court, yes- terday, received the final report of the Grand Jury for the May term. The jury was then discharged with the thanks of the court. The grand inquest and the several comm- mittees appointed to visit the various in- stitutions made a number of recommenda- tions, the former referring to the frequency of charges of wife-beating and urging that such offenders be punished by the lash rather than by the imposition of fines or by imprisonment. In its report the jury said it had consid- ered 263 cases from the sheriff's docket, 64 from the special docket and 1.009 from the grand jury docket. A total of 699 present- ments were found, 637 cases were dis- nussed, 281 tried, 45 persons acquitted and 236 convicted. There were 3,589 witnesses summoned. On the grand jury docket there were 634 cases presented. 375 dismissed; special docket, 54 presented and 10 dismissed, sheriff's docket. 11 presented and 252 dis- missed. The following was given as the classification of cases on the grand jury docket: Murder.... Assault Gambling. False pretenses Larceny. Peace Miscellaneив Violating liquor law. Total.. 9 161 S 31 396 140 230 34 1,000 The Foreman's Report. In his report for the jury Mr. Mark O. Shriver, the foreman, said: "I beg to call your attention to several matters that claimed our attention and which we believe, if put in practice, would be of benefit to all concerned. Of the many cases that come before the grand jury we find at least one-half of them of minor im portance; these cases, we think, should have been settled in the Police Court and not al- lowed a jury trial We refer to such trivial cases as drunkenness, disorderly conduct, disturbing the peace, minor cases of as- sault, theft of small articles of less than a dollar in value. If these cases could be set- tled by the police justice it would be a great saving to the taxpayers and relieve the Criminal Court very much. "About three-fourths of all the cases that come before the grand jury are negro cases. Many of these are the result of a violation of the civil and religious law, men and women living together as man and wife without any regard for the marriage tle. "In order to aid the police in locating stolen articles we thinkit would be wise to have a prepared blank to give to every li- censed dealer in second-hand goods, pawn- brokers, junk dealers and require them to make weekly reports to the police marshal of every article they have purchased dur- ing the week. giving a description of the party who sold or pawned the goods. their age, sex and color. Dealers in junk who make large purchases need only report the smaller articles bought and metals they buy of less quantity than 500 pounds. Perjury To Shield Offenders. "Regarding the liquor cases that come be- fore the grand jury, such as selling liquor to minors, selling during prohibitive hours, selling on Sundays, etc., we find it next to Impossible to present, as perjury in most cases is used to shield the offenders, both by the patrons and the saloonkeepers. We believe if the presentlaw was amended and a law enacted with the following condi- tions it would lessen the sale of liquor and at the same time keep minors out of the saloons and benefit all interested "Saloons should be on the most public streets The bar should be in the front 100m of the first floor of the house, facing the street. The front of the house should have plate-glass windows two-thirds the height of the ceiling, being but one foot from the floor, and two-thirds the width of the room. Over the bar there should be a light burning of at least 30 candle- power, and this should be kept burning all the time, so that passers along the street could have an unobstructed view of the in- Bide of the room, and always have the bar In full view This we believe would be a true temperance law and greatly benefit the public. "We think the law relating to wife-beat- ing could be used to good effect, and, there- fore, recommend that where the law ap- plies it be enforced and the whipping post be restored. "We think it would be advisable to have an expert accountant to examine the books of the different institutions that receive money from either the city or State and to publish the same in our daily papers. Tax- payers would be better satisfied if they knew how their money was spent in caring for the unfortunates committed to these different institutions. "A former employe of the House of Ref- uge made charges of harsh and cruel treat- ment of the boys confined in this institu- tion. We had some who were alleged to have been maltreated summoned before us. also the president and other officers, and are pleased to state that the charges were not proved. We believe them false, if not malicious. At Cheltenham. "By invitation of Rev. Thomas Broy- drick we visited the Colored House of the Good Shepherd, situated on the Calverton road. The Sisters have 81 colored children who have been committed to this institu- tion by the city and State. These children are required to do some work each day, having a certain task allotted which must be accomplished. Recreation is given every day, their health and morals are carefully cared for and every virtue instilled. The house was clean and neat and is a credit to the State and city. The chief occupation of the inmates is laundry work, which they are taught to do in a superior man- ner. We think the most efficient houses of correction are those which provide employ- ment for their inmates, and if the direct- ors of the different institutions would give this matter serious consideration they would assist the institutions to be self-sus- taining and greatly help the inmates by teaching them habits of industry. "The room' assigned to the grand jury has but one merit-its location. The ven- tilation is bad, the acoustics are worse, and the noise from the traffic on Calvert street makes the room anything but suit- able. The room should be adapted for the use of the grand jury, and if this cannot be done, then another room should be as- signed them." Commendation is extended to Mr. H. W. Rodgers, the stenographer, for his efficient work. Committees Make Reports. The various committees of the jury that visited and investigated the institutions to which they were assigned also made their reports, and these were presented to the Court with the general report. In many cases other members of the jury accom- panied the committees on their visits. The committee on sanitation reported that it found pressing necessity for measures presented to different juries. The grand jury room, it declared, is badly arranged, the acoustics are bad, there being an echo in the room and on account of the noise from Calvert street the windows have to be kept closed and the air becomes very of- fensive, Our city," the report continues, "wants a. larger storage system for the drinking water, which becomes muddy after heavy rains and has to be used in that condition. "The waterbeds supplying us should be most carefully policed to prevent infection. It is a shame that our drinking water is ever contaminated by negligence and the penalty is often disease, pestilence and death. There is no portable filter worthy of confidence in the hands of the average layman. Our neighbor, Philadelphia, has recently installed a filtration plant which is claimed to be a success. Need Of Sewerage. "We all know the great need of a sewer- age system, but the great trouble is to de- cide on the best. There is urgent want of a hospital for infectious diseases. It has not been long since we were promised one and the site selected. Alas! it proved to be a mere shadow, and not a reality. We need a better system of paving our streets and alleys to render them smooth and to have no ruts or deep holes to retain water and refuse matter to decay and pollute the at- mosphere. Cobblestones should be rele- gated to ancient history." Charles H. Cockey was chairman of the committee. The other members were Rich- ard. T. Martin, Alexander F. Murdoch, John H. Winkelman and Ignatius Smith. The committee which visited the House of Correction found that the new wing be- Ing built is very much needed for prober Reconimodation of the prisoners, and also recommended the provision of a better sewerage system. The committee reported that there, were 398 male and 39 female prisoners in the institution on August 20, the date of the visit. The manufacturing departments, said the committee, are under excellent control and management and the general condition of the prisoners seemed to indicate good care and treatment. St. Mary's Industrial School for Boys was reported to be in excellent condition, and special praise was given to the print- ing department. There were 481 boys in the institution the day the committee called. Warm commendation is bestowed upon Brother Dominic for his work of supervi- sion and direction. At The Penitentiary. The committee that visited the peniten- tiary reported it to be in first-class condi- tion. "The first impressions created," the committee said, "are of the absolute secur- ity and cleanliness, as well as in the re- duction of danger from fire to the lowest point. From interviews had with prisoners and by general observation we became im- pressed with the fact that the board of di- rectors have been most fortunate, as well as judicious, in obtaining and retaining the services of Mr. John F. Weyler, the very efficient warden." The committee that visited Springfield State Hospital, Mount Hope Retreat, Spring Grove Asylum, the House of Good Shep- herd, Industrial School for Colored Girls. Bayview Asylum, House of Refuge for Boys, Female House of Refuge and City Jail reported them to be generally in good condition and well managed. Increase Of Boys In Jail. The committee that visited the jail pro- nounced it to be overcrowded and empha- sized the need of a new structure. "We regret to see the large increase in the num- ber of boys under 16 years old." the com- mittee states. "This increase has occurred since the Juvenile Court went into opera- tion, about the middle of June. At that time there were three boys in jail; now there are 10. Relative to the Female House of Ref- uge, the committee visiting it said: "It cannot be too strongly emphasized that re- cent legislation made a radical and critical mistake when it fixed the age limit of girls placed in reformatories, such as this insti- tution, at 18 years The years between 18 and 21 are the critical ones in the definite fixation of character in girls, and it is in this period that the very highest good and best possible Influence of the institu- tion should be exerted as previous to 1900 such had been. Now this influence is lost. The compulsory closing of the cottage is also another serious drawback." The com- mittee recommends provision for a gymna- slum and that the city appropriate at least $5,000 a year for the institution. For New House Of Refuge. At the House of Refuge for Boys the committee visiting it recommended provi- sion of fire-escapes and that the present properties be sold and a more desirable location de bought farther out and new buildings erected. The jury, one of the members said, was harmonious in all of its deliberations. Purses of money were presented to Mrs. Malone, the matron, and Mr. Rogers, the stenographer. The jury was composed of Messrs Mark O. Shriver, foreman: James Clendenin, as-- sistant foreman; Leonard M. Levering, James S. Reese. Ignatius Smith. John W. King. Charles F. Ringgold. John Aftung, Alexander F. Murdoch. William H Scott. Robert M. Welch, Charles H. Cocker. Emile Caye. Robert L. Stevens, George C. Morrison. James King. Joseph J. Janner. Moses Daniel, Richard T. Martin. James A. Harris. James Owens, John H. Winkelman and John J. Jackson. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: BOY SENT TO JAIL
full_text: BOY SENT TO JAIL Cheltenham Being Full, There Is No Other Place. William Lee, a diminutive colored boy, who said he is 14 years old, presented a puzzling question when convicted in the Criminal Court yesterday of assault. The boy was convicted of cutting Hugh Taylor, a white boy, with a butcher knife on October 31 Inst. Deputy State's Attor- ney Poe sald there was no suitable place to send the boy, as Cheltenham is full. Judge Ritchie puzzled over the inatter for some time and finally sentenced Lee to Jell for three months. Lee was also charged with stealing the knife with which he did the cutting, but this case was stetted. Henry Johnson, an- other colored boy jointly charged with the assault, was acquitted. The cases of both boys were sent on from the Juvenile Court. Sailor Was A Droll Witness. Thomas Edward Thompson, a native of Ireland and a deep-water sallor, afforded much amuseinent in the Criminal Court yesterday while testifying in the case of John Turner, colored, charged with the lar- ceny of $2 from the cash drawer of a saloon at the corner of Bond and Thames streets. Thompson was in a back rooin of the saloon when the larceny occurred on October 30 last, and the grotesque manner in which he described the occurrence kept every- body laughing and the ballifts crying "Si- lence!" Turner was convicted and wa sentenced to six months in jail. Harry De Long Acquitted. Harry De Long, charged with feloniously assaulting Theresa Seguin, 14 years old. was acquitted in Part 2 of the Criminal Court yesterday. The case was tried before Judge Dobler, withouta jury, in the Judge's private room, Thomas J. Mason was at- torney for the defense. The alleged offenee was committed on October 20 last at 123 West Mulberry street. New Corporations. The Baltimore Fertilizer Company, for manufacturing fertilizers, was Incorporated, yesterday by H. Scott Roop, Newton S. Watts and Christian Rodekurt, of Balti- more, and E. Oliver Grimes, Jr., and Wil- llam T. Wilson, of Westminster, Md. The capital stock is $15,000, divided into 300 shares of $50 each. title: MR. SMITH URGES HASTE: WANTS SITES FOR HOSPITALS AND HOME SELECTED WITHOUT DELAY
full_text: - MR. SMITH URGES HASTE Wants Sites For Hospitals And Home Selected Without Delay. City Comptroller Smith had a confer- ence yesterday morning with Mayor Hayes in reference to the building by the city of an infectious-disease hospital, a home for consumptives and a parental home for a certain class of boys now at the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Chelten- ham. As explained in THE SUN last week, the city has an option on 130 acres of property near Bayview Asylum, and the plan under consideration is the erection of a colony of buildings for the care of persons now charges of the city. Comptroller Smith suggested to the Mayor that on the first- fair day this week the Mayor, Health Commissioner Bosley, the members of the Municipal Hospital Commission, members of the Board of Supervisors of City Chart- tles, himself and any others who may be Interested in the project make a trip of inspection over the land and select the most avallable sites for the proposed build- ings. The Mayor agreed that this step should be taken as speedily as possible. Mr. Smith said Inter that he belleved there should be no, delay in carrying out the idea of crecting these three buildings, as the situation was urgent. "No better Investment," he said, "according, to my judgment, could be made by the city, and it should be done at once. The land out there is eminently fitted for such build: ings, and there can be no reasonable ob- jection to any of them. In fact, there is no-one to object. "I have urged the Mayor to name a day. to go over the property with those infer- ested in the plan, and he has agreed. I suggested that the next fair 'day be se- lected." title: FOR A COLORED BOYS' HOME: THE CITY MAY HAVE AN INSTITUTION OF ITS OWN
full_text: FOR A COLORED BOYS' HOME The City May Have An Institution Of Its Own. the President Jeffrey K. Brackett, or Board of Supervisors of City Charities; Mr. John E. Dorsey, superintendent of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, and members of the board of directors of that institution appeared yesterday before the Board of Estimates and for more than an hour discussed the question of the city's entering into a contract with the institu- tion whereby a certain amount of money would be appropriated for its use next year. It was stated that there are now at the Institution about 100 city charges, who cost about $137 a year each for mainte- nance, and the suggestion was made that, the city should pay this sum for each boy committed to the place by the city. In the ordinance of estimates just passed $10,000 is set aside for the maintenance of colored youths, and the question of entering into a contract with the Cheltenham Home was to be determined later. Mr. Brackett made a suggestion that the city shouid establish a parental home for colored boys who are homeless or neg- lected, but not vicious, and said that the. lot of ground adjoining Bayview Asylum, recently purchased by the city, would be the proper place for its location. The Su- pervisors of City Charities, he said, had al- ready considered this plan and thought well of it., Messrs. Brackett and Dorsey and Secretary Grasty, of the Supervisors of Charities, were appointed a committee by the Board of Estimates to make an in- vestigation along this line and also to se- cure data concerning the number of city charges at Cheltenham who wouia de en- gible for transfer to such a home. title: ASK FOR MORE MONEY: THE CHELTENHAM DIRECTORS BEFORE BOARD OF ESTIMATES MANAGEMENT IS CRITICISED MR. MARK O. SHRIVER ALSO CONSIDERS MORAL TONE LAX--NEEDS OF BOARD OF CHARITIES
full_text: ASK FOR MORE MONEY The Cheltenham Directors Before Board Of Estimates. MANAGEMENT IS CRITICISED Mr. Mark 0. Shriver Also Considers Moral Tone Lax-Needs Of Board Of Charities. The Board of Estimates yesterday took up the request of the Board of Directors of the Colored House of Reformation. at Chel- tenham, for an appropriation of $15,000, an Increase of $6,000 over this year's allow- ance. The board listened to some severe criticism of the institution by Mr. Mark O. Shriver, a former member of the grand jury, who had made an inspection of the place. He said it was poorly managed and the moral tone was not what it ought to be. He admitted, however, that this might be remedied If the inmates were placed un- der closer supervision, which can only be accomplished if the Institution receives more money. The members of the board who were present to urge the claims of the reformatory declared that this was the only way by which the conditions there can be improved and that the disadvan- tages are due entirely to lack of money. title: SITE FOR CITY HOSPITALS: OFFICIALS AGREE ON LAND NEAR BAYVIEW ASYLUM 150 ACRES TO COST $50,000 PLAN IS TO ERECT HOSPITAL FOR INFECTIONS DISEASES AND HOME FOR CONSUMPTIVES NEAR EACH OTHER
full_text: PP SITE FOR CITY HOSPITALS Officials Agree On Land Near Bayview Asylum. 150 ACRES TO COST $50,000 Plan Is To Erect Hospital For Infec- tious Disenses And Home For Con- sumptives Near Each Other. The Health Department officials have notified members of the Board of Esti- mates that certain land in the vicinity of Bayview Asylum upon which the city has an option will be acceptable as a site for a hospital for infectious diseases. In con nection with this property it came to light yesterday that there is a broad, far-reach- Ing plan in process of development by which it is hoped to erect upon the land a colony of buildings for the care of the sick and other charges of the city. The matter Is, still in embryo, and has been kept ex- ceedingly quiet. Among the more Important buildings contemplated is a home for consumptives, to be built, entirely out of iron and glass, largely upon the general plan of a con- servatory. It was indicated yesterday that a new ordinance. would shortly be prepared for Introduction in the City Council repealing by Implication the present infectious-dis- cases hospital ordinance, which is perfected legislation, and providing that the hospital shall be erected upon the city's land near Bayview. City Comptroller's Statement. A week ago City Comptroller Smith, with other members of the board, went over the property for the purpose of gauging its availability for the erection of the various buildings contemplated. The site which is now being considered for the infectious- diseases hospital was carefully gone over, and he says that it appears to him to be an Ideal spot. It is a considerable distance from Bayview itself, and 'is entirely iso- lated from any surrounding buildings. Later a conference over the matter was held with Health Commissioner Bosley and Assistant Health Commissioner Jones, and yesterday it was announced that they had _notified Mr. Smith that the site was in every way acceptable. Condon Lot Not An Obstacle. The fact that the city is now engaged in a legal contest in which the owners of the Condon property, on the Reisterstownroad, are trying to force the city to take that lot, it is held, will not interfere with the new plan at all, and it is argued that the Infectious-diseases hospital is more nearly an accomplished fact now than it has ever been. Whether or not the city is forced to take the Condon property, the hospital can- not be erected there, as there is an act of the Legislature forbidding it. * The property near Bayview which the city is to buy contains in all about 150 acres, and $50,000 is appropriated in the ordinance of estimates for its purchase. Home For Consumptives. Immediately adjoining Bayview Asylum grounds and between it and the site for the infectious-diseases hospital is the site upon which it is hoped to erect the home for con sumptives. Comptroller Smith said yesterday that the Board of Charities and Corection had had this project in mind for some time, and an effort would be made to accomplish it next year. The plans and specifications will be prepared and the effort made later - to get the money. Physicians at the asy- lum, Mr. Smith said, are strongly in favor of the new building, and claim that it is not only bad for the other patients at Bay- view, but is unhealthy for the physicians attached to the institution to have to live -in the building with the large number of consumptives who are there. - Of Iron And Glass. The Idea of the Board of Charities and Correction, according to Mr. Smith, is to erect a large building of iron and glass, which will give the consumptive inmates of the asylum every advantage of sunshine and an open-air life: The building, It is claimed, could be so constructed as to be entirely warm and comfortable, and yet be adapted to the most modern treatment of persons afflicted with this disease. The Idea is to have as little woodwork as possi- ble about the building, and to surround it with ground enough to give the patients plenty of opportunity for exercise. Home For Boys. In addition to this, Mr. Smith says there is plenty of room on the property which the city is to buy, to erect the parental home for the care of a certain class of boys now at. the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham. The Board of Charities and Correction has already suggested the erec- tion of such a home to the Board of Esti- mates, and a committee has been appointed to look further into the matter and make a report as to the number of boys it would be necessary to accommodate, and other details of the scheme. Bayview Inmates To Work. Mr. Smith states that a part of the new, property will be apportioned off for farm Ing purposes, and will be worked by the in- mates of Bayview. This, too, is part of the general plan which is under way, and it is urged that the employment of the inmates in some work of this kind will improve conditions in the institution. title: Echo Of The Jamison Case
full_text: Echo Of The Jamison Case. The attachment taken out by Samuel H. Selfer against the Board of Police Commis- sloners to obtain possession of $100 found on Mrs. Mary Dill Jamison when she was arrested on the charge of passing bogus checks was quashed yesterday by Judge Phelps in the Superior Court. Mr.. Selfer's attachment was based on a check for $450 which had been passed on him by Mrs. Jamison. The Court ruled that funds in the hands of police officials may not be attached. Mrs. Jamison pleaded guilty and was let off with a light sentence. No Place For Colored Youths. The work of the Juvenile Courtis greatly hampered by the lack of some place to send the many colored boys who are brought before it. This is the opinion of Judge Heuisler, who presides over the court and who has well-defined Ideas of the work it should do. At present there is no place to send the colored juvenile offenders except to jail. Judge Heuisler does not want to commit them to that institution, but he is com pelled to do so in some cases. The Colored House of Reforination at Cheltenham is crowded and because of its great distance from the city it is not convenient to commit boys awaiting trial to that institution. Receivers For O'Neill & Fitzgerald. Frederick J. Singley and James J. Mc- Namara were yesterday appointed by con- sent receivers for the firm of O'Neill & Fitzgerald, manufacturers of porter and' ale, their bond being for $1,000. Daniel O'Neill and John Fitzgerald were the mem- bers of the firm. The appointment of re- ceivers was applied for in Circuit Court No. 2 on Friday by Mr. Singley, who is trustee in bankruptcy of Mr. O'Neill. It was alleged in the bill of complaint, among other things, that the firm is hopelessly In- solvent. Mr. Fitzgerald fled an answer yesterday admitting the allegations in the bill of complaint. Thomas T. Woodland's Will. The will of Thomas Theodore Woodland, admitted to probate in the Orphans' Court yesterday, bequeaths $50 to St. Peter Cla- ver's Church (colored) and $25 to St. Fran- cis Xavier's Church, colored, for masses for the repose of his soul. The balance of the estate is to be held in trust by Charles Frederick Woodland, brother of the testn- tor, who was also constituted executor, without bond. The net income is to be pald Sarah Jane Woodland, widow of the testator, as long as she lives, or until she marries again. If she remarries she is only to get $1 of the estate under the will. If the widow mar- ries again and one or more of the testator's four children die before reaching the age of 21 years, Rose Regina Braxton, niece of the testator, is to get the share of one child. In the event of the widow dying without' marrying again the entire estate is to be divided among the testator's four children when the youngest is 21 years old. The will was executed February 26 last.

Selfer against the Board of Police Commis- sloners to obtain possession of $100 found on Mrs. Mary Dill Jamison when she was arrested on the charge of passing bogus checks was quashed yesterday by Judge Phelps in the Superior Court. Mr.. Selfer's attachment was based on a check for $450 which had been passed on him by Mrs. Jamison. The Court ruled that funds in the hands of police officials may not be attached. Mrs. Jamison pleaded guilty and was let off with a light sentence. No Place For Colored Youths. The work of the Juvenile Courtis greatly hampered by the lack of some place to send the many colored boys who are brought before it. This is the opinion of Judge Heuisler, who presides over the court and who has well-defined Ideas of the work it should do. At present there is no place to send the colored juvenile offenders except to jail. Judge Heuisler does not want to commit them to that institution, but he is com pelled to do so in some cases. The Colored House of Reforination at Cheltenham is crowded and because of its great distance from the city it is not convenient to commit boys awaiting trial to that institution. Receivers For O'Neill & Fitzgerald. Frederick J. Singley and James J. Mc- Namara were yesterday appointed by con- sent receivers for the firm of O'Neill & Fitzgerald, manufacturers of porter and' ale, their bond being for $1,000. Daniel O'Neill and John Fitzgerald were the mem- bers of the firm. The appointment of re- ceivers was applied for in Circuit Court No. 2 on Friday by Mr. Singley, who is trustee in bankruptcy of Mr. O'Neill. It was alleged in the bill of complaint, among other things, that the firm is hopelessly In- solvent. Mr. Fitzgerald fled an answer yesterday admitting the allegations in the bill of complaint. Thomas T. Woodland's Will. The will of Thomas Theodore Woodland, admitted to probate in the Orphans' Court yesterday, bequeaths $50 to St. Peter Cla- ver's Church (colored) and $25 to St. Fran- cis Xavier's Church, colored, for masses for the repose of his soul. The balance of the estate is to be held in trust by Charles Frederick Woodland, brother of the testn- tor, who was also constituted executor, without bond. The net income is to be pald Sarah Jane Woodland, widow of the testator, as long as she lives, or until she marries again. If she remarries she is only to get $1 of the estate under the will. If the widow mar- ries again and one or more of the testator's four children die before reaching the age of 21 years, Rose Regina Braxton, niece of the testator, is to get the share of one child. In the event of the widow dying without' marrying again the entire estate is to be divided among the testator's four children when the youngest is 21 years old. The will was executed February 26 last.

title: BOYS ACCUSED OF BURGLARY
full_text: BOYS ACCUSED OF BURGLARY Three Said To Have Entered Houses • And Carried Off Fixtures. 1 Four houses are said to have been stripped of lead pipe and gas fixtures by three boys who were arrested by Sergeant Gasswein and Patrolmen Murphy and Jar- boe, of the Western district, Wednesday. The boys are Louis Ballock, 17 years old, - who was committed for court by Justice Loden; Louis Smith, 14 years old, commit- ted for court by Judge Heuisler, and Allen Truxton, 12 years old, colored, committed to the Industrial School at Cheltenham by Judge Heulsler. title: INSPECTED BY MR. GRIFFITH: SAYS COLORED HOUSE OF REFORMATION IS DOING WELL
full_text: INSPECTED BY MR. GRIFFITH Says Colored House Of Reformation Is Doing Well. Mr. Goldsborough S. Griffith. president of the Maryland Prisoners' Aid Association. has just returned from a visit of inspec tion to the Colored House of Reformation, at Cheltenham, Prince George's county. and yesterday made the following report on the fastitution: 1 "I was much gratified with the evidences upon all sides that earnest efforts are bei ing made by the superintendent. Mr. J. E. Dorsey, and the assistant superintendent, Mr. John B. Pyles, and other helpers to make the insilention a blessing to the State. There are now in the institution 167 boys. During the past two years the numbers: has been reduced by parole to parents of those whose conduct had so improved as to warrant it, and 48 have been placed out to responsible farmers, who have agreed to deposit In bank a certain amount annually. | subject to the order of the boy when he becomes of age. "There are 700 acres of land. 400 of which are under cultivation. There are 360 acres of timber. The land is of fair quality, and is being steadily improved. The crops pro- duced are better than those of surrounding 'l farms. So far as possible the boys are being instructed in farming. The farmer in charge is a most capable, up-to-date young man: but with only one assistant it is not possible for him to give the neces- sary attention to instructing the boys. There is general demand for farm labor in this and other States, and no hoy, properly instructed in farming, need leave the in- stitution to become an idler. From 60 to TO of the smaller boys have been employed In caning chairs. This has been of but Ilt- the profit to the institution and will be of but little benefit to the boys in after years. "There are four schools attached to the institution. A careful examination of these revealed satisfactory progress, especially in No. 2. under Mr. Fred Williams, and No. 5. under Mrs. Alice Mitchell: these are the highest grades. Mrs. Mitchell is the only colored teacher there, and is very pro ficient. "The Sunday-school which I organized soon after the institution was establisbed has been maintained ever since, and under Mr. J. E. Dorsey is in a better condition than ever before. The introduction of the merit system has had a salutary effect on the deportment of the boys. Four night watchmen have been employed, and a vis- itor to visit the homes to which boys are paroled, also to inspect the homes of appli- cants before boys are sent." title: William Graham's Will
full_text: William Graham's Will. The will of William Graham, admitted to probate in the Orphans' Court yester- day, leaves all his property in trust for the benefit of his unmarried daughters, with the privilege to them of occupying as a home his dwelling, 1220 North Caroline street, and using all its contents. The trust is to cease when all the daughters are married or dead. The estate is then to be divided equally among all of Mr. Graham's children, the children of any de- ceased son or daughter taking their par- ent's share. Letters on the estate were granted to Mr. Graham's son, William G. W. Graham, who was named as trustee and executor without bond. The will was executed May 21, 1897. The testator died May 22 last. The grand jury for the January term, of watch Mr. David Hutzler was foreman, finished its work and was finally dis- charged yesterday after handing the cus- tomary reports to Judge Stockbridge in the Criminal Court. No reference was made In any of the reports to the gambling in- vestigation made by the grand jury during Its term. A number of recommendations were made. Mr. Hutzler read the main report and Mr. George A. Pope read the report of the committee on the penitentiary, of which he was chairman. None of the other com- mittee reports was read. In discharging the grand jury with the thanks of the court Judge Stockbridge re- ferred especially to the statement in the main report that a comparatively small amount of crime was found to exist in the city. "The city is growing rapidly," Judge Stockbridge said, "but crime is not increas ing here in proportion to the increase in population. The records of this court show not only that there has not been an in- crease but that there has been a slight diminution in the number of indictments in the past five years. This condition, which is an anomalous one in some respects, is due to two things. One is the unusual freedom of this city from crime. The other is the wise discrimination shown by grand Juries. I know of no city which shows such an annual diminution in the number of indictments." In concluding, Judge Stockbridge sald that most of the recommendations made in the reports will require legislative action In order to be carried out. In this connec- tion he referred to the organization formed some years ago by those who had served on grand juries. Judge Stockbridge recom- mended that the members of the retiring grand jury take steps to bring their recom- mendations before the Legislature at the meeting next year. Mr. Hutzler's Report. The following is the report read by Mr. Hutzler: To His Honor Judge Henry Stockbridge, Crim inal Court of Baltimore, Md.: It is with pleasure we present a detailed report of the number of cases considered during the Jan- nary term, also the reports of the committees, which were appointed to visit and investigate various in- stitutions. Each institution was visited by the com- mittee; and in nearly all cases this inspection was supplemented by a visit by the entire grand jury. These reports justify us in congratulating the city on its excellent eleemosnary institutions, and the good work they perform. We find the amount of crime exceedingly small, and decidedly below the average, for a city the size of Baltimore; this being due to good citizenship, the influence of the various moral teaching institu- tions, to a most excellent police force and an ideal judiciary. The number of colored cases brought to our notice seams out of proportion to the white and black pop- ulation. No doubt heredity and environment are marked factors in this disproportion, but is it not aggravated by the delusive promises of immunity from the penalties of law by those having sinister nlterior motives? Herein lies a great future dan- ger, requiring prompt and discriminating action. The guilty should be severely punished and drastic measures adopted to prevent perverting our less in- telligent citizens. If, however, these excess cases indicate normal conditions, then it is obvious we must look to the schoolmaster, not the police for a remedy. The matter of taking affidavits over the telephone was carefully considered, and the prompt action of your Honor had the desired salutary effect. Public Improvements. The Sanitary Committee reports the early comple- tion of a smallpox hospital. The need of an infec- tious hospital has been a long-felt want, solicited by the medical authorities 'and the boards of trade over a decade. Why should it require years to se- cure a needed city improvement? If a private cor- poration does wrong, public clamor demands prompt remedial action, yet to municipal shortcomings it patiently submits. A city supplies water pronounced by the highest accredited authorites as unhealthy. A legislature defeats a coveted sewerage bill, needed to prevent infection and disease. Consistency on the part of the public would de- mand and insist on the city furnishing pure water. It would accentuate and persistently exact of the State, on all matters of strictly municipal interest, local autonomy. The affairs of the city should be managed in a business-like way; every want, after favorable con- sideration, should be promptly acted on, a director should see that all subordinates faithfully execute their duties and an auditor should compare, criti- cise and adjust all accounts of the various depart- ments, with a view to economic and satisfactory results. We fear incapable employes are not disciplined. We believe the new Charter-which has done so much to improve our city government-is evaded. The expending of large amounts in decisions just a trifle under the legal figures, to avoid public bids. is an evasion of the new Charter, which if not strenuously prohibited may lead to serious abuse. The "cocaine" habit promises to be a serious evil. It is practiced by those incapable of knowing that its continued use must result in mental and physi- cal wreck. It is now in its incipiency, where legal restriction as to the sale of this drug may arrest its demoralizing progress. Care Of The Insane. There are at present 348 insane patients at Bay- view. If these patients were placed at Springfield, or any other State insane asylum, it would be a hu- mane act, resulting in great benefit, and in accord with the consensus of expert opinion. Bayview could be used as a temporary reception hospital for alcoholic, nervous and suspected insane cases until the character of the case was clearly de- Aned. We appreciate the valuable and untiring services of Mr. H. W. Rodgers, our stenographer, whose notes must be a marked help to the court, as they have been to us. Statistics Of Work. The following is a summary of the grand Jury's work: Cases considered: the number of inmates on account of in- sufficient means. They recommended more liberal appropriations by the city and State. The system and discipline of the institu- tion were commended. The committee on the Female House of Refuge found that institution in splendid condition. The report states that the com- mittee was entertained "with several beau- tiful songs" by the inmates. The report also states that "the voices of some of the girls are really a wonder." The removal of the sign on the fence of the institution is recommended. The committee on the jail recommended in their report a new building, that all prisoners be compelled to work and earn at least the cost of their maintenance if physically and mentally capable and that a school be established for the youthful prisoners. A house of detention for juvenile offend- ers of both sexes, especially colored boys, Is recommended in the report of the com- mittee on House of Correction. The committee on the Male House of Refuge was surprised to find that with the antiquated buildings and obsolete facil- itles of the institution such good results are obtained. The committee agrees with the management that this institution should be moved beyond the city limits and the present property disposed of. Immediate steps for the erection of one large or two small buildings for the Indus- trial Home for Colored Girls, at Melvale, Baltimore county, are recommended in the report of the committee on that institution. The committee on sanitation states in its report that its investigation into the sani- tary condition of the city reflects great credit upon the able and efficient manage- ment of the Health Department. The Springfield State Hospital is com- mended in the committee report as the model institution of its kind in the State, and probably in the country. Exchanges Of Courtesies. Before going into court to be finally dis- charged the members of the grand jury held a pleasant social session in their room. Mr. Hutzler presented each of his fellow- jurors and a number of the court officials with a handsome silver matchbox. Each matchbox was engraved with the mono- gram of the recipient. Mr. Harry W. Rod- gers, stenographer of the grand jury, was presented with a heavy monogram gold ring by the grand jurors. Early in the afternoon Mr. Hutzler en- tertained his fellow-jurors and a number of court officials at dinner at the Hotel Rennert. The floral decorations of the table were handsome, the set pieces being representations of the Battle Monument and the scales of Justice. Among those present besides the grand jurors were Judge Stockbridge, Mr. Henry J. Broening, Clerk of the Criminal Court, and Mr. Harry W. Rodgers, the grand jury stenographer. State's Attorney McLane was invited to be present, but was unable to attend. During the dinner the following testimo- nial, handsomely engrossed and framed, was presented Mr. Hutzler: [Testimonial.] The undersigned members of the grand jury for the January term, 1903, assembled in this last meet- ing, are now to sever the connection which has held us together during the past four months in most pleasant personal relations We carry away regrets at parting and with mutual esteem and warmest wishes for the welfare of each individual member. We especially here express our hearty appreciation of the services of our foreman, Mr. David Hutzler, which have been characterized by his promptne-s and regularity in attendance; diligence and energy in conducting the business of the city; large sense of fairness, associated with justice, in its dealings with offending law-breakers, always tempered by the promptings of his warm sympathy for the unfortu- nate; his untiring patience in developing evidence of the witnesses; his earnest efforts to reconcile mis- guided complainants and to rescue juvenile delın- quents from further criminality, and his uniforu.. courtesy and amiable manner with impartial de- meanor towards every member. The committee on the penitentiary stated In their report, read by Mr. Pope, that in their judgment that Institution is fulfilling its purpose wisely and without a flaw in its conduct in the two aspects which they think a penal institution should be considered, namely, for the good of the prisoners who are enduring the deprivation of liberty as a punishment and of the State. Why should it require years to se- cure a needed city improvement? If a private cor- poration does wrong, public clamor demands prompt remedial action, yet to municipal shortcomings it patiently submits. A city supplies water pronounced by the highest accredited authorites as unhealthy. A legislature defeats a coveted sewerage bill, needed to prevent infection and disease. Consistency on the part of the public would de- mand and insist on the city furnishing pure water. It would accentuate and persistently exact of the State, on all matters of strictly municipal interest, local autonomy. The affairs of the city should be managed in a business-like way; every want, after favorable con- sideration, should be promptly acted on, a director should see that all subordinates faithfully execute their duties and an auditor should compare, criti- cise and adjust all accounts of the various depart- ments, with a view to economic and satisfactory results. We fear incapable employes are not disciplined. We believe the new Charter-which has done so much to improve our city government-is evaded. The expending of large amounts in decisions just a trifle under the legal figures, to avoid public bids. is an evasion of the new Charter, which if not strenuously prohibited may lead to serious abuse. It is now in its incipiency, where legal restriction as to the sale of this drug may arrest its demoralizing progress. Care Of The Insane. There are at present 348 insane patients at Bay- view. If these patients were placed at Springfield, or any other State insane asylum, it would be a hu- mane act, resulting in great benefit, and in accord with the consensus of expert opinion. Bayview could be used as a temporary reception hospital for alcoholic, nervous and suspected insane cases until the character of the case was clearly de- Aned. The following is a summary of the grand Jury's work: Cases considered: the number of inmates on account of in- sufficient means. They recommended more liberal appropriations by the city and State. The system and discipline of the institu- tion were commended. The committee on the Female House of Refuge found that institution in splendid condition. The report states that the com- mittee was entertained "with several beau- tiful songs" by the inmates. The report also states that "the voices of some of the girls are really a wonder." The removal of the sign on the fence of the institution is recommended. The committee on the jail recommended in their report a new building, that all prisoners be compelled to work and earn at least the cost of their maintenance if physically and mentally capable and that a school be established for the youthful prisoners. title: TEACHERS TO GET THEIR PAY: BOARD OF ESTIMATES REFUSES TO GIVE MORE MONEY TO CHELTENHAM
full_text: TEACHERS TO GET THEIR PAY Board of Estimates Refuses To Give More Money To Cheltenham. The Board of Estimates yesterday appro- priated the sum of $4,300 for the payment of the salaries of the public school teach- ers of Group M, whose money has been tied up through the failure of the City Trust and Banking Company. As stated in THE SUN yesterday morning, the matter was brough before the board by City Counellman Heintzeman, who urged that the money be loaned in order that the teachers might be relieved, many of them being in need of the money. City Solicitor Bryan made the motion that the money be appropriated, stating that the need of the teachers was an emergency that justifled such action, and pointing out that the City Council, having adjourned for summer, could not now do anything in the matter. No opposition to advancing the money was made by any member of the board. and is was provided that the city will receive back whatever money is recovered from the original deposit made by Group Principal Andrew J. Pietsch with the City Trust and Banking Company. There are about 139 persons interested in the matter, who were anxious to see the board advance the money. The board declined to grant a request for additional money for the House of Refor- mation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, made by Mr. N. G. Grasty, of the board of managers. Mr. Grasty made a plea for more money on the ground that it was ab- solutely needed to heat the building and to keep it clean. He declared that a crisis was at hand in the affairs of the institu- tion, and as an instance of this said he had just received the resignation of Gen. Thos. J. Shryock as president of the board because he would not be connected with an institu- tion in which there were not proper facili- tles for cleanliness and warmth. Mr. Grasty explained that for the good of the institution General Shrrock should not be allowed to withdraw from it, and that he was greatly needed in the manage- ment. Mayor McLane and the other members of the board agreed that General Shryock's resignation would be a blow, but did not think the emergency was great enough to warrant an additional appropriation, par- ticularly as the contingent fund of the board is not now more than $18,000 and the year is only half gone. The Mayor agreed with Mr. Grasty that the disposator colored boys was a great problem and that Chelten- ham is a valuable institution of its kind. but thought it better to wait until the emer- gency grew more acute before approprinting any more money. The Mayorsald he thought perhaps there were too many institutions al- together, and that if the fall could be made sufficiently large to accommodate all de- mands the community might be better off. Jones The Most Unconcerned. Of the three prisoners who faced Justice White yesterday morning the most uncon- cerned was Jones. With the same listless- ness that has characterized the young ne- gro's actions ever since he confessed to baving been Miss Link's slayer, Jones faced Justice White yesterday morning, and dur- ing the testimony of the officers the boy sat in the prisoners dock carelessly gazing at the persons and objects about him. When the Magistrate, at the conclusion of the testimony of the officers, asked him if he had anything to say, at the same time reminding him that anything he might say could be used against him during his trial, the boy, singularly enough, promptly re- plied in the negative, answering in a stolld manner: "No, sah." Shortly after 9 o'clock yesterday morn- ing Jones, Thomas and Young were taken from the Western Police Station to the Juvenile Court in the patrol wagon by De- tectives Bradley, Hall, O'Donnell, Dick and Kratz. A few minutes after the offi cers entered the courtroom with their pris- oners the case was called, the hearing be ing merely the formality as required by law of establishing a bona-fide case before a police magistrate. The statements of the detectives were, in substance, what has al- ready been printed in THE SUN, the offi- cers recounting the story of the murder. their parts in working up the case and Jones' subsequent confession to them and to Marshal Farnan and Captain of Detect- ives A. J. Pumphrey. Detective Tod Hall was the first witness called, and his state- ments were merely affirmed by his brother officers, What The Officers Said. Sergt. Patrick F. Tierner and Patrolman James L. Roche, both of the Western dis- trict, who, acting under orders from Cap- tain Fullem, arrested the boys, testified to their arrest. Thomas was the first of the trio arrested, and it was on the informa- tion of Thomas, implicating Young and Jonesin the Paca street till-tapping charge, that the two others were arrested. The two officers testified that at the time they arrested the trio they had no idea that Jones was in any way implicaed in the Link murder. As a matter of fact, according to the statements of the officers yesterday, while they had a suspicion from a conversation among the three overheard in a cell at the Western Station House that one of them knew something about the Link case, thes at no time suspected the smallest of the three-Jones. On the contrary they firmly believed that Thomas, the oldest and larg est of the group, was the one from whom some information of the woman's slayer could be gotten. Clear up to the celling he clambered, and then he thrust both legs through the bars and sat on the topinost horizontal bar, grin- ning like a simian and making faces at the little knot of officers who were amused witnesses of the performances. Suddenly letting go with his hands, the little negro allowed his body to fall backward and hung by his legs from the bar with his head downward. After hanging in this in- verted position for a few moments he went through a perfect series of grinnastic per- formances, displaying remarkable agility and strength for a boy of his age and size. Identification Mensurements.- Jones was taken to the Bureau of Identi- cation yesterday morning, where he was photographed by Sergeant Casey, chief of the bureau, and his assistant, Mr. William Higgins. A copy of this photograph is re- produced in THE SUN today. Jones displayed the most intense interest in the operation of having his "picter tuk," and expressed a wish to see the finished photograph. Sergeant Casey said that it would be use- less to take the boy's Bertillon measure- ments, as he would soon outgrow them. For the benefit of science, however, the Sergeant made a careful examination of the youthful slayer of Miss Link, with the following result: Height, 4 feet 5% laches; weight, 77 pounds; eyes, dark maroon; hair, kinky; complexion, dark brown; nose, rectilinear, elevated at base, medium height; nostriis, broad: forehead, medium height and width, reeeding; lower lip, protruding; chin, re- ceding; teeth, good; lobe of car, short and "gulfed"-this is very unusual and is not found once in 500 cases; arms, long and bent inward at elbow-this is also unusual; birthmark on left breast. While the Sergeant would not commit himself on the subject, it is said that the "gulfed" lobe of the ear and the bent arms denote animal nature. Jones can both read and write, having attended one of the public schools. He says he was born near Baltimore, but ex- actly where he cannot tell. To be frank, he has the appearance of being a very bad boy and one that would be hard to manage. The object of the so- ciety is not to coddle born criminals, but to extend a helping hand to those who fall through temptation and who are willing to begin life anew." Case Excites Interest. The case of Jones has excited consider- able interest among many persons in this city who are in one way or another interest- ed in the selence of criminology. Of more than ordinary interest is the case of Jones from the fact that the boy is to every ap pearance a born criminal. Although only 12 years old, he has during the last month, it is charged, participated in at least three crimes of a grave nature, including this last one of murder, while as early as 1809, when the boy was but 8 years old, he was before a magistrate on the charge of the larceny of a toy wagon. Twice in the following year he was be- fore a magistrate, once on the charge of stealing some books and writing paper and the second time for disorderly conduct. In 1901 he was before Justice Por at the Western Police Station on the charge of breaking a window with intent to steal. Last February he was charged with the larceny of a lot of hams. An unusual circumstance in connection with the criminal record of Jones is the fact that, although he was known to the police as a vicious boy and one who would hardly hesitate to commit a wrong, he was, up to the last time. Invariably dismissed of the different charges. Capt. G. W. Parker's Opinion. Capt. George W. Parker, who, by reason of the fact that he is secretary and agent of the Society for the Protection of Chil- dren from Cruelty and Immorality, comes in close contact with the vicious, hardened youthful element in this city probably more than any other man, explained yes- terday why Jones was dismissed so often In the face of what was probably convine- ing testimony of the boy's criminal tend- ency. "The boy." said Captain Parker: "was no doubt dismissed so often because the magistrates before whom he was arraigned had no other alternative hut to either dis- miss him or send him to jail. While there is a colored reformatory in this State for fractious colored boys, it is a hard matter to have them committed there. I refer to the House of Reformation for Colored Bors. This institution has all along refused to take colored boys from this city because, I understand, they belleve the appropria- tion from this city is insufficient. This fact being known to the police magistrates, who naturally consider the tender years of the prisoner, they hesitate a long time before committing the child to jail, the only other available institution for colored boys, and as a consequence mans who really do not deserve any leniency are dismissed. Should Have Been Sent To Jail. "I do not hesitate to say that it would have been far better had Jones, when his true nature became known to the police, been sent to jall. A hoy of Jones' type has no right to be running the streets free, as he is a serious menare to society. On the other hand, from what I have seen of the juvenile department of the city jail, the prisoners do not come into contact with the older prisoners, not even when brought to the Instirution, and rigid discipline is enforced at all times. This, I believe, in a case like that of Jones, would have a tendency to elevate the boy's moral charac- ter rather than lower it. "I am sorry to say that this city abounds with just such dangerous types of colored youth as that of which Jones is a fair ex- ample. There certainly should be a suit- able Institution established for them if we can't get them in at Cheltenham, for they are a serious menace to publie lte wel- fare and unless something is done to check it their type will continue to rapidly in- crease numerically." The sight of men working at the brick piles in the burned district with bare hands, chapped and stiff with the cold, has aroused the compassion of a leader of The Sun, who makes a suggestion in the following letter: Messrs. Editors: While walking through the burned district the other day I noticed the large number of laborers at work with bare hands. In this cold weather the hands become numb and are easily cut by the bricks, mortar and jagged edges of iron and wood. Their hands are no doubt in an-awful condition. I would suggest to the women of our city who have the leisure to devote a few min- -utes of it to making gloves for these men. No matter what the material, so it is heavy, or how crude the workmanship, they will be a protection. The Charity Organization So- ciety will, no doubt, see that they are dis- tributed. title: BANK CLERKS ON EXCURSION
full_text: BANK CLERKS ON EXCURSION Go To Annapolis And Receive Many Courtesies. Baltimore Chapter, American Institute of Bank Clerks, went on an excursion down the bay to Annapolis yesterday. The steamer Annapolis, which was char tered for the occasion, left Light Strest Pier No. 16 at 3.30 P. M. with about 600 people and arrived at Annapolis about 6 o'clock. Knight's Band was on board, and through the efforts of Congressman Wach- ter the Naval Academy Band gave a con- cert on the campus for the excursionists from 6.30 to 7.30. The party visited the new buildings at the Naval Academy, and through the courtesy of Governor War- field the State buildings were kept open for them. A crab supper was served at Carvel Hall, and the steamer left Annapo- lis about 8 o'clock, arriving in Baltimore about 10.30 o'clock. The object of the excursion was to pro- vide a pleasant outing for the Lank clerks and their friends and to raise funds for the educational work of the chapter next winter. The committee in charge of the arrange- ments consisted of A. Waller Morton (chairman), Walter Koppelman, James D. Garrett, James C. Fenhagen and Samuel M. Reid. The officers of the chapter are: Thomas B. Ewalt, president; Walter Kop- pelman, vice-president; Walter F. McCo- mas, secretary; Samuel M. Reid, treas- urer. SQRE ARMS AT CHELTENHAM General Vaccination Follows Dis- covery Of Smallpox Case. Dr. Marshall L. Price, assistant to Dr. John S. Fulton, secretary of the State Board, of Health, went to the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Chelten- ham, Prince George's county, Friday to investigate a report of a case of smallpox in the institution. He found that a col- ored boy 10 years old, who had been taken there from the City Jail on June 4, had a well-developed case of the disease. All of the other inmates were vaccinated and the patient was isolated. The fact that the eruption appeared on the 21st caused Dr. Helskell, the quarantine physician, to say that he thought the boy must have contracted the disease in this city, as he was hardly in the institution long enough for it to have developed if contracted there. A case of smallpox was gotten from the jail the day the boy was taken from there. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: J. J. JANNEY DIES AT HOME: FOR THIRTY YEARS OFFICER AT COLORED BOYS INSTITUTION
full_text: J. J. JANNEY DIES AT HOME For Thirty Years Officer At Colored Boys' Institution. -Joseph J. Janney, secretary and treas- urer of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, Md., a retired business man, Civil War veteran and member of the Society of Friends, died last night at his home, 1923 Park avenue, from the effects of a stroke of paralysis which he suffered two weeks ago yesterday. .: Mr. Janney was born in New Lisbon, now Lisbon, Ohio, Jan. 9, 1841, and was a son of the late Henry and Hannah Schelfield Janney. He came to Balti- more 50 years ago. He served through the Civil War, enlisting in this city in 1861 as a member of Purnell's Legion. He participated in the Virginia cam- paign and was slightly wounded before Petersburg, Va. After the war Mr. Janney entered the internal revenue service in this city. He later entered the commission busi- néss as a member of the firm of Pope & Janney, and later went into the coal business. He has been an official of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys during the last 30 years; was a life- long member of the Society of Friends, Erecorder of the Maryland Commandery of the Loyal Legion for many years and member of the Grand Army of the Re- public. Mr. Janney is survived by a daughter, Miss Bertha Janney; two brothers, Wil- liam H. and Dr. O. Edward Janney, three sisters, Miss Marian E. Janney, Mrs. Ellen S. Walton, of Glenburnie, N. Y., and Miss Hannah H. Janney. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

In an opinion filed in Part 2 of the City Court yesterday Judge Baer holds that the words "vagrant, habitually disorderly per- sou." as used in Section 314 of Article 27 of the Code of Public General Laws, de- scribe two separate offenses, and therefore it is proper to charge a person with va. grancy under the law. The question as to the judicial construc- tien of the language arose in the habeas corpus case of James Flanigan, who had been committed to six months in the House of Correction on the charge of vagrancy. Judge Baer states in the opinion that Judges Harlan and Dobler. who sat with him in the case, concur in his views. The question was whether the word "va- grant" should be construed as a noun or an adjective in the phrase quoted. The his- tory of the legislation on the subject and other words found in Section 314, together with the decision of the Court of Appeals in the Margaret Glenn case (54 Md., 572). led the Court to conclude that the word : "vagrant" should be construed as a noun. title: LADDER TO STEAL HORSE
full_text: LADDER TO STEAL HORSE Boy Was Too Short, So He Climbed Up To Put On Harness. James Gates, a little colored boy who says he is 10 years old, was arrested yes- terday by Patrolman Walter Burns, of the Northwestern police district, on the charge of stealing a horse, cart and harness. The horse and harness belonged to the Carroll Coal Company, 60 West Oliver street, and the cart to Edward Stabler, 58 West Oli- ver street. According to his own story Gates went to the stable of the Carroll Coal Company and by means of a stepladder took the har- ness from a hook. Being too small to place the harness on the horse he brought the stepladder into service again and finally arranged the harness on the animal. The horse was taken to a lot where the cart was standing and then Gates was pre- pared to do business. He had started out to find "work," as he termed it when l'a- trolman Burns was notified that the horse, cart and harness were missing and arrested Gates at Biddle street and Park avenue. The police say Gates has been paroled twice. Judge Packard, of the Juvenile Court, committed Gates to the Colored House of Refuge at Cheltenham. Murray Stole Whisky, Police Say. Alfred Murray, allas Cooper, colored, of 811 Mulberry court, was committed for court yesterday afternoon by Justice Lo- den, at the Western Police Station, on the charge of feloniously entering the ware- house of Meyer, Pitts & Co., whisky deal- ers at 415 West Camden street, and steal- ing several gallons of whisky on Septem- ber 27. Murray was arrested by Sergeant Rus- sell. Emil Koenig, a saloonkeeper at 310 South Eutaw street, testified that Robert 11. Bridges found several demijohns of whisky in an alley in the rear of the sa- loon and took them into his yard. Later Murray came to Koenig and claimed the whisky, offering to sell it. Mr. Bridges testified to having discovered the deuif- johns. Marray was arrested about a month ago on the charge of the Iarceny of six quarts of whisky, for which the police were un- able to find a claimant. Western Maryland's Schedule. The Western Maryland Railroad Com- pany announces that the regular fall and winter schedule will go into effect Sunday, October 2. The Blue Mountain express will be run as an extra train from Baltimore to the mountain resort points, and also to Hagerstown on Fridays and Saturdays, Oc- tober 7, 8, 14 and 15, leaving IIillen Sta- tion, however, at 3.20 P. M., five minutes earlier than at present. A new accommo- dation train to Union Bridge will leave Baltimore at 4.15 P. M. The fast Hagers- town express will leave IIiilen Station at 5 P. M. This train will run as a very fast express to Union Bridge, stopping only at Westminster, and beyond Union Bridge will make local stops. The York express will leave Millen Station at 5.25 P. M., which is earlier than heretofore. The new sched.. ule in detail can be found in the advertis- ing columns. Many Fine Pears Arrive. Large quantities of luscious Keifer pears are arriving at Light street wharf from the pear orchards of Kent and Queen Anne's counties. About 50 per cent. of the fruit consists of pears blown from the trees during the recent heavy storm. The Chester River Line, which brings most of the fruit from the two countles, has, In view of the large crop expected, re- duced the freight rates. This reduction will go into effect on October 1. The steamers of this line are arriving with large cargoes of pears. Prices on Keffer pears yesterday ranged from 15 to 20 cents, although exceptionally fine specimens went for 25 cents a basket, and the "windfalls," or fruit blown from the trees, were sold during the day for 12 cents a basket.
