title: CRITICISES CHELTENHAM: "MORE LIKE PRISON THAN REFORMATORY," SAYS GRAND JURY COMPLAIN_OF HEAT AND FOOD MANAGER HAVE PROMISED TO REMEDY ALL THE ALLEGED DEFECTS AS FAR AS POSSIBLE
full_text: CRITICISES CHELTENHAM "More Like Prison Than Reforma- tory," Says Grand Jury. COMPLAIN OF HEAT AND FOOD Managers Have Promised To Rem- edy All The Alleged Defects As Far As Possible. "At present it is more like a prison than a reformatory, and many radical changes seem to be absolutely required," is among the adverse criticisms of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Chelten- ham, Prince George's county, Md., made in a report on the institution by a committee of the grand jury for the September term, which finished its work and was finally dis- charged yesterday with the thanks of Judge Wright, in the Criminal Court. The com- mittee found much to condemn in the insti- tution, but the report states that the changes recommended will doubtless be promptly made. The report, which was made by the committee to Mr. Henry B. Gilpin, foreman, and submitted to the court with the other committee reports and the report of Foreman Gilpin, is as follows: "Two visits were made to the Chelten- ham Reformatory for Colored Boys by your committee and other members of the grand Jury. We found the institution poorly heated, and in many parts of we buildings no heat at all. "Complaint was made by many of the in- mates on account of insufficient food, and the occupants of the hospital claimed that they were not fed any better than the other boys. "Confinement in dark cells, without heat or light, and on a diet of bread and water for long periods is in vogue. "There are other objectionable features in this institution. "The committee is pleased, however, to report that the managers have promised to remedy all these matters as far as possible. "The institution should have more liberal appropriations, so that every part of it may he comfortably heated, and in order that it may in all respects be enabled to do the best work in the reformation of its wards. At present it is more like a prison than a re- formatory, and many radical changes seem to be absolutely required. "Now that the necessity for these changes has been called to the attention of the proper authorities they will doubtless be promptly made, and your committee re- spectfully suggests, in justice to the man- agement, that the attention of the incoming grand jury be called to our findings, so that the Court and public may hear later of the improved condition of the institution. "Perhaps no class of dependent minors need the wholesome influences of a properly conducted school or reformatory more than these colored boys." The committee was composed of Messrs. Maurice Laupheimer. Andrew Muncks, Wil- liam Vitzthum, Edward C. Johnson and George Filbert, all of whom signed the re- port. Mr. Preston Commended. The report of the committee on exits to public buildings states that without excep- tion all the buildings visited were found to be equipped with exits ample in size and sufficient in number to meet their respect- ive requirements. The committee noted with pleasure the diligence of the Building Inspector in locating buildings where fire escapes and additional means of egress were needed, and his promptness in demanding that these safeguards be put in such build- ings. "We desire to commend him for his work In this respect," the report continues, "and for his action in prohibiting the use of the turnstile doors in large and crowded build- ings. If it be needed, we would recommend the passage of such legislation as to make impossible the erection or use of such doors. That they would seriously impede the prompt passage of persons in an emergency cannot for a moment be questioned." Would Improve Milk Supply. The recommendations for a general sew- erage system, a hospital for infectious dis- eases and the filtration of the city water supply are repeated in the report of the committee on sanitation. The committee also recommends some plan by which the city may obtain better control over the milk supply. "Our system of inspection only applies to milk after its arrival in Baltimore," the re- port continues. "Endeavors should be made to require shippers to report to our Health Departments and receive instructions for the prevention of the pollution of the milk sup- ply. "Finally, your committee would urge a more active campaign against tuberculosis, and we trust Baltimore will not be long be- hind many other large cities in its endeav- ors to stamp out this dread disease." Penitentiary A Model. "We enthusiastically point to our institu- Lion as a model, for a model we think it 1s," the committee on the penitentiary say in its report. "Warden John F. Weyler we regard as the right man in the right place. "The committee recommend that the State adopt general supervision of all insti- tutions." In the opinion of the committee on the jail, that institution is too small, and a new, larger and more modern prison and workshops should be built. Foreman Gilpin's Recommendations Mr. Gilpin, the foreman, in his report, recommends severe punishment for wife- beaters, notifying persons required to have licenses, requiring junk dealers to report purchases to the police, more care in issu- ing licenses to hotels and clubhouses, and the establishment of a hospital for conta- gious diseases. The report says the protec- tion afforded by law to installment houses and chattel loan associations seems to be unfair. The report concludes with a summary of the work of the grand jury and a grateful acknowledgment of the attention, courtesy and efficiency of the court officials. The number of cases on the grand jury dockets during the term was 1,256, of which 707 The grand jury for the January term has were presented and 489 dismissed. been summoned for next Monday, when the term begins. title: AS THE OFFICERS SEE IT: POINT TO MANY IMPROVEMENTS MADE AT CHELTENHAM
full_text: AS THE OFFICERS SEE IT Point To Many Improvements Made At Cheltenham. In view of the report of the grand jury on the House of Reformation at Chelten- ham the following annual report, submit- ted to Mayor Timanus yesterday by Gen. Thomas J. Shryock, president of the insti- tution, is received with interest: "We are pleased to report that this in- stitution is in a more prosperous condition than for many years in its history. Owing to the liberality of the city and State in the financial support given the institution, we have been enabled to provide better maintenance for the boys who have been committed to its care, especially in the line of material comfort. "We have already made some improve- ments in the physical conditions at the in- stitution and have others in contempla- tion which will enable the officers to bring the reformatory influence to bear more ef- fectually than has been the case hereto- fore. "Our bathing facilities, which have been crude and out of date, have been greatly Improved by the introduction of the over- head-spray system and modern plumbing, with a view to proper sanitation, is being gradually installed in all the cottages. "The industrial training of the boys is the leading feature in the department of education, the idea being to give each boy such physical equipment as will enable him to make a living in some line of work when he leaves the institution. "There are now committed to the re- formatory 254 boys from the city of Balti- more, 91 from the various counties of Maryland and 37 from the Federal courts in the different States. "Our system of paroling boys to houses among farmers and others residing in rural districts is having good results. We have now 126 boys paroled in good homes in various parts of Maryland, who are earning wages, and these are, almost with- out exception, giving good satisfaction. "The increased confidence which has been shown and the more liberal support which we have received from both the municipal and State governments is greatly appre- ciated, and we trust that the results achieved will be considered as amply justi- fying the appropriations that have been made. The managers and officers certain- ly feel that they have cause to be encour- aged with the outlook, and it is their de- termination, if the financial support of the Institution in the future should be ade- quate, to make the House of Reformation one of the model reformatories of the coun- try." full_text: THE STATE CAPITAL Oyster Dredgers Walking Through The Snow To Baltimore, [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.) Annapolis. Md., Jan. 31. Six dredgers from an oyster schooner which is frozen in the lee some distance down the bay ar- rived in Annapolls late last night balf starved and cold, having walked from be- low West river, a distance of about 20 miles. The men said that they left the Jower section of the counts on Saturday sight and had been walking ever since, even through the blinding snowstorm of Sunday night. When they reached here they were placed in a police station for the night, after being fed, and this morning were given breakfast at the city's expense. They said that they lived in Baltimore, and being unable to make their way through the ice in the vesssel, they decided to walk. Learning their condition. the men were given transportation to Baltimore by the city authorities. The ice situation about here is becoming worse every day. The watermen think that the present freeze is the worst of the year, and the impression prevails that ship- ping, especially the smaller hay craft, may be tied up for weeks. Two large seagoing steamers, outward bound from Baltimore, this morning were apparently having a hard battle through the fields of ice. A FATAL LEAP William Sechrist, Aged 17, Killed Near Cheltenham, [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.) Hyattsville, Md., Jan. 31.-In attempt- ing to jump from a fast-freight train at Cheltenham, Prince George's county, Wil- liam Sechrist, 17 years of age, lost his life Sunday evening last. Accompanied by a colored boy, named John Hawkins, young Sechrist boarded the passenger train at Cheltenham about 6 o'clock and rode to Brandywine. There they caught the fast freight back to their home. When Chelten- ham was reached Hawkins leaped from the train, falling headlong into a deep snow- drift, escaping serious injury. He was on. top of the rear car. Young Sechrist was between the cars near the rear, and when he jumped the current from the fast-mor- ing train prevented him from making the drift, and he fell upon the track, his head striking the frog of the switch, crushing out his brains. The young man died in a few minutes and his body was removed to the home of his guardian, Mr. A. II. Se christ, near Cheltenham. The body was taken to l'ennsylvania today for interment. WASHINGTON COUNTY Body Of Unknown Man Found in Canal-Easton's Little Boy. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.) Hagerstown. Md., Jan. 31. The hods of an unknown man was found yesterday aft- ernoon under the ice in the Chesapeake sod Ohio canal near Pearre, about 10 miles west of Hancock. The body was in such a condition as to be scarcely recognizable as a human corpse. It is supposed the body is that of a la- borer who had been employed on the Wa- bash extension to Cumberland and who disappeared last fall. Flagman George Byerly, who was se- riously injured in the freight wreck on the Western Maryland railroad near Highfield, was removed to Johns Hopkins Hospital for an operation. Superintendent Jacob A. Ziegler, of the Orphans Home, today took preliminary legal steps to get possession of the S-year- old son of Fred Easton, who was convicted of manslaughter at Cumberland, and to place him in the home. The Washington County Commissioners today settled with ex-Sheriff M. Finley Sei- bert, who was sued last summer by the county for $1,500, alleged to be due. Mr. Seibert agrees to pay the county $600. Miss Lela L. Repp, of Big Pool, and Mr. Charles C. Grove, of Indian Springs, were married in Hagerstown yesterday by Rev. W. H. Lilley. Miss Pearl C. Jones, of Weverton, and Mr. Harry E. Nokes, of Brownsville, were married on Sunday at Brownsville by Rev. Noah P. Castle. Deaths In Washington County. Mrs. Anna Sophia Welty, formerly of Fair Play, died in Hagerstown of pneu- monia last night, aged 76-years. Relatives in Hagerstown received in- formation of the death on Monday at York, Pa., of David Syler Ziegler, in his seventy- sixth year. THE REFORMATION OF COLORED BOYS. The House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Cheltenham, Prince George's coun- ty, has been severely criticised by the grand Jury of Baltimore city. "At present it is more like a prison than a reformatory," says the grand jury, "and many radical changes seem to be absolutely required." Among the "objectionable features", discov- ered by the grand jury is the amiable cus- tom of confining boys in dark cells, with- out heat or light, and on a diet of bread and water, for long periods." It is provided by the laws of Maryland (Chapter 382 of the Acts of 1882) that when- ever any colored minor under the age of 16 years shall be convicted of any felony or other offense the judge or justice, "In his discretion and with reference to the char- acter of said institution as a place of re- form, and not of punishment, may order said minor so convicted to be removed to and confined in the said house of reforma- tion and instruction." In view of the disclosures of the grand jury such a provision seems a nockery. Any unfortunate convict might pray to be delivered from such a fate and committed instead to the penitentiary. If it had been contemplated when the "reformatory" was established that such methods would be used, then a humane Legislature would have provided, that the less hardened and vicious criminals should be removed from it to the penitentiary. full_text: ESCAPED AND WALKED HERE John Wesley Young Said He Was In Cheltenham. Footsore and weary and with his hands and feet cut and bruised, John Wesley Young, a 16-year-old negro, who says he escaped from the Cheltenham Reformatory last Thursday, was found exhausted near the Pennsylvania railroad near Fulton Sta- lion yesterday morning about 11 o'clock by Sergeant Pfennig, of the Northwestern dis- trict. title: HAS FAITH IN PROMISES: MR. MAURICE LAUPHEIMER SAYS CHELTENHAM DEFECTS WILL BE REMEDIED
full_text: HAS FAITH IN PROMISES Mr. Maurice Laupheimer Says Chel- tenham Defects Will Be Remedied. Mr. Maurice Laupheimer, chairman of the grand jury committee, which visited the Cheltenham Reformatory for Colored Boys and submitted a report criticising the man- agement of the institution, said yesterday that he believed the defects in the conduct of the institution would be remedied at once. Mr. Laupheimer said: "As chairman of the committee which vis- ited Cheltenham, I drew up the report. This was submitted and incorporated in the re- port of the foreman, Mr. Henry B. Gilpin. I know of nothing that I can say by way of supplement to the report, and I am satis- fied that the defects which we found and pointed out will be remedied at once. I am sure that my associates on the committee concur in this belief. "The institution is undoubtedly suffering from an insufficiency of funds. If sufficient money is provided the heating and lighting facilities will be improved, as they should be. . "The committee visited Cheltenham in its official capacity and reported what it found there. It did not go there for the purpose of 'white-washing' any defects that might be found, nor was the report intended as a 'roast' on the institution. The committee merely called the attention of the manage- ment to a number of defects found to exist in the conduct of the institution. A promise has been made that the defects will be rem- edied at once, and, as I know several of the gentlemen connected with the institution, I have every faith in the fulfillment of that promise." title: LOST, BUT LIVES HERE
full_text: LOST, BUT LIVES HERE Young Negro Is Unhappy; Justice Packard Is Perplexed. Although claiming to have lived in Bal- timore for the last five years, William H. Wardell, colored, 16 years old, who was before Justice Packard, in the Juvenile Court, yesterday on the charge of vagrancy, was unable to tell where he had lived. He was lost, totally lost; more completely lost, the authorities say, than any boy of his size they have ever seen-if his story was true. Several nights ago he was found sleep- ing on the softest side of a pine board in one of the lumber yards near President Street Station. ."Where do you live?" he was asked. "Wy - Weraa - Werth street," he an- swered. "What number?" "Five hundred block." "Then go back there." Then he said that he was lost. Five feet 6 inches in height, broad and with the marks of health scattered every- where over his round figure and fat face, he looked unusually well equipped by na- ture to take his place in the day's work and do a man's part. full_text: GOOD SHOWING OF J. H. U. MEN Baltimore Athletes Get Many Prizes At Georgetown Meet. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] Washington, March 3.-The eighth an- nual indoor athletic meet of the George- town University Athletic Association, held at Convention Hall tonight, was one of the most successful in the organization's his- tory. M. W. Sheppard, the world's mile cham- pion, won the mile run in 4 minutes and 23 seconds, a new record for the South Atlan- tic Association. Dick Dear, of the Uni- versity of Pennsylvania, beat Seitz, the in- door champion, in the 50-yard invitation. Seitz won the 50-yard handicap. The 50- yard scholastic event was won by H. S. Ducker, of the Baltimore City College, with C. Stollenwerck, of the Boys' Latin School, third. Johns Hopkins University took all three places in the 880-yard run. E. C. Lynch, of Johns Hopkins, followed this by taking first in the 50-yard novice. Indeed, Hop- kins was a prominent factor in nearly every event. The relay race between Army and Navy Preparatory and Boys' Latin School was one of the prettiest of the evening, the for- mer winning by a scant yard. The George- town Preparatory and Marston's School race furnished another close and exciting relay event, the Preps. winning by the good work of their last runner by 5 yards. All the Baltimore teams showed up well and many prizes were carried "Back, Back to Baltimore," Johns Hopkins walked away from George Washington in the relay race, the first man taking a lead of 15 yards and each successive runner increasing the dis- tance. The University of Pennsylvania re- lay team outran the Georgetown University four in easy fashion in the final event of the evening, winning by 25 yards after Widham, the last runner, had fallen, losing at least 25 yards. title: Cheltenham School
full_text: Cheltenham School TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: There have been several editorials which definitely advocated the erection of the proposed new Cheltenham School for Boys within the limits of Baltimore city. There are definite grounds for questioning this move and particularly if the South Baltimore site is to be used. The institution, irrespective of what State depart ment operates it, is a penal institution and so it cannot be built at the South Baltimore site.... The only commercial zoning near in the whole district are two grocery stores, and that portion of a lumber yard within the city line. These facts clearly explain the demand that the residential zone be retained. The South Baltimore property, in its pres- ent state, is a taxable asset of the city. A State institution would place the complete tract upon a tax-free basis, thus removing for all time the possible realization of taxes to the city. And unquestionably it would lower the assessment valuation of surrounding im- proved property. It may be very truthfully stated that this institution, legally, morally and according to all established customs, should not be located within the city boundaries. It is also possible that by using a portion of the appropriated money to rehabilitate the present site in Prince Georges county and the remainder to pay staff members a sufficient wage to insure their continued employment, the State could make the old institution very efficient. E. E. BOTSON, President Lakeland-Dorchester Heights Improvement Association. Baltimore, Jan, 28. Our Foreign Commitments TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: One year ago we were all saying, "Win the war and win the peace by occupying the enemy countries until 19-so-and-so." The length of time of occupation varied, depending upon the indi- vidual opinions, but all agreed that Ger- many and Japan should be occupied until such time as their warmaking potentialities were removed. That was one year ago. What a different picture is presented today! In the Philip- pines, in China, in Hawaii, in France, every. where, we find open rebellion against being kept abroad. Everywhere we find the desire to return home placed above the national security. The service man is probably not altogether responsible; some of the blame may be laid at the War and Navy departments' doors for a vacillating program, but certainly a large degrse of the blame rests upon Mr. and Mrs. John Q. Citizen back home. Most of the blame is brought about by lack of individual aware ness of the demobilization problem and the foreign commitments made by our State Department. ... I believe that the American people would follow the leadership if the President, or someone else in authority, would lay the issues squarely before us; half measures will no longer suffice. ARTHUR P. SEWELL. Baltimore, Jan. 28. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: SHE SUES FOR $10,000
full_text: SHE SUES FOR $10,000 Declares That She Was Injured By Cleaning Fluid At The Caswell. Elizabeth E. Hurley, by her attorneys, O'Mara & Angelmier, instituted suit for $10,000 damages against the Caswell Ho- tel Company in the Superior Court yester- -day. She.charges that her face, arm and body were seriously and permanently in- jured by a cleaning fluid containing acld. She was employed by the hotel's house- keeper to clean china, and she claims that she was not told that the cleaning fiuld con- tained acid or was poisonous. SENTENCED BY JUDGE MORRIS| Negro Who Passed A Bad Dollar Sent To Cheltenham. Clifton Wilson, colored, 15 years old, 26 Gould lane, was sentenced by Judge Morris to two years in the School for Colored Boys at Cheltenham on the charge of passing a counterfeit silver dollar. Judge Morris also sentenced Albert Salt- veldt, 30 years old, to 30 days in jail for passing. a. $1 bill which had been raised to $5. Jacob Niss and Gustave Myers were fined $25 each on the charge of smuggling two bottles of gin from the steamer Cassel on Saturday, March 24. Harrison Little was sent to jail for 30 days on the charge of assault and battery which took place on Government property at Annapolis. Royal Arcanum Appeal Heard. The appeal case of the Royal Arcanum Building Club from the assessment by the Appeal Tax Court of $29,800 on its prop- erty at 18 West Saratoga street was tried before Judge Sharp, in City Court, Part 2, yesterday. The previous assessment was $12,333. Judge Sharp announced that he would render a decision later. The appeal of Mrs. Isabelle Buckner from the assessment of $6,000 on property at 109 Centre Market Space was also taken up, but not concluded. The former assess- ment was $3.000. To Pay Belvedere Hotel Taxes, Judge Stockbridge yesterday signed an order directing Messrs. George Blakistone and Edgar G. Miller, Jr., receivers for the Hotel Belvedere, to pay $10,000 on account of the State and city taxes for the year 1905. The amount still owing by the Belve- dere in 1905 taxes is $10,178.36. title: CITY COLLEGE WINS: BALTIMOREANS CAPTURE TOME'S FIELD AND TRACK MEET DAVIS INDIVIDUAL CHAMPION HE GETS THE CUP FOR SCORING THE HIGHEST NUMBER OF POINTS--CENTRAL HIGH, WASHINGTON, SECOND
authors: Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun
full_text: CITY COLLEGE WINS Baltimoreans Capture Tome's Field And Track Meet. DAVIS INDIVIDUAL CHAMPION He Gets The Cup For Scoring The Highest Number Of Points-Cen- tral High, Washington, Second. [Special Dispatch to the Baltimore Sun.] Port Deposit, Md., May 12.-The fourth annual Interscholastic field and track meet of the Jacob Tome Institute was held here this afternoon. Excepting for a slight wind, the day was ideal for the events. A large crowd of Baltimoreans came on the steamer Susquehanna to witness the games, which were run off without a flaw. The Baltimore City College won the meet, and C. P. Davis, of that college, won the indi- vidual champlonship cup offered to the ath- lete scoring the highest number of points. The City College aggregate of points was 22, which does not take into consideration the junior events. The Central High School of Washington was second, with a total of 13 points. Four Tome and one State records were broken. In the hammer throw R. McCar- roll, of Brown Preparatory School; smashed the previous Tome record of 125 feet 10 Inches and established a new one of 134 feet 10 inches. H. S. Gamble, of Tome In- stitute, in the pole vault raised his own mark of 10 feet to 10 feet 6 inches. E. MII- ler, of Conway Hall, put the shot 43 feet 5 inches, breaking the previous record of 41 feet 0% inches, held by W. M. Hess, of the Central High School of Philadelphia. Garduer Ziegler, of the City College, low- ered the State interscholastic record of 55 1-5 seconds for the quarter-mile run to 54 3-5 seconds. This race was one of the hair-raising kind. The contestants started off at a break-neck clip. The entire Balti- morean contingent had their hopes cen- tered in Ziegler. By the time the runners turned into the homestretch he was a lit- tle too far back of the leaders for comfort, and the collegians began to despair, but the City College man then showed what was in him. He covered the last 100 yards with great speed and crossed the line fully three yards in front of the second man. In the broad jump C. P. Davis, who holds the Tome record of 21 feet 10 Inches for this event, failed to equal it, but, never- theless, won first place with a leap of 21 feet 1 inch. Davis won the 100-yard dash in fine style, going the distance in 10 2-5 seconds. He also captured second place in the high jump. From the very start it looked as if City College was going to have everything its own way. The entire three heats of the senior 100-yard dash were won by Duker, Davis and Ziegler, respectively. The junior 100-yard dash heats, which followed, were also captured by City College runners, but their triumphant march was stopped by the mile run, not one City College man win- ning a place. title: SIDELIGHTS ON THE HANGING: NEGRO PREACHER WILL TELL CONGREGATION OF WHAT HE SAW
full_text: SIDELIGHTS ON THE HANGING Negro Preacher Will Tell Congre- gation Of What He Saw. Commander Howard had never seen an execution, He saw Lee hanged. It was not due to any desire on his part, but was rather by accident. ! While the Sheriff was preparing for the Anale Commander Howard walked down the beach, standing with his back toward the scaffold. He turned his head, however, in the direction of the scaffold a moment later, Just in time to see the execution. Lec's spiritual adviser brought out a fact hèretofore unknown in the case. Lee ad- mitted to his minister that he was com- mitted to the Cheltenham School of Refor- mation for Colored Children when he was 12 years of age and romained there about two years. - Capt. John Wallop Sterling, who was among the crowd, said that the boy had been employed on his vessel about two years ago and that he had warned Lee to mend his ways or he would be hanged some day. - The members of the city detective force were each supplied with 15 rounds of am- munition. Having no use for it they will return it to headquarters. اجا Among the fishermen who saw the hang- Ing were three colored persons, who came ashore from their crabblag boats and seemed as much interested as the whites. The keepers of Smith's Island light low- ered their boat and joined those on shore, being unable to resist the temptation to see the execution. Several amateur photographers suc- ceeded in obtaining a number of pictures of the execution. Chief among them was Assistant State's Attorney O'Dunne, who kept his camera constantly working during the preparation for the hanging and after the execution. - The McLane arrived in Baltimore last night at 9.45 o'clock. Rev. Samuel A. Ward announced his in- tention of delivering a sermon to his con- gregation at the Fulton Baptist Church on Sunday next on what he saw at Lee's exe- cution. - It was one of the few executions to take place in Maryland on any day but Friday. title: SHOEDEALERS FOR TREE HIDES
full_text: SHOEDEALERS FOR FREE HIDES Appoint Standing Committee To Urge Change And Elect Officers. Boston, Jan. 24. At the annual meet- ing of the National Shoe Wholesalers' As- sociation of the United States held in this city today these officers were elected: President-R. F. Spencer, of St. Louis. Secretary-Treasurer-George C. Houghton, of Bos- ton. Vice-Presidents J. K. Orr, of Atlanta, Ga.; C. W. Durrell, of Cincinnati; John H. Gibbs, of Bos- ton, and Daniel T. Merritt, of New York. The question of free hides was discussed, but no action was taken, as it was felt that It would be useless to try to secure action on the subject at the present short session of Congress. A standing commitee, how- ever, will continue its efforts in the inter- est of promoting sentiment in favor of free hides.. Another matter under discussion was the efforts being made by the association to secure a reclassification of shoes by the transportation companies from first to sec- ond class, thus making a reduction in trans- portation rates. A committee will endeavor to bring about this change. MISS FOX NOW MRS. ELKINS Members Of Prominent Philadelphia Families Are Married. Philadelphia. Jan. 24.--In St. Paul's Church, at Cheltenham, a suburb. Miss Nat- alie Crozer Fox and George W. Elkins. Jr.. members of prominent Philadelphia fami- lies, were married today before an assem- blage of guests from New York. Pittsburg, Baltimore, Washington and other cities. The ceremony was performed by Rev. J. Thompson Cole, rector of the church, and the bridesmaids included Miss May Boy- den and Miss Jane Boyden, of Salisbury, N. C.; Miss Constance Johnson and Miss Mildred Grebel, of New York. CHINA FEEDS THE STARVING Mr. Coolidge Says It Is First Time In Her History. - San Francisco, Jan. 24.-J. G. Coolidge, former secretary of the American Legation at Peking, who arrived yesterday on the liner Korea, says that for the first time in its long history the Chinese Government is rendering organized rellef to famine vic- tims. The rice tribute from districts in the vicinity of the famine-stricken area has been directed for the relief of the sufferers and is being systematically distributed un- der Government direction. Refugees have been concentrated at Kang King and other large towns on the lower Yangtse, and the Government aid has been effectively administered. The refugees will have to be fed for four months, when a new crop is expected to re- store normal conditions in the famine belt. Mr. Coolidge believes there is little dan- ger of a renewal of the anti-American boy- cott. The danger spot is Canton, and there a new viceroy, friendly to foreigners, has taken the place of the arbitrary and very unpopular Governor under whose adminis- tration the boycott flourished. QUAKE AFFECTS OIL YIELD Gulf Field Loses And North Texas Field Increases Production. Galveston, Jan. 24.--The Gulf Coast oil fields have decreased their production over 45 per cent. within the last week, and the cause is attributed to seismic disturbances in Jamaica. The sudden-drop was noticed the second day after the Jamaica earthquake, and 17 wells in Texas and Louisiana went dry. After the VValparaiso .earthquake many wells ceased to flow, while an immense oil lake appeared out in the Gulf. The North Texas oil fields have increased 100 per cent. since the Jamaica shocks, and the product is much lighter in color. 1 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: FIFTH REGIMENT GAMES Field And Track Events On The Big Armory Floor. ALSO A COMPETITIVE DRILL Sergt. George Erler, Company D, Wins It-J. S. Hill's Hurdle Rec- ord Governor's Son Second. The fifth annual indoor games given by the Fifth Regiment at the armory last night were fairly well attended. While no records were broken the contests were all spirited and many of them resulted in close and exciting finishes. The entry list of contestants was large, but there were many entrants who falled to contest. While all of the events were entertain- ing the gallery was most pleased with the relay racing. Several of the officials originally appoint- ed failed to show up, and a delay ensued be- fore the start so that others could be found to fill the absentees' places. The games committee, consisting of Wash- ington Bowle, Jr., Frank S. Whitman, Geo. J. Turner, S. Johnson Poe, D. M. Jenkins and J. P. Houston, did their work well. The officials as finally appointed were busy fellows, and there was no idle time. In fact, there was much doing at all times. The local athletes carried off quite a bunch of honors. Hill's Hurdling Feat. In a trial heat in the 100-yard hurdle race D. S. Hill covered the distance in 12% seconds. Hill made the same time in the games held at the armory prior to last night's set, but the hurdles were not in cor- rest position. Last night the filghts were in correct position, there being eight of them, the first 15 yards from the start and the final one the same distance from the finish. In the finals Duker, of the M. A. C.; cар- tured first place, with Randall, Mount Washington, and Requardt, M. A. C., a close second and third, respectively. The two-mile roller skating relay race brought the crowd to its feet. The contest- ing teams represented the Walbrook and Mount, Washington Clubs, and the Wal- brook four won the medals. W. D. Randall, Jr., for Mount Washing- ton, nad Clark Jones, for Walbrook, were the third men on their respective teams. Randall is a big fellow, while his oppo- nent was a mite of a lad. Randall had a few yards start ahead of the little fellow, but the spectators went wild as Clark edged his way to the front on the second lap and won handily. The competitive drill among members of the Fifth Regiment was an interesting feature. The process of choosing the win- ners was one of elimination and reminded one of an old-time spelling match. A line of soldiers was stretched out along the floor, and the men were 'put through vari- ofis forms of drill. One by one the lads in blue were counted out until the winner stood alone in his glory. Sergeant George Erler, Company D, was first, with Cor- poral James Lyon, Jr., Company A, sec- ond, and Sergeant J. C. Scott, Company E, third. Te 440-yard dash was a close-pressed race, and two of St. John's College men won the first two places. A crowd of start- ers dashed off at the crack of the pistol, and there was much fouling, several run- ners falling. J. clean_text: FIFTH REGIMENT GAMES Field And Track Events On The Big Armory Floor. ALSO A COMPETITIVE DRILL Sergt. George Erler, Company D, Wins It-J. S. Hill's Hurdle Rec- ord Governor's Son Second. The fifth annual indoor games given by the Fifth Regiment at the armory last night were fairly well attended. While no records were broken the contests were all spirited and many of them resulted in close and exciting finishes. The entry list of contestants was large, but there were many entrants who falled to contest. While all of the events were entertain- ing the gallery was most pleased with the relay racing. Several of the officials originally appoint- ed failed to show up, and a delay ensued be- fore the start so that others could be found to fill the absentees' places. The games committee, consisting of Wash- ington Bowle, Jr., Frank S. Whitman, Geo. J. Turner, S. Johnson Poe, D. M. Jenkins and J. P. Houston, did their work well. The officials as finally appointed were busy fellows, and there was no idle time. In fact, there was much doing at all times. The local athletes carried off quite a bunch of honors. Hill's Hurdling Feat. In a trial heat in the 100-yard hurdle race D. S. Hill covered the distance in 12% seconds. Hill made the same time in the games held at the armory prior to last night's set, but the hurdles were not in cor- rest position. Last night the filghts were in correct position, there being eight of them, the first 15 yards from the start and the final one the same distance from the finish. In the finals Duker, of the M. A. C.; cар- tured first place, with Randall, Mount Washington, and Requardt, M. A. C., a close second and third, respectively. The two-mile roller skating relay race brought the crowd to its feet. The contest- ing teams represented the Walbrook and Mount, Washington Clubs, and the Wal- brook four won the medals. W. D. Randall, Jr., for Mount Washing- ton, nad Clark Jones, for Walbrook, were the third men on their respective teams. Randall is a big fellow, while his oppo- nent was a mite of a lad. Randall had a few yards start ahead of the little fellow, but the spectators went wild as Clark edged his way to the front on the second lap and won handily. The competitive drill among members of the Fifth Regiment was an interesting feature. The process of choosing the win- ners was one of elimination and reminded one of an old-time spelling match. A line of soldiers was stretched out along the floor, and the men were 'put through vari- ofis forms of drill. One by one the lads in blue were counted out until the winner stood alone in his glory. Sergeant George Erler, Company D, was first, with Cor- poral James Lyon, Jr., Company A, sec- ond, and Sergeant J. C. Scott, Company E, third. Te 440-yard dash was a close-pressed race, and two of St. John's College men won the first two places. A crowd of start- ers dashed off at the crack of the pistol, and there was much fouling, several run- ners falling. J. full_text: NEW YEAR'S TIPS COSTLY Americans In Paris Find Problem An Alarming One. NEW STREET AND SUBWAYS Authorities Planning To Rellere Congestion Of Trame-Chicago Geta A Valuable Picture, [Copyright, 1907, by New York Herald Compans.) [Special to the Baltimore Sun.f Paris, Dec. 28.-Americans of moderate means living in Paris are finding the New Year gift problem more than ever exact- ing. because every servant, even the post- man and butcher boy, demands a gratuity of at least a dollar. The total amounts to a considerable figure. What the Ameri- cans cannot understand is why the Gor- ernment not only recognizes. but approves, the postmen's and other Government em- ployes' annual demand on citizens. The feature of the New Year's approach is a group of nine lotteries, all to be drawn now or within three months. The maximum prize of any la no more than 500,000 francs ($100,000), but it is possible in the laws of chance for one person to win 30,000,000 francs ($6,000,000) on one set of nine tick- ets. French lotteries are permitted for charitable purposes only, and as such are approved by the Government. New Street To Cure Congestion. The congested appearance of the streets of Paris and the difficulty of regulating traffic has impressed the authorities with the necessity of Introducing a radical rem- edy. It is projected to create a new street, at først to run from the Madeleine to the Place Vendome and later to continue to the Avenue de l'Opera and Palais Royal. Old Paris is fast disappearing. A struc- ture in Place Louvois, where 100 years ago the opera stood, is now being demol- ushed. Here it was that Napoleon miracu- lously escaped a home thrown by Arena, where later Louvel was assassinated. More Subways To Be Built. The City Council has agreed to the con- struction by the Metropolitan Electric Railway of several new subways, Inchid- ing an extension of Subway 7 to Boulevard Morland, the extension of Line 3 to Porte des Lilas, the extension of Line 4 from Porte de Gentilly to Porte d'Orleans. The line from Porte Saint Cloud to l'Op- era via Trocadero is to be extended to the Carrefour Drouot. When the Boulevard Hausemann extension is completed several other lines will be built if the above sub- ways pay and a new loan can he raised. Mail Pouch Forgotten In Corner. = That American criticisms of French pos- tal methods are well founded is again proved. - A lawyer at Coret sent 80,000 francs ($10,- 000) in a registered letter to a contrere at Castelnaudary. Weeks passed without the arrival of the missive. Finally complaints: led to an inquiry, and a mall bag was found Intact forgotten in a corner at the Nar- bonne station. To facilitate rapid replies to letter cards sent by pneumatic tubes the postal authorl- ties have invented a card which contains a card for reply. This can be detached and a reply handed to a telegraph boy in walt- ing, saving the person from going to the nearest postoffice. Valuable Pleture For Chicago. The purchase by the Chicago Museum of the "Assumption of the Holy Virgin," by Greco, has given a new impetus to the movement for a law to prohibit the ex- portation of art treasures. The picture belonged to Infante Don Se- bastian, a brother-in-law of Queen Isabella II, who possessed one of the most valuable collections in Spain. It was for years in the Prado Museum. Left Legacy To Buy Toys. The Duc de Berry income of 25.000 francs ($5,000), a legacy, will shortly be distrib- uted to buy toys for poor children in Paris. M. Vincent, an admirer of Victor Hugo, following the poet's example on New Year's Day, heid a fete for children of the poor. Upon his death he provided by bequest to continue his generous charity. The French Government has just con- cluded an agreement with the muulcipal authorities of St. Germain-en-Laye for building a university for young women in that town. The institution will be fitted with all modern appliances for scientifle research, and will be conducted on the same lines as the great English colleges for women, such as Cheltenham and Bedford. Immense aigrettes, bunches of feathers and groups of swallows and hum- ming birds nave recently been employed as decorations for headgear. There is now a new rival. This is an owl's head, which adds to the charm of novelty its reputation as a mascot. Certainly this suits many pretty faces. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Angel Topples The angel-topped Centennial Fountain, between McMechen and Wilson streets, in Eutaw place, which several generations of Balti- moreans have liked to stroll around, crashed irreparably as the result of a one-sided burden of ice and snow. The 50-foot granite structure, which was first put into use May 19, 1877. had three basins, the outer one 48 feet in diameter. title: NEGRO INDUSTRIAL FAIR: MAYOR MAHOOL COMPLIMENTS THE EXHIBITORS
full_text: NEGRO INDUSTRIAL FAIR Mayor Mahool Compliments The Exhibitors, The negro State Industrial Fair opened last night in Centre Hall, Centre Market and Lombard street. The exhibits re- flected great credit on those who took part in their production, and the ball was hand- somely decorated for the occasion with bunting and national and State flags. Mayor Mahool delivered an address in which he commended those who had the affair in charge and the spirit that prompted them to show what the race could do. The fair was held under the auspices of the United Grand Lodge of Colored Masons, and different lodges were represented by booths in which were displayed articles of a wide variety. Among the lodges repre- sented,were those of Mount Horeb, Lebanon, King David, Hannibal, Zion, St. James, Friendship, Enterprise. St. John, King Soloman, Mount Olive and the United Grand Lodge... At the booths were exhibits which cov- ered a wide field and were interesting and In many cases Instructive. Perhaps the best exhibit of the fair was that from the Colored Industrial School, at Cheltenham. Numerous photographs showed what was actually being done at the school, which at the present time contains 273 boys. Specimens of vegetables grown on the farm, which is among the most productive In Prince George's county, were as fine as those seen in high-class markets. Every- thing the boys at the school eat and wear is made on the premises, and the preserves and bread made would do credit to the best, of cooks. From unbleached materials there were also exhibited shirts that had been made at the school and at the Female Colored Industrial School at Melvale. George H. Siddons, a local florist, had some clever de- signs in flowers, among others being good representations of a railroad train, Masonic designs, a fireman's hat, Elk's head and a large design bearing "In God We Trust." Pumpkins did not seem to be scarce on the farm of a negro bearing the title of Adam Washington, for he had one, said to have come from Anne Arundel county, which was enormous. 'Leaf tobacco grown by J. H. Halsey was also a good exhibi- tion of the productiveness of this county: In other departments there were ex- hibits of interest, in the department of antiques a picture of Baltimore in 1752 attracting considerable attention. The fair will continue every day, beginning at 1 P. M., until December 2..

title: NEW CHELTENHAM PROTEST TONIGHT: COMMUNITY GROUPS LAY PLANS FOR MASS MEETING
full_text: NEW CHELTENHAM PROTEST TONIGHT Community Groups Lay Plans For Mass Meeting - Representatives of half a dozen community and civic associations, meeting last night at Baltimore Highlands, completed plans for a mass meeting at 8.30 o'clock to- night in Lakeland Presbyterian Church to protest location of the new Cheltenham School for colored boys on a 122-acre site between the Hollins Ferry road and the Old Annapolis road. B. D. Hall, president of the First Precinct Community Improvement Association, presided at the meet- ing at which the State administra- tion was hotly condemned for its part in selection of the new site. All-Out Fight Pledged Representatives of six improve- ment associations with combined membership of 1,800 pledged an all-out fight to keep Cheltenham out of the section. Among those directing the fight against Cheltenham who attended last night's meeting were: Emmett Batson, president, Lakeland-Dor- chester Heights Improvement Asso- ciation; Mrs. George Grewe, treas- urer, Rosemont Improvement Asso- ciation; George Dorner, of the English Consul Progressive Asso- ciation; C. R. Zepp, president, Thir- teenth District Democratic Club, of Lansdowne; Joseph Smith, Jr., president, Lansdowne Civic League, and Mr. Hall, for the Baltimore Highlands community. Protest To Governor Spokesmen declared telegrams of protest had been sent Governor O'Conor. Mr. Batson was directed to in- vite the following persons to at- tend tonight's meeting: Répresent- ative Baldwin; City Councilmen from the Sixth district-Mrs. Ella A. Bailey, Edward A. Freburger and Louis W. Kotmair; State Sena- tor George Della and represent- atives of the Governor and of the Board of Public Works. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: BLANDFORD QUITS POST AT CHELTENHAM: RESIGNS FOLLOWING BOARD'S DECISION TO ABOLISH RACE SEGREGATION MANAGERS VOTED TO PROVIDE JOINT HOUSING FOR EMPLOYES
full_text: BLANDFORD QUITS POST AT CHELTENHAM Resigns Following Board's Decision To Abolish Race Segregation Managers Voted To Pro vide Joint Housing For Employes Joseph H. Blandford yesterday tendered his resignation as presi dent of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys following the board's decision to abolish all restrictions segregat. ing the institution's Negro em ployes from the white." In a letter to Governor O'Conor, Mr. Blandford stated his resigna- tion would become effective imme- diately, as he "could not go along with the board members who voted to establish an interracial situa- tion among the employes of the in- stitution." The board voted to provide joint dining and housing facilities for the Negro and white workers at a meet- ing held ten days ago. Away At Conference Mr. Blandford was away at a con- ference at Richmond, Va., and al- though he had authorized the meet- ing to be held in his absence, he said yesterday he did not know the employe question would be dis- cussed. Howard C. Hill, vice-president of the board, presided at the meeting attended by the nine other mem- bers. "I give credit to the board mem- bers for their full sincerity," Mr. Blandford stated, "but I think they are wrong. At least their views are different from mine and I cannot go along with them." Unhappy Over Decision The text of Mr. Blandford's let- ter to the Governor, dated April 10, is as follows: "I am very unhappy over the de- cision of the board of the school to establish an interracial situation among the employes of that institu- tion. "I feel as do practically all white people, as well as the great mass of (Continued on Page 22, Column 6) CHELTENHAM AIDE RESIGNS Blandford Quits Following Board's Decision To Abol- ish Race Segregation Managers Voted To Provide Joint Housing For Negro And White Employes (Continued from Page 30) colored people of Maryland, that the interests of both races is best served through race segregation rather than by interracialism. 26 Years With School "Indeed, it is my firm conviction after twenty-six years connection with this institution, together with a lifetime in that part of the State which has the largest proportion of Negroes to whites, that the princi- pal of interracialism is revolting to the senses of all our white people and is not desire1 by the Negroes themselves. "Since assuming the presidency of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys in 1937, ou policy has been to em- ploy Negroes in positions of close contact with the inmates-such as cottage masters, school teachers, etc.-leaving administrative and of- fice personnel in the hands of the whites, with separate eating, sleep. ing and recreational facilities for the two races. Apparent Satisfaction "This arrangenient has apparent- ly worked to the satisfaction of all concerned, and I know of no reason why it could not have been contin- ued indefinitely with beneficial re- sults to the inmates. In other words, we have had a bi-racial situation on the employment level and segrega- tion on the social level. "I have frequently referred to the fact that inasmuch as many of the boys will in the future work under white supervision, they should become accustomed to such supervision while at the school. "During the entire period of my incumbency as a member of this board I have diligently applied my self to the problem of obtaining so- cial and economic rehabilitation for these unfortunate boys, most of whom are at Cheltenham only for the reason that they were neglected in early childhood or for some cause got off to a bad start in life. "Definite Progress" : "I feel that we have made defi- nite progress in the direction of re- leasing boys with a sufficient amount of skill in such lines as laundering, shoemaking, dairying, canning, plumbing, vegetable grow- ing and other activities, as to en able them to render satisfactory service to their employers.: "Our main objectives have been to instill in the boys a desire to go straight and to give them the ability to earn an honest living. "During the past several months. however, I have observed these objectives losing ground and in their place has come a definite trend toward using Cheltenham as a laboratory for testing out un- wholesome experiments in social and racial problems. "Unalterably Opposed" "I am unalterably opposed to any attempt to divert Cheltenham from the purpose for which it was, and is, intended, or to waste State funds in providing a small radical group the opportunity to exploit theories that are offensive to the great mass of our citizens. "I am therefore submitting my resignation as a member of Chel- tenham, to take effect today." Mr. Blandford was named presi- dent of the board when the State assumed control of Cheltenham in October, 1937. Founded in 1870, the institution had been operated pri- vately until that time.

"I feel as do practically all white people, as well as the great mass of (Continued on Page 22, Column 6) CHELTENHAM AIDE RESIGNS Blandford Quits Following Board's Decision To Abol- ish Race Segregation Managers Voted To Provide Joint Housing For Negro And White Employes (Continued from Page 30) colored people of Maryland, that the interests of both races is best served through race segregation rather than by interracialism. 26 Years With School "Indeed, it is my firm conviction after twenty-six years connection with this institution, together with a lifetime in that part of the State which has the largest proportion of Negroes to whites, that the princi- pal of interracialism is revolting to the senses of all our white people and is not desire1 by the Negroes themselves. "Since assuming the presidency of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys in 1937, ou policy has been to em- ploy Negroes in positions of close contact with the inmates-such as cottage masters, school teachers, etc.-leaving administrative and of- fice personnel in the hands of the whites, with separate eating, sleep. ing and recreational facilities for the two races. Apparent Satisfaction "This arrangenient has apparent- ly worked to the satisfaction of all concerned, and I know of no reason why it could not have been contin- ued indefinitely with beneficial re- sults to the inmates. In other words, we have had a bi-racial situation on the employment level and segrega- tion on the social level. "I have frequently referred to the fact that inasmuch as many of the boys will in the future work under white supervision, they should become accustomed to such supervision while at the school. "During the entire period of my incumbency as a member of this board I have diligently applied my self to the problem of obtaining so- cial and economic rehabilitation for these unfortunate boys, most of whom are at Cheltenham only for the reason that they were neglected in early childhood or for some cause got off to a bad start in life. "Definite Progress" : "I feel that we have made defi- nite progress in the direction of re- leasing boys with a sufficient amount of skill in such lines as laundering, shoemaking, dairying, canning, plumbing, vegetable grow- ing and other activities, as to en able them to render satisfactory service to their employers.: "Our main objectives have been to instill in the boys a desire to go straight and to give them the ability to earn an honest living. "During the past several months. however, I have observed these objectives losing ground and in their place has come a definite trend toward using Cheltenham as a laboratory for testing out un- wholesome experiments in social and racial problems. "Unalterably Opposed" "I am unalterably opposed to any attempt to divert Cheltenham from the purpose for which it was, and is, intended, or to waste State funds in providing a small radical group the opportunity to exploit theories that are offensive to the great mass of our citizens. "I am therefore submitting my resignation as a member of Chel- tenham, to take effect today." Mr. Blandford was named presi- dent of the board when the State assumed control of Cheltenham in October, 1937. Founded in 1870, the institution had been operated pri- vately until that time.

full_text: This "Blackhand" Operator Colored Paul Toopence, colored, 15 years old, an amateur Blackhand operator, pleaded guilty In the United States District Court yester- day to sending a number of threatening and defamatory letters through the mail and was sentenced by Judge Morris to three years in the Colored House of Reformation, - at Cheltenham. The letters sent by Too- pence demanded money under threats of harm if the demands were not complied with. The boy was arrested in the Fidelity Building, after using the telephone to send a threatening message to a negro he had selected as a victim. Mrs. Elsie E. Hess Divorced. Elste E. Hess, 2100 Pennsylvania ave- nue, was granted an absolute divorce yes- terday from John L. Hess and the custody of their child. They were married July 13, 1902, and separated February 5, 1904, The divorce was granted for abandonment. Seaboard Cross-Bill Filed. A cross-bill of complaint for the appoint- ment of receivers for the Seaboard Air Line Rallway Company was filed in the United States Circuit Court yesterday by the Continental Trust Company, through Lemmon & Clotworthy, attorneys. The cross-bill is similar to the cross-bill filed by the trust company against the rallwaycom- pany in Richmond. Messrs. S. Davies War- field, of Baltimore; R. Lancaster Williams, of Richmond, and Edward O. Duncan, of Raleigh, who were appointed receivers for the Seaboard system under the bill of com- plaint filed by the railway company against the trust company, were also appointed Maryland receivers under the cross-bill. ALLENS COMING TO MARYLAND Immigration Burenu's Report Is Highly Optimistic. The second blennial report of the Bureau of Immigration of Maryland, which has Just been issued, contains a number of in- teresting satistics. The report declares that the bureau is bringing more immi- grants to Maryland at a smaller expense than are brought to any other State in the South. It is claimed that the bureau has greatly relieved the stringency of farm- hands. The statistics show that during the Host two years 21,704 Europeans landed in the United States with the intention of settling in Maryland. During the years of 1006 and 1907 there arrived at the port of Baltimore 120,974 allens, consisting of 90,- 344 males and 30,630 females. About 15 per cent. of the entire number found em- ployment in Maryland, while the remainder were shipped West by the railroads. The report also tells in detail of the new settlers in this State from other States in: the Union. The Board of Commissioners Is composed of Dr. W. Whitehill and Messrs. Henry S. Mancha and William T. P. Turpin. Mr. A. F. Trappe is the secre- < tary. 1

title: Good News About Cheltenham
full_text: Good News About Cheltenham Good news, for a change, about the Chel- tenham School for Colored Boys. For some time past the State has been committed to the construction of a new Chel- rtenham School, on a new site. The present a school, located deep in the heart of Southern e Maryland, is wholly inadequate as an insti- -tution for delinquent colored boys. For cor- e roboration see a long series of grand jury e reports and special inquiries, not to mention ☐☐ the unceasing flow of bad news that has temanated from the place. The plan has been, therefore, to start ■ afresh, locating the new institution close to = Baltimore; and there are good reasons for - so locating it. Location near Baltimore will - make it easier to obtain competent person- =(nel for the operation of the institution-and = personnel has been one of Cheltenham's chronic difficulties. Location near Baltimore will give the parents of inmates readier access. Location near Baltimore will make it possible to enter into arrangements for practical vocational training. And location near Baltimore, by giving access to the utilities, will simplify many problems of maintenance. The trouble is that suitable sites are scarce-and that most of the sites deemed suitable have, when proposed, aroused neighborhood objections. Now an adequate site has not only been found but has been bought and paid for. The deal is done. The site is on the southern periphery of the city, near the new Cherry Hill development. Though it is unbeautiful in its present condition, it is ample in size, satisfies every requirement, and has been approved by both the State Board of Wel- fare and the Cheltenham board itself. Thus the year begins auspiciously for Cheltenham. True, the plans have still to be drawn, and the plant to be built from them. So the new Cheltenham still lies a consider- able distance into the future. Even so, the acquisition of a suitable site is something positive and welcome. title: TOM SHAW'S HANDICAP

title: WHY THE DELAY?
full_text: WHY THE DELAY? The bill by which the reformatory for colored boys at Cheltenham is to be taken over and administered by the State has been in the State Senate's Finance Committee for several weeks and, although other bills have gone through the committee, is still un- reported. In view of the fact that the bill is the result of an agreement between the present Cheltenham trustees and the Board of State Aid and Charities, and was intro- duced by fourteen members of the Legis- lature representing both parties, this delay is strange and disturbing. It is doubtless true, as it is always true when changes of this sort are contemplated, that various interests are not entirely satis- fied, and it is sometimes true that unworthy political motives intrude to block measures which of themselves are not criticized. The arguments on this matter have been in progress for a long time, however, and the bill now before the Senate committee at Annapolis represents thought and investiga- tion by M. Hampton Magruder and Enoch Harlan for the Cheltenham trustees and Morris A. Rome for the State, and the willingness of all concerned to concede a point here and there for the sake of agree- ment on the proposal as a whole. That agree- ment has been reached by the parties in in- terest, and the agreement is represented in this bill. It ought to be reported promptly. If the delay is occasioned by genuine doubts about the bill itself, those who enter- tain such doubts should reveal them at once. The situation at Cheltenham calls for frank- ness and a willingness to subordinate any in- stinct to spar for political advantage to a greater necessity. Too much hesitation will convince the State that these qualities are not sufficiently represented at Annapolis. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: MARLBORO JAIL VISITED: PRISONERS' AID SECRETARY FINDS MUCH TO CRITICISE INMATES ALLOWED, TO MINGLE SANITARY CONDITIONS DECLARED TO BE THOROUGHLY BAD--NEW BUILDING RECOMMENDED
full_text: MARLBORO JAIL VISITED Prisoners' Aid Secretary- Finds Much To Criticise. INMATES ALLOWED TO MINGLE V Sanitary Conditions Declared To Be Thoroughly Bad-New Building Recommended. Mr. J. O. Stutsman, general secretary of the Prisoners' Aid Assocation, visited the Prince George's County Jail, at Upper Marlboro, and reported its condition to Mr. DeCourcy W. Thom, chairman of the county work. He says: "The building is constructed, of brick, two stories high, 25 feet square, and is sur- rounded by a tall stockade of boards about 70 feet square. This fence gives privacy, but not protection from within or with- out. Prisoners could easily vault it from within and a mob could easily batter it down from without. A public execution would be a public spectacle. It affords an- other evidence of the need of a central place for executions. "The building is antique in plan. Few cells face upon a central corridor. Each cell is entered by a door 2 feet 8 inches by 7 feet. The bars of the door are so close that a hand could not be inserted between them. The interior of each cell is well lighted. most of them having outside win- dows 28 by 48 inches and doubly barred. The cells and floors are all of brick. The cells are unuusally large, seven being 12 by 15 feet and the remainder 7½ by 12 feet. "Having these facilities in cell space and segregation, it was thoroughly inexplicable why the jall administration should find it necessary to confine 10 prisoners in two cells. In one cell there were five colored males, two of whom were young boys awaiting transportation to the Cheltenham Reformatory. It is very obvious that such an indiscriminate mingling of adults and juveniles is highly conducive to immoral- ity and habitual crime. Such a system must be thoroughly condemned and should be rectified at once by the jail administrators, "The beds are simply cheap mattresses placed on the bare floors. Some of the mattresses were very ragged, straw was scattered over the cell floor, while others were new and clean. Sewer Choked Up. "The sanitary conditions of the building were thoroughly bad. After my visit to this jall in the summer of 1907 I recom- mended the introduction of a sewerage sys- tem. The sewer was constructed; but at the time of my present visit the sewer was wholly clogged, and its mouth, which is close to the building, usually was full of putrid matter, filling the air with disease bacteria.. This sewer had been abandoned, and now buckets are used in the cells and are emptied into a hole outside of the prison enclosure-a system which thor- oughly disgusts a visitor, is a menace to the community and a disgrace to the coun- ty. The lay of the land adjacent to the jall offers abundant facilities for a good sewerage system. "It was noticed that the interior of the prison had been recently whitewashed and presented a more cleanly appearance than at the time of my former visit. ""There were 17 inmates-13 colored and 4 white; 15 males and 2 females. One only was a sentenced prisoner, one was imbe- cllic and should have been otherwise cared for, and 13 were awaitng trial for the October term of court. No Work For Prisoners. "Nothing at all in the way of industry was provided; the inmates were living out their days in idleness, being taught by the community to be public charges. It will be a blessed day for the State when the value and efficacy of industry are fully grasped for the prevention of crime-that It is contrary to good economics to have to sustain those convicted of delinquency entirely at the public expense. We also have here a further exhibition of the im- morality of detaining those suspected of crime for a long period before trial. "The dietary program consisted of two meals each day, which appeared perfectly wholesome and sustaining. "It is not unusual for the warden to lock up the jail while he is on other busi- ness throughout the town. "This jall is not at all adequate and should be superseded at once by a proper structure for the housing and care of those convicted of crime and those detained upon suspicion. This jall has more inmates usually than the average county jail owing to its proximity to Washington. There have recently been as many as 28 inmates in the jail at one time. "No systematic religious services have been held. "Efforts will be made to establish a local committee in Upper Marlboro for the im provement of conditions." Ball and Levitzky were sentenced to three years each in St. Mary's Industrial School. title: F. Reed Isaac To Head Board Of Cheltenham
full_text: F. Reed Isaac To Head Board Of Cheltenham + F. Reid Isaac, superintendent of the Strawbridge Home for Boys, near Eldersburg, has been named president of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys. He will assume his new duties immediately. Mr. Isaac was selected by the board of managers of Cheltenham at a meeting in the office of Harry C. Jones, State employment com- missioner. He will succeed Joseph H. Blandford, who resigned in April of this year, when members of the board decided to abolish all restrictions segregating the insti tution's Negro employes from the white. The board also elected Joseph C. Briscoe, Negro, principal of the Negro Vocational School, vice president of the board, and re elected Hal T. Claggett, secretary- treasurer. full_text: THIS BULLET A LIVE ONE Colored Lads Test It In Blaze And White Boy Is Hit. Samuel Goldenberg, 8 years old, 821 West Lombard street, was seriously injured In an unusual accident Monday. Jacob Chapman and Addison Jackson, two colored youths, stopped at Vine and Arch streets and began to discuss the com- bustible property of a number of pistol cartridges which Addison had. To prove that the cartridges were no good Chapman wrapped one of the bullets in a paper, and placing it on the pavement, lit the wrapper. Chapman guessed wrong. In a few moments the blaze had melted the shell of the car- tridge and it exploded with a bang, which caused Patrolman Garrigan to hurry to the scene. The discharged ball struck young Goldenberg, who was near by, in the chest. He was taken to the University Hospital, where it was said the bullet had struck a rib directly over the heart. Goldenberg was later taken to his home. At the hearing before Justice Loden, at the Western Police Station, yesterday morn- ing Jackson was sent to Cheltenham charged with incorrigibility, while Chapman was paroled in the custody of his father pending the outcome of young Goldenberg's injury. title: NO NEED TO PUT BOYS IN 'CUT,' CURRAN RULES: REFORMITORIES MUST RECEIVE YOUTHS UNDER 16, HE SAYS CURRAN CITES PENAL SCHOOLS URGES 16 AS MINIMUM AGE FOR BOYS SENT TO CUT
full_text: NO NEED TO PUT BOYS IN 'CUT,' CURRAN RULES Reformitories Must Re- ceive Youths Under 16, He Says William Curran, Attorney Gen- eral, said last night he saw "no reason why any male offender under the age of 16 should be sen- tenced to the House of Correction or to any other penal institution." Declaring that the State Board of Public Welfare has complete con- trol over policies of admission to the four State training schools, he said that, if the board were willing, no legal obstacle would stand in the way of an institution's accepting a youthful offender committed to it. If contrary institutional regula- tions exist, he said, the law calls for alteration of those rules.  Cites Training School Explaining that he was convinced the reformatories were ir a situa- tion which might call for some over- crowding, he said the same situa- tion existed in other institutions and in hospitals, hotels and homes, and that the question would have to be worked out accordingly. He pointed out that a minimum security unit for serious offenders with a capacity of 40 is in opera- tion with 44 inmates at the Mary- land State Training School for Boys. He said additional space could be provided at the school, inmates could be rotated from that unit to other departments and similar units could be established at the Cheltenham School for Boys-all under existing authority of the welfare board.  Replying To Inquiries The attorney general's statement -made in response to inquiries from J. Milton Patterson, director of the board, and Governor O'Conor regarding present legal provisions for handling juvenile delinquents -came on the eve of presentation of the matter for consideration by the Legislative Council. Senator James J. Lindsay, chair- man of the council, said yesterday he would place before the Council today at its meeting in the City Council chambers a request by the Governor that it study the need for establishment of one or more addi- tional institutions for supervision of juvenile delinquents. Governor O'Conor's message to the council, embodied in a letter from William J. McWilliams, sec- (Continued on Page 9, Cclumn 3) CURRAN CITES PENAL SCHOOLS Urges 16 As Minimum Age For Boys Sent To Cut (Continued from Page 24) retary of state, to Senator Lindsay, noted that previous studies made by the council of the State's sys- tem for handling youthful delin- quents would furnish a background so that determination of any addi- tional requirements might be made "in the light of recent develop- ments." His recommendatiion was put forward "in connection with sug. gestions that have been made by members of the judiciary and others that the State's system for handling juvenile delinquents should include new and specialized facilities for supervision of the more difficult cases."  Council's Aid Emphasized In the event that provisions for commitment to a new institution call for new legislation as well as expenditures, the assistance and advice of the council in these mat- ters would be helpful, the letter stated. Mr. Curran's statement follows: "Mr. J. Milton Patterson, di- rector of the State Board of Public Welfare, has asked the attorney general's office to advise whether the recently enacted Juvenile Court bill calls for a change in the department's rules adopted for training schools.  Request From O'Conor "This office has also been re- quested by Governor O'Conor to determine what institutions are, under the present laws, obligated to take care of the more difficult types of juvenile offender. "Our laws over the years and particularly in recent years have become more progressively en- lightened as they concern the juve- nile offender. "The State Board of Public Wel- fare now has complete control over the policy of admission to the four training schools: the Maryland Training School for Boys, the Montrose School for Girls, the Cheltenham School for Boys and the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls, "The sentencing judge has now an almost complete freedom of choice in sentencing a juvenile offender.  Intermediate Place Cited "Mr. Hall Hammond, the deputy attorney general, is advising Mr. Patterson that the right given to the court to sentence a juvenile offender to any public institution imposes a correlative right on the public institution to receive the child when sentenced to it. "If any of the rules or policies of admission of these institutions be to the contrary, the law as it has been developed calls for a change in the rules of the institution. = "Recently there has been much discussion as to the need for an intermediate institution to handle juvenile delinquents. In 1944 the so-called minimum security unit was established at the Maryland Training School to house youthful offc.ders convicted of serious crimes.  Now In Operation "That unit is now in operation with 44 inmates, 35 of whom are confirmed runaways. The remaining nine were committed by the Crimi- nal Court of Baltimore city. The unit's capacity is 40 boys. "Within the powers entrusted to the board of welfare by the Leg- islature, additional space could be provided in co-operation with the management of the Training School or some system of rotation worked out whereby certain in- mates of the security unit could be sent back to other departments of the school. "Similar units could be estab- lished at Cheltenham. There would seem to be no reason why any male offender under the age of 16 should be sentenced to the House of Correction or to any other penal institution.". Other business before the Legis- lative Council today will include hearings on the State divorce. and unemployment-compensation laws. 1

title: Ad Club Plans Party For Needy Children
full_text: Plans Under Way For Cheltenham Governor O'Conor has disclosed that negotiations are under way for purchase of a site for construc- tion of the projected new Chelten- ham School for Boys. "The State is even now making final arrangements for the purchase of a new location," he said, adding that the new school would be erect- ed as soon as building conditions permit. Present facilities at Cheltenham will be turned over to the De- partment of Mental Hygiene for the care of colored feeble-minded children.  Ad Club Plans Party For Needy Children Approximately a thousand tickets have been distributed for the Ad- vertising Club of Baltimore's an- nual Christmas party for under- privileged children to be held at 10 A.M. Sunday at the Hippodrome Theater. The tickets, including provisions for free transportation, were handled by the Babies Milk Fund Association and the Children's Fresh Air Society. E. Lester Muller, who plays Santa Claus an- nually to the needy children, is chairman of the party. The children will be entertained by a motion picture and several vaude- ville acts and will receive toys, fruit, candy and five pennies from Santa Claus. The Advertising Club's annual Christmas party for members and their guests will be held at 12:15 P.M Saturday at the Emerson Hotel.  Waverly Christmas Party Boys and girls of two Waverly organizations will be guests at a Christmas party to be given by the Square and Star Club of Waverly at 8.15 o'clock tonight in the parish house of St. John's Episcopal Church, Greenmount avenue and Thirtieth street. The guests will come from the Waverly Assembly No. 4, Order of the Rainbow for Girls and the Tuscan Chapter, Order of DeMolay. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Obituary
full_text: Obituary Frederick Lambden Frederick Lambden, a druggist at North avenue and Cumberland street for thirty years, died Saturday at the South Baltimore General Hospital, which he entered July 5. Services will be held at 10 A. M.. tomorrow in St. Gregory's Catholic Church, and burial will be in the New Cathedral Ceme- tery. : Mr. Lambden started his practice of pharmacy in 1902 after graduating from the old University of Maryland. For a time he was a pharmacist in Lauten- bach's drug store at Eutaw and Sara- toga streets. Then he opened his own store at Druid Hill and North avenues, moving from that site to the present one thirty years ago. Surviving are his widow, Mrs. Eliz- abeth Carroll Lambden, and three sons, F. Carroll Lambden, Francis H. Lambden and Harry P. Lambden, and one grandchild. : Mrs. Mary E. Toomey Mrs. Mary E. Toomey, widow of George W. Toomey, died Saturday at the home of her son, Lawrence W. Toomey, 1932 Griffiss avenue, Morrell Park. She was 83 years old and for sev- enty-seven years had been going to Sexton Methodist Episcopal Church, of which she was a member. She also was a member of the Martha Chapter, Order of Eastern Star. Her husband, who died ten years ago, was a miller connected with the Woodyear Mills that used to be lo- cated on Gwynn's Falls. The Rev. Ellis P. Frye, pastor of the Sexton church, will officiate at funeral services to be held at 10.30 Α. Μ. Wednesday at her son's home. Surviving, in addition to Lawrence Toomey, are another son, Joseph H. Toomey, and one daughter, Mrs. Jacob J. Foerster, fourteen grandchildren and six great-grandchildren. . John E. Dorsey John E. Dorsey, who was formerly superintendent of the Cheltenham School for Boys, died yesterday in Beverly Hills, Cal., according to word received here. Funeral services will be held in that city with burial in Baltimore at Druid Ridge Cemetery. Mr. Dorsey, who would have been 90 on July 25, was born in Baltimore and lived here until a few years ago.
