title: JUDGE MOYLAN OPPOSES NEW JUVENILE HOME: SAYS ONLY 11 OF 2,211 DELINQUENCY CASES WENT TO COURT IN 1944 NEW JUVENILE HOME OPPOSED JUDGE MOYLAN SEES NO NEED FOR ONE NOW
full_text: JUDGE MOYLAN OPPOSES NEW JUVENILE HOME Says Only 11 Of 2,211 Delinquency Cases Went To Court In 1944 Judge Charles E. Moylan, of the Supreme Bench of Baltimore City. said yesterday that he felt there was no need for another institu. tion for supervision of serious juve- nile delinquents. In a statement, he noted that nineteen boys under 16 years of agé had been sent to State penal institutions during the year ended last June 30. - "From my experience in dealing with more than 4,500 delinquent boys and girls in the Circuit Court of Baltimore City, Division for Juvenile Causes, I definitely feel that there is no need" for an addi- tional institution for serious cases, said Judge Moylan, who has been assigned to the juvenile court since September, 1943. Handled 2,211 Cases in 1944 "The Division for Juvenile Causes, as pointed out in its last annual report, handled 2,211 de- linquency cases in 1944-about half of which involved burglaries, rob- bery, larceny, or serious assaults- and waived jurisdiction in only eleven of them involving nine boys, five white and four Negro boys. "The dockets of the Criminal Court of Baltimore City show that only four of these nine boys were sentenced to penal institutions; one was placed on probation; one was found not guilty, and three were committed to training schools. "During the first six months of 1945, the Juvenile Division, out of approximately 1,300 cases of delin- quent boys and girls under 16 years of age, has waived jurisdiction in eleven instances, all involving boys. 10 Under 16 "Sent Up" - "Of these eleven boys the Crimi- nal courts of Baltimore city sen- tenced three to penal institutions, committed one to the Spring Grove State Hospital, and the remaining seven were sent by the Criminal Court to one of our training schools. "The Criminal Courts retained jurisdiction over the ten boys it had committed to the training schools. Subsequently, three of the ten were returned to Criminal Court for a subsequent offense committed at the school or while on escape from the school, and were sentenced to a penal institution. "Accordingly, during 1944 and the first six months of 1945, the Criminal courts of Baltimore city sentenced ten boys under 16 years of age to a penal institution. Ob- viously, Baltimore city needs no additional institution for this hand- ful of boys." 15 In State Sent To Prisons Judge Moylan said Harold E. Donnell, superintendent of prisons, had told him that during the fiscal year ending June 30, 1944, fifteen boys under 16 had been sent to penal institutions by all the courts (Continued on Page 8, Column 3)  NEW JUVENILE HOME OPPOSED Judge Moyian Sees No Need For One Now (Continued from Page 22) exercising criminal jurisdiction throughout the State, including committing magistrates of all counties, and that during the fol- lowing year, nineteen boys under 16 had been received in the penal system from the entire State. "Manifestly, the large expense of an additional intermediate institu- tion for a mere handful of boys would not be justified," his state- ment continued. : "The facilities of the State train- ing schools should be enlarged, and made sufficiently flexible to afford segregation of age groups, etc., where necessary; the security unit at the Maryland Training School for Boys improved and operated to reduce to a minimum its present acute problem of runaway boys and to accommodate the so-called 'tougher delinquents,' and a simi- lar security unit set up at Chelten- ham School for Boys, with safe- guards against the recurrence of medieval cells and of other much criticized abuses prevalent there in the past. Case Of One Boy Cited "Pending such amplification by the State Department of Public Welfare of our training-school pro- grams and facilities, should the Juvenile Division ever waive jurisdiction in any instance? An intelligent answer can be supplied only by reference to concrete cases. "A 15-year-old Negro boy. from Harford county ran away from Cheltenham School, came to Balti- more, attacked women on our streets and engaged in purse- Isnatching, and was remanded by the Juvenile Division to Chelten- ham on June 12, 1945. After being remanded, he again ran away from the school and engaged in burglary and pocketbook-snatching and was again brought to the Juvenile Division. "The superintendent of Chelten- ham advised the court that this boy had run away on many previous occasions and had been one of the worst problem boys in his many years of experience as administra- tor in training schools in Virginia and at Cheltenham, and was a disrupting influence generally. Despite this plea, I declined to waive jurisdiction and remanded him again to Cheltenham on July 3, 1945... Attacked Sleeping Boy "On July 15, 1945, this boy ma- liciously attacked a sleeping boy at the school with a wagon spoke. The unprovoked criminal assault required that the injured boy be sent to Freedman Hospital in Wash- ington, where he remained in a semi-conscious condition for sev- eral days. Three days after the assault this boy again ran away from Chelten- ham, and a warrant has been signed for his apprehension. He is now thought to be again in Baltimore and will probably be soon brought to court on a new offense. "Query? If this boy, although only 15 years of age, is returned to the Juvenile Division, should he again be sent to Cheltenham and afforded an opportunity to en- danger the lives of other boys now being rehabilitated at this school, over half of whom are wards of this court?, Should the court waive juris- diction to the Criminal Court? Judge Asks Question "What should be done in such a case until the training schools ad- just their facilities to meet just such immediate needs? Is it an an- swer to declare that the judge can force the school to accept the boy if he will almost surely again run away at will and be back on Balti- more streets within a week, thereby affording no opportunity for his own rehabilitation and no protec tion to the community?" Governor's Suggestion The Governor's suggestion had been put forward with a view toward using the security unit at the school exclusively for boys com- mitted by the criminal courts and "difficult repeaters" sent by the juvenile courts. Mr. Pratt protested that conver- sion of these facilities would in- terfere with the recreation pro- gram for other boys and make im- possible a later reopening of the machine shop. He said the gymnasi- um offered no security-sometimes needed in dealing with "chonic runaways"-and could serve at best only as a stopgap.

title: INSTITUTION FOR 'UNSOCIAL' YOUTHS URGED: TRAINING SCHOOL HEADS FAVOR INTERMEDIATE UNIT OF CORRECTION NEW JUVENILE UNIT IS URGED INTERMEDIATE INSTITUTION FAVORED BY SCHOOL HEADS
full_text: INSTITUTION FOR 'UNSOCIAL' YOUTHS URGED Training School Heads Favor Intermediate Unit Of Correction Establishment of an "intermedi-| ate" correctional institution for the detention of juveniles too young to be sent to penal institutions for adults, yet adjudged too "unsocial" to associate in correctional juvenile institutions with delinquent and de- pendent youths, was urged yester- day by heads of the State's four training schools. On the other hand, Harold E. Donnell, State superintendent of prisons, took the position that ex- isting institutions created for de- tention of delinquent and depend- ent juveniles "should and can be run to deal effectively with all types of juvenile delinquents below 16 years and possibly some cases between 16 and 18." Figures Presented Mr. Donnell presented figures showing that in the year ended last June 30, a total of 99 youths of 16 years and under were committed to the House of Correction and the Penitentiary, compared with 97 youths committed in the preceding twelve months to the same penal institutions. Mr. Donnell further disclosed that last year seven girls of 16 years and under were committed to the Maryland State Reformatory for Women at Jessup. Although each of the seven girls gave her age as 16, the superintendent expressed confidence that "several were not yet 16." Favored By Pratt James A. Pratt, superintendent of the Maryland Training School for Boys at Loch Raven, is in favor of immediate erection of a "spe- cialized institution." He further disclosed that the board of managers for the Loch Raven institution has approved transfer of sufficient land for the proposed institution, but "is averse" to having it connected in any way with the existing buildings, believ- ing that it should be "operated en- tirely separately from the regular training school for average boys." Basic or tentative drawings for the buildings to comprise the sug- gested institution to accommodate about 125 have been made, Mr. Pratt said, adding that plans called for an administration building, isolation section, hospital, shops, dormitory and classrooms, esti- mated to cost $400,000. Mr. Pratt said such an institution should not be run with the purpose of handling any specific age groups. Instead, he held it imperative that it should be of the intermediate training type with detention deter- mined solely by "the behavior of the individual." "In other words, we need an in- stitution that can handle difficult psychopathic cases that cannot be adapted to training for normal (Continued on Page 7, Column 2) NEW JUVENILE UNIT IS URGED Intermediate Institution Fa- vored By School Heads (Continued from Page 22) social life in an open-type school such as the State training schools," Mr. Pratt said. He pointed out that such an insti- tution was maintained in New York, and heads of regular training schools were authorized to commit difficult-to-handle cases to it with- out. first seeking court approval. "When such an institution is created, we ought to have careful psychological and educational tests of juvenile delinquents, so that we can commit to it those unsuited to open-type training school life," Mr. Pratt continued. "Such a unit, of course, should be carefully.se- cured, under constant guard, and made difficult to get out of, as con- trasted with our unfenced, open institutions. Also, it should have especial education and training fa- cilities suited to the type of indi- viduals that will be committed to it. "Such an institution could care for the disturbers, those who can't get along with the normal run of individuals until they are trained to do so. Most of those that would be committed will be found to be psychopathic cases. "It is very, difficult to handle such cases in the open-type school. At Loch Raven, for example, we have to put the worst cases in a special detention cottage. That requires that we have extra in- structors, extra guards. The play- ground is fenced; the door of the cottage is kept under lock and.key. "We find that very often, after two to five months of correctional training, the offender can be trans- ferred to our open-type institution and go on from there." Not Equipped To Handle Type Royal A. B. Crump, superintend- ent of the State School for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, discussing the difficult-to-handle juveniles, said: yesterday: "We actually are not equipped.to handle that type. We hesitate to have them come in contact with our regular boys of 11 years and up; the influence is not good. But on the other hand, we hesitate before refusing to handle them because there isn't any other place save the penal institutions open to them and they certainly should not be sent thero. "So often one of the difficult-to- handle lads runs away because we haven't the minimum security place to maintain him and he frequently gets into trouble with the law, so that he commits a criminal offense and thus is committed to a penal institution. "We feel that a separate unit should be built for such boys, but it ought not to be directly con- nected with the established train- ing school where we handle delin- quents and dependent boys as well. Many of the boys are ill-tempered, high-strung, emotionally unstable, and generally unsocial. "They should, therefore, be iso- lated from the rest of our plant. But there is definitely a place for such an intermediate training school in the comprehensive over- all training school program, yet it certainly has no place in the penal system." • Favors Special Institution Mrs. M. J. Spellman, assistant superintendent and acting superin- tendent of the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls at Glen Burnie, said: "Difficult-to-handle cases can best be accommodated in a special in- stitution. If there was such a place of detention it would make our job of rehabilitating girls for society much easier. But we must caution that the hard-to-handle ought not to be sent to penal institutions. "Many of these juveniles are re- claimable. They are simply out-of- hand. Putting them with normal juveniles makes it difficult to han dle the latter, and reformation of the hard-to-handle is impeded. If these unfortunates are sent to penal institutions, they will swing to the worst patterns of life invariably." Special Treatment Required Mrs. Edith Gardner, superin- tendent of the Montrose School for (white) Girls, said: "Fortunately we don't have too many of the hard-to-handle cases, but those we do get are generally psychopathic cases requiring spe- cial treatment to adjust them to conventions of society. "In institutions like our own. it is hard to segregate them and give them the special attention they deserve. "There should be a school be- tween ours and the State Reforma tory School for Women. The offend- ers should not be placed with the young children of our school, nor should they be thrown with adult offenders. "They demand specialized train- ing, and they can get it only in a separate institution," Cites Loch Raven Cottage Mr. Donnell pointed to establish. ment of the minimum security cot- tage at Loch Raven as "evidence of what can be done by operating our existing institutions to handle all of the juveniles committed to them." "Naturally some special facilities may have to be provided," he said. "But I don't think the youths with good minds have to be handled in a distinctly separate institution. It may be that the feebleminded and those of very low mentalities may have to be housed separately. But that is a problem for the mental authorities. In recent years there have been many of this type. For example, a recent murder at the Hagerstown reformatory was com- mitted by a lad who had been in Crownsville for four years." Expressing the belief that sep- arate institutions would have to be provided for white and colored boys, if it is decided to segregate the difficult-to-handle youths in the training schools of the State, Mr. Donnell said: "I don't see how we could afford to do this. Improved facilities at the respective institutions may be the answer. Institutions must adopt the policy of not trying to get rid of an offender because he is hard to handle; instead they should try to save a child from becoming a confirmed criminal through wrong- ful associations in a penal insti- tution."

title: NEGRO SCHOOL SITE PROPOSED: BAKER ESTATE SUGGESTED FOR CHELTENHAM LOCATION
full_text: NEGRO SCHOOL SITE PROPOSED Baker Estate Suggested For Cheltenham Location Governor O'Conor announced yesterday that Ingleside, the old Bernard N. Baker estate in Catons- ville, has been recommended as the site for a new training school for Negro boys. The State Board of Public Wel fare and the board of managers of Cheitennam School for Boys recom mended the 100-acre tract after making a joint study of prospective sites. The lot is located south of Johnnycake road. west of Ingleside avenue, and adjoins Douglass Park, a Negro ridential section. Option Obtained A 90-day option has been ob tained on the site, which must be approved by the Board of Public Works before further action is taken. Governor O'Conor said. W. W. Lanahan, chairman of the State Board of Public Welfare and F. Reid Isaac, president of the board of managers of Cheltenham.. submitted the recommendation to the Governor, Has Zoning Board Okay Their report to the Governor also included a letter from the Zoning Committee of Baltimore county approving the location of the State institution on the Catons- ville site, which is priced at $650 per acre. The selection of a site for the erection of a State training school for Negro boys is the first step in carrying out the law enacted in 1943 providing for the separation of normal and defective Negro boys. Both are now cared for at the Cheltenham School for Boys in Prince George's county. New Building Called For The State legislation provided for the construction of a new in- Estitution for normal delinquents, under the jurisdiction of the De partment of Public Welfare, and the utilization of the present build- ings for defective juveniles. If and when the Catonsville site is approved by the Board of Public Works, the Board of Public Wel- fare and the board of managers of Cheltenham will be advised to hegin a study of buildings for the new institution, Governor O'Conor said. title: APPROPRIATIONS APPROVED: BOARD OF ESTIMATES ALLOWANCES FOR REFORMATORY INSTITUTION
full_text: APPROPRIATIONS APPROVED Board of Estimates' Allowances For Reformatory Institution. The Board of Estimates acted finally in approving the appropriations for the vari- ous reformatory institutions at the meeting yesterday morning. The appropriation asked by the Maryland School for Boys was $1.500 less than last year, the reduction being on account of the fact that less repairs will be necessary, as the institution will leave its present home before the year is over. The appropriation this year will be $47,000, as against the ap- propriation for last year of $49,400. This appropriation, as is the case with the other reformatory institutions, only fixes the maximum amount which can he expended, the actual amount being gor- erned within the limits of the appropria- tion by the quarterly bills rendered to the city, according to the number of city in- mates. The St. Mary's Industrial School asked for $48,000, as against an appropriation of last year of $46.000, the authorities saying that they expected a large Increase in the number of inmates during the year. No improvements will be necessary at the Industrial Home for Colored Girls this year, and, as a consequence, the appropria- tion could be reduced from $8,400 last year to $6,000 this year. Owing to an increase in the number of city inmates from 65 to 71, the House of the Good Shepherd for Girls asked for an increase, which was granted, from $4.745 last year to $5,188 this year. The appropriation for the House of the Good Shepherd for Colored Girls was in- creased from $4,332 last year to $4,560 this year the increase being due to an increase in the per capita charge of $3, from $57 to $60. The Female House of Refuge appropria- tion this year will be $9,900, as against $10.120 last year, the reduction being due to the fact that fewer repairs will be neces- sary. Cheitenham, the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, was granted $23,200, a re- duction of $400, due to the smaller number of boys-200, against 205 of last year. The National Junior Republic granted $4,200, the same amount as last year, and the Home for Fallen Women was given $1.080, the same as last year. was The Universal Progressive School for Destitute and Neglected Colored Children was granted an increase of $160, making the appropriation $900, owing to an in- crease in the number of city lumates from 10 to 12. title: ARMSTRONG MAY ASK BASEBALL SUIT HEARING
full_text: ARMSTRONG MAY ASK BASEBALL SUIT HEARING Question Of Using Force To End Sunday Games To Go Be- fore Court. MAY 21 IS TENTATIVE DATE Case Probably Wil Go To Judge Walter I. Dawkins In Form Of Mandamus. A request probably will be made by Attorney-General Armstrong, through Assistant Attorney-General Allan H.. Fisher, that the initial hearing on the mandamus to compel the use of force by the Police Department to prevent Sunday baseball be granted a week from next Saturday. Judge Walter I. Dawkins probably will hear the plea of the Lord's Day Alliance in support of the mandamus, he having been assigned to all special cases in the City Court, the other judges attending to the routine work. The mandamus suit was filed several weeks ago by the Alliance asking the court to direct Police Commissioner Gaither to use force to prevent Sunday -baseball. Through Attorney-General Armstrong. Commissioner Gaither an- swered that he is enforcing the law as it should be enforced, by obtaining the names of alleged violators and pre- senting them to the grand jury. As the grand jury refuses to indict, the Police Commissioner holds he can go no further. A trial by jury, on questions of fact, is asked in the Gaither answer. To this answer the Lord's Day Alli- ance demurred, and it is on the demurrer that the original hearing will be held. Finish Fight Indicated In Strike Of Printers Both Sides Express Determination Not To Yield On 44- Hour Week. With no indications of an early set- tlement, the printers' strike entered its second week yesterday. Officials of the typographical, pressmen and bookbind- ers' unions announced that they are de- termined to carry the fight for the 4-4-hour week to the finish, while the employers declared they would not grant the shorter week if the strike lasted in- definitely. George K. Horn, president of the Typothete, said that four of the largest printing firms in Baltimore have come out for the open shop. They are, he said, the Williams & Wilkins Com- pany, Thomsen-Ellis Company, Meyer & Thalheimer and Kohn & Pollock. The industrial relations committee of the Typothetæ, it was announced by Mr. Horn, has decided that it considers all agreements, promises and offers at an end. 23 WOULD BE STATE BUYER Applicants Seek Post Of Purchasing Agent-Inquiry On Today. Twenty-three applications for the post of State Purchasing Agent had been received by Governor Ritchie yes- terday evening, but none had received anything but the most casual considera- tion. Nineteen of the applications are in writing and are accompanied by a long list of qualifications each applicant advances for himself. The four others have come in the form of recommenda- tions from political leaders. While the Governor is giving his at- tention to the selection of a Purchasing Agent the committee named several weeks ago to investigate the methods of the Purchasing Bureau and report on means to avoid friction will begin its work. Col. Claude B. Sweezey, chair- man of this committee, has called a meet- ing for this afternoon. Governor Ritchie probably will attend and help outline the course of the investigation. QUITS REFORMATION BOARD P. L. Goldsborough Sends His Res- ignation To The Mayor. Former Governor Phillips Lee Golds- borough yesterday sent to Mayor Broen- ing his resignation as a city director in the management of the House of Refor- mation for Colored Boys, Cheltenham. "This is done," Mr. Goldsborough said In his letter to the Mayor, "for the sole reason that I find my daily business en- gagements are such as to preclude prompt attendance upon the meetings of the board. "I had hoped to be able to render proper service, but now, finding that I shall not be able to attend meetings with regularity, it is but just to you that I should resign as a member of that body."

title: FROM $30 TO $100 AN ACRE: WHAT MR. HEITMULLER HAS DONE WITH WASTE FARM LAND
full_text: FROM $30 TO $100 AN ACRE What Mr. Heitmuller Has Done With Waste Farm Land. W. Charles Heitmuller, who owns a tract of land in Prince George's county, has solved the problem offered by aban- doned farm lands in Maryland. The tract is near enough to Washington so that its proximity to the District of Columbia gives the land a value as a pos- sible future addition to the city, regard- less of its lack of productive qualities when purchased by Mr. Heitmuller; but it is the same sort of land that in Maryland is generally regarded as unproductive and comparatively valueless. The land was bought four years ago at $30 an acre. In- telligent treatment and scientitle methods of cultivating have increased the value, be- cause of its increased productiveness, to $100 an acre. When Mr. Heitmuller bought the farm the land hardly produced weeds; last year 30 acres of it produced 6,000 crates of cantaloupes that in the Washington, Phila- delphia and New York markets brought twice as much money as New Jersey's. While the New Jersey cantaloupes were selling at from 75 cents to $1.50 a crate those from Mr. Heitmuller's farm in Maryland readily brought from $2 to $2.50 a-crate. "Waste Land" Proves Valuable. .This "waste land," abandoned because of its unproductiveness, is now producing 200 crates of cantaloupes to the acre that bring 50 per cent. more in price than the best grown in New Jersey and elsewhere. And they were not grown in the bottoms, but on the uplands. Mr. Ileitmuller says he is raising other crops to correspond on his land. The lands that are now offered at nomi- nal prices, due to impoverishment by ren- son of continuous farming without replen- ishment of the elements that contribute to plant growth, have only to be treated intelligently to be made to yield abun- dantly. How Population Affects It. The increase of population, requiring an increasing volume of products from the field and garden to supply the markets of the growing towns and cities, is causing people to consider what measures to take for maintaining the supply and increasing it. To facilitate the project of not only making two blades of grass grow where only one grew before, to enable the garden- ers and farmers to produce from their lands larger crops of, and better quality. and to promote rehabilitation of the soil. the Government is spending vast sums in educating the farming people how to farm scientifically. Mr. Heitmuller's achievement is not so easy as it sounds. He spent three years experimenting before he perfected the seed he believed would be adapted to the soil, and he learned how to treat the soll in a way to increase its productive powers. Finds Watermelons Unprofitable. He was asked whether he tried to grow watermelons. "No." he said, "watermel- ons don't bring more than about $25 a Lundred, and they are so heavy that the expense of bringing them to market is too much to justify the effort. If, however, a number of people were to go about raising cantaloupes, watermelons, small fruits and rården truck along the railway lines to ship in car lots, it would pay well. I am talking now about community farming- commercializing it. That is the only way by which refrigerator cars could be protit- ably utilized. I would like to see the lands adjacent to my farm rehabilitated. I am very well satisfied with my experiments. Two hundred crates of cantaloupes that bring an average of $1.55 a crate the sea- son through from ar acre of land that cost $30 is not a bad speculation. I expect to get better results next year." Mr. Heitmuller declares that there are thousands of young farmers earning a poor living from their lands who could make themselves comfortably well off if they would show the enterprise requisite to hard study and a respect for the scientiile knowledge of our day. In Warmed-Out" District. In Southern Maryland, right in the heart of the "farmed-out' district, is located the House of Reformation, for incorrigible colored boys. It is near Cheltenham Sta- tion, in Prince George's county. Forty years ago the several hundred acres of land belonging to the State as a part of the in- stitution was a "farmed-out" waste. In Capable, determined and energetic men have had charge since its inception. 1870 the land was unproductive. In the seventies Baltimore had not yet become fa- miliar with the electric trolley. 'The street cars were propelled by horse and muie energy. The management of the institu- tion obtained the right to use the manure from the street car stables. They also bought lime. The land was fertilized and selentifically cared for. It has been brought to a high stage of cultivation. It is an agricultural oasis in the midst of an agri- cultural land desert. It cost knowledge and effort to reclaim it. At the colored State industrial fair the exhibit of this farm was the best. Today that farm is producing enough to feed about 300 hungry, hardy colored boys on the "fat of the land' and is selling prod- ucts besides to assist in the maintenance of the reformatory. The land was fertilized and selentifically cared for. It has been brought to a high stage of cultivation. It is an agricultural oasis in the midst of an agri- cultural land desert. It cost knowledge and effort to reclaim it. At the colored State industrial fair the exhibit of this farm was the best. Today that farm is producing enough to feed about 300 hungry, hardy colored boys on the "fat of the land' and is selling prod- ucts besides to assist in the maintenance of the reformatory. . .

title: BYRD IS NAMED TO BOARD OF CHELTENHAM: NICE APPOINTS 4 OTHERS BESIDES PRESIDENT OF U. OF MD. GOVERNOR HOLDS PARLEY IN EFFORT TO IRON OUT RECENT DIFFICULTIES
full_text: BYRD IS NAMED TO BOARD OF CHELTENHAM Nice Appoints 4 Others Besides President Of U. Of Md. Governor Holds Parley In Effort To Iron Out Re- cent Difficulties To the multifarious duties of Dr. H. C. Byrd, president of the Univer- sity of Maryland and potent yet myş- terious figure in the State Democratic political picture, another was added yesterday. His name was placed by Governor Nice on the roster of the turbulent board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys. Dr. Byrd's appointment, with four others, to membership on the board was announced by the Governor short- ly before a conference was held at the Government House in Annapolis in an effort to solve the difficulties that have arisen since the Negro reform school was taken over by the State. The five appointees fill vacancies caused by expired terms on the six- teen-member board, of which the Gov- ernor is ex officio a member. Four Other Appointees The others named by the Governor are: JOHN L. BERRY, Negro, graduate of Howard University, former teacher at the Douglass High School in Baltimore, former member of the grand jury and active in civic af- fairs of his race. THE REV. ALBERT J. MITCHELL, Negro, graduate of Clark University and Gammon Theological Seminary, superintendent of the North Balti- more district of the Afro Methodist Episcopal Church and active in the raising of funds for Morgan College and other Negro educational insti- tutions. MISE IDA R. CUMMINGS, Negro, Mor- gan College graduate, sister of the late City Councilman, Harry S. Cummings, and a retired school- teacher. MISS BERTHA W. Pпостов, Negro pub- lie school teacher, president of the women's auxiliary of Morgan Col- lege and a social worker. Present At Conference Those who Inter conferred with the Governor on the squabble between the State and the board of managers were Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner; M. Hampton Magruder, Collector of Internal Revenue and a member of the board; Joseph H. Blandford, president of the board, and Howard C. Hill, member. Sitting with them also were Morris A. Rome, member of the Board of State Aid and Charities, and W. H. Blakeman, State Budget Director. A score of employes of the board at the reform institution were pro- nounced unfit for such employment by the State Employment Commissioner and when the State withheld pay to Lorce their elimination, with support of a majority of the board, mandamus proceedings were instituted to obtain the funds. Nice Gives Ultimatum The Governor stepped in with an ultimatum to the board to accept plans for reorganization, offer an acceptable substitute plan or resign. They declined to resign, but Mr. Ma- gruder, representing the board, and the State Employment Commissioner were named at yesterday's conference as a committee to seek a suitable com- promise solution. The Governor said the conferees had "an agreeable talk," but that he had stood on his request for a reorganiza- tion or for resignations of a majority of the board, and this group had stood on its denial. "Some Progress" Reported However, he added that he believed "some progress" had been made. The five new members on the board will not affect its attitude, the Gov- ernor added, since the five who retired were aligned against the majority in opposition to the State's demands. full_text: JONES REPORTS BRUTALITY AT CHELTENHAM Employment Commission. er Also Alleges Sadistic Treatment Of Boy Cottage Master Suspended For Beating Inmate-In- vestigation Made A cottage master at the Cheltenham School for Boys has been suspended for alleged "sadistic and brutal treat- ment" of an undersized 14-year-old in- mate, Harry C. Jones, State Employ- ment Commissioner, reported yester day to Governor Nice. Incarcerated in a barred cell for four days on suspicion of having stolen three cigars, the Negro boy was beaten up and a scalp wound was inflicted with a heavy iron padlock, Mr. Jones told the Governor.  Investigation Made The cottage master, Andrew Beck with, was ordered suspended after he was unable to give a "satisfactory ex- planation" of the occurrence at a per- Isonal investigation which the Employ- ment Commissioner conducted at the Southern Maryland reformatory Thurs- day. Mr. Jones said he would bring charges against Beckwith at a formal hearing, and if sworn testimony bore out the facts in his report he would refer the record to the State's Attor- ney for Prince George's county. title: FERRY COMPANY'S RATES ASSAILED: SHERBOW GIVES LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL PICTURE OF WHAT STATE COULD DO SAYS PASSENGER CHARGES COULD BE REDUCED AT LEAST 50 PER CENT.
full_text: FERRY COMPANY'S RATES ASSAILED Sherbow Gives Legislative Council Picture Of What State Could Do Says Passenger Charges Could Be Reduced At Least 50 Per Cent. [From a Staff Correspondent] Annapolis, April 10-Basing his re- marks on a heretofore unpublished re- port, Joseph Sherbow, People's Coun- sél for the Public Service Commission, today predicted that if the State took over the Claiborne-Annapolis Ferry Company for an "equitable" price, the following could result: Passenger rates reduced at least fifty per cent. Auto and truck rates cut one-third. Profits, despite the reductions, to permit amortization of the pur- chase bonds without cost to the taxpayer. A fast, high-frequency service in- stalled at once. Approved Generally Mr. Sherbow spoke before the Legislative Council. His statements on the situation on Chesapeake Bay transportation met general approval, particularly from Senator Dudley G. Roe (Dem., Queen Anne's). ■ "These figures," Mr. Sherbow said, "have been compiled on a basis of the same number of passengers and ve- hicles as are now carried by the ferry company. That, of course, is absurd, as there is not a bit of doubt that with the lower rates trame will be in- creased considerably and profits will be larger. I'm just stating the case mildly." Price Considered The attorney, who is endeavoring to have the Public Service Commission compel the ferry company to lower its rates, considered a purchase price of either $800,000, $900,000, or $1,000,000 in compiling his report. "I cannot be too emphatic when I say," he continued, "that the State must take into consideration, if it should purchase the ferry company, what the State has put into that com- pany." Between 1928 and the present, he declared, Maryland had put $165,000 in the concern, and before that date "a very substantial sum" which was impossible to estimate because the records of the predecessor company are in very bad shape." As other subsidies from the taxpayer he pointed to "all the roads direct to the ferry slips" and the deal with re gard to the ferry slip at Claiborne. "Maryland," 'he asserted, "purchased the land for that ferry slip for $4,100 spent $65,000 additional for mainte- nance, improvements and repairs, and then by an act of the 1929 Legisla- ture, the Board of Public Work sold it to the ferry concern for the origi. nal $4,100.", The speaker estimated the ferry company's valuation of its property was $750,000 too high, and said he would not "give a dime" for two of the ferries the Governor Ritchie and the Governor Harrington. Discussing valuations claimed by the company, the Council seemed agreed that "all the value has come from the State of Maryland and the man who paid his fare," : Calls Legislation Astounding Speaking of legislation concerning the company, Mr. Sherbow said the Ac: of 1935 "is one of the most astound- ing pieces of legislation ever put on the books.". In that statute, he as- serted, the State was committed to purchasing the concern for a mini- mum of. $1,200,000 in three per cent. bonds, if and when purchase was made. "This," he continued, "regardless of the fact that the State can sell its bonds for one and one-half per cent. in the open market." Other legislation provides that no competing ferries may be set up with- in twenty miles or ten miles of the two sites under consideration for the proposed Chesapeake Bay bridge. In addition, he declared, if the State does take over the ferry, it would be bound not to lower rates. All such legislation could be re- moved, and the way cleared for the State either to purchase the company or to found a competing transporta- tion system, by an act of the Legis- lature, Mr. Sherbow declared. Al- through members of the council ex- pressed opinions to the contrary, the attorney said he did not believe such legislation would get past the, law- makers. Speaks For Lower Bay Senator Roe asserted that "we ar building a magnificent bridge at th head of the bay, and certainly w should do something for the lowe bay. There should be a ferry fror Kent Island to Sandy Point, joinin the two shores the way they ought t be." In this vein, the Senator mentione also that it was of little moment to b talking of "money for doorkeeper. stenographers and so forth" with suc a problem to be discussed. Other members of the council als had something to say about recen criticism of the Legislature for pay ments to what the Baltimore count delegation in particular has charge were "an excessive" number of tem porary employes during sessions a Annapolis. On Legislative Expenses Senator Arthur H. Brice (Dem Kent) said several letters had bee received on the subject of costs a Annapolis and urged that Dr. Horac E. Flack, secretary of the council, b directed to make a survey of othe States on "legislative expenses." Thi was adopted. "I think there have been certain matters on which the newspapers hav not been explicit," said Delegate Pau L. Cordish, of Baltimore. "There wa mention of 108 extra employes. They were never here at one time. It is problem of definition." By that, he explained, he meant tha the so-called doorkeepers had beer used as clerks, runners and for putting up the daily journals. Cites Cost Of Session "One thing stands out," said Mr. Cordish. "We spend approximately $50,000,000 a year in Maryland, and the Legislature costs but $250,000 every two years. This is a veritable drop in the bucket. If there is any waste in this small sum, I would be glad to see it corrected, "There is bound to be a tremendous amount of wasted and confused effort in a ninety-day session. There are lays when we could have used more men, Other days we did not need those that were there." He suggested that "we accept the challenge, and determine either that the present budget is fair and ade- quate or that there are one or two men too many whom we could lop off." Senator Roe called newspaper com- ment a "lot of poppycock" and de- clared that "when you figure it out, the one hundred stenographers were equal to but forty on a full-time pasis, and the 'eighty doorkeepers represented eighteen." He commented also on a complaint that $25 for stamps vas an excessive allowance, and said any member of the Legislature who Ild not write 800 letters a susioni 'should not be elected." Wants Fund For Cheltenham Others who appeared, before the council were Joseph H. Blandford, hairman of the board of managers of The Cheltenham School for Boys, and Dr. John J. Rutledge, chief mine engineer for the Bureau of Mines. Mr. Blandford said Cheltenham was being transformed into a rehabilitation Institution instead of custodial, but hat problems of selection of the in- mates was a serious one standing "Two-thirds of our 420 boys are capable of the kind of education we are preparing to give them," he esti- mated. He said the mentality of the others was so low it would be a waste of time to use their methods on them, and that many of those were of a criminal type with an injurious effect on the other boys. Mr. Blandford indicated he would ask the next Legislature for funds from which to build an academic and industrial addition to the school, The Bureau of Mines head was greeted "as the first man who has come down here without asking for legisla- tion." Dr. Rutledge declared his de- partment suffered from too much legislation and complained he had to spend "ninety days at the last Legisla- ture guiding four or five bills through." It was his opinion, he added, that a technical man should not have to spend many hours at the Legislature's sessions guarding against legislation unfavorable to his department. : Stops Bootleg Coal He reported "quite a bit of success in stopping bootleg coal from Penn- sylvania," but did not appear en- thusiastic over the support he was getting in enforcement of the law from the State's Attorneys of the various counties. In one instance, Dr. Rutledge noted, he charged a county State's Attorney with using bootleg coal himself before getting any action. The next day, the speaker said, 300 licenses were issued to coal dealers. Senator Brice, chairman of the council, appointed committees to con- fer with the Insurance Commissioner, the Bank Commissioner, Employment Commissioner, Department of Welfare and the Commissioner of Motor Ve- hicles. Legislative proposals arising from such conferences will be given to the council for final consideration. = thwart such a move.

title: A Negro Problem That Is Headed For Solution
full_text: A Negro Problem That Is Headed For Solution sue 400vie suuge легman M. Moser nas Į had in finding a suitable place of commit- ment for an unusually obstreperous 13-year- old Negro boy should occasion no special furor, The State is developing a promising program for the handling of such cases and for improving generally the institutional facilities for Negro juvenile delinquents. The State's plans call for a wholly new training school for Negro boys, the site to be in the vicinity of Catonsville. This institution will cost approximately $1,500,000; the money for it has already been set aside in the special postwar building and rehabilita- tion fund. When this school is opened, the present inadequate Cheltenham School for Boys will be turned over to the State Board of Mental Hygiene for use in the care of Negro boys who suffer from mental diseases or are seriously retarded mentally. Those are the plans. When they are carried out, there should be an end to the problem of what to do with a Negro juvenile delin- quent though he be insane, moronic, tough or what not. Certainly our State officials can- not be planning to spend $1,500,000 on a new institution plus $300,000 or so at Cheltenham only to inform the public later that more money is needed to provide a facility for the care of a few unruly youngsters. The only question remaining is, therefore, how soon will the new school be built? The project has been given top priority by State officials. There has been some delay in acquir. ing a site, but progress here is expected to be somewhat more rapid in the next few weeks. Then detailed planning, and actual construc- tion, should follow promptly. To be sure, the new school will not he ready for occupancy for many months. But we And it hard to believe that in the mean- time tough boys of 13 cannot be provided for at Cheltenham. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: HOSE FLOGGING OF BOY INMATES NOT 'UNUSUAL': CHELTENHAM CHIEF, HOWEVER, DENIES YOUTH WAS "BEATEN BADLY" ANSWERS JONES' CHARGES, SAYS "NONE OF STATEMENTS ARE TRUE"
full_text: HOSE FLOGGING OF BOY INMATES NOT 'UNUSUAL! Cheltenham Chief, How- ever, Denies Youth Was "Beaten Badly" Answers Jones' Charges, Says "None Of State- ments Are True" B. B. Sunderland, superintendent of Cheltenham Reform School for Colored Boys, yesterday admitted it was "noth- ing unusual" for boys committed to the institution to be beaten with a rubber hose. Mr. Sunderland was asked for com- ment on charges made by Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commis- sioner, that 14-year-old Walter Thomas, an inmate, had been beaten severely by Andrew Beckwith, a cot- tage master, with a cell padlock. First Denies Jones' Charges, Mr. Jones, in addition, charged that John Beckwith, a brother of the cot- tage superintendent, had "flogged" Thomas with a piece of garden hose two and a half feet long and an inch in diameter before the boy had been released from confinement at Chel- tenham. Mr. Jones further alleged that John Beckwith had admitted the flog- ging. Answering Mr. Jones' charges, Mr. Sunderland first said that "none of the statements are true." "There is nothing wrong with the boy," he said. "The mother had a visit with him this morning and she was perfectly satisfied. We don't beat down here." As To Beating With Hose Then he was asked: "But what about the charge that Thomas was beaten with a rubber hose by John Beckwith?" "There is no question about not us- ing a hose," Mr. Sunderland replied. "You mean to say that he was not beaten with a hose?" he was asked. "No," Mr. Sunderland replied. "I didn't say that at all. I didn't say that at all." "Then he was beaten with a hose?" "Nothing Unusual," He Saya "That's nothing unusual. Don't for- get we get what you Baltimore city fellows are done with. The main ques- tion is to be fair to those boys." Questioned further about the Thomas boy, Mr. Sunderland said he was "not beaten badly" and repeated that "noth- ing was the matter with him." He said that Andrew Beckwith, the man charged with beating the Thomas boy with a cell padlock, and who was suspended from his duties after a per- sonal investigation conducted by Mr. Jones, had "taken a vacation for a day or two." "He needed it," Mr. Sunderland said. "He's a hard worker." Mother Appealed To Governor The Thomas boy is the son of a domestic employed in Baltimore. The mother appealed some days ago to Governor Nice to find out whether her son was "dead or alive." The Governor referred the matter to Mr. Jones. Mr. Jones said the officials at Chel- tenham, with whom he has been hav- ing a dispute about the capabilities (Continued on Page 12, Column 5) of the reform school's staff, pretended to know very little about the case. Then Mr. Jones charged that the Thomas boy first had been put in a barred cell for four days because he was suspected of the theft of three of Mr. Sunderland's cigars. Declared Ordered Locked Up "On or about Tuesday, July 26, the superintendent missed a few cigars from an open box on the mantel of his living room," Mr. Jones told the Gov- ernor, "and satisfying himsel that the boy had taken them, he ordered him 'locked up.' "The boy was taken by the assistant superintendent, Mr. Carroll, to cottage No. 1, over which a cottage master named Andrew Beckwith presides, and in the absence of Beckwith, 'locked' this boy in a barred cell. The Padlock Incident "On the next day, Thursday, July 28, another boy named Elwood Waters was locked in the same cell. It ap- pears that on Thursday evening the two boys got to playing with the bed in the cell and Andrew Beckwith, cottage master, who in the meantime had returned to duty, is alleged to have entered the cell with the cell padlock in his hand. "He appears to have gone after both boys with his fists. Thomas now has a partially healed scalp wound claimed to be the result thereof. Both boys testified they were 'beat up ter- rible.' ". . Not In Records, He Charges The evidence shows that Thomas was released on Monday by John Eeckwith, supervisor of boys and a brother of Andrew Beckwith. John Beckwith testified that at the time he released Thomas he logged him with a piece of garden hose two and a half feet long and an inch in diameter." Mr. Jones further alleged that none of the occurrences he charged had appeared in written records of Chel- tenham, although the institution main- tains a "conduct-card" record which is supposed to show all disciplinary action taken against inmates.

The mother appealed some days ago to Governor Nice to find out whether her son was "dead or alive." The Governor referred the matter to Mr. Jones. Mr. Jones said the officials at Chel- tenham, with whom he has been hav- ing a dispute about the capabilities (Continued on Page 12, Column 5) of the reform school's staff, pretended to know very little about the case. Then Mr. Jones charged that the Thomas boy first had been put in a barred cell for four days because he was suspected of the theft of three of Mr. Sunderland's cigars. Declared Ordered Locked Up "On or about Tuesday, July 26, the superintendent missed a few cigars from an open box on the mantel of his living room," Mr. Jones told the Gov- ernor, "and satisfying himsel that the boy had taken them, he ordered him 'locked up.' "The boy was taken by the assistant superintendent, Mr. Carroll, to cottage No. 1, over which a cottage master named Andrew Beckwith presides, and in the absence of Beckwith, 'locked' this boy in a barred cell. The Padlock Incident "On the next day, Thursday, July 28, another boy named Elwood Waters was locked in the same cell. It ap- pears that on Thursday evening the two boys got to playing with the bed in the cell and Andrew Beckwith, cottage master, who in the meantime had returned to duty, is alleged to have entered the cell with the cell padlock in his hand. "He appears to have gone after both boys with his fists. Thomas now has a partially healed scalp wound claimed to be the result thereof. Both boys testified they were 'beat up ter- rible.' ". . Not In Records, He Charges The evidence shows that Thomas was released on Monday by John Eeckwith, supervisor of boys and a brother of Andrew Beckwith. John Beckwith testified that at the time he released Thomas he logged him with a piece of garden hose two and a half feet long and an inch in diameter." title: LETTERS to the EDITOR: The Problem Of Cheltenham
full_text: LETTERS to the EDITOR The Problem Of Cheltenham ■ TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: I have just read in The Sun the excellent edi- torial on conditions at Cheltenham. I heartily agree with the suggestion that the Governor should arrange for a thor- ough investigation of the conduct of this reform school for colored boys, and if the court should decide that as the law now stands there cannot be the proper improvement, then the Governor should prepare the way for changing the law in the next session of the State Legisla- ture. In the letter from the Rev. George T. Bragg, Jr., in this same issue, voters are urged to support in the coming election candidates who will stand squarely for justice in this matter. This appeal should be taken to heart. Besides the obligation of public officials to look after the welfare of our State institutions, the main responsibility lies with the private citizens. If they were more interested and more coöperative, we might have more reason to be proud of our institutions. As a member of the Interracial Com- mittee of the Baltimore Branch of the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom and of the Committee on Juvenile Delinquency of the Baltimore Urban League, I have been gathering information about the reform school for colored boys at Cheltenham and the in- dustrial school for colored girls at Glen Burnie. In visiting these places I have found that the staff and the management of the school at Glen Burnie is far su- perior to that at Cheltenham. This dif- ference is due in large measure, I be- lieve, to the personal attention of an efficient board and to the unselfish co- operation of a large number of Negro and white women. When the public becomes as concerned about Cheltenham as many have been about the Glen Burnie establishment, it will be possible to have changes there that will tend toward the turning of delinquent Negro boys into good citi- zens. Baltimore, Aug. 9.' ESTHER J. CROOKS. 1 ! 1 i Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: STATE UNITS GIVEN TOOLS - Surplus Items Worth $66,000 Are Obtained Free ⚫ State correctional institutions) have obtained approximately $66,- 000 worth of surplus tools, machin- cry and equipment from the Fed- cral Government without cost, Gov. ernor O'Conor announced yester day on receiving a report from Jerome Sloman, chairman of the Commission to Study Prison Labor, The Governor said that in co- operation with heads of State pena institutions, Mr. Sloman and his commission were able to arrange for a transfer of the surplus prop. erty to equip the vocational reha- bilitation facilities of the Maryland State Reformatory for Males, the House of Correction the Maryland Training School for Boys and the Cheltenham School for Boys. Items Include Tractor Among the items obtained were a tractor and crushing screen for the State Reformatory for Males, ogether with drill presses, tire buffers, generators, grinders, en- Cine assemblies, tools, hack saws, wrenches and similar articles. Army officials at different posts in and near the State were most co-operative in making the property available, Mr. Sloman told the Governor. The equipment has been received from Fort George G. Meade, the Holabird Signal Depot, the Indiantown Gap Military Reser vation, the Lordstown Ordnance Depot and the Letterkenny Ord- nance Depot. Will Help Training Plans "Penal authorities were particu- !arly gratified that these items have been available," the Governor said, "inasmuch as they will make possible effectuation of the voca- tional training plans at the Mary- land Reformatory for Males and other institutions involved. "Throughout the period of the war the items needed for this prac- tice were practically unavailable, but now, thanks to the efforts of Mr. Sloman and his associates, and the co-operation of the army off- cials, the long-planned program can be put into effect immedi- ately." title: CHARGES ABUSES AT CHELTENHAM: JONES ACCUSES SOME COLLAGE MASTERS OF DISCIPLINING BY "FEAR AND FORCE" STATE EMPLOYMENT HEAD MAKES ALLEGATION IN REPLY TO MANDAMUS SUIT
full_text: CHARGES ABUSES AT CHELTENHAM Jones Accuses Some Cottage Masters Of Disciplining By "Fear And Force" State Employment Head Makes Allegation In Reply To Mandamus Suit Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, yesterday declared tha some cottage masters in disciplining Negro youths at the Cheltenhar School for Boys have used "fear and force." His charges were made in an answer filed in Superior Court, to mandamus proceedings brought by the board of managers of the school to force the commissioner to certify salaries of in- stitutional employes he has declared "totally unfit." Hearing Date Unset No date for a hearing on the man- damus suit has been set. Meanwhile, those employes declared unfit by Mr. Jones to continue on the institution's pay roll are being paid one-half of their wages out of a special $30,000 fund allotted to the school when it was taken over by the State. To support his contention that cer- tain employes of the school are unfit for further duty, Mr. Jones, in his answer, cited their records, their ex- perience and their attitudes. Mr. Jones stated that some of the employes in question were physically disabled or too old. "Case Histories" Cited "Case histories" of some of the insti- tution's employes were cited by the commissioner. One cottage master, he said, "settles all disciplinary problems himself by using the switch unhesi- tatingly and does not care whether he punishes the right boy." Another cottage master, Mr. Jones added, "handles disciplinary problems himself, chiefly by fear and force. This man . . . would probably be better adapted to his former grade of night watchman." title: STILL IN NEED OF REFORM
full_text: STILL IN NEED OF REFORM The transfer of Cheltenham to the State was undertaken largely with the idea that it would put an end to major abuses. The school had been a target of criticism for years. It was thought that if the State took the institution over it would be possible quickly to transform it into a reasonably effective agency for dealing with young Negroes gone wrong. Now, nearly a year and a half from the time the institution came under the ægis of the State, it is still necessary for the Employ- ment Commissioner to bring forward charges growing out of the alleged beating of a 14- year-old boy accused of stealing a few cigars. If the commissioner's charges are even par- tially true, the conclusion is inescapable that the benefits which were expected to flow from the State's assumption of responsibility have not materialized. If such a thing as he de- scribes can still happen at Cheltenham, the institution is still far from being the sort of place to which the State can send delinquent Negro boys in the hope of making them over and turning them out as decent citizens. The trouble seems to lie in the fact that, when the State took the school over, it was persuaded also to take its employés into the merit system without examination. When the Employment Commissioner held exami- nations for purposes of classification, he found that large numbers of those on the pay rolls at Cheltenham could not come up even to the minimum requirements of the merit sys- tem. He refused to classify them, or to ap- prove pay rolls on which these employés were listed. The Cheltenham board, however, which had also been taken over by the State, backed up the employés, and the case is still in the courts. RIDGELY DIES AT FAMILY HOME Former Executive Of Black & Decker Manufacturing Firm Was 85 Served As Director Of Cock- eysville National Bank Benjamin Talbott Ridgely, former vice-president of the Black and Decker Manufacturing Company and well-known Baltimore county farmer, died yesterday at his home, Barrett's Delight, near Towson. He was 85. Funeral services will be held at 1 P. M. tomorrow at the home. Burial will be in the family cemetery. A member of the old Talbott and Ridgely families, he was the son of Dr. Benjamin Rush Ridgely and Mrs. Catherine Todd Ridgely. The Ridgely farm has been in the family more than 200 years. Was Bank Director Besides taking an active interest in farming. Mr. Ridgely was a director of the Cockeysville National Bank and a director and vice-president of the Black and Decker Manufacturing Company at Towson. Surviving members of the family are his wife, Mrs. Elizabeth S. C. Talbott Ridgely; two daughters, Mrs. James T. Arrel, of Poland, Ohio, and Mrs. S. Duncan Black, of Towson; two sons, Neville R., of Towson, and Herbert W. Ridgely, of Atlanta; fifteen grand- children and six great grandchildren. Special Board Convenes On Cheltenham Post To Function In Selection Of New Superintendent For School For Boys The State's three-year attempt to smooth out the operations of the Chel- tenham School for Boys entered a final phase yesterday when a special board convened to review applications for the Cheltenham superintendency. The board was appointed by Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commis- sioner, to review the applications and prepare and conduct the merit system examinations. Fifty-one persons have applied for the post, vacated when Superintendent B. B. Sunderland resigned. When the new superintendent is named, Mr. Sunderland will return to his former post as chief parole officer of the Southern Maryland Negro Reformatory. title: NICE DENISE ROBERTS STORY ON CHELTENHAM: INSISTS BOARD WAS CONSULTED ABOUT MOVE FOR STATE CONTROL CLAIMS CHAIRMAN WAS "MISTAKEN" REFERS TO CONFERENCE ON ACQUISITION OF COLORED BOYS' REFORMATORY
full_text: NICE DENIES ROBERTS STORY ON CHELTENHAM Insists Board Was Con- sulted About Move For State Control CLAIMS CHAIRMAN WAS "MISTAKEN" Refers To Conference On Acquisition Of Colored Boys' Reformatory Governor Nice yesterday said that the board of directors of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Cheltenham, had been consulted when legislation looking to the acquisition of the reformatory was being dis- cussed at the last General Assembly. The Governor made this statement after Robert F. Roberts, president of the board, said "we have not been asked to state our position" on a move by the State to take over the operation of the institution. Roberts "Mistaken" "Mr. Roberts is entirely mistaken," the Governor said. "A number of the members of the board were in consul- tation with me and Thomas J. S. Wax- ter, director of the Municipal Depart- ment of Welfare, and Sidney Hol- lander, member of the Board of State Aid and Charities, during the last ses- sion of the Legislature. "The conference was held before legislation which would have set up the reformatory as a State institution (Continued on Page 15, Column 4) Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission. (Continued from Page 26) was introduced. The legislation after- ward was killed as the result of ac- tivities on the part of some members of the board. Situation Weighed "The situation as it exists was gone into very thoroughly and the con- sensus of the members present-and more than half were present-was to the effect that the board would neither approve or disapprove legislation looking to State control. "My personal reaction and memory is that the board was very decidedly of the opinion that the State should take over the institution. "And I am wondering how many visits, if any, Mr. Roberts has made to that institution since he has been president or even a member of the board." Mr. Roberts, before leaving for a three-month trip to the West Coast, said that in his opinion the "board will vote against turning the home over to the State." The last session of the Legislature passed a bill empowering the State to accept the property of Cheltenham if offered by the board of that institu- tion. A companion measure, which would have set up the home as a State institution, failed to pass. Mr. Waxter, while Juvenile Court judge, made an investigation of the institution and recommended at that time that Cheltenham be taken over by the State. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, yesterday opened the way for a court test of his right to re- fuse to accept twenty-six employes of the Cheltenham School, for Boys in the State classified service. title: SCHOOL EMPLOYES WIN FIGHT FOR JOBS: APPEALS COURT RULES JONES MUST CERTIFY 26 HE HELD UNFIT AT CHELTENHAM DECISION DOES NOT GRANT ASSEMBLY BLANKET MERIT SVSTEM POWER, HOWEVER
full_text: SCHOOL EMPLOYES WIN FIGHT FOR JOBS Appeals Court Rules Jones Must Certify 26 He Held Unfit At Cheltenham Decision Does Not Grant Assembly Blanket Merit System Power, However [By the Associated Press] Annapolis, Jan. 12-Twenty-six em- ployes of the Cheltenham School for Boys, held unfit for Merit System classification by Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, must be retained and paid by the State, the Court of Appeals ruled today. The Appeals Court upheld a Balti- more decision granting the house of reformation a writ of mandamus com- pelling Mr. Jones to certify the pay rolls containing the names of the al legedly unfit employes. Mr. Jones had refused to certify the pay rolls. The case arose from the ceding of the $400,000 house of reformation prop- erty, embracing 1,200 acres in Prince George's county, to the State for use as the Cheltenham School for Delin- quent Colored Boys. Provisions Of Law The 1937 Legislature passed enabling legislation to permit the transfer and accepted the specific condition laid down by the house of reformation that all employes should be retained in their posts after the deal. The bill also provided that successors to the present employes should be filled from Merit System eligible lists. Mr. Jones, soon after the trans- fer, held tests and found twenty-six employes unfit for classification and ordered their discharge. The house of meformation had retained its corpо- rate entity and $30,000 in funds at the time of the transfer, and promptly brought suit to compel retention of the employes ard payment of their sal- aries by the State, under the terms of the transfer agreement. When the Baltimore court granted the writ coupelling payment, it was for a time feared that a ruling ad- verse to Mr. Jones by the appellate court would open the way to blanket _nclusion of State employes now out- side the Merit System in the system by legislative enactment.. Rights Are Limited The decision today does not grant he Legislature wholesale rights to decree inclusion of any present em.. ploye under the Merit System. The court held that the house of reforma- Lion employes were beneficiaries of special legislation which was valid because of the great benefit accruing (Continued on Page 5, Column 6) (Continued from Page 22) to the Stat: through acquiring the $100,000 property. The principle of special legislation was frowned on, but the court held that the benefits to the State at large in the transaction made the act meri- torious. A case in Baltimore in which a rail- way system was granted freedom from taxes for two years in return for future tax concessions by the company which were greatly to the city's advantage was cited in the opinion as a type of specialized legis- lation comparable to the House of Reformation case because of the ulti- mate public good. Mr. Jones tonight said he would not comment on the case until after he had studied the appellate court's opinion. In another case decided today the conviction of two persons on charges of operating a bookmaking establish- ment within a block of the District of Columbia line was reversed by the court. Evidence in this case had been Jobtained by wire-tapping. t- Joseph J. Rowan and Eleanor E. Rowan were convicted by the M gomery County Court on charges of operating and maintaining a hand- book betting establishment in Takoma Park. on They appealed the conviction grounds that Sergt. Theodore F. Vol- ten, of the Montgomery county police, had engaged a telephone company maintenance man to tap the wires of the three telephones in the Rowan home. The appellate court held that the evidence which convicted the pair, Mrs. Rowan on two counts and Rowan lon nine, was inadmissible, as Sergt. Volten and his aides were unable posi- tively to identify the voices answering the Rowan telephones as belonging to the defendants, although the tele- phone listed to their home was regu- laraj answered. The court inferred that wire-tapp: ig evidence, provided the speaker was properly identified, might be admis- sible. A new trial was ordered for the Rowans. In still another case Frederick county was the loser in a suit to com- pel Alfred W. Gaver, supervisor of assessments, to repay $864 alleged over- payment in salary over a four-year period. The appellate court reversed a Frederick Circuit Court award to the county. :

title: ASSAIL CONDITIONS AT 2 INSTITUTIONS: THREE DELEGATES REPORT STATE CORRECTIONAL SCHOOLS ARE "VICIOUSLY INADEQUATE" MARYLAND TRAINING AND CHELTENHAM AMONG 5 INVESTIGATED BY GROUP
full_text: ASSAIL CONDITIONS AT 2 INSTITUTIONS Three Delegates Report State Correctional Schools Are "Viciously Inadequate" Maryland Training And Cheltenham Among 5 In- vestigated By Group Asserting that conditions in two of five of Maryland's correctional insti- tutions are "deplorable" and "viciously inadequate," and that remedial meas- ures should be taken in two others, William Heinekamp, of the House of Delegates (Fifth district), yesterday released the report of a survey he and three colleagues have made. Associated with Mr. Heinekamp in the survey, made for several months on their own initiative, were Edward A. Freburger (Sixth district), John T. Booth (First district) and Charles F. Argabright (Fifth district). Criticized severely in a statement issued by Mr. Heinekamp were the Maryland Training School for Boys and the Cheltenham School for Boys. Remedial steps to correct certain con- ditions were recommended for the Rosewood Training School for Girls Land the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls. The Montrose School for Girls was lauded. Recalls Juvenile Court's Action Mr. Heinekamp recalled that last week H. Hamilton Hackney, chief magistrate of the Juvenile Court, told the Assembly Club, consisting of members of the General Assembly, that the court was compelled to send southful offenders back on the streets because there is no room in correc- tional institutions for them Reports on mental and tubercular institutions which also were inspected by the Delegates are now being com- piled, Mr. Heinekamp said. The sur- veys were made, he added, to acquaint the legislators with conditions prevail- ing in the institutions so they could discuss intelligently their budgets when they are submitted at the next session of the General Assembly. At the Maryland Training School for Boys, the statement said, dormi- tories are overcrowded, facilities for recreation are limited, and food is so poor it is not touched by many boys. Yet, the statement said, the school has the highest food appropriation of any of the five schools. The boys, 11 was added, are living under very un- satisfactory conditions. Reports Fire Escapes Inadequate The statement said conditions at Cheltenham, where fire escapes are inadequate, are similar. "Many boys were barefoot on November 19." Boys complained of being beaten with a rubber hose. Kitchen facilities for storage and preparation of food were condeinned and "lots of things were found in the soup. Vegetables were full of sand, dirt and worms, and no sugar was used at meals," the state- ment added. Dormitories without night super- vision were reported at the Marylanıl Training School for Colored Girls Morale here appeared good At Rose- wood, the statement explained, "an infirmary constructed two years ago is complete with all the necessary hospital equipment ready for use, but as there were no funds provided in the 1939 budget for personnel, this modern hospital remains useless." Dormitories at the school are overcrowded, the report said. title: AT LONG LAST
full_text: G LAST After many months of negotiations between Mr. Morris Rome, for the State of Maryland, and Messrs. Enoch Harlan and W. Hanford Magruder, for the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, a deed to that insti- tution in the name of the State has been filed at Marlboro, Prince George's county, and the institution emerges under full State control as the, Cheltenham School for Boys. This is the culmination of a long campaign to secure State control over Cheltenham. Last January the Legislature passed a bill author- izing the State to take over the reformatory, and negotiations have been in progress since that time to work out the details of the trans- fer. These have now been decided upon and title to Cheltenham passes to the State, as every competent authority on such matters has advised for years. The men representing both parties to the transaction, including State Budget Director W. H. Blakeman, who worked out many of the financial details, deserve the gratitude of the people of the State for their patience and hard work in this excellent enterprise. Chel- tenham, under the former management, was harshly criticized and, even if there had been no criticism of its administration, it is surely fitting that the State should exercise direct control over this institution. An unpleasant chapter in Maryland history may now be - considered closed and a new one, with the State of Maryland exercising its full respon- sibility, is now begun. EQUESTRIAN PROBLEM ▼ A few days ago the jockeys of Great Britain gave' a dinner to Steve Donoghue, who at 53 is retiring from the saddle to be- come a trainer. Steve, whom Lord Lonsdale described as the only jockey in England who has never been called before the stewards for infractions of the rules of his trade, ex- plained in the course of his remarks at the dinner that one of the best horses he ever rode was Brown Jack, who won the Queen Alexandria Stakes at Ascot six years run- ning. He added that the owner of Brown Jack had rigged up a radio in the horse's stall so that Brown Jack could hear Steve's broad- cast tribute. "I can't see you, my beauty," concluded Steve, but "come on, Jack!" All this gives an idea of how the English feel about horses, but it also raises the point of the manner of address to a horse by his rider in the course of a race. With a horse named Brown Jack there is no problem. "Come on, Jack!" is the obvious formula. But how could a jockey be expected to shout, "Come on, Roentgenologist!" or "Come on, Napper Tandy!" or "Come on, Holluschickiet" or even "Come on, Eran de Persel" The namers of thoroughbreds seem as merciless on the riders as on the spectators, whose pronunciations of the names of racers have become almost another language. What this country needs is more horses named Jack. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: CHELTENHAM SECURITY UNIT TO BE RUSHED: TEMPORARY PLACE TO BE PROVIDED TO HANDLE MORE DIFFICULT BOYS
full_text: CHELTENHAM SECURITY UNIT TO BE RUSHED Temporary Place To Be Provided To Handle More Difficult Boys Immediate action will be taken to provide a temporary security unit at the Cheltenham School, the Rev. F. Reid Isaac, president of the board of managers of the institu- tion for Negro boys, announced yes- terday, following a meeting of the board.. At the same time the Rev. Mr. Isaac announced acceptance of the resignation of Royal A. B. Crump- superintendent since September, 1944-from the superintendency of the school. He had been asked by the board to remain, but insisted last week on immediate action on his resigna- tion, submitted in June. H. R. Harris, recently named as- sistant superintendent, was named acting superintendent. More Runaways Lately Yesterday's decision by the board to remodel one of the existing buildings at the institution for the housing of difficult offenders was based on a "larger number of run- aways recently," the Rev. Mr. Isaac said. He explained that the board had been working on the problem for several weeks, and that it had been decided the need for a building pro- viding more effective custody had to be filed immediately without waiting for construction of the per- manent security unit outlined in postwar plans for the school. "The school has been getting itself in shape to care for boys in the older group, from 16 to 18, who must be admitted under new regulations," he said. 1 Many Defectives There "Also, we still have a good many defectives." He said the building to be con- verted will provide complete segre- gation of its inmates from the "open" program of the rest of the school. Facilities and program for school- ing'and recreation will be worked out later, he said, pointing out that protection of the community from the runaways was the pressing problem. Meanwhile, the board of mana- gers of the Maryland Training School for Boys continued its con- sideration of the question of a suc- cessor to James A. Pratt, superin- tendent, whose resignation has been before the board for several months. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: 51 PERSONS SEEK CHELTENHAM POST Tones Names Special Ex- aminers To Hold Test To Fill Superintendency Employment Commissioner Hopes To Have Eligible List This Month Harry C. Jones, state employment commissioner, announced he had ap- pointed a special board of examiners Lo review applications and prepare and conduct a test for the superintendency of the Cheltenham School for Boys. The examination is necessary to fill vacancy created by the resignation of B. B. Sunderland. Mr. Sunderland, when a new superintendent is named, will return to his former post as chief parole officer of the institution. Advertised Position Commissioner Jones said the position had been advertised freely over a sixty-day period and that institutions similar to the Southern Maryland Negro reformatory had been canvassed for available applicants. Fifty-one persons subsequently filed applications. The examining board which will handle the reviewing and testing will consist of Mr. Jones, Dr. Thomas J. Pullen, assistant State superintendent of education, and Paul T. Beisser, executive secretary of the Henry Wat- son Children's Aid Society and a mem- ber of the Governor's commission on juvenile delinquency.
