title: Private School Meeting: Baltimore Association Holding Annual Gathering Thursday At Polytechnic Institute Dr. Fritz Redl, Austrian Psychologist, To Talk On "New Insights Into Adolescence"
full_text: Private School Meeting Baltimore Association Holding Annual Gath- ering Thursday At Poly- technic Institute Dr. Fritz Redl, Austrian Psychologist, To Talk On "New Insights Into Adolescence" T HE Baltimore Private School As- sociation, composed of nineteen private schools in and around Balti- more, will hold its annual open meet- ing Thursday at the Polytechnic In- stitute on East North avenue. Co- operating with the association in this meeting are the public schools, the various social and welfare agencies of the city and the museums. Believing that interesting and valua- ble experimental and research work has recently been done in the study of adolescents, the group has asked Dr. Fritz Redl, Austrian psychologist, to be the guest speaker at the meet- ing. Dr. Redl's topic will be "New In- sights Into Adolescence." Regional Conference The Baltimore meeting is prelimi- nary to the Middle States' Regional Conference of the Progressive Educa- tion Society, which is slated to be held Friday and Saturday at the Hotel May- flower, Washington, D. C. This confer- ence will continue the discussion of various phases of adolescence. Following eleven years of teaching in the Vienna public high schools, Dr. Redl became head of the psychological advisory clinics of the schools. While in Vienna he lectured at the University of Vienna on techniques of child guid- ance work, and only recently was a speaker at the two conferences of the New Education Fellowship-the Dutch Regional Conference and the World Conference at Cheltenham, England. Studying Adolescents Of late he has been working with Dr. Caroline Zachry on the committee on the study of adolescents. Dr. Redl has written extensively for scientific publications, for encyclopedias and is the author of two psychology books. The Baltimore Private School Asso- ciation, which was formed some years ago to promote better understanding among the schools and to encourage meetings at which both parents and educators could discuss those prob- lems in which they were both inter- ested, has brought to Baltimore at various times a number of outstand- ing figures in the educational world to lead its discussions. Donald Goodrich, of Calvert School, is president of the association. Other officers are: Louis Lamborn, McDonogh School, vice-president: Miss Agnes Elcock Greenwood, recording secre- tary; Edwin Zavitz, Friends, corre- sponding secretary, and Duncan McCulloch, Oldfields, treasurer. The committee in charge of Thurs- day's meetings is composed of Mr. Zavitz, Frederick A. Hahn, Boys' Latin, and Miss Elizabeth Jane Thorington, Bryn Mawr. title: King Tobacco again Seeks his Crown: BUMPER CROP AND BUMPER PRICES DAZE SOUTHERN MARYLAND
full_text: King Tobacco again Seeks his Crown SOUTHERN MARYLAND TOBACCO ROLLING INTO THE BALTIMORE WAREHOUSE Its progress from field to market is illustrated in today's Photogravure Section BUMPER CROP AND BUMPER PRICES DAZE SOUTHERN MARYLAND by MARK S. WATSON FOR all their beauty of natural scenery and of ancient manor houses, for all the allurement of their traditions of close to three centuries, for all the glory of their old families as highly satisfactory ancestors, the Five Counties of Southern Maryland. have been in a state of depression a good part of the time since the Civil War. Liberation of slaves had made tobacco growing enormously difficult. Prices for such tobacco as was grown and cured had been miserably low. Fine old mansions could not be kept up by impoverished purses and had fallen to ruin. Sons and daughters had moved away as rapidly as they could scamper out from so gloomy a neighborhood. Land had been left idle so that once trim fields were a tangle of thorns and weeds. Now and then a whole village had been depopulated, and its gutted dwellings left to the field animals or the buzzards or any other adventurer who chose to dally in them. But if anybody thinks that Southern Mary- land is anybody's poor relation in 1931 let him take a ride through the Five Counties more particularly through the sections where the tobacco plantations are in harvest. For 1931 is another year and Southern Maryland is rubbing its eyes in amazement over what looks to many of the growers like a return of the "good old days" that had ceased to exist save in memory and in the words of songs which accompanied an old-fashion hoc-down. NEW TOBACCO BARNS are being erected-the first that many of the plantations have put jup in decades. Old barns are being repaired, their tottering legs braced, their roofs patched, so that they may return to useful- ness in housing the biggest and best tobacco crop in the memory of most growers. Last year's sparse crop (it takes roughly a year and a half to grow and cure and market a crop) is commanding prices which twenty years ago would have sounded to anyone from the Five Counties like a mid-summer night's dream of 1850 when, one gathers, everybody was prosperous and deservedly so. Even a few bills are being paid-and that is a dazzling sight for crossroads merchants who carried their old neighbors through the 1930 drought. That disaster greatly reduced the money crop and the little garden crops as well and, coupled with the hard times gen- erally, caused most business to be done on a credit basis, and a very poor credit basis at that. Prosperity has not exactly rushed over the countryside, to be sure, but there is a livelier suggestion of it than has been seen in a long time-and this in a section of Maryland which had been immersed in economic gloom for years, and in a season when almost every other agricultural section of the country is in complete despond. They may be burning corn in Nebraska and feeding wheat to the hogs in bleeding Kansas, but from the Severn to the Potomac great heads of green tobacco are being hustled to the drying racks and on to the barns as rapidly as shrewd Mary- land eyes determine the crop is ready for cutting. AND WHY NOT, when first quality Maryland tobacco is selling as high as 55 cents a pound in the leaf, with the average running around 30 cents a pound-for the average includes, of course, the poor-quality stuff, which sells as low as 6 cents a pound right now. But if 30 cents should prove a fair average, bear in mind that this is 5 cents better than the average since the World War, and at least twice as much as it was before the World War got under way, with highly interesting developments for the Maryland tobacco grower. For years after the Civil War, there was only a beggars' market for prime tobacco from this section. Judge W. Mitchell Digges recalls that when he came home from college to Charles county, prime tobacco sold from his father's plantation for 6 cents. With tobacco the only important crop in that sec- tion it is easy to understand the dismay over how they were "gwine to keep 'em down on the farm." The wonder is that any of them stayed. The transformation in Southern Mary- land which the World War initiated is worth more than passing mention, for it involves a quality of the Five Counties' tobacco which makes it unique among the many varieties of the weed which America produces. It is the quality which makes prime Maryland leaf to- day more valuable per pound than the larger crops of Virginia and North Carolina or the vast crop of Kentucky burley (Kentucky produces a dozen times as large a poundage as Maryland, indeed almost as much as all the other States combined, but the price per pound is not high). The fine wrapper brand grown in Pennsylvania and Connecticut alone sells higher than prime Maryland; this is used solely for wrapping cigars. DURING THE DAYS of Southern Maryland's economic anguish there was no such price leadership. From Port Tobacco creek to the Severn the planters may have known they grew fine pipe tobacco (they never had any illusions about cigar possibilities), but they could not convince the market buyers that this was the case. The manufacturers wanted big acreages, which meant tremendous big concentrated crops, which meant that fac- tories could be built up in such areas with a minimum cost of transportation for the hogs- heads. Maryland had only 30,000 to 35,000 acres of good tobacco land, and this was not enough for them. So the factories put, up their buildings in Virginia and North Carolina and Kentucky. All they needed to import was some quick- burning tobacco to mix with their locally available crops, which, unfortunately, did not burn well enough to keep easily alight. This addition, naturally, they got from Turkey and Arabia, which long had supplied the English manufacturers with the essential quick-firing leaf for the English tobacco blends. As cig- arettes became more and more popular, in- creasing the demand for quick-burning leaf, more and more was imported from the Near East. AND THEN upon a booming cigarette market burst the World War. Consumption of ciga- rettes rose still more but the manufacturers were in a panic, for the war had cut off from the market every tobacco plantation in Tur- key and Arabia. Here was an unparalleled demand for cigarettes, factories eager to roll them, Virginia and Carolina components of the cigarette mixture ready in normal volume, but nothing to endow them with that quick- burning quality which was essential! In des- peration the manufacturers had their chemists experiment with every other tobacco they could find. They found Maryland tobacco, and their test showed that it had the precise quick-burning quality they were seeking. And it was cheaper than Near East leaf had been when it was available. 派 MARYLAND had been plodding sadly along for years selling its output where it could. More than half went to the French republic, which, as in royal and imperial days, still holds a tobacco monopoly, like its monopoly in matches. The frugal French bought in the cheapest market and that is why they came to Maryland, taking occasionally some poor stuff along with the good and making it all into cigarettes which many a disconsolate American has choked over despite the French tobacconist's assurance that it is "pure Mar-ee-lan." Of the remainder Germany had taken some and Italy a little, but Belgium (one of the largest per capita consumers in the world) and Holland had taken most- and the best grade; France never took the very best. Since that day Germany has ceased to buy here and Italy is doing its best with tobacco which the determined Signor Mus- solini is having grown on home soil, and even France through her chief buyer in America is complaining of late that Maryland is try- ing to work off poor quality on her, and threatening to stop buying here. So it is fortunate that Maryland tobacco has been discovered by America. The American cig- arette makers now buy about two-thirds of all Maryland raises. 业 IN 1916 Maryland tobacco prices jumped a good third, and have continued to show a mounting tendency, for even after the war the factories kept on with Maryland instead of returning to Turkey. Nineteen thirty-one is unusually high for two reasons: first, the 1930 crop (and it is that crop which is being mar- keted in 1931, of course) was very small ow- ing to the drought, and there is a resultant sharp demand for the small amount being of- Fered; second, the poorer quality has not been Coming into the market as liberally as usual and so price averages have been high. Generally speaking, the larger any crop the ower the price, of course. But this does not seem to be inevitable in the present case. There are growers who confidently declare that the unique tobacco of prime Southern Maryland can be used in still greater quanti- Lies to the advantage of the factories, and that with this the case the American market an absorb a much larger output from the Five Counties without depressing the price. Maybe. How much more could be grown in these counties is problematical, for there is noth- ing about the air of Southern Maryland, de- Hightful as it may be, which produces prime tobacco. It is a peculiar quality of the soil, and not all the soil at that, probably not more than a fifth of the whole area. Plenty of arable land there will produce excellent corn, but it does not produce true Southern Mary- land tobacco. Seed can be taken right out of Charles county and planted in Frederick or Montgomery county, where lately a good deal of tobacco has been grown, but even the first year's crop will not match Charles county tobacco and the third or fourth year's crop is very far from Southern Maryland standard. HERE is another oddity of that magic select soil. The seed is started in a clearing in a wood of white oaks "huckleberry soil," they call it and here it makes an ideal start, with no grass to choke it. But if left there it will not come to full fruition! It must be trans- planted into another kind of soil which gener- ations of experimentation have identified pretty closely. An old tobacco planter will tell you how he selects his tobacco land. He does not bother with chemical tests. He just looks for the area where locust, chestnut or sassafras has grown. There he sets out his plants, con- fident that they will find themselves at home. The very qualities of sandy loam which ap- peal to those trees appeal to the tobacco plant. Little else is needed in site selection, save that there must be proper drainage, for the plant does not like swampy soil. THERE HAS LONG BEEN a theory that South- ern Maryland planters burned out their soil by constant setting-out to tobacco. This does not seem to be borne out by study of the record. Judge Digges, whose great acreage on the uplands above Port Tobacco is a part of the original 6,000-acre Mitchell plantation, says that in the main the land is as good for tobacco as it ever was, and retains its virtue by a rotation of crops which early Mary- landers used and which their descendants em- ploy down to this day-one year of tobacco, one of grain, one of grass or clover, then a new cycle starting with tobacco. The same effect is being achieved by experimenters'. quick sowing of vetch as soon as the tobacco is cleared from the fields, and a plowing in of the vetch in time for the next spring's setting out of tobacco plants. When one sees magnificent stalks of to- bacco standing close to six feet, in land which has been so cultivated for nearly three cen- turies, it is hard to find basis for the theory of worn-out tobacco lands. There are plenty of acres in Southern Maryland which cannot be farmed, but they are not the 20 per cent. which was and is given over to tobacco. The good tobacco lands continue to turn out a hogshead (750 pounds) or more to the acre in normal years. This year they are doing better. The normal crop is around 35,000 hogsheads for the Five Counties; this year it should go well over 50,000. Why shouldn't Southern Marylanders look more cheerful than in many a year? Why shouldn't there be a grin on the face of the man driving his truckload of nine big hogs- heads or perhaps his little mule team with one hogshead into the tobacco warehouse in Baltimore? He's looking for a better price than he or his father or, perhaps, his un- lucky grandfather ever got. Why shouldn't the planter grin as he sends his cutters into the field where a bigger poundage is waiting for the knife than in many a year? * venture enough, as you can learn from any unhappy wretch who can see his whole labor of months completely undone in a few hours of hail, or wind, or grasshopper assault, or in a period too hot or too cold or too wet or too dry. The advantage that the grain grower or vegetable grower has is that he knows in the course of a few months whether he is wholly or only partly ruined. Not the tobacco planter. He takes a year and a half to trans- form his seed into dollars, and many a variety of pest he encounters on the way. His only ally is the tobacco plant itself, which has an almost unbelievable sturdiness-proving itself the "weed" which it has rightly been called. THIS IS THE PEAK of the tobacco year, of course, for the 1931 crop is being taken out of the fields at the very time that the 1930 crор, thoroughly cured and packed, is being rolled out of the barns and heaved up on a truck and sped for market. It is strange that in a community which owes its whole origin to tobacco culture, so little is known of the arts and mysteries of tobacco planting. City peo- ple are as unfamiliar with the stuff they smoke as they are with the stuff they eat- or drink, AS STATED, the planter searches out a spot in a white-oak wood where he can clear ade- quate space for his nursery, and there, in that favored soil, the surrounding trees will afford protection. Not the same spot each year, either, but always a different one, for reasons known only to the creator of plants and their mysteries. Here the land is broken and smoothed, and here in late January or early February the seed is sown, not in rows but broadcast-yet not "broadcast" as Mil- let's sturdy sower is pictured sowing his grain. For the tobacco seed is the smallest known to us, so infinitesimal as to make a celery seed seem gross. A single plant allowed to go to seed (which the planter permits only a few choice ones to do, that reproduction may be from his finest plants) will bear a million seeds, which ought to put it at the top of the vegetable kingdom for fertility. But each seed is nat- urally so tiny that only two tablespoonfuls are needed for sowing to capacity a nursery patch of 400 square yards! The only way this can be broadcast practically, therefore, is to thoroughly mix the two tablespoonfuls of seed with a peck or two of firmly powdered fer- tilizer, and then broadcast this diluted mix- ture over the allotted space, tread or roll it in lightly, and then let it alone. In March it is necessary to cover the young plants with a wide-meshed cotton cheesecloth, close enough to keep out the tobacco fly, which starts his maraudings then, wide enough to avoid weighting down the delicate plants. In May the space is thinned out so as to en- courage the strongest plants. In June they are transplated to the "locust-chestnut-sassa- fras soil" in even rows, a yard apart, and from then through July there is steady cul- tivating to keep down the rival weeds until the nicotine-bearing weeds can get their beight. August is a month mainly of watch- ful waiting, but at its end or in early Septem- ber starts the harvesting of the crop. There pest and his progeny, a long caterpillar, be- ween them can eat as much tobacco as an industrious office boy can smoke in a week. HARVESTING is not a job for an amateur. The expert watches the tobacco plants come to flower, and at the right time goes through his rows breaking off the flowers. Immediately there breaks out from the top of the maimed stalk a new growth of specially fine leaves which grow with extraordinary speed if the weather be precisely right. And three or four days later is the time to cut the field. That sounds easy. But perhaps instead of ideal weather the planter encounters drenching rains. If so, he cannot cut his crop. Yet the plant can and will grow with an exasperating genius for doing the wrong thing, and over each leaf will be put out a "sucker" which, to the city man, looks like a good cluster of new leaves but actually dries down to nothing at all and, worse yet, saps the strength which would have otherwise gone into the good leaves. And, too, the rain will spatter mud over the lower leaves which at best are "seconds," being inferior to the prime leaves which sprout from the middle of the stalk, and it will make them less valuable. When this un- seasonable rain stops, a crop of splendid promise may have deteriorated 20 per cent. in a matter of ten infuriating days. BUT EVEN RAINS will stop. And when they do, the planter sends his men out on the run, armed with a cutting knife as long as a sickel and heavier, but only slightly hooked. The stalk is cut close to the ground, and the felled plants gathered expeditiously by the next worker. Each plant he impales, near its thick pulpy base-very much like a corn- stalk-on a tobacco "stick" which only a greenhorn would confuse with any other stick. For the proper tobacco "stick," precisely four and a half feet long, has been rived from a chestnut log, the tool used in this process being a "fro," a long, heavy, crook-handled chisel which is driven into the log at the right point and twisted sharply, throwing out the squared stick precisely along the grain. One end of the "stick" then is sharpened, and over this sharpened end, to aid in impaling the tough stalks, the worker temporarily slips a wrought-metal spearhead. When on the "stick" are impaled at equal spaces four or five or six heads of tobacco, depending on their size, the metal spearhead is snatched off, to be placed on the next "stick" and go on doing its steady duty. The stout chestnut sticks, thus rived, will ground. Next the whole lot is collected-in Southern Maryland it is usually collected on mule-drawn cart and carried toward the Irying barns. Where space and weather per- nit, the "sticks" loaded with the tobacco stalks are laid across racks in the sun for a preliminary curing, but shortly, with or with- out the helpful sun curing, they go into the barns. NOW YOU UNDERSTAND why the stick is pre- cisely four and a half feet long, for the whole barn has been divided into lofty "rooms" precisely four feet wide reaching from floor to roof, and cross-divided into horizontal tiers (the true Southern Mary- lander calls them "tires") by a stout skeleton of beams and poles. When the barn is quite empty of tobacco the interior looks as though filled with a scaffolding all ready to be completed with planking which would create neat little cages four feet wide and five feet high and perhaps six to eight feet long. But no planking ever goes there. Instead the tobacco-loaded "sticks" are swiftly and accurately placed, horizontally, each end rest- ing on the proper beam, the stalk's stump up, the weight of the leaves holding them so that they will droop downward and will dry as flat as possible, Each compartment thus formed normally has a few inches of space between the tips of one set of leaves and the stalks of the tier immediately beneath. This space is needed, for the drying tobacco generates great heat and there must be currents of air or the too closely packed leaves will sweat and rot. The drying begins immediately, of course, and progresses at varying speed, depending on the weather, for Southern Maryland tobacco has to be cured by weathering, aided as it may be by the initial sun bath referred to. This is one of its unique qualities. The tobac- coes of Virginia or North Carolina (also those of Frederick and Montgomery) can be stripped from the stalk right in the field, and cured artificially and with great speed. When that is tried in St. Mary's or Calvert, Charles or Prince George's or Anne Arundel, the leaf crumbles away and is lost. It is strange that soil can so radically alter the whole constitution of a plant. BY NOVEMBER or December the drying is com- plete and, again watching the weather, which must be just right, the thrifty planter sets to work stripping the dry but flexible leaves from the stalk, keeping them whole and grad- ing them with practiced eye so that the four commercial grades are placed in four sepa- A TOBACCO BARN, BUILT IN 1778, NOW BEING REPAIRED TO HOLD THE 1931 CROP It stands on Judge Mitchell Digges' plantation, its wooden-pinned timbers still sturdy, its hand-rived shingles still shedding rain are no early or late varieties of tobacco, but the whole crop can be spread over a period of some weeks by a little ingenuity in the original planting, scattering the seed on two or three separate occasions so that one wave will have a proportionate lead on the others. All of this sounds fairly simple, and it is provided one has been alert to the peril of a later tobacco fly, a brawny brute with a body two inches long and a wingspread which look: to the planter as wide as an airplane's. Thi: last for decades; a sawed stick will hardly last a year. And that same stout old "fro," by the way, was used a century ago to rive out the enduring chestnut shingles which still shed rainwater from many a Southern Mary- land roof. It was a useful tool which is handled only by great deftness and no little strength. Three to five which grow nearest the ground ripen first and are gritty from the rains' spattering; they are of good value, light in weight, and very quick burning, but they are not prime, and so they are known to the trade as "sec- onds." There are three or four leaves at the very top, the so-called "tips" which of the whole marketable stalk are poorest in qual- Continued on next page ity. Next down on the stalk are perhaps three "dark" leaves which are only a little better for market. The first-quality leaves are the fifteen or twenty which sprout just below the "dark" leaves and above the "seconds." These are almost uniform in size and texture, weight and color, and even the unpracticed eye sees beauty in their rich, bright, light-saddle color. On a properly "made" crop they are not only by far the most valuable but, by a strange dispensation of nature, much the most plenti- ful, too. THE PLANTER does his stripping and grading, it was mentioned, when the weather is "right" as well as when the dried leaves are "in order." He can not do it in very dry weather or the leaves will crack and crumble; even moderately damp but excessively cold days will be hurtful. But moderately warm winter days with the air sufficiently moist are what he waits for. Happily, the work is such that he can do much or little at a time as suits his convenience. The leaves properly assorted, they are piled in neat little "bundles" of fif- teen, and a sixteenth leaf is twisted and tied about the stubs to hold the "bundle" to- gether. Then the bundles are piled in "bulks," still assorted in the four grades, and left there for a little more seasoning. The "sticks" re- tire from action, awaiting the next harvest. Not until August, normally, are these neatly arranged "bundles" touched again. It could be done earlier, to be sure, but the plantation hands are generally busy sowing and trans- planting and tending the new crop througlı spring and early summer, and not until Au- gust is there leisure for the final packing. Then the great hogsheads, also made on the farm, are brought to the barn. A skilled man, standing in the hogshead itself, takes the bundles as they are handed him and lays them in the bottom neatlý, stubs flush with the staves, leaf-tips toward the center. Two other men, also in the capacious hogshead, tread the bundles down as they are piled. When the cask is full and its contents trod down it is tilted on its side and further pres- sure applied with a winch which pushes an- other hogshead top against it. Then the top is nailed on, and at the planter's pleasure the hogsheads, weight three-eighths of a ton each,. are hustled off to the Baltimore warehouse. Three men can pack and "prize" fifteen to twenty hogsheads a day. 添 : THE SELLING PROCESS itself is much like that of grains, in that it is by sample. On the warehouse floor the hogshead is up-ended and by a derrick lifted free of its contents, which, well packed, keep their shape perfectly, standing on the floor like so many huge cakes. The inspector, walking about this extraordi- nary cake, with a little tugging pulls out three bundles from different parts, from them makes a selection of typical leaves, ties them into a new bundle, stamps it and the hogs- head from which the assortment is taken with identifying tags, and turns the sample over for examination by the commission men. One of the latter is allowed to take it to his place of business for exhibit to buyers. Here of course is a perilous policy. It is charged often enough that unscrupulous com- mission men stealthily pull out of the sam- ple bundle certain less-valuable leaves, so that the residue looks like undiluted prime quality, and sells the hogshead on the basis MUSICIANS, BY ELYSE LORD From Fine Prints of the Year 1930 (Minton, Balch & Co.) of that deceptive sample, with better profits to himself and the planter alike. Two efforts have been made to cure it. One in 1915 was through attempted legislation compelling the State inspector to keep the samples in his custody and compelling the commission men to bring their clients right to the guarded warehouse for their dickering. This failed. Now there is an attempt to band against commission men who are suspected of the fraud and refuse them business, so that the trade will clean itself up. The responsible commission men naturally are aiding. 业 THE STATE obviously has an interest in the reform, for.the good name of its output and the good faith of its inspection service. But it has a close financial interest as well, for under the inspection law the State is respon- sible for deception practiced under its pro- tection; if within ninety days a hogshead is proven inferior to the sample, claim can be made against the State itself. It is on this issue that M. Jarreville, the French agent, has lately made complaint, pointing out that not only have his clients been deceived but, owing to leisurely ocean freights, they have not discovered the decep- tion until the ninety days is over and so have been barred from the remedy at law. He has threatened to stop buying Maryland tobacco unless there is reform. If he carries out the threat, obviously Maryland would suffer seri- ously from the departure of a buyer who now takes about a third of the crop, including grades difficult to market in this country. TOBACCO'S HISTORY in the early colonies is pretty generally known. One of Columbus' companions, sent to explore Cuba, brought back word of the Carib Indians' addiction to the weed, which they smoked in pipes-indeed it was the name of the pipe, the tabaco, which actually gave its name to the weed itself in the Spaniard's lexicon. And a strange pipe it was, with two stems, one for each nostril, the Caribs taking smoke by the nasal route. A half century later the Spanish introduced the plant at home, and in 1558 Jean Nicot, French Minister to Portugal, sent samples of it and a description of its use to Queen Cath- erine de Medici in Paris; from his name comes the word nicotine, of course. It was in 1565 that Hawkins encountered the weed in Virginia and still later that Sir Ralph Lane sent a small shipment to Raleigh, who in- troduced Queen Bess herself to this strange American institution. It was culture of this new commodity, try where many a farmer could not grow cotton and would not grow his own vegetables. Hence, in 1624 (with more sense than the nation showed 200 years later) Virginia passed her "Two-Acre" act, requiring those who planted tobacco also to plant two acres of grain-and care for it so as to avert famine. Maryland did likewise, but was reluctant to join Virginia in the effort to cut down acreage so as to improve quality at the sacri- fice of quantity. The reasoning seems to have been that if the value per pound was raised the officials and the parsons (who got their pay in a fixed poundage) would get relatively a raise in pay and that thought was intoler- able! For years this strange obstinacy pre- vailed, but at long last in 1747 Maryland fol- lowed Virginia's lead, and tobacco planting again became profitable. Whether Maryland first got her tobacco from the local Indians or imported tested Vir- ginia seed is difficult to say definitely. We know that it was tried out almost everywhere in the Colonies, including the Eastern Shore, which grew tobacco until the Civil War but, with the depression which emancipation brought to the plantations, quickly shifted to more profitable enterprises. Latterly Talbot has experimented anew with tobacco, pro- ducing a very large leaf, but not planting any extended acreage. An Eastern Shoreman would be the last to admit it was because Talbot county could not produce tobacco as good as that raised across the Bay. THE VISITOR is struck by the few changes in methods as the centuries wear on. Little seems needed, but the University of Maryland is engaged in careful experimentation from year to year with soils and fertilizers and diseases, conducting some of its tests at Cheltenham, where there is an assured labor supply and adequate supervision of the physical work needed for the delicate tests and records. But in the main today's method is quite unchanged from the old days save in two respects. Machinery is now used to the ex- tent of employing a transplanting machine which saves a vast amount of time and effort and gains better results. The other is a fundamental difference from slavery days. For without slave labor it has not yet been found, practicable to farm the huge tracts of several hundred acres. Now half the tobacco is farmed by tenants, and often Negro tenants, on one-acre and two- acre tracts. Some day, no doubt, industry will move into the Five Counties and recreate great suddenly become valuable throughout West-tracts, with regimented laborers who under ern Europe, that hastened the colonizing of America. WATSON FOR all their beauty of natural scenery and of ancient manor houses, for all the allurement of their traditions of close to three centuries, for all the glory of their old families as highly satisfactory ancestors, the Five Counties of Southern Maryland. have been in a state of depression a good part of the time since the Civil War. Liberation of slaves had made tobacco growing enormously difficult. Prices for such tobacco as was grown and cured had been miserably low. Fine old mansions could not be kept up by impoverished purses and had fallen to ruin. Sons and daughters had moved away as rapidly as they could scamper out from so gloomy a neighborhood. Land had been left idle so that once trim fields were a tangle of thorns and weeds. Now and then a whole village had been depopulated, and its gutted dwellings left to the field animals or the buzzards or any other adventurer who chose to dally in them. But if anybody thinks that Southern Mary- land is anybody's poor relation in 1931 let him take a ride through the Five Counties more particularly through the sections where the tobacco plantations are in harvest. For 1931 is another year and Southern Maryland is rubbing its eyes in amazement over what looks to many of the growers like a return of the "good old days" that had ceased to exist save in memory and in the words of songs which accompanied an old-fashion hoc-down. NEW TOBACCO BARNS are being erected-the first that many of the plantations have put jup in decades. Old barns are being repaired, their tottering legs braced, their roofs patched, so that they may return to useful- ness in housing the biggest and best tobacco crop in the memory of most growers. Last year's sparse crop (it takes roughly a year and a half to grow and cure and market a crop) is commanding prices which twenty years ago would have sounded to anyone from the Five Counties like a mid-summer night's dream of 1850 when, one gathers, everybody was prosperous and deservedly so. Even a few bills are being paid-and that is a dazzling sight for crossroads merchants who carried their old neighbors through the 1930 drought. That disaster greatly reduced the money crop and the little garden crops as well and, coupled with the hard times gen- erally, caused most business to be done on a credit basis, and a very poor credit basis at that. Prosperity has not exactly rushed over the countryside, to be sure, but there is a livelier suggestion of it than has been seen in a long time-and this in a section of Maryland which had been immersed in economic gloom for years, and in a season when almost every other agricultural section of the country is in complete despond. They may be burning corn in Nebraska and feeding wheat to the hogs in bleeding Kansas, but from the Severn to the Potomac great heads of green tobacco are being hustled to the drying racks and on to the barns as rapidly as shrewd Mary- land eyes determine the crop is ready for cutting. AND WHY NOT, when first quality Maryland tobacco is selling as high as 55 cents a pound in the leaf, with the average running around 30 cents a pound-for the average includes, of course, the poor-quality stuff, which sells as low as 6 cents a pound right now. But if 30 cents should prove a fair average, bear in mind that this is 5 cents better than the average since the World War, and at least twice as much as it was before the World War got under way, with highly interesting developments for the Maryland tobacco grower. For years after the Civil War, there was only a beggars' market for prime tobacco from this section. Judge W. Mitchell Digges recalls that when he came home from college to Charles county, prime tobacco sold from his father's plantation for 6 cents. With tobacco the only important crop in that sec- tion it is easy to understand the dismay over how they were "gwine to keep 'em down on the farm." The wonder is that any of them stayed. The transformation in Southern Mary- land which the World War initiated is worth more than passing mention, for it involves a quality of the Five Counties' tobacco which makes it unique among the many varieties of the weed which America produces. It is the quality which makes prime Maryland leaf to- day more valuable per pound than the larger crops of Virginia and North Carolina or the vast crop of Kentucky burley (Kentucky produces a dozen times as large a poundage as Maryland, indeed almost as much as all the other States combined, but the price per pound is not high). The fine wrapper brand grown in Pennsylvania and Connecticut alone sells higher than prime Maryland; this is used solely for wrapping cigars. DURING THE DAYS of Southern Maryland's economic anguish there was no such price leadership. From Port Tobacco creek to the Severn the planters may have known they grew fine pipe tobacco (they never had any illusions about cigar possibilities), but they could not convince the market buyers that this was the case. The manufacturers wanted big acreages, which meant tremendous big concentrated crops, which meant that fac- tories could be built up in such areas with a minimum cost of transportation for the hogs- heads. Maryland had only 30,000 to 35,000 acres of good tobacco land, and this was not enough for them. So the factories put, up their buildings in Virginia and North Carolina and Kentucky. All they needed to import was some quick- burning tobacco to mix with their locally available crops, which, unfortunately, did not burn well enough to keep easily alight. This addition, naturally, they got from Turkey and Arabia, which long had supplied the English manufacturers with the essential quick-firing leaf for the English tobacco blends. As cig- arettes became more and more popular, in- creasing the demand for quick-burning leaf, more and more was imported from the Near East. AND THEN upon a booming cigarette market burst the World War. Consumption of ciga- rettes rose still more but the manufacturers were in a panic, for the war had cut off from the market every tobacco plantation in Tur- key and Arabia. Here was an unparalleled demand for cigarettes, factories eager to roll them, Virginia and Carolina components of the cigarette mixture ready in normal volume, but nothing to endow them with that quick- burning quality which was essential! In des- peration the manufacturers had their chemists experiment with every other tobacco they could find. They found Maryland tobacco, and their test showed that it had the precise quick-burning quality they were seeking. And it was cheaper than Near East leaf had been when it was available. 派 MARYLAND had been plodding sadly along for years selling its output where it could. More than half went to the French republic, which, as in royal and imperial days, still holds a tobacco monopoly, like its monopoly in matches. The frugal French bought in the cheapest market and that is why they came to Maryland, taking occasionally some poor stuff along with the good and making it all into cigarettes which many a disconsolate American has choked over despite the French tobacconist's assurance that it is "pure Mar-ee-lan." Of the remainder Germany had taken some and Italy a little, but Belgium (one of the largest per capita consumers in the world) and Holland had taken most- and the best grade; France never took the very best. Since that day Germany has ceased to buy here and Italy is doing its best with tobacco which the determined Signor Mus- solini is having grown on home soil, and even France through her chief buyer in America is complaining of late that Maryland is try- ing to work off poor quality on her, and threatening to stop buying here. So it is fortunate that Maryland tobacco has been discovered by America. The American cig- arette makers now buy about two-thirds of all Maryland raises. 业 IN 1916 Maryland tobacco prices jumped a good third, and have continued to show a mounting tendency, for even after the war the factories kept on with Maryland instead of returning to Turkey. Nineteen thirty-one is unusually high for two reasons: first, the 1930 crop (and it is that crop which is being mar- keted in 1931, of course) was very small ow- ing to the drought, and there is a resultant sharp demand for the small amount being of- Fered; second, the poorer quality has not been Coming into the market as liberally as usual and so price averages have been high. Generally speaking, the larger any crop the ower the price, of course. But this does not seem to be inevitable in the present case. There are growers who confidently declare that the unique tobacco of prime Southern Maryland can be used in still greater quanti- Lies to the advantage of the factories, and that with this the case the American market an absorb a much larger output from the Five Counties without depressing the price. Maybe. How much more could be grown in these counties is problematical, for there is noth- ing about the air of Southern Maryland, de- Hightful as it may be, which produces prime tobacco. It is a peculiar quality of the soil, and not all the soil at that, probably not more than a fifth of the whole area. Plenty of arable land there will produce excellent corn, but it does not produce true Southern Mary- land tobacco. Seed can be taken right out of Charles county and planted in Frederick or Montgomery county, where lately a good deal of tobacco has been grown, but even the first year's crop will not match Charles county tobacco and the third or fourth year's crop is very far from Southern Maryland standard. HERE is another oddity of that magic select soil. The seed is started in a clearing in a wood of white oaks "huckleberry soil," they call it and here it makes an ideal start, with no grass to choke it. But if left there it will not come to full fruition! It must be trans- planted into another kind of soil which gener- ations of experimentation have identified pretty closely. An old tobacco planter will tell you how he selects his tobacco land. He does not bother with chemical tests. He just looks for the area where locust, chestnut or sassafras has grown. There he sets out his plants, con- fident that they will find themselves at home. The very qualities of sandy loam which ap- peal to those trees appeal to the tobacco plant. Little else is needed in site selection, save that there must be proper drainage, for the plant does not like swampy soil. THERE HAS LONG BEEN a theory that South- ern Maryland planters burned out their soil by constant setting-out to tobacco. This does not seem to be borne out by study of the record. Judge Digges, whose great acreage on the uplands above Port Tobacco is a part of the original 6,000-acre Mitchell plantation, says that in the main the land is as good for tobacco as it ever was, and retains its virtue by a rotation of crops which early Mary- landers used and which their descendants em- ploy down to this day-one year of tobacco, one of grain, one of grass or clover, then a new cycle starting with tobacco. The same effect is being achieved by experimenters'. quick sowing of vetch as soon as the tobacco is cleared from the fields, and a plowing in of the vetch in time for the next spring's setting out of tobacco plants. When one sees magnificent stalks of to- bacco standing close to six feet, in land which has been so cultivated for nearly three cen- turies, it is hard to find basis for the theory of worn-out tobacco lands. There are plenty of acres in Southern Maryland which cannot be farmed, but they are not the 20 per cent. which was and is given over to tobacco. The good tobacco lands continue to turn out a hogshead (750 pounds) or more to the acre in normal years. This year they are doing better. The normal crop is around 35,000 hogsheads for the Five Counties; this year it should go well over 50,000. Why shouldn't Southern Marylanders look more cheerful than in many a year? Why shouldn't there be a grin on the face of the man driving his truckload of nine big hogs- heads or perhaps his little mule team with one hogshead into the tobacco warehouse in Baltimore? He's looking for a better price than he or his father or, perhaps, his un- lucky grandfather ever got. Why shouldn't the planter grin as he sends his cutters into the field where a bigger poundage is waiting for the knife than in many a year? * venture enough, as you can learn from any unhappy wretch who can see his whole labor of months completely undone in a few hours of hail, or wind, or grasshopper assault, or in a period too hot or too cold or too wet or too dry. The advantage that the grain grower or vegetable grower has is that he knows in the course of a few months whether he is wholly or only partly ruined. Not the tobacco planter. He takes a year and a half to trans- form his seed into dollars, and many a variety of pest he encounters on the way. His only ally is the tobacco plant itself, which has an almost unbelievable sturdiness-proving itself the "weed" which it has rightly been called. THIS IS THE PEAK of the tobacco year, of course, for the 1931 crop is being taken out of the fields at the very time that the 1930 crор, thoroughly cured and packed, is being rolled out of the barns and heaved up on a truck and sped for market. It is strange that in a community which owes its whole origin to tobacco culture, so little is known of the arts and mysteries of tobacco planting. City peo- ple are as unfamiliar with the stuff they smoke as they are with the stuff they eat- or drink, AS STATED, the planter searches out a spot in a white-oak wood where he can clear ade- quate space for his nursery, and there, in that favored soil, the surrounding trees will afford protection. Not the same spot each year, either, but always a different one, for reasons known only to the creator of plants and their mysteries. Here the land is broken and smoothed, and here in late January or early February the seed is sown, not in rows but broadcast-yet not "broadcast" as Mil- let's sturdy sower is pictured sowing his grain. For the tobacco seed is the smallest known to us, so infinitesimal as to make a celery seed seem gross. A single plant allowed to go to seed (which the planter permits only a few choice ones to do, that reproduction may be from his finest plants) will bear a million seeds, which ought to put it at the top of the vegetable kingdom for fertility. But each seed is nat- urally so tiny that only two tablespoonfuls are needed for sowing to capacity a nursery patch of 400 square yards! The only way this can be broadcast practically, therefore, is to thoroughly mix the two tablespoonfuls of seed with a peck or two of firmly powdered fer- tilizer, and then broadcast this diluted mix- ture over the allotted space, tread or roll it in lightly, and then let it alone. In March it is necessary to cover the young plants with a wide-meshed cotton cheesecloth, close enough to keep out the tobacco fly, which starts his maraudings then, wide enough to avoid weighting down the delicate plants. In May the space is thinned out so as to en- courage the strongest plants. In June they are transplated to the "locust-chestnut-sassa- fras soil" in even rows, a yard apart, and from then through July there is steady cul- tivating to keep down the rival weeds until the nicotine-bearing weeds can get their beight. August is a month mainly of watch- ful waiting, but at its end or in early Septem- ber starts the harvesting of the crop. There pest and his progeny, a long caterpillar, be- ween them can eat as much tobacco as an industrious office boy can smoke in a week. HARVESTING is not a job for an amateur. The expert watches the tobacco plants come to flower, and at the right time goes through his rows breaking off the flowers. Immediately there breaks out from the top of the maimed stalk a new growth of specially fine leaves which grow with extraordinary speed if the weather be precisely right. And three or four days later is the time to cut the field. That sounds easy. But perhaps instead of ideal weather the planter encounters drenching rains. If so, he cannot cut his crop. Yet the plant can and will grow with an exasperating genius for doing the wrong thing, and over each leaf will be put out a "sucker" which, to the city man, looks like a good cluster of new leaves but actually dries down to nothing at all and, worse yet, saps the strength which would have otherwise gone into the good leaves. And, too, the rain will spatter mud over the lower leaves which at best are "seconds," being inferior to the prime leaves which sprout from the middle of the stalk, and it will make them less valuable. When this un- seasonable rain stops, a crop of splendid promise may have deteriorated 20 per cent. in a matter of ten infuriating days. BUT EVEN RAINS will stop. And when they do, the planter sends his men out on the run, armed with a cutting knife as long as a sickel and heavier, but only slightly hooked. The stalk is cut close to the ground, and the felled plants gathered expeditiously by the next worker. Each plant he impales, near its thick pulpy base-very much like a corn- stalk-on a tobacco "stick" which only a greenhorn would confuse with any other stick. For the proper tobacco "stick," precisely four and a half feet long, has been rived from a chestnut log, the tool used in this process being a "fro," a long, heavy, crook-handled chisel which is driven into the log at the right point and twisted sharply, throwing out the squared stick precisely along the grain. One end of the "stick" then is sharpened, and over this sharpened end, to aid in impaling the tough stalks, the worker temporarily slips a wrought-metal spearhead. When on the "stick" are impaled at equal spaces four or five or six heads of tobacco, depending on their size, the metal spearhead is snatched off, to be placed on the next "stick" and go on doing its steady duty. The stout chestnut sticks, thus rived, will ground. Next the whole lot is collected-in Southern Maryland it is usually collected on mule-drawn cart and carried toward the Irying barns. Where space and weather per- nit, the "sticks" loaded with the tobacco stalks are laid across racks in the sun for a preliminary curing, but shortly, with or with- out the helpful sun curing, they go into the barns. NOW YOU UNDERSTAND why the stick is pre- cisely four and a half feet long, for the whole barn has been divided into lofty "rooms" precisely four feet wide reaching from floor to roof, and cross-divided into horizontal tiers (the true Southern Mary- lander calls them "tires") by a stout skeleton of beams and poles. When the barn is quite empty of tobacco the interior looks as though filled with a scaffolding all ready to be completed with planking which would create neat little cages four feet wide and five feet high and perhaps six to eight feet long. But no planking ever goes there. Instead the tobacco-loaded "sticks" are swiftly and accurately placed, horizontally, each end rest- ing on the proper beam, the stalk's stump up, the weight of the leaves holding them so that they will droop downward and will dry as flat as possible, Each compartment thus formed normally has a few inches of space between the tips of one set of leaves and the stalks of the tier immediately beneath. This space is needed, for the drying tobacco generates great heat and there must be currents of air or the too closely packed leaves will sweat and rot. The drying begins immediately, of course, and progresses at varying speed, depending on the weather, for Southern Maryland tobacco has to be cured by weathering, aided as it may be by the initial sun bath referred to. This is one of its unique qualities. The tobac- coes of Virginia or North Carolina (also those of Frederick and Montgomery) can be stripped from the stalk right in the field, and cured artificially and with great speed. When that is tried in St. Mary's or Calvert, Charles or Prince George's or Anne Arundel, the leaf crumbles away and is lost. It is strange that soil can so radically alter the whole constitution of a plant. BY NOVEMBER or December the drying is com- plete and, again watching the weather, which must be just right, the thrifty planter sets to work stripping the dry but flexible leaves from the stalk, keeping them whole and grad- ing them with practiced eye so that the four commercial grades are placed in four sepa- A TOBACCO BARN, BUILT IN 1778, NOW BEING REPAIRED TO HOLD THE 1931 CROP It stands on Judge Mitchell Digges' plantation, its wooden-pinned timbers still sturdy, its hand-rived shingles still shedding rain are no early or late varieties of tobacco, but the whole crop can be spread over a period of some weeks by a little ingenuity in the original planting, scattering the seed on two or three separate occasions so that one wave will have a proportionate lead on the others. All of this sounds fairly simple, and it is provided one has been alert to the peril of a later tobacco fly, a brawny brute with a body two inches long and a wingspread which look: to the planter as wide as an airplane's. Thi: last for decades; a sawed stick will hardly last a year. And that same stout old "fro," by the way, was used a century ago to rive out the enduring chestnut shingles which still shed rainwater from many a Southern Mary- land roof. It was a useful tool which is handled only by great deftness and no little strength. To return to the tobacco field; once the "stick" is loaded with its four or six stalks of tobacco, it is stacked with others on the Most farm or garden crops go through ad . . rate piles on the barn floor. The normal stalk has twenty-five or thirty leaves. Three to five which grow nearest the ground ripen first and are gritty from the rains' spattering; they are of good value, light in weight, and very quick burning, but they are not prime, and so they are known to the trade as "sec- onds." There are three or four leaves at the very top, the so-called "tips" which of the whole marketable stalk are poorest in qual- Continued on next page ity. Next down on the stalk are perhaps three "dark" leaves which are only a little better for market. The first-quality leaves are the fifteen or twenty which sprout just below the "dark" leaves and above the "seconds." These are almost uniform in size and texture, weight and color, and even the unpracticed eye sees beauty in their rich, bright, light-saddle color. On a properly "made" crop they are not only by far the most valuable but, by a strange dispensation of nature, much the most plenti- ful, too. THE PLANTER does his stripping and grading, it was mentioned, when the weather is "right" as well as when the dried leaves are "in order." He can not do it in very dry weather or the leaves will crack and crumble; even moderately damp but excessively cold days will be hurtful. But moderately warm winter days with the air sufficiently moist are what he waits for. Happily, the work is such that he can do much or little at a time as suits his convenience. The leaves properly assorted, they are piled in neat little "bundles" of fif- teen, and a sixteenth leaf is twisted and tied about the stubs to hold the "bundle" to- gether. Then the bundles are piled in "bulks," still assorted in the four grades, and left there for a little more seasoning. The "sticks" re- tire from action, awaiting the next harvest. Not until August, normally, are these neatly arranged "bundles" touched again. It could be done earlier, to be sure, but the plantation hands are generally busy sowing and trans- planting and tending the new crop througlı spring and early summer, and not until Au- gust is there leisure for the final packing. Then the great hogsheads, also made on the farm, are brought to the barn. A skilled man, standing in the hogshead itself, takes the bundles as they are handed him and lays them in the bottom neatlý, stubs flush with the staves, leaf-tips toward the center. Two other men, also in the capacious hogshead, tread the bundles down as they are piled. When the cask is full and its contents trod down it is tilted on its side and further pres- sure applied with a winch which pushes an- other hogshead top against it. Then the top is nailed on, and at the planter's pleasure the hogsheads, weight three-eighths of a ton each,. are hustled off to the Baltimore warehouse. Three men can pack and "prize" fifteen to twenty hogsheads a day. 添 : THE SELLING PROCESS itself is much like that of grains, in that it is by sample. On the warehouse floor the hogshead is up-ended and by a derrick lifted free of its contents, which, well packed, keep their shape perfectly, standing on the floor like so many huge cakes. The inspector, walking about this extraordi- nary cake, with a little tugging pulls out three bundles from different parts, from them makes a selection of typical leaves, ties them into a new bundle, stamps it and the hogs- head from which the assortment is taken with identifying tags, and turns the sample over for examination by the commission men. One of the latter is allowed to take it to his place of business for exhibit to buyers. Here of course is a perilous policy. It is charged often enough that unscrupulous com- mission men stealthily pull out of the sam- ple bundle certain less-valuable leaves, so that the residue looks like undiluted prime quality, and sells the hogshead on the basis MUSICIANS, BY ELYSE LORD From Fine Prints of the Year 1930 (Minton, Balch & Co.) of that deceptive sample, with better profits to himself and the planter alike. Two efforts have been made to cure it. One in 1915 was through attempted legislation compelling the State inspector to keep the samples in his custody and compelling the commission men to bring their clients right to the guarded warehouse for their dickering. This failed. Now there is an attempt to band against commission men who are suspected of the fraud and refuse them business, so that the trade will clean itself up. The responsible commission men naturally are aiding. 业 THE STATE obviously has an interest in the reform, for.the good name of its output and the good faith of its inspection service. But it has a close financial interest as well, for under the inspection law the State is respon- sible for deception practiced under its pro- tection; if within ninety days a hogshead is proven inferior to the sample, claim can be made against the State itself. It is on this issue that M. Jarreville, the French agent, has lately made complaint, pointing out that not only have his clients been deceived but, owing to leisurely ocean freights, they have not discovered the decep- tion until the ninety days is over and so have been barred from the remedy at law. He has threatened to stop buying Maryland tobacco unless there is reform. If he carries out the threat, obviously Maryland would suffer seri- ously from the departure of a buyer who now takes about a third of the crop, including grades difficult to market in this country. TOBACCO'S HISTORY in the early colonies is pretty generally known. One of Columbus' companions, sent to explore Cuba, brought back word of the Carib Indians' addiction to the weed, which they smoked in pipes-indeed it was the name of the pipe, the tabaco, which actually gave its name to the weed itself in the Spaniard's lexicon. And a strange pipe it was, with two stems, one for each nostril, the Caribs taking smoke by the nasal route. A half century later the Spanish introduced the plant at home, and in 1558 Jean Nicot, French Minister to Portugal, sent samples of it and a description of its use to Queen Cath- erine de Medici in Paris; from his name comes the word nicotine, of course. It was in 1565 that Hawkins encountered the weed in Virginia and still later that Sir Ralph Lane sent a small shipment to Raleigh, who in- troduced Queen Bess herself to this strange American institution. It was culture of this new commodity, try where many a farmer could not grow cotton and would not grow his own vegetables. Hence, in 1624 (with more sense than the nation showed 200 years later) Virginia passed her "Two-Acre" act, requiring those who planted tobacco also to plant two acres of grain-and care for it so as to avert famine. Maryland did likewise, but was reluctant to join Virginia in the effort to cut down acreage so as to improve quality at the sacri- fice of quantity. The reasoning seems to have been that if the value per pound was raised the officials and the parsons (who got their pay in a fixed poundage) would get relatively a raise in pay and that thought was intoler- able! For years this strange obstinacy pre- vailed, but at long last in 1747 Maryland fol- lowed Virginia's lead, and tobacco planting again became profitable. Whether Maryland first got her tobacco from the local Indians or imported tested Vir- ginia seed is difficult to say definitely. We know that it was tried out almost everywhere in the Colonies, including the Eastern Shore, which grew tobacco until the Civil War but, with the depression which emancipation brought to the plantations, quickly shifted to more profitable enterprises. Latterly Talbot has experimented anew with tobacco, pro- ducing a very large leaf, but not planting any extended acreage. An Eastern Shoreman would be the last to admit it was because Talbot county could not produce tobacco as good as that raised across the Bay. THE VISITOR is struck by the few changes in methods as the centuries wear on. Little seems needed, but the University of Maryland is engaged in careful experimentation from year to year with soils and fertilizers and diseases, conducting some of its tests at Cheltenham, where there is an assured labor supply and adequate supervision of the physical work needed for the delicate tests and records. But in the main today's method is quite unchanged from the old days save in two respects. Machinery is now used to the ex- tent of employing a transplanting machine which saves a vast amount of time and effort and gains better results. The other is a fundamental difference from slavery days. For without slave labor it has not yet been found, practicable to farm the huge tracts of several hundred acres. title: WILL TAKE OVER CHELTENHAM: WILL OPERATE AND MAINTAIN REFORM INSTITUTION TOR NEGRO BOYS AGREEMENT FOR NEW CONTROL ANNOUNCED BY MEMBER OF CHARITIES BOARD
full_text: STATE WILL TAKE OVER CHELTENHAM Will Operate And Maintain Reform Institution For Negro Boys Agreement For New Contro Announced By Member Of Charities Board Directors of the House of Reforma- tion for Colored Boys at Cheltenham have ratified an agreement by which control of the institution will be turned over to the State, Morris A. Rome, a member of the Board of State Aid and Charities, announced yesterday. Mr. Rome and Enoch Harlan, acting president of the institution, were ap- pointed Monday as a committee to "see what could be done toward hav- ing the State take control" of Chel- tenham. They held a conference Wednesday, drawing up a tentative agreement which, Mr. Rome said, was satisfactory to the Board of State Aid and Chari- ties. When the agreement was pre- sented to the Cheltenham board yes- terday, favorable action was taken. Mr. Rome said he had been informed by Mr. Harian, "Full Accord" "We are in full accord now," Mr. Rome said. "We have been trying to accomplish this for fifteen years, and now all that remains is the mechanical procedure of drafting a bill to be presented to the Legislature next month." Under the agreement, according to Mr. Rome, Cheltenham will turn over to the State its entire property, repre- senting an investment of approximate- ly $500,000, and the State will control and maintain the institution. Conditions at Cheltenham have been investigated a number of times by grand juries, committees of the Board of State Aid and Charities and other groups interested in social problems and the care taken of delinquent Negro youths. At a meeting of the Board of State Aid and Charities Monday, Governor Nice criticized conditions at the in- stitution as "deplorable," although he said an improvement had been noted in the last year or two. Privately Owned Cheltenham is a privately owned in- stitution supported by a State appro priation of $20,000 a year and payments of $180 a year from the counties anc city for each boy committed. Balti- more, it was said, contributes about $60,000 annually. The board of directors of Chelten- ham consists of a self-perpetuating group of twelve persons and four oth- ers, two appointed by the State and two by the city. At present, there are approximately 450 Negro boys confined there. A bill authorizing the State to take over control of the institution was introduced in the Legislature in 1935 but after being passed by the Senate it was defcated in the House of Dele- gates. At that time, Cheltenham di. rectors were opposed to relinquishing control. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: CHELTENHAM
full_text: CHELTENHAM It has long been the belief of those best able to pass judgment on the matter that Cheltenham should be taken over by the State. It is a privately owned institution for the reformation of colored boys of 10 to 21 years of age, the management of which has come under frequent criticism. It has been in receipt of $20,000 a year from the State, and the city contributes to it approximately $60,000 a year for support of boys sent there by the city. Those sent from the counties are charged $180 a year. At best, wise direction of the affairs of Cheltenham is a difficult job and under the present arrangement dissatisfaction with the way they are handled could not easily be avoided. The best solution of the problem is for the State to assume control of it. The reported assent of the managers of the insti- tution should eliminate the remaining obstacle | to that procedure. full_text: U. S. JUMPERS LEAD IN BRITON J. H. Whitney's Thomond II And Clark's Sorley Boy Run One, Two ANOTHER PLACES Dusty Foot Loses By Nose In Hunt Chase At Cheltenham [By the Associated Press] Cheltenham, Eng., March 2-Two American-owned horses finished first and second today in the Seven Springs Handicap Steeplechase over two and a half miles for £350. J. H. Whitney's Thomond II, at 7 to 1, won by. four lengths from J. Am- brose Clark's Sorley Boy, 100 to 6, and 16 others. Whitney's Grand National candidate, Dusty Foot, almost made it two in a row for the American sportsman in the National Hunt Chase over a four-mile course, but was nosed out by Major Noel Furlong's Robin A Tiptoe. Dusty Foot, the 7-to-4 favorite, ran a game race and staged a thrilling finish with Robin A Tiptoe. The English horse was at odds of 100 to 6. The two leaders were ten lengths in front of the third horse, Steady Johnny, owned by K. Urquhart. Ten horses of the 32 starters fell during the race. full_text: Largest Crowd Of Week Visits Automobile Show Many Line Up To Take Driver's Reaction Test-Exhibit Will Close At 11 O'Clock Tonight The week's largest crowd visited the Automobile Show at the Fifth Regi- ment Armory yesterday afternoon and evening. John E. Raine, manager of the show, said last night. Many persons in the throng lined up and awaited their turn to test their reactions to typical dangers confront- ing a driver on the highway. title: SOCIAL HELP SEEN IN FREUD'S THEORY: PSYCHIATRIST SAYS STUDY OF CONFLICT OF TENDENCIES WILL AID WORKERS DR. KARL MENNINGER ADDRESSES MEETING OF STATE CONFERENCE OF WELFARE
full_text: SOCIAL HELP SEEN IN FREUD'S THEORY Psychiatrist Says Study Of Conflict Of Tendencies Will Aid Workers Dr. Karl Menninger. Ad- dresses Meeting Of State Conference Of Welfare Sigmund Freud's theory of the con flict in every human being between constructive and destructive tenden- cies was extolled to 400 maryland so- cial workers last night as the means by which they might raise the stand- ards of mental hygiene. If you can think of your beings as interactions of these two, then you can work out a mental-hygiene program," Dr. Karl Menninger, author and head of a psychiatric clinic in Topeka, Kan., told a meeting of the Maryland State Conference of Social Welfare in the Lord Baltimore Hotel. : Some Do, Some Don't "Some master their destructive or aggressive inhibitions," he continued. "Some don't; and externally, they may become criminals; or internally, they may evidence it by suicide or drinking themselves to death'." Social workers, he said, could strive to help those who have little mastery over their inhibitions to sublimate their destructive energy into construc- tive goals. In this connection he men- tioned President Roosevelt as one who has applied "psychiatric principles to sociological problems" as no Presi- dent has ever done before. The Civilian Conservation Corps he called "a won- derful example" of this. Games And Dances Can Help "Play is another thing in which a psychiatric approach can help mental hygiene," Dr. Menninger declared. "The furtherance of games, socials and dances at institutions is a scientifically justified part of mental hygiene. They get rid of destructive energy and build up constructive energy," People often complain that pris- oners or those in mental instiutions are being "coddled" when they find such programs arranged, the psychia- trist said. Such feelings he called "foolish" and added that "it is about the only kind of mental hygiene I know much about." Dr. Menninger was introduced by Dr. George H. Preston, State Commis- sioner of Mental Hygiene. Governor O'Conor, delayed by another engage- ment, appeared at the end of the meeting and welcomed the social workers as engaged in work of "im- measurable benefit to the State." Building At School: Improvements in, personnel and buildings at Cheltenham School for Colored Boys are well under way, but the "very bad problem" presented by the mixture of feeble-minded and normal inmates is yet to be worked out, Dr. Thomas G. Pullen, Jr., said ina luncheon address to the con- ference. "The fundamental problem," con- tinued Dr. Pullen, who is assistant State superintendent of education, "is the wide range of intelligence among the boys. Sixty per cent. are feable- minded and only ten per cent. of su- perior intelligence. The position of supervisor of educa- f'on at the school, created under recommendations made by an in- vestigating group last August, will be filled shortly, Dr. Pullen said. Program Of Training Two cottages and a new auditorium- gymnasium have been constructed on the campus, the speaker added, and a program of inservice training for the school personnel nearly completed. In an address at one of the confer- ence's numerous seminars, Judge Charles W. Hoffman, of the Court of Domestic Relations, Cincinnati, Ohlo, branded as "the merest lies" stories that family life is disentegrating. "The family has withstood the rigors of modern civilization as well as any institution we know and cherish," he declared. "The best available figures indicate that only one marriage in one hundred and twenty-six is a failure." Incapacity To Work Among the afternoon seminars was one discussing the problem of inca- pacitation for work at which J. Douglas Coleman, executive director of the Associated Hospital Service of Baltimore, presided. There is no organized group, it was pointed out, to determine the exact status of a person's "incapability to work." 1 The main address today will be de- livered by Clarence Pickett, execu- tive secretary of the American-Friends Service, Philadelphia, who will dis- cuss "Personalizing the Objectives of the Social Worker." Officers of the conference include Mrs. Adolf Gutt- macher, president, and J. title: Another Superintendent For Cheltenham
full_text: Another Superintendent For Cheltenham Cheltenham School for Boys, which has been without a superintendent since last February, now has that vacancy filled by the appointment of Lawson Jerome Veney, for merly parole superintendent of a reforma tory school in Washington. A graduate of Howard University, Mr. Veney was selected for the Cheltenham post by the institution's latest board of managers and comes highly recommended. It would be difficult to name an incoming public official more in need of administrative ability, patience, luck and all the public sympathy he can muster. The Cheltenham School for Boys has been branded a disgrace to Maryland by succes- sive grand juries and official investigating groups for the past twenty years. title: New Sites Studied For Cheltenham
full_text: New Sites Studied For Cheltenham Two "very excellent" sites near Baltimore are under consideration for the projected new Chelten- ham School for Boys, Thomas B. Sprague, president of the Chelten- ham board of managers, said yes- terday. He announced that a special com- tee of the board was making a care- ful investgation of the tracts in- volved, and said the board had "every reason to hope for early suc- cess" in selecting a site. A fund of $1,500,000 has been set aside for construction of the proposed new training school for Negro youths. The present school is situated in Prince Georges county. Earlier attempts by the board to purchase property, first at Catons- ville and later near Mount Winans, were unsuccessful. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: ACCORD IS SOUGHT ON CHELTENHAM: EFFORTS RENEWED TO HAVE STATE TAKE OVER HOUSE OF REFORMATION INSTITUTION "BLOT ON GOOD NAME OF STATE," GOVERNOR NICE SAYS
full_text: ACCORD IS SOUGHT ON CHELTENHAM Efforts Renewed To Have ! State Take Over House Of Reformation f Institution "Blot On Good Name Of State," Governor Nice Says 1 Efforts to have the State take over control of the House of Reformation at Cheltenham were renewed yester- day with the appointment of a com- mittee of two to effect an agreement between the board of directors of the institution and the Board of State Aid and Charities. The action was taken after Enoch Harlan, vice-president and acting president of the Reformatory for Negro Boys, asked the Board of State Aid and Charities to include in its budget funds for certain repairs and additions at Cheltenham. Conditions Called Deplorable After a discussion, in which Gov- ernor Nice and members of the board criticized conditions at Cheltenham as "deplorable," Samuel E. Shanna- han, chairman of the board, appointed Morris A. Rome, a member of the board, and Mr. Harlan to act as a committee to "see what could be done toward having the State take control" of the institution. In addition to Mr. Harlan, repre- sentatives of sixteen other State-aided institutions were given hearings yes- terday on their requests for 1937-38 and 1938-39 allotments. Governor Nice recalled that the board of directors of Cheltenham two years ago "gave him to understand" that they favored the State taking con- trol of the institution, but that this stand later was reversed and as a result the Legislature failed to take Retion. The Governor asked Mr. Harian whether he could explain the present view of the board. Race Question Raised Mr. Harlan replied that the majority of the board was opposed to the change because of the possibility that the in- stitution would be placed under Negro management. Governor Nice replied that he had pledged himself to main- taining an equal balance between Negro and white officials and attend- ants. "I am sure," the Governor said, "that the Negro population of the State is not concerned so much with who is in control as to the improvement of con- ditions at Cheltenham. "There have been a series of reports from grand juries and committees and other investigating bodies, all criti cizing conditions at Cheltenham. 1 have come to the conclusion that the institution is a blot on the good name of the State."
