title: CHELTENHAM PLANS VIEWED: NEW SUPERINTENDENT TELLS OF HIS PROGRAM
full_text: CHELTENHAM PLANS VIEWED New Superintendent Tells Of His Program A system for diagnosis and classi fication of every person entering the institution will be set up at the Cheltenham School for Boys, ac cording to plans of the new super Intendent, Lawson Jerome Veney who will take over his duties on or before March 1. Mr. Veney said yesterday that the classification system he con templates would not require addi- tional personnel but would be done by members of the staff as part of their duties. Classification committees, con- sisting of the superintendent, his assistant and the supervisors, have been functioning in this manner for years in institutions under the Fed- eral Bureau of Prisons, he ex- plained. Wants All To Participate Mr. Veney does not believe in "a one-man school," but said his idea is for "the entire staff to par- ticipate on various levels. "There must be delegation of authority and responsibility." Even "the youngsters them- selves" would help with the plan- ning, he continued, adding that "sometimes types of programs that we think are suitable for a child from the adult point of view do not appeal to the youngsters' interests or fit his needs. "The program should be geared to fit the youngsters and the pro- grams have to be flexible" because different groups in the institution at different times have different needs. Diagnostic Procedures Under Mr. Veney's plan, diagnos tic procedures for every youth would include psychological and medical examinations as well as so cial workers' studies. Such a system, he said, "will in- sure the fact that the youngsters' problems are not only fully known to the staff but also understood by them." To give real help, "we have to know the conditions which contrib- uted toward making the child the kind of youngster who gets in trouble." As To Training Period He said that "for the average youngster, two weeks should give each staff member time to spend an hour or more with him to decide what can be done in the way of training and treatment." Thereafter. "each youngster would be seen by supervising per- sonnel at least every two months or at any other time when any of the personnel feel that the youngster's program is not satisfactory for him." If one program does not fit the child's need, he will be reclassified, it was said. Seeks Maximum Attention Mr. Veney said a good classifica- tion program aims at maximum pos- sible attention for each youngster and the establishment of proce- dures to insure adequate training. "Any institution that provides merely custodial care is doing noth- ing for the child but keeping him out of the community," he declared. "A training school that does not fulfill the functions of training will be a breeding ground for adult of- fenders." Mr. Veney said he could not comment on reports of bad condi- tions existing at Cheltenham be- cause "I have had no opportunity at all" to inspect the institution; that he had last visited the institu- tion two years ago "just for a few hours" and not for the purpose of inspecting it. Wants To Study Problem : "I understand there is a pretty big job to be done there," he con- tinued. "I want to study the pro- gram, personnel and budget, then move on from there to see what progress we can make to insure satisfactory training and treatment for the youngsters under our care." Mr. Veney said he did not know how soon his proposed classifica- tion program can be established. "Staff training for participation is necessary," he explained. "However, I'm sure it can be done." Asks More Advise He said he could not give more specific plans "until I've had a thor- ough opportunity to work with the staff at Cheltenham, learn the con- ditions under which they are work- ing and the handicaps, as well as the children and their needs. "One thing I'm sure of-Chel- tenham can be and will be the type of training school of which the people of Maryland can be proud, "It will take a great deal of time and work by the staff and the people in the community" to ac- complish this end, he added. Regarding public responsibility, he said "this is a publie agency, and the people in the community should be aware of developments." Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: OBJECTORS SOUGHT FOR FARM LABOR: PRISONERS ALSO URGED TO FILL SHORTAGE NEAR HAGERSTOWN WASHINGTON AND FREDERICK COUNTY MEN OFFER SUGGESTIONS
full_text: OBJECTORS SOUGHT FOR FARM LABOR Prisoners Also Urged To Fill Shortage Near Hagerstown Washington And Freder- ick County Men Offer Suggestions By GEORGE C. DORSCH Staff Correspondent of The Sun Hagerstown, Md., May 9-Farm- ers of the section of Maryland hugging the Mason-Dixon Line, where highways follow roller- coaster patterns over some of the richest land in the State, have a suggestion that they think might about solve their problems result- ing from the draft and from the grand exodus of farm labor to de- fense industries in this city and elsewhere. They would supplement the little labor available for planting and harvesting with conscientious ob- jectors and with inmates of penal institutions. Of course, there would always be the women of the farm to give a hand where and when they could. Insist This Should Be Done There have been no conferences among the farmers, nor have they called in any authorities for round- table talks on the subject. Yet the farmers of Washingtor county and those of the upper reaches of Fred- erick county, far from being de- jected, insist that this should be done. They point out that the Mary- land State Penal Farm at Roxbury is only a short distance from Ha- gerstown and that a great number of the Washington county farms are within easy transportation dis- tance of the institution. Moreover, some farmers further pointed out that coupled with a statement of Maryland officials recently that vegetables would be canned at the penal farm was the announcement that this would keep only a frac tion of the inmates busy. Objectors Trimming Fences It was recalled that some South- ern Maryland farmers had sug- gested that boys at Cheltenham (correctional institution for col- ored boys) be farmed out in that section where farm labor is at a premium. W. K. Marker, operator of a large farm near Ringgold, ex- pressed more eloquently and elabo- rately what other farmers said. "Look over there at a crowd of conscientious objectors trimming bushes and making fences when folks in the city are expecting us to grow and harvest the food they and the military will eat," he said. Has 90 Acres Of Land "There they are down there in the hollow a very fine place, too- when they ought to be working on the farms. Sure there are only about twenty-five of them here, but one man to a farm would be a great help. And some more could be taken from their camps and put to work where it would do (Continued on Page 17, Column 4) OBJECTORS MAY FARM Prisoners Are Also Sought To Fill Labor Shortage Near Hagerstown Washington And Frederick County Men Call Sugges- tions Solution : By GEORGE.C. DORSCH (Continued from Page 20) them the most good. It would at least increase their appetites." Mr. Marker has ninety acres of tillable land and only a son, who may be drafted, to help him. If the son is called, Mr. Marker will have nobody to help him get his wheat and other commodities in barns. The call for farm hands races through. Washington county as else- where in the State. | Horse Selling Revived From the slopes of South Moun- tain where extensive acres of raspe. berries stand like regiments of green- coated soldiers, to the State line there is a demand for the help which, it is asserted, has left to find work either at the Fairchild aviation plants outside Hagerstown or for employment at larger wages in, Baltimore, Washington, Edge- wood and Aberdeen. And, while the Washington county farmers are worrying what to do, there is developing in the top stretch of Frederick county-at Thurmont, to be exact-a renais- sance of the business which once made that section of Maryland particularly prominent. It is horse selling. Imported From All Over Nation Horses are being shipped in from all parts of the country-even as far away as Minnesota. And the customers are coming from many places looking for horses to sup- plant their motor-driven wagons and private machines. But, while this progresses, the farmers carry on their daily tasks with hope that something in the form of aid will show up. What? They won't even guess, but they can hope. Wheat is the pay crop of Washington county and, according to M. D. Moore, 'county agent, yields about 800,000 bushels a year. Raspberries also are of prime importance. This year there are about 800 acres of berries planted. Stops Planting Extra Trees Between the berry and the apple country are the Fairchild plants. The newest, still incomplete, spreads out over wide areas ad- jacent to the city airport. Here hundreds of former farm hands come daily to earn, in many in- stances, in a week what they for- merly earned on the farm in a month. And there are many others who once planted and har- vested Washington county soil who motor daily to work at defense plants in near-by Waynesboro, Pennsylvania. "Apple Dan" Martin, who has ten apple orchards scattered through this part of the State, or about 300 acres of apple land with thirty trees to the acre, has usually shipped between 60,000 and 70,000 bushels of apples a year. Now he has stopped planting additional trees. And the trees need at least eight sprayings. "From April 1 to July 1 they should be sprayed every week or ten days," Mr. Martin said. "I have two big sprayers for the purpose, and we paid men on a weekly basis, ranging from $18 to $30, and they still walked out. I've got six men for spraying, but I don't know when they'll go. Have To Let Them Drop And Rot "Then at the harvest time, any- where from September to Novem- ber, the apples have to be picked and packed. We've paid 35 cents an hour for sixty hours. "If the draft and defense indus- tries continue to take the help we have-other apple growers and my- self-we'll just have to let the apples drop and rot. And I have, for example, 8,000 crates and trucks to handle them. "I suggest that inmates of the State Penal Farm at Roxbury be sent into the orchards. We could use them. Now it is a community idea. Everybody helping everybody else. And we'll have to do the best we can in this fashion and not be sure of the results." "We'll Help Each Other Out" Benjamin Risser has a farm of 150 tillable acres, of which forty are in wheat and ten in barley. He indorsed Mr. Martin's statement about community work. His fertile fields, incidentally, are across the road from the air- port and within view of the new Fairchild plant, which has attracted farm hands who otherwise would be working for him. "I have a thrashing machine and we'll help each other out," said Mr. Risser. "Nothing is ever too bad that it couldn't be worse, and we'll all go along together." That theme is sounded in nearly every section of Washington county. There is a close-snit neigh- borliness about the people in this part of Maryland.

title: Verdict Of $779,812 Upheld On Appeal
full_text: Verdict Of $779,812 Upheld On Appeal Receivers For Davison Realty Company Win Suit Against C. Wilbur Miller Attorneys for the receivers of the Davison Realty Company yesterday were informed by the rederal Cir- cuit Court of Appeals, at Charlotte, N. C., that a verdict of $779,812 ob- tained a year ago against C. Wilbur Miller, former president of the com- pany, had been affirmed. The sum represents, with interest, amounts which Mr. Miller is said to have borrowed from the company on eight promissory notes. The original verdict, returned in November, 1934, by a jury in the United States District Court here, was appealed by Mr. Miller, who con- tended the loans were not personal obligations, but were for the benefit of the Davison Chemical Company, of which he then was head. Mr. Miller was represented by Isaac Lobe Straus and J. Wallace Bryan, while the re- ceivers' case was presented by Hilary W. Gans, James U. Dennis and George Moore Brady. Cheltenham Man Asks Probe Of Reformatory John A. Hurley Writes To Nice, O'Conor And Grand Jury About Disturbance Cheltenham, Md., Jan. 6 (AP)-In- vestigation of conditions at the House of Reformation here was asked of Governor Nice today by John A. Hurley, of Cheltenham. Hurley ex- pressed apprehension over an alleged growing tendency toward violence among the 400 Negro inmates of the institution. He reported a near-riot in the re- formatory last Friday, in which four guards were injured and several win- dows broken as Negro boys hurled pots, pans, bottles and dishes at break- fast time. Hurley also charged in letters sent to the Governor, Herbert R. O'Conor and the Baltimore city grand jury that some inmates were mistreated, Hal B. Kearns, superintendent, is to ap- pear before the investigating body on Wednesday. Confession Reported In Slaying Of Hermit Former Hagerstown Man Quoted As Admitting Part In Virginia Killing Hagerstown, Jan. 6 (P)-Carl Turner, 26, formerly of Hagerstown, was quot- ed by police here tonight as having confessed to complicity in the robbery- slaying of John Looker, aged hermit of Elkton, Va. Looker was shot near his barn De- cember 7. Virginia authorities held Turner and Lester Looker, a nephew of the victim, for questioning. Until today neither admitted guilt. Looker is being detained at Harrisonburg, Va. Turner was brought here from Elkton today by State police, osten- sibly to attempt identification of a suspect. Officers said no identification was made, and that Turner broke under a prolonged grilling. Garey Declares State Must "Clean Up" Courts "Stop Fixing Traffic Charges," Says Head Of Police-Plans Safety Campaign Major Enoch Barton Garey, super- intendent of the Maryland State po- lice, disclosed plans for a highway safety campaign yesterday with a charge that Maryland must "clean up" its courts. "We must stop the fixing of traffic charges," Major Garey said. "We have reports of judges being fixed, of juries allowing themselves to be talked into freeing guilty men by lawyers." Major Garey said that the second major phase of the safety campaign must be the education of the public to the point where it will support such a drive. Plans for the campaign will be discussed at the next meeting of the Governor's advisory council. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: QUIET MARKS ASSEMBLY OPENING; ADMINISTRATION FORCES IN FULL CONTROL: PATRONAGE DISPENSED UNDER DIRECTION OF GOVERNOR WITH NO DISPUTE NO CHANGE IN PRESIDING OFFICERS; O'CONOR GIVES BIENNIAL REPORT
full_text: QUIET MARKS ASSEMBLY OPENING; ADMINISTRATION FORCES IN FULL CONTROL Patronage Dispensed Under Direction Of Gov- ernor With No Dispute No Change In Presiding Officers; O'Conor Gives Biennial Report By LOUIS J. O'DONNELL [Annapolis Bureau of The Sun] Annapolis, Jan. 1--Encountering not the slightest ripple of opposition, a smooth-clicking administration ma- chine carried the General Assembly tonight over the opening-day hurdles of its ninety-day biennial session. Patronage allotments were signed, and sealed in Governor O'Conor's office and delivered to the Democratic caucus for ratification only a few hours before the executive mounted the rostrum in the House of Delegates chamber to give an accounting of his two усага in office. As for the presiding officers of the Senate and the House, no change was expected. And there was none; Senator Arthur H. Brice (Dem., Kent) retained the Presidency of the Senate, and Thomas E. Conlon (Dem., Fifth, Bal- timore) again will preside in the House.  Nothing Startling There were a few indications-such as in the appointment of Frank F. J. Daily, long a follower of Mayor Jackson, as chief clerk in the House of a further consolidation of the O'Conor political forces but otherwise nothing startling appeared on the sur- face in the apportionment of jobs. The list forwarded from the execu- tive office and rubber-stamped by the caucus was identified mainly, as the handiwork of the Governor, Howard Bruce, his political mentor; Clarence W. Miles, his legislative field marshal, and William Curran, E. Brooke Lee Unnoticed Nowhere at least openly-did Dele- gate E. Brooke Lee (Dem., Montgom- ery), former Speaker, Montgomery county boss and generalissimo in the Ritchie administrations, show up in today's preliminary organization of the Assembly. He's back in the House in place of a member who resigned. So far as could be learned, he is not slated to cut a big figure if the ad- ministration has its way, but he was being pointed out to those who are comparatively strangers to the State House corridors as the man who can upset the best of apple carts if he has a mind to do so. The Governor didn't burden the legislators-many of them still holi- day-minded-with a recitation in ita entirety of his 24,000-word report on the operation of the State government since he took over on January 11, 1939, Only Hits High Spots Instead, he skimmed through the lengthy document and spent forty- five minutes hitting its high spots, emphasing the need for legislation that will mesh the State's activities with the national defense program. Without making specific recom- mendations, he pointed out that with- in the State's borders are many im- portant defense manufacturing and armament plants for which the tracks must be greased and around which safeguards must be thrown. The Governor appeared before the legislators shortly before 9.30 P. M. after both Houses had been through the formalities of installing presiding officers and heard their brief speeches of acceptance. Ten minutes after the Governor had finished speaking, the State House was almost deserted.  Adjourn Till 11 A. Μ. Both Houses had been adjourned until 11 o'clock tomorrow morning, at which time the bills prepared by the Legislative Council will be presented. The Assembly will adjourn tomorrow afternoon until Tuesday night, accord. ing to current plans, at which time committee assignments will be com- pleted. The Governor in his message indi- rectly warned the legislators that the administration-and the public-ex- pects the Assembly to get down to work without the usual dilly-dallying. He reminded them that the State Treasury's figures show that Maryland is in the soundest financial position it has ever enjoyed-with balance as of September 30, 1940, of $6,151,955-and that he will recommend that this good fortune be passed on to the taxpayers. In fact, he told the legislators that he has practically completed the de- tails of the fiscal recommendations he will pass on to them with his proposed (Continued on Page 4, Column 6) (Continued from Page 1) budget for 1942-43 and that they can expect this program next week. This early preparation of the budget, the Governor advised the legislators, is his contribution to a general effort that should be made to forestall the usual closing-hour rush. Road Plan Is Ready Affairs of the State Roads Commis- sion are in such shape, the Governor said, that he is prepared to put be- fore the Assembly a most ambitious highway program-an accomplishment made possible by the fact that no gaso- line-tax funds have been diverted by his administration and none will be diverted. It is up to the Legislature, he added, to forge a new link in State trans- portation by ratifying the purchase of the Claiborne Annapolis ferry-a move that will mean lower rates. In the first year of his administra- tion, the Governor reported, 110.18 miles of road was built and, during this year, 87.68 miles are under con- struction or contract. The Governor's summary of opera- tions of various institutions was de- tailed, designed primarily as a hand- book for the legislators. Projected Plans In the case of some, however, the Governor projected the plans of the administration for improvement or expansion. For example, in the case of the Cheltenham School for Boys, the State's institutional sore spot for years, the Governor said that the fact that further improvement in facilities and operation is imperative must be faced squarely by the administration and the Legislature.. To meet this need, he informed the Assembly, he has made a generous provision in his budget. He reviewed the progress of the State Health Department; expansion of hospitals for tuberculosis and mentally afflicted and indicated that appropriations for such purposes would be increased rather than held down in his forthcoming budget. On the subject of conserving the State's natural resources, the Governor spoke briefly of the fact that the ad- ministration's plan for a separate com- mercial fishery commission was de- feated at the polls in November and then issued a plea for considered and unbiased action on the problem during this session. Dismisses Sectionalism In reaching a solution, the Governor asked the legislators to "lay aside pre- conceived notions and any sectional or political viewpoints and be guided by what is best for the future of the State." Maryland has been fortunate, the Governor said in connection with the State welfare program, in that ex- penditures are being handled "capably and properly" to the end that, as com. pared with other States, the cost here is relatively light. He indicated that his recommenda- tions on welfare appropriations must await the fiscal proposals that will ac- company his budget. Praises Magistrate System The trial magistrate syster that was created by the legislators at the 1939 session, the Governor told them, has worked so well that it can be said in no two-year period heretofore have such rapid advances been made in the administration of justice in Maryland. Dr. H. C. Byrd, president of the University of Maryland, was paid ex- ceptional tribute by the Governor in his reference to that institution. "Under the able leadership of Dr. Byrd," the Governor's report asserted, "the University of Maryland, and all its related activities are being effici- ently conducted and are offering services of great value to the State." "Very Noteworthy" "Very noteworthy," said the Gov- ernor, is the growth of the physical plant at the university-a growth made possible mainly by Dr. Byrd's per- suative work with Federal fund- dispensing agencies in Washington. However, the Governor added that "the educational advancement of the university has keep pace with the ad- vancement in physical facilities." Fiscal aspects, often the subject of great controversy in the past, of the university were left for the budget message. In keeping with the new demands That will be made on State agencies by the national defense program, the Governor informed the Assembly that the Public Service Commission has approved expansion plans of the pub- lic utilities that will provide adequate service and he revealed plans to train members of the State police force for specialized duties. To Increase Police Additions to the force that he will recommend-and provide for in the budget-the Governor said, will make possible this special training of the State policemen and increase their usefulness as well as make more of them available for patroling the high- vays. It was indicated, in his remarks on The unemployment compensation di- ision, that the Governor plans to ask The Legislature to make changes in The law that will simplyfy its adminis- ration and relieve employers of some f the mass of detail now necessary in he keeping of records. Reminds Membership Paving the way for the approximate- seventy measures that the Legisla- ive Council will lay before the As- embly as a whole with its recommen- Lation for adoption, the Governor re- minded the general membership of the Legislature that the council had not usurped any of the rights of the legislators as a body. The Governor said he desired to "lay emphasis" on the fact that the bills the council will persent are open to the same discussion as any other measure that may come before the Assembly. Cites Constitution "The elected representatives of the people, including every member of the Senate and every member of the House of Delegates," he said, "are the legislative branch of the government. "The Constitution provides for that, and no provision by law (such as creation of the council or otherwise can deprive the members of their rights. "Accordingly, it will be the entire membership of the General Assembly that the public will look for final decisions on all the matters under consideration. That the Senate and the House will meet their responsibilities I have no doubt."

title: A Baltimore Philanthropist: ENOCH PRATT WAS FRUGAL IN SMALL THINGS, LIBERAL IN LARGE
full_text: A Baltimore Philanthropist ENOCH PRATT WAS FRUGAL IN SMALL THINGS, LIBERAL IN LARGE* by MARK S. WATSON JUST fifty years ago today the Enoch Pratt Free Library, at that time the largest of free libraries functioning by private gift, was opened to the public. Appropriately Book Borrower's Card No. 1 was issued to Enoch Pratt, whose donation of $1,145,833 had made it possible. The semi-centennial anniversary is well observed by the library with its publication of a short life of the shrewd old Yankee phil- anthropist, written by Richard II. Hart, of the library's present staff, the handsome typography designed by Norman T. A. Mun- der, who is responsible for a great deal of fine Baltimore printing, and the book itself issued under the imprimatur of the library. Too little is known of Enoch Pratt, whose intluence on fellow-men was not limited by his life's span. A very few years after he set foot in South Charles street in 1831 he be- came a man of importance and so continued until his deata in 1896. Baltimore has ample continuing evidence of his devotion to the public good. So has the Massachusetts hamlet where he was born. And so, whether they know it or not, have a hundred cities and villages where Enoch Pratt never set foot, for in them Andrew Carnegie planted his own free libraries by dozens and scores after learning from Mr. Pratt, to whom bonnie Andy pointed as his instructor, how a rich man could spend his money. IT IS STRANGE that of so useful and so pic- turesque a person so little is known, for niany a surviving raconteur must have known Mr. Pratt. His biographer surmises that one reason for his adopted city's curious lack of acquaintance may well be in the continuing if unexpressed hostility between the methodical, industrious Yankee and the leisurely Mary- landers who surrounded him. There were many points of difference. Enoch Pratt was born in Titicut parish, which only a microscopic search of the maps uncovers, not far from Plymouth Rock, where seven generations earlier one Phineas Pratt had trod as early as 1623. In the family tree, no doubt, were a few clergymen and other bookish people, for they were nu- merous in every New England family, but for the most part the Pratts were farmers wrest- ing a living from a stubbornly resisting soil, and supplementing that meager living with a small revenue from boat building, or fishing, or ironworking. Enoch's father, Isaac, for example, bought iron rods from Sweden and Russia and in his little smithy drew them out and sheared them and hammered them into nails for general sale. To the respect that a little boy working 'ine bellows must have had for each separate nail, Mr. Hart suggests one can trace the old man's later addiction to pulling up his car- riage horses, dismounting and picking up a nail his keen eyes had observed in the thick dust of Baltimore's streets. Such frugality made his Maryland-born neighbors snicker. Not many of them emulated him then or later, either in picking up old nails or in endowing new libraries. HIS SCHOOLING ENDED at 15, the boy went to nearby Boston, became clerk in a wholesale hardware store, stayed there for seven years, presumably building up credit and confi- dence, for in 1831, when he was 22, he moved to Baltimore and immediately opened his own warehouse in South Charles street, about where No. 23-25 now stands. It must have been largely on credit from the Boston houses through which he bought his nails and horseshoes, but it was not long before he had capital of his own. Mr. Hart gives a quick but graphic picture of the growing town of that year-the same year in which an unrecognized poet named Edgar A. Poc came to Baltimore. It was second among the young republic's cities, its clippers becoming famous. The Independent Church, now the Unitarian Church, was already standing at Charles and Franklin (young Mr. Pratt promptly joined it) and the McKim Free School was rising over in East Baltimore. Stage coaches and Conestoga wagons rumbled through the streets, their owners not yet greatly worried over the new- fangled railroads already under way. Half the city jail's inmates were in prison not for crime but for debt, and only a few years earlier two highwaymen had been put to the ordeal by blood, which we like to think of as a long outgrown medieval enterprise in ENOCH PRATT FREE LIBRARY THE NEW MODEL penology. An industrious Quaker merchant named Johns Hopkins was already winning respect and profits. BY 1847 the Yankee hardware merchant was so much a part of the town that he was made treasurer of the church society. While in office he found the church worried by two problems, the maintenance cost of its old cemetery out at Belair road and Broadway, and the interest charges on its outstanding bonds. The astute Mr. Pratt offered genially to relieve them of both worries at one blow. He acquired the bonds and gave the whole collection to the church in exchange for the old cemetery. Then he had the cemetery abandoned, moving the graves to a new loca- tion and selling the old and now valuable site, for real-estate development for a price higher than he had paid for the bonds. In- stead of two continuing losses, there was one substantial profit. He was entitled to it, be- cause for years he met the church's deficit, he paid for the organ and for some of the statuary, and he met part of the cost of the parish house. IHe must have accumulated his first mil- lion by about 1855. Anyway, having worked for twenty-five years without a vacation, he decided to take one, and invited his wife on a European tour. She did not like to travel and declined, so Mr. Pratt went alone. Then he came back and resumed work, and profit. Like Johns Hopkins and another resolute Baltimorean of that day, John Garrett, of the Baltimore and Ohio, he was an ardent Union- ist. He opposed slavery and was willing to aid in the African recolonization movement. Later he was proud to learn that Negroes were using his library and, determined to help the newly freed people, led in the upbuilding of the Cheltenham reformatory for colored children who presumably had not been spending their free time in the library. He gave his 750-acre farm as a site. Interest in the work done there was demonstrated by his employing on his own country place nu- merous Negro gardeners who had been trained at Cheltenham. Mr. Hart gives a too brief summary of ear- lier American library experiments, many of which must have been studied by the shrewd old merchant. In 1865 Mr. Pratt is discovered giving financial aid to the Pratt Free School at Titicut Parish and urging development of its free circulating library, not only for school children but for the community. This gift to his boyhood home came twenty-six years before Mr. Carnegie's gift of a library to Dunfermline, and eighteen years before the great gift to Baltimore. 业 IT WAS in the late seventies, Dr. Weld, of the Unitarian Church, recalled, that Mr. Pratt spoke to him about the city's prime need. As he saw it, it was a library, and not a library for scholars such as George Pea- body had given, nor for the well-to-do, such as the old Mercantile Library, but a library, somewhat like that of his Workingmen's In- stitute, for "all, rich and poor, without dis- tinction of race or color, who, when properly accredited, can take out the books if they will handle them carefully and return them." Having reached that decision, Mr. Pratt set about the enterprise in his own way. He acquired needed property in West Mulberry street and began digging a large hole. There was much speculation about what was going there, but no answer to the mystery until it suited the old man to make his own an- nouncement. Then he informed the Mayor that he had in mind building a central library with five branches, and endowing it with $833,333.33, if the city in exchange would agree to appropriate $50,000 each year for maintenance. The city gladly accepted, and Mr. Pratt thereupon went ahead. When the central library was completed and turned over to the public on January 5, 1886, it developed he had spent $250,000 for site and building, plus $50,000 for four branches already com- pleted, and tucked in $12,500 for cash in hand-a total of $1,145,833. Other branches followed in time, but the next big impulse came in 1906 when Mr. Carnegie gave $500,- 000 for twenty new branches, with the grace- ful remark that this was intended simply to extend the pioneering enterprise of his old friend Mr. Pratt. Incidentally, the fund ran out before the fifteenth new branch was up. THIS NEW BIOGRAPHY introduces a number of anecdotes, sometimes amusing, generally illuminating, of this vigorous old man whose rule the biographer identifies as "frugality in small things, open-handedness in large." Не hated waste. He favored women employes on the thrifty reasoning that "women are THE OLD MOD steadier workers and more reliable; besides, they require less wages than men in the same position" but Mr. Hart quotes the old gentleman's bitter comment that "when a woman has an extra dollar it gets spent on zewgaws." ABOUT his new library (where at the outset a brass rail separated male and female read- ers) he prowled at all hours, so earnestly hat a new and conscientious janitor once went to a library assistant with a warning that "that old gentleman needs watching." One of his proudest visits was that of 1890, with Mr. Carnegie as his much-interested com- panion. There are other stories, too, of his im- mense aid to the Sheppard-Pratt Hospital; of his service to the city as finance commis- sioner, particularly his part in refinancing the city stock on a lower interest basis, guaran- teeing to take up himself all that was not subscribed for; of his other lively interests in the adopted home, plus a continuing in- terest in his birthplace, and in the Unitarian theological seminary he aided. Further research may well produce addi- tional information about this remarkable phil- anthropist. Mr. Hart's volume is an encour- aging contribution. title: REPORTS PROGRESS AT CHELTENHAM: HEAD OF REFORMATORY NEGRO BOYS CITES IMPROVEMENTS HAL T. KEARNS GRAND JURORS' ASSOCIATION
full_text: REPORTS PROGRESS AT CHELTENHAM Head Of Reformatory For Negro Boys Cites Improvements Hal T. Kearns Addresses Grand Jurors' Asso- ciation Hal T. Kearns, superintendent of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, last night told members of the Grand Jurors' Asso- ciation of improvements which have been inaugurated at the institution. He said he had begun the develop- ment of a case-work system, by which each boy entering the institution is given individual study and treatment. He added that the housing problem had been revised so that the inmates were segregated according to type and age. Reformatory Overcrowded The reformatory is overcrowded, he told the former grand jurors, there be- ing 400 boys at Cheltenham while there are normal accommodations for 300 only. "There are two classes of boys who should not be there," he continued. "They are the definitely feeble-minded and those with pronounced criminal tendencies. "Maryland has not made provision for the feeble-minded, however, and the Crownsville State Hospital 'is crowded. The ages of the boys at the institution range from 10 to 16 years." Improvement of the academic school by the employment of three young Negroes, graduates from Howard Uni- versity, was reported by Mr. Kearns. He also said the former policy of having a consultant physician visit the institution once a week had been dis- continued, and another Negro, a young doctor, graduate of the same univer- sity, gives the infirmary his full time. Mr. Kearns also said plans were being made for construction of a can- nery, extension of the farm work and hog raising. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: O'Conor Suggests $1,500,000 For 2 Chronic Hospitals By THOMAS J. O'DONNELL [Annapolis Bureau of The Sun] Annapolis, Jan. 7-Governor O'Conor -today recommended that $1,500,000 of State funds from a $4,172,000 pro- posed bond issue be set aside for the construction of two chronic disease hospitals, one on the Eastern Shore and the other on this side of the bay, to replace the numerous and much- criticized almshouses in the various counties.  The plan for the two new hospitals provides that the counties maintain them on a per-capita basis, with the amount each would contribute gov- erned by the number of persons sent to the institutions. Again, the appropriation for opera- tion of the institutions has been in- creased, the new funds amounting to $62,432.2 The State Health Department was not overlooked.. A recommendation that $250,000 be appropriated from the bond issue for the erection of a build- ing to house the offices and labora- tories of the department was the main consideration. Rental for the building now occu- pied by the department is $14,500 per year. Increase Asked to congregate for athletic and recrea- tional purposes. An additional $10,000 was recom- mended for a sewerage system at this school. The State's only school for the edu- cation of the deaf, the Maryland State School for the Deaf, would receive $15,000 from the bond issue for equip- ment and improvements. The operating appropriations for the department would be increased by $21,230, all of which would be used for new activities. The most important new function would be the establishment of a di- vision of industrial health within the Health Department. Governor O'Conor asserted that this addition to the department has been urged by many industries and by the Federal Government for the protec- tion of workers in plants having na- tional defense corſtracts. Necessary professional personnel would be employed to study occира- tional hazards in plants with the aim of correcting conditions which cause illness in industrial workers. The Governor pointed out that the appropriation probably would not be sufficient for all the personnel needed in the proposed industrial division, but said he had reason to believe that Federal funds will be available by next year to supplement the State ap- propriation. Cheltenham Provisos Nearly half a million dollars more new construction has been proposed for the State's correctional, or train- ing, schools. Cheltenham School for Boys, which has long been a bone of contention. would be allotted $255,000, of which $95,000 would be for a building for vo- cational education; $70,000 for erection and equipment of a new cottage; $50,- 000 for extension of sewerage and water-supply systems; and $40,000 for additional power plant facilities. An increase of $31,266 in the main- tenance budget also was recommended for Cheltenham, the additional money to be spent for an increased amount of food, additional fuel and new educa- tional and vocational supplies and equipment. Would Get $125,000 The Maryland Training School for Boys would receive $125,000 from the bond issue, $115,000 of which would be for the construction of a new cottage and $10,000 for needed improvements and equipment. There also will be an Encrease in the maintenance budget, amounting to $1,636. Montrose School for Girls would be given $24,000 from the bond issue, $15,000 for the equipping of a voca- tional building, which recently was completed; $7,000 for remodeling Wil- son Cottage, in order to accommodate more girls, and the remaining $2,000 for kitchen and dining-room equip- ment. Needs $50,000 The Maryland Training School for Colored Girls needs $50,000 to complete the gymnasium and assembly hall, the Governor said, and this amount was recommended, with the notation chat at present the girls have no place . .

title: ROBERTS DEFENDS CHELTENHAM WORK: BOARD PRESIDENT REPLIES TO CRITICISM OF CHILD WELFARE LEAGUE
full_text: ROBERTS DEFENDS CHELTENHAM WORK Board President Replies To Criticism Of Child Wel- fare League - Robert F. Roberts, president of the board of directors of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys al Cheltenham, yesterday defended the institution against criticism leveled at it in a report of the Child Welfare League of America, Inc. At the same time a local attorney, Erwin I. Feldman, representing a group of Negroes, announced they would seek to have the management of the reformatory taken over by the State. Conditions Condemned The report of the league, which was made public Saturday, recommended that the State take charge of the insti- tution. Physical and health conditions there were severely condemned. "We have a good institution and it has been doing a good piece of work for the State," Mr. Roberts said last night. title: NICE REVENUE COMMITTEE IS NOW COMPLETE: PERSONNEL OF GROUP TO SEEK NEW SOURCES OF FUNDS IS DISCLOSED LOOKS LIKE RUSH JOB, SAYS CASEY CHAIRMAN CALLS FIRST MEETING OF MEMBERS FOR TOMORROW
full_text: NICE REVENUE COMMITTEE IS NOW COMPLETE Personnel Of Group. To Seek New Sources Of Funds Is Disclosed LOOKS LIKE RUSH JOB, SAYS CASEY Chairman Calls First Meeting Of Members For Tomorrow By LOUIS J. O'DONNELL [Annapolis Bureau of The Sun] Annapolis, Jan. 12-The personnel of Governor Nice's committee charged with seeking sou ces of additional State revenue was disclosed today. Under the chairmanship of William J. Casey, director of the Baltimore Commission on Governmental Effici- ency and Economy, the committee will canvass the revenue field and advise Governor Nice what sources should be tapped to finance such leg- islation as relief, old-age pensions and unemployment insurance. Appointment of Mr. Casey, who is regarded as an expert on taxation and fiscal matters, was announced some months ago. He also will head a "su- per-committee" to be composed of the chairmen of various groups intrusted by the Governor with the task of draft- ing legislation for his social program. Members Named The members of the committee that will function under Mr. Casey on revenue questions include: ADAM J. HAZLETT, president of the Eastern Rolling Mills Company, a director of the Baltimore Associa- tion of Commerce and a member of the Baltimore Emergency Relief Commission, OSCAR LESER, minority member of the State Tax Commission and an authority on taxation. ALBERT D. HUTZLER, department store president, former president of the Associated Jewish Charities and of the Baltimore Association of Com- merce. CHARLES C. WALLACE, City Solicitor in the first administration of Mayor William F. Broening. ALLAN SAUERWEIN, director of the Baltimore Association of Com- merce and legal member of the Baltimore NRA Compliance Board. JAMES E. HOOPER, vice-president of the W. E. Hooper Cotton Mills and a director of the Baltimore Asso- ciation of Commerce. First Meeting Monday Mr. Casey said last night that the committee would hold its first meeting Monday afternoon. It will be, he said, an advisory body, the function of which will be to iay before Governor Nice reports on the effect various forms of proposed new taxes would have on the ecenomic sit- uation and various industries. "Our committee," said Mr. Casey, "will cover the entire field, dealing with the problem of where additional revenue will come from and its gen- eral effect on business. We do not ex. pect to develop any legislation. Looks Like "Rush Job" "It looks like a rush job that must be done in a hurry, and we'll do the best we can with it. "Of course, it is understood that we cannot adopt any permanent reorga- nization of the State revenues in this emergency situation." Mr. Casey said any widespread re- adjustment of the Maryland system of taxation would entail months of work. The job before them, he pointed out, must be completed in a brief space of time, because the Legislature will be in session only until April 1. There will not be time, he said, for many meetings of the committee and he expects that the members will have to devote much of their time to ac- complish. their task in the period al- lotted them. Group Fully Qualified The committee, he added, is to his mind "most representative" and fully qualified for the task entrusted to them. Governor Nice pointed out that the personnel of the committee had been selected from among men who previ- ously had been making a study of the taxation problem. "They have been investigating and giving the best of their thought and talent to the task of helping to solve the financial problems of the State of Maryland," he said. "The very men- tion of the names of these gentle- men is in itself a guarantee that these problems will receive thoughtful and intelligent consideration, and that their findings will be constructive, (Continued on Page 22, Column 2) FUNDS COMMITTEE COMPLETED BY NICE Personnel Of Group To Seek New Sources Of Revenue Is Disclosed By LOUIS J. O'DONNELL (Continued from Page 24) equitable and in the best interest of all the people. Expresses Gratitude "I am under a deep sense of obliga- tion to all of these men for their very great kindness in coming to my aid and to the aid of the people of the State. "It is, of course, my purpose to lay before the Legislature various meth- ods for the raising of revenue, and, as I have said, it will be the duty of the Legislature to select from among these methods one, two or all, as it may think best, or in lieu thereof, inaugurate a program of its own. I expect, among other things, to lay before both houses the result of the labor and intelligent study of the members of this committee." Judges Discuss Report On Negro Reformatory Grand Jury Committee Suggests Institution Be Taken Over By State Judges of the Criminal Court yes- terday were considering a report filed by a special committee of the retiring grand jury which suggested that the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham be taken over by the State. Now supported almost entirely by the State, Baltimore city and the counties, the institution, according to the report, is overcrowded and lacks the proper medical facilities. The "rec- reational and social expression and development of the boys at Chelten- ham seem non-existent," the report says. The report recommended that all the boys receive training in "produc- tive work," suggesting agriculture, poultry raising, husbandry, small fruit farming, landscape gardening and manual training. title: SIMPLER TRAFFIC LAWS ARE URGED: RETIRING JURY ALSO FAVOR REVOCATION OF CHRONIC OFFENDERS' LICENSES REPORT ALSO SAYS "REASONABLE DOUBT" PREVENTED INDICTMENTS IN ELECTION FRAUD CASE
full_text: SIMPLER TRAFFIC LAWS ARE URGED Retiring Jury Also Favors Revocation Of Chronic Of- fenders' Licenses DEALS WITH ACCIDENTS Report Also Says "Reasonable Doubt" Prevented Indictments In Election Fraud Case Simplification of traffic laws to suit - present conditions and the revocatior of the licenses of chronic offenders were among four recommendations to effect a decrease in the number o이 fatal automobile accidents made yes. terday by the retiring September grand jury. : The suggestions were made in a re- port filed with the clerk of the Crimi- nal Court by Richard C. Williams, foreman of the jury. Vote Fraud Cases Cited In connection with its investigation Into the alleged fraudulent vote count- ing in Fourth district precincts during the election, the report said: "We exhausted every possible means of information regarding the irregu- larities in the last general election, and recounted the ballots in an effort to fix responsibilities for them. Fraud Admitted "In some precincts these were due in our judgment to fatigue and not to fraudulent intent. In other cases, un- doubtedly fraud was practiced, and while the evidence pointed toward cer- tain persons as being guilty, there still remained, however, as to them, a reasonable doubt in our minds. "Under such circumstances we were unwilling to make presentments which might result in placing the stigma of a criminal prosecution on innocent parties." Accidents Referred To Referring to automobile accidents, the jurors reported: "The ever-increasing toll of death and serious injuries due to automobile accidents has been of grave concern to us. While doubtless just how to di- minish the number of such accidents is a matter of continuous study by the proper authorities, we recommend: "1. A simplification of traffic laws to suit present conditions. "2. Such reorganization of Traffic Court and the Automobile Com- missioner's office as my be neces- sary to make readily available at the Traffic Court, as part of his trial, the record of each traffic offender. "3. We recommend that the license to drive of chronic offenders be taken from them. The law should be changed so that the person seeking reinstatement of his li- cense should prove beyond a rea- sonable doubt, his fitness to ex- ercise this privilege. "4. In view of the conflicting testi- mony as to facts easily ascertain- able at the time of a crash, or shortly thereafter, we recommend that in serious cases certain of the police be assigned to investigate and file written reports of such accidents." Sherman Praised In addition, the foreman's report commended the Police Department and the State's Attorney's office, "in particular the workings of the office dealing with non-support cases which has been so ably, administered by John A. Sherman and Albert H. Blum during this term." Mr. Sherman and Mr. Blum formerly were Assistant State's Attorneys, Concerning State and city institu- tions, the foreman suggested that "the State and City Forester be instructed to survey all the State and city insti- tutions and funds be provided to plant wherever desirable forest trees and native shrubs from the State nurs- eries." Teacher Needed The grand jury committee appointed to investigate the Montrose School for Girls reported that an instructor to teach handicraft was needed, as that department was closed. The former instructor received only $5 a week, which "is not sufficient compensation," the report stated. The committee which investigated the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham reported that it could not "condemn too strongly the health conditions, especially tubercu- losis," there. It asserted boys with tu- berculosis should be transferred to Henryton for proper treatment. Prison Committee Reports The Penitentiary committee report disclosed that of the 276 inmates at the State penal farm at Roxbury, in Washington county, the average age was 21 years and that the average school grade reached by the inmates was the fifth. The report showed also that during its four-month term of office the jury acted on 1,630 cases. Of the defendants in these, 1,491 were indicted, 122 dis- missed and the remainder reconsid- ered and ignored. Of the indictments 15 were for mur- der; 12, manslaughter; 121, false pre- tenses and forgery; 126, assault and assault and robbery; 297, burglary; 41, liquor without license; 547, larceny; 64, gambling; 8, bets on races; 36, re- ceiving stolen goods, and 74, non-sup- port. Witnesses summoned to appear before the jurors totaled 3,604, it was disclosed. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: CHELTENHAM TO GET FULL NEGRO STAFF: BOYS' SCHOOL BOARD RESOLVES UPON ACTION 'AS SOON AS PRACTICABLE' HOWARD C. HILL SAYS STEP 'EVENTUALLY' WILL INCLUDE SUPERINTENDENT
full_text: CHELTENHAM TO GET FULL NEGRO STAFF Boys' School Board Re- solves Upon Action 'As Soon As Practicable' Howard C. Hill Says Step 'Eventually' Will Include Superintendent The Cheltenham School for Boys will be staffed "as soon as practi- cable" entirely by Negroes. The order to replace present white teachers and other employes with Negroes was entered in the form of a resolution by the school's board of managers at a meeting yesterday afternoon. The meeting, originally sched- uled for next Thursday, was moved ahead for the convenience of some of the members. : To Include Superintendent Asked if the order included the position of superintendent, Howard C. Hill, acting president, replied: "Yes, eventually." The new move is meant to end the controversy that reached a climax more than a month ago when the board adopted a resolu- tion to end the segregation of white and Negro employes at the school. In its resolution yesterday it re- affirmed the principle which it had set forth at that time. Resolution Adopted 1 The resolution adopted yester- day said: "The board feels that its resolu- tion of March 25, adopted after very careful consideration of a crisis which had already arisen at (Continued on Page 20, Column 1) (Continued from Page 26) the institution, was justifiable and an expression of a general demo- cratic principle which we reaffirm." At this point, it was noted paren- thetically that "Mr. Hal T. Clag- gett, secretary-treasurer of the board, who was not present at the meeting on March 25, stated his opposition to the resolution. "However," the resolution con- tinued, "it is the unanimous sense of the board that it is to the best interests of Cheltenham that the institution, as soon as practicable, be staffed entirely by Negroes and that the board will proceed upon this basis with due regard to the rights and interests of the white employes now at the institution." Opportunity For Transfer Mr. Hill said the resolution means that the white employes will be given an opportunity to be transferred to other institutions or to seek other. employment be- fore the replacements are com- pleted. Asked if the approval of the principle of the former resolution. meant that efforts would be made. pending organization of a Negro staff, to abolish the segrega- tion at the school, Mr. Hill said: full "I can't answer that categorically, but we are seeking better housing for some of the Negroes. "We have very few places where more than one or two people live together. There are a few familięs at the school, but not many. We are leaving it entirely to the superin- tendent to handle it in a way that could not be objectionable to any- one." All Members At Session Mr. Hill said all nine members of the board of managers attended yesterday's meeting. He said he did not know until after the meeting that Governor O'Conor had ap- pointed Joseph P. Healy to member- ship on the board. The controversy that raged since the board's resolution of March 25 resulted in the resignation of Joseph H. Blandford, president of the board. Resignations of several employes followed. The latest of these, re- ported to Mr. Hill, are Leroy Chisholm, teacher of plumbing, a graduate of Hampton Institute, and Walter C. Hones, elementary teacher for the last five years, who charged that Vance E. Thomas, superintendent, "bungled the chance" to settle amicably the racial segregation problem.

title: CHELTENHAM CONDITIONS ARE CENSURED: DETAILED REPORT ON RE FORMATORY FOR NEGRO BOYS FILED IN COURT STATE CONTROL RECOMMENDED MENACES TO HEALTH AND LIFE OF INMATES ALLEGED IN SURVEY
full_text: CHELTENHAM CONDITIONS ARE CENSURED Detailed Report On Re- formatory For Negro Boys Filed In Court STATE CONTROL RECOMMENDED Menaces To Health And Life Of Inmates Alleged In Survey Censuring the health standards, diet, dormitories, clothing and vir- tually all other living conditions at the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, the Child Wel- fare League of America, Inc., has recommended that the State take it over. The league's report on the institu- tion, based on a study made last year, came to light last week in con- nection with a petition filed in court for the release of one of its inmates. Executive director of the league, which has offices at 130 East Twenty- second street, New York city, is C. C. Carstens. The secretary is Kenneth L. Messenger. Criticized By Grand Juries Frequently criticized by grand juries and other investigating bodies, the institution most recently came under fire in the report of the retiring Sep- tember term grand jury, and Gover- nor Nice subsequently reiterated his campaign assertion that the State should take charge of the reformatory. title: A Move To End Controversy At Cheltenham
full_text: A Move To End Controversy At Cheltenham The decision of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys to give the institution a full Negro staff is obviously designed to end the contro- versy occasioned by the board's earlier. action ending racial segregation among employés. It looks, therefore, in the right direction. To carry out the board's plan, however, will take time. The filling of vacancies in a staff of a school like Cheltenham is difficult at best, if qualified personnel is to be obtained. It is particularly so now, when teachers and institution managers find it so easy and so attrac- tive to accept positions in private indus- try and in the Federal Government. The board recognizes this problem when it says that the all-Negro staff will come "as soon as practicable." Those who realize that the inmates at Cheltenham are wards of the State and that controversy and criticism cannot help but be detrimental to the housing, feeding and education of those wards, will hope that the board can carry out its newly announced policy without un- due delay. And they will hope that the introduction of a full Negro staff will remove all causes of complaint and fric- tion and place the Negro institution on the sound footing which the public interest demands. In the meantime the board's action should end racial friction and permit the school to push its program to the advan- tage of those intrusted to its care. . title: NEW CHELTENHAM SITE ABANDONED: TITLE TO PROPERTY PURCHASED FOUND 'DEFECTIVE'
full_text: NEW CHELTENHAM SITE ABANDONED Title To Property Purchased Found 'Defective' | Because a highway to connect with the new municipal airport is planned to pass through the site purchased by the State for a new Cheltenham School for Boys, the Cheltenham board of managers has withdrawn its approval of the tract, Thomas B. Sprague, president of the board, announced last night. The 1222-acre site lies between the Hollins Ferry road and the Old Annapolis road between Mount Winans and Cherry Hill. Its pur- chase last January for construc- tion of a Negro training school brought protests from residents of the area. Clear Title Not Obtainable A price of $45,000 was paid for the land to the Whitaker Iron Com- pany, of Wheeling, W.Va. Mr. Sprague, in a statement, said a preliminary report and survey by the Maryland Title Company, en- gaged by the State to ascertain the condition of the title to the Whit- aker tract, showed that a clear title. could not be obtained, "among other things due to the fact that there is planned a highway through the heart of the property." "This highway is to connect with the projected new airport," he con- tinued. "Although the highway had been planned prior to the signing of the contract to purchase the tract, this fact was not known to the board of managers until a title search had been made. Another Site To Be Sought "It is, therefore, with regret that the board has recinded its former action approving the purchase of this tract of land, as it feels that were it not for this defect in the title, the site would be a suitable one. "The board further authorized me to as promptly as possible seek out another location for the school. This will be done." Mr. Sprague said the question of disposition of the property ac- (Continued on Page 13, Column 2) New Cheltenham Site Abandoned (Continued from Page 30) quired would be turned over to the State Law Department. This is the second site the Chelt- enham board has had to abandon in recent months. Plans to con- struct the school on the Bernard N. Baker estate at Old Frederick road and Ingleside avenue, Catons- ville, also subject of much protest, were halted when it was discov- ered the Board of Public Works lacked condemnation powers in connection with the project. + A fund of $1,500,000 has been set aside for construction of the training school.

title: IMPROVEMENT PLAN URGED AT CHELTENHAM: O'CONOR, 2 SPECIAL COMMITTEES AND SCHOOL BOARD BACK PROGRAM APPOINTMENT OF QUALIFIED EDUCATIONAL DIRECTOR AMONG PROPOSALS
full_text: IMPROVEMENT PLAN URGED AT CHELTENHAM O'Conor, 2 Special Com- mittees And School Board Back Program Appointment Of Quali- fied Educational Director Among Proposals A far-reaching program to improve conditions at the Cheltenham School for Negroes was unanimously recom-: mended yesterday at a conference among Governor O'Conor, two spe- cial committees and members of the school's board.  The board of managers of the re- form school was requested to "lake initial steps to put into force" the recommendations which are based on studies made of the institution by a committee of the State Department of Education and by a committee ap- pointed recently by the Governor. Board To Get Report Thursday Yesterday's recommendations and a complete report on the school, com- piled by the education committee after a year's study, will be placed before the board of managers for action at its meeting Thursday, the Governor announced. Studies of Cheltenham were under- taken after repeated reports of bru- tality, starvation and mismanagement emanated from the school. The recom- mendations made at the conference follow: 1 Appointment of a qualified educa- tional director. Appointment of an advisory com- mittee on education, consisting of at least five members. Establishment of a program of in- service for present employes. Expansion of the testing program to determine the abilities of present trainees and those, entering the school. Regrading of the school and pro- vision for an opportunity class. Coordination of practice and related information in practical arts train- ing. Installation of a graded system of credits in habit training. Installation of an adequate system of physical examination and rec- ords thereof. Establishment of a plan of intake control based on the objectives which may properly be assigned to a training school. Construction of a building to serve as a gymnasium, school building, assembly hall and industrial build- ing. Establishment of an optional recre- ational program and purchase of the necessary equipment for its operation. Governor O'Conor, who released a statement on the program, declined to enlarge on it or make any further comment on the institution. However, he said the program, if adopted, would modernize the handling of the reform school. Governor's Statement The Governor's statement follows: "Governor O'Conor met today with six members of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys, a committee of the State Department of Education, appointed in March, 1938, at the request of the board of managers of Cheltenham, to study the educational situation at the institu- tion, and the committee appointed re- cently by him at the request of the president of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School. "The board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys in March, -1938, asked the State Department of Education to study conditions at the school and to make recommendations in respect to the educational program. "In May, 1939, the president of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School had an interview with the Governor and requested him to ap- point a committee to study the con- ditions at Cheltenham and to report its findings to the Governor. Educational Director Urged "The committee of the State Depart- S ment of Education has finished its study of the institution. The commit- 5 (Continued on Page 5, Column 4) tee appointed by the Governor had access to this report and had con- ferences with those who drew it. "The meeting today was an amicable one and everyone present was actuated by the desire to do whatever is best for the school. "Cheltenham is the institution to which colored boys who are homeless, who have no proper care and who have other problems, are sent. The State Department of Education has recommended that an educational di- rector be appointed immediately to take charge of all matters connected with the training and education of the boys and has outlined a long-term program of general improvement." Secret Committee Governor O'Conor declined to re- veal the identities of the three mem- bers of his special committee, which he named early in June. He did say, however, that their work was now completed. Unfavorable reports have emanated from Cheltenham ever since it was taken over by the State in 1937. Last year former Governor Nice asked the board of managers of the school to adopt a plan of reorganiza- tion advanced by Harry C., Jones, State Employment Commissioner, pre- sent a satisfactory alternative plan or resign. The board then informed him. it would not resign or comply with his demands. The school's board consists of fifteen members. There will be five vacancies on the board this summer for Gov- ernor O'Conor to fill.

title: CHELTENHAM'S NEEDS
full_text: CHELTENHAM'S NEEDS Governor O'Conor has made public a long scries of proposals for the improvement of conditions at Cheltenham School for Negro Boys. The nature of the proposals makes it clear that the unnamed committee which worked with the board of managers in sur- veying conditions at the school has consid- ered not merely the physical aspect of things but the nature of the training offered and the quality of the personnel which gives that training. Cheltenham is one of the oldest and the most difficult of the State's correctional prob- lems. The dissatisfactions and open scandals which it has produced are almost number- less. Bitter condemnation has been visited upon it by one grand jury after another. In private hands it was unendurable; now, for two years the property of the State, it still arouses suspicion and dissatisfaction. The proposals made public by the Gov- ernor sound well in theory. But adequate buildings and a staff of improved education and character are not all that Cheltenham has needed. It has needed, especially, a dif- ferent sort of management; it has needed a new approach and new standards among its trustees. The proposals put forward by the Governor do not touch on this essential. Most Marylanders will hope that silence on this point does not mean that it has not received the consideration it needs. title: APPEAL TO END 'JIM CROW' LAW SENT TO LANE: STATE COMMISSION ALSO ASKS ALL-NEGRO BOARD FOR CHELTENHAM
full_text: APPEAL TO END 'JIM CROW' LAW SENT TO LANE State Commission Also Asks All-Negro Board For Cheltenham Repeal of the "Jim Crow" law. appointment of an all-Negro board of managers for the Cheltenham School for Boys and a change in its own name were recommended yesterday to Governor Lane. The recommendations were made by the Commission to Study Prob- lems Affecting the Colored Popu- lation. The second of the proposals al- ready is on the way toward being placed in effect. Members of the Cheltenham School's present board recently submitted their resigna- tions, recommending to Governor Lane as they did so, the appoint- ment of an all-Negro board. The Governor is understood to be preparing now for appointment of such a board. Makes Other Suggestions The three recommendations. were contained in letter of transmittal of the commission's first public report since March, 1943. The commission, first ap- pointed by Governor O'Conor and later established permanently by the. Legislature, has been in exist- ence since 1942. Joseph P. Healy is chairman, Besides the specific recommenda- tions, the commission also pointed up needs and made other sugges- tions in its review of employment, housing, health and welfare, law enforcement, transportation, educa- tion and other fields where prob- lems were found to exist for the Negro population. The report itself does not discuss the "Jim Crow" law or set forth the commission's reasons for proposing a change from the mixed board now managing the training school for Negro boys at Cheltenham. New Title Suggested The commission's third recom. mendation already has received at tention, also. Last month, when Governor Lane placed several new members on the commission, he said he would suggest the change in title-to "Commission on Racial Relations"-to the Legislature. In its letter of transmittal, the commission said the report showed the State was making "progress in the intelligent, sympathetic and thorough understanding" of mi nority problems, but noted that "the complete solution of the prob- lem will await the distant future." "We have sought to analyze and determine in so far as possible the social and economic factors which are the cause and basis of these problems, and to suggest means of solution deemed practicable within the framework of the tra- ditions and policies of the State," the commission stated. Evidences Of Improvement The report is divided into sec- tions, some merely setting forth the problems found, others showing progress or lack of advancement and still others containing sugges- tions for future action. In its study of employment, the commission found three main evi- dences of improvement: An in- crease in the absolute number of Negro employés; employment by industries and companies which never before used Negro workers, and promotions within industries! and companies which formerly em-)! ployed Negroes only in limited capacities. It found also, however, that the Negro since the war had lost some of his gains in industrial and agri- cultural employment made in the war period. 2 Licensed Electricians Specific complaint was made that properly trained Negro applicants for plumbers licenses have met an "insurmountable barrier" in Balti- more city and that admission to the electrical vocation presents the same obstacles. There are in the State, according to the report, only two licensed Negro electricians, one at Cam- bridge and one in Baltimore city, and only one licensed "plumber and steam-itter," at Pocomoke city. As to housing, the commission was less optimistic. It found resist- ance against movement of Negroes to new areas to establish homes "as strong as ever" and com- mented: "There still seems to have been but little progress made with this toughest of Negroes' problems." Overcrowding Deplored Deploring overcrowding, it rec- ommended that existing facilities "at least be brought up to a mini- mum standard by strict enforce- ment of Health Department regu- lations" and said "undeveloped jareas in and adjacent to the city of Baltimore must be made avail- able for Negro housing to take care of the present overcrowded situa- tion and for future development." "The three present inspectors of the Health Department cannot possibly enforce the rooming house, housing and trailer camp rules," the commission said. With regard to health, the com mission recommended: Utilizationn of professional and technical personnel nnel without gard to race, creed, color or na- tional origin. re- Integration of qualified mem- bers of minority groups in nurse training schools. "The gross death rate among Negroes emphasizes the social consequence of discriminatory practices in hospital services," it said. Training For Doctors It found need for adequate facili- ties for training of Negro doctors, training opportunities for Negro nurses, sufficient beds for the mentally ill at Crownsville and relief from the "overcrowded" condition at the Henryton Tuber- culosis Sanitarium. In 1946 and 1947, it noted, "the death rate for tuberculosis of the colored race was nearly four times that of the white population, the rate for pneumonia over twice that for the white; the rate for syphilis nearly ten times that for the white." The commission found the "im- proved relationship existing be- tween the police and the large sec- tions of the Negro community," particularly in Baltimore city, one of the "most tangible indications of interracial progress in the State." Police Co-Operation "The Police Department under Commissioner Atkinson has been unusually co-operative in inves tigating alleged abuses of police authority and general complaints of brutality and discourtesy," it said. "More Negroes have been inte- grated into the department in the city and in four of the county seats throughout the State. Negro offi cers are beginning to be rated on the basis of merit and ability and promotions made accordingly." In the section of the report on newspapers the commission found. newspapers on the whole "extraor- dinarily sympathetic to the cause of inter-group understanding" and said The Sun "deserves credit for its recognition of its social respon- sibility as a public servant for bet- tering human relations; for its de cision and policy to fight against all forms of prejudice and discrimi- nation and for its extraordi- nary sympathy to the cause of in- terracial understanding and good will." . Newspapers Approached Newspapers throughout the State have been approached in an at- tempt to "change attitudes of news reporting, race labeling, etc.," the commission continued. It noted "general complaints among Negroes that some news- papers, in reporting crime, un- necessarily describe the defendant as a Negro" and said, "Negro lead- ers are inclined to think and feel the use of 'Negro' or 'colored' in such cases is seldom necessary." Discussing transportation, the commission said the "numerous" complaints about taxicab facilities avialable to the Negro population were "justified and well-founded," but added that discriminatory prac- tices by drivers had been "some- what alleviated." It reviewed educational pro- grams for Negroes in the State, going into the vocational training picture in Baltimore at some length. In the area of higher education it recommended that an effort be made to supply at Morgan College uate' and professional study. part of the demand for postgrad- Throughout the report mention is made of appointments of individ- ual Negroes to boards of State, city and private agencies, and of contributions Negroes have made to the community.

title: CHELTENHAM BOARD SUES: SEEKS TO RECOVER PAY FOR 24 DROPPED BY JONES
full_text: CHELTENHAM BOARD SUES Seeks To Recover Pay For 24 Dropped By Jones Upper Marlboro, Md., May 3 (AP)- The board of managers of the Chelten- ham School for Boys filed a mandamus suit today to recover salaries of twenty-four employes of the institu- tion. The employes were cut off the pay roll by Harry C. Jones, State Employ- ment Commissioner, on the ground they were unfit. The suit said that the legislative act of 1937, which made the school a State institution, provided For blanketing in the present employes without examination. title: NICE INVITES CHELTENHAM BOARD TO QUIT: CALLS FOR RESIGNATION IF JONES' REORGANIZATION PLAN IS REJECTED GIVES MANAGERS ALTERNATIVE OF PRESENTING SATISFACTORY PROGRAM
full_text: NICE INVITES CHELTENHAM BOARD TO QUIT Calls For Resignation If Jones' Reorganization Plan Is Rejected Gives Managers Alterna- tive Of Presenting Satis- factory Program [By the Associated Press) Annapolis, May 11-Governor Nice) today requested the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys either to adopt immediately the plan for reorganization of the institution submitted by Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, present a satisfactory alternative plan, or resign. He made the request in a letter to Joseph H. Blandford, president of the board, and asked that a special board meeting he called on receipt of the letter. "I have kept in close touch with the negotiations between Col. Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commis- sioner, and the board of managers of your institution." the Governor wrote. Quotes Official Record - "I approved the statute, authorizing the State to accept the Cheltenham property, on April 15, 1937; but. due to delayed action on the part of your board, your resolution, implementing the act. was not passed until Septem- ber 28, 1937. "The record, furnished me by the State Employment Commissioner, showed that his department started on the work necessary to induct the em- ployes of the institution into the State service on October 5, 1937, and that his survey, analysis and the necessary fit- ness tests were completed and for- warded to you on March 4, 1938. Cites "Grave Deficiencies" "The record shows that, in addition to inviting the attention of your board to the grave deficiencies in your man- agement and your employes, as shown by his survey, the State Employment Commissioner made constructive rec- ommendations, not only for reorgani- zation of the institution along the lines of other State juvenile correc- tional institutions, but for the neces- sary redistribution of your budget for 1938-1939 in the interest of reor- ganization and higher efficiency. "In making this survey and these recommendations, the State Employ- ment Commissioner acted under the provisions of Section 6. Article 647. Acts of 1920, which requires that the State Employment Commissioner in- vestigate the efficiency of all classified employes, methods of administration, etc., and make recommendations for increased efficiency and economy. "It appears that your board has failed to remedy the conditions com- plained of, and continues to delay and obstruct reorganization of your insti- tution in a manner which can no longer be tolerated. Cheltenham is now a State institution, and the conditions, which have been a source of complaint for years past, will not be permitted to continue. "I, therefore, request, immediately upon receipt of this letter, that you call a special meeting of the board of managers for its consideration, and, at that meeting, you either adopt the State Employment Commissioner's en- tire recommendations for reorganiza- tion and redistribution of your budget. or present a satisfactory alternative. "If the members of your board are unwilling to perform their duties as managers of Cheltenham by taking the action that is vitally necessary to its reorganization, I request that all the members of the Cheltenham board forward to me their resignations forth- with, and thus permit me to appoint, as successors, citizens who will assume this important public duty and carry it to a prompt conclusion." Blandford, president of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys, declined comment today on an ultimatum from Governor Nice de- manding board agreement to Chelten- ham's reorganization or the managers' resignations. - Blandford said he would make no statement until he had received the letter.
