title: PROBE ADVOCATED FOR CHELTENHAM: GRAND JURY CRITICIZES ADMINISTRATION OF SCHOOL FOR NEGRO BOYS WOULD HAVE RIGID SURVEY MADE BY COMMITTEE APPOINTED BY GOVERNOR
full_text: PROBE ADVOCATED FOR CHELTENHAM Grand Jury Criticizes Ad- ministration Of School For Negro, Boys Vould Have Rigid Survey Made By Committee Ap- pointed By Governor A complete investigation of the Cheltenham School for Boys, a Negro reformatory, by a committee appointed by Governor Nice was recommended yesterday by the grand jury. In a special report filed in Criminal Court, the jurors, through their fore- man, C. Delano Ames, criticized the administrative and physical facilities of the institution, which was taken over by the State by a legislative act in 1937. Types Of Training Advocated The investigating committee, the report said, should be composed of Negro and white members "from prop- erly trained institutional executives who would set up a proper course of training and management along the lines of the Maryland Training School for Boys at Loch Raven." The report advocated: Military training. Vocational and academic education. Parole and supervision. Dietary and sanitation training. Moral and religious training. Segregation of communicable dis- case cases. Installation of a group of Negro teachers, cottage masters and in- stitutional executives under mixed board of managers, the members of which would not re- ceive compensation or hold execu- tive positions. a Lack Of Cooperation Charged The jury also recommended the im- mediate adoption of a report made by Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, which said that in- capable and unfit employes should not remain on the institution's pay roll. "From our observations and in- quiry," the jury report said, "there is apparently no responsible head of this institution to whom the other em- ployes can look for leadership or ad- vice. There is a very decided lack of cooperation between the parole de- partment, vocational training and ex- ecutive departments of this institution, and it would appear to use that this lack of cooperation begins at the top. In other words, with its board of man- agers. Committee On Report "It would be our recommendation that if this board is not willing to act upon the recommendations of the var- ious departments of the State in the solution of their difficulties that they step out or be replaced by the Governor with a suitable board which will definitely take the matter to heart and make a job of it." The special report was submitted by a grand jury committee headed by Alfred D. L'Esperance, and consisting of W. Emerson Brown, Philip G. Schwaab, Sr., and George H. Harper.

title: RITCHIE SAYS HE'LL RENAME MANY TO POSTS: WILL SEND "GREEN BAG" TO SENATE THURSDAY FOR CONFIRMATION JANNEY SUCCESSOR IS NOT DECIDED ON GOVERNOR HAS NOT ANNOUNCED WHO WILL BE INSURANCE COMMISSIONER
full_text: RITCHIE SAYS HE'LL RENAME MANY TO POSTS Will Send "Green Bag"To Senate Thursday For Confirmation JANNEY SUCCESSOR IS NOT DECIDED ON Governor Has Not An- nounced Who Will Be In- surance Commissioner [Annapolis Bureau of The Sun] Annapolis, Feb. 17-With a few minor exceptions, Governor Ritchie's "green-bag" appointments will con- tinue in office those now holding the positions affected, the Governor said todas. The "green bag" will be sent to the Senate Thursday for confirmation. Thursday is the fiftieth day of the present session of the Legislature, and, according to the State, Constitution, the appointments must be presented to the upper house on or before that day. The appointments confirmed will become effective Mag 1. Janney Successor Not Included A proposed appointment for a suc- cessor to Stuart S. Janney, director and chairman of the State Board of Welfare, will not be sent to the Sen- ate, Governor Ritchie said. Mr. Jan- ney submitted his resignation Decem- ber 21. asking that it "take effect at your' (the Governor's) convenience." "The appointment of a successor to Mr. Janney," the Governor said, "will require considerable time and thought. title: B. B. SUNDERLAND SUCCEEDS KEARNS: CATONSVILLE MAN NAMED ACTING SUPERINTENDENT OF CHELTENHAM VISITING AGENT IN CHARGE OF PAROLED BOYS PICKED BY COMMITTEE
full_text: B. B. SUNDERLAND SUCCEEDS KEARNS Catonsville Man Named Act- ing Superintendent Of Cheltenham Visiting Agent In Charge Of ☐ Paroled Boys Picked By Committee Benjamin B. Sunderland, of Catons- ville, for many years a visiting agent in charge of boys on parole from the House of Reformation at Cheltenham, yesterday morning was named acting superintendent of the institution in place of Hal T. Kearns, who resigned. The announcement was made by Enoch Harlan, chairman of a commit- tee that has been operating the insti- tution temporarily. Mr. Harlan said Mr. Kearns' resignation, said to have been asked because of a lack of cooperation between Mr. Kearns and the personnel of the Negro boys' reform school, was accepted at the same time Mr. Sunderland was ap- pointed. "Mr. Sunderland is well and favor- ably known to the entire Cheltenham staff, and they received notice of his selection with the greatest satisfac- tion," Mr. Harlan said. "When the 400 inmates were noti- fied at their noon meal, there was a spontaneous handclapping, for they also know and have great respect for Mr. Sunderland. The committee, of course, is very much pleased with these demonstrations of good will." The committee headed by Mr. Har- lan, who also is one of the Baltimore city representatives of the institution, includes also M. Hampton Magruder. Hal Claggett and John E. McCormick, Mr. Sunderland's home is on Frederick avenue in Catonsville. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Down The Spillway
full_text: Down The Spillway THE latest version I have heard of the old, old variation on the old, old story of the boy who wanted to see the ball game and asked his boss well, anyway, the latest version I have heard is that of a colleague who has just got- ten passes for "Anthony Adverse" and is now applying for two days off in order to use them. NOW THAT the celebration of Har- vard's tercentenary has reached its height it may not be amiss to reproduce from Samuel Eliot Morison's history of the university this brief refrain which was popular in the eighteen-sixties: In the good old colony times, When we lived under the king, Each Saturday night we used to get tight, A-pouring down gin-sling. And Hollis used to roar, And Stoughton used to sing, When the rollicking rabble lay under the table, A-pouring down gin-sling. Professor Morison adds that in his opinion the year 1759 marks the "all- time high of student potation." It was in this year that the Board of Over- seers repealed the law prohibiting drinking of punch, decreeing that "it shall be deemed no offense if the schol- ars shall, in a sober manner, entertain one another and strangers with punch (which, as it is now usually made, is no intoxicating liquor)." HARVARD, of course, has not devoted herself exclusively to the consumption of alcohol, although her students, like students from the earliest time, have been inclined to mention this phase of activity more frequently than any other. I rather suspect there is less of this kind of vain boasting now than there used to be. Motor cars and other in- fluences have made college life very much like life in general and there is less need for those satisfying examples of exhibitionism, funny hats and drink- ing songs. FROM THE racing pages of the English newspapers, I cull the headline "Heel Trouble Epidemic," and pause to ob- serve that "heel trouble" is by no means confined to the turf. WHEN ONE enlists in a cause, it is a fine trait to be wholehearted in espousal of it. But I should hesitate to approve in a political campaign such thoroughgoing loyalty as a Republican woman speaker from New York urges upon Baltimore women. Her audience was told that, before entering a taxicab, she always asked whether the driver was a Democrat or Republican. In patronizing a restaurant she makes it her business to ascertain the politics of the waiter. When she buys shoes, it is only from a Republican clerk. In other words, she becomes a human interrogation point, upon the political persuasion of all with whom she comes in contact and refuses to traffic with the enemy. THAT MAY be a good rule for those who like that sort of rule. But if every- body followed it, there would be a pretty how-to-do. One's soup might be- come cold before proper understanding was had with a non-intellectual waiter as to his political alignment. A shoe salesman might be hard to convince that his liking for one or another candidate had anything to do with the proper fitting out of the customer. And as for taxi drivers, being shrewd readers of character, they would find no diffi- culty in changing their political coats to suit the fancy of the fare. Moreover, how are converts to be made if one eschews converse with opponents? On the whole, it is not easy to see how the scheme of things would be improved if Democrats dealt only with Democrats and Republicans only with Republicans. Only by close contact with the erring can brands be snatched from the burning. In a recent issue of the London Sun- day Observer there is an interesting article on the difficulties which the English General Postoffice encounters in its sorting of the mails from foreign parts. Of course, the problems of ex- traordinary handwriting and remark- ably wrong addresses are common, I suppose, to postoffices the world over. But it is my guess that, if only because of its vast and elaborate empire, the English postoffice does have to untanglea more of these puzzles than any other and that as a consequence its employés are, therefore, more adept in brilliant deductions and solutions. The writer in the Observer gives an example. He was shown a letter ad- dressed to some one at "Schlten- hammggos." The American might make a futile stab at supposing that the word was the name of some Welsh town, But, according to the English reporter, the sorter of the mails knew at once what it was. "Obviously," he said, "this is a letter to Cheltenham, Glos." Imagine that being "obvious" to anyone. It is, I think, of particular interest to note that the Observer's reporter was also told: "At present, we are having a very busy time, for nearly every mail from the United States contains from 80 to 150 doubtful cases' "-i. e., cases of handwriting so illegible or of place names so absurdly spelled that even the astonishing sixth sense of the expert "sorter" is baffled or left in a state of uncertainty. I wonder if the number of letters received here from England which prove equally perplexing to the American mailmen is as large. JOHN O'REN, Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: MANY CHANGES ADVOCATED AT CHELTENHAM: NEW OFFICIAL WOULD RAZE SEVERAL BUILDINGS AND EXPAND EDUCATION
full_text: MANY CHANGES ADVOCATED AT CHELTENHAM New Official Would Raze Several Buildings And Expand Education Dwight II. Ferguson, head of the State Department of Public Wel- fare's new division on institutions, yesterday asserted that all except four buildings at the Cheltenham School for Boys should be razed and replaced with well-constructed, modern units. Following a tour of the school Saturday, Mr. Ferguson described the administration building and six cottages now in use as obsolete. Earlier, J. Milton Patterson, head of the State Department of Public Welfare, declared the school was "a medieval penal institution." Would Keep Only Recent Ones Mr. Ferguson said the only build- ings that should be left standing are the recently constructed gym- nasium, hospital, boiler room and mule barn. The six cottages which house the Negro juvenile delinquents, school- rooms and workshops have been in use since the school was built in 1872, he said, "and do not seem worth repairing." He also recommended that the administration building. which houses offices, officers' quarters. dining room and kitchen, should be replaced with a new structure. Points Out Shortcomings Vance E. Thomas, superintend- ent of the school, pointed out to Mr. Ferguson and Lee L. Dopkin, a member of the board of directors of the Welfare Department, inade- quate toilet facilities, places where buildings were disintegrating and unsanitary kitchen facilities. Inmates of the institution, it was explained never have eaten with any utensil but a spoon, from cereal-type bowls. The kitchen floor constantly is wet from steam emitted from huge cooking pots and food is stirred with long wood- en sticks. The new welfare official also as- serted that a combination school and workshop building should be erected and that an athletic field should be provided for the boys in the institution. Needs Are Cited Needs cited by Mr. Thomas were: Installation of modern elec trical equipment to train the boys for vocational work such as tailoring, shoemaking and me- chanical lines. Provision of adequate shower facilities and replacement of bathroom facilities in use for more than thirty years. Hiring of approximately fif- teen staff members and teachers in addition to the present staff of fifty, which includes several conscientious objectors. Progress now is being made, Mr. (Continued on Page 14, Column 3) Changes Urged At Cheltenham (Continued from Page 18) Ferguson said, in establishing definite rules which would permit entrance of boys between twelve and sixteen years only and would bar admission of feeble-minded youngsters. 20% Are Mental Cases. Of the present inmates, approxi- mately twenty per cent. should have been committed to mental institutions, he said, and a number are either over age or too young to be committed to any reforma- Lory. Mr. Ferguson assumed his post this month, after serving for three years as director of the Child and Family Service, a private organiza- tion, at Honolulu. He was graduated from Oregon State Teachers' College, where he studied horticulture, and in 1927 received his Master of Education degree at Northwestern University. For the following thirteen years ne worked in family agencies in Chicago and Minneapolis.

The others are the Maryland Training School for Boys, the Montrose School for Girls and the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls. Mr. Ferguson has not made a study of these institutions as yet. full_text: Assembly Holds Brief Session, Then Adjourns Until Monday COMMITTEE POST FIGHTS SETTLED Judiciary And Chesapeake Bay Appointments Break Session's Monotony 17 Bills Introduced Before Assembly Adjourns Until Next Week [Annapolis Bureau of The Sun] Annapolis, Jan. 13-Maryland's legis- lators left for their homes tonight after a dull routine session had been ad- journed until Monday night. The only breaks in the monotony of today's gathering were settlement of fights over the chairmanships of two House of Delegates committees and the introduction of seventeen bills, the first to come into the 1937 session in any numbers. full_text: TRUSTEES APPROVE CHELTENHAM BILL Reformatory's Board Passes On Proposal For State Control Measure To Be Introduced In General Asscıńbly By Republicans A bill to give the State control of Cheltenham Reformatory for Negro Boys has been drawn up and approved by the reformatory's board of trustees, Morris A. Rome, member of the Board of State Aid and Charities, announced yesterday. It will be introduced to the General Assembly by a number of Republican Senators as an administration measure, Mr. Rome said. Among those sponsor- ing it will be Senator Melvin L. Fine of Baltimore and Senator J. David Baile of Carroll county. Board Is Named The bill provides that the institution shall be known henceforth as the Cheltenham School for Boys. All of its property in Prince George's county is to be deeded to the State, with the exception of $30,000 in cash, which is to be kept by the present trustees and invested as a trust fund for the school and employes. The following are named in the bill as a board of managers: The Governor of Maryland, to serve ex officio. WILLARD W. ALLEN, JOSEPH C. BRISCOE, FREDERICK DOUGLASS, GEORGE MC- DONALD and JOHN O. SPENCER, to serve for a period ending June 1, 1938. ENOCH HARLAN, HOWARD C. HILL, JOHN E. MCCORMACK, BLOSSIE R. MILLER and JAMES E. STEUART, to serve for a period ending June 1, 1939. JOSEPH H. BLANDFORD, HAL B. CLAGETT, J. AMOS DAVIS, WILLIAM H. GIBBONS and M. HAMPTON MAGRUDER, to serve for a period ending June 1, 1940. At the expiration of their present terms the managers may be reap- pointed, or their successors appointed. for a term of three years, the bill provides. title: A LAND OF PROMISE: SOUTHERN MARYLAND IS AFTER THE RIGHT SORT OF PEOPLE FARMS FOR THOSE WHO WORK THE EXACT SITUATION AS TO THE NEGRO--SOME LIGHTS AND SIDELIGHTS ON THE GREAT PROBLEM
full_text: A LAND OF PROMISE FARMS FOR THOSE WHO. WORK Southern Maryland Is After The Right Sort Of People. The Exact Situation As, To The Ne- gro-Some Lights And Sidelights On The Great Problem. [From a Staff Correspondent.1 La Plata, Charles County, Md., April 25. Down at the southern extremity of the Western Shore of Maryland, where the Chesapeake's noble waters sweep onward to the sea, and where the broad Potomac rolls in its southeasterly course to join the Chesapeake there is an Eden of beauty and sunshine, of flowering hilltops and emerald fields and of fringes of woodlands bursting into the freshest green of the springtide. And as these words are penned there comes through the open windows the heavy fragrance of lilacs. They have been in full bloom for four weeks now. The fruit trees have blossomed and the dog- wood has broken out its banners of white and gold. The birds are in a very riot of music. Bless them they demand no guar- antee fund. They are singing all the operas of nature and now is heard the crystal. pure note of Bob White to let you know that he, too, is in the company and that he promises to raise two families this season. Down in this angle of the Potomac and the Chesapeake lie the counties of Charles, St. Mary's and Calvert. This is the land of promise. This is the Southern Mary- land that is about to be discovered as the new Canaan. The 40 years are about up. Everybody here wants to forget them. The Climate Prodigal. Here the climate is prodigal, the soil rich and the land plenty, but the white people are comparatively few. The old white stock of Charles county is land-poor in having so many acres, and money-poor in not having enough division of intelligent white labor to bring forth riches from the earth's bosom. The State Bureau of Immigration has already sent a number of fariners to this section. These have received a hearty wel. come and are doing well. Some are grow- ing rich. There was told in the first article of this series that the exact situation con- cerning the negro would be shown. The population of Charles county in 1900 was 17,662. In the year 1909 there were 1,801 white voters registered and 1,913 colored voters, being a colored majority of 112. To read of this difference in times of political excitement would lead the aver- age person to suppose that there must be a constant warfare between the races. Nothing is further from the truth. The white people are uniformly kind to their colored help and neighbors, and the ne- groes are polite to all, whether they oc- cupy the positions of servants to the white gentry or are independent workmen and farmers. "We-Sort" A Peculiar Word. There is no spot on earth where the two races dwell together in greater harmony, no spot where a white Democrat would more promptly rush to the defense of his black or "we-sort" friends. By the way, "we-sort" is a word that belongs to this locality. It is the people of mixed blood and is a name that they have bestowed upon themselves. As the white people are true to the ne- groes, so are colored people, with all their frailties, loyal to their Caucasian employ ers, landlords or friends. Each needs the other. The black man depends upon the counsel of the white and the opportuni- ties given to him to live in plenty and se- curity. The farmer needs the labor of the colored help and wishes that double the number lived in the county. Cases of long and continuous service are common. The little black boy who drove the writer five miles from Bel Alton to La Plata proudly boasted that he had worked three years for Mr. Wills, and told that his late father had been in the same service for 26 years and was the best driver in the county. But They Dominate Politically. But all this does not alter the fact that the white men of affairs, the owners of thousands of acres, the proprietors of banks and stores and hotels, the men who own sawmills and all who pay taxes are dominated politically by the negro major- Ity when it comes to administering public affairs and building up the county to where she should be with her generous natural resources. It so happens that the intelligence and means are on one side and the votes on the other. It is an actual fact that the negroes of La Plata and its vicinity did not know of the vetoing of the Digges bills until eight days after the Governor's act. One or two residents, more as a joke than any thing else, told them that the bills had been signed and that they could never again vote. That news spread among them rapidly enough, but they dismissed it as something they could not help, and, in fact, they did not seem to take it greatly to heart. That the real truth was so long in finding its way about exhibits the grade of intelligence that is common among them. And He Threw Shad Roe Away. Last Tuesday Mr. Walter M. Page, man- ager of the New. Wills Hotel, bought some fine fat roe shad, fresh from Port To- bacco Creek, for the dinner that day. Mr. Harry Malcolm, formerly of Baltimore, slapped the writer on the leg and said: "Set your mouth for a shad roe break- fast tomorrow morning, my boy." A few minutes later Mr. Malcolm dashed breathless into the hotel looking for Mr. Page. Then he darted out again and ran to the kitchen. Then he came out per- spiring and growling. "Never saw anything to beat it," he said. "Here's a nigger who was fairly raised on the banks of a creek that pro- duces the best shad in the world, and he's gone and done that!" "Done what? Who is the villain?" "Why. that big black fellow. Pearl, had those fish to clean. He cleaned out en- trails, roe and all, and there it is Iying on the ash heap.". There was no fish roe for breakfast next morning, and every time Mr. Malcolm sees Pearl now he says: "There goes that price- less jewel, that black pearl." Why Dr. Owens Lost A Vote. The writer went to a stable yard with a gentleman of La Plata whose horse, while being unhitched, showed signs of a cold. The black stable hand, very sympathetic, said: "I dunno what make he cough dat way." "Wait until we get out of here," whis- pered the owner. "I want to tell you a story about that colored voter." Outside he said: "That intelligent elector was go- ing to support Dr. T. S. Owens for the Legislature. Suddenly he announced that the Doctor should by no means get his vote. He was pressed for a reason. His reply was: "I know all 'bout him and what he do in de Legislatur. He jes' want to go dere and eff he git dere he gwine to put up de price on all medicines. I hear all about it. Den ef I need a little bit o' quinine to stop a cold, stid o' payin' 10 cents like I does now it'll cost me jist $1. Yo' think! Doc's a nice man, a wery nice gentleman. I got any dollahs to throw away? No, sah. but he look out fo' hissef an' I gotter look out fer myself. I don't blame him none."" An Easy Way To Carry Goslings. Here's another one. They're all true stories from life, too. Mr. Adrian Posey has a boy from Cheltenham School, bound to him until he becomes 21 years old. Ar- thur is a "we-sort." Mr. Posey had a pet goose, which, with 13 handsome goslings, went down to the creek to go swimming and mosey around for tid-bits. Arthur was sent down late in the afternoon to fetch home the goose and her brood. He returned after a time and said be couldn't somehow get the flock together and start them homeward as they had minds of their own. "Now, you go down there and get those geese," ordered Mr. Posey, "and don't you come back without them." Arthur did it all right. He drove the mother goose home and carried the goslings, but he took pre- caution to kill every gosling in the batch. He had them all. For some reason or other Arthur jumped away from home that even- ing and wasn't caught for several days afterward, but the trouble is all patched up now. It is this high grade of intellect that the men of affairs do not quite relish in the responsibilities of state and in decisions on momentous questions of county govern- ment; but there all feeling ends, and you'll have a better chance with a Charles county freeholder if you'd maltreat his driving horse or kick his hunting dog than if you'd injure one of his faithful servitors. They May Give Some Away. But the Charles county man is going to populate his county. His mind is made up to that. He sees that he owns too much land severally and individually. One of them has 2,700 acres in one piece. These farms are going to be cut up into smaller ones, and the new people are going to come into the social and industrial life of the region if they have to give some farms away to start the ball to rolling. Said Mr. W. Mitchell Digges: "I think I know of at least 100 men who will give an average of 50 acres apiece, if necessary, to attract a thrifty class of people here so that we can develop our great resources. "The main thing to do, howeler, is to have a company with headquarters in Bal- timore and with a capital of from $250,000 to $500,000 to buy up our riduculously cheap lands, resurvey them and divide them up into convenient farms of mod- erate size for the new settlers. As it is now, farms are of certain sizes, and if halved or quartered sometimes they are still of the same total acreage and do not always admit of the best partition to suit the needs of the newcomers. For Less Than $3 An Acre. "Our lands are going up some in price, and those which are in particularly pic- turesque locations, particularly those which overlook the Potomac river, are eagerly sought for homes. Yet all the prices are low. I sold recently a 1,200- acre tract for $3,400. That was actually less than $3 an acre. In fact, some of our laud has sold as low as $1 an acre, and any quantity of desirable land can be bought for $10 an acre. "We can already see the signs of the times in the movement of real estate. I know of one attorney in Baltimore who is backed by $100,000 to buy up cheap lands here, especially at trustees' sales. The movement for the establishment of smaller farmsteads is also well under way, since there are now many containing from 125 to 150 acres only. That this is the cor- reet thing I have no doubt, for there are many large landowners who are making absolutely nothing on their places. It cannot but be wise for them to sell por- tions of their property and thus obtain capital to work the remainder by the best agricultural methods and by the most mod ern of labor-saving machinery. A Chance For Capital. "When we consider the problem of the world's food supply there is every incen- tive to work this naturally rich county to its utmost productiveness, and then will money flow in to us, then will come more and better transportation and every com- fort and convenience, and our people will be better off. "Even now the chance for the invest- ment of capital is gilt-edged. The pres ent enhancement of values would pay a very great interest, while the advance over the prices of a few years ago would show a tremendous gain. With a monered interest in us in Baltimore the people there would direct immigration this way, and the newcomers would find nothing to dis courage them, but everything to make them happy and prosperous. "Our lands are kind and fertile, and they vary from a rich brown loam to the stiff white oak soil. There are at least 50.000 acres of this land easily and cheaply obtainable. Our lands are particularly adapted to alfalfa and the grasses, and this suggests great dairying operations and cattle-raising right between the two fine markets of Baltimore and Washington. There are fine opportunities for grazing sheep on the high hills. Only a week ago one farmer sold two hogs at $65, and he is selling lambs at $12 apiece and calves at $15 each. "Fruit thrives finely nearly everywhere when attention is paid to it. I have in mind an old orchard which had been pro- ducing the verlest scrubs of apples. The owner's brother had been appointed as- sistant to the State Entomologist. This brother went home, sprayed the trees three times, and the results were magical, for finer apples were never seen than those trees have since borne. "So, too, with wheat. Some have thought that our lands were unfavorable since. while a good stout straw was produced, in some places the heads were not satis- factory. Then it was found that the soil needed liming, and when this was done the best of wheat was produced. Tobacco Giving Way A Bit. "The old tobacco crop has been done away with by some of our farmers for what they consider better paying things. With many owners the efforts used to be expended on a few acres, while the rest of their lands went to waste. Then it is always 12 months before there is any money return for the tobaced, owing to the time required in the curing. "But all that is past now, and the new spirit of Charles county is coming into its own, and prosperity will be the word from now on." S. C. A. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Lions Club Gift Used For Equipment For Boys
full_text: Lions Club Gift Used For Equipment For Boys Of a $500 gift by the Baltimore (Downtown) Lions Club to the Bal- timore Youth Commission, $250 has been used to finance and equip a a drum and bugle corps at the Cheltenham School for Boys, Judge Charles E. Moylan, of the Supreme Bench of Baltimore and commis- sion chairman, said yesterday in a letter to the club. An additional $28 was used to buy soft balls and bats for the boys at the Maryland Training School for Boys, the jurist said. Baltimore Lions, his letter added, "can be very proud of the fact that they are helping in the rehabilita tion of the boys at both schools. 1 happen to know that the boys them- selves are most appreciative of these needed gifts.". title: Mabel Boll's Boy Friend Tries To Kill Himself
full_text: Mabel Boll's Boy Friend Tries To Kill Himself Professional Hoofer Found On Nice Estate Of "Queen Of Diamonds": : Nice, France, May 15 (AP)-A dancing boy friend of Mabel Boll shot himself on the lawn of her new villa here today, but if he was trying to kill himself, the police said, his aim was inaccurate. Also, if the 27-year-old professional hoofer, Georges Charlot, was despair- ing because the "Queen of Diamonds" was about to throw him over, which is the police theory, the Countess Dela Porcerie (Mabell Boll's present name) wouldn't confirm it. The countess, who is divorced from the man who gave her the title, found Charlot in a pool of blood on the lawn when she returned to her villa at Saint Jean Capperrant after a shopping trip to Nice. A bullet was extracted from Char- lot's side, and physicians at the Nice Clinic said he will recover. full_text: An English Village Remembers GOSSIP OF TURPIN AND CHAUCER HANDED DOWN FROM FATHER TO SON WHAT by CECIL ROBERTS WHAT little things put us on the trail of discovery! I live in a tiny village of the English Chilterns, those hills that command a view of the Thames on one side and of the Oxford plain on the other. I suppose it is more correct to call my village a hamlet, it is so small. It possesses two inns, but one of these is on the highway to Oxford and does not really belong to us. But we are grateful to it, for the whole of my village hides away behind it. It is optimistically called the Trav- eler's Rest and stands at a point, after a straight mile, where motorists are "all out" to tackle the hill behind it, while those com- ing down are equally "all out" to see what they can touch or the level. The travelers seldom rest; therefore, they go past at anything from sixty to eighty miles an hour. Nor can I assert that they miss much. It is a large gabled house, flat-faced and roofy. Its drabness is relieved by two things: a well-painted sign and a well-kept garden in front. The original Traveler's Rest, where travelers by horse or carriage, in the old days when ten miles an hour was good going in fair weather, probably did rest-this is across the road and is now a picturesque private house. 业 THE OTHER INN, the real inn of the village, has both history and beauty. I discovered one day, almost by accident, that it is linked with romance, as we see it today. Mine host, Mr. Harris, an old soldier, is adept with a gun, a tankard of ale, a handful of darts, a skittle ball, a row of kidney beans, a ferret in a bag, a car that wants "looking at," or anything else in which an all-round man with unfailing good nature can excel. My admirable Mr. Harris one day gave me a start. I had been looking at the Golden Ball and had come to the conclusion that it had once been a coach station. It has a space in front of the old taproom that suggested a former inn yard into which the flying coach had come for a change of horses or for addi- tional horse power to tackle the old Oxford road that winds up behind. The inn itself has a delightful bay window that juts out into the road where it curves through the heart of the village. The Golden Ball shines gaily in the sun with its red tiles HOME and yellow washed walls, and seen from the surrounding hills its shape, color and position in the floor of the valley are altogether a per- fect example of the English scene. I HAD KNOWN Mr. and Mrs. Harris for three years before their bombshell was dropped on me. As they kept an ever open door and heart, I had turned to them a hundred times in do mestic emergencies. When a sudden descent of visitors for tea had used up all the bread, it was to Mrs. Harris that my servant fled for supplies. When a field rat attacked my larder, again its was Mr. Harris, with a ferret, Sally, and his dog, Ponto, who delivered us from the raider. When I had a houseful and another had to be "slept," it was Mrs. Harris who took him in. A sudden shortage of matches or candles, a breakdown in the newspaper de- livery, a demand for stamps after. postoffice hours-the Golden Ball never failed me. This readiness to help was all the more gracious because I was the inn's worst cus- tomer. I am neither a drinker nor a smoker by choice. I make the effort in sheer socia bility, but I should never be aware of the absence of either of these things. There is always a smile in the Golden Ball at my ef- forts to drink beer. Any friends gifted that way I eagerly take along to make up for my deficiency. I like to sit in the parlor and hear the vanishing Oxfordshire, as opposed to the expanding Oxford accent. You meet there men still wise in the way of horses, followers of the plow, builders of ricks, thatchers, men who seemed doomed to be the last of a great line extinguished by the machine. But for some reason I had never regarded Mr. Harris as a repository of local history. Compared with some of the Methuselahs of the village he is a mere boy and a newcomer. The air of the sergeant, the old soldier with Indian experience, the retired Oxfordshire constable, redoubtable in the tug-of-war, still hangs about him, for all his handiness with a beer pump or a spade. I MENTIONED my suspicions abut the coach station. It was as if I had touched a spring. All I had surmised was correct. He showed me the place where the incoming mail coach from Aylesbury to Henley turned in, also the "Tantivy" from Birmingham; a red coach; the "Magnet" from Cheltenham, a blue; the "Alert" from Oxford, and the Gloucester and Stroud Mails. "No wonder Tom King and Dick Turpin hung about here," said Mr. Harris. He was building a hen coop at that mo- ment and I was glad he did not see my face. Astonishment quickly changed to incredulity. Of course, this was the kind of local yarn one might expect. Dick Turpin was a hero of mine at 7. I can recall now the sore place on my thumb made by a pair of scissors, and the mess of gum on my fingers and clothes. My father had returned one day with a large colored cardboard sheet on which was painted the wonderful pictorial history of Dick Tur- pin's great ride to York. I worked feverishly by night cutting out and pasting up on the plan the toll gate, the astonished keeper, the six-barred gate, the leaping horse and the great Dick going over it, masked, with pistol cocked. There was rebellion when I had to go to bed without the tollhouse's roof on. Waking early, I descended through a sleep- ing house and in cold room returned to the scissors and the gum pot. Oh! that ecstacy of childhood, evoked by colored cardboard and gallant, defiant Dick! DICK TURPIN had ridden to York along the Great North road. I could not believe that brave Black Bess had cantered past my gar- den, or that, booted and spurred, the high- wayman had darkened the threshold of the Golden Balt. "Haven't you seen his hiding place?" asked Mr. Harris, driving home a nail. "No," I answered, and added, half in pro- test: "But Turpin couldn't have been here- he was on the Great North road!" "Well, he was born in Essex and worked all round London. He knew every inch of the Chilterns. He'd places to 'dive' in when it got hot for him. Come and have a look, sir." I followed Mr. Harris, determined not to be led away by the mere thirst for romance. The old ostlers' taproom is now a private living room, but in the old days it commu- nicated with the parlor for the gentry. Be- tween these two rooms there is a thick chim- ney stack. As is usual with these old chim- neys, there is a bend in it. This bend had been completely hidden by boarding. To my surprise Mr. Harris opened a cupboard door, revealing a narrow staircase leading to a bed- room above. There was also a space in the bend for a man to stand and look down THATCHING ROOF IN RURAL ENGLAND Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. There was a main staircase to the room above. Fur- ther inquiries elicited the fact that Turpin and King had "worked" the Oxford and Wash- ington roads. Mr. Harris's exciting news was largely confirmed. 业 WITHIN a week I had a second shock. At that time I was employing an old gardener. He was so old he was counting up the eighties-that he could not go up a ladder because of dizzi- ness, kneel because of rheumatism or dig be- cause of lumbago. He had been born in the village, as had his forebears. He had spent his pennies, he told me, in my drawing room, when it was a sweetshop, and had seen my tall poplars arrive on a hand barrow. One day I asked him what he had done with the grass from the lawn mover. "I've put it on the Roman road," he said. "The what?" I cried, jumping out of my skin, "The Roman road, sir." "Where is the Roman road?" "Why, this lane, sir. It was the Oxford road when I was a boy, but we always called it the Roman road." "Who's we?" "Oh, everybody. My dad and my grand- dad always called it the Roman road. It was the way them Romans walked to Dorchester, They came over by the ford at Henley and up Friday street and down the Mile, and along 'ere and up the hill where this lane runs into the new Oxford road again, I've 'eard my granddad say 'is granddad said that Mr. Chaucer, the King's poet, used to walk this way. And King Charles, when he was skeered out of Oxford, came down 'ere and went into them woods to avoid Henley, where they were waiting for him. And 'e 'ad a friend up at Fawley Court, who was now against 'im, but 'e winked and let King Charles go by. Ev course, I've only 'eard this, and none of us was scholars." I LET the old man go on, though my head was reeling and a hundred questions came to my lips. When he had finished and started clip- ping again, I went straight into the house to keep calm. There were certain headlines to. this astonishing information. My lane was a Roman road before it was the old Oxford road. "Mr." Chaucer had walked along it. King Charles had fled down it. I have heard that local tradition is often more trustworthy than the written word. My gardener was 85. The recollections of his grandfather could carry back an additional seventy years, say. The grandfather's grand- father, therefore, might well have been liv- ing in the village on the day King Charles fled through it. It should not be difficult to find whether the King had come this way. That he had been at Henley and Oxford, I knew. It seemed probable. he might have journeyed this way, by the hedge of my garden. But I wanted to pursue the Chaucer trail, Charles could wait. I returned to the garden and found some- thing to do by the hedge, where the old man was clipping. "I suppose," I said casually. "Mr. Chaucer was on his way to Oxford when he went past here?" The old man stopped clipping. "Not at all, sir. He was going to visit 'is son at Ewelme." "Ewelme?" "It's about ten miles from here, sir; just off the Oxford road, Mr. Chaucer's son's buried there, where old Henry VIII 'ad 'is 'oneymoon-one of 'em. My granddad said the poet was very fond of the country. He wrote a lot about it, an' 'e was a bit bawdy, too." I HAD HEARD this criticism before, but I never expected to hear it from a gardener. My curi- osity was aroused. I had not seen Ewelme. That afternoon I went there. I have not yet recovered from the fact that for three years I lived near to anything so lovely and surprising without discovering it. Surely it is one of the loveliest old churches in England. It has a battlemented exterior, a gargoyled tower and an alms chapel added Continued on next page tomb, was Alice Chaucer. And this Alice Chaucer was the daughter of the Thomas Chaucer, whose tomb lies near by. Duke John gave to the church his mother's-the duchess-tomb, the front cover and the shields on the tomb of Thomas Chaucer, bis grandfather. And this Thomas Chaucer, who died in 1434, was the son of Mr. Chaucer the poct. THE FACTS, therefore, so far as the records in this church go, are not incompatible with my gardener's astonishing story. All the bedrooms have dormer windows, with a sitting room below each. Near by there is a chapel, also of Tudor brick, with square-headed, stone- mullioned windows and rectangular drip- stones. This noble group of buildings clings to the hillside, with the village and its water- cress bed below... But it was concerning Mr. Chaucer that I had come hither, so I hurried into the church. I must not digress, though sorely tempted. I could write pages about the roofs. YET.it is the tombs that make this church so rich in interest. That of the Duchess of Suf- folk is a masterpiece. She has a ducal coronet grandfather. That was getting well back into history. It is almost safe to assume that these ancestors were "illiterate," which meant that they relied on hearsay. They had not read about King Charles or Mr. Chaucer or the Roman road. The legacy of oral tradition ac- counts for their knowledge. IN THE matter of King Charles, I was soon able to confirm the legend by strict historical fact. The King fled from Oxford on April 27, 1646. Disguised as a groom, he rode toward Fawley to avoid the town, then in the hands of the Parliamentarians. He turned aside and went by a bridle path through Hen- ley Park and spent the night at Hambledon Manor. The friend who "winked," according to my gardener, and let him go by, was Sir Bulstrode Whitelock, then living at Fawley Court. All that my gardener told me coin- cided also with the facts concerning Bulstrode Whitclock. He loomed very importantly in the life of that strange woman, Christina of Sweden, to whose court he was sent to Crom- well. At the time of his arrival at court she had already made plans to abdicate the throne, at a considerable price, and settle in Rome. There she became a Catholic, to the rage and consternation of Protestant Sweden, kept a salon, turned the head of a cardinal and, in turn, flouted and courted the Pope. 业 BUT at the time of Whitelock's arrival, in 1653, no one except the Queen dreamed of the Roman adventure. She took a liking to the pompous Ambassador. Gradually he gained her favor. Then one day she took him aside. "I have great confidence in your honor and judgment, and therefore, though you are a stranger, I shall acquaint you with a busi- ness of the greatest consequence to me in the world." In the open space below the tomb-the sexton supplies a cushion and loves to make you go down on your hands and knees there is a gruesome, emaci- ated figure of the duchess in death. title: PEDESTRIAN IS KILLED WHEN AUTOS COLLIDE: POLICE UNABLE TO LEARN WHICH CAR STRUCK MISS EDITH MASER BOTH OF DRIVERS TO FACE CHARGES VICTIM WAS CROSSING PARK HEIGHTS AVENUE AT TIME OF CRASH
full_text: PEDESTRIAN IS KILLED WHEN AUTOS COLLIDE Police Unable To Learn Which Car Struck Miss Edith Maser BOTH OF DRIVERS TO FACE CHARGES Victim Was Crossing Park Heights Avenue At Time Of Crash A 27-year-old woman, walking across Park Heights avenue, at Violet avenue, last night, was almost instantly killed when two automobiles collided at the intersection and one or both of them hit her. After questioning the drivers for three hours, Northern district police were unable to tell whose machine had killed Miss Edith Maser, assistant buyer in a downtown department store, and charged both with having caused her death. Had Stepped From Trolley Miss Maser, going from her home at 2117 Presbury street to visit her sis- ter, Mrs. Charles Yaker, at 2814 Violet avenue, had stepped off a northbound trolley car and started to walk across Park Heights avenue when the two machines collided. One, southbound on Park Heights avenue, was driven by Albert W. Boss, 57, of the 3100 block Sumter avenue. The other, operated by Edward J. Offit, 29, of the 4600 block Park Heights avenue, was eastbound on Violet ave- nue. After the crash, Miss Maser was found unconscious in the trolley-car tracks. She was taken to the West Baltimore General Hospital by an- other motorist, Morris A. Richmond, of 3701 Park Heights avenue. She died of a skull fracture a few minutes after admission to the hospital. Question Put Up To Coroner The question of whose automobile killed Miss Maser will be placed be- fore Dr. Hubert Gurley, automobile coroner, at an inquest November 20. Several other persons were injured in other accidents in and near the city. James Cannon, 51, of 3211 Bayonne avenue, suffered a scalp laceration which required eleven stitches to close when his car overturned after the steering wheel broke on the Crain Highway near Cheltenham. He was treated at the South Baltimore Gen- eral Hospital. Accused Of Drunken Driving Ralph Grogan, of Fullerton, was charged with driving under the in- fluence of liquor after his automobile allegedly sideswiped another car on the East Joppa road, about two miles from Towson. The other machine was driven by Edward Brown, of Media, Pennsylvania. Grogan was arrested by Patrolman Martin Chenoweth, who stopped him as he drove into Towson. Boy Knocked From Bicycle A 16-year-old Negro was seriously injured when he was knocked from his bicycle by one car and struck by another automobile as he fell. The accident occurred on Myrtle avenue, near Lanvale street. Elwood Ross, 1100 block Stockton street, was bumped from the bicycle by a car driven by Samuel Skurow, 3000 block Oakmont avenue, according to police. The second automobile which struck the boy was coming from the opposite direction, and was driven by William Williams, Negro, 700 block Barnes court, police said. Ross was taken to the University Hospital, where physicians said he had suffered severe skull injuries. Williams was charged with driving without an operator's license. No charges were placed against Skurow. Three Escape From Fire Three persons escaped with slight Injuries from a burning truck which had struck a pole and overturned on Dulany Valley road, several miles north of Towson. The vehicle was de- stroyed by fire. Blair F. Kluger, his wife and infant child, of Sunbury, Pa., were treated at the office of Dr. R. O. Sellman, of Towson, for shock and slight cuts and bruises. Kluger told Sergt. Talbott Kelly, of Towson police, he had lost control of the vehicle on a curve. The owner of the truck, Vincent Palmayano, also of Sunbury, who was following in an- other truck, took the Kluger family homes. The Towson Fire Department ex- tinguished the blaze. Aided By Grid Team's Doctor A doctor attending a football team playing in Herring Run Park found his services utilized by a boy who was injured in an automobile accident. Samuel Brocato, 7, of the 4500 block Harford road, was hit by a car driven by John P. Jenkins, 21, of the 2300 block Southern avenue, a player who had just left the game. Jenkins took the lad back to the field, where Dr. Joseph Castagna, physician and coach of the Iroquois team, took seven stitches in a cut over the boy's left eye. Samual later was taken to St. Joseph's Hospital. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: NEGRO BOY OF 15 HELD AS SLAYER OF BRILLIANT: SAID TO HAVE FIRED FROM ALLEY WHILE CELEBRATING CHRISTMAS FRIENDS GIVE TIP; POLICE LOCATE GUN YOUTH DENIES SHOOTING, BUT ADMITS OWNING GUN FOUND IN MATTRESS
full_text: NEGRO BOY OF 15 HELD AS SLAYER OF BRILLIANT Said To Have Fired From Alley While Celebrat- ing Christmas FRIENDS GIVE TIP; POLICE LOCATE GUN Youth Denies Shooting, But Admits Owning Gun Found In Mattress A 32-caliber pistol in the hand of a 15-year-old Negro celebrant of Christmas was said last night by po- lice to have caused the death of 23- year-old Hyman Bradiant carly Wednesday. The shooting occurred at Milliman street and North Broadway. Held under arrest at the North- eastern District Police Station was 15- year-old Virtus Lucas, 1.ho police as- serted admitted ownership of a .32- caliber nistol found sewed into a mattress at his home in the 1600 block of East Madison street. Lucas taken into custody on information furnished by two young Negro friends. Displayed Gun According to the story told by the two Negroes, whose names police re- fused to reveal. Lucas had spent Christmas Eve at the Ashland avenue home of one of them and during the evening had displayed a revolver with the remark: "This is my new pistol and I'm going to celebrate Christmas by trying it out." was Lucas later told them, the two Negroes informed police, that he had started to his Madisch avenue home about 1 A. M. and had stopped in an alley that runs between Milliman and Madison streets. There he decided to fire off his revolver, but, fearing the weapon might backfire, huddled against a fence while he stuck the gun around the corner into Milliman street. Had Just Left Girl At that moment, police believe. Bril- liant had just swung into Broadway from Madison street, where he had left a friend, Miss Sara Hawtof, at her home in the 900 block after spending the evening with her. on As Brilliant, walking south Broadway, stepped into the Milliman street intersection, police say, Lucas pulled the trigger of his pistol three times. One bullet struck Brilliant, po- lice believe, and he staggered to the corner of Broadway and Monument street, where a taxicab driver picked him up and took him to the Johns Hopkins Hospital. There he was pro- nounced dead. Meanwhile, Lucas' friends told t police, the Negro youth heard a scream r follow his shots and fled to his home. Peering from his window, they said. he saw police cruisers appear in the vicinity and search the neighborhood. Warned To Keep Silent The next day Lucas again came to the Ashland avenue home of one of the Negro youths, showed them the pistol he had displayed the night be- fore and said he had shot a man early that morning. After warning them to keep silent about the matter, he left the house, they asserted. In the meantime police were work- ing on the theory that Brilliant had been shot accidentally, probably by one of a group of Negroes engaged in an argument. John T. Beatty, the cab driver who took Brilliant to the hos- pital, declared Brilliant had muttered, "I've been shot three times by a Negro." At the hospital, however, it was found only one bullet had struck the youth, piercing his chest. Residents in the neighborhood, however, reported having heard three shots. Friends Tell Of Threat Thursday night, Lucas' friends said, the Negro youth came to one of them and threatened him because he "knew too much." Yesterday afternoon the youths decided to go to Capt. John R. Scheuler of the Northeastern po- lice district, and tell him their story. Captain Scheuler immediately sent a squad of officers to Lucas' home, but the youth was not there. Later he was arrested at the home of friends in the 1600 block of Milliman street. Still later police searched Lucas' home and found the pistol secreted in the mattress. Admits Owning Gun Lucas, who Captain Scheuler said had been an inmate of Cheltenham several times, refused to admit the shooting, despite several hours of questioning by police. He did admit ownership of the gun, however. Police said they would have the weapon ex- amined by ballistics experts today in order that its markings may be com- pared with the bullet removed from Brilliant's body. Brilliant graduated from Baltimore City College in 1929, and was said to be the sole support of a widowed mother, five brothers and a sister. He was employed as an accountant by an oil company and lived at 2236 Orleans street. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: HALF WAY
full_text: HALF WAY By passing last week the bill providing for State ownership and control of the Chelten- ham reformatory for colored boys, the Senate at Annapolis has done its part toward - the liquidation of a particularly unfortunate situation. The bill, which is the result of agreement between the Cheltenham trustees, including M. Hampton Magruder and Enoch Harlan, and the Board of State Aid and Charities, now awaits similar action by the House of Delegates. In view of the agreement among the lead- ers upon the desirability of the purposes of the measure, there is reason to expect that prompt consideration will be given it by the Delegates. The bill's sponsors stand ready to satisfy the curiosity of members upon any of its features, and it is clear that the opinion of penologists, welfare leaders and others who have given much thought to the plight of delinquent and vagrant colored boys is wholeheartedly behind this necessary meas- ure. The principal risk would appear to be that the bill might be lost in the confusion of the last ten days of the session. To avoid such an unfortunate conclusion to a good job, it is to be hoped that more than the minimum of delay can be avoided. POOR RELATION? Dexter Fellows is not available at the moment, but it ought not to be long before he is heard from in respect to the news from Italy that William F. Cody (Buffalo Bill to millions) was really an Italian "full of Fas- cist courage and daring." This will be a great surprise to some millions of Americans. Perhaps the Italian editor who made this surprising revelation had been reading the Dictionary of American Biography, which makes this observation about Buffalo Bill: "He dealt with facts in a large, free way, and he had a tendency after he became famous to make himself the central figure in the epi- sodes which he recounted. Most of his state- ments are inaccurate; many of them are preposterous, and he sanctioned, on the part of his publicity agents, a gross indulgence in fiction." This is a somewhat solemn descrip- tion of a man in the circus business, and the qualities mentioned do suggest fascism in its more innocent aspects. Mussolini being also in the circus business, ane of his editors may be forgiven for finding spiritual kinship. The incitement to all this Italian research into the life of Buffalo Bill appears to be a suit brought by alleged Italian heirs to re- cover a "large fortune" which Cody is sup- pased to have left in the United States. If Buffalo Bill left anything more than a hat and a pistol, it will be news to a lot of people; a fact which, when known in Italy, may dampen at least a little of the desire for consanguinity with the American plainsman. title: Cheltenham Board Tours Institution
full_text: Cheltenham Board Tours Institution Members of the new, all-Negro board of managers of the Chelten- ham School for Boys toured the institution's buildings and grounds yesterday during their second meeting. They also inaugurated a detailed study of the school through the six committees appointed at the board's organizational meeting last Friday at Annapolis. Next Meeting April 5 Comments and recommendations on the subjects of the investiga- tions will be made at the next meeting, scheduled for 1 P.M. Monday, April 5, at the training school. Fields being covered by these studies include curriculum, pupil activities, physical facilities, staff and supervision, administration and the philosophy and purpose of the school. All Members Present Dr. William E. Henry, president of the board, reported that all nine members were present for the day- long meeting at the school. It had been decided at the board's initial session that first- hand knowledge of the institution was essential for each member and that'a prompt inspection of facili- ties was desirable. At present the school lacks a superintendent, and no acting superintendent has been named by the new board. Dr. Henry has been delegated by the board to work closely with H. R. Harris, assistant superintendent. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: HENRY HEADS NEW BOARD AT CHELTENHAM: GROUP MEETS FOR FIRST TIME, PLANS VISIT TO SCHOOL MONDAY
full_text: HENRY HEADS NEW BOARD AT CHELTENHAM Group Meets For First Time, Plans Visit To School Monday By ANNE W. HUTCHISON [Sun Staff Correspondent) Annapolis, March 5-Members of the new, all-Negro board of man- agers of the Cheltenham School -for Boys held their first meeting here today and made plans for an all-day visit at the Negro training -school on Monday. Prior to the meeting, which was held in the Senate chamber of the State House, the board met with Governor Lane in the executive aoffices. e Dr. William E. Henry, president e of the Bowie State Teachers Col- lege, was elected president of the nine member group. Co-operation Promised Governor Lane assured the board members of his fullest co-operation and said he had "great confidence in the future of Cheltenham" under their guidance and management. "The fact that for twenty years Cheltenham has had a reputation for bad conditions and not fulfill- ing its purposes has not discour aged me," he said. "I am confident that something can be done about it." Thanking the new board mem- bers for agreeing to serve, he said he had selected their names from between 75 and 100 recommended to him. He said that both Thomas B. Sprague, chairman of the retir- ing mixed board and Wallace Reidt, associate director of the Criminal Justice Commission who had been working with the school in recent months, would be avail- able to the new board for advice on any questions and problems which might arise. Early Survey Planned In the course of the organiza- tion's meeting it was decided that the full board should make a sur- vey of the institution as soon as possible to learn the conditions that exist there. A number of committees were named by Dr. Henry to give spe- cial attention to certain points during the initial visit Monday which is scheduled for 10 A.Μ. Serving on these committees will be: Curriculum - Edward Wilson and Mrs. Violet Hill Whyte. Staff and Supervision - Mrs. Whyte and Mrs. Bertha B. Proctor, Physical Facilities-The Rev. John Thomas Colbert and Dr. James Arthur White. Activities of Pupils-Lieut. Col. William Brady and Charles E. Cornish, Philosophy and Purpose of School-Mr. Wilson and Willard W. Alten. Administration-- Mr. Allen and Mrs. Whyte. Mr. Sprague, who was present at the meeting, pointed out that II. R. Harris, assistant superintend- ent of Cheltenham, at present had no official status as acting superin- tendent, and it was suggested that Dr. Henry work closely with him. title: SPRAGUE DEFENDS DISMISSAL OF KIAH: SAYS ACTION OF OLD CHELTENHAM BOARD WAS UNANIMOUS
full_text: SPRAGUE DEFENDS DISMISSAL OF KIAH Says Action Of Old Chelten- ham Board Was Unanimous Thomas B. Sprague, president of the former board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys, yesterday reiterated his statement that the board was unanimous in its action leading to dismissal of Cal- vin L. Kiah as superintendent of the institution. "This action of the board was unanimous," Mr. Sprague said. "By that I mean it was unanimous with regard to the.six of the nine mem- bers present." Mr. Sprague made his statement after Dr. R. L. Jackson, Negro mem- ber of the recently resigned board, criticized the board for dismissing Mr. Kiah. Final Act Of Old Board The dismissal of Mr. Kiah, after a six-month probationary period, was the final official act of the re- tiring board. In his statement Dr. Jackson charged that, himself, J. Marshall Stewart and J. Grayson Luttrell were absent from the meeting and that Carroll Hynson, of Annapolis, another board member, asked to be excused from voting on the dismis- sal of Mr. Kiah. Dr. Jackson also charged that imeetings were held at irregular hours, and that it was impossible to know the time and place of board meetings. Lane To Meet With Board Mr. Sprague, in commenting on this criticism, stated that the board meeting of February 24 was set on January 26, and that mem- bers of the board were notified in plenty of time for the meeting, al- though no time was set. Mr. Sprague also said that due to his work along with two other members of the board serving grand jury duty, it was impossible to hold the meeting on February 24 before 3 P.M. It was after the February 24 meeting that Mr. Kiah was notified of his dismissal. Governor Lane will meet with the newly appointed nine-member all Negro board at an organization meeting at 3 P.M. today at the State House. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. O'DONNELL [Annapolis Bureau of The Sun] Annapolis, March 5-After almost two months' labor ostensibly directed toward effecting economies in State expenditures, the Legislature tonight brought forth a gross increase of $303,- 000 in the budget for the next two years-with roughly one third of the additional funds going to the Uni- versity of Maryland.  Actually, the net increase in the budget, however, will amount to only $87,000 in the two-year period, since Governor O'Conor, to meet pressure of the General Assembly, cut the ap- propriations to the Department of Welfare for 1942-1943 by approximately $216,000.  One Cut Is Made The months of labor of both the House Ways and Means Committee and the Finance Committee of the Senate, which received the $106,664,000 biennial appropriations bill early in January amid declarations for economy and reduced expenditure, produced only one cut. title: WILLIAM H. JANNEY DIES AT AGE OF 84: RETIRED AS SECRETARY-TREASURER OF CHELTENHAM INSTITUTION 18 MONTHS AGO SERVED FOR 14 YEARS FUNERAL SERVICES TO BE HELD TOMORROW WITH INTERMENT IN FRIENDS' BURIAL GROUND
full_text: WILLIAM H. JANNEY DIES AT AGE OF 84 Retired As Secretary-Treas- urer Of Cheltenham Insti- tution 18 Months Ago SERVED FOR 14 YEARS Funeral Services To Be Held To- morrow With Interment In Friends' Burial Ground William Henry Janney, secretary- treasurer of the House of Reforma- tion for Colored Boys at Cheltenham until his retirement eighteen months ago, died suddenly at his home in the Plaza Apartments, Park avenue and Wilson street, at noon yesterday. He was 84 years of age. Funeral services will be held in the parlors at 802-4 Madison avenue at 11 A. M. tomorrow. Burial will be in the Friends' Burial Ground. Engaged In Banking Mr. Janney was born in Washington, the son of Henry and Hannah Schol- field Janney. During the early part of his life he was engaged in the banking business and served as presi- dent of the National Bank of Smyrna, Delaware. He came to Baltimore about twenty- five years ago and had been connect- ed with the Cheltenham institution for approximately fourteen years. His wife, who was Miss Elizabeth Brooks, of Baltimore, died in 1919. He was a brother of the late Dr. O. Ed- ward Janney. His survivors are two daughters, Miss Phida Janney, of Bal- timore, and Mrs. F. D. Davis, of Buf- falo, N. Y., and a son, Henry Janney, of Baltimore. He was a member of the Society of Friends. title: ASKS PAY INCREASE IN NEGRO SCHOOLS: STATE INTERRACIAL BODY URGES ADDED EDUCATIONAL FACILITIES IN REPORT LETTER SENT TO NICE COMMISSION RECCOMMENDS LABOR PROBE, REPEAL OF SEGREGATION LAWS FOR PUBLIC CARRIERS
full_text: ASKS PAY INCREASE IN NEGRO SCHOOLS State Interracial Body Urges Added Educational Facili- ties In Report LETTER SENT TO NICE Commission Recommends Labor Probe, Repeal Of Segregation Laws For Public Carriers Asserting that intelligence. health, morality and industry are prime fac- tors in the development of the Negro as well as any other group-these being included in the term "equal opportunity"-the report of the In- terracial Commission of Maryland to Governor Nice and through him to the General Assembly was made public yesterday. The report recommended, among other things that: Negro teachers and supervisors get the same salaries as other teachers and supervisors. The Princess Anne Academy-East- ern Shore branch of the Univer- sity of Maryland ultimately should have a four-year course, the first two years being liberalized to make them more advantageous to those wishing to pursue other than agricultural subjects. Morgan College get increased sup- port as the only standard college for Negroes in the State. A preventorium for Negro children exposed to a tubercular environ- ment be established in some part of the State where climatic conditions are favorable. Laws prescribing regulations for the separation of white and Negro passengers on public carriers be repealed. Additional features at the House of Reformation for Negro boys at Cheltenham be extended to include appropriate industrial training, and recreational features there be in- creased. Labor Probe Asked In a letter to the Governor that ac- companied the report, the commission consisting both of white and Negro members emphasized that "suitable provision should be made for a search- ing survey of labor conditions as re- lated to the Negroes of the State." "No racial or social group of Ameri- can citizens will long remain con- tented if denied a fair and equitable share in the education, social and economic benefits due the people gen- erally," the letter continued. "All efforts that deny the steady flow of these benefits are doomed to ultimate defeat. The 'golden rule' is not merely a tenet of religion, but an inexorable law of social progress. If checked or hindered for a time in its application, it ultimately succeeds through the weakness and folly of those who deny its truth. Urges "Fearless Honesty" "Recent events clearly show that this State is not exempt from the most cruel manifestations of racial antipathy. There seems to be no cure for these social outbreaks, but the cultivation of fearless honesty in deal- ing with interracial relations. A dis- crimination which begins by denying the daily rights, public and private, may end by denying the right of life itself." In 1920, it was pointed out in the report, there were only four county high schools for Negro pupils of Maryland in addition to the high- school work then offered at the Bowie Normal School. There are now twenty- seven high schools, Howard county being the only county that does not provide high-school training for its Negro youth. Baltimore county pro- vides for such high-school work in the Baltimore city system. Equal Costs Cited "If the colored teachers of Maryland are to make long continued prepara- tion for efficient professional service," the report said, "they must see the reward for their sacrifice in reason- able remuneration. No human being can remain satisfied with less. When colored teachers make special prepara- tion by advanced study, it costs them as much as similar preparation costs other teachers." The State appropriated annually $276,750 to eight colleges open to white students and $23,400 to Morgan College. The report stated that "with the Ne- groes constituting one-sixth of the population of the State, they receive less than one-twelfth of the sum ap- propriated in aid. We respectfully sub- mit that this is not a fair and equitable division of State funds." ! Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: The Varied Jobs Required To Run A Railroad
full_text: The Varied Jobs Required To Run A Railroad SOME people think of railroad workers as brakemen and engineers, riveters and the husky laborers who stand aside when the train edges through a work squad. Others think of them as porters and conductors, stewards and ticket salesmen. Some people even include chefs, night watchmen, hostesses and business executives in the group, but not many would name magicians. musicians, or geologists as connected with the business of railroading. 125 Vocations Are Listed On The B. & O's Pay Roll All these trades and many more are repre- sented among the 40,000 employes of the Balti- more and Ohio Railroad. Among the company's 6,400 workers in Baltimore alone, you can find a diversity of trades sufficient to put any small community well on the way to being self-suf- ficient-clockmakers, printers, wireless opera- tors, chemists, designers, writers, bootblacks, dietitians and public speakers. One hundred and twenty-five different vocations are listed on the company pay roll. If the entire personnel voted on the most unusual job in the organization, it is likely that a healthy number of ballots would go to Arthur D. Gans, who knew Thurston as a boy and for years dreamed of following in his foot- steps. He got as far as recognition on the variety. stage and eventually the job of head magician for the B. & Ο. Meetings Were Going Flat- In Need Of Showmanship The job was born during an intensive safety campaign throughout the railroad's territory. Statistical speeches and otherwise tedious meet- By HARRY HALLER ings were going flat, needed showmanship. Gans stepped on the platform, poured water on a flower pot. Nothing happened. Then he tried whisky. A plant zoomed up three feet in the air. He dangled a pair of women's stockings before the audience, placed them in a box and handed it to a young lady. She opened it, and three white rats jumped out. The attention of the audience was his and the railroad's. She Began As A Clerk In Car-Service Department "That's nothing," says Miss Margaret T. Stevens, who during twenty-three years' service with the Baltimore and Ohio has held enough different jobs to staff an average office. "It took Houdini to get me started on a career." She began as a clerk in the car service department, where "you reported for work at 8.30 and not 8.31 and sorted records without even talking to your desk-mate until lunch hour at 1. On the way up to work in the elevator one morning a member of the Transportation De- partment told her that there was a good job open there. "Why don't you apply?" he asked. "Applications must be in by 1." "Small chance," Miss Stevens said. "Nothing but a circus parade on Baltimore street could get us an intermission before lunch. And this isn't circus season." But that position was more on her mind than the records she was sorting, and at 11 o'clock there was a tumult of horns (auto and musical) in the street outside, and everyone rushed for the windows. With one eye on the chief clerk. Miss Stevens whisked about the room until she found a piece of paper and pen. Nervously she scratched out the application and just managed to deposit it with a passing clerk from the transportation department as her colleagues were filing back to their desks. "What was all the commotion?" she asked. Even Without Houdini She Would Have Succeeded "Houdini," someone replied. "He was hang- ing from The Sun Building, advertising a theater program." But one suspects that even without Houdini's assistance, Miss Stevens would have landed in the unusual brackets. Next day's promotion to the transportation department soon led her to the distinction of being the first woman to work in the mine-rating bureau. During lunch hours she helped the chief file clerk, and before the World War had his job, with five assistants working under her. In spare moments, Miss Stevens organized the first B. & O. toy shop to brighten Christmas for furloughed employes' youngsters, acted as the first hostess on any train and got six words out of Calvin Coolidge, supervised the railroad's exhibit at the Chicago World Fair, wrote the scripts for the Fair of the Iron Horse pageant; and for the "Story of Baltimore Town," the pageant celebrating Baltimore's two hundredth anniversary. In 1923 she was one of three B. & O. women elected by the employes to go to France for rehabilitation work. 10,000 Railroading Objects Go Through Stenographer's Hands Twenty-five years ago A. J. Bitter was hired as a stenographer in the railroad's test depart- ment at Mount Clare, but in his spare moments he has amassed a general knowledge that would soon exhaust the average stenographic worker. Over 10,000 objects relative to railroading, from brooms to girders, pass through Mr. Bitter's hands on the way to the testers. The soap you use in the train washroom, the stationery in the lounge car, the nuts and bolts that hold a train together, the waste used by the engineer to wipe grease from his hands and the glass panes through which you watch the passing country- side must all come here first for testing. Upstairs a large and elaborately equipped chemical laboratory ($54,000 went into its appointments) is presided over by Dr. Wilbur M. Stedman, chief chemist for the railroad. Here are tested drinking water, many varieties of oil, ink, copper and everything used by the line subject to chemical analysis. During a thirty-year building period Dr. Sted- man achieved national recognition for the labor- atory. At one time he had a staff of dozens of chemists working full time. Then the railroad's employes numbered 75,000. Now Dr. Stedman has only one assistant, and you detect nostalgia for former busier days as he strolls about the deserted tables and cabinets. "So much work undone," he sighs. Too Much Work To Do With Time On His Hands "So much work to do," gulps Samuel A. Wil- son, Baltimore and Ohio horologist, as he looks at myriad clocks cluttering the shelves, tables and floor of his Mount Royal Station workshop. Ranging in size from a watchman's timepiece to great station clocks, they have come from Illi- nois and Missouri and more nearby States for repair. Twenty-five thousand company time- pieces come under his supervision. Bustling about one of the company's busiest offices is William H. Hoffman, manager of the telegraph room in the Charles and Baltimore streets building. Twenty-four hours a day, wire- less machines and telephones chatter in this nerve center of the railroad as 6,400 messages are handled daily. Messages vary from how many tons of coal are being shipped from Pitts- burgh to St. Louis at 11.45 P. M. to a sleeping- car reservation on a Chicago-New York ex- press. All day and night, this room keeps officers and officials informed of transportation developments throughout the system. Originator of a telegraphic office for Enoch Pratt and installed at the Cheltenham Reforma- tory, and later in charge of telegraphic oper- ations at Union Station during the Spanish- American War, Mr. Hoffman's experience pre- pared him for B. & O. responsibilities. Functioned Without Interruption During Baltimore Fire During the Baltimore fire, company wires in his charge continued functioning with no inter- ruption. When flames began to sweep down near the building emergency paraphernalia was imme- diately connected at Camden Station and calls for help went on. For a while the B. & O. wires were the only contact with the outside world. Previous experience also paved the way to Dr. George P. Grimsley's job as B. &. O. geolo- gist. A Hopkins doctor in geology, his record as assistant State geologist of West Virginia inter- ested the company when the employment of a geologist was found necessary. A plea to the rail- road from a mid-Western clay or cement com- pany for suggestions as to an adequate Eastern location brought about the necessity. Miss Helen Foreman Candidate For Gulliver Honors As director of the women's division of the Cooperative Traffic Program, Miss Helen Fore- man is probably the most traveled of the railroad's specialized employes. Responsible for pepping up eighty-seven clubs of women em- ployes and company wives, scattered throughout the country, she averages 2,500 miles a week. Her job is to talk the club members into talk- ing their friends into using the railroad. "Some- times I need more than a magician to win their attention," Miss Foreman says. But, according to the records, 2,400 railroad fares were sold during two months through this program.
