The soap you use in the train washroom, the stationery in the lounge car, the nuts and bolts that hold a train together, the waste used by the engineer to wipe grease from his hands and the glass panes through which you watch the passing country- side must all come here first for testing. Upstairs a large and elaborately equipped chemical laboratory ($54,000 went into its appointments) is presided over by Dr. Wilbur M. Stedman, chief chemist for the railroad. Here are tested drinking water, many varieties of oil, ink, copper and everything used by the line subject to chemical analysis. During a thirty-year building period Dr. Sted- man achieved national recognition for the labor- atory. At one time he had a staff of dozens of chemists working full time. Then the railroad's employes numbered 75,000. Now Dr. Stedman has only one assistant, and you detect nostalgia for former busier days as he strolls about the deserted tables and cabinets. "So much work undone," he sighs. Too Much Work To Do With Time On His Hands "So much work to do," gulps Samuel A. Wil- son, Baltimore and Ohio horologist, as he looks at myriad clocks cluttering the shelves, tables and floor of his Mount Royal Station workshop. Ranging in size from a watchman's timepiece to great station clocks, they have come from Illi- nois and Missouri and more nearby States for repair. Twenty-five thousand company time- pieces come under his supervision. Bustling about one of the company's busiest offices is William H. Hoffman, manager of the telegraph room in the Charles and Baltimore streets building. Twenty-four hours a day, wire- less machines and telephones chatter in this nerve center of the railroad as 6,400 messages are handled daily. Messages vary from how many tons of coal are being shipped from Pitts- burgh to St. Louis at 11.45 P. M. to a sleeping- car reservation on a Chicago-New York ex- press. All day and night, this room keeps officers and officials informed of transportation developments throughout the system. Originator of a telegraphic office for Enoch Pratt and installed at the Cheltenham Reforma- tory, and later in charge of telegraphic oper- ations at Union Station during the Spanish- American War, Mr. Hoffman's experience pre- pared him for B. & O. responsibilities. Functioned Without Interruption During Baltimore Fire During the Baltimore fire, company wires in his charge continued functioning with no inter- ruption. When flames began to sweep down near the building emergency paraphernalia was imme- diately connected at Camden Station and calls for help went on. For a while the B. & O. wires were the only contact with the outside world. Previous experience also paved the way to Dr. George P. Grimsley's job as B. &. O. geolo- gist. A Hopkins doctor in geology, his record as assistant State geologist of West Virginia inter- ested the company when the employment of a geologist was found necessary. A plea to the rail- road from a mid-Western clay or cement com- pany for suggestions as to an adequate Eastern location brought about the necessity. Miss Helen Foreman Candidate For Gulliver Honors As director of the women's division of the Cooperative Traffic Program, Miss Helen Fore- man is probably the most traveled of the railroad's specialized employes. Responsible for pepping up eighty-seven clubs of women em- ployes and company wives, scattered throughout the country, she averages 2,500 miles a week. Her job is to talk the club members into talk- ing their friends into using the railroad. "Some- times I need more than a magician to win their attention," Miss Foreman says. But, according to the records, 2,400 railroad fares were sold during two months through this program.

title: Letters To The Editor: Cheltenham School
full_text: | Letters To The Editor Cheltenham Schoo TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: As a member of the board of man- agers of Cheltenham I would like to express my reaction to the re- port of the grand jury on that insti- tution. Grand juries have been dragging the skeleton out of the closet at Cheltenham and exposing it to the public for twenty years without re- sults. I have shared their disgust and have been on the brink of resig. nation. I am fully aware that after the publication of this letter my resignation may be a must, The grand jury did a good and thorough job with brutal frankness in condemning the physical plant and the substandard efficiency of the staff. Your editorial likewise exposed the plausible weakness of a normally good board of directors. But constructive criticism should. be followed by practical solutions, long overdue at Cheltenham. A careful survey. and estimates have been made of the cost of reno- vating the present location, and the figures approximate those for build- ing a new school on a new site. Onę possibility is that a new school for Cheltenham could be built on the State-owned land adjacent to the Maryland School for Boys at Loch Raven. Several other sites have been offered, including one on the Washington boulevard. Several major problems cannot and will never be solved as long as Cheltenham remains at its present location, 55 miles from Baltimore. This means as high as 15 and 20 per cent vacancies on the staff with- out much choice in getting better qualified help. Cheltenham should be moved to within 10 or 15 miles of Baltimore. Ninety 'per cent of the boys are from Baltimore city. There is a plan pending for the erection of a new dining room and building at Cheltenham at the cost of about $270,000. This, I think, is a mistake and extravagant if the State is sincere in giving us a new school at a new site. This large sum of money should go immediately into the construction of a new school. A superintendent for Chelten- ham should, for obvious reasons, be appointed at the earliest possible time. And a rational purge should be made of the entire board of trus- tees, let the chips fly wherever they may. This, if done without any per- sonal feelings, will go a long way in solving one of Cheltenham's major problems. I also agree with The Sun that, because of circumstances and for the present at least, the school's best chance for getting out of its deep rut is to have a mixed board. That is Maryland's pattern as ex- emplified at Morgan College. I wish it to be clearly understood that I do not believe in or defend Maryland's policies in making a distinction be- tween races. We simply have no practical alternative for Chelten- ham except to fall in line with Morgan. That is to say, to cut our cloth to fit the pattern. JAMES A, WHITE, Baltimore, Dec. 22. ! title: MENTAL HOSPITAL NEED FOUND VITAL: FIRE HAZARDS, LACK OF PROPER SEGREGATION FACILITIES ARE REPORTED
full_text: MENTAL HOSPITAL NEED FOUND VITAL Fire Hazards, Lack Of Proper Segregation Facilities Are Reported | The Maryland Commission on Post-War Reconstruction and De- velopment had before it yesterday a story of fire hazards, lack of proper segregation for patients and unsuitable housing facilities for attendants at State mental hos- pitals. Walter N. Kirkman, State direc- tor of budget and procurement, said projects to remedy the condi- tions should be placed high on the schedule for post-war construction. In the fire-hazard class he par- ticularly noted the industrial build- ing at Spring Grove State Hospital. The present building, he said, would offer little resistance to con- Nagration. Mattresses and other in- flammable objects are made there. He submitted a proposal for a new building to cost $120,000. Cottages Wanted Mr. Kirkman said there is a lack of proper segregation for patients at Springfield State Hospital. Re- (Continued on Page 16, Column 2) (Continued from Page 24) quests are on file, he said, for cot- tages for one hundred women; at a-cost of $150,000, and a cottage for one hundred men patients, also at $150,000. An attendants' home for fifty employes is asked at the same hos- pital. It would cost $115,000. Mr. Kirkman said the Legisla- ture, often sympathetic with the needs of patients, is inclined to re- ject proposals for the comfort and convenience of hospital employes. This, he contended, is one reason for the difficulty in keeping proper personnel at tire institutions. Equipment Limited When, the cost of lighting, re- frigeration and sewerage for an at- tendant's home comes into the pic- ture, he said, the Legislature will say: "You have a dynamo at the main plant, you have a sewer. Just hook them up with the new build- ings." "They don't realize," he said, "that those pieces of equipment have limitations." An admitting building for 120 women patients at Spring Grove would cost $220,000 according to the proposal. The building, he said, is needed to make it possible to properly assign patients for treat ment. Such assignments, he de- clared, offer the best opportunities for recovery. More farm land-an estimated $28,000 worth-also is needed at Spring Grove, he said, because much of the land there now is not suitable for farming and doesn't provide the prescribed half acre a patient. Building For Alcoholics The Eastern Shore State Hos- pital, he said, is badly in need of a building for alcoholics. The pro- posal calls for a structure to house! eighty patients at a cost of $100.- 000. At present, he said, it is neces- sary to house them with psycho- pathic cases. "They are not psychopathics," ■ he said; "and it would be to the ad- vantage of both the psychopathics and alcoholics if they were treated in separate hospitals." A total of $480,000 is asked for improvements at Cheltenham School for Boys. The school. he pointed out, has been the subject of controversy for years. The buildings are all very old and a complete vocational and educational program is needed. Environment Important "To train those boys," he said, "you must provide a proper en- vironment and a proper staff." The proposals call for a voca- tional building and equipment, re- modeling and reconditioning of four old cottages, additional facili- ties for the staff and supplemen- tary services. A new women's dormitory, he said, is needed at Morgan State College. Improvements sought at the tuberculosis sanitoriums would cost $262,000 at Maryland State Sanitorium: $3,000 at Salisbury and $65,000 at Henryton, $6,889,396 Urgent All the proposals listed as urgent total $6,889,396. Listed as slightly less urgent are projects totaling $3.533,028. Members of the commission pointed out that the $2,000,000 set aside by the State for post-war improvements is "only a drop in the bucket" and would be so even with most of the $4,000,000 in the current emergency funds. Dr. Abel Wolman, vice-chairman of the committee, pointed out there have been years in the past-even with no unemployment emergency -when the State spent as much as $40 000 000 on public works.

title: Cheltenham-By Any Other Name
full_text: Cheltenham- By Any Other Name Beginning next month there will be no Cheltenham School for Boys, with all the memories of filth, brutality and bad man- agement that name conjures up. The in- famous reformatory school for Negro boys will be known officially as "Boy's. Village of Maryland." A full-time psychologist and a part-time psychiatrist will be added to the staff at that time to carry out the "Boy's Town" tradition of close personal guidance and moral rehabilitation. Perhaps the most significant change that is taking place at Cheltenham is a shift in the age group being handled by the institu- tion. The State Reformatory at Breatheds- ville is being used for older delinquents from. 16 to 23 years of age, while the younger boys-including those only 8 and 9 years old are being sent to Cheltenham. Under the guidance of the new Cheltenham superintendent, Mr. Lawson J. Vency, the younger boys are being encouraged to com- pete on a friendly cottage-to-cottage basis in housekeeping, athletics and academic progress. This is not the first time that there have been reports of reform measures under way at Cheltenham. There have been many such reports in the past, and always they have been followed by later reports that the institution was too antiquated and poorly located to make it an effective train. ing school. Mr. Veney gives at least one hint that the basic things wrong with the school have not changed much for the better when he speaks of his "terrific problem getting an adequate staff." The public, periodically shocked by bad reports on Cheltenham, will certainly be on Mr. Veney's side if he can make Cheltenham by any other name smell better than it used to. But, while wishing Mr. Veney the best of luck, the public has justification for keeping its fingers.crossed. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: UNIDENTIFIED MAN HELD IN SLAYING: CHARGES PREDICTED TODAY IN YULE SHOOTING OF AUGUST MATT QUARREL THEORY CITED VICTIM CALLED FROM HOME BY ASSAILANT PREVIOUS TO MURDER
full_text: 3 UNIDENTIFIED MAN HELD IN SLAYING Charges Predicted Today In Yule Shooting Of Au- gust Matt QUARREL THEORY CITED Victim Called From Home By Assailant Previous To Murder [By the Associated Press] Upper Marlboro, Md., Dec. 26-An unidentified farmer was held today in connection with the Christmas Eve slaying of August Matt, 40. Police said murder charges probably would be filed tomorrow. Matt was shot through the abdomen by a man who drove a car into the yard of his Cheltenham home, called him by name and fired when Matt came out of the house. Quarrel Theory Advanced Authorities worked on the theory the slaying resulted from a quarrel involving Mrs. Leta Bredhaute, said to have been employed at one time as a housekeeper by the suspect in the shooting, and more recently engaged in the same capacity by Matt. Mrs. Brodhaute found Matt lying on the ground mortally wounded after the shooting. Christmas Play Proves Fatal To Child At York [Special Dispatch to The Sun] York, Pa., Dec. 26-Christmas joys were turned to sorrow today at the home of Mr. and Mrs. Jacob Sweitzer, when their son, Richard, 20 months, died from injuries sustained in a fall while playing with one of his toys. While the boy was running with a two-wheeled toy, he tripped over a raised floor board, his head striking a rocking chair on which his mother sat with an infant in her arms. The impact inflicted a fractured skull and brain concussion, which proved fatal. The former Cuban President, who tis wanted by the present Cuban Gov- ernment on a killing charge, was ar- rested in a French hospital on a war- rant issued by Garrett W. Cotter, United States Commissioner, at the request of counsel for the Cuban Government. Herrera is suffering from a com- pound fracture of the skull received sin an automobile accident. title: PLANS TO HOLD UP 2 ISSUES OF BUILDING BONDS: BOARD OF PUBLIC WORKS MAY DEFER $1,458,000 IN SECURITIES ACTION FORCED BY HIGH CONSTRUCTION COSTS AND LACK OF MATERIALS
full_text: PLANS TO HOLD UP 2 ISSUES OF BUILDING BONDS Board Of Public Works May Defer $1,458,000 In Securities Action Forced By High Construction Costs And Lack Of Materials Governor O'Conor announced last night that the Board of Public Works la, planning to withhold the sale of $1,458,000 of construction bonds, re- mainder of an issue approved by the last session of the Legislature. Approximately one third of the issue, amounting to $859,000, was sold last July 15 at the rate of .098 per cent. interest. The General Assembly au- thorized a total issue of $2,317,000. Reason For Action The Governor explained that the proposed action by the boardis prompted by the present high cost of construction and by the scarcity of essential materials. Within the last few days the Office of Production Management has ad- vised State, county and municipal of- ficials that they will be budgeted next year for the purchase of iron and steel products and other commodities needed for national defense. In fact, Maryland has been selected as one of three States where OPM will.. conduct a survey to determine the pro portionate amount of strategic mate- rials required by each State to main- tain hospitals, water mains, sewers and other essential public health services. The other test-tube States are Virginia and New Jersey, Equipment Affected According to Walter N. Kirkman, State director of budget and procure- ment, OPM has advised State authori- ties that the steel restrictions also will apply to such equipment as typewrit- ers, Aling cabinets, laundry machines, automobiles and motorcycles. Baltimore, together with Chester, Pa., and Bridgeport, Conn., also will be used by OPM to determine future municipal requirements for essential products. Governor O'Conor explained last night that money obtained last summer now is being used for the construction of a new hospital wing at the Maryland Tuberculosis Sana- torium and for several other projects. Loan Authorization. According to the terms of the bond issue, as approved by the Legislature, the State was authorized to borrow $859,000 Inst July, $807,000 on January 15, 1942, and $651,000 on July 15, 1942. - Should the Board of Public Works finally decide to forego the other two bond issues, the State will have to defer a number of construction and improvement plans provided for when the bond issue was authorized. However, the Governor emphasized last night that the hospital wing at Continued on Page 6. Hospital Construction In addition to the hospital wing, Governor O'Conor said the board has approved the construction of a new building at the Spring Grove State Hospital and a number of improve- ments at the Crownsville State, Hos- pital. The contracts for these projects have been approved, priority ratings have been given, and work is about ready to begin. Furthermore, the board also has awarded contracts for the erection of a gymnasium at the Towson State Teachers' College and for the building of a new power plant at Morgan State College. New Dormitory The board further has given its approval for the construction of a new dormitory at the Princess Anne branch of the University of Maryland, but the Governor said last night tha this project is still being considered by the board. The Governor explained that $115, 000 had been set aside originally for the Princess Anne project but that the lowest bid for the dormitory ex- ceeded $135,000. After certain revisions are made in the building plans, however, bring. ing the cost down to the budgetary provision, the go-ahead signal will be given for erection of this structure Destroyed By Fire One of the dormitories at Princess Anne was destroyed by fire last April, According to the terms of Senate Bill 67, which authorized the bond issue, provision of $100,000 was made to the Maryland Council of Defense "for such projects of State defense as may be approved by the State Board of Public Works." / Also included in the bill were funds for the erection of a dormitory at the Rosewood State Training. School for Boys, a vocational building at the Cheltenham School for Boys, and for the remodeling of a cottage at the Montrose School for Girls. Projects Outlined Since the expenditure of a large por- tion of the $875,000 already has been planned by the board, many of the projects provided for in the bill will have to be abandoned temporarily. Among the projects outlined in the bill are: To the University of Maryland, Col- lege Park, for a new armory, $100,- $000. For an addition to University Hos- pital Nurses' Home, in Baltimore, $65,000. For Improvements and equipment at Princess Anne branch of the university, $35,000. To the Military Department for com- pleting airport and naval militia building and improvement and re- pairs to armories in the State and at Camp Ritchie, $100,000. To the Maryland State School for the Deaf, for improvements and equipment, $15,000. To the Board of Public Works, for ***Improvements to the Court of Ap- peals building and other public buildings in Annapolis, $75,000. To the Springfield State Hospital for laundry equipment, $25,000; for repairs and improvements, $12,000; for additions to sewerage disposal, $35,000; for farm land, $10,000; for addition to attendants' home, $10,000. Additional Projects Additional projects also were pro- vided for at the following: St. Mary's Female Seminary. The State Teachers College at Bowle and Salisbury. The Maryland State Penal Farm. The Maryland House of Correction. The Maryland Training School for Colored Girls. The Eastern Shore State Hospital. It could not be determined last night which of the projects will be post- poned, or if some of them will be allowed partial appropriations. Last January the Governor origi- nally asked the Legislature for au- thorization of a $4,172,000 issue. How- ever, as he pointed out last night, he visualized the possible scarcity of building materials and the rising cost of construction and later requested that only $2,317,000 be allowed. Several Proposals With the additional funds the State would have erected two chronic dis- ease hospitals, at the total cost of $1,500,000, one to be located on, the Eastern Shore and the other on this side of the bay. The original bill proposed an appro- priation of $250,000 for a Health De- partment building and laboratories to replace the present departmental headquarters at 2400 North Charles street. An allotment of $225,000 had been set aside for the addition to the Com- missioner of Motor Vehicles' office at Guilford avenue and Twenty-first street. But these projects were eliminated at the request of the Governor when he advised the Legislature "that the material and labor which might be necessary for the construction of these buildings might be sorely needed dur- ing the next year or two."

Governor O'Conor explained last night that money obtained last summer now is being used for the construction of a new hospital wing at the Maryland Tuberculosis Sana- torium and for several other projects. Loan Authorization. According to the terms of the bond issue, as approved by the Legislature, the State was authorized to borrow $859,000 Inst July, $807,000 on January 15, 1942, and $651,000 on July 15, 1942. - Should the Board of Public Works finally decide to forego the other two bond issues, the State will have to defer a number of construction and improvement plans provided for when the bond issue was authorized. However, the Governor emphasized last night that the hospital wing at Continued on Page 6. School for Boys, a vocational building at the Cheltenham School for Boys, and for the remodeling of a cottage at the Montrose School for Girls. To the Military Department for com- pleting airport and naval militia building and improvement and re- pairs to armories in the State and at Camp Ritchie, $100,000. To the Maryland State School for the Deaf, for improvements and equipment, $15,000. To the Board of Public Works, for ***Improvements to the Court of Ap- peals building and other public buildings in Annapolis, $75,000. To the Springfield State Hospital for laundry equipment, $25,000; for repairs and improvements, $12,000; for additions to sewerage disposal, $35,000; for farm land, $10,000; for addition to attendants' home, $10,000. The Maryland House of Correction. The Maryland Training School for Colored Girls. The Eastern Shore State Hospital. It could not be determined last night which of the projects will be post- poned, or if some of them will be allowed partial appropriations. Last January the Governor origi- nally asked the Legislature for au- thorization of a $4,172,000 issue. How- ever, as he pointed out last night, he visualized the possible scarcity of building materials and the rising cost of construction and later requested that only $2,317,000 be allowed. Several Proposals With the additional funds the State would have erected two chronic dis- ease hospitals, at the total cost of $1,500,000, one to be located on, the Eastern Shore and the other on this side of the bay. The original bill proposed an appro- priation of $250,000 for a Health De- partment building and laboratories to replace the present departmental headquarters at 2400 North Charles street. An allotment of $225,000 had been set aside for the addition to the Com- missioner of Motor Vehicles' office at Guilford avenue and Twenty-first street. But these projects were eliminated at the request of the Governor when he advised the Legislature "that the material and labor which might be necessary for the construction of these buildings might be sorely needed dur- ing the next year or two."

title: SETS TEST FOR HEAD OF CHELTENHAM: JONES SAYS EXAMINATIONS TO PICK SUPERINTENDENT WILL BE HELD THIS FALL HIGH QUALIFICATIONS IN EXPERIENCE AND TRAINING WILL BE REQUIRED
full_text: SETS TEST FOR HEAD OF CHELTENHAM Jones Says Examinations To Pick Superintendent Will Be Held This Fall High Qualifications In Ex- perience And Training Will Be Required i An examination for superintendent of the Cheltenham School for Boys' will be held this fall at the request of the school's board of managers, State Employment Commissioner Harry C. Jones said yesterday. The superintendency was included in a schedule of twenty-two merit system examinations issued by Jones for the next quarter year. Requirements High Jones said the post woull pay $4,000 a year, and require "high qualifica- tions in experience and training." The superintendent would "plan, direct and supervise" staff and activities of the school for Negro boys, under di- rection of the board of managers. The announcement is the latest in a long controversy over operation and personnel of the school, which was taken over by the State in 1937, A court suit was instituted after Jones held tests and reported twenty- six school employes were "unfit for the merit system," but the Court of Appeals in January, 1939, ruled in favor of the employes. To Be Reclassified Jones said yesterday that Benjamin B. Sunderland, now acting superin- tendent of the school, would "be re- classified into his old position as parole officer." The board of managers is composed of: JUDGE JOSEPH H. ULMAN, Baltimore. DR. G. CANDY ROBINSON, Baltimore. DR. FRANK R. Isaac, head of the Strawbridge Home for Boys. JAMES A. PRATT. JOSEPH H. BLANDFORD. HAL B. CALGETT. The first three were appointed and the latter two reappointed by Gov- ernor O'Conor last May. Dates for the superintendency ex- amination and the twenty-one other tests will be announced later, Jones said. Applications for all twenty-two posts are to be mailed to the Employ- ment Commissioner's office not later than October 30. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Golf Ball "Explodes" And Caddy Is Injured
full_text: Golf Ball "Explodes" And Caddy Is Injured Fluid Squirts into Boy's Eye While He Cuts Golf Ball In Half Joseph Frank Dickerson, 15-year-id eaddy, won't be cutting golf balls in half again for awhile, He tried it yesterday afternoon after caddying a round 011 the Elkridge Country Club course and wound up with visits to two hospitals. It wasn't the first but the "Afteenth or twentieth" one he had cut, but he never before had cut one without removing the rubber bands, When his blade got to the center of the ball "it exploded," he said, and the fluid from the center of the ball squirted into his eyes, Two members of the club took him to the Union Memorial Hospital where his eyes were bothed, then he was recommended to the eye clinic at the Johns Hopkins Hospital where further treatment was given. From there he went to his home in the 6000 block Staunton avenue, Legislator Is Victim Of Spinal Meningitis Luther P. Jefferson, 35, Was Mem. ber Of House Of Delegates From Cecil Elkton, Md., Aug. 8 (M)-Spinal meningitis today proved fatal to Luther P. Jefferson, 35, member of the House of Delegates from Cecil county and a well-known farmer, live-stock dealer and auctioneer. Mr. Jefferson, who had been ill only a short time, died in Union Memorial Hospital, Baltimore. Surviving are his wife, his father, James Jefferson, of Chesapeake City, and a sister, Mrs. Reginald Walworth, of Hartford, Conn. Funeral services will be held here tomorrow afternoon, Burial will be in Cecil County Cemetery, near Chesa- peake City. 2 Boys At Cheltenham. Freed On Habeas Corpus Youths Sald To Have Been De. tained At Cheltenham. After Sentence Expired Two Negro youths, who were de dained, at the Cheltenham School for Boys after their one-year term had expired, were released yesterday and Thursday on habeas corpus proceed- Engs by Chief Judge Samuel K. Dennis, The youths, Lucius Boyd and Arthur Andrews, were sent to the reforma- Hory in July, 1940, for one year each on a carnal knowledge charge. They vere eligible for release last July 29. Joel G. Hochman, attorney for the souths, told the court that the insti- Lution authorities told him and the parents of the boys that they were not required to free the youths, but hat they were considering probation. title: New High Speeds By Modem Trains
full_text: New High Speeds By Modern Trains From the Kansas City Times The railroads have begun to catch up with the boys who are bearing down hard on the accelerator, and high speed, along with safety and comfort, has become an obsession-high speed, wheth- er obtained by steam, Diesel or elec- tricity, each having its partisans and cach streamlining until there isn't a wrinkle left on the surface. The English point with pride to the famous Cheltenham Flyer, which runs between London and Cheltenham, 122 miles, at an average speed of 52.3 miles an hour, making 71.4 between Swindon and London. But in point-to-point tim- ing, the Santa Fe's new Super Chief (with no desire to start an argument) can probably claim to be the fastest train in the world. We were waiting one frigid night last winter for a south- bound Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul train on the platform of that road's station in Milwaukee. It was fifteen minutes before train time. title: PARLAY SCARES ENGLISH BOOKS: ODDS ON GOLDEN MILLER IN GRAND NATIONAL DROP AS FLAMENCO WINS
full_text: PARLAY SCARES ENGLISH BOOKS Odds On Golden Miller In Grand National Drop As Flamenco Wins [By the Associated Press) Liverpool, England, March 27-On the eve of the ninety-seventh running of the Grand National Steeplechase at Aintree England's bookmakers faced a crisis following the victory today of Lord Rosebery's heavily played Fla- menco in the Lincolnshire, first big event of the flat-racing season. If Dorothy Paget's Golden Miller gets over the hurdles first in the Grand National test Friday it is believed he will bring bankruptcy to scores of the country's oldest and richest commis- sion houses. Flamenco and Golden Mil- ler have been heavily backed by doubles players, while the Lincoln- shire winner also has been coupled with John Hay Whitney's American- owned Thomond II in many combina- tions. Odds Drop Tο 5 Το 2 One middle-sized commissioner ad- mitted to the Associated Press that his firm stood to drop around £50,000 ($237,500) unless something happens Friday to the sure-footed Miller, which won the world's greatest jumping race Last year. "But that's only chicken feed to what will happen to some of the bigger boys." As the result of the critical situation a special callover was held at the Vic- toria Club in London tonight to give the bookies an opportunity to ease their liabilities. Golden Miller was knocked down from 7 to 2 to the al- most unheard-of price for a Grand National candidate of 5 to 2. Thomond II was shortened to 6 to 1, while the French-bred Tapinoise remained third choice at 9 to 1. Race Crowds Swelling The odds on George H. Bostwick's' Castle Irwell, which the young Amer- ican sportsman will ride himself, were cut to 20 to 1, and Whitney's Royal Ransom was reduced to 25 to 1. That's the darker side of the situa- tion. There's nothing but sunshine and Toy in the hearts of thousands pouring into this city from every part of the world. The hotels already are choked to capacity. The sidewalks are over- lowing with those arriving in time to witness the opening of the meeting to- morrow. The weather kept peace with their spirits, deluging the famous Ain- tree course with hot sunshine. While America's hopes of thwarting the great Golden Miller encountered a slight setback in the anticipated scratching of J. B. Snow's Delaneige, second last year, other American own- ers were far from conceding anything. Five American-owned jumpers re- mained in the field of 27. Whitney Confident Whitney believes :: Thomond. II, third in the 1934 renewal, will run the legs off the favorite. "In view of his fine fight against Golden Miller in the Cheltenham Gold Cup, in which he finished less than a Rength behind, I think he has a great chance to turn the tables," declared the young American sportsman, who has tried many times but never won a Grand National: "Remember he will have an eight-pound pull in weights chis time." "I consider we have an excellent Outside chance," said Bostwick. "I'd Just as soon ride him as any horse in the race. He proved what he could do over Aintree fences when he won the Molyneux Chase in November." May Be Horizontal Champ Morgan Blair, owner and trainer of Fouquet, was "just hopeful." "He might do well if in right mood, out fact remains he tumbled in three ecnsecutive races. He promises to be- come the horizontal champion." If Thomond II fails, Whitney still has Royal Ransom, rated one of the leading ong shots. The other American entry, Jesse Metcalf's Theras, also was given only an outside chance. title: MAY CLOSE PLANT AT CHELTENHAM: HUNGERFORD REFUSES TO CLASS BROOM FACTORY AS SHELTERED WORKSHOP APPEAL MAY BE TAKEN ACTION WOULD RESULT IN ANNUAL LOSS OF $5,000 AND RESULT IN IDLENESS OF FORTY
full_text: MAY CLOSE PLANT AT CHELTENHAM Hungerford Refuses To Class Broom Factory As Shel- tered Workshop APPEAL MAY BE TAKEN Action Would Result In Annual -Loss Of $5,000 And Result In Idleness Of Forty The broom factory at the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham may be closed as a re- sult of a refusal yesterday by Arthur E. Hungerford, NRA Compliance Di- rector, to allow the factory to be classed as a "sheltered workshop," thereby removing it from the author- ity of that industry's code. Should Mr. Hungerford's decision be upheld by the National Sheltered. Workshop Committee at Washington, the factory will be closed with a loss of $5,000 per year to the institution and the idleness of about forty inmates. Conditions Under Fire Cheltenham, which is a private in- stitution receiving aid from the State, has been under fire recently because of alleged conditions at the institu- tion. A plan also has been suggested whereby the State would take over the institution. As far back as 1923 the Baltimore Federation of Labor complained about the broom factory, declaring it reduced the Negro boys to a "form of peon- age." Several months ago the Child Welfare League of America, in a re- port, condemned the health standards, diet, dormitories, clothing and virtu- ally all other living conditions at the home. Revenue Cited The broom factory, which A. S. Ripple & Bros. established at the insti- tution more than twenty-seven years ago, at present pays into the institu- tion 50 cents per day for every boy who works in the factory. In denying the broom concern the right to classify 'ts plant as a sheltered workshop, Mr. Hungerford told the representatives of the home and the company that they could take the mat- ter to the National Sheltered Work- shop Committee for a final ruling. Mr. Hungerford explained that a sheltered workshop was one operated for the benefit of handicapped workers, such as the Goodwill Industries, Inc. "The broom factory at Cheltenham is not a sheltered workshop," Mr. Hungerford said, "since the institu- tion never has applied to be classed as such, and, in my opinion, the fac- tory is a member of the broom indus- try, and must observe the code pro- visions of that industry." Robert F. Roberts, president of the board of managers of the institution, who attended yesterday's meeting with Enoch Harlan, vice-president of the board, was optimistic about the re- sult of the appeal to be made to Washington. He admitted, however, that the clos- ing of the shop "would be a hard- ship." Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

Jones, State Employment Commissioner, yesterday notified 200 officeholders who were blanketed into the Merit System recently by Gover- nor Nice's executive order, they must pass standard tests. title: ENOCH HARLAN DIES WHILE ON VACATION: BALTIMORE ATTORNEY VICTIM OF PNEUMONIA AT ST. PETERSBURG, FLA FORMERLY HEADED BOARD OF HOUSE OF REFORMATION, CHELTENHAM
full_text: ENOCH HARLAN DIES WHILE ON VACATION Baltimore Attorney Victim. Of Pneumonia At St. Petersburg, Fla. Formerly Headed Board Of House Of Reformation, Cheltenham Enoch Harlan, senior member of the law firm of Harlan & Harlan and former president of the board of the House of Reformation at Cheltenham, died yesterday in St. Petersburg, Fla., where he was on vacation. Mr. Harlan, according to word received from his wif who was ac- companying him, was removed to a hospital and placed in an oxygen tent Thursday after developing pneumonia. He died at 9 A. M. yesterday. Native Of Delaware Born at Wilmington, Del., November 15, 1867, Mr. Harlan was graduated from the University of Maryland Law School in 1897. In 1898 he married Mary Susanna Benson. He became president of the House of Reformation Board before the in- stitution was taken over by the State, and remained as one of its directors after the change. He also was a member of the board of the Boys' Home Society and of the board of the Thomas Wilson Fuel Saving Society. He was a member of the Friends Society and of the Bar Association of Baltimore City, the Maryland Bar Association, and the American Bar Association. Formed Law Firm In 1935 In 1935, with his twin sons, Edwin and Joseph Harlan, he founded the law firm of Harlan & Harlan. Edwin yesterday left by plane to meet his mother in Florida and to make plans for the funeral, In addition to his wife and twin sons, Mr. Harlan is survived by a daughter, Mrs. Helen Harlan Bag- galey, of Chicago; another son, Enoch L. Harlan, two sisters, Mrs. Cora H. Johnson, of Seattle, and Mrs. Helen H. Marshall, of Evansville, Ind., and a brother, J. Paul Harlan, of Oxford, Pa. Mr. Harlan lived at 2914 Garrison Boulevard. full_text: TWO STRIKERS FACE ASSAULT CHARGE Women Arrested After Al- leged Tussle With Rain- coat Plant Worker POLICE BREAK UP FIGHT Pickets Remain In Front Of Hanover Street Shop-Union Complains Of Wage Cot Two striking employes of a raincoat company in the first block South Han- over street, were arrested yesterday afternoon after a brief tussle with a woman worker leaving the plant. The fight was broken up by police, and the employes, who had been pick- eting the plant with about thirty fel- low-strikers, were charged with as- saulting Mrs. Genevieve McDevitt, 1316 West Lombard street. Those arrested and later released in $26 collateral for a hearing this after- noon, were Mrs. Louise Watts, 27, of the 300 block North Fulton avenue, and Miss Angela Banebace, 800 block Hamilton Terrace. Mrs. Watts was also charged with assaulting Miss Mary Brock, 4308 Parkwood avenue. Pickets Remain At Plant Carrying signs, the pickets walked in front of the plant for about an hour after their companions had been taken into custody, but no further disturb- ances were reported. Officials of the Garment Workers' Union said the employes had struck ast Thursday because the company old them they would receive a see- nd cut in wages and their hours would be increased to forty-four a week. A company official, however, said he employes had been asked to work orty-two and a half hours a week and were told they would be paid on a piece-work rate for overtime. They were told, he said, that wages would not be cut, but that the NRA minimum would be maintained. Offices Of Cheltenham Colored School Picketed Picketing yesterday in front of the local offices of the House of Reforma- tion for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, 225 East Redwood street, failed to have any apparent effect on the office. title: CENSURES SCHOOL AT CHELTENHAM: GRAND JURY CALLS EDUCATION FARCE--URGES PURCHASE BY CITY AND STATE MOVIE EXITS CRITICIZED CLOSING OF THEATERS LACKING SAFETY OUTLETS RECOMMENDED IN REPORT
full_text: CENSURES SCHOOL. AT CHELTENHAM Grand Jury Calls Education Farce-Urges Purchase By City And State MOVIE EXITS CRITICIZED Closing Of Theaters Lacking Safety Outlets Recom- mended In Report Charging that the education inmates receive at the institution is a farce, the retiring grand jury for the January term yesterday criticized the manage- ment and, conditions at the Chelten- ham School for Colored Boys and reс- ommended the purchase of the place by the city and state. 1 The recommendation was contained in a report to Judge Robert F. Stan- ton in the Criminal Court. The grand jury for the May term will be organ- ized Monday. Cites Sullen Obedience Pointing out that Cheltenham was privately owned, although aided by city and state, the report said "history fails to reveal a triumvirate that was successful or lasted for any great length of time." Discussing the pre- vailing educational system, the re- port continued: "The method in vogue does not awaken interest. It does not lead out of the mind of the boss many latent and useful qualities-many of God's plans die because no teacher, improp- erly prepared, can inspire respect and love, but all he gets is sullen obedi- ence. "We recommend the purchase of the place by the city and state and the selection of trained Afro-Americans who will give the boys selective work, some recreation and much education." Melvale School Called Poor Of the eleven institutions visited by members of the jury, Melvale School for Colored Girls was declared the poorest. The city and state, accord- ing to the report, are falling short of their obligation at the school and should arrange for a new home. The jurors praised the officials at Melvale for the work they are accom- plishing with the poor facilities. Movie Exits Condemned Hazardous exits in a number of East Baltimore street motion-picture thea- ters were criticized by the jurors. They pointed out that if a fire should occur in the picture booth of any of the houses concerned the patrons would be trapped. The rear exits were declared to be no exits at all, as they open on blind alleys or alleys littered with boxes and other obstructions. The report recommended the closing of the theaters until proper rear exits could be installed. The jurors also pointed out the lack of a regulation governing the number of persons who can stand between the rear seats and rear wall of a motion- picture theater. They, recommended that such a regulation be instituted. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: LAUREL'S FINE RACING: HARNESS AND RUNNING HORSES MAKE SPLENDID TIME TRACK IS HALF-MILE WONDER LARGE CROWD GATHERS ABOUT COURSE TO SEE EVENTS ON PROGRAM OF BIG FOUR-COUNTY FAIR
full_text: LAUREL'S FINE RACING Harness And Running Horses Make .. Splendid Time. 1 ! TRACK IS HALF-MILE WONDER Large Crowd Gathers About Course To See Events On Program Of Big Four-County Fair. The Laurel (Md.) Four-County Fair and race meeting began yesterday under most encouraging auspices. For an opening day the attendance was large. The race track was a curiosity to the horsemen. It is a full half-mile course. The building of the track was started August 19, and it was finished, last week. Forces worked night and day for 40 days. They accomplished a work which was thought by many to be Impossible. Time made in the races yesterday showed the capabilities of the course. The many horsemen present had no fault to find with the track, and as there are 178 horses entered for the harness races alone this is the best evidence of the track being a good one. It is a Fuler's earth base and mixed loam topping. Both harness horses and runners took to the going kindly. The track has good, long stretches, broad turns and is 60 feet wide on the homestretch. It is nearly as wide on the backstretch. The association has land enough to extend the homestretch by a chute and have seven-eighths of a mile straightaway if such is necessary. Fast Time By All Classes. Besides harness and flat races there will be hurdle races this season, and next fall a steeplechase course will be added. Yesterday the 2.25 class pacers stepped in 2.23, the 2.24 class trotters worked in 2.234 and the 2.35 class (county horses) in 2.28. In the one running race, an inau- gural at one-half a mile, the distance was run in 52 seconds, and had the winner had occasion he could have won in 50 seconds. That the races were hotly contested was proved when it took six heats under the new elimination rules to settle the 2.24 trot. The first event was for the 2.25 pacers. Nine started. The first heat was the feature of the race. Elegant Boy, en- tered from Baltimore, Happy May, from Mount Vernon, and Helen, from Townsend, Del., raced home in the lead. There were not 24 inches between these three, who finished in the order named. While the second heat was faster, it did not result in so grand a finish. Ele- gant Boy was forced out in the final heat In fast time. The 2.24 trot had 17 entries and 11 scratched. It was a race of uncertainties to the finish. The first three heats were each won by different horses. One was distanced, one was out under the rules, but four were left to race three more heats before Alexander I., owned and driven by Gipsy Haight, of Savannah, Ga., landed a winner. Miss Kushan, a Washington mare, was first under the wire in the fin- ish heat, but was set back one position for running. Race For Horses Of Four Counties. The 2.35 pace was for houses owned in the four counties-Prince George's, Mont- gomery, Howard and Anne Arundel. It was a better race than such specials usu- ally result in. It was won by Cora Wig- gens, from Bladensburg, in straight heats. Tuscarora, a gelding entered from Sandy Springs, was second in the first heat, but as he belongs in Washington, he had to be drawn after the heat. The inaugural running dash, at half a mile, was won handily by Pio Pico, a horse which had previously won 13 races this season. Despite this the books laid 3 to 1 against him. The management decided to offer a $50 bonus to the horse making the fastest mile, on a trot or pace, at this meeting. Results Of All Events. 2.25 class pacing; purse $300. title: Two Charities To Share In Enoch Harlan Estate
full_text: 1100 10 Share In Enoch Harlan Estate ... 3. VVVVI n buyo Home Society Among Bene- ficiaries Under Will Two charitable institutions yester- day were named to share in the esti- mated $60,000 estate of Enoch Harlan, senior member of the law firm of Harlan & Harlan and former president of the board of the House of Reforma- tion at Cheltenham, according to the will filed in Orphans' Court. Mr. Harlan died last Friday while on vacation at St. Petersburg, Fla., He Deft $100 each to the trustees of the McKim Free School and the Boys' Home Society of Baltimore, for which he served as a member of the board. Four friends were named to re- ceive $100 each and Mr. Harlan's four children each were to receive $1,000. The residue was left to his wife, Mrs. Mary B. Harlan, who was designated executor of the estate. Mr. Harlan lived at 2014 Garrison Boulevard. full_text: WASHINGTON COUNTY'S NYA WORK TO HALT All Projects, Including Defense Training, To Stop April 1 Brown Also Says Some State Programs Will Go On War List  With National Youth Admin- istration programs in Maryland being, curtailed as a result of an order by Aubrey Williams, NYA administrator, all NYA projects in Washington county, including training for defense industries, will be terminated by April 1, Glen D. Brown, State NYA director, an- nounced yesterday.  Mr. Brown, who made a four- day reorganization survey in West- ern Maryland last week, also said that some NYA programs in the State hitherto considered non-de- fense activities will be transferred to defense lists of the organization following Mr. Williams' order to eliminate all projects that are not training workers for war produc- tion.  Mr. Brown, it was disclosed, made his survey trip after he had been visited here by Mr. Williams. This conference, ten days ago, was not revealed until yesterday. title: LAUREL'S CLASSY RACES: HARNESS AND RUNNING HORSES PLEASE BIG CROWD MANAGEMENT COMPLIMENTED BLACK WIG, FROM YORK, WINS IN 2.16 CLASS--OCCIDENTAL TAKES 6-FURLONG DASH WITH EASE
full_text: LAUREL'S CLASSY RACES Harness And Running Horses Please Big Crowd. MANAGEMENT COMPLIMENTED Black Wig, From York, Wins In 2.16 Class Occidental Takes 6- Furlong Dash With Ease. [From a Staff Correspondent.] Laurel, Md., Oct. 11. The racing today at Laurel's Four County Fair was fully up to the high standard set Monday, the opening day of the meeting. The weather conditions were excellent. Racing over the track is doing the track good. Horse- men today pronounced the footing to be all that could be desired. The management came in for a lot of favorable comment for the wisdom shown in constructing such a course. Some of the officials were saying this evening that they believed the new Laurel track to be the best half-mile circle in Maryland. That the track is a good, safe one is a certainty. The attendance today was larger than that of the opening day, and, with good weather, it is anticipated it will grow daily. Meeting Is Well Conducted. So far the race meeting has been fric- tionless. The moment the starter an- nounces the result of a race he invites the money winners to come to the stand and they are promptly paid the money parts of the purse their horses won. The wide stretch-60 feet-enables big fields to score away on more even terms than is possible on many tracks. Because of the shortness of the day's light and the large entry list, the harness races, have to be started at 1.30 P. M. so that the running horses may have their chance.. There was much greater speculation on the results of today's racing than on that of Monday's. : The afternoon's sport began with a race for the 2.16 class-pacers. It was won in straight heats by Black Wig, a gelding from York, Pa. Minnie Tillian, a mare from Bath, N. Y., forced Black Wig out in 2.164. The 2.20 trot was won off the reel by Mald of Athens, from Governor, N. Y. Little Joe Wiesenfeld's Expedition, Jr., was the Maid's warmest contender. The country folk took much interest in the race for country horses of the 2.40 class. Brosene Bros.' mare, Wannetta, from Ellicott City, won the first heat and, though she was the only one able to race Van March, from Cheltenham, she just did not have speed to do more than force Von March to a record of 2.26%. Occidental Takes The Dash. The six-furlong running race was won by Occidental, owned by W. R. Hall, of Car- uthsville, Md. She was ridden by Mc- Carthy, who took Ice from Elaborate to the last furlong. Occidental, the favorite; when let down, showed a burst of speed and won by a neck from Elaborate, who beat Lady Fitzherbert by three-fourths of a length. R. E. Biggs, who started the runners, got them off in great shape. His starting of the trotters and pacers also was well done. Summary Of The Races. First Race-2.16 class, pace; purse $300. clean_text: LAUREL'S CLASSY RACES Harness And Running Horses Please Big Crowd. MANAGEMENT COMPLIMENTED Black Wig, From York, Wins In 2.16 Class Occidental Takes 6- Furlong Dash With Ease. [From a Staff Correspondent.] Laurel, Md., Oct. 11. The racing today at Laurel's Four County Fair was fully up to the high standard set Monday, the opening day of the meeting. The weather conditions were excellent. Racing over the track is doing the track good. Horse- men today pronounced the footing to be all that could be desired. The management came in for a lot of favorable comment for the wisdom shown in constructing such a course. Some of the officials were saying this evening that they believed the new Laurel track to be the best half-mile circle in Maryland. That the track is a good, safe one is a certainty. The attendance today was larger than that of the opening day, and, with good weather, it is anticipated it will grow daily. Meeting Is Well Conducted. So far the race meeting has been fric- tionless. The moment the starter an- nounces the result of a race he invites the money winners to come to the stand and they are promptly paid the money parts of the purse their horses won. The wide stretch-60 feet-enables big fields to score away on more even terms than is possible on many tracks. Because of the shortness of the day's light and the large entry list, the harness races, have to be started at 1.30 P. M. so that the running horses may have their chance.. There was much greater speculation on the results of today's racing than on that of Monday's. : The afternoon's sport began with a race for the 2.16 class-pacers. It was won in straight heats by Black Wig, a gelding from York, Pa. Minnie Tillian, a mare from Bath, N. Y., forced Black Wig out in 2.164. The 2.20 trot was won off the reel by Mald of Athens, from Governor, N. Y. Little Joe Wiesenfeld's Expedition, Jr., was the Maid's warmest contender. The country folk took much interest in the race for country horses of the 2.40 class. Brosene Bros.' mare, Wannetta, from Ellicott City, won the first heat and, though she was the only one able to race Van March, from Cheltenham, she just did not have speed to do more than force Von March to a record of 2.26%. Occidental Takes The Dash. The six-furlong running race was won by Occidental, owned by W. R. Hall, of Car- uthsville, Md. She was ridden by Mc- Carthy, who took Ice from Elaborate to the last furlong. Occidental, the favorite; when let down, showed a burst of speed and won by a neck from Elaborate, who beat Lady Fitzherbert by three-fourths of a length. R. E. title: MORE RIGID CURB ON PARKING URGED: GRAND JURY GROUP FAVORS COMPLETE BAN ON MAIN DOWNTOWN STREETS CREATION OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO DRAW TRAFFIC RULES ALSO ADVOCATED
full_text: MORE RIGID CURB ON PARKING URGED Grand Jury Group Favors Complete Ban On Main Downtown Streets Creation Of Special Commit- tee To Draw Traffic Rules Also Advocated Abolition of parking on major thor- oughfares in the downtown area and creation of a special committee with the power to draw regulations govern- ing traffic are among the recommen- dations which have been submitted by the traffic committee of the retiring grand jury. The parking situation on Charles street, which has been discussed, pro and con by almost everybody for the past few years, again was given a prominent position. The outgoing body advocated the prohibition of parking on that street between Centre and Baltimore streets. : Other Streets Mentioned Other streets on which a no-park- ling law was advocated are: Franklin street between St. Paul and Paca streets. Howard street between Richmond Market, or the south end of the Howard street extention, and Madison street. North avenue between Charles street and Madison avenue. More one-way streets with more intersections carrying a left-hand turn ban also were suggested, as was the substitution of a block system of traffic- light control instead of the present wave system now in use on many thoroughfares. Market Situation Cited As for the traffic situation around the Lexington Market, that was de- scribed by the grand jury committee as a "classic traffic abuse." With a view to studying and cor- recting traffic conditions throughout the city the committee, headed by Henry C. Miller, advocated the crea- tion of a special traffic committee to be added to the City Planning Commis- sion, with powers to set up regulations f use of the streets. There was a divergence of opinion in the report by the committee on Cheltenham, the house of reformation for Negro boys. Report Of Majority The majority report was signed by David W. Bridges, committee chair- man; Louis G. Groener and Mr. Mil- ler. The minority report was filed by Howard H. Murphy, Negro member of the grand jury and one of the Chel- tenham committee. • .. In the majority report, management of the institution was called "satis- factory and efficient considering the difficulties they are working under in respect to more or less antiquated equipment, old buildings and a limited budget." The minority report claimed "the cows and hogs get much better atten- Lion than the boys themselves" and The barns and cowsheds are in better condition than the dormitories. Negro Staft Urged Replacement of the present staff with a Negro personnel also was sug- gested in the minority statement. It also was said that "Prince George's county seems to regard Chel- Lenham as a private political plum and through its control of the board mem- bership foists upon this institution the incompetent political employes whom Commissioner Jones (Harry C. Jones, Employment Commissioner), says are unfit." Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: BEISSER RESIGNS FROM AID SOCIETY: TO TAKE WELFARE POSITION WITH 2 ORGANIZATIONS AT ST. LOUIS HAS SERVED 17 YEARS AS GENERAL SECRETARY OF HENRY WATSON GROUP
full_text: Aid Society Secretary Accepts St. Louis Pos UFU PAUL T. BEISSER BEISSER RESIGNS FROM AID SOCIETY To Take Welfare Positio With 2 Organizations At St. Louis Has Served 17 Years As Gen eral Secretary Of Henry Watson Group - LIGIUULL UL Saul L. DUIDser as general secretary of the Henry Wat- son Children's Aid Society and his - acceptance of the duties of secretary - and manager of the St. Louis Chil- dren's Aid Society and the Provident Association, was announced yesterday by Philip W. Ness, president of the local society. Mr. Beisser's duties in St. Louis will begin on September 1, Mr. Ness said. The two Missouri organizations cover the family welfare work of the city of St. Louis and the child-welfare work of that city and St. Louis county. Has Held Post Here 17 Years .Mr. Beisser has been general secre- tary of the local society for seventeen years. He is a graduate of the Univer- sity of Pennsylvania, the Wharton School of Finance and the New York School of Social Work. Before coming to Baltimor he served as secretary and legislative agent of the Children's Division, Public Chari- ties Association of Pennsylvania; re- search secretary, American Association of Social Workers; field secretary, New York School of Social Work, and as an economist in the Federal Bureau of Labor and Statistics. Made Several Surveys In addition to his other duties he has made community surveys in Hart- ford, Providence, Rochester. Stam- ford, Kansas City and Honolulu; was active in the Home Relief Bureau of New York city; secretary of the Gov- ernor's Commission on Juvenile De- linquency in 1940, and a member of the commission to study Cheltenham School for Colored Boys in 1939. From 1929 to 1933 he was president of the Maryland State Conference on Social Welfare; was a member of the executive committee, National Con- ference of Social Work from 1933 to 1935, and president of the Child Wel- fare League of America from 1938 to 1940. His Work Lauded James M. Hepbron, director of the Community Fund, of which the Henry Watson Children's Aid Society is a member, said yesterday, "Mr. Beisser's professional attainments are of the highest order and he is generally rec- ognized, not only locally, but through- out the country as one of the leaders in the child-welfare field. "He came to Baltimore seventeen years ago and has done more to raise the general social work and welfare standards of this city than any other one individual. "Successive governors and mayors have called upon him to head com- missions and in working out legislative matters. Other cities in the country have consistently sought his services for surveys in his particular field. He has been an outstanding asset to the city and I greatly regret that he is leaving us." Wishes Beisser Success Mr. Hess said, "I speak for our en- tire board of managers when I say that it is with real regret that we lose Mr. Beisser to St. Louis, and we wish him every success in his new position with its enlarged opportunities and responsibilities.. "During the last seventeen years in which Mr. Beisser has been our gen- eral secretary, the Henry Watson Chil- dren's Aid Society has made vast strides forward in the child-welfare work in this community, and we pro- pose to continue this much-needed work at its present high standards under a new executive." Mr. Beisser is married and has two sons, Paul, Jr., 21, and James E., 18. He is a member of the University Club of Baltimore. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: CHELTENHAM HOME CHARGES ARE DENIED: REPORT ON NEGRO INSTITUTION "CREATLY EXAGERATED" BOARD SAYS
full_text: CHELTENHAM HOME CHARGES ARE DENIED Report On Negro Institution "Greatly Exaggerated," Board Says. That reports regarding mismanage- iment of the House of Reformation for Colored Boys, at Cheltenham, Prince George's county, are "greatly exagger- ated," but that an investigation by dis- interested parties is welcomed, was the sentiment expressed yesterday by the board of managers of the institution at a special meeting. The board met in executive session in the Vickers Building at the request of William J. Ogden. secretary of the State Board of Aid and Charities, and Nathaniel G. title: ATTACK ON A NEWSBOY: NEGRO FINED FOR STRIKING LAD SELLING EVENING SUN
full_text: ATTACK ON A NEWSBOY Negro Fined For Striking Lad Selling Evening Sun. As a result of the animosity of certain newsboys to boys who sell THE EVENING Sus, John Parraway, a 16-year-old negro, living at 219 North Parrish street, was fined $1 and costs, amounting to $2.45, by Justice Stanley, at the Southwestern Police Station, yesterday morning. Parra- way was convicted by the magistrate of assaulting Thomas Wells Cole, living at 241 North Fulton avenue, a 12-year-old white boy, whose only offense in the eyes of the negro was that he sells THE EVENING SUN. What inspired the hostility of the young negro to THE EVENING SUN may be gathered from the fact that an employe of the circulation department of another afternoon newspaper deposited $20.45 at the police station Thursday afternoon to secure the release of Parraway, and an- other employe of the circulation depart- ment of the same paper paid the fine after he had been permitted to withdraw the collateral which his fellow-employe had deposited. The assault on Cole is only an instance of the hostility that has been incited throughout the city against boys who han- dle THE EVENING SUN. In some сабек the papers have been taken from the boys and torn into pieces and the youngsters made to fleet in terror. l'arraway's assault was committed at Gilmor and Saratoga streets, where THE EVENING SUN newsboys have been fre- quently molested by those who sell other papers. It is understood that the word has been passed along that the boys must not handle THE EVENING SUN. Cole is so diminutive in size that his face just appeared above the ralling in front of the magistrate's desk as he told his story. He said that he was getting on a car with his papers, when Parraway pushed him off and kicked him, causing him to fall to the ground and narrowly escaped being run over. Mr. Howard S. La Salle, a wholesale agent of THE EVENING SUN, who ordered Parraway's arrest, testified that he saw the negro strike the white boy. The agent said he had been stationed on the corner to see that the boys who sell THE EVENING SUN were not molested. Some newsboys have been instructed, Mr. La Salle also said, not to sell THE EVENING SUN and have been run away from the corner when they did not obey instructions. These had been made timid by the threats, but Mr. La Salle told them he would look out for them. Patrolman Frederick, who made the ar- rest, said the newsboys have been having trouble on that corner. The patrolman warned the boys Thursday afternoon. While he was away from the corner a few minutes the assault occurred. Charles Johnson, colored, 430 North Gil- mor street, testified that he saw Cole get on the car and Parraway strike at him. When this testimony had been heard Parraway admitted striking Cole, but de- nied kicking him. Justice Stanley, in deciding the case, told the boys that they must understand that they are at liberty to sell any news- papers they desire. He told Parraway that he ought to be sent to the Colored House of Reformation, at Cheltenham, and that he would be severely punished if arrested again on such a charge. full_text: $9,334,270 ASKED BY PLANNING UNIT Sum Would Go For Capital Improvements In State Institutions Work To Be Completed In Next Six Years Under Proposal A six-year capital improvement pro- gram for State agencies and institu- tions, calling for a total expenditure of $9,334,270, was recommended by the State Planning Commission in a 169- page report issued yesterday. The report, compiled by the commis- zion in collaboration with the De- partment of Budget and Procurement, covers the most urgent needs of the State in the fiscal years from 1941 to 1947. It recommends to Governor O'Conor and the 1941 General Assembly that $4,172,000 be provided for the fiscal biennium beginning October 1, and that the State figure tentatively on spending $1,722,560 in 1943-44 and 1944- 45 and $3,439,710 in 1945-46 and 1946-47. From Agency Requests These figures, the report stated, were worked out from requests of the agencies and institutions themselves, which asked altogether for $18,509,051 for the six-year period. Largest Items For 1944 Largest items in the 1943-44 and 1944- 45 biennium are $592,000 for State men- tal hospitals. $252,000 for Rosewood State Training School, $180,000 for Morgan State College, $146,000 for the Cheltenham School for Boys and $164,- 000 for tuberculosis sanatoria. In the 1945-46 and 1946-47 list are $1,626,000 for mental hospitals, $6-12,- 500 for Rosewood, $266,000 for Chelten- ham, $268,000 for Maryland Training School for Boys, $208,500 for Maryland Training School for Colored Girls and $428,000 for Morgan State College. Both the lists for the second and for the third bienniums in the six-year period will be subject to review two years hence. To finance the immediate $4,172,000 program, the State Planning Commis- sion recommends a bond issue for this amount to be authorized by the cur- rent General Assembly. $33,865,000 Debt This would bring the State bonded indebtedness in 1943, after bonds com- ing due in the meantime have been retired, to $33.865,000. title: GRAND JURY OFFERS UCB PROPOSALS: RECOMMENDS THAT A COMMISSIONER REPLACE 3-MAN BOARD
full_text: GRAND JURY OFFERS UCB PROPOSALS Recommends That A Commissioner Replace 3-Man Board Naming of a commissioner of employment to replace the present three-man board in the administra. tion of the affairs of the State Un employment Compensation Board was recommended in a special re port submitted yesterday by the retiring September-term grand jury. In a lengthy review of the ne tivities of the UCB and a discus sion of the large number of frauds recently brought to light after a series of articles appearing in The Sun, the grand jury suggested immediate action to prevent further frauds. It also urged replacement of un- qualified personnel and a program of publicity to acquaint employés with the nature, purposes and sources of the UCB fund. Favor Amendments In addition, the jurors said they believed the present unemploy- ment compensation law should be amended and greatly strengthened, and indorsed in principle the 23- point program adopted by the Legislative Council and presented to the State Legislature. The grand jury stated that when it first took office last September, it was called on to deal with a large number of cases involving frauds against the UCB. "This situation," the jurors re ported, "produced a feeling of grave concern in the minds of the jury, for fresh in our memories were the allegations in the morn- ing press of incompetency and vari- ous abuses and laxities found in the administration of the fund by the Unemployment Compensation Board." Witnesses Were Questioned The jury stated that it was then decided that the public interest re- quired an investigation into the op- cration of the board. In furtherance of the probe, a great number of wit- nesses were questioned, the report said. The report continued, saying that an aftermath of the recent war was the closing down of many war in- dustries and the resultant layoff of workers. The UCB suddenly found itself deluged with workers seeking (Continued on Page 11. Column 6) unemployment compensation, par ticularly workers who refused to seek other jobs at lower salaries. Large numbers of discharged vet erans also were added to this pool. forming what the jurors termed "complacent '52-20' club, whos members were satisfied to take vacation at public expense." Employes Lacked Experience Called upon to increase its per sonnel, the board acquired a num ber of incompetent employés whos lack of experience was responsibl for some erroneous payments, the jurors continued. "In our study of the unemploy ment compensation law of the State of Maryland," the report of the jurors said, "the committee noted the far-reaching negation of the high purposes of the act, which was conceived as a measure to as sist those unemployed through no fault of their own, and to encourage employers to provide more stable employment conditions, "Contrary to those purposes are payments, permitted by statute, for voluntary quits, layoffs for mis conduct connected with work and willful acts endangering safety of others. The result of our present public policy is a weakening of moral fiber in many individuals, who seek recompense from the State for not working. "Not In Best Interests Of State" "This deplorable state of affairs probably can be attributed to dis. interest on the part of the general public, which up to now has seen no immediate cause for concern.. "On the other hand, those indi- viduals in our State, whose inter- ests, whether individual or politi- cal, lie with the cause of labor, have been active over a period of years to further all possible bene- ties, which have found expression in some phases of our State law in our opinion, are not in the best interests of the State and country.' The jurors found that the UCE is handicapped in the prompt de tection of frauds due to the time interval between benefit payments and submission by employés o earnings lists as required by law The investigating body contended that "prompt detection is a mos effective deterrent." Meet Three Times A Week "In reviewing the activities o the three members of the board we have found that the board meets three days each week to hold hear ings on cases of appeals from de cisions of reviewing referees. "The present chairman has been the most active member of the board and, while he is eminently qualified for this position and has compiled an imposing record dur- ing his years with the board, he has found that his private business re- quires as much time as he spends in the business of the board. As far as we have learned, the associate members of the board have been active mainly in the hearings of ap- peals, with few or no administra- tive assignments." Higher Salaries Urged The board recommended adop tion of corrective measures ad. vanced by the Legislative Council subcommittee for benefit payments for other than voluntary unemploy ment. Higher salary classifications to permit the best possible type of personnel also were proposed. Another recommendation of the jurors was that employers immedi- ately notify the board of all new employés to help in the prevention and prompt detection of frauds. The report on the UCB was sub- mitted by William J. Bullen, R. Harwood Bagby, Edgar L. Heaver and Edward F. Requard. In the main grand jury report signed by John B. Duvall, foreman, the jurors noted the "deplorable conditions" at the Cheltenham School for Boys.

"This situation," the jurors re ported, "produced a feeling of grave concern in the minds of the jury, for fresh in our memories were the allegations in the morn- ing press of incompetency and vari- ous abuses and laxities found in the administration of the fund by the Unemployment Compensation Board." In furtherance of the probe, a great number of wit- nesses were questioned, the report said. The report continued, saying that an aftermath of the recent war was the closing down of many war in- dustries and the resultant layoff of workers. The UCB suddenly found itself deluged with workers seeking (Continued on Page 11. Column 6) unemployment compensation, par ticularly workers who refused to seek other jobs at lower salaries. Large numbers of discharged vet erans also were added to this pool. forming what the jurors termed "complacent '52-20' club, whos members were satisfied to take vacation at public expense." A DAY IN JUVENILE COURT Wayward Boys And Girls Developed Into Good Men And Women, HOW JUDGE WILLIAMS WORKS Finds That A Lecture Is The Best Remedy For The Wayward-Syrı pathy Better Than Severity: There was a little baby that no ona would have; a boy who would not behave, a negro urchin who had an ice-pick that did not belong to him and several other cases in the Juvenile Court yesterday. Despite the stifling heat Judge Williams looked over his "specs" at each case and tried each time to make the world better. It was just an ordinary sort of day for cases at the court, but it seemed to bring out the contrasts, which showed what a force and guide for good it is in Baltimore. The boy who would not behave was given a lecture by the Judge, the kind his father would give him. He probably will not be back again on charges. Ten years honce the boy will be a good citizen. If he had not been taken to the court he might have grown up a thief or a burglar. It was hot. The Judge fanned and the court attaches fanned, and the little boys and girls on the benches looked very pent- tent and very scared. The mothers and fathers appeared worried. All were warm, uncomfortable warm. But then Judge Williams put on his "specs," pecullar "specs" that perch on the end of his nose and will not let him look harsh and severe. Then he began. The Negro Boy With The Pick. First was the negro boy with the ice pick. IHe was 10 years old and talked like he was 40. He had found the ice-pick, he sald, and he certainly did not steal it. A man had seen it the same time he did, ly ing in the street, but he got it first,, and when he tried to sell it on Harrison strect the big policeman got him. He said he lived on "West Wolfe street" and had never seen his "real father." He lived with his aunt, and he did not steal the plek, anyhow. So the Judge told him to go home and be good. He went quick, his eyes glancing apprehensively back. Then the little baby, whom no one wanted, was talked of. His mother had become Insane and been sent to Bayview. IIis father was dend. The Supervisors of City Charities found it out and took the baby to its mother's relatives. The aunt did not want it, the cousin could not care for it-nobody wanted a baby in hot weath. er. The Judge thought maybe the Sisters at St. Elizabeth's Home would not mind adding just another to their home, and so the baby slept last night in its foundling cot. A wide-eyed negro boy, with spine trou- ble, was next brought up. His mother died yesterday morning at Bayview. He had been living with a "bad, bad man." Two negro women said they had telephoned for "Parker," meaning Captain Parker, of the Society for the Protection of Children. Judge Williams saw the negro boy's eyes fill and his lips quiver. He smiled at him over the specs and he stopped crying. Then he sent him to the House of Reforma- tion for Colored Boys at Cheltenham, and the negro women went out "thanking Gawd." Watch And Chain Her Downfall. The next was a little negro girl, a coun- try girl from Rock Hall, who came to Bal timore to be a mald. But her mistress went out several days ago and left her alone in the house. The sight of a gold watch and chain broke down the barriers of her Sun- day-school lessons and she took them. Patrolman O'Donnell caught her in half a day. The Judge looked serious. He asked Julia why she took it, but Julia did not know. The only thing Julia did know was that she wanted to get back to that old "mammy" in Kent county. And Judge Williams directed his bailiff to see her safe- ly on the bont today and dismissed the case. Julia will think a long time before doing wrong again. Two boys came up for shooting off fire- crackers. The biggest one said he knew it was wrong, but he "Just did it." He said his "gang" was with him, so the Judge commissioned him to break up the gang. And the boy demurred and said maybe he could not do it, but he is coming b Thursday to report progress. Ife the Judge calls "one of my missionaries A boy with a slungshot was told that "what goes up, must come down." He had not thought of that while shooting, and he was penitent. He sald manfully he was sorry and was dismissed. Said Jail Would Ruin Him, The next case was hard. A negro child. was accused of stealing five pool balls. The colored lad denied it. He reckoned. he had been with the boys who stole them, but he did not take any of the balls. The Judge sald: "This is a case where a detention house Is necessary. This boyeshould not be al lowed to go, and yet I will not send him to jail. It would ruin him." "Jimmy" was paroled in the custody of a probation officer. The Judge also deliv ered a lecture to the boy's mother. "It seems to me," he said, "that the col ored women of Baltimore do not exercise, in most cases, any control whatever over their children or seek to do so. They let them run wild and allow them to develop into criminals without trying to correct them. Something must be done." The last case was the little boy who would not behave. He had been to St Mary's Industrial School for two months, but he liked home better, so he said he would certainly behave this time. The Judge thought so, too. And then his day's work was over. That happens every day in the Juvenile Court. The Washington authorities say it is the best in the coun try. Baltimore does not realize it yet.
