title: GRAND JURY HITS ORDER ON CHELTENHAM: PRINCE GEORGE'S URGES ACTION OF BOARD BE NULLIFIED RECOMMENDS DISMISSAL OF 19 OBJECTORS AND 6 NEGRO EMPLOYES
full_text: GRAND JURY HITS ORDER ON CHELTENHAM Prince George's Body Urges Action Of Board Be Nullified Recommends Dismissal Of 19 Objectors And 6 Negro Employes Immediate nullification of the order to abolish race segregation in the staff dining and housing facili- ties at the Cheltenham School for Boys and prompt dismissal from the institution of nineteen conscien- tious objectors and six regular Negro employes have been recom- mended to the school's board of managers by the April grand jury of Prince George's county. 1 In its report to the judges of the Circuit Court the grand jury charged that "a radical group com- posed of Negro and white conscien- tious objectors to military service, who comparatively recently have been detailed to the institution for public service, and certain of the regular Negro employes are de- manding that the policy of social interracialism adopted by the board be put into effect," and that they "appear to be primarily responsi- ble" for the "deplorable situation" found in the jury's investigation. Cites "Chaotic Condition" "This action by the board of managers appears to have resulted in a chaotic condition within the institution," the report said. It continued that, in addition to practically all white employes, "a certain group of Negro employes who appear to definitely want race segregation continued, have taken the definite position that they will sever their connections if any at- tempt is made to put the board's in- structions to the superintendent into effect." A third recommendation of the grand jury was that "in the future all vacancies on the board of man- agers and in administrative posi- tions on the staff be filled with per- sonnel very carefully chosen to reasonably insure the continued successful operation of the institu- tion in line with established prece- dents." : Hill Reserves Comment Howard C. Hill, acting chairman of the board of managers, yester- day said he had not seen the grand jury report and would have no com- ment to make until he has read it fully. Mr. Hill is acting in the place of Joseph H. Blandford, who re- signed the chairmanship as a result of the board's action against segre- gation. Mr. Blandford was absent from the meeting on March 25 ------ 4-1--- The grand jury report, copies of which were ordered sent to Gov- ernor O'Conor and each member of the board of managers, said: "The conflicting peremptory de- mands of the two groups referred to have resulted in a situation which is not only very serious but is potentially dangerous, and it ap- pears obvious that an immediate solution of the problem is necessary and urgent. Called Repulsive "Aside from what may be the immediate result of the board's action within the institution itself it is the feeling of this body that any policy of social interracialism there would be very definitely re pulsive to the great mass of both white and Negro citizens of the State, not be for the best interests of the inmates themselves and would defeat the very purpose of the institution's existence, namely, to prepare and equip Negro youth of Maryland for future employment in gainful occupations under white supervision in a country where most certainly for generations to come general social interracialism between the white and Negro races probably will not be tolerated." The grand jury said it was satis- fied that the "recommendation con- cerning the removal of certain per- sonnel can be followed without any serious result in so far as the op- eration of the institution imme- diately following such removal is concerned, and we sincerely selieve that all recommendations made are for the best interests of the institu- tion itself, its inmates and all others concerned or interested." title: CHELTENHAM ACCORD SOUGHT: "FAIRLY RADICAL" COMPROMISE MOVE BY BOARD OF MAN- AGERS SEEN MATTER TO BE CONSIDERED IN LIGHT OF RECENT DEVELOP- MENTS, HILL SAYS
full_text: CHELTENHAM ACCORD SOUGHT "Fairly Radical" Compromise Move By Board Of Man- agers Seen Matter To Be Considered In Light Of Recent Develop- ments, Hill Says A "fairly radical" compromise move by the board of managers of The Cheltenham School for Boys to settle the controversy over its re- cent order to abolish segregation of white and Negro employes was seen yesterday as Howard C. Hill, acting president, planned to call a special meeting at the school before the end of the week. Mr. Hill said the matter would be considered in the light of recent developments, particularly the re- port of the Prince George's county grand jury which described a "de- plorable situation" and "chaotic condition within the institution" as a result of the board's order, but in- dications were that the action would fall far short of the grand jury's recommendations that the non-seg- regation order be nullified and nineteen conscientious objectors assigned to the staff and six regular Negro employes be "promptly re- moved." "Issues Confused" Meanwhile, at Philadelphia, it was indicated the American Friends Service Committee, as- signor of the conscientious objec- tors who, according to the grand jury report, were "primarily re- sponsible" for the action of the board and the existing conditions, was ready to cooperate in any solu- tion, but "prefers not to act in any way that would embarrass the board." Kenneth W. Morgan, educational director of the Civilian Public Serv- ice section of the Friends Service Committee, said representatives of the committee have been to Chel- tenham to investigate the situation and were expecting to be called "very soon" to a meeting of the board of managers. Mr. Hill, however, announced it was not planned to call represent- atives of the Friends Committee to the meeting, which probably will be held Thursday or Friday. "While there will have to be something fairly radical done," he continued, "it will have to be a solution on which intelligent groups can meet. If you dismiss the con- scientious objectors, there will be repercussions. There will be other repercussions from some of the em- ployes if the order is rescinded, and still others if we seek to enforce it."! Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: APPOINTED HEAD OF CHELTENHAM: OFFICER AT ATLANTA PENITENTIARY TO TAKE CHARGE IN FEW WEEKS
full_text: APPOINTED HEAD OF CHELTENHAM Officer At Atlanta Peni- tentiary To Take Charge In Few Weeks The board of managers of the Chel- tenham School for Boys yesterday named Vance Errett Thomas, 49, chief parole officer at the Atlanta Federal Penitentiary, superintendent of the Negro reformatory in Prince George's county. Thomas is expected to assume the $3,500-a-year superintendency within four or five weeks after he finishes his duties at Atlanta, said Howard C. Hill, of Baltimore, president of the Chel- tenham board of managers. B. B. Sunderland, present superin- tendent, will resume his former posi- tion as chief parole officer when Thomas takes over. Thomas was second on a list of five eligibles certified for the superintend- ency by Harry C. Jones, State Employ- ment Commissioner, after an examina- tion taken by twelve applicants. The board sent his name back to Jones for final certification. Native Of Kansas Hill said. Thomas "has had a good deal of experience in administrative work, vocational placement and parole work." Thomas is a native of Kansas and was a parole and social worker at the Petersburg, Va., Federal re- formatory before going to Atlanta in 1937. He is married and has two daugh- ters, 6 and 11. Cheltenham was taken over as a State institution in 1937. It receives Negro boys on commitment by any court, Juvenile Court or magistrate. Baltimore city or the counties from which the Negrocs are committed must pay the State $200 a year for their care and training. The remaining amount necessary is paid by the State Treasury. Jones, State Employmen Commissioner, last night announce an eligible list of five men for thi post of superintendent of the Chelten ham School for Boys, Negro reforma tory. title: JUDGE ULMAN SUCCUMBS TO HEART ATTACK: ASSOCIATE OF SUPREME BENCH OF BALTIMORE DIES AT HOME JURIST WAS OF NATIONAL REPUTATION AND WIDE ACTIVITIES
full_text: JUDGE ULMAN SUCCUMBS TO HEART ATTACK Associate Of Supreme * Bench Of Baltimore Dies At Home Jurist Was Of National Reputation And Wide Activities Judge Joseph N. Ulman, of the Supreme Bench of Baltimore, a jurist and penologist of national reputation and former president of the Prison Industries Reorganiza- tion Board by appointment of Pres- ident Roosevelt, died suddenly yes- terday morning at his home, 2615 Talbot road, Windsor Hills. Death was due to a heart attack. Judge Ulman was also a member of the American Law Institute, an organization of especial importance in the legal profession devoted to research in the law; a leader in ac- tivities of the Baltimore Urban League, which he served many times as president; a member of the board of the Cheltenham School for Boys; a former member of the Alumni Council of the Johns Hop- kins University, and a leader in Jewish activities, local and national. In Apparent Good Health The jurist apparently was in per- fect health when he awakened yes- terday morning. The day before he took his usual long walk and last week attended to his court duties and to other interests. As he was preparing for break- fast, Mrs. Ulman noticed that her husband did not look so well as usual, although he made no com- plaint. Dr. Samuel Wolman was summoned -but Judge Ulman was dead when he arrived. News of the judge's death spread quickly and many of his colleagues on the bench called at his home during the afternoon. Because of Judge Ulman's energy and appar- ent health his death came as a de- cided shock. Governor And Mayor Shocked Both Governor O'Conor and Mayor Jackson said they were shocked by Judge Ulman's death. "I am shocked beyond expression since it was only Friday that Judge Ulman spent several hours at my Annapolis office going over matters of State importance with me," Gov- ernor O'Conor said. "Maryland' has suffered an irre- parable loss because Judge Ulman not only was an exceptional and eminent jurist, but also because for many years he has been an out- standing leader in humanitarian movements in our State. Missed Train To Make Plea "His was an unflagging interest in what he considered just and in the cause for right. Indicative of this was a plea he made to me Fri- da in the interest of a convict seeking parole. He was so intense, so interested, that he missed his train to Baltimore. "Baltimore and Maryland have lost a truly great citizen." Mayor Jackson recalled that Judge Ulman only a week ago pre- sided at a large meeting dealing with Jewish humanitarianism. "It was indicative of the man, an honored citizen of our city, a jurist of highest ideals, of courage and vision," the Mayor said. "In his death Baltimore suffers a loss it can ill afford," Born Here in 1878 The son of the late Nathan and Dina Oppenheim Ulman, he was born in this city on August 9, 1878. His father was a member of the distilling firm of Ulman, Boykin, and Company. He attended Baltimore's public schools and Marston's University School before he entered the Johns Hopkins University, where he re- ceived his bachelor of arts degree in 1898. He later received his mas- ter of arts and law degrees at Columbia University. He was admitted to the Maryland Bar in 1901 and started his law practice as an associate of Samuel J. Harman. In 1902 he became a member of the law firm of Harman, Knapp, Ulman and Tucker, which later became the firm of Knapp. Ulman and Tucker. Appointed By Governor Ritchie He rotired from the arm when he was appointed to the Supreme Bench by the late Governor Ritchie in 1924 to succeed the late Judge Charles W. Heuisler, who had reached retirement age. From 1908 to 1928 Judge Ulman was a member of the faculty of the University of Maryland Law School He served as president of the Prisoners' Aid Association from 1910 to 1912. It was in this capacity that he attracted especial public attention and established an activi- ty on which he was to center his attention for more than a quarter of a century. During a period of widespread agitation over the management of the Maryland Penitentiary, Judge Ulman urged former Governor Phillips Lee Goldsborough to ap- point a commission to study condi- tions in the State's penal institu- tions, probation, parole and kindred subjects. A legislative bill author- izing the commission was passed (Continued on Page 4, Column 2) JOSEPH N. ULMAN. Jurist who died suddenly Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. JUDGE ULMAN DIES SUDDENLY Member Of Supreme, Bench Of Baltimore Stricken By Heart Attack He Was Active In Many Lines, Juristic And Social, Local And National (Continued from Page 22) and the reform movement in Maryland's penal institutions was started. Meanwhile, Judge Ulman served as treasurer of the Montrose School for Girls from 1920 to 1924; presi- dent of the Hebrew Benevolent So- ciety of Baltimore from 1925 to 1928; a member of the executive committee of the Community Fund from 1925 to 1930; president of the Urban League of Baltimore from 1931 to 1934; vice-president of the Baltimore branch of the American Jewish Congress from 1937 to 1941; a consultant of the Public Works Administration beginning in 1938. Wide Activities He also was a director of the National Probation Association, the National Urban League, the Legal Aid Bureau of Baltimore; a mem- ber of the advisory commission on criminal justice of the American Law Institute; member from 1938 to 1940 of the committee on edu- cation and practice of criminal law of the American Bar Association; member of the American Socio- logical Society, of the Maryland Commission on Prison Labor and of the Phi Beta Kappa, Phi Alpha and Omicron Delta Kappa fraterni- ties. He was a former president of the Johns Hopkins University Alumni Association. In 1933 Judge Ulman wrote a book that attracted national atten. tion, "A Judge Takes the Stand." In the volume he talked about jus- tice in Maryland and about spe- cific cases he had tried. In the same year, he amplified sections of the book in a speech before the Ameri- can Prison Association convening in Atlantic City. It was at this meeting that he told the delegates that the coun- try's penal system "would be ludicrous if it were not so tragic." And in 1933 he urged Governor Ritchie to sponsor a strong anti- lynch law. On Federal Committees The following year Judge Ulman was named chairman of a newly formed prison-labor committee of the American Prison Congress and chairman of a subcommittee of the National Industrial Relations Board. Also in 1934. President Roosevelt appointed Judge Ulman head of a committee to make a study of prison labor and the jurist was excused from court duties until the committee's report was compiled. Meanwhile, Judge Ulman was ap- pointed by the late Governor Nice to a State committee to investigate idleness in Maryland prisons. The following year, 1935, President Roosevelt again called on Judge Ul- man, appointing him chairman of the newly created Prison Indus- tries Reorganization Board, which sought to ease competition between prison-made goods and those of private manufacturers. He resigned from this board in 1936. Urges Revision Of Law In 1937, addressing a meeting of Federal judges, prosecutors and lawyers of the Fourth Judicial Cir- cuit, he said a radical revision of the criminal law was urgently needed. Two years later, at a meet- ing of the International Association of Chiefs of Police in San Fran- cisco, Judge Ulman submitted a program for administration of criminal justice to afford the maxi- mum protection of society and give an opportunity for rehabilitation of the offender. In recent years his attention to juvenile crime and delinquency be- came a major part of his life. As late as last month he insisted that Baltimore ought to have a juvenile court in which cases could be heard in decent privacy. He was the author of many magazine articles and pamphlets dealing with criminal law and as- sociated subjects, and was an asso- ciate editor of Criminal Law and Criminology. Married In 1903 Judge Ulman married Miss Ella Guggenheimer, daughter of Isaac Guggenheimer, of the printing and stationery firm of Guggenheimer and eil, on June 23, 1903. Fond of the outdoors, he had as hobbies tennis, canoeing, walking and fishing. He maintained a sum- mer lodge in Maine, where he in- dulged in outdoor sports every summer for the past thirty years. Judge Ulman never was without his r'pe. He carried it, always one with a curved stem, wherever he went. He is survived, besides his wife, by two children, Joseplı N. Ulman, Jr., of Detroit, and Miss Eleanor Ulman, and two grandchildren, Bar- bara and Barry Ulman. Funeral services will be held this afternoon at 3.30 o'clock at his home. They will be conducted by the Rev. Dr. Charles Rubenstein, former rabbi of Har Sinai Congregation. The active pallbearers will be Albert D. Hutzler, Sidney L. Ny- burg, Victor S. Jelenko, Major Manfred S. Guttmacher, Dr. Alan F. Guttmacher and Sidney Hol- lander. Members of the Supreme Bench will act as honorary pallbearers. Meanwhile, Judge Ulman was ap- pointed by the late Governor Nice to a State committee to investigate idleness in Maryland prisons. The following year, 1935, President Roosevelt again called on Judge Ul- man, appointing him chairman of the newly created Prison Indus- tries Reorganization Board, which sought to ease competition between prison-made goods and those of private manufacturers. He resigned from this board in 1936. Two years later, at a meet- ing of the International Association of Chiefs of Police in San Fran- cisco, Judge Ulman submitted a program for administration of criminal justice to afford the maxi- mum protection of society and give an opportunity for rehabilitation of the offender. In recent years his attention to juvenile crime and delinquency be- came a major part of his life. As late as last month he insisted that Baltimore ought to have a juvenile court in which cases could be heard in decent privacy. He was the author of many magazine articles and pamphlets dealing with criminal law and as- sociated subjects, and was an asso- ciate editor of Criminal Law and Criminology. Married In 1903 Judge Ulman married Miss Ella Guggenheimer, daughter of Isaac Guggenheimer, of the printing and stationery firm of Guggenheimer and eil, on June 23, 1903. Fond of the outdoors, he had as hobbies tennis, canoeing, walking and fishing. He maintained a sum- mer lodge in Maine, where he in- dulged in outdoor sports every summer for the past thirty years. Judge Ulman never was without his r'pe. He carried it, always one with a curved stem, wherever he went. He is survived, besides his wife, by two children, Joseplı N. title: MOSER CITES NEED IN NEGRO JUVENILE CASE: FAVORS MAXIMUM SECURITY UNIT FOR COLORED AS WELL AS WHITE BOYS
full_text: MOSER CITES NEED IN NEGRO JUVENILE CASE Favors Maximum Secur- ity Unit For Colored As Well As White Boys Some provision for a maximum security unit should be made for. difficult Negro juvenile offenders, Judge Herman M. Moser said yes- terday after suspending a four-year sentence to the House of Correc tion that he had previously im- posed on a 13-year-old Negro boy. "There is just as much need, pos- sibly a greater one, for the estab- lishment of such a unit for these 'tough' Negfo offenders as for white boys," declared Judge Moser. "I am in favor of the State insti- tutions which now take care of juvenile cases being made the. places for the establishment of these security units." Recommitted To Cheltenham The boy whose sentence was sus- pended was convicted last Feb- ruary for participation in a series of burglaries. He was sentenced to the Cheltenham School for Boys and ran away from the institution last May 27. On June 14 he was given a four- year sentence to the House of Cor- rection by Judge Moser on charges of burglary committed after he escaped from the reformatory. This latter sentence was sus- pended by the jurist, who recom- mitted the defendant to Chelten- ham. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: HERSHEY CITED AS WITNESS IN DRAFT CASE: HIS AUTHORITY TO ASSIGN CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTORS TO CAMPS QUESTIONED OTHER OFFICIALS ARE WANTED AT TRIAL HERE OF CHARLES BUTCHER
full_text: HERSHEY CITED AS WITNESS IN DRAFT CASE His Authority To Assign Conscientious Objectors To Camps Questioned Other Officials Are Wanted At Trial Here Of Charles Butcher Maj. Gen. Lewis B. Hershey, di- rector of selective service, and the adjutant general of the United States Army, or their accredited representatives, and other high- ranking draft officials have been summoned as witnesses by Charles Butcher, Harvard graduate, who will be tried in Federal Court to- morrow on a selective service viola- tion charge. Butcher contests the authority of General Hershey to assign conscien- tious objectors to public service camps, and contends that although the law says specifically that ob- jectors' camps shall be under ci- vilian control, the control actually is almost entirely in military hands. Accused Of Refusing To Quit Camp Butcher, a conscientious objector, is accused of refusing to leave a camp at Cheltenham, Md., and re- port to a camp at Marion, N. C. He had been serving as a counselor at the Cheltenham Reformatory for Negro Boys and prior to that had served at two other objectors' camps, it was testified at a pre- liminary hearing. Wilfred T. McQuaid, counsel for Butcher, has requested that sub- poenas be served on General Her- shey and the adjutant general of the army or their representatives; Col. Lewis F. Kosch, chief of the camp operations division of selec- tive service, and Lieut. Col. Frank- lin A. McLean, of the camp opera- tions division. Records Requested These officials were requested to bring certain records with them, some having to do with military promotions and citations given to officials in the draft system and others having to do with adminis- trative procedure of the camp operations division. Also summoned were Joseph Weaver, executive secretary of the National Service Board for Re- ligious Objectors, and George B. Reeves, of the National Committee on Conscientious Objectors. Butcher is 26, single, and lives in Cambridge, Mass. ! Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: FOOD WAS FUGITIVES' UNDOING: ATE SO MUCH THEY FELL ASLEEP AND WERE ROUNDED UP
full_text: FOOD WAS FUGITIVES' UNDOING Ate So Much They Fell Asleep And Wero Rounded Up. Inmates Nos. 3430, 2664, 2057, 3436, 2699 and 2756, all colored, and all escaped from the Cheltenham Reformatory, were dis- covered yesterday morning by Mrs. John Wengers, near Westport, on the Annapolis road, lying asleep on her kitchen floor. She screamed for help and her husband and several neighbors came to her aid, called Constable Muul and Patrolman Me- Kay, of Mount Winans Police Station, and held the negroes until the officers of the law appeared. All six, the oldest of whom is 21 and the youngest 15, told their tale to Justice Charles J. Hull, of Mount Winans, yester- day morning. title: Coal Miners And Their Work
full_text: Coal Miners And Their Work TO THE EDITOR OF THE Sun-Sir: In your editorial on John L. Lewis April 14, you dogmatically state that the miners "certainly are not working harder." Unless someone has made a com- plete survey with a gadget which measures the exact amount of physical as well as nervous energy expended by each individual miner, I don't see how you can be certain that they are not working harder. I, personally, agree with Mr. Lewis. MRS. PETER B. OLNEY 2D. Baltimore, April 16. The two major operations in soft-coal mining are cutting the coal out of the coal veins and loading the stuff on cars for transport out of the mines. In 1918 mechanical labor-saving devices for loading coal accounted for less than one per cent. of the total output. In 1942 40.7 per cent. of total out- put was loaded by labor-saving me- chanical devices. In 1918 only 56.8 per cent. of total output was cut by means of labor-saving mechanical devices. In 1942 89 per cent. was cut by such devices. In 1923, the earliest year for which the statistical abstract of the United States has such figures, the prevailing hours of labor per week for the overwhelming proportion of bituminous wage earners were 44 to 52 hours, and some worked up to 62 hours and more. It is unlikely that working hours were shorter in 1918, a war year. But in February. 1943, average weekly working hours were 37.3-Editor, The Sun. On The Cheltenham Case TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: I was shocked beyond words when I read the statement which accom- panied the resignation. of Mr. Joseph H. Blandford as president of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys. I have always respected the views and opinions of others even when they differed from my own and I am willing to concede that Mr. Blandford had the right to express himself as he felt about the matter of racial discrimination at the in- stitution which he served for so many years. I write this letter to you in the hope that Mr. Blandford will ex- amine himself, his ideas, and his philosophy of life, in the light of the generic story of the creation, La part of which story was used by that great American, Thomas Jef- ferson, in writing the Declaration of Independence which states among other things, "that all men are created equal...." title: 21 THREATEN TO RESIGN AT CHELTENHAM: WHITE EMPLOYES TO ACT IF SEGREGATION POLICY IS ABOLISHED RULING TO, BE EFFECTIVE WHEN "ADMINISTRATIVELY PRACTICABLE"
full_text: 21 THREATEN TO RESIGN AT CHELTENHAM White Employes To Act If Segregation Policy Is Abolished  Ruling To, Be Effective When "Administra- tively Practicable"  Twenty-one white employes of the Cheltenham School for Boys have informed Howard C. Hill, act. ing president of the board of man agers of the institution for Negroes, that they plan to resign if the board's program abolishing restric- tions segregating Negro employes from white is put into effect. The board of managers voted sev- eral weeks ago to provide for joint dining and housing facilities for both whites and Negroes. Mr. Hill said it was not the in- tention of the board to put the pro- posal into effect immediately, but that it was to be effected as soon as Vance E. Thomas, superintend- ent, "found it administratively practicable."  Effective April 20 Following the board's announce- ment of its plan, Joseph H. Bland- ford, president, tendered his resig- nation to Governor O'Conor and the latter said yesterday. "there ap- parently is nothing else to do but accept it," although he has not formally done so. Six of the group of white classi- fied State employes, who informed Mr. Hill of their intention to re- sign, set April 20 as the date for their resignation unless the reso- lution of the board was rescinded. The remaining fifteen stated the time of their resignation would de. pend on their ability "to work out a solution to our own individual problems by means of retirement, transfer to other State departments or to other employment." With the exception of the con- clusions, the letters of the two groups, were identical. The text of the identical part fol- lows: "The present conflict concerning the prospects of interracial living for the employes at Cheltenham School for Boys has created a most unfortunate situation. We are anx- ious to present to the board of managers our thoughts and convic- tions concerning this matter. "The recent resolutions approved by the board of managers are abso- lutely administratively imprac- ticable. The board has placed the superintendent in an impossible situation. They have, by the action of one meeting, destroyed all that has been accomplished by the pres- ent administration and staff for the pact two years  Welfare Jeopardized "They have seriously jeopardized the welfare of the 325 boys at the school. If the board does not take steps immediately to instruct the superintendent to continue with his policy developed during the last two years, even more serious consequences are imminent. "We should like to make it clear to the board that we are anxious to continue serving in our present capacities for the continued wel- fare of the institution provided there is no further attempt to im- pose interracialism. "It is not for the best interests of the Cheltenham School for Boys to arbitrarily declare interracial- ism. We cannot subscribe to such a policy. We feel these convictions so strongly that we shall be forced to offer our resignations."  To Confer With Thomas Mr. Hill said he was going to confer with Mr. Thomas to deter- mine whether the situation was "imminent or urgent" enough to call a special meeting of the board or wait until next regular meeting date, the first Thursday in May, to act on the protests. Those who signed the letter set- (Continued on Page 20, Column 3) (Continued from Page 30) ting April 20 as the resignation date were: H. HUNTLEY LLOYD, JR., classi- fication director. HILDA L. SPICER, junior account clerk. RUTH HYRONS CARTER, dieti- tian. GARY A. BRAY, head cook. FRANK M. FRIEND, statistical clerk. LOIS E. SPICER, junior stenog- rapher. The names of those who said they were "not in a position to leave immediately because of our family obligations and prospective loss of retirement benefits accumu- lated over a period of years," follow: FOSTER WERNER, night super- visor. FRED C. WERNER, carpenter. HARRY S. Carroll, assistant superintendent. NELSON GRIMES, chauffeur. MATILDA WERNER, laundry supervisor. JOHN S. BECKWITH, supervisor of boys. JOHN HUTHMAN, watchman. GEORGE A. SHANE, Vvocational instructor in carpentry. CLAUDE, L. SUTHARD, vocational instructor' in farming. MARGARET D. THOMAS, senior account clerk. JAMES M. Thomas, carpenter. JOHN L. MOORE; blacksmith. THOMAS LAROQUE, painter. CHARLES H. SMITH, farm man- ager. EVA V. SMITH, dining room supervisor. Founded in 1879, Cheltenham, which is located at Crownsville, Anne Arundel county, was private- ly operated until 1937, when the State assumed control through an act of the Legislature.  Blandford Made Head Mr. Blandford was named presi- dent of the board at that time. He was in Richmond, Va., at the time the board acted to abolish the segre- gation policy and last Saturday sent his resignation to the Governor. The controversy came about after twenty-three conscientious objec- tors had been obtained from a morthwestern State to work at the institution. There were seventeen: white and six colored men. The conscientious objectors re- sented the segration of white and colored and their protests resulted: in the board's action.

full_text: SEEK SOLUTION OF JUVENILE DELINQUENCY Heads Of Institutions Re- ply To Criticisms At Gavel Club. Lack Of Facilities For Mentally Retarded Chil- dreh Cited The State's juvenile delinquency problem boils down to the fact that there are not sufficient facilities for mentally retarded children, it was in- dicated last night by heads of insti- tutions that were criticized at a Gavel Club open forum, The only institution equipped to care for juvenile public wards of feeble minds is Rosewood State Train- ing School, and there is a waiting list of about 200 at that institution. Rosewood is the only place per- mitted, under fairly recent regula- tions of the Board of State Aid and Charities, to take mentally retarded cases.  Situation At St. Mary's Brother Gerard Joseph, superin- tendent of St. Mary's Industrial School, which formerly received num- bers of these cases, revealed the exist- ence of this rule, "Recently," he said, "we have been raising our standards to comply with the new ruling of the Board of State Aid and Charities which says no in- stitutions that care for normal chil- dren may take in mentally retarded individuals, who might be bad in- fluences upon the normal children. "The rule relieves us of the neces- sity of receiving cases we are not equipped to handle, and for whom we can do nothing. In addition, it gives our normal charges better chances for rehabilitation, since they are not in contact with the mental cases."  Stand Taken By Stanton At the Gavel Club forum, Monday night, Robert F. Stanton, Commis- sioner of Police, said the Juvenile Court often turned loose children who should be in custody. These chil- dren, he asserted, were "repeaters" in crime, and gave the police much trouble. Dr. James W. Harry, supervisor of probation for the Juvenile Court, rose to the court's defense, saying it often had trouble in getting institu- tions to accept "repeaters," most ef whom were mental cases. Some of the speakers contended the State needed a committing agency that could force the institutions to accept whatever cases were sent to them.  Last night, Dr. Harry said, he felt the solution was the appropriation of more funds, either to build more facilities at Rosewood, or to estab- lish another institution for mentally retarded juveniles. 1 "There are really two types for whom we have no place now," he explained. "There is the very low mentality class for which Rosewood was designed, and there is a class superior to these, but not fitted to be placed with normal children in other institutions."  James A. title: MORGAN HEAD GIVES PLAN FOR NEGRO SCHOOLS: ASKS PRINCESS ANNE SHIFT TO TEACHER-TRAINING, JUNIOR-COLLEGE ROLE
full_text: MORGAN HEAD GIVES PLAN FOR NEGRO SCHOOLS Asks Princess Anne Shift To Teacher-Training, Junior-College Role By ANNE w. HUTCHISON Dr. Martin D. Jenkins, president of Morgan State College, recom mended yesterday that Morgan be made the center of undergraduate education for Negroes except for training of county elementary teacliers, junior-college work and engineering. He proposed that. Negroes be ad- mitted to all graduate and profes- sional courses at the University of Maryland and to undergraduate engineering courses there. Under his proposals for a radical reorganization of Maryland's pro- gram for higher education of Negroes, the teacher-training pro- gram at Bowie State Teachers Col lege would be transferred to Prin- cess Anne College, now a branch of the University of Maryland and the land-grant college for Negroes. Proposal For Use Of Bowie Bowie's facilities would be used for the State training school for Negro youth, now the Boys Village of Maryland, at Cheltenham, or for some other State purpose. His recommendations, presented to the commission recently ap- pointed to study higher education for Negroes, were these: 1. Designation of Morgan as the land-grant college for Negroes with future work in this field to be de- veloped under administration of the board of trustees of Morgan. 2. Transfer of Bowie to Princess Anne and addition of strong junior- college courses in arts and sciences, agriculture and trades to the teacher-training program, which (Continued on Page 22, Column 5) Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission. NEGRO SCHOOL PLAN OFFERED Morgan President Asks Shift In Princess Anne Role By ANNE W. HUTCHISON (Continued from Page 32) would remain under the State Board of Education. 3. Education of elementary schoolteachers for the Baltimore city schools at Morgan after Cop- pin Teachers College, now operated by the city, is closed in June. 4. Admission of Negro students to existing curricula at the Univer- sity of Maryland in graduate and professional fields and undergradu- ate engineering. 5. Abolition of the out-of-State scholarship fund. a step which would "save the State at least $2,- 000,000 over the next ten-year period." Dr. Jenkins told the commission he found Negro students "disillu- sioned and cynical" because of the way the University of Maryland had handled the question of ad- mission of Negroes. He referred to it as "that sort of playing about with Negro educa- tion" and cited a court case last week as an example. Declarations Contrasted He pointed out that the Board of Regents had declared formally last October that nobody was being rejected because of race but that the reason given in court for re- jecting an 18-year-old applicant to the University of Maryland School of Nursing was that she was a Negro. "We are trying to educate cer. tain ethical viewpoints into our Negro students, and you set the example," he said. "We hope it will not be the example of expediency shown in this case." Dr. Jenkins said it would cost about $2,000,000 for land and facili- ties for a land-grant program at Morgan. He said at least two pre- vious study commissions had made a similar recommendation. Advantage Noted In Location Advantages of conducting the program at Morgan, he said, include Morgan's location in the center of the Negro population, availability of housing and jobs and elimination of the need for conducting dupli- cate basic college programs at two State institutions. He spoke of the "depressing history of neglect of Negro educa- tion with the University of Mary- land" and said he doubted that the university had a "sincere interest" in Negro education despite its recent activities. He noted also that throughout the Southern pattern of segrega- tion, except in Maryland, it was "universally" true that Negro institutions were under control of members of their own race. Eastern Shore Need Seen In connection with the proposed transfer of Bowie to Princess Anne he recognized a need for a college for Negro youth on the Eastern Shore. He said that since Bowie now has a large proportion of boarders, they could go equally well to Princess Anne. He described Bowie as "isolated in an area with insufficient popula- tion for an enlarged practice school." He said the Princess Anne plant would require "little if any. major expansion" to accommodate the teacher-training program. In discussing the proposed open- ing of the university's graduate and professional schools and under- graduate engineering courses to Negroes. he said it was "less ex- pensive than any other plan" and feasible. Changes In South Noted On the point of feasibility, he said that despite the tradition and history of segregation in the South, several states and schools have modified their policies in recent years. Delaware has opened graduate and professional schools to Ne- groes, he said. In West Virginia, Negroes have attended the graduate and profes- sional schools for a number of years. Kentucky has admitted Negroes to graduate and professional work this year for the first time. Universities of Texas and Arkan- sas are admitting Negroes to their medical schools. The University of Oklahoma is. admitting Negroes to graduate work and its law school. The University of Maryland, accepts Negroes in its law school "In none of these instances bas there been the slightest amount of difficulty." Dr. Jenkins said. title: LANE ASKS $39,912,300: SEEKS $16,373,000 BOND ISSUE, NEARLY THIRD OF IT FOR U. OF M.
full_text: LANE ASKS 1 $39,912,300 FOR BUILDING Seeks $16,373,000 Bond Issue, Nearly Third Of It For U. Of M. U. of M. psychopathic unit plans full liaison with mental hospitals. executive says Page 32 Court writ orders Lane unit to show cause why mental report should not be disclosed.. Page 32 By ANNE W. HUTCHISON 【Annapolis Bureau of The Sunl Annapolis, March 15-Governor Lane tonight asked for a $16.373,- 000 bond issue to help finance a $39,912,300 construction programı and proposed that nearly one third of the bond proceeds go to the Uni- versity of Maryland. The administration bond bill, in- troduced in both houses of the General Assembly, provides $5,061.. 500 for the university-$2,033,900 more than recommended by the State Planning Commission, but $11,391,892 less than requested by the university.. Includes Princess Anne Work Included in the $5,061,500 total is $865,000 for construction at Princess Anne College, where the State Planning Commission recom- mended no capital improvements next year. The university had re- quested $3,755,000 for Princess Anne. The university item is the largest single-department total in the bill. [Editor's Note: The day the plan- ning commission's recommenda- tions were published, the Governor said, with regard to the university: "It is not so much a question as to whether the cuts recommended from the university should be re- stored as it is whether the amount allocated nay have to be reduced still further.") 11 ( Requests Exceed $101,000,000 The $16,373,000 bond issue com-f bined with the $23,539,300 alloca- tion from surplus for capital expenditures comprise the admin istration's total construction pro-1 gram. Departmental requests for capital funds had exceeded $104.000.000. Governor Lane already has rec ommended that $19,994,800 of the surplus be used for improvements and construction at the five State mental hospitals and that the re- maining $3,544.500 go toward con struction at the tuberculosis sana- toria. Tonight's bill includes an addi tional $2.187,055 to fill out the total $5,731,000 construction program proposed for the sanatoria. No message accompanied the bill when it was presented to the Legis- Jature. Tax Rise Indicated The 4.93-cent tax rate called for to finance the bonds indicates a 1950 property tax rate of 11.18 cents as compared with the present rate of 11.15 cents. Governor Lane said earlier in the session that if no bonds were issued the tax rate would be 6.25 cents. title: WASHINGTON MAN NAMED TO CHELTENHAM: NATIONAL TRAINING SCHOOL OFFICIAL, L. J. VENEY, TO HEAD INSTITUTION
full_text: WASHINGTON MAN NAMED TO CHELTENHAM National Training School Official, L. J. Veney, To Head Institution By ALBERT W. QUINN [Annapolis Bureau of The Sunl Annapolis, Jan. 28--Vacant since the ousting of Calvin L. Kiah, eleven months ago, the superin Tendency of the Cheltenham School for Boys was filled today with the appointment of Lawson Jerome Veney, of Washington. The appointment, made by the school's board of managers, was announced from the office of Gover- nor Lane. Mr. Veney, 38 years old, now is parole supervisor of the Training School for Delinquent Boys in Washington-a post he has held since September, 1944. Prior to that time, he was intake supervis ing probation ofliver of the Juvenile Count in Washington, Howard University Graduate Mr. Veney is a graduate of Howard University, Washington. where he received degrees of bachelor of arts and master of arts. He is married and the father of six children. There were ten qualified candi dates for the post of superinten dent. Two of them failed to attend the oral examination. Of the eight who took the examination, thred failed. Those Who Gave Test The examination was given for the Department of State Employ ment and Registration by a panel of three, selected by that depart- ment. The members of the panel were: Frank Loveland, assistant direc tor of the Bureau of Prisons, United States Department of Jus tice, Washington. Mrs. Anna D. Sanford, member of the Division of Juvenile Causes, Circuit Court of Baltimore City. Dr. F. Lovell Bixby, deputy com- missioner in charge of correction and parole, Department of Institu- tions and Agencies, Trenton, N.J. Interviewed By Board The five men who passed the examination were interviewed by the Cheltenham board of managers. which selected Mr. Vency. a Mr. Kiah, former superintend ent, was appointed after an exami- nation in which he received higher rating than some of the other applicants because of his status as a veteran of the second World War, After his six months' probation- ary period in the job, during which time there were many complaints about administration, Mr. Kiah was dismissed by the board. Office Remains Vacant Later there was an effort by some of the members to reinstate him, but the Department of State Em- ployment and Registration inter- fered, and the office remained va- cant. In the interim, supervision was conducted by members of the board of managers with the assistance of trusted members of the staff. Management of the institution for Negro boys has been one of the main points of contention in the State for years. About six months ago, the old board resigned and a new board, made up entirely of Negroes, was appointed by Gover- nor Lane. Members of that board gave as- surance yesterday that they will give full support to the new super- intendent.

title: Church Tribute Paid To Founder
full_text: Church Tribute Paid To Founder Representing all spheres of com- munity life, hundreds of men and women yesterday filled Douglas Memorial Community Church, Mad- ison and Lafayette avenues, to pay tribute to the Rev. Dr. Frederick Douglas, founder of the Negro congregation, on the first anni- versary of his death. The large church was crowded at morning services at which the Rev. Joseph M. Evans, pastor of Metro- politan Community Church in Chi- cago, was the speaker. The Rev. Marion C. Bascom, present rector of Douglas Community Church, con- ducted the service. Music consisted of the favorite hymns of Dr. Douglas, Miss Viola Jones, a trustee of the church, was the soloist. Praised In Many Roles congregation Another large gathered for the actual memorial exercises at 4 P.M... The Rev. Wilbur H. Waters, pastor pastor of Emmanuel Community Churen. spoke of Dr. Douglas as a minister; Elmer W. Henderson, assistant superintendent in the Baltimore Department of Educa- tion and director of Negro schools, and George W. F. McMechen, a member of the School Board, paid tribute to Dr. Douglas as an edu- cator. Former Mayor Howard W. Jack- son spoke of him as a citizen who, among other things, had been a parole officer at Cheltenham School for Boys, a member of the rationing board during World War II and a member of the grand jury. Dr. Dwight C. W. Holmes, presi- dent emeritus of Morgan College, emphasized the characteristics of Dr. Douglas as a friend. Music By Combined, Choirs Other remarks were made by the Rev. J. J. Barnes, pastor of Or- chard Street Methodist Church, who represented other denomina- tions. Music was by the combined seni- or, young people's and Gospel choirs of the church. The soloist was Simon Scott, a trustee. The Evangel Singers, a female sextett, also sang. John H. Murphy, Jr., presided. ". At the morning service and the commemoration ceremonies the altar was banked with white flow- ers presented by different church organizations and friends of Dr. Douglas. The congregation he founded now has an enrolled membership of more than 1.000. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: REIDT IS GIVEN HEPBRON'S JOB: NAMED DIRECTOR OF CRIMINAL JUSTICE COMMISSION
full_text: REIDT IS GIVEN HEPBRON'S JOB Named Director Of Criminal Justice Commission Wallace Reidt was appointed managing director of the Baltimore Criminal Justice Commission yes- terday, succeeding James M. Hep- bron who became executive vice president. The apointment was made at a meeting of the commission's board at the Emerson Hotel. Both Mr. Reidt and Mr. Hepbron have been with the commission since its organization 26 years ago. Born in Baltimore in 1898, Mr. Reidt attended city and Baltimore county public schools, the business school of the Young Men's Chris- tian Association and obtained his law degree at the University of Battimore Law School, He served with the Canadian Army in World War I and was seriously wounded in 1917. Made Many Surveys He joined the staff of the com- mission as secretary and statis- tician in January, 1923, and. since then, has made many surveys for the city and State as well as the commission. He held the rank of captain in the Maryland State Guard in World War II and was chairman of a spe- cial panel board of the selective service that arranged for the indue tion of prisoners from State penal Institutions into the nation's armed forces. He has made for the past several years an annual survey of the coun- Ly jails in Maryland for the State Department of Correction. At the request of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys, Mr. Reidt recently acted as execu- tive secretary for the board and submitted a report that recom- mended an all-colored board for the school. Author Of Manual He is the author of a recent manual prepared for the board members of the Montrose School for Girls. He became assistant man- ager of the Baltimore Criminal Justice Commission in 1938. Mr. Reidt is a member of the boards of the Ulman Foundation, the Baltimore Eye, Ear and Throat Hospital and the Montrose School. He is secretary of the Baltimore Youth Commission and a member of the Youth Commission of Balti- more county. He is a Mason and a member of Boumi Temple, Shrine. title: CHELTENHAM GETS TROPHIES: SHOULD HELP SOLVE PROBLEMS, JUDGE MOYLAN SAYS
full_text: CHELTENHAM GETS TROPHIES ! Should Help Solve Problems, Judge Moylan Says | At courthouse ceremonies mark ing the presentation of eight trophies to Cheltenham School for Boys, to be competed for by var sity and cottage teams, Judge Charles E. Moylan yesterday de- clared that the awards should help solve disciplinary and run-away problems at the school. In turning over the trophies to the athletic director of Cheltenham, Judge Moylan pointed out that whenever the school has been the target for criticism, leaders in the child-welfare field have called for enrichment of the educational and extracurricular program, Praises Ex-Umpire The judge said, in line with that thought, that in the past several years he has been interested in the organization of a band, a glee club and a drum and bugle corps. The judge said Doll Derr, former International League umpire, "has demonstrated a real interest in the welfare of these boys and has been most helpful" in the efforts to aug- ment the sports program at the school. One of the trophies, to be used in connection with senior basket- ball, was donated by Judge Moylan. A junior basketball trophy was donated by Dr. Walter B. Clemson.! Other Donors Named Other presentations were don- ated by: Luke Duffy-wrestling. Dick Matthews-junior softball. American Legion, Department of Maryland-junior football, W. Austin Baughman - volley ball. James J. Lacy-track. Dillon Smith-boxing. Judge Moylan declared that no college in the State has a campus better adapted for a real sports program and few Baltimore high schools have athletic fields com- parable to the one at Cheltenham. title: JURORS URGE EARLY CLOSING FOR ALL_BARS: MAY-TERM BODY WOULD ALSO PROHIBIT LIQUOR SALES ON SUNDAY
full_text: JURORS URGE EARLY CLOSING FOR ALL BARS May-Term Body Would Also Prohibit Liquor Sales On Sunday Closing of bars at midnight on weekdays and all day Sunday was advocated yesterday by the retiring May-term grand jury in a report to the judges of the Criminal Court. The proposed restrictions, it was explained, would apply to all types of establishments selling alcoholic beverages. The jurors said they had ob- served minors visiting taverns and being sold liquor. The investigating body also contended that it had seen card-playing for money in such places. Advocating that all bars be closed at midnight and not be re- opened until 8 o'clock the next morning-two hours later than the present law permits-and that they remain closed all day Sunday, the grand jury said it observed that most disturbances occur after mid- night. Criticize Jails, Hawkers The jurors also complained of overcrowding and idleness in the State's adult penal institutions. urged the elimination of sidewalk hawkers on downtown streets and suggested that parents exert them. selves in the care and raising of their children to prevent both juve- nile and parental delinquency. The jurors further urged that a line be drawn on the floor near the front of streetcars and busses and that passengers be required to re- main behind that line, thus afford- ing the operator clear vision to his right and freedom to operate the vehicle. Painting of the city markets also was proposed by the grand jurors, who pointed out that visitors usual ly make it a point to visit those landmarks. particularly Lexington Market. Cheltenham Needs Cited The reports said many improve- ments have been made at the Cheltenham School in recent months, but declared that one of the major problems there is the lack of trained personnel. There also is a lack of equipment for: training boys in the trades, the jurors said. If the school is to serve as a cor. rective institution, boys must leave with more knowledge of how they can go about making an honest daily living, the jurors declared. The jury had words of praise for the Baltimore Police Depart- ment and for the State's attorney's office. Myles Katz, foreman, in his re- port. urged citizens to support a $8,000,000 loan for public build- ings because part of the money is to be used for a 300-bed tuber- culosis hospital at the City Hos- pitals. title: BUILDING COST EXCEEDS FUND: 3 STATE COLLEGE STRUCTURES TO BE $35,000 MORE
full_text: BUILDING COST EXCEEDS FUND 3 Stato College Structures To Be $35,000 More Completion of three faculty buildings at Maryland State Col lege at Princess Anne is expected to cost $35,000 more than the money avaliable, and the Board of Public Works is going to ask the University of Maryland to find the money. John B. Funk, chief engineer and head of the State Department of Public Improvements, reported to the board yesterday that two un- expected developments had oc curred to upset his department's $88,000 cost estimate for the faculty apartment house. "In arriving at the required fund of $88,000, we assumed that stu- dent labor would be furnished without charge or at a nominal cost," he said. Wrong On Installation "We were also under the inpres- slon that the plumbing and heating Instructors in the college could in- stall the plumbing and heating system. "Both of these assumptions prove to be in crror." "The college authorities were also under the impression that they were given authority to build one cottage on January 6 and another cottage on March 22, 1948, and have, therefore, constructed two cottages." He reminded the board that it had approved construction of one cottage, using student labor, March 22. Governor Lane inquired how much of the $32,634.31 paid out of the $88,000 for pay rolls repre- sented payments to students. Mr. Funk said student wages, at 75 cents an hour, constituted "80 to 90 percent" of that total. The Governor then observed that the "change in policy" about paying student labor apparently had caused the need for the extra money being sought by the univer- sity. "That plus the fact that they built an extra cottage," Hooper S. Miles, State treasurer, added. "Left-Handed Scholarships" Governor Lane referred to the payments for student labor as "left- handed scholarships.". Both he and Mr. Miles agreed that the university would have to find the money needed to complete the faculty housing project. James J. Lacy, State comptroller, had been unable to attend the meeting. Mr. Funk's written report to the board said his department had ob tained a breakdown of usage of the $88,000 "after repeated requests." Other developments at the board's meeting, held at the Gover nor's office in the Davison building Included: 1. A recommendation by Mr. Miles that, subject to the Legisla- ture's approving purchase of the O'Sullivan Bulding for a 'State office building, the State sell the seven-story building at 110 East Lexington street now occupied by the State Roads Commission. 2. A statement by Governor Lane that moving of Cheltenham School for Boys to a new location lacked priority, in his considera- tion, over "many other projects that have to be done for the State, such as those at the mental hós- pitals and the tuberculosis sana- toria." 3. Allocation of $65,575 from the General Emergency Fund for a variety of items, leaving a balance of less than $50,000 in the fund for the remainder of the fiscal year ending next June 30. Would Inform Public Mr. Miles's recommendation for sale of the Roads Commission Building was included in a three- page statement designed to give the public and tenants of the O'Sul- livan Bulding the "fullest informa- tion" as to plans for the building. Governor Lane, who said he was in accord with making such data available, described as "unin- formed and outrageous" the recent statement by Councilman Buckler as to the reason for the projected purchase of the building on which the State has taken an option. "Rumors are flying around town," Mr. Buckler told the City Council last week,. "that the present owner of the O'Sullivan Building was about to raise the rent of the Balti- more National Bank, that the exec- utives of the bank are close to the State administration and that this would be a clever way to avoid that rent increase by transferring own- ership of the building to the State." Mr. Miles's report included, in- formation about the amount of space the State would take over In the O'Sullivan Building and the amount that would be left vacant in other buildings in the downtown area by the shift of State offices from their present locations. title: KIAH TO HEAD CHELTENHAM SCHOOL AGAIN: WILL HOLD POST PENDING STATE EMPLOYMENT CHIEF'S EXAM
full_text: KIAH TO HEAD CHELTENHAM SCHOOL AGAIN Will Hold Post Pending State Employment Chief's Exam Calvin L. Kiah will again become superintendent of the Cheltenham School for Boys on Friday. His appointment to the post which he left last February is temporary, pending examination by the State Employment Commis sioner. He previously served under a former board of managers which rejected him for permanent ap- pointment at the end of a six-month probationary period. The new appointment was made Thursday by the present board of managers, composed entirely of Negroes. at a meeting at the school. The vote was 5 to 0, with the president and secretary of the board abstaining. Two members were absent. Later Ruling Given Edward N. Wilson, secretary of the board, explained yesterday that while the board first had been in- formed that Mr. Kíah, formerly principal of a Negro high school at Cambridge, was ineligible for reap- pointment, a subsequent ruling by the attorney general held that he could take an examanination and qualify for the post. Mr. Wilson said that it also had been ruled that Mr. Kiah, mean- while. might be reappointed pend- ing examination. . He had refrained from voting, Mr. Wilson went on. because con- sideration previously had been given to changing the qualifications for the position of superintendent, in line with a study of the school's educational program carried out by the State Department of Education. Favors Discussion He said he had felt further dis- cussion on that point was war- ranted before the board acted on Mr. Kiah's appointment. Dr. W. E. Henry, president of the board, who also did not vote, is in Georgia and could not be reached for comment. Mr. Wilson said the movement for reappointment of Mr. Kiah ap- peared to be well under way when he arrived at the meeting. follow- ing an early afternoon hearing in (Continued on Page 18, Column 5) Baltimore before the State Plan- ning Commission on the institu- tion's capital improvement pro- gram. Mr. Kiah first went to the school September 1, 1947, having been selected by a board headed by Thomas B. Sprague. That board, last February 26, announced that because Mr. Kiah had "failed to demonstrate the prerequisite ad- ministrative ability, judgment. tem- perament and leadership." would not receive a permanent ap- pointment at the end of his proba- tionary period. Action Criticized he One member of the board sub- sequently said that the action dis- missing Mr. Kiah had been taken in the absence of three members and with one member "strenuous- ly" objecting and declining to vote. There was public criticism of the board's action and shortly thereafter the board resigned to make way for a new all-Negro board. The education study to which Mr. Wilson referred proposed that the superintendent direct his attention to an in-service training program for employés. This, he explained yesterday, called for the superintendent's be- ing trained in abnormal psychology and in handling delinquent boys. The school has not had a super- intendent since last February. Not Yet Informed Walter D. Owens, State employ- ment commissioner, said yesterday The had not yet been informed of the new appointment. Mr. Wilson said the temporary- appointment order had been signed at the board's meeting and that he assumed it was now on its way to Mr. Owens's office.. He added that Mr. Kiah's formal acceptance had not been received, but that he had no reason to be- lieve he would refuse the appoint- ment.

title: 9 BOYS HUNTED AFTER ESCAPE
full_text: 9 BOYS HUNTED AFTER ESCAPE 12 Flee Cheltenham School; 3 Found In Hiding State police and St. Marys county authorities early this morn- ing were searching for nine in- mates who escaped from the Cheltenham School for Boys. Charles Cephas, supervisor of the school, said twelve boys fled from a cottage last night after kicking out a window screen. They range in age from 13 to 15. Three of them were found hiding on the school grounds. Watchman Finds Broken Screen The escape was discovered by Daniel Ragsdale, a roving night watchman, who noticed that the sereen was broken in Washington cottage. The cottage houses 40 boys, Mr. Cephas said. The watchman ghecked the oc- cupants and discovered that twelve were missing. He notified State police and then began the search of grounds which led to the discovery of the three boys shortly after midnight. full_text: $93,000 SITE REASSESSED 74 Acres Offered For Chelten- ham Listed At $12,180 The 74-acre tract of land in Cur tis Bay, assessed at $6,865 and of fered for sale to the State fo $93,000 as a proposed new site fo the Cheltenham School for Boys has been assessed at $12,180 fol 1949, Joseph H. A. Rogan, chair man of the State Tax Commission said yesterday. Mr. Rogan said that the old as sessment on the land, made in 1937 valued the land at $50 an acre and the improvement on it at $3,150 making a total of $6,865. :. Reassessed. This Year Under the continuous assess ment law, passed several years ago, he said, the tract was reassessed this year for 1949. Eight acres ad jacent to a State road have been assessed at $200 each, while the remaining 66.31 acres have been assessed at $100 an acre for a total of $8,230 for the land. The improvements now are as sessed at $3,950, making the com- plete assessment $12.180. Mr. Rogan said that, under the continuous assessment law, prop- erty is assessed according to its classification and utility. Acreages Used As Basis "The land in question consists of acreage of farm land, and is assessed like other comparable farm land at so much per acre, and my understanding is that the acre- age so assessed is in uniformity and on equality with comparable farm land." Mr. Rogan said. Mr. Rogan said that what a land owner would like to obtain for his land "is not a criticism or a stand- ard of its market value." title: COURT WARNS DELINQUENTS: TELLS JUVENILES THEY FACE TERMS IN TRAINING SCHOOLS
full_text: COURT WARNS DELINQUENTS Tells Juveniles They Face Terms In Training Schools Judge Charles E. Moylan In the Division of Juvenile Causes yester-! day announced that because so many juvenile delinquents released on probation are becoming repeat offenders, he will have to resort to more frequent commitments of such offenders to training schools. Judge Moylan announced his new policy after sentencing four Negro boys, ranging in age from 8 to 12, to the Cheltenham School for Boys. The judge disclosed that a training program has been developed for younger delinquents. Twelve Burglaries In One Month He said the boys were involved in twelve burglaries in one month. Some of the offenses were com- mitted Immediately after the boys bad been arrested on similar charges, but released in care of their parents, the judge pointed out. One of the boys, who is 8, has been before the Court eight times, while a 9-year-old boy was making his ninth court appearance, the judge pointed out. Two 12-year-old boys had been before the court seven and four times, respectively. 2,293 Delinquency Cases In 1948 "The probation officers and the presentatives of the Department of Public Welfare recommended that the boys be committed to the training school, despite their youth, as there are no alternate facilities in the community equipped to deal with young delinquents of this type," the judge asserted. "During 1948, of 2,293 delin- quency cases, 592, or about 25 per cent, involved youngsters under 12 years of age; ten of them were brought to court on four separate occasions charged with delin- quency; eight appeared in court on five occasions during the year, and one of them on seven different occasions. 1 1 Urged By Welfare Agencies "This condition grows out of the Court's reluctance to commit children in this age bracket to the training school. As a result of this reluctance, there were practically none of this age from Baltimore city in the training schools of Mary- land during 1946, 1947 and 1948." The judge said welfare agencies were unable to cope with the in- crease in serious delinquencies and have urged commitment as the only possible alternative. After conferences between social agencies, welfare organizations and the Court, a training program has been devised in the training schools for younger delinquents, the judge said. title: 3 MEN IN CHARGE AT CHELTENHAM: TO STAY ON JOB PENDING CHOICE OF SUPERINTENDENT
full_text: 3 MEN IN CHARGE AT CHELTENHAM To Stay On Job Pending Choice Of Superintendent Cheltenham School for Boys is being administered by a three-man' committee pending appointment of 1 new superintendent, it was learned yesterday. Edward N. Wilson, secretary of the board of managers, said the temporary administration was working out successfully, that morale at the institution was good and the buildings and grounds were in well-kept condition. Committee Members Serving on the committee are Charles Cephas, in charge of social service; Robert Scott, business man- ager, and George Crawford, who is on loan from Bowie State Teachers College to develop the educational program at Cheltenham. The school has been without a superintendent for several months, and its assistant superintendent, H. R. Harris, resigned June 15 to become superintendent of a boys' training school at Hanover, Va. Meanwhile, the board of man- agers is having a job analysis made of the superintendent's post in light of recent recommendations result- ing from a study of the institution by the State Department of Educa- tion. title: What Cheltenham Needs Is A Steady Course
full_text: What Cheltenham Needs Is A Steady Course. The news that the State Planning Commis sion is once again considering plans to re build the Cheltenham School for Boys at a site closer to Baltimore should make many readers feel that this is where they came in five years ago. Proposals and counterpro posals regarding the future of Cheltenham have been in the news since 1943, when the General Assembly, on the advice of the Maryland Commission on Juvenile Delin- quency, voted to build a new institution for normal delinquent Negro boys in less rural surroundings and to utilize the old school at Cheltenham for mentally defective ones. The need for a new Cheltenham was gen- erally accepted during Governor O'Conor's administration and the money for the proj- ect was included in Maryland's postwar construction fund. Governor Lane, however, scrapped the plans for the new institution and shifted the money earmarked for, its construction into the general funds of the State. Governor Lane held to the theory that Cheltenham, despite its poor location and advanced state of deterioration, could be suitably patched up. In line with this idea, the State Board of Public Works, last October, approved an "emergency" expendi- ture of $128,300 to repair the old buildings. Now the Cheltenham board of managers and Mr. J. Milton Patterson, director of the State Department of Public Welfare, are urging anew that Cheltenham be rebuilt from the ground up at an entirely new loca- tion. Their arguments are the same valid ones advanced by the juvenile-delinquency commission and the 1943 Legislature. It re- mains largely for Governor Lane to decide whether it will be better in the long run to spend a large sum now for the erection of a modern training school for Negro boys (and then decide how to finance it, now that the funds set aside for this very purpose have been spent otherwise) or to continue spending smaller sums to meet the periodic and inevitable emergencies arising at the present institution. The important thing is to have an early decision on what the future of Cheltenham is to be. Five years of vacillating plans and emergency programs have done little to improve conditions at Cheltenham to date. 1 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: BOYS' TRAINING SCHOOLS SEEK BUILDING FUND: MARYLAND AND CHELTENHAM ASK AUTHORITY TO SPEND $6,000,000
full_text: BOYS' TRAINING SCHOOLS SEEK BUILDING FUND Maryland And Chelten- ham Ask Authority To Spend $6,000,000 | Maryland's two training schools for boys are seeking authority to spend nearly $6,000,000 for capital improvements in the two-year period beginning July 1. 1950. The Maryland Training School for Boys at Loch Raven has pro- posed expenditure of $2.213.000 on construction including a separate group of buildings for younger boys, a new cottage in the present group, a gymnasium and a building to house 70 staff members. Plans of the Cheltenham School for Boys primarily are for con- struction of an entirely new train- ing school for Negro boys at a new location at an estimated cost of $3,645,994 in the first two years of construction. Expenditure Breakdown Its proposed expenditure of $125.950 at the present institution is described as "construction and repairs to conform with instruc- tions of fire and health depart- ment," with $100.000 of the amount allocated to the boiler house and $20,000 toward building a shed for cattle. Taken together, the programs of the four training schools, including the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls and the Montrose School for Girls, present a total proposed expenditure during the biennium of $7,310,305. Each pro- gram is to undergo review by the State Planning Commission. The Maryland Training School for Colored Girls wants permission to spend $830,011 including $237,- 068 for a central heating plant, $200.000 for two new cottages for girls, $150,000 for a reception cen- ter and infirmary, $136.418 for an addition to the administration building. $65.000 for a sewage con- nection and $25.000 for a superin- tendent's home. Would End Overcrowding Montrose has proposed expendi- tures of $113.100 for a staff build- ing, $128.000 for a dormitory for 25 girls, $211,900 for a school build- Ing addition and auditorium, $9,600 Tor a swimming pool and $33.700 for furnishings, or a total outlay of $496,300. In presenting its case to the State Planning Commission for the new junior cottage group, the Maryland Training School for Boys Lirged "immediate" building of the Limit "to eliminate overcrowded conditions and take out 68 children with us now who are twelve years and under." "These children are mixed with (Continued on Page 16. Column 5) SCHOOLS SEEK BUILDING FUND Maryland And Cheltenham Would Spend $6,000,000 (Continued from Page 24) the older group, and there is no planned program for the needs of these younger children," its memo- randum pointed out. "The board felt we should immediately, on an emergency basis, get started. with four of these units and the school building." Costs were estimated as follows: Cottages, $100,000 each; school building, $300,000; utilities, $200,- 000. Treatment Of Children "There should be a definite type of treatment as applied to children 13 years of age and under as against that used for 14 years and up," the institution's statement said. "This is sound in light of the whole educational philosophy of America as well as the normal behavior patterns of those 13 and under and those above puberty. "It is also felt that the Mary- land Training School should be planning to take care of all white delinquents in the State of Mary- land looking toward the closing of St. Mary's (Industrial School. "In line with this and even if the population of both institutions is kept at a possible minimum as against past years, we will need to look toward a population of 400 in the near future with a possible increase of 40 to 50 in later years. Eight Cottages Needed "With the treatment of children in units of not more than 30 for those boys of high school and in advanced age, and 25 with the younger children who require more individual education, and after consulting with Mr. Funk (John B. Funk, chief engineer of the State), the board felt that a unit consisting of eight cottages, with proper educational building with an auditorium for church and chapel, should be established for the junior group. "These figures indicate at least five boys in each unit more than is generally advocated in better-run delinquent schools. "When we stop to consider that in the State only three children are recommended for boarding home care (no more than five) and that these children are not delinquents in any way, but are just boarders. it is beyond the conception of good treatment procedure to expect a couple to handle more than 25 boys. "We feel that we should have fewer boys in the cottages but the cost of this to the State would be too great." For New Negro Institution The Cheltenham board of man- agers placed itself on record some months ago as favoring construc- tion of a new Negro institution closer to Baltimore city. Estimates of initial costs include purchase of site, $150,000; ten cot- tages for 25 boys, $1.000.000; superintendent's residence. $25,000; staff quarters, $91,200; gymnasium, $300,000; boiler house, $165,000; vocational building. $400,000: aca- demic building. $215,000; culinary department, $343,700; administra tion building, $132,000; farm and auxiliary buildings. $39.500; equip- ment, $195.000; sewage disposal, $175.000, and garages, $30,000. Other expenditures estimated in connection with the new institu- tion are landscaping, $84,840; utili- tfes, $117.108, and architectural and engineering fees, $182.046. Four-Year Expenditures Additional classrooms for $155,- 1000, and auditorium for $200.000 and other improvements costing $355,000 would be carried out in the next two years, and in the succeeding two-year period $100.- 000 would be spent for bleachers and a swimming pool, $100,000 for an athletic field and $334,872.70 for other improvements, Commenting on the programs of the four institutions, J. Milton Pat- terson, director of the State De- partment of Public Welfare, which oversees their operation, told the Planning Commission: "We believe these plans repre- sent concretely a State plan for a responsible service for children and equal opportunity for all chil- dren receiving the service of the training schools. Cheltenham Needs Vital "We cannot say that any one plan, except that of Cheltenham. takes precedence. Cheltenham needs immediate repairs and improve- ments requested to provide for the safety and health of children. It cannot provide a training program without what is included in the building request for the next two years. "You will note that the Chelten- ham board, with regard for the ulti- mate costs to the State, has re- duced expenditures on the present plant to provide only the minimum essentials for health and safety." Mr. Patterson's letter pointed out that the department was "con- cerned" about what the planning at the institutions amounted to at present-day costs. It added: "How- ever, we believe that the expendi- tures now will ultimately repre- sent a saving in money to the State."

full_text: CITATIONS NOTE POLICE FITNESS Courage, Alertness And Mem- ory Given Praise Police Department. citations awarded to eight policemen this week gave recognition to a variety of accomplishments, including "ex- emplary courage" shown by one policeman in exposing himself to an armed bandit; alertness in de- tecting a fire; good memory work, and the ability to track down a wanted person on description. Three patrolmen who received commendations were praised for doing their work on their own time. These were Patrolmen Peter Politis, Morris Stein and Henry F. Plunkett, all of the Southern dis- trict. In Battle With Bandit Sergt. James W. Tyler, attached to headquarters, was the policeman cited for "exemplary courage." On May 19, the sergeant saw a Negro leave a liquor store on West Baltimore street and fire two shots at a white man who followed him out. When the sergeant ordered the armed man to stop, the bandit faced the policeman and pointed a 45-caliber automatic pistol at him. Sergeant Tyler fired two shots, and the man fled. Three times he fired back at the pursuing sergeant, who returned the fire. As the bandit crouched in an alley, the sergeant, now without ammunition, ordered two other po- licemen to approach from the end of the alley. They rushed the man, who was semi-conscious from wounds.
