full_text: IMPETUS FOR FORESTRY  Possibilities If Well Directed A Maryland Need Neglected.  CHARGES FULL MAPLE LANDS  Interesting Address Before the Federation of Women’s Clubs. The Need of Conservation.  The Maryland Federation of Women’s Clubs held a meeting yesterday at the Hotel Belvedere. The morning session was devoted to business, and in the afternoon the members listened to an address by Mr. F. W. Besley, State Forester, on “Forestry in Maryland.” Mr. Besley said: “Maryland is not generally considered a forest State, yet it has within its borders 2,100,000 acres of woodland, which is 33 per cent, of the total land area of the State. This is a considerable area, and if properly handled would be a source of great wealth to the State. As it is, the forests are being depleted at an alarming rate, and unless something is done to check this waste the time is not far distant when Maryland will be practically without forests. “The forests of Maryland are of two general types, the hardwood forests of the western counties and the pine and hardwood forests of the coastal plain. The hardwood forests are composed largely of oak, chestnut, hickory, maple, beech, birch, ash, walnut, cherry and other valuable species. The pine forests are composed of loblolly pine, shortleaf pine, pitch pine and scrub pine. The hardwood forests are found in the coastal plain, mixed with the pines. “The forests of Maryland are being depleted by fire, insects, disease and wasteful cutting. Fire is the greatest enemy of the forest. It destroys the young growth, kills the trees and injures the soil. Insects and disease also cause great damage to the forests. Wasteful cutting is another great source of loss. Trees are often cut before they are mature, and the tops and branches are left to rot on the ground. “The forests of Maryland are a valuable resource, and they should be conserved. Forestry is the science of managing forests so as to produce a continuous supply of timber and other forest products. Forestry also includes the protection of forests from fire, insects and disease. “The State of Maryland has a forestry department which is charged with the duty of protecting and managing the forests of the State. The forestry department is doing a great work, but it needs the support of the people of the State. “The people of Maryland can help to conserve the forests by preventing fires, by planting trees and by practicing forestry on their own lands. The forests of Maryland are a valuable resource, and they should be conserved for the benefit of future generations.”

full_text: BRITON'S AUTO STRUCK BOYS, POLICE ALLEGE Naval Officer Is Charged With Fatally Injuring One Of Trio A British naval officer yesterday was charged by Anne Arundel county police with manslaughter and leaving the scene of an acci- dent in which three brothers were injured, one of them fatally. Meanwhile, a woman was killed and six other persons---all of them North Carolinians were injured in two collisions between automo- biles and parked trucks in Prince Georges county. Sergt. Edward C. King identified the British officer as Lieut. Com. Gregory Haines and said that he was charged with driving the car which struck the Negro boys near Galesville Friday night. • Commander Haines, who is sta- tioned in Washington, was charged after he reported to Annapolis police that his car had "struck something" as he drove toward his home in St. Margarets from the capital, according to the sergeant. Victim Identified Police had been searching for a damaged vehicle after finding a running board, headlight rim, and pieces of glass at the scene of the accident. They identified the victim as Joseph Brown, 11, son of Mr. and Mrs. George Brown, of Davidson- ville. He died early yesterday at Emergency Hospital in Annapolis of a skull fracture and internal Injuries, according to police. 11. was reported that young Brown, with his brothers, Stanley, 16, and Earl, 13, were struck white returning to their home from a store about 7.30 P.M. Last night Stanley was being treated at the hospital, but Earl's injuries were said not to be serious, Commander Haines also was charged with reckless driving in the warrant sworn out by Patrol- man Robert Williams. Was Passenger In Car In the fatal Prince Georgès county accident, police identified the victim as Mrs. J. R. Mobley, 42, of Greenville, N.C. They said that she was a pas- senger in a car, driven by Blanco Hardee, 27, also of Greenville, which struck a parked truck about. a mile north of Cheltenham. Mr. Hardee was admitted to a Washington hospital in a serious condition suffering from head in- juries, and his wife, Mabel, was admitted in a critical condition. Police said that those injured in the other accident were Harold Adams, 25; of Midway Park, N.C.; Sergl. Benny Tumbarello, 19; Pfc. Pasquale Caprio, 18, and Pfe. J. K. Hefferman, 19, all of Camp Lejeune, N.C. Hospital attachés said that none of them was seri- ously injured. Injured last night in a two-car collision near Randallstown, John W. Meanwhile, Mrs. Roy D. Whit- lock, president of the Maryland Federation of Women's Clubs, called on the State's 10,000 club- women to support the President's food-conservation measu measures, in- volving meatless Tuesdays, and eggless and poultryless Thursdays. title: Judge Moylan On Cheltenham
full_text: Judge Moylan On Cheltenham TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: The Sun has for many years been most helpful in promoting needed reforms in our juvenile institutions. However, I must take issue with your editorial of November 16. There is not the slightest inconsistency in my report to Governor Lane on Cheltenham and my more recent plea for more adequate facilities and personnel for our two State schools for the feeble-minded. In my report to the Governor I definitely did not propose any patchwork of the present Cheltenham plant. 1 urged the construction of a school building with adequate classrooms and vocational shops, as did the State Board of Education in 1939. I recommended the re- placement of the present administration building, erected in 1872. The cost of these and other suggested improvements, however, would be but a fraction of the cost (the lat- est estimate, as reported in the columns of the Sunpapers, is $6,000,000) of buying a new site and erecting thereon all new build- ings. I set forth just how many conditions which impelled State officials in 1939, and later in 1943, to advocate the removal of the school, no longer existed. The advantages of the pres ent site, with its 1,230-aere farm, Including 30 acres of attractively landscaped campus and 400 acres of woodland, along with sev- eral new buildings erected within the past several years at a cost of $250,000, are such that, with the improvements suggested, the faulty educational and disciplinary practices that have plagued Cheltenham, for many years can be corrected and a good training school conducted at the present site. These proposals are entirely consistent with my recent request that the public sup- port efforts of the Board of Mental Hygiene to relieve the congestion at the Crownsville and Rosewood schools for feeble-minded chil- dren. Your statement, in referring to Chel- tenham, that "kids are committed to State schools which are jammed to the doors" is inaccurate but leads you on to a renewed advocacy of a new Cheltenham to relieve a congestion there which does not exist and simultaneously, you feel, the present Chelten- ham plant's use for Crownsville's overflow will ease the overcrowding at the latter in- stitution, which does exist. Unlike the Rosewood and Crownsville in- stitutions for the feeble-minded, each with large waiting lists, neither Cheltenham nor any of our other six training schools has a waiting list for admissions. The Cheltenham student body has declined nearly 50 per cent, from 413 in 1939 to 219 at present (the State Reformatory for Males, at Breathedsville, having been established several years ago). The combined student bodies of all seven training schools total less than 1,000, about 45 per cent less than the total enrollment of 1,457 at our two institutions for feeble-mind- ed children. Nor does it follow at all that Cheltenham, designed and constructed as a training school for healthy, nonfeeble minded, delinquent boys, 11 to 16 years of age, would be suitable or adapted to a school for the feeble-minded, or to an institution for "defective delin- quents." The facilities required, the therapies and techniques of treatment needed, and the whole setup of these two types of schools are entirely different. One may as well argue that the Maryland Training School for Boys should be moved to a new location in order to relieve conges. tion at the Rosewood School for the Feeble- Minded, or that our Public School for Phys- ically Handicapped Children, in Baltimore city, could just as well be operated at an abandoned school building originally designed and used as a school for normal children. The simplest and soundest way to start re- lieving the current congestion in our schools for feeble-minded children is found in the plan considered by the Board of Mental Hy- giene from time to time of removing from Rosewood several hundred adults, divorcing the management of the Crownsville School for the Feeble-minded from that of the Crownsville State Hospital, and the operation of both institutions as schools for children. The number of adults there now is larger than the combined waiting lists of both schools. Similarly, when the need of a separate insti- tution for "defective delinquents" is met (ac- tually two institutions would be required if the color line is adhered to), further relief would be afforded. CHARLES E. MOYLAN, Judge, Supreme Bench of Baltimore City. Baltimore, Nov. 19. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: The Cost Of A New Cheltenham
full_text: The Cost Of A New Cheltenham TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: Your con- roversy with Judge Moylan relative to the proposal to establish a new training school for colored boys to take the place of Chelten- nam at an estimated cost of $6,000,000 is perplexing. 1 -Based upon the present population of 219 nmates at Cheltenham (which may decline with more adequate facilities for feeble- minded children elsewhere), the extravagant and ill-considered program which you severe- My criticize Governor, Lane and Judge Moylan for discarding would cost the State $27,400 to provide a home for each of its delinquent colored boys. If the State is going to be so generous as to provide such a luxurious home for each de- linquent colored boy, then perhaps all of us should, become delinquent colored boys, for but few of our citizens can afford such ex- pensive living quarters. Governor Lane and Judge Moylan are en- titled to the thanks of the community for scuttling this costly scheme. Baltimore, Nov. 22. WILLIS R. JONES. ! The Sun has never advocated building a new training school for colored boys to take the place of Cheltenham for $6,000,000-or for any other specific figure. Back in 1943, the State Legislature decided to proceed with such an institution, but did not appropriate funds nor specify the amount to be spent- reasonably enough, since plans had not been drawn. Toward the end of 1943 a tentative figure of $1,500,000 was proposed for this project. This figure was not far out of line with the figure of $1,253,691 for the Maryland Training School For (White) Boys-and the present Cheltenham would have remained available as a new institution for the feeble- minded and other defective children. Still nothing was done. By 1945, the State Planning Commission estimated that the cost of such an institution would be around $2,424,000. By July of this year, in the peak of a building boom and runaway building costs, the figure of $4,486,000 emerged. Mr. Jones uses the figure of $6,000,000, and his reference to luxurious homes for delinquents are mere debating points.-THE EDITOR. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: PUBLIC WORKS FUND BOOSTED BY $3,000,000 Total Includes $1,000, 000 From Unearmarked Postwar Sums More than $3,000,000 has been placed at the disposal of the Board of Public Works during the cur- rent biennium for expenditure at the board's discretion. Not the least of the amounts making up the total-but certainly the least publicized is the slightly more than $1,000,000. in unear- marked postwar funds which re- mained after $5,260,993.95 was transferred to general funds to balance the current budget. Another $1,000,000 was made available to the Board of Public Works in the General Emergency Fund for the biennium-$500,000 for 1948 and $500,000 for 1949. title: Letter From Germany
full_text: Letter From Germany Sir: TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN Inclosed you will find a copy of a letter my daughter received from Germany. I thought you might be Linterested in publishing it. A. C. SUSEMUIL. Baltimore, March 18. [INCLOSUREI Dear Mary Virginia Susemihl My daughter, Hille Gutman, 8 years old, got the American Junior Red Cross parcel you filled. She was very glad to get it and she would express her gratitude for the fine things. My daughter is learning English in her first year at school, but she is not able to write in English, so she asked me to write for her. We are D.Is now in a camp in Germany. We had our native coun- try on the Baltic Sea, our beautiful Estoria. We had there a fur life, but our homeland is occupied by Russians and we cannot return. You and your parents are very happy people, because you can live in freedom in your homes in the U.S.A. We had such a life, but it is as a fairy tale now. We all here would like to go to America, but There are no possibilities. HILDE GUTMAN. Augsbury, Hochfield, Bavaria, Germany, Feb. 28. Maryland Artists' Exhibition TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN Sir: In commenting upon the pictures That won the awards in the Mary- land artists' exhibition, my 8-year- old son hit the nail pretty squarely on the head when he said: "Looks as if they were done by kids. Look at this one pointing to the one of the bird that won a prize for the best draftsmanship), It looks like some kind of puzzle and they put the wrong parts together!" K. JONES. Baltimore, March 18. Cheltenham School Sir: TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN It seems to me that the action of the "lame duck" board of the Chelton- ham School in summarily discharg ing Mr. Calvin Kiah from his position of probationary superin- tendent is open to question. I am not so sure that Mr. Kiah was given a chance to demonstrate his ability to manage the school and put into effect his modern, pro gressive program. If he had been given the sympathetic assistance of his board and the wholehearted co operation of his staff, there is every reason to believe that he would have made Cheltenhain a reform school of which the State of Mary- land could be proud. In the field of public relations Mr. Kiah did an outstanding piece of work.. He personally visited the homes from which his charges come and thereby gained first-hand information concerning their back- ground.. An honor system was introduced and to this the boys re- sponded well. It seems quite clear that Mr. Kjah is entitled to be removed from the category of an inenicient ad ministrator and given an opportu nity to prove his worth. JOHN W. WOODHOUSE Baltimore, March 18. title: Luttrell Given Cheltenham Post
full_text: Luttrell Given Cheltenham Post J. Grayson Luttrell, vice presi- dent of MeCormick & Co., Inc., has been named a member of the board of managers of the Chelten- ham School for Boys, it was an- nounced yesterday at Governor Lane's office. He will fill the vacancy on the board caused by the death of How- ard C. Hill, educator and social worker. Mr. Hill's term was to ex- pire in 1951. Mr. Luttrell is a former presi- dent of the Rotary Club of Balti- more and is a director of the Fed- eral Home Loan Bank of Winston- Salem, N.C. title: CHELTENHAM STEP ADVISED BY BOARD: MEMBERS RESIGN, MAKING WAY FOR ALL-NEGRO GROUP
full_text: CHELTENHAM STEP ADVISED BY BOARD Members Resign, Making Way For All-Negro Group Declaring that conunions am me 5 Cheltenham School for Boys could - be improved by an all-Negro board of managers, the entire board, com- posed of five white members and four Negroes, yesterday resigned. S S ב a ... In accepting their resignations, Governor Lane said that he ex- pected to appoint a new all-Negro board "as soon as it can be done.. with the expectation that this board can continue the progress which has been made toward the rehabili- tation of Cheltenham." The resignations were submitted following a meeting of the board at which it unanimously approved a report of Wallace Reidt, assistant director of the Baltimore Criminal Justice Commission, who had been serving as executive secretary of the board. Until New Board Is Appointed In submitting their resignations, the board, composed of Thomas B. Sprague, president; J. Grayson Lut- trell, Hal B. Clagett, Joseph P. - Healy. J. Marshall Stewart. Car- eroll H. Hynson, Mrs. William B. e Proctor, Joseph II. Neal and Dr. Robert L. Jackson, said they would continue to function until a new one is appointed. The recommendation for an en- - (Continued on Page 7, Column 3) Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission. Lire Negro board was based on the premise that such a board would be able to gain more confi- dence from the Negro staff at Chel- tenham and, at the same time, hold the staff to a more strict accounta- bility. Three Deficiencies Noted Made at the request of Mr. Sprague, Mr. Reidt's report listed recent improvements at the insti- tution and listed three outstanding deficiencies to be corrected in the future: 1. The eficiency of the staff at the school is "very low." Many em- ployés are only temporary and do not have the listed qualifications for the positions they are holding, al- though the salaries pald and pre- requisites for employment are good. A recruiting campaign for good personnel should be inaugurated. 2. "A careful survey should be undertaken as to maintenance and some better utilization of existing facilities be made until such time as additional facilities can be pro- vided. No additional living quarters should be bullt, however, that pro- vide for unit cooking and eating by the staff." Habits Of Cleanliness 3. "It cannot be too strongly Impressed upon the staff that good eitizenship begins with habits of cleanliness and that, unless this fact is constantly brought home to the boys through teaching and inspection, they will be slovenly at the school and upon their return to the community. Much remains to be done in this connection." The report recommended that the State Board of Welfare clearly define the responsibilities of the State board, the board of managers and the superintendent of the insti- tutions and define minimum stand. ards of maintenance for the staffs and a diet for the children. Periodic Reports Called For It also recommended that the board of managers be given periodic reports showing the situa- tion of the school as viewed by the supervisor of training schools, and that personnel qualifications and practices be standardized for the four State training schools. Since there may be many of the present staff qualified for positions different from those they now hold. the report recommended a survey to see what positions they should hold regardless of their present classifications. New members should be screened carefully. White Members' Situation In reference to the board of man- agers, the report stated: "The white members of the hoard have earnestly tried to un- derstand and appreciate the prob- lems and viewpoints of the staff. "Little opportunity is afforded, however, for confidences between the white board members and the staff, and, indeed, there may pos- sibly be some resentment against a staff member by his fellow em- ployés who attempted to establish such contacts. "On the other hand, colored board members may meet staff members at church and social fune- tions and establish pleasant rela- Honships that can be most helpful. "Helpfulness" Seen As Past "However, there is respect on the part of the white board members for those staff members who are striving to do a creditable job. "I believe that it has been help- ful to the school to have had white board members in the past who might assist in interpreting its pros gram to the entire community, but this advantage is no longer neces- sary. "A most important function of the board at the present time is the recruiting of a proper staff. "I know that a large number of colored organizations and agencies have exhibited a new interest in this school and its needs and that there are available excellent col- ored people who would be willing willing to work earnestly and intelligently on this problem. Girls School Board Cited "After a full consideration of all the many factors involved, it is my opinion that the best Interests of The institution and its charges will be served by setting up an all- colored board of managers. ""There are no white members on the staff at the present time and there is no real reason for mixed board. The Girls School at Glen Barnte has an all-colored board. "An all-colored board is likely to hold the staff to a more strict accountability than a mixed board, It is my firm conviction that such a board, wisely chosen, will not tolerate some of the conditions that have existed in the past at the school." title: The Cheltenham Plan Had A Double Purpose
full_text: the fact remains that the State's plan for doing this job at a new institution would, if carried out, have made Cheltenham avail- able for the care of feeble-minded children and other defectives. title: BOARD SEEKS NEW SITE FOR CHELTENHAM: NEW ALL-NEGRO GROUP CONTENDS INSTITUTION IS TOO FAR FROM CITY
full_text: BOARD SEEKS NEW SITE FOR CHELTENHAM New All-Negro Group Contends Institution Is Too Far From City In its first official recommenda- tion, the new board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys yesterday advocated moving the school to a site nearer Baltimore. In discussion preceding their action, members of the new all- Negro board expressed the hope that, in any move to a new site, the name of the institution and the less pleasant aspects of its past history "be left behind." The board immediately wired Governor Lane of its recommen- dation.  Remoteness Cited ✓ A formal report will be made to the Governor as quickly as pos- sible, according to Edward N. Wil- son, registrar of Morgan State College, who is secretary to the board. Several reasons were given for the desire to move the Cheltenham School from its present site in Prince Georges county. Most of these reasons dealt with the disad- vantages of the remoteness of the school from Baltimore. : The decision that a move would be advisable followed a meeting which the board of managers held at the school with John B. Funk, chief State engineer. Report Of Subcommittee 1 At the meeting, the board con- sidered the report of a subcommit-1 tee which had been asked to weigh the arguments for and against relo- eating the school. Dr. James A. White, surgeon dentist, and the Rev. James T. Col- bert, a Presbyterian minister, both momhore of the hoard were on the subcommittee. Dr. William E. Henry, president of the State Teachers College at Bowie, is chairman of the board of managers. The vote of the board was unanimous with all of its nine members present.  Supervision Program Also considered by the board was a report from officials of the school that 214 former inmates are at present on parole and badly need an adequate supervision program., The fact that Cheltenham is 55. miles from Baltimore makes the task of supervision difficult and at times impossible-and the situation is especially serious since 90 per cent of the boys who are sent to the school are from Baltimore, the board was informed. Dr. White and the Rev. Mr. Col- bert reported they felt that a new school probably would remedy the deficiencies at the present institu- tion in facilities for vocational and industrial training.  Programs Hindered If the school is close to Baltimore when an adequate program of voca- tional instruction is put into effect, several board members asserted, it would be easier to place boys in jobs in industry and supervise their progress on the way toward re- habilitation. Another disadvantage of the pres- ent location, according to the sub- committee report, is the fact that the distance from Baltimore hinders development of adequate sports or "cultural" programs. Explaining how this has affected the school, Mr. Wilson said: "If they want to have a band con- cert, it turns out that they can't get an audience. "If they organize a sports team, they are too far away to get op ponents."  Visits Prove Difficult Parents, who should be able to help authorities to correct thein delinquent children, frequently are unable to make visits to the school because of the distance, Mr. Wilsor added. No mention was made of a pos sible new site for the institution In its telegram to Governor Lane the board requested a meeting with: the Governor, at his convenience to discuss the entire matter. title: CHURCH HERE BURGLARIZED, RANSACKED: GRACE AND ST. PETER'S IS ENTERED, AND ANOTHER RECEIVES THREATS
full_text: CHURCH HERE BURGLARIZED, RANSACKED Grace And St. Peter's Is Entered, And Another Receives Threats : The Grace and St. Peter's Episco- pal Church, at Park avenue and Monument street, was burglarized and ransacked Sunday night or early yesterday, Central district po- lice reported. Meanwhile, it was learned that Northwestern district police are searching for the author of several threatening letters addressed re- cently to the First Presbyterian Church, a' Park avenue and Madi- son street, only a block away. Police were alerted to be espe- cially watchful of Grace and St. Peter's following discovery of the burglary.  Synagogue Broken Into Only two weeks ago, vandals broke into the Ohr Knesseth Israel Synagogue, in the 700 block of West Franklin street, and wrecked the interior of the building. Val uable sacred objects were de stroyed. Two boys were arrested in con- nection with the desecration of the synagogue and one of them, 13 years old, has been sentenced to four years in the Cheltenham reformatory. Police said that entrance to the Grace and St. Peter's Church was gained through a window on the Park avenue side, which was forced.  Tabernacle Door Pried Open The door of the tabernacle in the church had been pried open, po- lice reported, and cigarette bults were strewn on the altar. In an adjoining room, vestments had been thrown to the floor, ac- cording to a police report. Following an inventory yester- day, the Rev. Daniel Corrigan, rec- tor of Grace and St. Peter's, sald, however, that he found nothing missing. Father Corrigan said there were numerous signs that the church had • been ransacked.  Garments Scattered Drawers had been pulled open, he said, and on an upper floor, garments which had been collected by churchwomen for a rummage sale were scattered on the floor. Police also said they found a screwdriver and half a burned candle in the church basement, The burglary was discovered by Webster Thomas, Negro sexton, when he went to work at 7 Λ.Μ. Lieut. Albert Hanssen, acting commander of the Central district, and Lieut. George Galkas investi- gated.  Unusual Sequence Of Events The police reported that a smoker's pipe was found beneath the window which had been forced. An unusual sequence of events preceded discovery of the burglary. Father Corrigan said that late Sunday night he looked from his bedroom window and saw a num- ber of policemen around the church. He went to find out what was the matter, he said, and was told that police had received a call that someone had broken into Grace and St. Peter's. : The call was from a woman who refused to give her name, police (Continued on Page 8, Column 2) (Continued from Page 30) reported. She said she had seen a tall Negro in a tan raincoat and a light cap breaking into the church.  Heard Nothing Suspicious Father Corrigan sald he told the police that he had heard or seen nothing suspicious. He and the police investigated immediately, he said, but saw nothing wrong. The letters sent to the 'First Presbyterian Church, received over a period of several weeks, were described as "violent," "disjointed" and "containing vague threats." Police are reported to believe Ithem the work of a crank. cran The Rev. Dr. John H. Gardner is pastor of the church. In February, 1945, the North Avenue Presbyterian Church was damaged seriously by youthful vandals.

title: CHELTENHAM HEAD SLATED: C. L KIAH, VETERAN AND EDUCATOR, LIKELY TO GET POST
full_text: CHELTENHAM HEAD SLATED C. L. Kiah, Veteran And Edu- cator, Likely To Get Post Appointment of Calvin L. Kiah a principal of Cambridge, Md., as superintendent of the Cheltenham School for Boys, Negro training school in Prince Georges county. was indicated yesterday at a joint meeting of the institution's board of managers with the State Board of Public Welfare. Prompt appointment of a super- Intendent, thorough physical ex amination of the school's plant by the chief engineer of the State and procurement of new buildings, pos- sibly quonset huts, to serve as ad- ditional staff quarters, dining room, kitchen and vocational shops, were decided upon at the meeting as immediate steps to be taken. Lane Attends Session Governor Lane, who had asked for a "full report" on conditions at the training school, was among those present at the discussions held in the offices of the State Department of Public Welfare. He promised his co-operation in the program to be undertaken. Mr. Kiah, a 36-year-old veteran, tops the eligible list from which the Cheltenham board of managers is expected to name the superin- tendent at a meeting next week. Thomas B. title: Judge Moylan Argued Against Himself
full_text: Judge Moylan Argued "Against Himself In committing a feeble-minded Negro boy, aged 12, to Crownsville for vandalism, Judge Charles E. Moylan declared that juvenile au- sthorities cannot afford to defer commitments in such cases in spite of the large waiting lists for admission to State institutions. Judge Moylan said that many of the recent cts of vandalism were done by feeble-mind- ed youngsters, awaiting entrance to State schools. He also cited two cases of homicide by children whose commitments as feeble- minded patients had been postponed. "Con- gestion or no congestion," the judge said, the court could not "legally commit children to'a waiting list." Judge Moylan has pointed up the dis- tressing shortage of facilities for the care of delinquent Negro children, but he has failed to recall that there was a sound plan in the works for the partial elimination of that shortage. The General Assembly in 1943 passed the necessary laws to enable the State to build a new training school for de- linquent Negro boys and to keep the present school at Cheltenham for mentally defec- tive colored children. The money for the new school was earmarked in Governor O'Conor's Postwar construction fund. The plan was later shelved by Governor Lane, who wiped But the funds set aside for the purpose. - to When interest in a new Cheltenham school was revived once again this fall, it was none other than Judge Moylan who declared in a special report to the Governor that there was no need to spend $3,400,000 for the pur- chase of a new site and buildings for the colored training school. Judge Moylan told the Governor that the present school could the patched up, and so it could. But no amount of patching up will solve the problem of what is to be done with kids who are com- mitted to State schools which are already jammed to the doors. If, as Judge Moylan says, our juvenile authorities cannot afford to defer commitments of feeble-minded van- dals, then it must follow that the State can- not afford to defer the enlargement of our facilities to handle those vandals. Either the Judge is wrong in saying that feeble-minded children should be put away for safekeeping For he is wrong in saying that we do not need a new school for colored delinquents. For twenty years Mr. Hill was an inspector of county prisons for the State Board of: Welfare and later held the same position with the Department of Correction. title: KIAH TERMED INELIGIBLE AS SCHOOL HEAD: CAN'T BE REINSTATED AT CHELTENHAM, BOARD PRESIDENT SAYS
full_text: KIAH TERMED INELIGIBLE AS SCHOOL HEAD Can't Be Reinstated At Cheltenham, Board President Says Dr. W. E. Henry, president of the board of managers of Chelten- ham School for Boys, said last night that Calvin L. Kiah definitely was not eligible for reinstatement as superintendent of the Negro train- ing school, He made the statement following receipt of an opinion from the State Law Department that, while ' Mr. Kiah retained his place on the elig- ible list for the classification of su- perintendent, he could not be re- appointed to the head post at Chel- tenham, There is, however, no other po- sition in the State service for a male superintendent in a Negro training school. List Set Up Year Ago The eligible list established nearly a year ago will expire June 18, and since the new all-Negro Cheltenham board has not yet moved to make an appointment from the list, it is expected that the board will request a new list when the time limit on the old one has run out. Mr. Kiah was appointed to the superintendency last September 1, pending a six-month probationary period. Just before the proba- tionary period expired February 26, he was rejected by the old board for permanent appointment. Dr. Henry, who also is president of State Teachers College at Bowie, said a delegation supporting Mr. Kiah had appeared before the board of managers yesterday dur- ing its regular monthly meeting at the institution and that he had ex- plained the ruling by Richard W. Emory, deputy attorney general, to the group. Harris Is Assistant He explained last night that H. R. Harris, who recently requested the employment commissioner for a ruling on his status, is assistant su- perintendent, a position he holds under the Merit System, and that the new board had not made Mr. Harris acting superintendent.. During yesterday's board meet- ing, Dr. Henry said, a temporary building program recommended by John B. Funk, chief engineer of the State, was approved by the board. It is expected Mr. Funk will submit the plan to the Board of Public Works on behalf of the school, he said. The construction program in- volves erection of a new building containing a dining room, kitchen and classrooms and renovations to several of the old buildings, par- ticularly the administration build- ing, it was explained. title: Mr. Kahl Promises To Keep The Public Informed
full_text: Mr. Kahl Promises To Keep The Public Informed The announcement by Mr. Christian H. | Kahl, president of the Board of Commission- ers of Baltimore county, that the public will be kept fully informed of all the details in the investigation of the Baltimore County Police Department should be well received by the residents of Baltimore county. Corrup- tion, abuse of authority or favoritism in a law-enforcing agency are things that no healthy community will stand for. Almost five months have passed since the start of the inquiry into the county's police department. During that time the public has been told little more than that three cases in which traffic tickets were "fixed" have been uncovered, that seven members of the police department have been either demoted, fined or transferred and that a clerk to a police magistrate has been dismissed. Five months of investigation is a lot of investigation to produce these results. However, the inquiry is not over. And the residents of Baltimore county now have Mr. Kahl's announcement that the public will be kept informed. A note of that announcement will be filed for future reference by those interested in protecting Baltimore county's welfare. One Way Of Learning How To Swim : There has never, within the memory of the oldest inhabitant, been any good news about the Cheltenham School for-Boys. Its history has been a sordid account of neglect, inadequate facilities and mismanagement. For awhile it looked as though Chelten- ham might be given a fresh start, beginning from the ground up with a new and properly Jocated building. There was provision for such a building in Governor O'Conor's.post- war construction program. But the Chelten- ham project was crossed off the list by Governor Lane, and since then we have had a resumption of the usual sordid news. Now the Cheltenham board of managers has had to appoint a new superintendent for the institution, Mr. Calvin L. Kiah. The most experienced superintendent obtainable, on going to Cheltenham, would find most of the cards stacked against him. For all we know, Mr. Kiah may turn out to be just the man whom Cheltenham needs. The fact re- mains that the board has gone out of its way to state that Mr. Kiah has had no previ- ous "institutional experience." The board has put him on a six-month probationary appointment. It is said that one way to learn how to swim is to be tossed overboard-a harsh method, but effective. Mr. Kiah is being tossed overboard into just about the deepest and most treacherous institutional waters in these parts. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: The Rich Harvest At Solomons
full_text: The Rich Harvest At Solomons This is the first of two short articles on the remarkable bar- gain which the State got when it acquired the amphibious training base near Solomons Island from the Navy last fall. The second article will describe some of the potentialitics of this base for the State when the present big sal vage operation is finished. The State government is bring- ing in a rich harvest from the 118- acre peninsula between Back and Mill creeks near Solomons Island. The harvest consists of an immense quantity of building supplies- finished building supplies: electric wiring and lighting fixtures, oak flooring, radiators, windows and doors and their frames, wood joists and heavy roof beams, pipes of many kinds and sizes. There is just about everything required to build a house, a small office build- ing or any other relatively simple structure. And each item is there to be harvested in abundance. The materials are being taken from what is known in official rec- ords as the United States Naval Operational Development Center (Atlantic). But the tract is better known as the amphibious training base. It was there that many of the men who fought in the Pacifie learned about beach warfare. In its heyday five years ago the base could house thousands of troops. It was a small but complete city, with its own modern water a system, its own electric power and heating plants, its own sewage- disposal plant. In addition, the base had numerous barracks, a large hospital, recreation centers, series of substantial piers, a marine railway-all the facilities of a thriving community and an armed services center. But when the war ended the Navy had no further use for the base.. -0- It was then that an agreement was reached between the Navy and the State government. On payment of $5,000-just $5,000-the State was given the authority to strip the peninsula of the improvements made by the Navy. The only ex- ceptions are the sewage-disposal, water and power plants and a few other selected items that will not readily deteriorate and could be put to use more or less swiftly if the base were needed in the future. The State began its stripping operations last fall, By the first of this month building materials with a value of $200,000 had been re- claimed and segregated. The total will be increased to $250,000 before this phase of the job is completed, To date, materials valued at more than $106,000 have been delivered to State institutions for public- building, projects. Reference to the minutes of the State Board of Pub- lic Works provides evidence of the many uses to which these materials from Solomons are being put. Last month, on the recommenda- tion of Mr. John B. Funk, the State chief engineer, the board author. ized the Cheltenham School for Boys to convert a farmhouse into two apartments for school em- ployés. There will be no expendi- ture of State funds; the materials will come from Solomons and the labor will be furnished by the personnel at Cheltenham. The construction of twelve small apartments, one large apartment and twelve single bedrooms at Princess Anne College also was authorized on the recommenda- tion of Mr. Funk. The use of ma- terial from Solomons will make an appreciable reduction in the cost of the new living quarters. At the same time the board authorized the use of materials from Solomons for the construction of employés' cottages at Crowns- ville State Hospital and for a ga- rage at the Eastern Shore State Hospital. And slop tanks were al lotted to the Spring Grove State Hospital. At every board session there is some talk about materials from the old Navy base. -0- Needless to say, the stripping of the base and the distribution 'of the materials are not being done for nothing. Both jobs are being done under the direction and super- vision of Mr. Funk. The actual work of tearing down the build- ings and the segregation of the many items is being done by prison labor, The prisoners-usually there are about 80 of them, including cooks and helpers-live at the base in a partly reconditioned building. As of June 1 the prison labor bill had mounted to $38.500. The total includes the pay for the guards and the $3 per month given each pris- oner for his work. But all of that $38,500 is not lost to the State. About half of it goes into the State industries account of the Depart- ment of Correction and will be used to help finance the penal in- stitutions. So, while the State has been paying out $38,500 on one hand, it has been receiving $20,000 back on the other hand. Just a bookkeeping item, in part. There is also an item of $20,000 for operating costs, which includes the financing of actual operations at the base and the delivery of ma- terials to the sites of construction. That $20,000 is money spent. It isn't going back into another pocket. of the State. But, all in all, the State has not spent more than $45.000, including the $5,000 pay- ment to the Navy. That means that for every dollar the State has paid out for the stripping opera- tions, it has received $4 in return. That is the kind of business trans- action one rarely if ever finds in the operation of public enterprise. E. V. BAUGH, JR. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. The harvest consists of an immense quantity of building supplies- finished building supplies: electric wiring and lighting fixtures, oak flooring, radiators, windows and doors and their frames, wood joists and heavy roof beams, pipes of many kinds and sizes. There is just about everything required to build a house, a small office build- ing or any other relatively simple structure. And each item is there to be harvested in abundance. The materials are being taken from what is known in official rec- ords as the United States Naval Operational Development Center (Atlantic). But the tract is better known as the amphibious training base. It was there that many of the men who fought in the Pacifie learned about beach warfare. In its heyday five years ago the base could house thousands of troops. It was a small but complete city, with its own modern water a system, its own electric power and heating plants, its own sewage- disposal plant. In addition, the base had numerous barracks, a large hospital, recreation centers, series of substantial piers, a marine railway-all the facilities of a thriving community and an armed services center. But when the war ended the Navy had no further use for the base.. -0- It was then that an agreement was reached between the Navy and the State government. On payment of $5,000-just $5,000-the State was given the authority to strip the peninsula of the improvements made by the Navy. The only ex- ceptions are the sewage-disposal, water and power plants and a few other selected items that will not readily deteriorate and could be put to use more or less swiftly if the base were needed in the future. The State began its stripping operations last fall, By the first of this month building materials with a value of $200,000 had been re- claimed and segregated. The total will be increased to $250,000 before this phase of the job is completed, To date, materials valued at more than $106,000 have been delivered to State institutions for public- building, projects. Reference to the minutes of the State Board of Pub- lic Works provides evidence of the many uses to which these materials from Solomons are being put. Last month, on the recommenda- tion of Mr. John B. Funk, the State chief engineer, the board author. ized the Cheltenham School for Boys to convert a farmhouse into two apartments for school em- ployés. There will be no expendi- ture of State funds; the materials will come from Solomons and the labor will be furnished by the personnel at Cheltenham. The construction of twelve small apartments, one large apartment and twelve single bedrooms at Princess Anne College also was authorized on the recommenda- tion of Mr. Funk. The use of ma- terial from Solomons will make an appreciable reduction in the cost of the new living quarters. At the same time the board authorized the use of materials from Solomons for the construction of employés' cottages at Crowns- ville State Hospital and for a ga- rage at the Eastern Shore State Hospital. And slop tanks were al lotted to the Spring Grove State Hospital. At every board session there is some talk about materials from the old Navy base. -0- Needless to say, the stripping of the base and the distribution 'of the materials are not being done for nothing. Both jobs are being done under the direction and super- vision of Mr. Funk. The actual work of tearing down the build- ings and the segregation of the many items is being done by prison labor, The prisoners-usually there are about 80 of them, including cooks and helpers-live at the base in a partly reconditioned building. As of June 1 the prison labor bill had mounted to $38.500. The total includes the pay for the guards and the $3 per month given each pris- oner for his work. But all of that $38,500 is not lost to the State. About half of it goes into the State industries account of the Depart- ment of Correction and will be used to help finance the penal in- stitutions. So, while the State has been paying out $38,500 on one hand, it has been receiving $20,000 back on the other hand. Just a bookkeeping item, in part. There is also an item of $20,000 for operating costs, which includes the financing of actual operations at the base and the delivery of ma- terials to the sites of construction. That $20,000 is money spent. It isn't going back into another pocket. of the State. But, all in all, the State has not spent more than $45.000, including the $5,000 pay- ment to the Navy. That means that for every dollar the State has paid out for the stripping opera- tions, it has received $4 in return. That is the kind of business trans- action one rarely if ever finds in the operation of public enterprise. E. V. BAUGH, JR. . .

title: The Cheltenham Appointment
full_text: The Cheltenham Appointment TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: If the editorials in your issues of August 6 and 7 are intended as an implied criticism of the State employment commissioner in certify- ing Mr. Calvin L. Kiah as eligible for ap- pointment as superintendent of Cheltenham School for Boys, then it is not justified. Under the law that placed the training schools under the jurisdiction of the Board of Public Welfare it was specifically provided that that board "shall prescribe the minimum qualifications" for the personnel of the train- ing schools of which Cheltenham is one. The State employment commissioner had no au- thority to amend, change or alter the qualifi- cations so prescribed, and the examining board, created for the purpose, after person- - al interview and oral examination, found that Mr. Kiah did possess the minimum qualifica- tions for the position of superintendent of Cheltenham School for Boys with a passing mark of 90.04 per cent. In these circum- stances the State employment commissioner had no alternative other than to certify Mr. Kiah for appointment, and, as the law also provides that a qualified veteran "shall be certified for appointment, employment, rein- statement or re-employment before non- veterans," and Mr. Kiah, being a qualified veteran, he went to the head of the eligible list. W. D. OWENS. State Employment Commissioner. Baltimore, Aug. 16. No criticism of the State employment commissioner was intended. -THE EDITOR, Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Nothing New At Cheltenham
full_text: Nothing New At Cheltenham The new board of managers at Cheltenham School for Boys has made its first report to Governor Lane. This report echoes the recommendations of nearly every board and special commission in the past ten years that has studied the chronically unsatisfac- tory situation at Maryland's lone reforma- tory school for colored boys. The new board, like the old ones, urges that Cheltenham be rebuilt at a site closer to Baltimore. Plans regarding Cheltenham have com- pleted a full circle since 1943. That was the year that the General Assembly, on the advice of the Maryland Commission on Juvenile Delinquency, voted to build a new institution for normal delinquent Negro boys nearer to Baltimore city and to utilize the old school at Cheltenham for mentally defective Negro boys. Money for the new school was set aside in Governor O'Conor's postwar construction fund. Governor Lane scrapped the plans for a new Cheltenham last year and shifted the money earmarked for its construction into the general funds of the State, That left Cheltenham in the advanced state of de- terioration that Governor Lane found so deplorable when he made a surprise visit to the institution last June. Then, in Octo- ber, the State Board of Public Works ap- proved an "emergency" expenditure of $128,- 300 to patch up the old school. The action was taken after Governor Lane read a report • showing that there was some improvement in the operation of Cheltenham since Cal. vin L. Kiah had taken charge. Mr. Kiah, whose work during six months at Cheltenham had been considered proof that the old school could still be rehabilitat. ed, was abruptly dismissed last month. Chel. tenham at this point has neither a superin- tendent nor the means to train properly the boys in its custody. The new all-Negro board of managers is. impressed by the hope- lessness of attempting to plan for the future on the basis of the present site and facilities at Cheltenham and urges a return to the 1943 plans for a modern school. The decision is largely in the hands of Governor Lane, who should see by now that five years of vacillating plans and "emergency" programs have done nothing to benefit Choltenham. What the State needs is a long-range pro- gram for Cheltenham that will give its managers a permanent basis for their oper- ations.

full_text: IMPROVEMENT UNIT IS ACTIVE State's New Department Has Building Program Role Maryland's new Department of Public Improvements, one of the smallest of the State departments with a prospective staff of six and an annual budget of $38,455, al ready is playing an integral part in the State's large building pro- gram. This program, according to John B. Funk, chief engineer and head of the department, amounts to more than $10,000,000 a year and embraces alt State construction and public works, including the new Federal-aid hospital program. It does not, however, include the State roads program. title: CONDITIONS BETTER AT CHELTENHAM: BOARD OF MANAGERS INSPECTS NEGRO TRAINING SCHOOL
full_text: CONDITIONS BETTER AT CHELTENHAM Board Of Managers Inspects Negro Training School : BY ANNE w, HutchISON Sun Staff Correspondent] Cheltenham, Md., July 17-Mem- bers of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys, who met at the Negro train. ng school here today, found con- litions somewhat improved since last Saturday night but gave assur- inces that the preliminary clean- ing job that had been done was not a whitewash, An inspection showed that not only had the "filthy" conditions complained of in the wash rooms been remedied to a large extent but emergency repairs already were under way in some of the buildings. Board members admitted, how ever, that there still was much to be done both in immediate and longer range repairs. Toilets Back In Working Order They found today that toilets. which prior to their Saturday in- spection reportedly had not been Mushed "for days" at least, were back in working order, Shower systems in the collages were being overhauled, Repairs were projected on, the hand sinks. Floors had been cleaned and were slated for further scrubbings, Many Showers Out Of Order Stair rails had been strengthened But some of the toilet facilities still were not functioning. Many of the showers were out of order pending repairs, and the only (Continued on Page 8, Column 1) CHELTENHAM STATUS BETTER Reported "Filthy" Conditions Found Remedied By ANNE W. HUTCHISON (Continued from Page 28) water for washing purposes in one cottage housing 35 boys was a single tap. Some hand sinks operated only on a makeshift basis; one not at all. Conditions in the wash room of one of the cottages prompted Wal- lace Reidt, newly appointed execu- live secretary to the board of man- agers, to say: "If you think this is bad, you should have seen it Satur- day night." Mr. Reidt. who conducted a tour of the buildings, has been engaged this week in an inspection to de- termine emergency needs at the school, and the cleanup and repairs to date have been under his super- vision. To Have Windows Washed He said screens, now lacking in many windows, were "one of my first orders of business." "And," he said, "I am going to have the windows of Cheitenham washed so that God's good sunlight can get in and these boys can get some of it." Some of the windows aledy had been washed. In the statement issued after its mercing, the board described condi- tions which had been found Satur day night by its president, Thomas B. Sprague, and Mr. Reidt on a sur- prise inspection trip. These men summoned other board members to the institution that night. Besides the unsanitary situation discovered in three cottages a stran was found in the desk at the secur ity cottage. Number Of Boys Whipped "A check of the boys." the state ment said, "disclosed that a num ber of them had been whipped re- cently in violation of the orders of the board that no boy should be whipped unless in the presence of the acting superintendent." The statement noted further that a boy whose tonsils had been re- moved last Thursday at Provident Hospital was found Saturday "to have been placed in the security cottage without proper attention." It said the board was "consider- ing appropriate deciplinary action against the staff members involved" in the circumstances uncovered. Further light on the situation in the security cottage was offered to- day by Mr. Reidt, who described finding what "in my opinion was a booby trap" in one of the unlighted basement rooms and said there was "every indication that the boys had been using these rooms for a kan- garoo court." Supervisor Discharged The "booby trap" consisted of a door balanced at one end on a pipe against the wall and held up at the other on a piece of window sash. One cottage supervisor was dis- charged Sunday as a result of the board's Saturday night inspection. That inspection was described to- day as the beginning of "a series of inspections on the part of the board. Jorking to needed improvements." Before the Saturday visit the board had called on the State's new chief engineer, John B. Funk, and the Department of Budget and Procurement for a thorough study of the institution's physical needs. This morning Dr. H. C. Byrd, president of the University of Maryland, conferred here with Mr. Sprague and other officials on possible improvements in the farm program.

title: BOY, 13, GETS 4 YEARS FOR VANDALISM: YOUTH SENTENCED TO CHELTENHAM FOR DAMAGING SYNAGOGUE
full_text: BOY, 13, GETS 4 YEARS FOR VANDALISM i Youth Sentenced To Cheltenham For Dam- aging Synagogue After he was convicted of being delinquent because he participated in acts of vandalism in the Ohr Knesseth Israel Synagogue last October 27, a 13-year-old boy yesterday was sentenced to four years in the Cheltenham School by Judge Charles E. Moylan, of the Division for Juvenile Causes.. Meanwhile, Adolph Foster, 16- year-old Negro, was held in $2,000 bail pending grand-jury action on a charge of being 'the other youth who took part in the acts of van. dalism, which resulted in damage estimated at $5,000. Held For Court Action Foster was held for court action by Magistrate James H. Ellis, Jr., in Northwestern Police Court, on charges of twice burglarizing the synagogue, the first time on Sep- tember 25 when $45 were stolen from a poor box. : The older youth pleaded guilty to the charges. The younger defendant, also a Negro, lives near the West Frank- lin street synagogue, Judge Moylan was told. Foster gave an address in the 300 block West Biddle street. Locks Had Been Forced Although the second unlawful entry of the synagogue was attrib uted by the younger defendant to Halloween pranks, police contend. ed that a quest for money was the real motive, pointing out that locks on drawers and windows had been broken or forced. According to Lieut. Louis Vinup. and Sergt. Joseph Koenig, the vandals destroyed many sacred reli- gious papers and desecrated the in- terior of the building by spreading scrolls and other religious articles on the floor and then walking on them. Whisky and beer bottles were found strewn over the building and some of the liquid contents had been poured over the religious em- blems, the police testified before Judge Moylan. They also asserted that the van- dals had broken a sacred pointer, had moved and overturned the pul pit, broke and crushed sacred candles, spread religious robes and crowns on the floor and crushed them and poured salt water into pipes. title: CHELTENHAM HEAD NAMED: CALVIN L. KIAH CHOSEN BY BOARD OF MANGERS
full_text: CHELTENHAM HEAD NAMED Calvin L. Kiah Chosen By Board Of Managers Calvin L. Kish, high school principal at Cambridge, Md.. yes terday was appointed superinten- dent of Cheltenham School for Boys by the institution's board of man- agers. The board also: Approved a motion to ask the Legislature to remove the Chel- tenham superintendency from the Merit System, applicable to Mr. Kiah's successor. Approved the adoption of a handbook of rules and regula- tions to govern the staff of the Institution. Mr. Kiah will assume his posi tion around August 15. Three board members-J. Marshall Stewart, Howard C. Hill and Miss Bertha Proctor-will serve as an advisory committee to him for 30 days. Selection Delayed Mr. Kiah, as a veteran, held first place on the Merit System eligi bility list, but his selection was delayed because he lacked previous experience, in correctional institu tion work. After considerable discussion the board agreed to give him the per mitted six-month probationary period and to aid him in every way possible to "make a go" of the position. The group pointed out that the heads of all correctional and penal institutions in Maryland, except three-one of which is Chelten- ham-now are out of the Merit System and may be selected solely by their own boards of managers. Merit System Factor: Walter D. Owens, State employ- ment commissioner, who supplied the list of five names for the posi- tion, had informed the board previ- ously that Mr. Kiah, because of his veteran's status, could not be passed over in favor of any of the other applicants on the list unless the board could prove he was not qualified. The board asserted it often was hindered in obtaining qualified su- perintendents because of the Merit System arrangement, Requirements in' Handbook The handbook will be ready for distribution among the staff mem- bers of the school at the end of his week. At that time Thomas B. Sprague, chairman of the board, and Richard W. Emory, deputy at- torney general, will visit the school and explain what the staff will be required to do. The handbook sets forth that the staff, must have discipline among its members and each member must set an example for the in- mate by being neat in, personal appearance and living habits and not using profane language. The regulations prohibit smok- ing while supervising the boys, prohibit alcoholic beverages or firearms on the school grounds. The staff cannot buy any clothing or personal belongings of a boy or accept any gifts from the boys or their relatives, nor shall a staff member wear any article of State clothing. No staff members shall be absent from duty without written permis- sion signed by the head of his de partment and approved by the superintendent or his assistant, nor punish à boy by force or corporal means unless with special permis- sion and under personal supervi sion of the superintendent or his assistant. No staff member can permit a boy to leave the school grounds with- out permission of the superinten- dent or his assistant, and each mem ber shall be held to a strict account- ing of the boys assigned to him. Mr. Sprague appointed a finance committee to investigate expendi tures of the school. Members are Joseph P. Healy, J. Marshall Stew- art, Hal B. Clagett, Carroll H. Hyn- son and Joseph H. Neal.

title: BOARD LENDS CRAWFORD TO CHELTENHAM: EDUCATION STAFF MEMBER TO SERVE SCHOOL ON PART-TIME BASIS
full_text: BOARD LENDS CRAWFORD TO CHELTENHAM Education Staff Member To Serve School On Part-Time Basis At the request of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys, the State Board of Edu- cation agreed yesterday to lend the services of George Crawford, assist- ant supervisor of curriculum, to the Negro training school, Mr. Crawford, staff member of The State Department of Educa- tion, will serve at Cheltenham on La part-time basis "for an indefinite time, maybe until a superintendent is selected," according to the ap proved request by the institution's board. The request, made through Edward N. Wilson, secretary of the Cheltenham board, said the board wished Mr. Crawford "to work with the cottage masters and the director of education in formulat- ing a program of activities." Dr. Thomas G. Pullen, Jr., who was re-elected State superintendent of schools for another four-year term at yesterday's meeting, ex- plained, when the assignment was questioned, that Mr. Crawford's duties would be to help set up the institution's educational program. Similar Aid Given In Past He said the State Department of Education gave similar assistance to other training schools. Dr. W. E. Henry, president of the State Teachers College at Bowie, recently was elected head of the new all-Negro board of man- agers of Cheltenham, As yet that board has taken no action on appointment of a new superintendent of the training school. A vacancy has existed in the position since February 27 when Calvin L. Kiah was rejected for appointment as permanent superin- tendent after serving a six-month probationary period. In the interim, H. R. Harris, as- sistant superintendent, is serving as acting superintendent. Board Officers Named The State Board of Education opened its session with re-election of Tasker G. Lowndes as president and election of Nicholas Orem as vice president. Mr. Orem was nomi- nated by Wendell D. Allen, vice president since 1942. The board voted to acknowledge an appeal taken by the City Barber School from the State superintend- ent's action in ordering the school closed April I because it had failed to meet requirements for approval under the new licensing law. It was planned that a hearing in the ease would be held at the board's next meeting, probably in June. The school is permitted to continue operations pending the hearing, the first requested under the licensing law. Also in connection with the licensing program for nonpublic schools, the board adopted a resolu- tion exempting from the program day nurseries, child care centers (Continued on Page 23. Column 8) "The and like institutions where no spe cific educational program is given. The resolution states: "Th board will exercise no jurisdiction over day nurseries and similar in- stitutions, and they shall not be permitted to use the word 'school' in their names." : In view of reports by the depart ment's consultant architect and the State engineer that the condition of the president's house at Bowie State Teachers' College was such that expenditure of funds for its Improvement would be a waste, the board initiated action toward con. struction of a new house +' It adopted a suggestion that the Board of Public Works be request. ed to approve the building of a new esttage on the school grounds "with fands to be made available by the Board of Public Works or front the funds to be returned from the public school fund." Retirement Request Approved Reversions from public-school appropriations to the general treas ury of the State at the end of the. current fiscal year, June 30. are expected to be in the neighborhood- of $1,000,000. A specific appropria- tion by the Legislature, however, is understood to be required if some of these monies are to be put to.. other purposes. The board approved the retire- ment request of Miss Bessie C. Stern, director of finance, statistics and educational measurements, eflective August 1. Miss Stern has been with the department since 1921. She will be succeeded by David Zimmerman.

title: CHELTENHAM REPORT GIVEN: SCHOOL GROUP TO STUDY DATA FOR POSSIBLE ACTION
full_text: CHELTENHAM REPORT GIVEN School Group To Study Data For Possible Action Reports by members of the staff of the Cheltenham School for Boys on conditions discovered at the Negro training school a week ago Saturday were referred yesterday to a special three-man committee of the institution's board of man agers, At a meeting of the board held at ofices of the State Department of Public Welfare, the reports, assem- bled by H. R. Harris, acting super- intendent of the school, were turned over to the committee with- out discussion of their contents. The committee, named by Thomas B. Sprague, president of the board, will go over the reports with Richard W. Emory, deputy attorney general, and report back to the board at its regular meet- ing August 5 on possible grounds for disciplinary action. Unsanitary Conditions During a surpise inspection of the institution, Mr. Sprague and Wallace Reidt, executive secretary to the board, reported they had found unsanitary conditions in some of the cottages, evidences that boys in the security unit had been whipped in violation of the orders of the board and lack of proper attention for one of the in- mates who two days before had been operated on at Provident Hos pital, 1 The board had ordered reports from all the staff concerned, Serving on the special committee which will study the reports are Howard C. Hill, Dr. Robert L. Jack son and J. Marshall Stewart, all of Baltimore. The committee also were dele gated to initiate preparation of a printed manual of regulations for guidance of the Cheltenham staff. They will be assisted by Mr. Emory and Mr. Reidt. Rules Will Be Studied Included in this work will be a review of regulations now on the minutes of the board of managers and of rules and regulations pro mulgated by the State Department of Public Welfare. Regulations now in effect at the Maryland Training School for Boys at Loch Raven will be studied, A report on this phase of the committee's work also is scheduled for e next regular heard meeting As had been expected, appoint- ment of a permanent superinten dent for the institution was de ferred until August 5. The board y conferred with Walter D. Owens, State employment commission, on regulations affecting the appoint ment, me 11 also Interviewed George Crawford, of Westminster, the only one of the five candidates on the eligible list who had not appeared before the board. Mr. Crawford had visited the institution last week and gave the board his views of what he would do if they should appoint him. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: POLICE BEAT 2 BOYS ON HEAD, ATKINSON TOLD: JUDGE MOYLAN ALSO COMPLAINS THAT THE YOUTHS, AGE 14, WERE NOT FED
full_text: POLICE BEAT 2 BOYS ON HEAD, ATKINSON TOLD Judge Moylan Also Com- plains That The Youths, Age 14, Were Not Fed | Judge Charles E. Moylan. presid- ing in the Division for Juvenile Causes, yesterday lodged a com- plaint with Hamilton R. Atkinson, police commissioner, that two 14- year-old Negro boys had been beaten with nightsticks by police Thursday night after the youths were arrested in connection with an attempted burglary. full_text: KIAH REJECTED FOR TOP JOB AT CHELTENHAN i Decision Made By Boar After 6-Month Proba- tionary Period nejection of Calvill. nian as permanent superintendent of the Cheltenham School for Boys was announced yesterday by the board of managers of the Negro training school, Mr. Kiah, a veteran and former high school principal at Cambridge had been appointed last September 1 to head the institution, subject to a six-month probationary period. Harris Is Renamed H. R. Harris, assistant superin tendent, who served as acting superintendent from October 8 1945, when Royal A. B. Crump re signed, until Mr. Kiah's appoint ment, again was named acting superintendent. In terminating. Mr. Kiah's ap pointment as of yesterday, Thomas B. Sprague, president of the board of managers, told Mr. Kiah, in a letter, that the board felt he had not shown he possessed the qualifi cations required of a permanent ad ministrative head of the institution. Mr. Sprague said the board's action, based on a committee re port, had been taken unanimously Appeals For New Site Mr. Kiah, in a statement issued late yesterday afternoon, 'appealed for an immediate decision on a new site for the school and for the launching of a building program to bring the institution "out of the Dark Ages." He said that while he had beer given an opportunity to resign fron the Cheltenham post, he had fel such a step would be "unfair to the school, the boys and the genera putne who have sau conndence in me." "I took what the press described as an impossible task and was able to achieve some major reforms," he said, "After six months at Chel- tenham, I have become aware of the underlying causes of the lack of progress there. "Resigned In Frustration" "Under great obstacles and handicaps, I was able to institute improvements by dint of great per- sonal sacrifice. and untiring effort. "I am aware that my predeces- sor, a man of many years of in-1 stitutional experience, resigned in frustration at what seemed to him a hopeless task. However, I am not as pessimistic. "As a native Marylander, with fifteen years' administrative expe- rience in the educational system of our State, I believe in the possi- bilities within our boys and am convinced that with the proper philosophy governing the board, staff and community, Cheltenham can be a leading institution for the redirection and reclamation of the boys in our State who have never had a chance. "Must Not Be Work Farm" "Cheltenham must not be a penal work farm but a training school. "I want personally to thank the community for its wholehearted support, and appeal to the citizens and the Governor of our State to decide on the permanent site for the school, and to launch a building program at once to bring Chelten- ham out of the Dark Ages." In a report on Cheltenham, which supplemented his statement, he fur- ther recommended that the new all-Negro board shortly to be ap- pointed to replace the present mixed board be "composed of con- scientious citizens who are con- cerned not with personal honor but with the all-important task of rehabilitating and developing good citizens out of the human beings who come to Cheltenham." "I cannot overemphasize this great need," he said. List Of Accomplishments During his tenure, is reрогі stated, the following was accom plished: 1. The number of runaways was reduced from a peak of 65 in March of last year to a low of one this month, with six the highest number for any month since Mr. Kiah tool office. 2. Kitchen, dining hall, cottage: and grounds have been improved. 3. An "outstanding" dietitian ha: been employed; food is "wholesome  well balanced, attractively pre- pared." 4. A "public relations" program has greatly increased the number of religious, fraternal and social organizations, community leaders from Baltimore and other parts of the State and others who have visited the school, 5. General staff efficiency 'has been increased. Farm Program Described. Mr. Kiah also described progress in the farm program, the educa- tion program and the "boys' life" program during his term at the school. As yet no plans are under way for finding a new permanent super- intendent. Unless an appointment is made from the current eligible list of four names, no other ap pointment can be made until the list expires June 18. The board of managers of the institution recommended at the time of Mr. Kiah's appointment that the Legislature remove the position from the Merit System, the action to apply to Mr. Kiah's successor. At present the superintendencies of two training schools, Chelten ham and the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls, are under the Merit System. 2 Recommendations Made J. Milton Patterson, director of the State Department of Public Welfare, has recommended to the Legislative Council that the tor posts at Montrose School for Girls and the Maryland Training School for Boys also be brought into the Merit System. ! Since Mr. Crump's resignation more than two years ago, the State employment commissioner has scheduled three examinations for superintendent of Cheltenham, The first, for which the closing date for applications was January 15, 1946, attracted no qualified ap- plicants and no examination, was held. The salary range for the posi- tion at that time was $3,600 to $4,500. Salary Raised August 1, 1946, was the closing date for the second examination, with the salary still $3,600 to $4, 500. The test was given September 19, 1946, and an eligible list of one, Mr. Harris, the acting super- intendent, was certified to the board of managers October 31. No appointment was made. When the third examination was scheduled last year, with a closing date of March 15, the salary had been raised to $4,500 to $5,625. The test was given May 27, and Mr. Kiah appointed three months later.

title: Filth And Brutality At Cheltenham
full_text: Filth And Brutality At Cheltenham The latest report of filth and brutality at the Cheltenham School for Colored Boys follows a pattern that has been going on for twenty years. Cheltenham has long been one of those civic disgraces that everyone talks about and no one does anything about. Now Thomas B. Sprague, the current president of the board, has ordered a thorough investiga. tion of reports that the boys are being whipped and abused. It is to be hoped that he can do something to improve conditions in that medieval rattrap that Maryland so graciously calls a reform school for young Nezroes. Mr. Sprague has been told by the inmates that whipping with a strap and a cat-o-nine- tails is common practice at Cheltenham. Mr. Sprague himself, on a surprise visit to the institution, found a large leather lash in a supervisor's drawer, Mr. Sprague also found that three of the five cottages were "inexcusably filthy." Worst of all, he found & young boy locked and unattended in a wire storage cage who was just recovering from an operation and was still running a fever. Such abuses Mr. Sprague should be able to correct. There is no excuse for brutality or filth. At the same time, the State should not entertain the notion that the expenditure of large sums of money will do much to Improve the situation at Cheltenham. The school is hopelessly outmoded, overcrowded and useless. Nothing except a new school will cure the basic things wrong with Cheltenham. And the funds for a new school were set aside by Governor O'Conor as a part of Maryland's postwar construction pro- gram. Governor Lane wiped out the funds for a new Cheltenham, and it is now up to Governor Lane to see to it that those funds are restored. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: CHELTENHAM BOARD MEETS: INTERVIEWS FOUR CANDIDATES FOR SUPERINTENDENT
full_text: CHELTENHAM BOARD MEETS Interviews Four Candidates For Superintendent The board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys yes- terday interviewed four candidates without selecting a new superin- tendent for the State training school for Negroes. They also asked two State agen- cies for help in determining what can be done to improve the school, which cares for 215 to 235 boys assigned there by juvenile courts. Governor Lane several weeks ago said his attention had been called to conditions which needed immediate correction. A joint conference between the board of managers and State Wel- fare Department officials decided the first step to be taken was ap pointment of a new superintendent. The institution has been admin. istrated for more than eighteen months by H. R. Harris, acting superintendent. Candidates Considered He was one of those considered yesterday by the board of man agers. The others were: Calvin L.. Kiah, a school prin- cipal from Cambridge, Md. Benson C. Tipton, an employé of the National Traninng School for Boys at Washington, Garland J. Gilliam, principal of Bet Alton High School in Charles county, near La Plata, A fifth candidate asked that his name be withdrawn. He was George M. Crawford, principal of Robert Moton High School at Westminster. The board accepted the resigna- tion of James W. Childs, who for less than a year had been director of security and acting assistant superintendent. Decisions Reached After discussing conditions brought to light in the joint con- ference with the Welfare Depart- ment, the managers decided to: 1. Ask the Department of Public Improvements and John B. Funk, chiet engineer, to make a survey of the physical plant at Chelten ham and suggest what new con- struction is needed. 2. Ask Walter Kirkman, director of the State Department of Budget and Procurement, to make a simi- tar survey on the condition of present facilities. The board also decided to hold regular monthly meetings the first Tuesday in each month, beginning August 5. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner.
