title: Three Cheltenham Escapees Captured
full_text: Three Cheltenham Escapees Captured | Sunderland, Md., Sept. 6 (AP)- Three youthful fugitives from the Cheltenham Training School for Negro Boys were recaptured at gunpoint today by a garage owner with whose automobile they were tampering. State Trooper Walter Wahl reported. Thomas Blake, owner of Blake's Garage, was roused by a noise early this morning and encoun- tered the trio busily engaged with the automobile. Keeping the lads in check with a rife, he notified the State trooper and Sheriff Roy C. Howard. Wahl identified the escapees as Elvon Garrison, 15; Cornelius Scott, 14, of Baltimore, and Robert Smallwood, 14, of Easton. He said the boys evidently fled the State correctional institution sometime last night. Bartender Freed On Bail On Slot-Machine Charge Paul Navgrocjis, 27, a bartender in the 300 block of South Paca street, was released yesterday on $500 bail, pending action by the grand jury on charges of permit- ting a slot machine to be operated for profit at that address. He was arrested by Sergt. Thomas Joyce, of the vice squad, yesterday afternoon and pleaded not guilty before Magistrate Pres ton A. Pairo in the Western Police Court. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: 2 ABSOLVED BY ATKINSON Policeman Cleared Of Charge Of Beating Youths After studying full reports on the case, Hamilton R. Atkinson, police commissioner, said yester day there was no foundation for charges by two 14-year-old Negro boys that police beat them with nightsticks as they were being ar rested for attempted burglary last week. In absolving two Northeastern district patrolmen, Commissioner Atkinson said the boys' charges "may have been made to excite sympathy with the view to obtain- ing leniency, particularly because both boys had previous records of burglary and larceny extending since 1944." "There Was No Brutality" Mr. Atkinson asserted he was convinced the policemen were not guilty of mistreating the boys. "I will not stand for any bru- tality-but in this case there was no brutality," he said. The boys made their complaint in Juvenile Court Friday morning. Arrested Thursday night, they com. plained also that they were not given breakfast before being taken to court the next morning. Judge Charles E. Moylan, who presides in the Division for Juve nile Causes, reported the allega tions to Commissioner Atkinson) after interrogating the boys. The judge had convicted the youthful defendants and sentenced them to the Cheltenham School for Boys. As they were leaving the courtroom he noticed marks on the forehead of one and on the side of the head of the other boy. In a statement on the case, Com missioner Atkinson said the boys had broken into a store directly across the street from the North- eastern Police Station. title: CHELTENHAM FUND APPROVED: $128,300 PROVIDED FOR CONSTRUCTION PLAN AT SCHOOL
full_text: CHELTENHAM FUNDAPPROVED $128,300 Provided For Con- struction Plan At School Annapolis, Oct. 7 (AP) The Maryland Board of Public Works today approved an emergency con- struction plan for Cheltenham School for Negro Boys to cost ap- proximately $128,300. The board provided $75,000 from money turned back to the State by the State Planning Commission and authorized the expenditure of other funds available to the, institu- tion: In other action the board:. 1. Adopted a standard of archi- tects' fees for work performed for the State. Rosewood Request Rejected 2. Rejected a request from Rose- wood Training School for Girls for approximately $8,000 to provide a bus and station wagon and $9,132 for annual operation and mainte- nance to accommodate their per- sonnel. 3. 'Gave the go-ahead to com- plete negotiations for the Solomons Island amphibious base in Calvert county for use of the Board of Natural Resources. 4. Approved spending up to $21,000 to eliminate the backlog of work in the Department of Motor Vehicles, The action on Cheltenham was taken after consideration of a re- port, submitted by John B. Funk, State engineer. The report was drawn up after visits of a various State officials to the institution. Improvement Noted The emergency program for the school-which was chosen instead of a long-range relocation plan- was adopted after Governor Lane read a report showing there was some improvement in the operation of the institution since Calvin L. Kiah, 36-year-old war veteran, had taken charge. Mr. Funk's report stated: "It is suggested that, no matter what re- pairs are affected in the institution, and regardless of what new build- ings and accommodations are pro- vided, the value of such improve- ments will be worthless if staff and adminstration officials of the insti- tution do not organize Cheltenham and run it in such manner as to keep it clean and habitable." The report recommended that the present dining hall, kitchen and food-handling facilities be aban- doned in the present' administra- tion building.. New Use Of Structure The structure would be con- verted in part to living space for the staff; the dining room would be made into office space; the laundry retained but adequately lighted and provided with steam exhaust, and fumigation and rodent control would be carried out. Cottages would be generally re- paired, and changes made in the heating system.. A new dining room and kitchen would be constructed of concrete blocks and of a type that could be improved later, when more money was available. The basement of this building would be used also as a pasteurization plant and a food storehouse. Architects' Fees Set The architects' fee standard was set after proposals were submitted by the Maryland Chapter of the American Institute of Architects. Hereafter the pay will range from 6 to 3 per cent contract fees on simpler types of building; 10 to 61½ per cent on specialized work, and 7 to 6 per cent on the type of plans most frequently drawn. On all types of building plans, the State will pay the highest rate for the first unit of any group and 3 per cent on any identical plan. Under the permit and sale of the Solomon's base as proposed by the Navy; the State would be required to maintain certain buildings on the property and could buy others for a price up to $5,000. If the State failed to comply with the Navy's conditions, the Federal Government could take _ over the property. State Labor To Be Used Mr. Funk said state labor would be used to dismantle the property of over 100 bulldings in order that the materials may be used in other state repairs or construction. The Department of Motor Vehi- cles will have a clean-up of its backlog of work by January 1 un- der the $21,000 program approved by the board. W. Lee Elgin, motor vehicles commissioner had asked the board for $51,736 from the emergency fund to take care of office work which needs to be done in the bureau. Aftera study of the bureau, Griffenhagen and Associates rec- ommended new procedures be in- stituted and that the back work be accomplished speedily. Under the plan approved $9,000 would go to the International Busi- ness Machine Company, $6,000 to a "task force" of workers and $6,000 to Griffenhagen, whose officials would supervise the job and pre- pare procedures for the entire de- partment to use in the future. title: CHELTENHAM BARN BURNS; BOY BLAMED: 12-YEAR-OLD INMATE ACCUSED OF STARTING $10,000 BLAZE
full_text: CHELTENHAM BARN BURNS; BOY BLAMED 12-Year-Old Inmate Ac- cused Of Starting $10,000 Blaze Fire, blamed on a 12-year-old inmate, early yesterday razed a storage barn and destroyed farm equipment for a total loss of more than $10,000 at the Cheltenham School for Boys, Prince Georges county. It was the last storage barn left standing at the school, three others having been destroyed by fire in the past eighteen months, accord ing to Thomas B. Sprague, presi dent of the school's board of man agers. Cause Not Determined Cause of the three previous fires has not been determined. Mr. Sprague and Wallace Reidt, executive secretary of the board, who together personally investi gated the blaze, said the boy admitted under questioning by State police that he had set the two-story frame building afire. School officials said the barn. which is about 2 city blocks from the main buildings of the institu- tion, seemed to burst into flame throughout the entire structure. Blaze Spreads Quickly They attributed the quick ad- vance of the blaze to fire spreading to 20 tons of hay, stored in the building. Also destroyed were pieces of field machinery, including harvest- ing equipment and wheat-binders, and about 100 iron beds which were stored in the building. Called immediately to the scene the Upper Marlboro Fire Depart- ment. located 7 miles away, arrived to find the building completely enveloped in flames. Firemen worked to isolate the fire to prevent its spread through dry grass to neighboring boring buildings. Naval Unit Sends Help Fire equipment from the naval air station near Upper Marlboro also responded, Mr. Sprague said. So rapidly was the building con- sumed that it was impossible to form school inmates into fire fight- ing crews. Mr. Sprague said he was told by officials at the school. He said he was first informed of the fire, which then had been burn- ing for about 20 minutes, when he made a telephone call from Balti- more at 11 A.M. on other school business. title: The Cheltenham Mess And A Broken Promise
full_text: The Cheltenham Mess And A Broken Promise Governor Lane will have to demonstrate his fanciest political footwork to sidestep a charge that he ſumbled an opportunity to correct the wretched conditions that exist at the Cheltenham School for Colored Boys. Cheltenham has been a public disgrace for twenty years. Repeated grand jury investiga- tions have found its physical equipment 'deplorable," its morale "bad" and its dis- cipline "nonexistent." Perhaps worst of all, for an institution of correction, it violates all the rules of child training by crowding to- gether both disciplinary cases, which will re- spond to a rehabilitation program, and men- tally defective youngsters, which require permanent custodial care. What had the State planned to do about Cheltenham? The State, under Governor O'Conor's administration, decided to do the only thing that could be done for Chelten- ham-build a new training school for de- linquent (not feeble-minded) Negro boys and keep the present institution as a home for mentally defective Negro boys. The General Assembly in 1943 passed the neces- sary laws to carry the plan into effect. The money was carmarked in Governor O'Conor's Postwar Construction Fund. Indeed, the re- placement of Cheltenham by a new and ade- quate institution was a matter of formal public policy, with a high postwar priority. But what did Governor Lane do about Cheltenham? He shelved the plans for a new school and wiped out the funds set aside for the purpose. He fixed it so that nothing of permanent value could be done to improve Cheltenham, because the present setup is beyond help. And now he has put himself in the position of being an innocent bystander by announcing that he has asked for a "full report" on conditions at Cheltenham and declaring that "there is no justifiable reason why conditions such as have been reported to me should prevail at this State-operated correctional institution." There is every reason, albeit unjustifiable, for the conditions prevailing at Cheltenham, Any additional "reports" will only repeat what was said as far back as 1934, when the executive director of the Child Welfare League of America reported that Chelten- ham was among the worst reform schools in this country. Cheltenham has no facilities for an ade- quate training program. It is so far in the country that it is impossible to get an ade- quate staff to work there. The buildings are designed in a way that defeats their purpose, and delinquent children are still thrown in with feeble-minded ones. Any money spent in trying to patch up the present institution is money wasted. What the State needs is the new training school which it was promised. It is now up to Governor Lane to reinstate the funds previously set aside for that purpose. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: A Thankless Task For Mr. Kiah
full_text: A Thankless Task For Mr. Kiah We certainly wish the very best to Mr. Calvin L. Kiah, who is slated to become the new head of the Cheltenham School for Boys. But any number of good wishes will do Mr. Kiah little good, for he is up against an almost impossible task: making a success of the present Cheltenham. For one thing, Mr. Kiah will, in effect, be asked to run not one but two schools at Cheltenham: one for mentally defective Negro boys, the other for delinquent Negro boys. Surely it is impossible to expect a man to devise and carry out parallel and simul- taneous programs for delinquents and men- tal defectives living together. The delin- quents must be trained to resume produc- tive life outside; the mental cases can only hamper that training. On the other hand, the kind of training needed by mental defec- tives can be very had medicine for the de- linquents. And the influence of one group on the other from their life in common can hardly work to the betterment of either. Mr. Kiah will be faced, too, with the prob- lem of providing occupational training for the delinquents at a school located in the country, far from shops or other trained personnel. He will be asked to refit many of the delinquent boys for urban life with- out a fair chance of teaching them city techniques. Without these, the boys will be further handicapped in readjusting to normal society. Quite clearly, another school in addition to Cheltenham for delinquent boys must be built: the new school that Governor Lane removed from the State budget last spring. Such improvements as can be made at Chel- tenham are all to the good; it isn't yet in a position to perform either of its purposes adequately or hopefully. But all the im provements at Cheltenham will not remove the underlying need for another school for Negro boys. This has been long recognized; the plans for it long held in abeyance. It is, indeed, a little sad that at this point a new superintendent can have no better oppor- tunity for doing his best for either class of Negro boys confined at Cheltenham. Mr. Kiah has a tough job on his hands a job he won't really be able to perform until the Governor and the other members of the Board of Public Works have done theirs. A New Twist In Plans For Cheltenham The announcement that the State Board of Public Works has authorized the expendi ture of $128,300 on capital improvements at the Cheltenham School for Boys will come as a surprise to many people. It was gener- ally understood-in fact, it was the official State opinion-that the only answer to the Cheltenham problem was the construction of a new school at a new site. The State had adopted a program in line with that opinion. True, the specific program was discarded early this year by Governor Lane. The funds which had been earmarked for the new school were withdrawn and no new funds were made available in the bond issue bill approved at the recent session of the Gen- eral Assembly. The amount involved is not very large, but it is too large an amount to invest in any make- shift, too large to invest in what might be called temporary appeasement of critics of the Negro institution. It is not unreasonable to assume from the board's action that the plan to build a new school at a new site is slated for discard. title: CHERRY HILL RECREATION CUT ATTACKED: MOYLAN JOINS IN ASKING BOARD TO RESTORE FUNDS IN NEW BUDGET
full_text: CHERRY HILL RECREATION CUT ATTACKED Moylan Joins In Asking Board To Restore Funds In New Budget  As one of the speakers who yesterday criticized the Board of Estimates for cutting recreation budget requests, Judge Charles E. Moylan said that one boy sent to Cheltenham, possibly because of a lack of recreation facilities, costs the taxpayers $400 more in a year than the cost to parents of sending a boy to the University of Mary- land. Discussing generally the board's reduction of a $96,000 request for an expanded playground program, and particularly the deletion of $5.000 asked for staffing a com- munity recreation center at the Cherry Hill Negro housing devel- opment, Judge Moylan told the board: "One of those youngsters from Cherry Hill will come before the court tomorrow, or the next day, or next week, and he will be sent to Cheltenham. That will cost the tax- payers more in one year than it would cost you to educate your boy or girl at the University of Mary. land." Cost About $1,300 A Year Questioned later, he said he is advised that the annual cost for a boy at Cheltenham-State training school for Negro boys-is between $1,300 and $1,400 a year, Head of the Division of Juvenile Causes, before which such boys are tried. Judge Moylan was before the Board of Estimates yesterday as chairman of the Baltimore Youth Commission. He was preceded by several other speakers, including Otho Pinkett, project manager at the Cherry Hill housing project, who surprised some board members by reporting that the comparatively new, Gov- ernment-built Cherry Hill school already is overcrowded and that next year at least eight classes will be on part time. Questioned By Kelly He cited the overcrowded condi- tion of the school as another reason why the Negro children of the area will need more in the way of rec- reation facilities. "Do you mean to tell us," asked C. Markland Kelly, president of the board, "that that new school is al- ready overcrowded?" "It has been overcrowded since the day it was opened," Mr. Pinkett replied, "How could that have hap- pened?" asked Mr. Kelly. "It appears," he was told, "that proper survey was not made before it was built. It was built only for the housing project but must serve the entire Cherry Hill area." Can't Place The Blame "You mean," Mr. Kelly pressed. "that the Federal Government slipped up in planning the school?" "I'm not in a position to place the blame," replied the project manager. title: Late Starters' Course In Care Of Children
full_text: Late Starters' Course In Care Of Children SUPERFICIALLY, the class being held at 311 St. Paul place resembled many of the evening parent-education classes con- slucted by the department of adult educa. tion. There were six mothers and one father present all neatly dressed persons who lis tened intently to the instructor, a motherly looking woman. The meeting was slow in starting, but since this was the opening of a new and unusual course, it was natural that there should be confusion about where to go, whom to see, what was going to happen. Back of the course is the Baltimore Youth Advisory Board, an alert and intelligent group of students, who last spring proposed that a school for parents of young delinquents be set up in Baltimore as a further measure in the campaign against juvenile delinquency. Like many other proposals, this was "studied by city authorities" for several months. Un- like the majority of such proposals, it has become an actuality. Slow To Warm Up "Learning for Living" was announced as the topic of the first meeting and under this heading, the teacher offered suggestions, with examples, on "fHow to Train Your Child." For about half an hour sho talked in a down. to-carth manner about children in relation to planning, patience, co-operation, punish. ment and humor, frequently asking for comments and questions. But the parents re- mained cold and quiet. "Let's express ourselves," she would say, but her audience was unresponsive. The pe culiar circumstances of their attendance at the course prevented them from being natural and relaxed people, and tongue-tied them, Finally, in answer to the repeated ques- tion-"What makes a happy family?"-one mother meekly asked: "Could it be love?" Of San Francisco Origin With these words, the chill left the barren classroom. The first of a series of eight classes for parents of delinquent children in Balti- more seemed to have a good chance of be- conting more than an empty talk. The teacher. berself a mother of two sons, and the parents were reaching an understanding. Members of the Youth Advisory Board do not take credit for this plan. explaining the BY DIANA GORDON they heard of a similar school in San Fran- cisco and thought the idea worth trans- planting. "Despite the recently announced decrease in juvenile delinquency," says N. Ellsworth Bunce, Jr., president of the board, "we think that there is enough delinquency in the city to call for further measures. We've tried things like reks and sports, and while they've done good, they haven't been enough." The students feel that the course's merit is that it will reach parents of delinquents. Points Out Parents' Mistake "Too often the blame for delinquency has been placed on the children when it properly belongs on the parents." Pat Maguire, of Notre Dame School of Maryland, comments. Charles Dunzee, a student at Douglass Ifigh School, likewise feels that the fault is often with the elders. "One of the biggest mistakes that parents make," he says, "is refusing to admit that a teenage person is no longer a child and can't be restricted to a child's hours and activities." When parents take the course, they will be more careful to see that younger children, if any, don't get into trouble, reason two Girls' Latin School pupils. Gail Phillips, of 3808 Tudor Arms avenue, and Nancy Hanna, of 219 Woodlawn road. While the board members display natural youthful elation at the adoption of their pro- posal, they regret that attendance at the course has not been made compulsory. Be- cause enrollment is voluntary, they predict that many parents to whom the course would be most beneficial will not attend. Judge Moylan Explains The reason for not making attendance com. pulsory is explained by Judge Charles E. Moylan, of the Circuit Court of Baltimore, division for juvenile causes. After he had received the board's resolution for the estab; lishment of such a school last spring, he studied the setup of the San Francisco school and similar projects elsewhere with Thomas A. Van Sant, director of the department of adult education, and Mrs. Sarah W. Davis, superintendent of the department's parent- education classes. They agreed, Judge Moylan says, that the school would fill a vital need here if: "First, it would he conducted by trained and experienced teachers in the field of parent education and not made, as the San Francisco school is, a springboard for lectures by law enforcement officers and other public officials. We favored a sounder and more conservative approach to the need. "Second, that the benefits of the course might well depend upon making it available to those parents whose children have had problems and have had brushes with the law who can be prevailed upon to seek the help the course will offer. In this fashion, no parent will regard his attendance as involving any stigma." Discovered Uujust Condition The function of the court, the judge con- tinues, has been to furnish the enrollment, which has been done by him and the court's staff of probation officers: Bernard M. Mc- Dermott, Mrs. Emma Quinlin and Mrs. John 2. Sanford. The course will run for eight weeks, with classes Tuesday nights for white parents and Wednesday nights for colored parents. As evidence of the need for such a school, Judge Moylan tells how he talked with the supervisor of every training school in the State during the summer, asking why certain boys and girls were being held for periods longer than two years. "At Cheltenham School for Boys," he re- marks. "the acting director, H. L. Harris, re- ported that 25 boys had earned their return to the community and would have been paroled if there had been adequate and proper homes to which to return them. This condition seemed grossly unfair to the boys, whose rehabilitation had been vouched for if a proper placement back in the community could be effected. Talked With Many Parents "I sent for the 25 parents or sets of parents and talked with them about their children, their failure to visit them, to write to them, and to improve conditions in their homes." Judge Moylan says that every parent in this group said he or she would start imme- diately to overcome the faults pointed out to them. They all enrolled in the parent-educa- tion classes.

full_text: REPORT IS ASKED ON CHELTENHAM Lane Calls For Complete Data; Pledges Action Announcing that he has asked for a "full report" on conditions at Cheltenham School, Governor Lane yesterday asserted "there is no jus- tifiable reason why conditions such as have been reported to me should prevail at this State-operated cor- rectional institution." title: 'CRIME SCHOOL' HEAD, FATHER OF 25, JAILED: MAN, 76, GETS TWO YEARS FOR BUYING STOLEN FOOD FROM CHILDREN
full_text: 'CRIME SCHOOL' HEAD, FATHER OF. 25, JAILED Man, 76, Gets Two Years For Buying Stolen Food From Children Described by Judge Charles E Moylan as the operator of "a schoo of crime for 11 and 12-year-old boys," Fred Sheppard, 76-year-old father of 25 children, yesterday was sentenced to two years in the House of Correction for contribut ing to the delinquency of five Ne gro boys. Three other adults were fined and two of them received three months' suspended sentences on the same charges. All the defendants are Negroes. Sheppard, who said he had eight children by his first wife and seven- teen by a second wife, was charged with buying hams, turkeys, chick- ens, sugar and other articles of food stolen by the five boys in Lexington Market recently. He also was alleged to have bought a stolen radio and bicycle.  Youngest Child is 14 The elderly defendant told the Court that his youngest child is 14 years old and that his second wife died about five years ago. On ques- tioning by the court, he revealed that none of the children was the result of a multiple birth. Before sentencing the man, Judge Moylan said the evidence showed that the boys made "pop's place" their "hangout" and that they made several trips a day to the market to steal articles.  "Clear As A Bell" The judge declared the case might have presented a problem to the court, but that he believed that Sheppard's mind was "as clear as a bell" and that the accused knew what he was doing. The five juveniles were given hearings at the same time and all of them were found to be delin- quent. One of the boys already is an inmate of the Cheltenham School for Boys and was brought from the school for the hearing. Four of the boys had been in the hands of juvenile authorities previ- ously, according to court officials. Judge Moylan asked for additional reports on three of the boys before disposing of their cases.  Boy Put On Probation He placed on probation the fifth boy, who, although it was testified he had been present when articles were taken and when they were sold, was not said to have partic- ipated in the thefts or to have re- ceived any money from stolen goods. It was said in court that the thefts occurred during November and December. In most of the cases, it was said, the boys simply (Continued on Page 20, Column 2) grabbed up articles of food and rar away with them. The youngsters were small and could easily lose themselves ir the crowded market, it was added Fled With Turkey Most of the thefts occurred ir the preholiday period. In one case a small boy was said to have carrieċ away a giant turkey, weighing 22 pounds and almost half as large as the boy himself. Sheppard alleged ly bought the turkey. It was also testified that Shep- pard kept money-as much as $73 on at least one occasion for the boys. Testimony disclosed that at least some of the money had been stolen. Besides the theſts in the market, the boys were alleged to have taken foodstuffs and other articles from parked automobiles.  "Expensive Ham" Sheppard's daughter-in-law, identified as Agnes Sheppard, was one of the three others convicted of contributing to the boys' delin- quency. She was fined $50 and given a three-months' suspended sentence. The same penalty was imposed on Percy McCloud, a neighbor of the Sheppards. McCloud's mother, who allegedly bought a stolen ham, was fined $25 with Judge Moylan commenting: "That will be the most expensive ham you ever bought."  Convicted 50 Years Ago Two other adults who appeared on the same charges were acquitted by Judge Moylan. Questioned concerning his past record, Sheppard said he thought he might have been convicted of assault about 50 years ago. The case was in the Division for Juvenile Causes. Sheppard lives in the 200 block of North Pearl street. 4

title: LANE ATTACKED FOR FOOD CUTS: ASSEMBLY TOLD OF NEEDS IN STATE YOUTH INSTITUTIONS
full_text: LANE ATTACKED FOR FOOD CUTS ssembly Told Of Needs In State Youth Institutions By ALBERT W. QUINN [Annapolis Bureau of The Sun] Annapolis, Feb. 27-Criticism of Governor Lane's cuts in requests for food allowances at two of the State's training schools featured to- day's joint session of House and Senate committees for the study of the 1948-1949 biennial budget. E. L. Fletcher, superintendent of the Maryland Training School for Boys, also complained about the de- Metion of a proposed new job-su- pervisor of recreation at $1,900 for the fiscal year of 1948 and $1,995 for 1949. Mr. Fletcher said his school is the only one of its kind in the State without a recreation supervisor. and that such an officer is needed for the proper rehabilitation of the boys committed to the institution. Present recreation, he said, is "makeshift," and supervised by various teachers and others on their own time. Says Food Is Important Item But food, he said, is the most im- portant of all items for growing hoys. He said his request would have provided for 75 cents a day for the feeding of the inmates of the school-a figure established some time ago by a dietician of the State Health Department. A later figure, he said, is 81 cents. The Governor cut the item, Mr. Fletch- er stated, to a figure that would provide only 56 cents a day per boy. The total request for food in the Maryland Training School budget was for $92,500 for each year of the biennium. The budget as submitted to the Legislature calls for $55,700 for each year. For the present biennium, the appropriations were $49,275 for 1946 and $37.625 for 1947. Weekly Food Needs Given Mr. Fletcher said the needs for the weekly feeding of each boy in such an institution as his are: Seven quarts of milk, four pounds of potatoes, one half pound of beans, two pounds of citrus fruit, three pounds of yellow vegetables, four pounds of all other vegetables, two and one half pounds of meat, poultry or fish, seven eggs, five pounds of break cake, one and one half pounds of fats and oils, three fourths of a pound of sugar-at a total cost today of about $5.70. His figures of fiscal needs to pro- vide the food, he said, take into consideration the production on the school's farm. Addressing the joint committee, Mr. Fletcher said: "In making that cut, you have absolutely not studied the food needs of boys." "If you have been cut," replied Senator Robert B. Kimble (R., Al- legany), "you were cut by the Gov- ernor, not by the committee." 21-Cents-A-Day Allowance The entire requests for the school were $430,463 for 1948 and $429,774 for 1949. The Governor reduced these to $357,263 and $358,579. Mrs. Muriel Johnson, superin- tendent of the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls, said when she took over the institution a year ago the food allowance was 21 cents a day, the girls had one dress apiece and the school was nothing more than a custodial institution. - She requested $25,000 for each year of the next biennium for food, - which the Governor cut to $21,900 for each year. The appropriations for the current biennium were $10,898 for 1946 and $10,000 for 1947. Mrs. Johnson, however, said she had to go to the Board of Public -Works on several occasions for ad- ditional funds in all branches of maintenance. For 1947, to date, she said, the school has received $38,- 000 additional. Satisfied With Funds The entire requests for the school were $159,377 for 1948 and $127,003 for 1949. They were cut to $118,571 and $119,311, Mrs. Edith P. Gardner, superin- tendent of the Montrose School for Girls, said the food allowance of $15,000 a year about 46 cents a day for each girl-is "quite satis- factory. She pointed out, however, that the school has a "very good farm." Her appropriations for 1948 and 1949 are $153,578 and $151,163, compared with requests of $168,- 297 and $163.702. II. R. Harris, superintendent of Cheltenham School for Boys, said the entire allowance in the Gov- ernor's budget of $53,965 for 1948 and $56,066 for 1949 is necessary if the school is to be more than a place of detention. He had re- quested $61,585 for 1948 and $62,166 for 1949. Dwight Ferguson, director of the Bureau of Child Welfare, said the Governor's supplemental budg- et will propose $190,000 for a State-wide program of juvenile de- tention. Fletcher, superintendent of the Maryland Training School for Boys, also complained about the de- Metion of a proposed new job-su- pervisor of recreation at $1,900 for the fiscal year of 1948 and $1,995 for 1949. Mr. Fletcher said his school is the only one of its kind in the State without a recreation supervisor. and that such an officer is needed for the proper rehabilitation of the boys committed to the institution. Present recreation, he said, is "makeshift," and supervised by various teachers and others on their own time. Says Food Is Important Item But food, he said, is the most im- portant of all items for growing hoys. He said his request would have provided for 75 cents a day for the feeding of the inmates of the school-a figure established some time ago by a dietician of the State Health Department. A later figure, he said, is 81 cents. The Governor cut the item, Mr. Fletch- er stated, to a figure that would provide only 56 cents a day per boy. The total request for food in the Maryland Training School budget was for $92,500 for each year of the biennium. The budget as submitted to the Legislature calls for $55,700 for each year. For the present biennium, the appropriations were $49,275 for 1946 and $37.625 for 1947. Weekly Food Needs Given Mr. Fletcher said the needs for the weekly feeding of each boy in such an institution as his are: Seven quarts of milk, four pounds of potatoes, one half pound of beans, two pounds of citrus fruit, three pounds of yellow vegetables, four pounds of all other vegetables, two and one half pounds of meat, poultry or fish, seven eggs, five pounds of break cake, one and one half pounds of fats and oils, three fourths of a pound of sugar-at a total cost today of about $5.70. His figures of fiscal needs to pro- vide the food, he said, take into consideration the production on the school's farm. Addressing the joint committee, Mr. Fletcher said: "In making that cut, you have absolutely not studied the food needs of boys." "If you have been cut," replied Senator Robert B. Kimble (R., Al- legany), "you were cut by the Gov- ernor, not by the committee." 21-Cents-A-Day Allowance The entire requests for the school were $430,463 for 1948 and $429,774 for 1949. The Governor reduced these to $357,263 and $358,579. Mrs. Muriel Johnson, superin- tendent of the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls, said when she took over the institution a year ago the food allowance was 21 cents a day, the girls had one dress apiece and the school was nothing more than a custodial institution. - She requested $25,000 for each year of the next biennium for food, - which the Governor cut to $21,900 for each year. The appropriations for the current biennium were $10,898 for 1946 and $10,000 for 1947. Mrs. Johnson, however, said she had to go to the Board of Public -Works on several occasions for ad- ditional funds in all branches of maintenance. For 1947, to date, she said, the school has received $38,- 000 additional. Satisfied With Funds The entire requests for the school were $159,377 for 1948 and $127,003 for 1949. They were cut to $118,571 and $119,311, Mrs. Edith P. Gardner, superin- tendent of the Montrose School for Girls, said the food allowance of $15,000 a year about 46 cents a day for each girl-is "quite satis- factory. She pointed out, however, that the school has a "very good farm." Her appropriations for 1948 and 1949 are $153,578 and $151,163, compared with requests of $168,- 297 and $163.702. II. R. Harris, superintendent of Cheltenham School for Boys, said the entire allowance in the Gov- ernor's budget of $53,965 for 1948 and $56,066 for 1949 is necessary if the school is to be more than a place of detention. He had re- quested $61,585 for 1948 and $62,166 for 1949. Dwight Ferguson, director of the Bureau of Child Welfare, said the Governor's supplemental budg- et will propose $190,000 for a State-wide program of juvenile de- tention. Because of a lack of such facilities, he said, holding of juve- nile delinquents in jail, pending commitment to an institution, is a "common practice" 1 1 1 . .

title: ATHLETIC GEAR GIVEN SCHOOL: JUDGE MOYLAN URGES MORE GIFTS TO CHELTENHAM
full_text: ATHLETIC GEAR GIVEN SCHOOL Judge Moylan Urges More Gifts To Cheltenham In furtherance of the expanding recreational program at the Chel- tenham School for Boys, Judge Charles E. Moylan, of the division for. Juvenile Causes of the Supreme Bench of Baltimore, yesterday pre- sented $500 worth of athletic equip- ment and games to the institution. Money for the gifts came from the North Baltimore Optimist Club and the Downtown Lions Club, Judge Moylan said, after he had told the organizations the story of an unused gymnasium building and needs of Cheltenham. Pool Table Also Given Yesterday's presentations in- cluded outdoor basketballs, volley balls, sets of badminton, table ten- nis, indoor and outdoor quoits, boards for indoor games, checkers, dominoes, and other games for the younger boys in the cottages of the school. Judge Moylan announced also that a hand-carved pool table, with all equipment, had been contrib- uted by Martin R. Crook, of Balti- more. The table will be delivered and put into use as soon as it can be dis- mantled, moved and reassembled, the jurist said. Other Gifts Requested "There are some members of the board of governors who can afford to give the school other tables," Judge Moylan said. "I can- not understand how boards of gov- ernors can meet month after month and fail to realize that the job of rehabilitation of these boys can- not be accomplished just on the taxpayers money, but only if each man personally tries to help." H. R. Harris, acting superintend- ent, told the assembled staff and student body how instruments for a 26-piece band, provided more than a year ago by the Morres Schugar Lodge in Baltimore, had been allowed to gather dust in an attic until Judge Moylan insisted they be put to use. Bugle Corps Outfitted Mr. Harris told also how Judge Moylan had been instrumental in inspiring the Downtown Lions Club of Baltimore to provide instruments for a Drum and Bugle Corps for Cheltenham. The 271 boys, ranging in age from 12 to 18, who are now in the school, were slicked up for the occasion and gave an enthusiastic demonstration for Judge Moylan and members of his staff. Choruses from the cottage dormi- tories sang, and other youngsters put on an impressive tumbling act under the direction of Robert Anderson, supervisor of recreation. Boy Scouts Raise Flag The small Boy Scout troop, under Scoutmaster L. C. Chisholm, conducted flag-raising ceremonies with military precision, to the ac- companiment of the drum and bugle corps. Judge Moylan, during the cere- monies inside the gymnasium, urged more and larger Boy Scout troops to take advantage of the 1,200 acres which make up the grounds of Cheltenham. The judge also made a presenta- tion of his personal trophy, awarded to the winning basketball team of the season, to the quintet from Carver cottage. Boys To See Orioles Mr. Harris told the boys that he hoped to arrange for twelve of their number to see the Baltimore Orioles play baseball once a month during the season-with Mr. Harris guaranteeing transportation, and Doll Derr, loaned by the commis- sioner of motor vehicles, organiz- ing the program. The privilege of being taken to Baltimore to see the games would be earned, Mr. Harris said. Judge Moylan, commenting on the record of runaways from Chelt- enham which reached a high of 700 for one year, said: "It seems to me that here we have a chance to establish a new track record. I'm told there is only one home-made high-jump on the track. We can't forget that some of the world's greatest athletes have been Negroes. I'm interested now in building up a real track team." No Escapes In April Since the institution of the rec- reational program, with equipment provided, the run-away figures have dropped from 117 last September to a low of 13 in January, Judge Moylan said. There was a climb to 17 in March, but up until last night there had been no escape in April, the jurist said. "I can't send these boys here or other boys and girls elsewhere and just forget them," Judge Moylan said. "Under the law they are still the wards of the court and I stand in loco parentis to them. Action Vs. Talk "I am told that no county judge in the State has ever visited Chel- tenham, and that in the face of many condemnations from outside ( mothing has been done. "I don't see why we should wait for long-range planning when there( are certain definite steps which can be taken while interminable meet- ings are being held." Judge Moylan, members of his staff, and other visitors were guests at dinner in the home of Mr. and Mrs. Harris. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Cheltenham To Get $36,000 For Repairs
full_text: Cheltenham To Get $36,000 For Repairs Approximately $36,000 has been made available by the Board, of Public Works to the Cheltenham School for Boys for new refrigera- tion and general repairs at the Negro training school, it was an- nounced yesterday. Sprague, president of the institution's board of man- agers, said the improvements would greatly simplify administra. tion of the school and that efforts were being made to get the work underway as soon as possible. title: COUNCIL ASKED FOR PENALTIES UPON UNIONS: LEGISLATIVE GROUP HEARS DEBATE ON MUNICIPAL EMPLOYE ORGANIZING
full_text: COUNCIL ASKED FOR PENALTIES UPON UNIONS Legislative Group Hears Debate On Municipal Employe Organizing Severe penalties, "comparable to those imposed for treason," were recommended yesterday before the Legislative Council for persons who organize in an association "for the purpose for preventing or ob- structing any of the normal opera- tions of government until their demands are met." The proposal was among several put forward against unionization of public employés by Willis R. Jones, attorney, who, with Walter IH. Buck, represented two taxpay. ers in a recent suit against Balti- more city and a teamsters' union local with which the city had en- tered into a contract. Contract With Chauffeurs A contract between the city and the Municipal Chauffeurs, Helpers and Garage Employés Local Union No. 825 now is in effect. This and earlier contracts, as well as ne- gotiations leading up to the con. tracts, were the basis of much of yesterday's discussion. Mr. Jones also proposed: • That legislation be enacted to prevent any State, county or municipal agency of government from deducting union dues from the earnings of public employés and from paying such dues to any union or association of employés. That public employés of any such agency of government be forbidden to belong to any union or association of employés which advocates resort to strikes or work stoppages or threats of strikes or work stoppages against any such agency of government to force compliance with their demands. That any public employé who engages or participates in any strike or work stoppage to pre- vent the orderly functioning of any agency of government shall forfeit this right to be employed by any agency of government within this State and be subject to prosecution for disloyal and subversive activities against the government. Mr. Jones was interrupted in the carly part of his remarks to the Council when he asserted that the government of Baltimore city was "to a very large extent under the control of one man," identified the man as Harry Cohen, president of the Teamsters Joint Council No. 62. and said: "If Mr. Cohen wants to fix municipal wages, he should run for public office." Senator Kimble Objects Senator Robert B. Kimble oh. jected to the interjection of "per- sonalities." Commenting upon the city's posi- tion, Simon E. Sobeloff, city solici- (Continued on Page 13, Column 3] ANTI-UNION PENALTY ASKED Legislative Unit Hears Debate On Municipal Organizing (Continued from Page 30) tor, said the city was faced with an "intensely practical problem" of "dealing with a union in order to get public work done." He questioned the Council's in- quiry into what he described as a "purely local matter being handled with satisfaction all along the line," and said there was no need to enact legislation, no public call for it and no practical necessity. Sobeloff's Assertion Mr. Cohen had pointed out that there was "no collective bargaining agreement with any other political subdivision in Maryland," and said that "Baltimore is big enough to hold its own potato, no matter. how hot." Mr. Sobeloff asserted that it was better to negotiate with a union be- fore a strike was called than after. Grievances are settled by collective bargaining in the last analysis, he said. Taking up Mr. Jones's recom- mendations to prohibit unioniza- tion of government workers, he said adoption of the provision pre- venting organization for the pur- pose of obstructing government operations until demands are met. punishable by "severe penalties," would make the legislators the "laughing stock of people ex- perienced in legislation." "Voluntary" Checkoff System He defended the city's "volun- tary" checkoff system-upheld by the Court of Appeals-as an ex- tension of a privilege accorded such organizations as the Red Cross, and the Classified Munici- pal Employés Association. The union pays the city the estimated cost of collecting, he said. With regard to outlawing strikes among government employés, he pointed out that the city's contract with the Teamsters Union con- tained a no-strike clause and said the proper way to proceed was to establish sensible and decent labor relations. The union, he said, had been willing, because of the decent atti- tude shown, to renounce strikes and agree to have the city engineer the final arbiter for all grievances. One Of "Mildest" Agreements Mr. Cohen described the agree- ment between the union and city as "one of the mildest that could possibly be written or accepted by a labor organization" and said the union "recognized its lawful and dutiful obligations to Baltimore city." During the union's regime, since June, 1941, he said, there has been one "unauthorized work stoppage" of twenty minutes in one district of the city and a strike of less than a day's duration when Mayor Jackson delayed in signing a contract. Wages of the union workers have risen from 40 cents an hour in 1941 to approximately 80 cents at pres- ent-still about 10 cents below the level in industry, he told the Council. "Humiliating Language" Mr. Buck, appearing against or- ganization of government workers, cited a resolution of the Board of Estimates in February, 1944, in which it was stated the "annual crisis and strike" had been avoided by "making slight concessions in wages and working conditions" to the union. This he characterized as the "most humiliating language any public officials ever permitted to come out in this State before." Also testifying before the coun- cil were Jack C. Flaherty, execu- tive secretary of the Baltimore In- dustrial Union Council, and Car- lyle Barton, attorney, representing the teamsters local union. Dr. Preston Presents Memorandum OnSchool A memorandum of legislation: which will be needed when the Cheltenham School for Boys is turned over to the State Board of Mental Hygiene for an institution for defective delinquent Negro boys was presented yesterday to the Legislative Council by Dr. George H. Preston, commissioner of men- tal hygiene. The training school, in Prince Georges county, is occupied at pres- ent by delinquent Negro youths for whom construction of a new school has been authorized and is under consideration. Dr. Preston's memorandum calls for establishment of a board of managers, consisting of six to nine members, which would operate the institution under the supervision of the Board of Mental Hygiene. All-Negro Staff Urged Its members would be appointed by the Governor for staggered terms of six years, and "should include persons familiar with the problems of feeblemindedness, de- linquency, education, medicine and institutional administration." The superintendent would be a physician experienced in the care and treatment of defective delin- quents, and all staff appointments subject to the merit system. Dr. Preston said his board recommended that the board of managers and all employés of the institution be selected from com- petent Negroes. Per-Patient Charges Annual maintenance costs were estimated at $180,000. In addition, extensive changes in buildings to make dormitories more secure, pro- vide a large fenced recreation yard and an adequate dining room and kitchen would cost "at least $200,- 000," it was estimated. The memorandum further states that each county should pay the State comptroller $180 a year for each patient in the institution com- mitted from that county, and the same for Baltimore city.

title: 2 PLANS OFFERED FOR DELINQUENTS: KIRKMAN URGES NEW PLANTS OR ANNEXES FOR DIFFICULT CASES
full_text: 2 PLANS OFFERED •FOR DELINQUENTS Kirkman Urges New Plants Or Annexes For Difficult Cases Two alternative methods for han- dling especially difficult juvenile offenders in Maryland were placed before the Legislative Council yes- terday by Walter N. Kirkman, State budget director. 7 The proposals, for the housing of an estimated 100 white and 100 Negro serious youthful delin- quents, were: That a new and separate insti- tution be erected. That especially designed secu- rity units be incorporated in the present boys' training - school plants. Discussion of expansion of train- ing-school facilities followed sev- eral hours of discussion before the council of the State liquor laws, particularly as they apply to Balti- more city. Hearings Continued Hearings on both subjects will be continued October 3 at the next. regular session of the council. In presenting his proposal, Mr. Kirkman said a new and separate juvenile institution would be "very expensive." However, he said, the cost of a new security unit at the Maryland Training School for Boys at Loch (Continued on Page 10, Column 1) 2 DELINQUENCY PLANS OFFERED Kirkman Proposes New Plant Or Addition To Present Ones [Continued from Page 30] Raven, separate and distinct from the regular units but utilizing the present property and water, power and other services, would not ex- ceed $250,000. He said the security unit for Negro boys could be included in the $1,500,000 training school soon to be built to replace Cheltenham, the present Negro school. The State administration, he continued, was eager that construc- tion of this new school, to accom- modate between 100 and 350 boys, be begun soon. Purchase of a site near Catonsville was under con- sideration, he said, Cheltenham, after construction of the new school, would be placed under the Board of Mental Hygiene for use for the care of feeble-minded de. linquent Negro boys. In discussing the financial aspects of these proposed im- provements in the training-school system, Mr. Kirkman said he had consulted State officials concerned, including J. Milton Patterson, di- rector of public welfare; Harold E. Donnell, superintendent of prisons, and James A. Pratt, superintendent of the Maryland Training School for Boys. Separate Handling These men, he said, were agreed that construction of security units at the two boys' institutions would best fill the gap in the training- school setup. He said he had been advised that use of buildings at Montrose School for Girls and the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls could be altered so that the limit- ed number of particularly difficult girls committed to those institu- tions could be handled separately. The consensus among officials with whom he talked, he said, was that care of delinquents under 16 was definitely a training-school problem. Final action on any new con- struction rests with the Department of Public Welfare and the Board of blic Works.

title: Wilkerson To Speak At Communist Meeting
full_text: Wilkerson To Speak At Communist Meeting In a Lincoln-Douglass anniver sary meeting. sponsored by the Communist party of Maryland and the District of Columbia, Monday night, Doxey Wilkerson, former Howard University professor, will be among the speakers. The meet ing will be held in Baltimore Garden, formerly the 104th Medi- cal Regiment Armory. Mr. Wilkerson is now a member of the national committee of the Communist party, U.S.A.; is a vice president of the International La- bor Defense, and instructor in the Carver School and the Jefferson School. Other speakers will be William Z. Foster, chairman of the Com- munist party, U.S.A., and Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, also of the national Communist committee. Muriel Rahn, star of "Carmen Jones," and Richard Dyer-Bennett, ballad singer, will entertain. Cheltenham School Post Applications Accepted Because an insufficient number of qualified persons applied for the position of superintendent of the Cheltenham School for Boys, the State Employment Commissioner again is taking application for the post. Notice of the vacancy has been sent to other states in the hope that qualified applicants may be found, it was learned. The State Department of Em- ployment and Registration also cur- rently is receiving applications for the assistant superintendency of the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls. Penn Alumni To Hear University President Dr. George McClelland, presi- dent of the University of Pennsyl- vania, will address the Penn alumni dinner to be held at 7.30 P.M. Tues- day at the Hotel Stafford. Movies of last fall's football games will be shown by George Munger, Pennsylvania football coach. Leonard Dill, secretary of the general alumni association, also will be present. The committee in charge of the arrangements includes Harry Wood, Joseph Archer, Harry Allers and Paul Morris. 1 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: Council Adopts School Resolution The City Council last night | adopted a resolution calling upon the Board of School Commissioners to make a survey of the O'Donnell Heights and Graceland Park areas to determine whether there is need for a new school building in that area. The O'Donnell Heights section has been brought to public atten- tion recently by a strike of pupils of School No. 288 over the lack of public transportation from their homes. Other Action Refused While adopting the public-school resolution, the Council refused to take immediate action on another resolution calling upon the Mary- land Board of Public Works "to reconsider its action in acquiring the property near Westport in the Sixth legislative district for use as a correctional institution." .. The Board of Public Works has designated an area in the district as a new site for the Cheltenham school for boys-a Negro institu- tion. .. • The resolution, introduced by the three members from the Sixth dis- trict, Councilmen Freburger and Kotmair and Councilwoman Bailey, said "so much property has been taken for industrial uses that very little land is left for develop. ment for residential purposes" and that "it is desirable that land now zoned as residential property should be retained for this pur- pose." : Urges Immediate Attention Councilman Freburger said the resolution "requires our immediate attention." - Citing an ordinance that forbids Federal infringement on city land without city approval, he said "there should be a similar ordi- nance against State infringement." The resolution was sent to the Committee on Buildings and Build- ing Regulations. The Board of Pub- lic Works was invited to attend a hearing at 2 P.M. Monday. title: GRAND JURY SUGGESTS NEW LIQUOR LAWS: PROPOSES MANDATORY TO BAR LICENSE TO ANY WITH CRIMINAL RECORD
full_text: RAND JURY SUGGESTS NEW LIQUOR LAWS roposes Mandatory Rule To Bar License To Any With Criminal Record Legislation making it mandatory for the Board of Liquor License Commissioners of Baltimore to re- fuse a liquor license to any person having a criminal record was pro- posed yesterday by the Baltimore grand jury in a term-end report submitted to Judge Herman M. Moser in Criminal Court. The jurors also advocated that liquor-dispensing establishments be required to close at midnight on week days and that such places remain closed all day on Sundays. Acute Shortage Of Help Reporting on inspections of the State's penal and medical institu- tions, the grand jury noted that in practically every one of the institu- tions there is an acute shortage of adequate help, occasioned largely by inadequate wage scales. The main jury report, submitted by Alfred E. B. Jones, foreman, pro- posed that court reporters be as- signed to police courts to record testimony as given in the first in- stance, shortly after the happening of the event under inquiry. The jurors noted that frequently it has been found that some wit- nesses' memories have proved to be at fault or recollections became hazy when the case reached the criminal courts. Having stenogra- phers in the police stations would dend to discourage attempts to in- fluence witnesses who are called upon to give the same testimony in the higher court, the jury con- tended. Grand Jury's Report The grand jury made the follow- ing reports on the institutions: Maryland State Reformatory for Males-This institution should be used as an example of what can and should be done in a prison. The place is a credit to the State of Maryland and the city of Balti- more. Springfield State Hospital-Un- lerstaffed, but the buildings are clean and well managed. Pay for doctors, nurses, ward helpers and others is very inadequate. A total (Continued on Page 5, Column 3) of $800,000 has been allocated for postwar building. Baltimore City Hospitals-New- er buildings in excellent condition, but the old infirmary building is poorly lighted and dismal, Many buildings were closed during the war because of lack of help. Jurors suggested they be reopened. "Remarkably Clean" Crownsville State Hospital- Buildings in excellent condition and "remarkably" clean and well managed. This institution is under- staffed and unable to offer proper treatment for the criminally insane. Jurors suggested survey be made to determine whether special facili- ties for the criminally insane can be provided. Spring Grove State Hospital- Buildings in good condition, but in- stitution overcrowded and under- staffed. One building is over 100 years old and is dark and dreary. House of Correction-An over- crowded condition tends to create unhealthy and dangerous situation. Present buildings are inadequate. Maryland State Reformatory for Women-Interior and exterior of building immaculate and orderly. High praise given to Mrs. Helen de Corse MacArthur, head of the institution. Jurors suggested study of venereal disease problem, enlargement of the institution and more work to keep idle hands busy. Institution equipped to handle 145 prisoners. Now houses 189 prison- ers More State-Used Goods - a Maryland Penitentiary Clear and orderly. More gainful occupa tions for inmates proposed. Sug igest manufacture of more State used goods and installation of run ning-water facilities in each cell City Jail-Building old and out moded. No recommendations made in view of city committee's studies of a proposed new jail. Proposed that committee make special provi sions for persons held as State's witnesses and those adjudged insane. Montrose/School for Girls-Gives impression of an exclusive private school. Buildings "cool, clean and inviting." Girls healthy, well-uni formed and well-trained. House of Good Shepherd for White and Colored-Conditions ex cellent. Buildings clean and food good. Training School Overcrowded Maryland Training School for Boys-Overcrowded, but cottages in excellent condition. Additional furnishings and some sanitary im provements needed. St. Mary's Industrial School- Sanitary and well equipped. Maryland Training School for Girls-Understaffed, but buildings in good physical condition. Some need paint. Cheltenham School for Colored Boys-Jurors recently filed lengthy report on conditions. New build- ings are to be erected near Balti- more.

title: PUBLIC WORKS JOBS LISTED: $16,404,474 WORTH READY TO START DAY WAR ENDS
full_text: PUBLIC WORKS JOBS LISTED $16,404,474 Worth Ready To : "Start Day War Ends Maryland and Baltimore city are ready to go ahead with 98 public works projects, at an estimated cost of $16,404,474, on the day after materials are released at the close of the war with Japan, Henry P Irr, chairman of the Maryland Commission on Postwar Recon struction and Development, an nounced yesterday. Bids could be advertised today on these projects, for which plans and specifications have been drawn and approved, he said. They are part of a total of 655 projects over the State in varying stages of con- sideration and preparation. involv- ing an estimated expenditure of $212,171,356, the chairman said. Of the plans completed and ready to be put into operation im- mediately, twenty involve capital state improvements, estimated at $1,298,354; seventeen are under the State Roads Commission, estimat- ed at $7,894,730; 39 are sponsored by the counties and municipalities at an estimated cost of $1:687,090; 21 are Baltimore city projects esti- mated at $4,589,200, and one is a sanitary district plan estimated at $25,000.. 196 Being Completed Mr. Irr said that an additional 196 plans, involving the spending of $81,795,686, are now in process of completion. Proposals have been made, but no plans drawn, for 361 more projects to cost an estimated $113,971,299, he said. Among the capital state improve- ments which can be started as soon "as the green light is given" are an $844,400 addition to Spring Grove State Hospital; a $377,194 improve- ment at the Cheltenham School for Boys; a $20,000 piggery for the Maryland State Penal Farm; a $119,200 addition to the Mary- land Training School for Boys at Loch Raven; additions to Morgan State College valued at $428,000, and a $258,000 addition to the Maryland Tuberculosis Sanatorium at Sabillasville. A 1-year-old baby boy who was found in a partially filled trash barrel in an alley behind the 200 block of South Conkling street by Corporal Frank Fox, 19, was identi- fied as Albert Lee Wise, son of a soldier. The baby's mother, who disappeared with the child last week end, and could not be located when the baby was found in the container, was charged with desert- ing the infant. The "trash-barrel baby's" picture, that of a plump, blond little boy, has inspired doz- ens of families to seek his adoption. The estate of Edwin G. Baetjer, Baltimore attorney and world traveler, filed in Orphans Court at Towson, listed total assets at $3,031,402.86.  Need A Ladder? David Hobbs, 31, was locked out of his room at 32 North Chester street by his landlady, so he went in quest of a ladder with which to get up to the second floor. Not a man to avoid the easiest way out of a predicament, Hobbs pulled a fire alarm from the corner of Fair- mount avenue and Chester street. When firemen arrived and found no fire, Battalion Chief W. S. Leid- lich saw Hobbs standing near the box. Questioned, Hobbs told the fire chief of being locked out and said that he wanted to "borrow" a ladder from the Fire Department so he could get up to the second floor of the house. The chief informed Hobbs that no ladders were available, but that alternate quarters at the city's ex- pense could be furnished. Hobbs was taken to the station house and lodged in a cell. The next day he was charged with sounding a false fire alarm. While out walking, Corporal Frank Fox found this blond baby boy in a trash barrel in an alley behind the 200 block of South Conkling street. He' wrapped his coat around the baby and took it home. Sports At A Glance Racing returned to Pimlico again last week when the Maryland Jockey Club opened a 35-day meet. J. R. Steinman's Pink Devil crossed the finish line to win the first by a neck with Zito and Mechaniador second and third, respectively. Service Edition THE MORNING EVENING SUN Baltimorc, Md., Sunday, October 28, 1945 Navy personnel, from seamen first class, to four-stripers, and their families invaded the town last week as thousands arrived for the Navy Day celebration. Downtown Balti- more took on the traditional Sat- urday night air of hustle and bustle as the lads in the bell-bottomed trousers rushed for eating places, night spots, movie houses, roller skating rinks, bowling alleys, bur- lesque houses, photograph gal- leries, penny arcades, and all of the so-called playhouses that attract the gob out for an evening of amusement.  Most of the men were from the eleven vessels that arrived on Wed- nesday and Thursday for the big day, yesterday. The huge carrier Randolph, the heavy cruiser Can,- berra, three destroyers, one de- stroyer escort, four submarines and one APD boat described as a light- attack transport steamed into har- bor and cleared the decks for the public inspection on Friday, yes- terday and today. The carrier Randolph's pinup girl, Joan Lilley, a Baltimore girl, was formally introduced to the ship's crew last night at a ban- quet. The week end was a busy one for her, as she kept a date with 3,000 doting gobs at the Navy League's Saturday night's formal ship's party and at a special pinup dance.  Navy Day itself started off with a public award ceremony at which Commander Slade Cutter, former football star at the Naval Academy and now commanding officer of the submarine Requin, preserited med- als and letters of commendation to thirteen crew members from the submarines Requin and Flying Fish. A colorful parade from the 5th Regiment Armory to Memorial Plaza via Howard and Baltimore streets followed the award cere- mony. SUNDAY News From Home Five Hurt In Charles Street Fire The 70-lane Charles Bowling Cen ter located in the 1700 block North Charles street, the fourth largest in the nation, was completely burned out Tuesday morning in a six-alarm fire which caused damage estimated at $400,000 and injured five persons. A series of heat ex- plosions accompanied the three hour blaze, described as one of the trickier and more dangerous the Fire Department has had to fight for some time because of vacuums and backdrafts caused by the open expanse of the alleys on both floors.  Times Theater Emptied Soon after the first alarm sound- ed, police directed the removal of more than 300 patrons of the Times MISS JOAN LILLEY Had a date with 3,000 gobs Theater, next door to the bowling alleys. The bowling center is a two-story brick structure, the south section of which formerly had been used as a streetcar barn, Although the fire was confined mainly to the second-floor alleys in the south section, extensive damage was caused throughout the remainder of the structure by smoke and water. It is believed that it will be several weeks before the unburned alleys are ready for play. The bowling center was one of the more elaborate in the East.. It occupied more than half of the 1700 block of North Charles street, along with several small shops, which sustained severe smoke and water damage.  Former Policeman Arrested Paul M. Maenhoudt, 43, a former policeman, was charged at the Central Police Station with 56 cases of burglary and attempt to burglarize, involving more than $27,000 cash and merchandise. Two of the burglaries with which he was charged had been attributed to a self-styled "phantom burglar." Setting an all-time record for the number of charges made against any one defendant at any one time, Maenhoudt is being held in $53,000 bail which actually re- quires the posting of more than $100,000 in property.  Many of the burglaries charged against Maenhoudt were on posts he was working as a patrolman and records at the Central Station show that in some he himself took the reports on them, interviewing the victims and ostensibly aiding in the investigations. title: Petition Changes Cheltenham Plans
full_text: Petition Changes Cheltenham Plans Governor O'Conor last night announced that Ingleside, the Baker estate in Catonsville, will not be the site of the new Chelten- ham School for Boys. The Governor said that condem- nation proceedings on the property have been abandoned on the advice of W. Wallace Lanahan, chairman of the State Board of Welfare, and of F. Reid Isaacs, president of the board of governors of Cheltenham. Protests against the site began early this month shortly after the Governor had anounced that it had been chosen for the school. A petition signed by nearly 2,000 residents of the First district of Baltimore county was recently forwarded to the Governor by the Board of County Commissioners. The Governor did not announce immediate plans for choosing an alternate site. Annapolis Negro Found Guilty Of Manslaughter : Annapolis, Oct. 24 (P)-Tried on an indictment charging murder, Robert Forrester, 35, Negro, was adjudged guilty of manslaughter by Associate Judge James Clark, sitting without a jury, in Anne Arundel County Circuit Court today. The accused was charged with causing the death of Charles W. Willford, 40, another Negro, which occurred under unusual circum- stances. The two engaged in a quarrel that led to a fist fight in Annapolis last September 6, during which Forrester dealt Willford a heavy blow that fractured the latter's jaw. Lockjaw developed and Willford died twelve' days afterward. Judge Clark has reserved sentence in the case. title: The Case Against The Site For Cheltenham Is Weak
full_text: The Case Against The Site For Cheltenham Is Weak Consider the case being presented by the opponents of the State's plan for a new Cheltenham School for Negro Boys to be located on a 122-acre tract between the Hollins Ferry and Old Annapolis roads. The tract in question is zoned for residential use. The opponents of the plan claim that the school. proposal violates the zoning law in that that law prohibits the erection of either a correctional or penal institution in a residential area. The claim does not hold much water. While the proposed school site is zoned for residential use, its present use and character are definitely not residential. The tract is nothing more than waste land; its extreme eastern section is neavily scarred with abandoned ore pits. Just outside its perimeter there are to be found an auto- mobile graveyard, a lumber yard and several taverns.. And somewhat to the north and east of the property is the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad's right of way to the Curtis Bay-Fairfield industrial area. Such condi- tions do not invite residential development. The charge that the school is a correctional or penal institution is also open to some question. The school is not under the State Department of Correction as are the Peni- tentiary, the House of Correction and the re- formatories at Breathedsville and Jessups. It is under the State Department of Welfare. And the plans call for a school with support- ing cottages and appropriate planting and not for something resembling the City Jail. But even if the school were held to be a correctional or penal institution, there is nothing to prevent the City Council from changing the zoning designation to permit the use of the proposed location. Such a step could hardly be classed as spot zoning, and we fail to see how the surrounding areas could be affected adversely. In this connection it is worth noting that when those who had the responsibility of selecting a site were making their studies some fault was found with the location - eventually decided on because it did not have better surroundings. But it was decided that these conditions could be overcome and the immediate neighborhood given a lift by a well-planted and commodious school ground. The opponents of the State's plan for Cheltenham have not made out a case. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Enoch Pratt Library Case
full_text: Enoch Pratt Library Case TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: May I challenge the closing paragraphs of your edi- torial,. "A New Challenge for Negroes," in which, in, regard to the recent court decision admitting qualified colored applicants to the Enoch Pratt Free Library training course, you warn: "Now that the court ruling removes this racial distinction they must not expect special consideration because they are Negrocs must win their way on indi- vidual merit." . Anyone familiar with the strenuous efforts which colored citizens have had to make to gain admission to the University of Maryland, which is supported by their taxes, to be ac- cepted for employment on the police force, to be employed as social workers, knows that there is no danger of any colored citizen re- ceiving special consideration because of his race. To an observer with a simple sense of justice it is clear that the colored people have never expected special consideration, only equal treatment. ... As a practical excursion into the realities of the color question, have your writers inter- view just a few of the hundreds of skilled, business, and professional job applicants among young colored citizens and listen to their experiences. A colored citizen always has to be more skilled, better qualified, able to - double the qualifications_of a white citizen, to get a job, and then in the majority of cases he is barred simply because of his race.... JUANITA MITCHELL, Director, Citizens Committee for Justice. Baltimore, Oct. 22. Palestine And The Future TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: Allow me to thank you for the very interesting and de- tailed reports by Faul W. Ward, of your Wash- ington Bureau, about Palestine. To me, and thousands of other readers, Palestine and its future is a very dear and interesting topic. We could almost prophesy what's in store for our world by the attitude that this same world will assume toward the yearning of the rem- nants of European Jewry to settle in Pales- tine. If the leading nations will do justice to the Jews and return Palestine to them-then they will also be just in their international relations with one another and a finer and nobler world will emerge from the chaos of World War II. If, on the other hand, the great nations or their leaders will break sacred pledges and.condemn a tortured people to per- petual dispersion-then they lack a sense of justice and will eventually abuse one another, and that will lead to conflict which will put a finish to human civilization. Thus the degree in which Jews are enabled to fulfill their aspirations in Palestine serves, to me, as a barometer of the conscience of mankind. And, whereas we could do little to change the course of human destiny, we should at least be well-informed. And such information. Paul W. Ward's correspondence provides in a splendid manner. Baltimore, Oct. 21. DR. JACK SHOBIN. Cheltenham School For Boys TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: I have been instructed by the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys to express to you our appreciation of the editorial of October 15. We feel that you presented the facts in the situation most accurately, clearly and persuasively. You may be interested to know that the contractor has promised us the use of our security unit within three weeks. While it is a makeshift use of very poor present equip- ment, we think that it will provide custody of chronic runaways and protect the community. The only satisfactory answer to the prob- lem is the building of the new school, which will furnish these facilities at their best. Then we can really give the boys a good training program while providing the custody that will safeguard any community. President, Board of Managers, Chelten- ham School for Boys. | Cheltenham, Md., Oct. 22. F. REID ISAAC,
