title: REFORM SCHOOL BACKERS LOSE: CHELTENHAM SITE SUPPORTERS DENIED NEW COUNCIL HEARING
full_text: REFORM SCHOOL BACKERS LOSE Cheltenham Site Supporters Denied New Council Hearing Refusing to accept disclaimers of racial prejudice in the opposition to the locating of Cheltenham School for Boys near Westport in South Baltimore, supporters of the site yesterday requested and were denied a new hearing on a Council resolution condemning the State's selection of the South Baltimore tract. The resolution, introduced by Councilmen Freburger and Kot- mair, and Councilwoman Bailey, all of the Sixth district, was adopted following a noisy hearing of about 500 South Baltimore residents who indulged in frequent applause, foot- stamping, whistles and occasional catcalls, depending on the nature of the testimony. Galleries Warned It was not until near the end of the hearing that Councilman Bon- nett, chairman of the Committee on Buildings and Building Regula- tions, warned by galleries that their behavior was not in keeping with procedures in Council hearings. Selection of the site, which has been purchased outright by the State, was defended by Thomas B. Sprague, president of the Chelten- ham Board of Managers, and J. Milton Patterson State director of public welfare. Joseph P. Healy, chairman of the Governor's Commission to Study Problems Affecting the Negroes, urged the Council committee to treat the question "the same as though you were considering the proposed location of a white insti- tution." "If now or later you are going to permit training schools in the city, don't discriminate against this Negro institution," he said. There were protests from the sponsors of the resolution and from some of the objecting citizens. Shouting In Galleries "If you were here," Councilmar Freburger told Mr. Healy, "repre senting a brick yard, you'd have no better chance of getting this land rezoned than Cheltenham has." Whistles, shouts and stamps of approval broke out in the galleries. The Rev. Louis F. Hoffman, pas tor of the Lakeland Presbyterian Church, supporting the resolution against the location of the school, said he hated "to see the race ques- tion injected into the discussion." There was more applause. But Leo V. Miller, a member of the National Association for the Ad- vancement of Colored People and a member of the board of managers lat Crownsville State College, charged that "90 per cent of the protestants to this location are thinking in terms of color." There were whistles of derision. "The institution," he said, "could never harm the beauty of the neigh- borhood" because the "State is careful of its architecture." 'Precedent Will Be Set' Del Rasin, Negro, a member of the Baltimore Community Youth Centers, told the committee that "every site in Maryland with 100 acres or more-large enough for the proposed new Cheltenham-is in a predominantly white area. We will have the same opposition on all sites. The precedent will be set here today." Mrs. Lillie May Jackson, presi- dent of the Baltimore Branch of the National Association for Colored People, urged the committee to "give us a chance to present the other side.". "I have a son in Germany and another in Saipan because Hitler couldn't be reasoned with," she said. "Let us be reasonable here." "It's going to be hard," said the Rev. James Gray, who said he rep- resented 165 Negro Baptist min- sters, "to locate the school near Baltimore because sometimes it's lifficult even to get a house to live n unless you white folks agree to [it." The proponents of the site said they were not prepared for a com- plete argument on the question yes- terday. Mr. Rasin asked that a later date to be set for the hearing. He said he disagreed with a statement by. Councilman Kotmair that Cher- ry Hill Negro residents were op- posed to locating the training school in their vicinity. Freburger Speaks "I think they should be allowed to speak for themselves," he said, Councilman Freburger told the committee the people of the area are against changing any residen- tial zones in the Sixth district "re- gardless of the purpose." "I am not satisfied," he said, "for any State or Federal body or any other to come into the corporate limits of Baltimore city and set up an institution that violates the code of Baltimore city in respect to zon- ing. If this thing is allowed, we may as well throw the Commission on City-Plan, with all its plans, out the window." "We'll fight to the last ditch against it," said Councilman Kot- mair. Emmett Batson, a resident of the district, said the location of the institution on the 115 acres of open land "eliminates the possibility of $1,500,000 in taxable basis." James K. Cullen, United States. Commissioner, told the committee: "I can't imagine anyone interested in the development of Baltimore city taking any position other than that Cheltenham should be located in a rural district." Meade At Hearing Hugh H. Meade, an Assistant Attorney General, representing the Board of Public Works and the Cheltenham board, said he was "not here to oppose the resolution." "That is entirely a matter for the Council and then it will be up to the Board of Public Works to decide what action it will take." Mr. Sprague said the site was selected because it "is close to the city of Baltimore and has all trans- portation and utility facilities." He said an act of the Legislature requires the moving of the insti- tution for delinquent boys from its present location in Prince Georges county. The existing institution will be used for mentally deficient boys. Councilman Kotmair asked Mr. Sprague. how many boys escaped from. Cheltenham in the past two years. "Some place it as high as 700," he replied. "There has been only one escape so far this year. There were 31 in December." Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: O'CONOR BACKS $12,550,000 POSTWAR FUND: TO ASK LEGISLATURE TO APPROVE MEANS FOR CONSTRUCTION PROGRAM
full_text: O'CONOR BACKS $12,550,000 POSTWAR FUND To Ask Legislature To Approve Means For Con- struction Program & By LOUIS J. O'DONNELL [Annapolis Bureau of The Sun] Annapolis, March 15-Governor O'Conor announced that he will ask the Legislature to approve a $12.550,000 construction program to be undertaken immediately as materials are available and to be financed partly by surplus treasury funds and a bond issue. Legislation he will propose to the General Assembly would pool $6,000,000 from treasury surplus, $1.725.000 in unspent appropria- tions for postwar construction and a bond issue of $4,825,000. Funds Not Dedicated The construction-loan bond issue will differ from those of the past in that the funds they would raise would not be dedicated specifically to any project. Bonds would be issued only after the $7,725,000 on hand had been expended on what- ever projects are first undertaken. Included as a project to be financed from the $12,550,000 pool is the proposed recreational area somewhere on the shores of the Chesapeake Bay. Pooling the funds on hand and the bond issue, without dedicating the proceeds of the bonds to any specific project, the Governor ex- plained, will enable the State to proceed with the building program in the order in which materials be- come available and as other circum- stances dictate, and at the same time save carrying charges by rea- son of not having to issue bonds immediately. Listed On Program Listed in the immediate postwar construction program, for which the Governor will ask this session of the Legislature to authorize and make fiscal provisions, are: Three chronic disease hos- pitals. A new Cheltenham School for Boys. Additions to mental hospitals. Construction for Training Schools for Boys. Construction at penal institu- tions. The University of Maryland building program. Teachers' colleges. Additions to tuberculosis sana- toria. The bay-front recreational area. Morgan State College construc- tion. A new State Police headquar- ters. A new State Department of Health building. A new Commissioner of Motor Vehicles headquarters. The Governor said that any pro- posal for a State office building in Baltimore, to be purchased or con- structed, would be handled sepaа- rately and not as a part of the State's construction program. He said there was a possibility that the Legislature would receive at this session recommendations relative to a centrally located office building in Baltimore. title: Are The Plans For Cheltenham Being Snarled Up Again?
full_text: Are The Plans For Cheltenham Being Snarled Up Again? 1 Are the plans to build a new Cheltenham School for juvenile delinquent Negroes about to be snarled up again? On paper, the present plan is to build a wholly new school on a site near Baltimore and to turn over the present plant in Prince Georges county to the Board of Mental Hygiene for the care of mentally defective Negro youths. The idea is that a new insti- -tution close to Baltimore could be more readily visited by parents, would be in a better position to make arrangements for employment and training with urban indus- tries, and would have less difficulty in at- tracting a staff. But this plan is encountering obstacles. The State has been unable so far to acquire a suitable site; and the Board of Mental Hy- giene appears distinctly cool to the proposal that it take over the old institution. Here and there the question is being heard: Why not rebuild on the present site? Certain arguments for rebuilding on the present site are plausible. The site com- prises 1,200 acres, and agricultural labor fits well into the training program of any such institution. The property could easily be linked with Baltimore or Washington by bus. And, being farther from the city, such a location discourages in some degree the inevitable runaway boys. Thus, there are plausible arguments on both sides-for building the new institution near Baltimore or for building it on the present site. This is the kind of decision on which most people will accept the judgment of those State officials who will be held re- sponsible for the successful operation of the school. But one point ought to be made abundantly clear. This is the absolute neces- sity for a new Cheltenham School-not a patching up of the old one. The present one is not only old and inadequate: it is jinxed. Those who have followed the incessant troubles of Cheltenham have long since been convinced that the only way of getting rid of them is to start afresh. If Cheltenham moves to a new location there will be a new school. If the decision is to keep the institu- Lion where it is now, then it must also be a new school. title: The Present Cheltenham Cannot Be A Good School
full_text: The Present Cheltenham Cannot Be A Good School The blast by the Prince George's county grand jury against the Cheltenham School for Boys follows a pattern which has become almost a norm for criticism of the State- owned and State-operated training school for delinquent Negro boys. The physical equip- ment at the institution is "deplorable," morale is "bad" and discipline is "nonex- istent." Such are the charges that have been made and, continue to be made. Where does the fault lie for the inexcus- able situation at Cheltenham? Does it lie on the doorstep of the board of managers? Con- sider these facts: Some of the key buildings at the school are 50 and more years old, and they have long since served out their useful- - ness. There has been no real effort to mod- - ernize them. The school has an authorized staff of 75 persons, but there are 32 vacan- cies. Much hard work has been done to fill open positions, but the manpower shortage - occasioned by the war and the location of the - school have made recruitment almost im- possible. : The problem of maintaining discipline and morale has become particularly difficult in the last year or so. This results from the fact that the school has had to accept an increas- ing number of youths in the upper-age brackets. Many of these youths cannot be controlled in an open institution, and the place lacks a security division. It is these older youths who, in the main, have figured in the escapes and "depredations". com- plained of by the grand jury. On top of all this is the fact that the school has some inmates who should very properly be in an institution for the feeble-minded. The board of managers in the last year or two has taken steps to improve conditions at the school and, in so far as the younger in- males are concerned, there are indications that there have been improvements. But the only hope for a real solution in the Chelten- ham problem lies in the plans now being formulated for a wholly new institution. The responsibility for these plans does not rest primarily with the board of managers but with the heads of the State government. It is the latter who set the policies and see that the money is forthcoming. Until we have a new Cheltenham, not on the drafting board but in reality, there will be solid grounds for criticism of the school in Prince George's county. title: 2 New Buildings For Cheltenham
full_text: 2 New Buildings : For Cheltenham Annapolis, Nov. 25 (AP)-Con- struction of a dining hall and culi- nary unit to cost $150,000 at Cheltenham School for Boys was authorized today by the State ad- ministration measure. as an emergency Governor O'Conor said the new buildings would help relieve "an acute situation at the institution." To avoid delay in the construction, the Board of Public Works used its emergency powers and directed the payment from the emergency fund created by the last General As- sembly, Governor O'Conor said. Urged By Lanahan F. Reid Isaac, president of the Cheltenham board of managers, and W. Wallace Lanahan, chairman of the State Department of Public Welfare, requested the Board of Public Works to authorize the im- mediate construction. The new allocation from the Femergency fund is in addition to the $45,000 made available last month for construction of staff quarters at the school. Approved By Dr. Preston The Governor, anticipating the transfer of the present location of Cheltenham School to the Board of Mental Hygiene for the Housing of Negro Defectives, said Dr. George H. Preston, commissioner of mental hygiene, approved the plans for the new dining hall and culinary unit. The building will fit in with the program for defectives, the mental hygiene board said. 'Junior Class' Of 1904 At City Meet Again Thirty of the original 80 mem- bers of the "junior class" of 1904 of City College, some of them from New York and Philadelphia, last night held their 16th annual re- union at the Southern Hotel. The junior class was so called because its members were gradu- ates of the four-year curriculum, then an innovation, while other graduates in the same year had at- tended five years of school. Among those present were Wal- ter N. Kirkman, State Budget Di- rector; Walter Huff, class president, now an official of the Railway Ex- press Agency in Philadelphia; Guy H. Reese, class treasurer, a Balti- more broker, and Thomas M. Bart- lett, former football star, now at- torney for the Maryland Casualty Company. Virginia Convict Caught Frank Clark Fields, who a month ago escaped from the Fairfax (Va.) jail where he was confined after being convicted of robbery, has been apprehended at Poolesville. Montgomery county, by agents of the Federal Bureau of Investiga- tion, it was announced yesterday.

title: O'CONOR AIMS FOR LOW TAXES: PREPARING TO DRAW BUDGET FOR NEXT TWO YEARS
full_text: O'CONOR AIMS FOR LOW TAXES Preparing To Draw Budget For Next Two Years By LOUIS J. O'DONNELL By constitutional mandate, Gov- ernor O'Conor and his fiscal ad- visers are about to embark on a job that requires them to estimate what the per capita income of Marylanders will be, not in 1945, but in 1946 and 1947-the prepara- tion of the State budget for that biennium. Under the budget provisions of the Constitution, the Governor not only must prepare a schedule of appropriations for all State gov- ernmental operations for those two years, but he is required to base these allotments of funds on his estimate of what the revenues for that period will be. Cost Increases Foreseen Only one thing is certain at this point in the preparation of the biennial appropriations bill for sub- mission to the General Assembly within 20 days of its convening in Annapolis next January 3 - that there will be substantial increases in the cost of operating all of the (Continued on Page 8, Column 3) O'CONOR AIMS FOR LOW TAXES Preparing To Draw Budget For Next Two Years By LOUIS J. O'DONNELL (Continued from Page 24) State's institutions and heavy de- mands for replacement of equip- ment unobtainable during the war period. Governor O'Conor, he disclosed yesterday, is approaching the task before him with certain definite objectives in mind, which include: Avoidance of any new State taxes. Holding the State tax rate on real and personal property at its present figure of 12 cents per $100, if possible. Steering clear of any attempt to resolve uncertainties in the long-range cost of governmental operation by generous recourse to contingent funds. In short, the Governor plans to construct a budget as nearly as pos- sible along normal lines, he said yesterday, and recall the Legisla. ture in special session if and when conditions warrant or require a re- vision of appropriations or reve- nues as the post-war economic pic- ture develops. Salary Speeds Legislators In this connection, the Governor pointed out that the State's legis lators now are on an annual salary and can be called into special ses- sion at comparatively little extra expense, and furthermore that the new method of remuneration ap- parently encourages them to handle the business before them in ex traordinary session with dispatch. He cited the four-day special ses- sion on soldier-voting legislation last March. The Governor's disclosure that he wishes to avoid any new taxes, land hold the real estate levy at its present figure, indicates that Mary- landers may expect to resume pay- ing the full two per cent. Income tax in the next budgetary period, which starts July 1, 1945. Reduced By Proclamation Under special powers granted it by the Legislature, the Board of Public Works by proclamation re- duced income-tax payments in 1943 and 1944-on 1942 and 1943 in- come-although the levy remains at a two per cent. rate on the stat- ute books. In 1943 income-tax payers were permitted to deduct one third of the amount due after computation of the levy by the Board of Public Works proclamation. In 1944 they had to pay only one half of the amount due under a two per cent. levy. Maryland began the current fiscal year-1945-on July 1 with a surplus of $8,961,000, of which $2,000,000 was earmarked as "work- ing capital." Governor Must Decide A substantial amount of the sur- plus will be needed, in the way of a transfer into the debt fund, to keep the real and personal property tax at the current figure of 12 cents per $100. In order to hold it at 12 cents this year it was necessary to add $450,000 from surplus to revenues from taxes on real estate and personal property to fulfill interest and retirement obligations on the bonded indebtedness. As a matter of policy the Gov- ernor will have to decide whether to make further heavy drafts on surplus funds for general govern- mental operation in order to con tinue kick-backs to income-tax payers, or begin to exact the full two per cent. tax. With payments halved by the Board of Public Works proclama- tion, the levy on 1943 incomes pro- duced $6,400,000, or roughly 25 per cent. of the total "general fund" revenues of $24,000,000 appro- priated for general governmental operations. "General Fund" Category It is estimated by Walter N. Kirk- man, the director of budget and procurement, that the yield of the levy on 1944 incomes-at the half- rate figure-would produce about the same amount. It is in the "general fund" reve- nue category that the budgeteers are up against it in preparing esti- mates as a base for the 1946-1947 budget. These revenues-the in- come tax, taxes on beer and liquor, racing and levies on the gross re- ceipts of utilities are reflected by the per capita income. The tax on real and personal property is dedicated totally to the debt retirement fund and can be estimated with a relative degree of accuracy, dependent solely on per- centage of the levy collected. Dedicated Funds The dedicated funds, such as revenues from the gasoline tax, motor-vehicle licenses, etc., while they affect the departments and agencies which draw their support from them and govern the amount to be expended on the State's high- ways, are not reflected in the budg- et for general governmental pur- poses. Mr. Kirkman, whose job it is to prepare revenue estimates for sub- mission to the Governor, said yesterday that he is "not ready to predict" what the State can expect in 1946 and 1947. He does know, however, that the individual budget requests of the State's departments and institu- tions will make urgent demands for replacement of equipment that has worn out during the war and for replacement of automotive equip- ment. More Funds For Welfare It seems likely, according to Mr. Kirkman, that the Department of Public Welfare will have to be granted additional funds on a con- tingent basis to be prepared against increasing unemployment after the war. Mr. Kirkman also believes the general cost of operating institu- tions will be greater than during the present budgetary period be cause of increases in the cost of textiles, food and fuel. 000 more than was allowed in the current budget. Two Correctional Institutions There are no more mental pa- tients than there were a year ago, the institutions have the buildings and beds, but are at present short on help. It is the considered opin- ion of those in charge of the insti- tutions that a three shift schedule must be instituted for personnel to enable them to recruit attend- ants and "get the kind of people they want." The State is committed to build-and, of course, maintain- two new correctional institutions a new Cheltenham and an insti- tution for white boys of a type between a reformatory and prison. Teachers To Seek Raise. Due to an increase in their case- load of bed-fast tuberculosis pa- tients, the tuberculosis sanatoria are expected to ask an increase of $250,000 in their appropriation. Except for minor adjustments, the salary schedule of State em- ployes in general, now fixed by the State salary standards law, is ex- pected to undergo no change. The State's schoolteachers, how- ever, are expected to seek increases in their salary schedules. They are not included in the salary stand- ards law. As an example of increases due in the cost of operating institu- tions, Mr. Kirkman cited the proh- lem of the State's five mental in- stitutions. full_text: Can't They Have Knives And Forks At Least? ▼ Back in the Dark Ages a grand jury took the trip down to Cheltenham School for Colored Boys, near Upper Marlboro, and, after deploring condi- tions in general, expressed surprise that cach boy ate all his food out of a single dish and had nothing to eat it with except a large tin spoon. In subsequent years, numerous other grand.juries, not to mention State com- missions and independent investigators, have gone down to inspect Cheltenham and, after deploring conditions in gen- eral, have expressed surprise that the boys ate all their food out of a single dish and had nothing to eat it with ex- cept a large tin spoon. Last week Mayor McKeldin, accom- panied by several other gentlemen equally distinguished for their interest in social betterment, took the trip down to Cheltenham. Like their numerous predecessors, the members of this party all expressed surprise that the boys had no eating utensils except tablespoons. Cheltenham, as we all know, is one of the skeletons in the State's institu- tional cupboard. When the war is over there is going to be a new Cheltenham. The General Assembly has said so. The Board of Public Works, after some back- ing and filling, has said so. Everybody now agrees that there is going to be a new Cheltenham-a fine, sanitary, well- designed, wholesome institution for the rehabilitation of delinquent Negro boys. But, though it would be obviously foolish to try to fix up the present Chel- tenham, pending the construction of the fine new post-war Cheltenham, is there any reason why the boys, in the mean- time, shouldn't be given knives and forks as well as spoons? Cheltenham is supposed to rehabilitate-that is, to train these youngsters to play a useful rôle in society. And, though we would be the last to claim that good table man- ners are synonymous with good char- acter, the fact remains that a child is better equipped to take his part in the world if he knows how to eat like a civi- lized human being. War or no war, we believe that the Board of Public Works, or whatever other public authority has the power, should authorize the purchase of enough knives and forks to go around at Cheltenham. 4 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: STATE FUNDS RECOMMENDED FOR J.H.U. UNIT: PUBLICWORKS BOARD BACKS POSTWAR PROJECT FOR ENGINEERING SCHOOL
full_text: STATE FUNDS RECOMMENDED FOR J.H.U. UNIT Public Works Board Backs Postwar Project For Engineering School The allocation of State funds for planning the construction of two buildings for the engineering school at the Johns Hopkins University was recommended to the Board of Pub. lic Works yesterday by the Mary- land Commission on Postwar Recon- struction and Development. Commission members said it is understood that Johns Hopkins officials also will ask the Legisla- ture to appropriate funds for the construction, estimated to cost $1,250,000.  First Of Its Type It was noted at the commission meeting that the recommendation was the first made by the group for the use of State planning funds on any but a strictly public institution. Acting on reports by the commit- Lee on public activities, the commis- sion also voted approval of con- struction at an estimated cost of $4,274,000 for the University of Maryland; the establishment of a new Maryland Training School for Colored Boys, at an estimated cost of $1,600,000; buildings at Morgan State College, at an estimated cost of $957,000; at the Maryland Train- ing School for Boys, $166,500; at Montrose School for Girls, $161,820; for the Maryland State police, $290,500, and at the Women's Prison, $21,500.  Laboratory And Classroom E. Brooke Lee, chairman of the committee on public activities, said the committee's action on the Johns Hopkins plans was taken at a meet- ing called at the request of Gov- ernor O'Conor. The university was represented at the meeting by Dr. Isaiah Bowman, president; Dean W. B. Kouwenhoven, of the School of Engineering, and Dr. A. G. Chris- Cie, professor of mechanical en- gineering. The proposed buildings, are a (Continued on Page 8, Column 2) laboratory and classroom building at an estimated cost of $500,000, and a laboratory for industrial re- search, estimated at $750,000.. Mr. Lee said he previously had discussed the question with Wil- liam C. Walsh, Attorney General, and had been advised that the project could be legally financed by legislative action, "probably along the same lines that were fol- lowed when the 1912 session made $600,000 available for the construction of the present build- ings of the engineering school" at the university. Mr. Lee also pointed out that the State is now appropriating $93,- 000 a year toward the operating cost of the engineering school and that the State is receiving scholar- ships to the school in return.  Cites Number Of Graduates Dr. Bowman told the committee that the average number of engi- neering school graduates for 1939, 1940 and 1941 from both Johns Hopkins and the University of Maryland was 106 a year, which, he said, represented a 50 per cent de- ficiency in the number of engineers annually graduated in Maryland as compared to such graduation in the nation. Dr. Bowman emphasized "in con- siderable detail," Mr. Lee said, "the importance of Johns Hopkins University work in industrial re- search both in connection with the prosecution of the present war and in connection with improved industrial processes." He said the details could not be made public because of war secrecy.  Plans For College Park The plans for the University of Maryland include a building for engineering, chemistry and physics to cost $750,000, to be built at Col. lege Park. Other College Park buildings include general class- rooms, an agriculture building, a building for girls' activities, three girls' dormitories, two men's dor- mitories, and additions and im- provements to the plant at an esti- mated cost of $3,111,000. Approved for the University of Maryland in Baltimore are a psy- chopathic hospital, additions to the dental building and nurses' home, a recreation hall, and completion of the twelfth floor of the Univer- sity Hospital, at a cost of $695,000. New University of Maryland con- struction at Princess Anne would include a men's dormitory, eight faculty cottages and one faculty apartment house, a dining hall and kitchen, reconditioning of the agri- culture building, an athletic field and stands and other improvements at a cost of $468,000.  For Normal Colored Boys The proposed Maryland Training School for Colored Boys would be for normal boys now sent to the Cheltenham School for Boys from juvenile courts. Cheltenham would be continued for the mentally de- ficient. The proposed location of the school is near Catonsville, Mr. Lee said. It would house only 243 boys, but unlike Cheltenham, where some boys remain for several years, it is believed that each boy sent to the new school would re- main not more than three years. It would be under the super- vision of the Department of Public Welfare, while Cheltenham would be under the Department of Mental Hygiene.  Morgan Proposals The Morgan proposals include a classroom building, a dining hall for 350 persons, a women's dormi- tory, a men's dormitory, an audi- torium and quarters for the col- lege staff. The committee said the college is crowded beyond capacity and that many more students, some of them now in the armed forces, are expected to enroll after the war. The Maryland Training School for Boys construction includes liv- ing quarters for the staff and an addition to the power plant. The Montrose School projects are an addition to the vocational building, a dormitory and a school addition. For the Maryland State Police department, the committee recom- mended a new headquarters and training school at Pikesville, build- ings at Waldorf, Cumberland and Frederick. The Women's Prison would get a new canning and storage building and an attendants' home,

title: Mr. O'Conor Can Settle The Cheltenham Issue
full_text: Mr. O'Conor Can Settle The Cheltenham Issue Governor O'Conor's statement regard- ing plans for the Cheltenham School for Boys is reassuring in one respect. He says that nothing yet has been de- cided by the Board of Public Works. This gives the board an opportunity to fall back into line with the State's formally adopted policy regarding Cheltenham. What is behind all this? To put it briefly, Cheltenham is a kind of hodge- podge institution to which delinquent Negro boys are sent. Traditionally, it has made no distinction between boys who are normal and susceptible to train- ing and eventual return to society and boys who are abnormal-feeble-minded, epileptic, etc.--and likely to require per- manent custodial care. Obviously these two categories of boys ought to be kept separate. Following persistent public criticism over many years, Mr. O'Conor's own Commission on Juvenile Delinquency finally came out with recommendations regarding Cheltenham, in its big report of January, 1943. In essence, it recom- mended that Cheltenham be devoted solėly to feeble-minded cases, and be placed under the Board of Mental Hygiene. To carry out the original pur- pose for which Cheltenham was founded, it recommended the building of an en- tirely new training school for delinquent (not feeble-minded) Negro boys, and it recommended, for a variety of sound reasons, that this new training school be located much closer to Baltimore. A few months later the General As- sembly formally ratified these recom- mendations as an expression of State policy, writing them into law. The as- sumption was that the construction of the new training school would take place at the earliest possible time- which means that it should be high on the list of post-war projects. But last month the State Board of Public Works, without consulting the Cheltenham Board, the Department of Public Welfare or the Board of Mental Hygiene, dusted off an ancient set of recommendations regarding Chelten- ham and began the consideration of them. These recommendations ante- dated the action of the General Assembly by many years, and in view of the Assembly's subsequent action are now obsolete and irrelevant. To adopt them would be to brush aside the consid- ered opinion of the Commission on Juve- nile Delinquency, the decision of the General Assembly, and the desire of in- formed citizens generally to see the whole Cheltenham question settled prop- erly, once and for all. Why has the Board of Public Works gone off on this tangent? If it did so through oversight and misunderstand- ing, then things can quickly be straight- ened out. If it did so in response to local pressure for the maintenance of a train- ing school in its present location, then Mr. O'Conor will know how to deal with that. In the past, Mr. O'Conor has more than once been confronted with a choice between yielding to local pressure and taking action directed to the welfare of the whole State. When he has resisted local pressure and stood by the State's best interest, he has gained greatly in stature and public esteem, and has con- firmed the confidence of his supporters. Once again, in this matter of the Chel- tenham School, Mr. O'Conor has an op- portunity to show that the welfare of the whole State is the deciding factor in This decisions. | Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: More Trouble Brewing Over Cheltenham?
full_text: More Trouble Brewing Over Cheltenham? It looks as though the affairs of Chel- tenham School for Boys are getting badly snarled up again. Cheltenham is the State training school for Negro youngsters in Prince George's county. For years it was the focal point of criticism. Independent investigators and a succession of grand juries reported conditions at the insti- tution to be unsatisfactory from almost every point of view, and there devel oped a determined campaign, either to improve the institution or to replace it with another. These efforts came to a head in Janu- ary of last year, when the report of Governor O'Conor's own Commission on Juvenile Delinquency urged not the patching up of the institution as it was then but its present abandonment and the construction of a wholly new institu tion, closer to Baltimore and designed especially for the work in hand. It was suggested that on the construction of a new institution the old institution be turned over to the Board of Mental Hygiene for the care of defective colored juvenile delinquents, a use to which it is suited. Within a month or two of the appear- ance of this report, the recommenda- tions regarding Cheltenham were writ- ten into the law, as follows: The Board of Public Works is here- by authorized and empowered, as soon as conditions permit, and to the extent that funds may be set aside for the purpose in a capital account in the budget, to proceed with the acquisition of an appropriate site and the con- struction and equipment of...a new training school for non-defective col- ared juvenile delinquents. under the supervision of the State Department of Public Welfare to take the place of Cheltenham School for Boys, which Institution shall then be converted into an institution exclusively for defective colored juvenile delinquents, under the supervision, direction and control of the Board of Mental Hygiene. Thus the replacement of Cheltenham by a new and adequate institution is a matter of formal public policy. It is a settled issue.. Settled? Not quite. For the State Board of Public Works has given evi- dence of intention to disregard the law. On April 15 the secretary of this board listed a series of projects, running into some hundreds of thousands of dollars, for the improvement of Cheltenham. These were not mere repairs, to keep the present institution in shape until its successor can be built. They were major undertakings looking to the con- tinuance of Cheltenham in its present location. And the Board of Public Works adopted this program without reference to the views of the Chelten. ham Board, or to those of the Depart- ment of Public Welfare or the Board of Mental Hygiene. Why has the Department of Public Welfare so chosen to act in defiance of settled public policy? It owes the public an explanation and a speedy return to the guidance of the law. Since Governor O'Conor is a member of the Board of Public Works and dominates its pro- ceedings, the explanation for this curi- ous disregard of the law might properly -come from him. 4 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: CHELTENHAM BOARD HEAD QUITS POST: REV. F. R. ISAAC FEELS HIS EFFORTS FRUSTRATED; T.B. SPRAGUE NAMED
full_text: CHELTENHAM BOARD HEAD QUITS POST Rev. F. R. Isaac Feels His Efforts Frustrated; T.B. Sprague Named | The Rev. E. Reid Isaac has re- signed from the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys, it was learned yesterday. partly because he felt "frustrated" in his efforts as president of the board and believed he was "getting no- where." He said he asked Governor O'Conor to relieve him of his duties in connection with the school for delinquent Negro youths so that he might devote full time to his posi tion as general superintendent of the Board of Child Care of the Methodist Church. Concerned Over New Site Explaining that he had found work in the Cheltenham board time-consuming and that it had placed him under considerable strain, he said: "I seemed to be working all the time and getting nowhere." The Cheltenham board recently has been particularly concerned with seeking a site for the proposed new school and with coping with the immediate need for closer su- pervision of chronic runaways at the school. Thomas B. Sprague Named One of the school's cottages currently is being converted for use as a security unit. Thomas B. Sprague, who served on the January (1945) term of the Baltimore grand jury, was elected president of the board Monday. He had been appointed to the board last Thursday, when the Rev. Mr. Isaac's resignation became effective. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: NEGRO FACILITY TO BE BUILT: STATE TO PROVIDE STRUCTURE FOR NORMAL DELINQUENTS
full_text: NEGRO FACILITY TO BE BUILT State To Provide Structure For Normal Delinquents Governor O'Conor said yester- day the State would proceed with plans for a new institution for normal delinquent Negroes, who now are committed to the Chelten- ham School for Boys with defective youths, as soon as a tentative loca- tion and plans for buildings are submitted by the State Department of Public Welfare. He said what appeared, in a re- cent report of his Commission on Post-War Reconstruction and De- velopment, to be disapproval of this plan and its replacement by one calling merely for the improvement of existing facilities at Cheltenham was due to the failure of the Wel- fare Department to submit plans or a suggested location. He said he had expressed satis- faction with the commission's re- port, including a program to im- prove the present Cheltenham School near Brandywine, but to retain both normal and defective inmates in the same institution, because he realized the commission at present could "go no further" without a basis for plans. Became Law In 1943 The Governor pointed out that a recommendation by the Mary- land Commission on Juvenile De- linquency to provide a new institu- tion for normal delinquents and to make the present Cheltenham School an institution exclusively for defective boys was approved by him and later was made law in 1043. "This fact alone leaves no lati- tude for change or disapproval of the plan to erect new facilities for normal boys," he said. title: Why Pick On Cheltenham?
full_text: Why Pick On Cheltenham? Alas, it is necessary to write another chapter in the confused and unhappy history of Cheltenham School for Boys. Cheltenham is a school for delinquent Negro boys, located in Southern Mary- land. It has long been recognized as being hopelessly inadequate for its pur- pose. Back in January of 1943 the Mary- land Commission on Juvenile Delin. quency recommended that Cheltenham be transferred to a new building on an entirely new site and that the present school property be made into an institu- tion for defective Negro boys exclusively and placed under the State Board of Mental Hygiene. The present Chelten- _ham undertakes the impossible task of dealing with both defective Negro boys and boys who are susceptible of rehabili- tation. The gist of the recommendation was that these two groups be separated. The recommendation was approved by Governor O'Conor and subsequently written into-law by the Legislature. In spite of this, the Governor's im- E posing Maryland Commission on Post- War Reconstruction and Development has persistently refused to accept the State's policy regarding Cheltenham. In October of last year it published a formal report listing State post-war improve- ment projects. In the list was a program for the patching up of the present Chel- tenham-an obsolete and inadequate program which had long since been junked by the State administration. When this fact was discovered, there followed a brief uproar, which was quieted when the Governor announced that, regardless of his imposing Com- mission on Post-War Reconstruction and Development, the State's declared policy regarding Cheltenham would nev- ertheless be followed. And now what? The Commission on Post-War Reconstruction, etc., has just issued another progress report; and the Governor has expressed satisfaction with it. What does this latest report have to say about Cheltenham? Once again, the Commission on Post- War, etc., trots out the obsolete, inade- quate and oft-repudiated scheme for patching up the present Cheltenham. Evidently the Commission on Post- War, etc., learns slowly. Its recommen- dations regarding Cheltenham is wholly out of line with State policy. If its other recommendations, filling many pages, are as beside the point as its recommen- dations on Cheltenham, then the proper filing place for this report is the nearest wastebasket. Won't someone in Annapolis. please tell us once and for all what the official administration line is regarding Chel- tenham, and then see that that line is adhered to? title: Enlarging The State's Postwar Works Program
full_text: Enlarging The State's Postwar Works Program The recommendation on Monday, by the State's Commission on Postwar Reconstruc- tion and Development, of a long list of addi- tional projects is a reminder that the State's postwar public-works program has been making steady headway. In developing this program, several steps are involved. First, the commission surveys all the various proposals, winnows the wheat from the chaff, and makes recommendations to the State Board of Public Works regard- ing desirable projects. So far the commis- sion has recommended projects amounting to no less than $16,900,000. Having received the recommendations, the State Board of Public Works acts upon them in due time. So far it has definitely adopted as part of the public-works program some $9,400,000 worth of projects. It has projects amounting to $7,500,000 still to act upon- most of these being the recommendations made by the commission on Monday and sent to the board yesterday. Yet the program cannot reach the action stage until the General Assembly has appro- priated the funds. Funds are already allo- cated only in the case of a few relatively small projects. The General Assembly, which is to meet next month, will have the consid- eration of this great program as one of its principal duties. The sum involved is a large one for Mary. land. Yet the State is not wholly unprepared. There exists already a postwar building fund which will yield a net of approximately $2,000,000 for actual construction. In addi tion, a State surplus of somewhere around $8,000,000 will be available. Thus funds suffi- cient to pay for more than half of the pro- gram as so far recommended are already on hand, if the General Assembly chooses to use them for the purpose. That is a pretty good start. As for the list of works recommended on Monday but not yet approved by the Board of Public Works, it includes a number of im- portant projects which have long been under discussion. One of these is for the establish- ment of a new Maryland training school for colored boys, an institution designed to re- place that least admirable of State institu- tions, the Cheltenham School. Improvements for the Maryland Training School for Boys and the Montrose School for Girls are like- wise included. These appropriations lie in the realm of rehabilitation and training. The recommen- dations regarding higher education bulk even larger. A program. for the University of Maryland adds up to the substantial sum of $4,274,000, most of it going into the further expansion of physical plan at College Park. But this list also includes provision for a new psychopathic hospital, or ward, in connec- tion with the university's medical school in Baltimore. Baltimore is a great center of medical education, and the field of psy. chiatry is represented by the world-famous Phipps Clinic. But the institution now being recommended would have a different func- tion, being a sort of clearing house for acute psychiatric cases. The lack of such an institu- tion, not only as an important direct service to the public but as a clinical aid to medical teaching, has been felt for a long time. Finally, the commission has recommended the financing by the State of substantial addi- tions to the engineering school of Johns Hop- kins University. Though Johns Hopkins is a private institution, the State has had a heavy interest in the engineering school from its inception. After the war, the demand for men trained in the several branches of engi. neering is going to be very heavy, owing partly to the shortage of trained engineers occasioned by the war and partly to con- tinued advance in the engineering arts. And this will be coupled with equally heavy de- mands on our engineering schools for basic and applied research-extensions, after a fashion, of the kind of research which Johns Hopkins and other institutions have carried on in connection with the war. Additional State assistance should therefore prove to be money well spent. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Plans For Cheltenham
full_text: Plans For Cheltenham TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: After reading two recent editorials in The Sun dealing with plans for Cheltenham, 1 desire to make the following statement on behalf of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys: The Cheltenham board is working in coöperation with the State Department of Public Welfare on plans for the pro- posed training school for colored boys to be located elsewhere than at Chelten- ham, Md. This new school will not carry the name of "Cheltenham," but will prob- ably be called the Maryland Training School for Colored Boys. At the request of the Board of Public Works, a committee is in search of a site for the new school in the vicinity of Bal- timore. Furthermore, we have a definite program outlined for this new school. All of this is in accordance with the law passed by the last Legislature, and also is in response to the request of the Mary- land State Planning Commission. Fur thermore, in a recent meeting with the Cheltenham board of managers and over seventy-five outstanding citizens of the colored group Governor O'Conor ex- pressed his interest in and his support of the program. As soon as the board has completed its studies pertaining to the location, number and type of buildings, school and recreational facilities which will be needed to serve these particular hoys, we shall submit the plan to the Maryland State Planning Commission. In the meantime, certain alterations and additions are being planned and re- quested for the present site for the pur- pose of creating decent living conditions as well as adequate facilities for the housing of staff and further carrying out of the present program. Capable persons are available as cottage supervisors, aca- demic and vocational instructors, but we are lacking any living quarters for them. New dining-room accommodations are also being requested along with a re- ceiving cottage for the study of new boys. These recommended improvements have been discussed with Dr. Preston, who has told us that they will fit into the needs of the institution when operated by the Board of Mental Hygiene. The Governor and the Board of Pub- lic Works have already approved the installation of adequate sanitary facili- ties in each of the six cottages. This work is now being done. Mr. Royal A. В. Crump, the new superintendent, is doing admirable work in cleaning up and mak- ing the present buildings more usable. We appreciate the concern and interest of The Sun in its endeavor to keep the public informed concerning the progress toward a new school for the colored boys of Maryland. F. REID ISAAC, President, Cheltenham Board of Managers. Baltimore, Oct. 11. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: YOUTH DETENTION HOMES CROWDED: NO FACILITIES FOR MENTALLY DEFECTIVE CHILDREN
full_text: YOUTH DETENTION HOMES CROWDED  No Facilities For Mentally De- fective Children  There is no State-operated place in Maryland to care for or detain a juvenile delinquent.  There is no State-operated place to care for or detain a mentally de fective juvenile.  There is no State-operated place to care for a neglected child.  These facts were revealed yester day by the State Department of Public Welfare; the State Board of Mental Hygiene and the Baltimore Council of Social Agencies.  Room For Six More Girls Of the four juvenile correctional institutions in the State only one, the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls, is not filled to or beyond capacity, and this institu- tion has room for exactly six more girls.  Cheltenham School, for colored boys, which has a current operat- ing capacity of 240, now houses 270 boys, at least 50 of whom are mental defectives, who, officials agree, should not be there at all. There is no segregation of these mental cases from the other boys.  Montrose School for Girls is filled to its capacity of 125, and there is a "limited waiting list." There is "a very small percentage" of mental defectives in this school, and there is no provision for their segregation from the other girls.  Overcrowding Maryland Training School for Boys has a current operating ca- pacity of 240, but there are 286 boys crowded in the institution. At the present time there are no men- tal defectives.  Until three months ago feeble- minded children, along with de- linquents, were committed to the four correctional institutions be- cause there was no room for them elsewhere.  There still is no room for these mental defectives, but they no longer are being committed to the correctional institutions. They are not being committed anywhere.  Nothing Could Be Done Dr. George H. Preston, of the State Board of Mental Hygiene, was asked yesterday what could be done if the need arose during the day to take care of a mentally defective child.  "Absolutely nothing," he replied.  Crownsville State Hospital for mentally defective Negro men and women, boys and girls, from city and State, has 190 beds "constantly full," Dr. Preston said.  "Beyond that there are no other provisions for feeble-minded Negro children," he said.  "Beyond Capacity" There are 1,200 beds at Rose- wood, the institution for mentally defective white children, both boys and girls, from the city and coun- ties, and it is "crowded beyond ca- pacity," Dr. Preston said.  "There is literally nothing which can be done at present to expand facilities.  "The problem is, how are we going to divide existing facilities which cannot be expanded?" Dr. Preston said.  "No Other Place" In this connection, Dr. Preston said the advisory committee at Rosewood will meet next Monday to confer with Dwight H. Ferguson, director of institutions of the State Department of Public Welfare.  This may result in the resump- tion of the practice of sending men- tally defective children to the four correctional institutions, it was in- dicated. He asserted that plans for the expansion of facilities (Continued on Page 7, Column 2)i 1 for mental defectives had been submitted to the State Planning Commission on a number of occa- sions dating back at least eight years.  With no more room in the correc- tional institutions for delinquents or neglected children-"serious de linquents" somehow will be crowd. ed into the institutions-the State Department of Public Welfare hopes to solve the placement prob- lem by putting delinquent children on probation or by finding them foster homes. - Big Waiting List" Right now there is a big waiting list of more than 100 neglected and dependent children, while ap- proximately 700 children are being cared for in less than 300 foster homes, according to the Council of Social Agencies.  To assist the State Department of Public Welfare in its plan to find places for delinquent or neglected children the Council of Social Agencies plans to conduct a drive in Baltimore and Baltimore county to find 300 additional foster homes with accommodations for 400 chil- dren.  In order not to conflict with a Red Cross campaign, the drive for the foster homes will not begin until April 1.

title: 50 BOYS UNDER 12 AT CHELTENHAM: SOME AS YOUNG AS 7, SUPERINTENDENT SAYS
full_text: 50 BOYS UNDER 12. AT CHELTENHAM Some As Young As 7, Superin- tendent Says Juvenile authorities throughout the State are committing delin- quent Negro boys under 12 to Cheltenham School for Colored Boys, in violation of the institu- tion's new intake policies, because of a critical shortage of foster homes, Vance E. Thomas, superin- tendent, asserted yesterday. Although the new intake rules, established last January by the State Department of Public Wel- fare, provide that only Negro boys 12 or over shall be committed, Mr. Thomas said some as young as 7 are being admitted. Fifty of the 300 boys at the insti- tution are under 12, he asserted. Problem Outlined To Mayor "The tendency over the last year and a half has been to commit younger boys," he added. "This is in violation of the new intake policies, but the practice will have to continue until more foster homes are found and home-finding agencies are enlarged." Mr. Thomas outlined this prob- lem, to Mayor McKeldin, who visited the institution Thursday, accompanied by T. J. S. Waxter and Francis. A. Davis, director and chairman, respectively, of the Balti- more Department of Public Wel- fare, and G. Cheston Carey, active in child-welfare work in the State. Mr. McKeldin said he visited Cheltenham because a large num- ber of Baltimore boys were sent there, and he wanted to see at first- hand the care they received. Program Criticized, Approximately 80 per cent. of the boys at the school have been committed by the Baltimore Divi- sion of Juvenile Causes, Mr. Thomas said, the terms of commit- ment averaging from 15 months to two years. The city pays $180 a year for each boy it commits. The visitors noted that the boys were given only tablespoons with which to eat, 'and suggested that knives and forks be supplied. They expressed surprise at the inade- quate sanitary facilities and the "dungeonlike kitchen" in the base- ment of the school's administra- tion building. Mr. Thomas. pointed out, how- ever, that a 'law enacted by the 1943 session of the Legislature called for construction of a new Cheltenham after the war and de- clared it would be useless to make expensive improvements of the an- tiquated buildings now in use. Drop In 'Feeble-Minded The superintendent said there has been a slight decrease in the number of feeble-minded delin- quents committed to Cheltenham since the State Department of Pub- lic Welfare assumed control of the State's four training schools last June 1. "Borderline cases," with I. Q.'s ranging between 60 and 70, still are being admitted in consid- erable numbers, however. Under the new intake rules, which permit municipal authorities to order temporary commitments not to exceed 45 days, 83 boys have been admitted temporarily since January 1. Of these, 43 have been released on probation and 22 com- mitted permanently. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Two Hopeful Proposals For Correctional Schools
full_text: Two Hopeful Proposals For Correctional Schools By a pleasant coincidence, yesterday's paper recorded potential advances in the handling of Maryland's juvenile de- linquents in two respects. Neither ad- vance is revolutionary, but both show an appreciation of present shortcomings. Governor O'Conor announced that a unit at the Maryland School for Boys will be set aside, on October 1, for boys from 16 to 18 who have been convicted of serious crimes. Up to the present time, such boys have been sent either to the House of Correction or to the Penitentiary, both equally bad from the penologists' point of view. Hereafter they will be incarcerated not with adult prisoners but with boys of their own age and, presumably, rehabilitation tech- niques will be used. This plan is obviously a stop-gap, and - the Governor makes no greater claim for it. It still leaves out of account the younger criminals-those of 14 and 15- and it is doubtful, in addition, that it is wise to have proven criminals, even in a separate inclosure, in so close an asso- ciation with the other boys at the train- ing school, most of whom are there for less serious offenses. Yet it is an at- tempt to deal with part of the larger problem and as such is to be commended. The other announcement is more stimulating. Only recently, the board of trustees of Cheltenham School, which alls for colored boys roughly the place which the Maryland Training School fills for whites, announced the appoint- ment of a new superintendent, Royal A. B. Crump, a colored man. Now the new superintendent announces his program. His aim is to make Cheltenham some- thing more than a mere place of deten- tion. He wants to give it, in fact, the status of an accredited school, the in- mates of which can continue their studies, whether academic or vocational, precisely as if they were free. This is bold thinking, and Mr. Crump deserves all credit for making his views known. That there will be administrative difficulties in carrying out such a pro- gram everyone can see. But the board and citizens generally should give the new superintendent every support in his effort. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Again, Not A Word About Cheltenham
full_text: Again, Not A Word About Cheltenham Cheltenham, the State's school for de- linquent Negro boys, has long struggled under a double burden-that of caring for defective Negro boys and that of caring for delinquents capable of reha- bilitation. It is generally agreed that these two functions should be taken care of by separate institutions. Back in January of 1943 the Maryland Commission on Juvenile Delinquency recommended just such a separation. It recommended that an entirely new insti- tution be built for trainable Negro delin- quents and that the present Chelten- ham, after suitable alterations and im- provements, be turned over to the State Board of Mental Hygiene as a school for defective Negro boys. The General As- sembly approved this recommendation. Yesterday Governor O'Conor an- nounced the State's post-war program for medical-care institutions, including mental patients. The Governor's list of projects in- cluded badly needed work at Spring Grove, an expansion program at Spring- field State Hospital and programs of expansion at Crownsville State Hospital, Eastern Shore State Hospital and a number. of other institutions. Nowhere in the list is any reference to the new rôle of the present Chelten- ham. Cheltenham is absent from the list despite the fact that the post-war pro- gram for Cheltenham is supposed to be settled public policy. Why is it that the program for Chel- tenham is so consistently disregarded? Only last week the Governor's imposing Commission on Post-War Reconstruction and Development published a list of post-war projects which made no refer- ence to the new Cheltenham program. Now Cheltenham has been skipped again. The Governor, or the State Board of Mental Hygiene, or the Commission on Post-War Reconstruction and Devel- opment, owes the public an explanation of this. title: SEEKS EXPANSION OF CHELTENHAM: O'CONOR CALLS NEED MORE PRESSING THAN FOR NEW UNIT
full_text: SEEKS EXPANSION OF CHELTENHAM O'Conor Calls Need More Pressing Than For New Unit The Board of Public Works may ask the next session of the Legisla ture to amend the State law pro viding for construction of a new Cheltenham School for Boys to per mit instead early expansion and alteration of the present institu tion, Governor O'Conor said last night. • Explaining that a recent Board of Public Works plan to spend a large sum of money for the improvement of Cheltenham was still under con sideration, the Governor said the alterations could be made during the war to expand crowded facili- tles, while construction of a new school would have to wait until after the war, New School Authorized The law, as passed by the Legis- lature last year, authorizes the board to proceed with construction of a new training school for non- defective Negro Juvenile delin- quents, under the supervision of the State Department of Public Welfare. to replace Cheltenham School for Boys. Cheltenham then would be con- verted into an institution exclu- sively for defective Negro juvenile delinquents, under the supervision of the Board of Mental Hygiene. "We are not proceeding in viola- tion of the law," Mr. O'Conor said. "No construction has been author- ized on the present institution. The project that was put out for plan- ning was in accordance with the plans of the Post-War Planning Commission. More Pressing Need "The Board of Public Works is considering asking the Legislature to amend the law to permit alter- ing the present institution instead of building a new one. The need for expanded facilities for normal Negro delinquents is much more pressing than that for facilities for feeble-minded Negroes. "In view of wartime construction difficulties and the length of time it would take to erect an entirely new school, the board feels expan- sion and alteration would be more practical at the present time. "The entire matter is before the board. Nothing will be done of a final nature until it is determined if the State policy will follow the law or ask the Legislative Council or Legislature to introduce an amendment changing the law." title: CREDITS PROPOSED FOR CHELTENHAM: OTHER IMPROVEMENTS URGED BY NEW SUPERINTENDENT
full_text: CREDITS PROPOSED FOR CHELTENHAM Other Improvements Urged By New Superintendent | The Cheltenham School for Boys, which now serves as a corrective and disciplinary institution, will become an accredited school whose students may proceed to advanced grades in regular educational insti- tutions, according to a program proposed by Royal A. B. Crump, the school's new superintendent. Mr. Crump's administrative plan has been approved tentatively by the school's board of managers, and will be submitted to appropriate State authorities for further ap- proval and financial support. ☑ Mr. Crump developed this type of educational program as superin- tendent at the Hanover (Va.) Training School for Boys which, like Cheltenham, has a student body of about 400 delinquent Ne- gro boys. The proposal provides for correlated vocational and academic departments from which students may go on to higher grades in other schools.. Other Improvements Urged - Other major improvements advo- cated in the new program for Chel- tenham include: The replacement by State- hired instructors of the approxi- - mately 14 conscientious objec- - tors employed in Federal civil C service as instructors at the - school, The remaining white staff members, numbering about 20, also would be replaced gradually by qualified Negrocs. A student self-government pro- gram, under strict supervision by authorities, with merit awards for deserving pupils, will be in- stituted, Church and Sunday-school pro- grams of an undenominational. nature, which at present are not included in the school's program, will be started. Accreditation of Cheltenham seems to Mr. Crump the most im- portant single objective of his pro- posed administration. Like Grade School When it is accomplished, a stu- dent, after being classified for vo- cational or academic training upon entrance, will advance in grades corresponding to those in any school. title: NEGRO NAMED CHELTENHAM SCHOOL HEAD: O'CONOR SAYS RACE WILL GET CHANCE TO SHOW MANAGEMENT ABILITY
full_text: NEGRO NAMED CHELTENHAM SCHOOL HEAD O'Conor Says Race Will Get Chance To Show Management Ability Royal A. B. Crump. Negro, yes- terday was appointed superintend- ent of the Cheltenham School for Boys by Governor O'Conor, thus bringing the school under an all- Negro management. The Governor said the move was made in the "belief that Negroes should be given an opportunity at least to demonstrate their ability to manage institutions harboring only Negro inmates." Mr. Crump formerly was assist- ant superintendent of the Hanover (Va.) Training School for Negro Boys. He will assume his new duties on September 1. He succeeds Vance E. Thomas, outgoing superintendent, who will act in an advisory capacity while Mr. Crump is "becoming acquainted with his duties," the Governor said. Whites To Be Transferred The few remaining white em- ployes at the school soon will be transferred to other institutions so that the policy of a complete Negro administration likely will be achieved in the near future, Mr. O'Conor said. Mr. Crump said last night that his contemplated administration program for Cheltenham, sub- mitted some time ago to the institu- tion's board of managers, places emphasis on "vocational education rather than a reformatory or penal system." "We plan to make Cheltenham an accredited school where an edu- cation comparable to that of any other vocational school, whether or not a reformatory, will be avail- able," he stated. From Recommended List Since he has not as yet visited the school, practical administration details have not been worked out, The added. Selected as superintendent of Cheltenham from a list of per- (Continued on Page 13, Column 4) sons recommended by the State Employment Commissioner, Mr. Crump was assistant superintend- ent at Hanover for 16 years. Previously, after serving as a lieutenant of infantry in the first World War, he helped found and served for five years as director of a social settlement for Negroes in South Bend, Ind. He was recommended for the Cheltenham post by Negro educa- tion leaders, including Walter R. Brown, dean of men at Hampton Institute, Virginia, from which Mr. Crump received diplomas in voca- tional training and education. Mr. Crump and his wife will make their home at Cheltenham. They have no children.

title: Obituary
full_text: Obituary Dr. James Burch Joyce Funeral services were held on Tuesday for Dr. James Burch Joyce, of 3809 St. Paul street, retired physician and former mem- ber of the city health department, who died last Sunday after a short illness. Burial was in Greenmount Cemetery. Dr. Joyce, who was 72, was a graduate of St. John's College and the University of Maryland. He was a member of Grace Methodist Church. Roland Park, and served as layman to the Methodist Epis- copal General Conference in Kan- sas City in 1928. He also belonged to a number of Methodist church organizations. He is survived by two daughters, Mrs. Joseph T. Hazen, of Joyce, Md., and Mrs. Frederick A. Weiss, Jr., of Baltimore; two brothers, Cyrus N. Joyce and Dr. John C. Joyce, and a sister, Mrs. Walter C. Munroe, all of Joyce. His wife, the former Miss Flora Bolgiano, of Baltimore, died nine years ago. Charles C. Carver Charles C. Carver, proprietor since 1915 of the firm of Charles F. Eareckson & Co., manufacturers of sails, awnings and tents, died Thursday at his home, 2801 Elsinor venue. Funeral services will be held at 11 A. M. today at funeral par- lors at North and Pennsylvania ave- nues. Burial will be in Druid Ridge Cemetery. The Rev. Allen J. Miller, of the Protestant Episcopal Church of the Messiah, will officiate. Surviving Mr. Carver in addition to his wife, the former Marian Gould Travers, is a sister, Mrs. Richard W. Worthington. Problem Boy Goes To Welfare Unit A 13-year-old Negro boy yester- day was turned over to J. Milton Patterson, of the Department of Public Welfare, after the boy was refused admission to Cheltenham School for Colored Boys and Crownsville State Hospital. The action was taken by Judge Charles E. Moylan, of the division of juvenile causes, after he found the boy to be a delinquent. Judge Moylan announced that he had or- dered the boy held in a station house after efforts to place him in an institution had been unsuccess- ful. The judge pointed out that the boy had been before the court on various charges since August 1943 involving thefts of a re- volver, a bicycle and some cash. Judge Moylan explained that under a special provision of the new Juvenile Court setup, when a minor is refused admission to one of the State institutions, the case is turned over the Department of Public Welfare for solution. He said he did not intend to release the boy on probation since that type of action had failed on pre- vious occasions. He revealed that the court psy- chiatrist had reported that the boy was not a fit subject for Crowns- ville and that Cheltenham had re- fused admission to the minor be- cause of a low intelligence quotient. title: TRIO CHARGED WITH LARCENY: MEN HELD AFTER PURSE-SNATCHING BY BOYS
full_text: TRIO CHARGED WITH LARCENY Men Held After Purse-Snatch- ing By Boys A purse-snatching by two 11-year- old Negro boys resulted in the ar- rest of three young Negro men on a larceny charge, it was testified in the Southern District Police Court yesterday when the men were held in $2,500 bail each for action of the grand jury. According to the testimony of one of the 11-year-old boys, the story begins early on the night of January 12. That night, it was testified, the two boys snatched a purse contain- ing $35 from Mrs. Olive E. Rensch, of 6913 Kenleigh road, as she was walking near Charles and Mont- gomery sts. Is Thrown In Churchyard After taking the purse, the two boys ran north on Charles st. and, suddenly losing their nerve, threw the pocketbook in a churchyard at Charles and Hill sts. Shortly thereafter, the two boys met the three men, who asked them what they were running away from. The boys, it was testified, told them of the purse-snatching and where they had thrown the pocket- book. Later, upon hearing that the men had gone to the churchyard and found money in the purse, one of the boys, becoming increasingly afraid of what he had done, told the police his story. Three Held For Grand Jury The three held for the grand jury by Magistrate Solomon Liss were identified by police as Raymond Robertson, 18. of the 600 block Dover st.; Vernon Matthew. 18, of the 1000 block West Vine st., and Willie Lee Smith, 23, of the 500 block Sharp st. - One of the boys already has been committed by the Juvenile Court to the Cheltenham School for Colored Boys for his part in the purse snatching. The other has been re- leased in the custody of his parents for a hearing. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: A Negro Delinquent Case And The Cheltenham Problem
full_text: A Negro Delinquent Case 'And The Cheltenham Problem The Board of Public Works has in- structed the board of managers of Chel- tenham School, working with the State Department of Public Welfare, to find a new site for this institution. In so doing the board has acted wisely, as all thoughtful people will agree. Chelten- ham has been the target of sharp eriti- cism for years. Its buildings are old and ill-fitted for the training of delinquent boys; its teaching staff has not been maintained at desirable standards. A new school is the obvious answer, and this fact has been recognized for some time. The inadequacies of Cheltenham were given special attention by Governor O'Conor's Commission on Juvenile De- linquency. It recommended that the present school property be turned over to the State Board of Mental Hygiene for use as an institution for "trainable defective Negro boys" and that a new Cheltenham at a new site be established for normal and border-line delinquent youths. Within a month or two after the appearance of the commission's recom- mendations they were written into law by the General Assembly. If anyone doubts that the Commis- sion on Juvenile Delinquency, the Legis- lature, and now the Board of Public Works, have taken the right course, we recommend the reading of a news arti- ele which appeared in The Sun yester- day. The article tells of the case of a 13- year-old Negro boy found to be a delin- quent by Judge Charles E. Moylan. The Cheltenham School refused to accept the youth because of a low intelligence quotient; the court psychiatrist reported that the boy was not a fit subject for the Crownsville State Hospital. There was no place to send the boy, and Judge Moylan refused to release him. He has been turned over to the Department of Public Welfare. What this agency will do with him is, of course, the question. There will be a ready answer in such cases when the new Cheltenham has been built on its new site and the present school proр- erty has been converted to the use proposed by the Legislature and now approved by the Board of Public Works. title: CRUMP HEADS CHELTENHAM: NEGRO FORMALLY PRESENTED BY GROUP TO O'CONOR
full_text: CRUMP HEADS CHELTENHAM Negro Formally Presented By Group To O'Conor Annapolis, Sept. 14 (Special) - Governor O'Conor today told 75 Negro business and professional leaders of the State and the board of Cheltenham School for Boys, a Negro institution, that first steps have been taken by his administra- tion for the post-war construction and equipment of a new training school for colored juvenile de- linquents. The group gathered in the ex- ecutive offices in the State House for the installation of Royal A. B. Crump, the new superintendent of Cheltenham and the first member of his race to hold such a position in Maryland.  Succeeds Thomas He succeeds Vance E. Thomas, who has resigned. Before coming to Cheltenham, Mr. Crump was con- nected with a Negro boys school in Hanover county, Virginia. The Governor said Mr. Thomas "voluntarily and graciously' has given up his position in favor of a new superintendency because he was convinced that such action would be for the good of the school and its pupils in whose progress he was very genuinely interested." The post-war correctional school, the Governor said, will take the place of Cheltenham, which will be turned into an institution for the care of Negro mental defectives under the Board of Mental Hygiene.  Post-War Cheltenham "Intensive consideration has been given by the Department of Public Welfare and the Cheltenham School board concerning the selec- tion of a site for the post-war school," the Governor explained. "Provision is being made in the program of the Maryland Post-War Commission for the necessary buildings." The Governor reviewed the money spent on Cheltenham since 1939, when the Legislature pro- vided $85,000 for new facilities. Two years later, he said, an addi- tional $131,000 was provided and since then the Post-War Commis- sion has programed approximately $900,000 for post-war construction when conditions permit.  $2,000,000 Since 1938 Besides, he said, $900,000 for operating expenses has been pro- vided, making a total of $2,000,000 "that has been put into the insti- tution and its operating expenses since this administration came into office." Nothing could be more hearten- ing to Mr. Crump and his associ- ates, the Governor said, than "the knowledge first of all that the State administration was heartily in ac- cord both with his appointment and with the new policy which such an appointment indicated." "Your presence here today in the executive offices, at my invitation, would certainly give ample evi- dence of the favorable view which this administration has of condi- tions at Cheltenham at the mo ment," the Governor continued.  "Favorably Impressed" "We have been most favorably impressed with the selection of the board because of Mr. Crump's ad- mitted experience and proven capa- bilities in previous work of this kind. { "The very fact that the installa- tion is being held here would cer- tainly give emphasis to our desire to impress upon all concerned that we are heart and soul in line with Cheltenham's new policies and de- lighted, indeed, to see the school at last on the road toward permanent solution of its problems."  "Program Of Education" Mr. Crump was appointed in an announced effort by the Governor to place the entire management of Cheltenham under Negroes. Mr. Crump, who was introduced by Dr. Frank S. Isaac, president of the school's board, said he will advance "a program of education for boys who have not had opportunities." Dr. Isaac described the condi- tions at Cheltenham to those at- tending the meeting and asked that a new dining room, apartments for employes and an intake cottage be constructed as soon as possible. He said the intake cottage might be used to house boys still awaiting sentence by the courts.  "Almost A Hog Pen" He said that at present the kitch- en at Cheltenham "is almost a hog pen" and that the school has been "indoor sport for one grand jury after another in making investiga- tions and reports." Following short statements by architects to the effect that priori- ties could be obtained for the con- struction of the new kitchen imme- diately, the members of the board were introduced to those present by Dr. Isaac and the meeting was adjourned. Cheltenham board members who attended included, in addition to Dr. Isaac, Joseph P. Healy, Jr., Dr. G. Canby Robinsoh, Junius Gray, Howard C. Hill, Joseph C. Briscoe, John L. Berry and Bertha в. Proctor.
