title: State Funds Available To Hospital And School
full_text: State Funds Available To Hospital And School Annapolis, Feb. 12 (Special) - State funds totaling $33,313 were made available today for the Spring Grove State Hospital and the Cheltenham School for Boys. Of $27,735 for labor and material items at the hospital, $8,835 will be used to pay overtime and bonuses to employes in accordance with a recent request by hospital officials for additional wage funds for attendants, farm hands, cooks and steam firemen. The allotment was made from unused funds in the hospital's budget which resulted from inabil- ity to obtain much-needed replace- ments for mechanical equipment and repair work. Of $5,578 made available for Cheltenham, $3,500 will be trans- ferred to the live-stock feed ac- I count of the school. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: Two Important Bills On Juvenile Delinquency
full_text: Two Important Bills On Juvenile Delinquency One of the major responsibilities rest ing on the General Assembly during the final week of its deliberations will be the adoption of bills to revise the Juvenile Court setup in Baltimore city and to provide for the care of juvenile delin quents in State institutions under the over-all direction of the Department of Public Welfare. The first of these bills conforms in a general way to the recommendations which the Bond Commission made on the subject of the Juvenile Court. It provides that one of the judges of the Baltimore Supreme Bench shall pre- side over the Juvenile Court. The Juve- nile Court will have original and exclu- sive jurisdiction over offenses (except capital crimes) committed by persons under 16 years of age, and also over cases of neglected, dependent and feeble- minded children. It will have power to commit the children of whose cases the court takes jurisdiction to the care of the Department of Public Welfare which will report to it. The second bill, based on recommen- dations by the Commission on Juvenile Delinquency, provides that the State Welfare Department take over the cus- tody of juvenile delinquents. To this end the department is provided with supervisory powers over the Maryland Training School for Boys, Montrose School for Girls, Cheltenham School for Boys and the Maryland Training School for Colored Girls. An appropriation to allow the department to handle the juvenile-delinquency cases is included in the supplemental budget which went to the General Assembly on Friday. Governor O'Conor emphatically in- dorsed the two bills in a broadcast a week ago. He urged their enactment as a means of ending the disgraceful prac- tice of confining juvenile delinquents in State penal institutions along with mature offenders. The bills have now been reported out by the Senate Com- mittee on Judicial Proceedings, whose chairman, Senator Byrnes, was also sec- retary of the Juvenile Delinquency Com- mission. Certain amendments were made, all of which were accepted by the commission, and only one of which raises any misgiving. This one amend- ment deprives the Welfare Department of the veto power which the original bill would have given it over the ap- pointment of superintendents of the four institutions concerned by their respective boards. It would have been better to retain the provision under which the superin- tendents would have been appointed subject to the Welfare Department's approval. But opposition to this pro- vision from the boards of the institutions concerned had arisen, and the Judicial Proceedings Committee thought it best to make the change. Its judgment of the situation must be reluctantly accepted. The main thing now is to get the bills passed and end the conditions the Governor described in his broad- cast. Every precaution should be taken to insure that these measures do not get lost in the last-minute shuffle. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. To Start With U. Of Md. The leadoff budgetary request, that of the University of Maryland, is one which Dr. H. C. Byrd, presi- dent of the university, described recently as eliciting "silly and ridiculous misconceptions" on the part of members of the Legislature. At a recent meeting of the Legis- lative Council, Dr. Byrd declined to discuss the university budget, except as pertained to the medical and law schools and then only in a general fashion. He told members of the Legis- lative Council that he wanted to make a public statement about the budget before it was submitted officially either to the council or to the Legislature. At the office of Walter N. Kirk- man, director of the Bureau of Budget and Procurement. it was learned that Dr. Byrd has sub- mitted a total budget request for $4,044,112.48 for 1944 and 1945. Special funds, which are gained from current revenue, were esti- mated at $2,600.000, and the gen- eral funds sought from the State amounted to $1.444.112.48. Although the House of Delegates in the last session of the General Assembly adopted a resolution call- ing for the submission of all State department budgets not later than October 15 of the year in which the budget was to be drawn, some of the budgets have not been sub- mitted to the Bureau of Budget and Procurement, it was announced yesterday. Two of the largest requests will come from the Bureau of Education and the State Roads Commission, it was said. Causes Of Delay Cited Delay in the budget of the De- partment of Education was said to be because the State school sys- tem had to determine first how many students were going to be en- rolled in the 1944-1945 period, in addition to determining how many teachers would be needed because of either replacements or the need for new teachers. As for the State Roads Commis- sion, it was said at the office of the Bureau of Budget and Procure- ment that the budget of that de- partment was being held up be- cause final figures had not been received on the budgetary requests of such departments as the State Police Department and the office of the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles which depend for revenue on the income from the gasoline tax. title: A Negro Superintendent For A Negro Institution
full_text: A Negro Superintendent For A Negro Institution Of the many troubles which have be- set the Cheltenham School for colored boys, one of the most persistent has had to do with the skin color of its superin- tendent and staff. An all-white staff was intolerable to the Negro community. A mixed staff has been the source of con- stantly recurring friction, to the detri- ment of the institution. Now a Negro superintendent, Mr. R. A. B. Crump, has been appointed, bringing that particular controversy to an end. Those who have followed Chelten- ham's rather sordid history will wish him well. He comes to the institution with a background of experience and accomplishment. On his shoulders rests the task of demonstrating the practi- cability as well as the propriety of Negro management for Negro institutions. Other things being equal, the demon- stration should not be too difficult. Unfortunately, "other things" are not equal. Cheltenham falls considerably short of the ideál, as such institutions go. The ghosts of innumerable past contro- versies and administrative ineptitudes haunt its ancient and badly battered corridors. Its buildings are an unsatis- factory medley of obsolescence and im- provisation. It is overcrowded. It has for years been a dumping ground for all sorts of "problem" cases-waiſs in want of parental care and guidance, delin- quents, the feeble-minded and the men- tally ill. The successful administration of such a hodgepodge institution would tax the capacities of Solomon himself. The State is in part responsible for this sorry situation, and at last has recognized its responsibility. Provision for a new institution to replace Chelten- ham is on the list of the State's post-war projects. When that is finally built, the old institution will still be available for a part of its present task-the care of feeble-minded Negro boys--and the new one will then be able to concentrate on the education and rehabilitation of the normal delinquents. : Until then, we may expect no miracles from Cheltenham. The people will ob- serve the efforts of the new superin- tendent with sympathy and good will. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: CHELTENHAM SHOWS SOME AWARENESS OF ITS PROBLEM
full_text: CHELTENHAM SHOWS SOME AWWARENESS OF ITS PROBLEM The appointment of Claude D. Jones, now superintendent of the National Train- ing School for Boys at Washington, to be director of education at the Cheltenham School for Negroes, seems to be a good nove. The appointee was on a list of three certified to the board by Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner. More than that, he has had experience in the sort of work he is employed to do, both at Washington and, earlier, at Denver. These facts apparently indicate that the appoint- ment is not political.. As to the desirability of having a trained man in that post there can be no question. The special committee which made a survey of Cheltenham strongly recommended this move, for reasons that are obvious. The director of education in such a place must be more than an ordinary teacher, because he is handling more than ordinarily difficult pupils. Boys who are easy to deal with don't go to Cheltenham. At the same time, if the school is to serve a social purpose useful enough to make it worth its cost, the educational side of its work should be strongly developed. The institution's excuse for existence is the hope that it may prevent problem children from becoming habitual criminals, and all experience goes to show that mental and physical training plays an enormously im- portant part in realizing that hope. To the extent that appointment of a trained direc- tor of education shows awareness of the existence of that phase of the problem on the part of the governing authorities, the appointment is encouraging. title: THE LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL AND THE PENAL SYSTEM
full_text: THE LEGISLATIVE COUNCIL AND THE PENAL SYSTEM Maryland's penal system, particularly the setup for handling young men and boys, has been criticized severely in the last few days. Judge Edwin T. Dickerson and Judge George A. Solter, now presiding in the Criminal Courts, and Mr. J. Bernard Wells, State's Attorney, have each emphasized the need for a special institution for the older youth definitely disposed toward crime. The offender they have in mind cannot be sent to the Maryland Training School for Boys, the St. Mary's Industrial School or the Cheltenham School for (Negro) Boys. And he should not be sent, they say, to the Penitentiary, the House of Correction or the penal farm and allowed to mix with adult, hardened criminals. Such offenders, however, are being sentenced to these insti- tutions because there is no other place for them. Yesterday Mr. Robert F. Stanton, Police Commissioner, added an emphatic criticism to the same effect. That the four attacks on the penal system came one immediately after the other and with almost exquisite timing, may have been accidental. It may also have been accidental that three of the four critics decided to speak, on the very heels of the meeting here last week of the Big Brothers Association. It will be remembered that at that meeting Mr. James V. Bennett, director of the Fed- eral Bureau of Prisons, said that "behind almost every adult criminal is a juvenile delinquent." He pleaded for a concerted drive to "prevent the youth from becoming an adult criminal." But accidental or planned timing, the attacks by the four critics and the address by Mr. Bennett have served to direct atten- tion to Maryland's penal system. This at- tention should not be wasted. Maryland now has a Legislative Council that functions between sessions of the General Assembly. The council might begin to 'consider whether changes in our penal system are in order. title: NOT TOO FAST
full_text: NOT TOO FAST After several months of study, the com- mittee of the State Department of Educa- tion assigned to make educational recom. mendations for the Cheltenham School for Boys has made public its report. On the whole, the committee has done a thoughtful piece of work. It has placed its emphasis where it should be placed on the need of a real rehabilitation program at Cheltenham, to educate and train its inmates so they can be fitted for return to the community. But in one respect the committee seems to go too fast. It recommends that the insti- tution be restricted to boys of sufficient in- telligence to benefit from educational train- ing. To this end, it suggests that Cheltenham be given the power to set its own standards and reject those applicants it does not want. Specifically, this would mean turning more than one hundred feeble-minded boys over to Crownsville State Hospital, it appears, while the House of Correction would be asked to take those who seem to have crimi- nal tendencies. The desire to improve standards at Chel- tenham is an entirely laudable one, but the principle advocated here is dangerous. If each State institution is empowered to set its own admission standards, the courts of Maryland are likely to be left with a resid- ual group of urgent cases which no institu- tion will take. This condition already has been reached with regard to white boys and girls in the defective delinquent category, and some extremely vicious cases are at large in Baltimore at this moment. It would be highly undesirable to have a similar situa- tion exist with regard to Negro boys, for whom Cheltenham now makes provision. To recommend that the feeble-minded be sent to Crownsville is no solution, because Crownsville has room for only a limited number-about thirty-odd, at present. It may be equally impracticable to divert the younger criminal type to the House of Cor- rection. Rather, the solution would seem to be a proper type of segregation within Cheltenham itself. No plan for raising stand- ards can be accepted offhand which leads to the institution shirking its basic and residual responsibility for taking care of those Negro boys who must somehow be institutionalized. O'DONNELL Annapolis, March 14-Members of the State Legislative Council were told today that Maryland's relief bill -barring unforeseen and unpredict- able conditions-probably will be sta- bilized at its present figure, approxi- mately $5,000,000 a year. This information was given to the legislators by J. Milton Patterson, director of the State Department of Public Welfare, one of four public officials who made their appearance today before the special committee of the General Assembly. "Analyzing the present situation as well as it is possible to do at this time," said Mr. Patterson, "I believe that this department should not re- quest an increase in funds for the next biennium, but should attempt to meet the need within the present appro- priation of approximately $5,000,000." Will Have Figures To Show "I say this not because I believe that all need for assistance is now being taken care of adequately. For example, general public assistance is now far from adequate in many cases. When the time comes for preparing the budget we shall have the figures to show what the picture is. title: NATIONAL LEAGUE HITS "RIPPER BILL": CIVIL SERVICE REFORM GROUP ASKS GOVERNOR O'CONOR TO KILL MEASTIRE JONES' WORK DEFENDED AS BEST MERIT SYSTEM HAS EVER HAD
full_text: NATIONAL LEAGUE HITS "RIPPER BILL" Civil Service Reform Group Asks Governor O'Conor To Kill Measure Jones' Work Defended 'As Best Merit System Has Ever Had An organization outside of Mary- land yesterday aligned itself. with the opposition to the bill that would legis- late Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, out of office. The National Civil Service Reform League urged Governor O'Conor in a letter to disapprove House Bill 240, the so-called "ripper bill." The league described the three-man board which the bill proposes to sub- stitute for the employment commis- sioner as a "dubious experiment" and a threat to the Merit System. Fears Much. Loss E Stressing the advantage of a paid employment commissioner over three-man board, the letter said: "To abandon the present form of adminis- tration seems to us a change liable to result in much loss and no apparent gain." The letter, which was signed by H. Eliot Kaplan, executive director of the league, said States where there is a single commissioner or director have "won places in the scale of civil service administration far higher than most of the States with multi-mem- bered civil service commissions." Bill Passed By House Attacking the setup provided by the bill, which has been passed by the House and has been reported favor- ably in the Senate, the letter con- tinued: "A bipartisan board is all too fre- quently exactly what the adjective implies-representative of two politi- cal organizations, and its deliberations are apt to bow to political expediency. "Multi-membered control,. over, tends toward delay, uncertainty of action and the spreading of re- sponsibility which ought to be defi- nite." more- Mr. Kaplan will be the speaker at a massmeeting tomorrow night at the Polytechnic auditorium, sponsored by the Maryland Classified Employes Association, to rrotest, any and all inroads into the State civil service system by the Legislature. Uphold Jones' Work Local officers of the Civil Service Re- form League from time to time have upheld Mr. Jones, saying that he "is giving the Merit System the best ad- ministration it ever had in Maryland." At the very time the "ripper bill" was introduced, it was pointed out yesterday, legislation prepared under Mr. Jones' direction to standarize the salaries of thousands of Merit System employes was being introduced in both houses of the Legislature. The bills represented an aim of the Unemployment Commissioner since 1935. Walter H. Buck, a pioneer in civil service work, charged that the bill was aimed solely at Mr. Jones, and its purpose was to "get rid of" him "in the middle of his term when he is doing a good job.", Mr. Jones' attempts to raise the standards of employes at Cheltenham School for Boys, defeated by a legal decision, have been cited by several of the organizations that are protesting the move to legislate him out of office. The commissioner ordered the board at the school to dismiss twenty-six members of the staff as "physically and otherwise unfit" for duty. The board resorted to the courts and it was ruled - the staff at Cheltenham had been blanketed into the Merit System when the school came under State cirection. Other Efforts Mentioned Further mention was made of the commissioner's successful efforts last fall to prevent Merit System employes from engaging in political activity. Though the "ripper bill" was intro- duced by Delegate John S. White, majority floor leader in the House, Governor O'Conor has said it is not an administration measure, and has declared a hands-off attitude. Repeatedly on the floors of both houses the charge has been made that the bill is nothing but a "political maneuver" to shoot holes through the Merit System and open patronage fields to Democrats. title: STATE BONDS SOLD: ISSUE OF $1,587,000 PURCHASED BY SYNDICALE FOR 100.0577 MONEY TO BE USED FOR CONSTRUCTION AND EQUIPPING OF INSTITUTIONS
full_text: STATE BONDS SOLD AT RECORD FIGURE Issue Of $1,587,000 Purchased By Syndicate For 100.0577 Money To Be Used For Con- struction And Equipping Of Institutions (By the Associated Press] Annapolis, July 25-The sale of $1,587,000 in State bonds at the best price in Maryland's history was an- nounced today by the Board of Public Works, which will use the funds for construction and equipping of State institutions. The purchasing syndicate, headed by Blyth & Co., Inc., of New York, and Owen Daly & Co., of Baltimore, which submitted the bid, agreed to purchase the bonds, which bear 1½ per cent. Interest coupons, for 100.0577. The State will obtain the money at an average interest cost of 1.24 per cent. The next best sale was made July 27, 1938, when $3,413,000 on 1½ per cent bonds went for 101.182, an average cost to the State of 1.48 per cent. This was in the term of Governor Nice. Budget Balanced Governor O'Conor, chairman of the Public Works Board, said: "It is most gratifying to note the exceptionally high price at which Maryland bonds were sold today. This s positive proof that those who are in the best position to know consider the State's fiscal affairs in splendid con- lition. "For years, emphasis has been laid upon the necessity of having a balanced budget. We have now accomplished this result. Furthermore, it has long been felt that our State should not live on borrowed money and defray cur- rent expenses through loans. Financial House In Order "The program we have adopted adheres strictly to such a policy. An- other important factor is that after pursuing the most painstaking effort to determine the total State require- ments for the next two years, we Lackica the probiem and pui ini ward a tax program which would produce an adequate amount. All these con- siderations undoubtedly are reflected in the high bids. "I am pround that throughout the country our securities are valued so highly and that it is the consensus that our financial house is in order." title: O'CONOR PLANS INQUIRY INTO CHELTENHAM: WOULD END REPORTS OF BRUTALITY, STARVATION AND MISMANAGEMENT GOVERNOR SILENT AS TO WHETHER HE WILL REORGANIZE INSTITUTION
full_text: O'CONOR PLANS INQUIRY INTO CHELTENHAM Would End Reports Of Brutality, Starvation And Mismanagement Governor Silent As To Whether He Will Reor- ganize Institution By LOUIS J. O'DONNELL Governor O'Conor is determined to put an end to the oft-recurring re- ports of brutality, starvation and mis- management emanating from the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Cheltenham. He let it be known yesterday that he intends to make a personal investi- gation of conditions at the Prince George's county institution taken over by the State two years ago. The Governor revealed his plans! after a visit to his Annapolis office of a delegation-the third in as many days-protesting against the treatment of the Cheltenham inmates. Silent On Remedy + Whether he has in mind a reorgani- zation of the institution, or a complete shift in its personnel, the Governor declined to say. "I am going to find out what is nec- essary for me to do to rectify condi- tions that certainly must exist at Cheltenham," he said, "and then I am going to do it." The Cheltenham question has been in the news almost constantly since the State took it over in 1937. By court order the State was obliged to take over the personnel that operated it as a private institution. Refers To Charges From time to time inmates, investi- gators and ex-members of the staff have called practices there intolerable, - citing incidents of underfeeding and Ibeating of inmates and unsanitary and disease-breeding conditions. !, The personal investigation planned by the Governor is in line with a new policy he inaugurated yesterday- surveying State institutions and de- partments and attending meetings of various boards and commissions. Yesterday he attended a session of the Maryland Tuberculosis Sanatoria Board of Managers at the office of Dr. Warren H. Buckler, chairman. Will Study Data He came away with a mass of data and statistics for further study, in- cluding per capita cost comparisons with other States, a report on exist- ing facilities and needs and a break- down of the sanatoria's fiscal setup. He expects in the future to attend sessions of the State Roads Commis- sion, the State Tax Commission, the Board of Welfare and other such com- missions, and to make periodic calls on the heads of various other depart- ments. The Penitentiary, House of Correc- tion and Penal Farm and all the in- stitutions for handicapped and delin- quent children will be visited. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: REORGANIZATION ACTION DEFERRED: PUBLIC WORKS BOARD SEEKS MORE DATA ON STATE ROADS PROPOSAL PLANS TO REQUEST CHAIRMAN WHITMAN TO APPEAR BEFORE NEXT MEETING
full_text: REORGANIZATION ACTION DEFERRED Public Works Board Secks Morç Data On State Roads Proposal Plans To Request Chairman Whitman To Appear Before Next Meeting [By the Associated Press] Annapolis, Oct. 10-Approval of the State Roads Commission reorganiza- tion plan, which would oust eight present employes, was deferred today by the Board of Public Works. Governor O'Conor said the board felt additional data should be made available before the board takes final action. The board voted to call Ezra B. Whitman, chairman of the State Roads Commission, before its next meeting. Date for Whitman's appearance was not fixed, as the board meets on call of the Governor, To Abolish 23 Jobs Whitman's reorganization program calls for discontinuance of eighteen classified and five unclassified jobs. Transfers to other posts in the service would take care of all but eight pres- ent jobholders. The eight would be placed on the eligible list. Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, has approved the pro- posals, but approval of the Board of Public Works is necessary before the action becomes final. O'Conor said the board spent the balance of the five-hour session con- sidering budget amendments petitioned by the various divisions of the State government. Some Affect 1939 Budget Some of the changes sought affected items in the 1938-39 budget, and others pertained to the 1940-41 budget. O'Conor said the Cheltenham School for Negro Boys was granted per- mission to transfer $18,000 in unex- pended 1938-39 funds to a building fund for improvements at the school. In all, some fifty budget amendment applications were considered. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: FATE OF JONES' JOB HANGING IN BALANCE: SENATE GROUP'S VOTE TIED ON REPORT ON BILL ABOLISHING POST BALLOT INDICATES NO ACTION BY ADMINISTRATION TO SIDETRACK MEASURE
full_text: FATE OF JONES' JOB HANGING IN BALANCE - Senate Group's Vote Tied On Report On Bill Abolishing Post Ballot Indicates No Action By Administration To Sidetrack Measure [Annapolis Bureau of The Sun) Annapolis, March 21-The job of Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, teetered in the balance tonight so far as the Legislature is concerned. By a vote of 6 to 6, with one member not voting, the Senate Finance Com- mittee tied on the question of whether a favorable report should be returned on a House bill that would legislate Mr. Jones out of office and replace him with a three-man policy-making board. The Senate committee's vote indi. cated that nothing has been done by the administration forces of Governor O'Conor to sidetrack the measure, which has been described as a "ripper". bill, holding dire possibilities for the State's Merit System. The Senate committee's vote on the Jones bill was taken during a three- hour session that body held tonight in an effort to clear its files. Defends His Policies !! Mr. Jones, the employment commis sioner, had appeared before the com- mittee this afternoon to answer charges of the author of the ripper bill that he administered his office in a "czaristic" and "arbitrary" ma....er.; - The bill's sponsor is Delegate John S. White (Dem., Prince George's), ad- ministration floor leader in the House, which already has approved the move to fire the employment commissioner. - Some of the Senators who balloted for the bill tonight, it was said, did so with the understanding that Mr. Jones would be included in the three- man board which would set the policy for a director of State employment under the terms of the White bill. There is no way, unless this would be included specifically in the White bill, that the Legislature could have any assurance that Mr. Jones would be continued as a member of the board. The board, proposed under the White bill, would be unsalaried, whereas Mr. Jones now is paid $6,000 a year and his term of office runs until 1941. Long Session Held The Senate committee's meeting to- night was one of the longest it has held and, when it was adjourned, Senator Dudley G. Roe (Dem., Queen Anne's), majority floor leader and chairman, announced that twenty measures had been voted favorable reports during the three-hour session, "Our files are practically clear," he said. "So far as the Finance Com- mittee is concerned, we could go home (Continued on Page 4, Column 2) FATE OF JONES' JOB HANGS IN BALANCE Senate Committee's Vote Is Tied On Report On Bill Abolishing Post Ballot Indicates Lack Of Ac- tion By Administration To Sidetrack Measure (Continued from Page 26) within the next few days. There are only three controversial measures still to be acted upon the fireworks bill, women's jury service and the Jones bill. "There have been 360, bills intro- duced in the Senate, and, of these 206 have been passed, not to mention those that will be left to die in committee." To Have Choice Senator A. Raymond Marvel (Dem., Talbot) is the sponsor of a bill that would require primary elections pre- paratory to the filling of Congressional vacancies. He will be given his choice as to whether the measure shall die in committee or be killed on the floor. The Finance Committee voted for an unfavorable report tonight. Appearing at the invitation of the Finance Committee, Mr. Jones this afternoon told the Senators that he rarely ever made an important move in the administration of the Merit System without consulting the At- torney General. And, he added, the Attorney General from whom he asked for most of the opinions he has on file to guide him was Governor O'Conor. Received Forty Opinions "Where the previous Employment Commissioner from 1920 until 1934 asked for and received but one opin- ion," he read to the committee from a letter he had sent Senator Roe, the chairman, "from 1935 to date I have asked for and received forty opinions, and I have conducted the Merit Sys- tem strictly in accordance therewith. : "Does this look as if I have con- ducted this department in an arbitrary manner, or exhibited any of the at- tributes of a czar?" After Mr. Jones had talked for two hours, reading his letter, answering questions and making his recom- mendations on his department's budget, a member of the committee, Senator Wilmer C. Carter (Dem., Third, Balti- more) jumped to his feet and said: "I know it is out of order, but I wish it were possible for this committee to give you a vote of complete confi- dence. The State is lucky to have such a man as you in public office. : "I hope to God the Senate, by an overwhelming vote, will defeat this bill." The measure would replace the pres- ent Employment Commissioner with an unpaid, three-man body, which would hire a director with duties similar somewhat to those of Mr. Jones. During House debate, while the pro- posal was going through the lower chamber, it was said that Mr. White had introduced it solely because of Mr. Jones' actions in attempting to get rid of employes of Cheltenham Reform School for Negro Boys, which is in Mr. White's home county. |.

Jones, State Employment Commissioner, teetered in the balance tonight so far as the Legislature is concerned. By a vote of 6 to 6, with one member not voting, the Senate Finance Com- mittee tied on the question of whether a favorable report should be returned on a House bill that would legislate Mr. Jones out of office and replace him with a three-man policy-making board. The Senate committee's vote indi. cated that nothing has been done by the administration forces of Governor O'Conor to sidetrack the measure, which has been described as a "ripper". bill, holding dire possibilities for the State's Merit System. The Senate committee's vote on the Jones bill was taken during a three- hour session that body held tonight in an effort to clear its files. Defends His Policies !! Mr. Jones, the employment commis sioner, had appeared before the com- mittee this afternoon to answer charges of the author of the ripper bill that he administered his office in a "czaristic" and "arbitrary" ma....er.; - The bill's sponsor is Delegate John S. White (Dem., Prince George's), ad- ministration floor leader in the House, which already has approved the move to fire the employment commissioner. - Some of the Senators who balloted for the bill tonight, it was said, did so with the understanding that Mr. Jones would be included in the three- man board which would set the policy for a director of State employment under the terms of the White bill. There is no way, unless this would be included specifically in the White bill, that the Legislature could have any assurance that Mr. Jones would be continued as a member of the board. The board, proposed under the White bill, would be unsalaried, whereas Mr. Jones now is paid $6,000 a year and his term of office runs until 1941. Long Session Held The Senate committee's meeting to- night was one of the longest it has held and, when it was adjourned, Senator Dudley G. Roe (Dem., Queen Anne's), majority floor leader and chairman, announced that twenty measures had been voted favorable reports during the three-hour session, "Our files are practically clear," he said. "So far as the Finance Com- mittee is concerned, we could go home (Continued on Page 4, Column 2) FATE OF JONES' JOB HANGS IN BALANCE Senate Committee's Vote Is Tied On Report On Bill Abolishing Post Ballot Indicates Lack Of Ac- tion By Administration To Sidetrack Measure (Continued from Page 26) within the next few days. There are only three controversial measures still to be acted upon the fireworks bill, women's jury service and the Jones bill. "There have been 360, bills intro- duced in the Senate, and, of these 206 have been passed, not to mention those that will be left to die in committee." To Have Choice Senator A. Raymond Marvel (Dem., Talbot) is the sponsor of a bill that would require primary elections pre- paratory to the filling of Congressional vacancies. He will be given his choice as to whether the measure shall die in committee or be killed on the floor. The Finance Committee voted for an unfavorable report tonight. Appearing at the invitation of the Finance Committee, Mr. Jones this afternoon told the Senators that he rarely ever made an important move in the administration of the Merit System without consulting the At- torney General. And, he added, the Attorney General from whom he asked for most of the opinions he has on file to guide him was Governor O'Conor. Received Forty Opinions "Where the previous Employment Commissioner from 1920 until 1934 asked for and received but one opin- ion," he read to the committee from a letter he had sent Senator Roe, the chairman, "from 1935 to date I have asked for and received forty opinions, and I have conducted the Merit Sys- tem strictly in accordance therewith. : "Does this look as if I have con- ducted this department in an arbitrary manner, or exhibited any of the at- tributes of a czar?" After Mr. Jones had talked for two hours, reading his letter, answering questions and making his recom- mendations on his department's budget, a member of the committee, Senator Wilmer C. Carter (Dem., Third, Balti- more) jumped to his feet and said: "I know it is out of order, but I wish it were possible for this committee to give you a vote of complete confi- dence. The State is lucky to have such a man as you in public office. : "I hope to God the Senate, by an overwhelming vote, will defeat this bill." The measure would replace the pres- ent Employment Commissioner with an unpaid, three-man body, which would hire a director with duties similar somewhat to those of Mr. Jones. During House debate, while the pro- posal was going through the lower chamber, it was said that Mr. White had introduced it solely because of Mr. Jones' actions in attempting to get rid of employes of Cheltenham Reform School for Negro Boys, which is in Mr. White's home county. |.

title: As To Cheltenham And Discipline
full_text: As To Cheltenham And Discipline TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: I have been much distressed lately over the situation at Cheltenham and fear great injustice is being done the personnel down there. I have known the institu- tion for nearly thirty years and have had a succession of boys from there dur- ing that time. These hoys lived in my home and came to look on me almost as a mother. They confided in me as any small boy would, and the most severe punishment they told me of was heing locked up on bread and water when they needed dis- cipline. Some of these boys were pretty tough characters too, but none com- plained of being beaten or ill-treated physically. Some of the boys, I am glad to say, were such good children we be- came much attached to them. ... After reading the articles that have appeared in the papers from time to time, I am beginning to believe the fire that is being set to burn under officials there is because they could not be re- moved from the institution legally, as their contract, when it was turned over to the State, called for the continuance of all employés. Now I fear this agita- tion over cruelty to the boys is being fanned to a flame of indignation, so the employés can be separated from their livelihood. I've known the very able superintend- ent, Mr. B. B. Sunderland (affection- ately known to several generations of boys as "Big Ben"), for many years. As placing agent for the boys, who were sent to farm homes, he visited my home and the boys twice a year. Knowing him as I do, I cannot believe him guilty of cruelty, or inhumanity, nor do I be- lieve he would allow it in a subordinate. I also believe he, or any other superin- tendent, would need to govern with a very firen hand, if he is to keep control of several hundred colored boys. Many so incorrigible that they were a menace and nuisance in their own communities, and who have no respect for any man who is easy and unable to enforce his rules physically. After all it must be kept in mind that this is a penal institution and the boys are sent there to learn to respect some authority. I challenge any of the critles to keep such a collection of boys in order for one week and see if they can command respect and obedience, unless backed up by physical discipline. I fear the present-day leaders of youth are depending too much on per- suasion. In raising six fine men and women in my own family, I found a little physical punishment would do much more to clear the atmosphere and impress a child with the need for obedi- ency. If this course of training goes much further I very much fear our country will be filled with inconsiderate girls and boys who have no respect for God or man. Mns. GEORGE DAVIDSON. Annapolis, Aug. 10. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

title: Seeks To Fix Blame For Beating Of Boys: Employment Commissioner Places Charges Against Cottage Master At Cheltenham
full_text: Seeks To Fix Blame For Beating Of Boys Employment Commissioner Places Charges Against Cottage Mas- ter At Cheltenham An effort to determine who is re- sponsible for the alleged beating of inmates at the Cheltenham School for Colored Boys will be made by Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commis- sioner, Mr. Jones yesterday placed charges against Andrew Beckwith, a' cottage master at the school, for allegedly assaulting two Negro boys, about 14 years old, when they tusseled over a bed in the cell to which they were confined. Beckwith has five days to answer the charges. Mr. Jones explained he wanted to find out whether such beatings were wanton acts of individual employes at the institution, or on orders from the superintendent, B. B. Sunderland. If the beating of inmates is Sunderland's policy, then Beckwith cannot be blamed, Mr. Jones said. ! Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: CHELTENHAM RIOT BY 125 IS QUELLED: STATE AND COUNTY POLICE ARE CALLED AS BOYS SMASH WINDOWS, BENCHES TWO ALLEGED RINGLEADERS ARE PUT IN SOLITARY AFTER UNEXPLAINED REVOLT LLEIIVLLY ARMED .SQUADS OF SLATE AND LOCAL POLICE WERE RUSHED TO THE NEARBY CHELTENHAM SCHOOL FOR BOYS TONIGHT TO QUELL A RIOT OF INMATES.
full_text: CHELTENHAM RIOT BY 125 IS QUELLED State And County Police Arc Called As Boys Smash Windows, Benches Two Alleged Ringleaders Are Put In Solitary After Un- explained Revolt Special Dispatch to The Sunl Marlboro, Md., Sept. 15-Heavily armed squads of State and local police were rushed to the nearby Chelten- ham School for Boys tonight to quell Ja riot of inmates. The disturbance had been ended, about 125 boys participating had been herded into a cottage and two alleged ringleaders placed in solitary confine- ment by attendants by the time the officers, armed with shotguns and tear gas, arrived. Begins At Lunch The mutiny began at lunch, when hoys living in two cottages at the Negro Reformatory began hurling the luncheon dishes at each other. At dinner they refused to say grace, then surged into a yard, smashing windows and breaking up playground benches. B. B. Sunderland, superintendent, said the damage to the institution was slight. Blames "Troublemaker" He described one of the boys placed in solitary as a chronic troublemaker, and said the other was being held on suspicion of helping incite the riot. Neither he nor the police who an- swered the riot call could ascribe any definite reason for the outbreak. Police, who said the food was good and the discipline not severe, said they believed it was "just plain devilment." Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: CONTINUING SCANDAL
full_text: CONTINUING SCANDAL Cheltenham, the reform school for colored boys, has been a continuing stench for more years than most people can remember. It was a discredit to the State when it was run as a private institution. Now that it is publicly owned and operated, tales of in- competence and cruelty continue to emanate from it. The explanation offered for the situation is that, under the terms of the law by which the State took title, it was impossible to oust the previous management. It is a fact that Governo: Nice asked the members of the board to resign so that he might appoint their successors and that the mem- bers refused. It is further true that Colonel Jones, the State Employment Commissioner, did make a valiant but unsuccessful fight to replace the present personnel with one that had stood the test of the State Merit System. But the legal obstacles thus cited are hardly a sufficient excuse for the continuation of a régime which one grand jury after another has seen fit to condemn. The people of Maryland pay for the support of the place. It is hardly creditable that, having control of the purse strings, they are forever estopped from saying how their oney should be spent. Governor O'Conor is a resourceful man, both in politics and in the law. It should not be beyond his capacity to find a way to break through the barrier which the board and managers of Cheltenham have set up about themselves, so that some light may shine in the dark places. THE OPPOSITION Mayor Jackson issued a call. Monday night for the defeat in the coming Mayoralty elec- tion of City Councilman Daniel Ellison. Why Mr. Jackson in his exuberance singled 'out Mr. Ellison. for special slaughter was not made clear. It probably was due to the fact that Mr. Ellison is a Republican breakwater against which Democratic hopes have been dashed for sixteen long years. For twelve of those years Mr. Ellison was the sole repre- sentative of his party in the City Council. All this can mean but one thing. A majority of those who go to the polls in the Fourth district like the representation they get through Mr. Ellison. ۱ It is not difficult to applaud the Fourth district for the support it has given Mr. Ellison in the past or to hope the support will be continued next month. As the lone Re- publican in the City Council, Mr. Ellison has served a useful purpose. His has been too often a voice in the wilderness, but the voice was there if the Democrats wished to follow it. Without Mr. Ellison in his usual place in the front row, meetings of the City Council would be even more deadly than they are now. Mr. Jackson might be "satisfied" if Mr. Ellison does not go back to the City Council, but why wreck what has become a public institution merely to please Mr. Jackson's too ardent partisanship? : Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: CROWNSVILLE IMPROVEMENTS COMPLETED: FOUR ADDITIONS TO STATE HOSPITAL TO BE INSPECTED WEDNESDAY INSTITUTION TO TAKE MANY CHILDREN FROM 500 NOW ON WAITING LIST
full_text: CROWNSVILLE IMPROVEMENTS COMPLETED Four Additions To State Hospital To Be Inspected Wednesday Institution To Take Many Children From 500-Now ン On Waiting List Four additions to the Crownsville State Hospital, have been completed and are to be inspected Wednesday by the board of managers of the in- stitution, it was announced yesterday. Two of the additions are to the building for feeble-minded children, and will enlarge the capacity from 90 beds to 200. The other additions are to the main building, to provide -more space for occupational therapy and add to the employes' dining room. 500 On Waiting List.. Dr. Gustave H. Faubert, resident physician of the feeble-minded chil- dren's group, said that as soon as the buildings could be equipped-in a month or two-the hospital would take children from the 500 now on the waiting list to fill the new beds. The children will come from the Cheltenham School for Boys and other Negro institutions which have been housing the children until they could get hospital care, he explained. Improvements Cost $140,000- The Crownsville building program has been undertaken with State ap- propriations to the institution supple- mented by a forty-five per cent. grant from the Public Works Administra- tion. Cost, of the four additions was approximately $140,000. The architects were Crisp & Edmunds, of Baltimore. The institution is the only one in the State for Negro insane and feeble- minded. The first unit for feeble- minded patients was completed in 1937. The superintendent' is Dr. R. P. Winterode. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: CHELTENHAM Ii disorders at Cheltenham require the summoning of police officers to quell the dis- turbance, it is strongly indicated that the management of Maryland's reformatory for colored boys is not yet up to the expectations of the people of the State. When the institu- tion was taken over by the State, it was assumed that the glaring defects in adminis- tration at Cheltenham would be promptly remedied so that there would be an end to the procession of rumors and dismal stories from that stepchild among Maryland institu- tions. title: BECKWITH RESIGNS CHELTENHAM POST: COLLAGE MASTER DENIES HE BEAT BOY, BUT ASKS NO HEARING LETTER ACCUSES JONES OF CONSTANT INTERFERENCE AT INSTITUTION
full_text: BECKWITH RESIGNS CHELTENHAM POST - Cottage Master Denies He Beat Boy, But Asks No Hearing Letter Accuses Jones Of Con- stant Interference Ai Institution Andrew T. Beckwith, suspended cottage master at the Cheltenham re- formatory, resigned his post yesterday in a letter to Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner. Beckwith denied Jones' charges that he brutally beat and manhandled two Cheltenham inmates. His letter did not ask for a hearing but criticized the employment com- missioner for "constant interference" in the affairs of the Southern Mary- land Negro institution. Beckwith was suspended by Jones after an investigation ordered by Gov- ernor Nice. He was given until yes- terday to answer the complaint and request a formal trial before Jones, as is customary under the State civil service law. Incompetence Charged Charges against him included in- competence and inemciency, "wantonly careless or negligent or brutal" treat- ment of inmates; "wantonly offensive" conduct, and a general charge of con- duct unbecoming a State employe. Jones said Beckwith was accused of beating one Negro boy over the head with a padlock, whipping him and otherwise manhandling him, as well as beating another inmate. "Your charges are absolutely un- founded," Beckwith's answer asserted. "I have the unsolicited evidence of five witnesses who were present that I did not assault the boys as you allege." Says Boys Tried To Escape Beckwith said the "real facts" were that the two boys, Walter Thomas and Elwood Waters, were attempting to escape by propping a bed up be- neath the window of a cell in which they had been placed for punishment. The cottage master said he dis- covered the escape attempt when he carried in the youths' supper and ordered the bed removed. "I merely shook Thomas and did not beat either of them," Beckwith asserted, adding the cell padlock re- mained on its insp after he entered the room. The night watchman, Beck- with's wife and three other inmates would testify to those facts, he con- tinued. "I understand that you have fled the charges against me and that you (Continued on Page 4, Column 5) BECKWITH RESIGNS CHELTENHAM POST Cottage Master Denies He Beat Boy, But Asks No Hearing Letter Accuses Jones Of Con- stant Interference At Institution (Continued from Page 200 also expect to hear the charges against me," his letter continued. "In other words, you would be both the prosecu- tor and the judge. Fortunately I will not be placed in the position of having such a prejudiced judge. Obtains Another Position "While I was away (on a trip to Maine) 1 obtained a position in a place where I had worked many years before and which is a far better posi- tion than the one I have at Chelten- ham... "Your constant interference with things at Cheltenham has made it very hard for everybody there. You seem possessed of a great desire to run things and feel that nobody else has any sense. I am very glad per- sonally to be rid of you but feel sorry for the rest of the officers and cm- ployes at Cheltenham or any other place you may have anything to do with." Commissioner Jones said Beckwith "had every opportunity to say all that at the preliminary henring but failed to do so." "It is evident that he had adequate assistance in preparing his letter," Jones added. "So far the boy (Thomas) is concerned, he was either struck by a padlock or a meteor."

title: Thirty-five Years at Morgan College: RETIRING, DR. SPENCER LEAVES A COLLEGE BUILT BY HIS ACTIVITY
full_text: IT Thirty-five Years at Morgan College RETIRING, DR. SPENCER LEAVES A COLLEGE BUILT BY HIS ACTIVITY by GRACE S. PARKS LT was in 1002 that Dr. John F. Goucher, from whom Goucher College took its name, wrote to the principal of the Hudson River Institute at Claverack, N. Y., and invited him to head Morgan College-at that time a small Baltimore institution with two strug- gling branches, a woefully small faculty and student body, and a deficit. The Claverack principal, John Oakley Spencer, already knew about Morgan, and was aware of the need for a much more ener- getic school for the higher education of Ne- groes. He accepted Dr. Goucher's tender, but with the condition that the board of trustees grant him the privilege of mapping out and carrying out his own program, which he made clear was for swift improvement of the col- lege's educational facilities. How faithfully the board's pledge was kept is illustrated by a member's humorous summary of its be- havior: "He proposes; we agree," he ob- served. It seems to have been a good policy, anyway. Now, having spent thirty-five years of hard driving for Morgan College, Dr. Spencer will retire from the presidency next Wednes- day, to be succeeded by Dwight O. W. Holmes, lately dean of Howard University's Graduate School. As president emeritus, how ever, Dr. Spencer will continue his contact with the college until the stadium is com- pleted and a library erected. The stadium is a Federal project; the Maryland General Assembly this year appropriated $100,000 for a library building.  THE LIBRARY in the St. Paul street home of Dr. Spencer is lined with bookshelves, with a new book occupying a place of prominence. It is called "A Resolution: a faint gesture to indicate the permanent place which he will hold in the love and esteem of those who this day have gathered to honor him.. ." It is signed by the four hundred persons who met to pay tribute to the veteran educator at a testimonial banquet last May. That was a notable occasion for a modest scholar, but Dr. Spencer laughingly says he attracted still more attention on one occasion in 1857. During that year people for miles around visited his birthplace on a farm near the Wyoming Valley, Pennsylvania. The at- traction in the old red house there was the 1 pound 7-ounce baby of Sarah Rachel and Henry A. Spencer named John Oakley. The farm clung to a spur of mountains on the Indian trail where the Delawares had fashioned arrowheads. Dr. Spencer cannot understand why his grandfather, who went to Pennsylvania to survey Connecticutis "West- ern Reserve," ever settled in such a rough and rugged place, but maybe it was to de- yelop a rugged grandson. When a weaving "bee" day arrived and the neighbors brought rags to weave carpets at his home, Dr. Spencer asys, his mother was ill. But the "bee" had to be fed, so he cooked the dinner, carrying the ingredients for the cake and biscuits to his mother's bedside, where, following her directions, he prepared them for baking. When some one asked who cooked the dinner the abashed boy hung his head and fled from the house. Dr. Spencer remembers, too, the vicissi- tudes of farm life following the Civil War, when barter was the medium of exchange for commodities. Two events connected with that period are etched on his memory; one, the - return of the soldiers at the close of the war; the other, his grief-stricken father staggering into the house and crying out, "Lincoln is shot!" MOST of his 80-year span of life has been spent in. schools and colleges. When he was a baby, in order to relieve his mother of his care, a cousin, who taught a "select school," carried him to school with her. At the age of 5 he was a pupil in a small country school. title: NOTHING UNUSUAL
full_text: "NOTHING UNUSUAL" The more we hear about the state of affair in Cheltenham the more in need of thorougl investigation the conduct of that institution seems to be. The news was bad enough on Saturday, when the State Employment Com missioner, Mr. Jones, reported to the Gov ernor that a cottage master had hit one of the inmates on the head with a padlock and that the boy, on emerging from several days' con finement for the theft of a few cigars, had beer further beaten with a rubber hose. Now the admission of Mr. Sunderland, the head of the school, that beating the boys with rubber hose is nothing unusual makes the picture all the worse. This admission needs to be considered in connection with the statement of the Employ- ment Commissioner that the conduct card of the boy, whose punishment is in question in the charges against the cottage master, showed no record of confinement in a cell, nor a beating. If it is usual to flog boys at Chelten- ham with a rubber hose, as Mr. Sunderland says, and if careful records of such floggings are not kept, then it would seem that disci- pline is on a very helter-skelter basis. And it is decidedly against the public interest to have discipline on a helter-skelter basis in an insti- tution dedicated to the reclamation of young Negro delinquents. The work of reforming colored boys, and making them into good citi- zens who will not be menaces to society when they are discharged, is too serious a task to be handled except in the most careful and discriminate manner. The admission as to the usualness of rubber-hose beatings raises issues entirely too broad to be settled at a hearing on charges against a single cottage master. The State's responsibility in this matter requires that the Governor take a hand and arrange for a thor- ough ventilation of what goes on at Chelten- ham. If the courts should decide that as the law now stands there can be no house-clean- ing at this institution, it will be imperative for the next Legislature to change the law, and it is in order for the Governor now to take appropriate steps to prepare the way for such a contingency. title: 11 Jailed After Second Riot At Cheltenham: Disorder Termed "Reactive Hangover" From Thursday's Trouble At Reformatory
full_text: 11 Jailed After Second Riot At Cheltenham Disorder Termed "Reactive Hang- over" From Thursday's Trouble At Reformatory Upper Marlboro, Md., July 17 (AP). The second riot in two days at the House of Reformation, in nearby Cheltenham, resulted today in the jailing of eleven Negro youths whom Superintendent Sunderland of the re- formatory termed ringleaders. Arthur Hepburn, superintendent of police of Prince George's county, said all 105 inmates of one cottage smashed tables, benches and windows last night in what he described as a "reactive hangover" from a riot Thursday night when 100 boys escaped. All were re- captured. Hepburn said the youths iailed prob- ably would appear before Police Court Judge George B. Merrick Monday. State's Attorney Alan Bowie had not determined what charges he would lodge against them. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: Negro Sent To Jail After Year At Cut Term Doubled By Magistrate Eck- hardt For Violation Of Traffic Laws + A Negro said to have been released from the House of Correction nine days ago, after serving a year for auto- mobile larceny, yesterday was sen- tenced to serve two years in jail on similar charges. He was James Miller, 21, of the 100 black West Preston street. Magistrate George Eckhardt, Jr., sentenced him (in Traffic Court to serve a year for unauthorized use of an automobile, a year for operating the automobile after his application for a license had been refused, to run consecutively, and Gued him $5 and costs on each of two minor charges. title: ASKS CHELTENHAM ACTION BE QUASHED: O'CONOR FILES PETITION IN CIRCUIT COURT FOR PRINCE GEORGE'S COUNTY SAYS BOARD'S SAIL SHOULD HAVE BEEN FILED IN BALTIMORE--CONFERENCE PLANNED
full_text: ASKS CHELTENHAM ACTION BE QUASHED O'Conor Files Petition In Cir- cuit Court For. Prince George's County Says Board's Suit Should Have Been Filed In Balti- more-Conference Planned Herbert R. O'Conor, Attorney Gen- cral, fired the first gun in the State's legal battle with the board of the Chel- tenham School for Boys by filing a petition yesterday in the Circuit Court for Prince George's county, asking to have the board's suit quashed. The suit was filed on behalf of Joseph K. Cox, one of the Cheltenham employes, to test the right of the State to refuse to accept a group of more than twenty employes classified unfit for the State service. as Called Preliminary Skirmish Mr. O'Conor contended the suit should be quashed because it was un- reasonable to expect Harry C. Jones. State Employment Commissioner, to answer it in a part of the State where ne does not reside. The suit should have been brought in Baltimore, the Attorney General said, The Attorney General's action is re- garded as a preliminary skirmish. which will be followed eventually by a court argument of the State Employ- ment Commissioner's powers. Parley With Nice Planned Meanwhile, a committee of the Ne- gro reformatory's board prepared to go to Governor Nice to discuss the whole situation with him. It will comprise Howard C. Hill, Dr. John O. Spencer, M. Hampton Magruder and Joseph Blandford, chairman, The board contends that, in taking over Cheltenham, the State is com- pelled to receive its employes into the Merit System, regardless of fitness. The State refuses to accept them unless they pass the same fitness test applied to other State employes. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: LINKS POLITICIANS WITH CHELTENHAM: REV. DR. FREDERICK DOUGLAS EXPLAINS HIS RESIGNATION FROM BOARD CONTINUES IN HIS POST AS CHIEF PAROLE OFFICER, HOWEVER
full_text: LINKS POLITICIANS WITH CHELTENHAM Rev. Dr. Frederick Douglas Explains His Resignation From Board Continues In His Post As Chief Parole Officer, However Hints at political maneuvering at the Cheltenham School for Boys were made last night by the Rev. Dr. Fred- erick Douglas, pastor of Douglas Me- morial Community Church, in explain- ing his resignation and that of three other Negro members of the school's board. Dr. Douglas, however, will continue as chief parole officer at the institu- tion. Called "Wonder Workers" The four who resigned, including Willard W. Allen, Joseph Briscoe and Dr. George McDonald, quit in order to make room for "wonder workers" to be appointed by Governor Nice, Dr. Douglas said. The Governor recently demanded the board accept reorgani- zation plans, submit plans of its own, or resign. The board has refused to comply. "There are pioneers in every great movement, and I am profoundly grate- ful to our good Governor for making it possible for me to be one of the pioneers in initiating the much-needed reforms that are being so strongly urged at this time," Dr. Douglas said in a statement. Competent Man Needed "Together with the Messrs. Mc- Donald. Briscoe, Allen, Spencer and Hill, I have helped make Cheltenham a State institution, and when the mat- ter came before the board for the selection of a superintendent, six members, namely, Dr. George Mc- Donald, Prof. Joseph Briscoe, Willard W. Allen, Dr. John O. Spencer, Howard C. Hill and myself, contended that the institution needed a competent super- intendent. "We felt that it ought to be the chief concern of the board to select a man specifically trained for that work, and that was the most impor- tant thing to be considered. Hence, we went on record as being opposed to the present incumbent, but, being in the minority, our wishes were de- feated. Cites "Political Leaders" "We had been told by some so-called political leaders of our own group that we ought to contend for an entire Negro personnel. "We should like to see the wish of these folk gratified, but we fail to find a way in which this can be accom- plished immediately, because anybody with two grains of common sense ought to know that six men can never outvote nine, and, even if it were pos- sible to so maneuver Roberts' rules of order to the effect that a minority vote should have precedence over the majority, there are any number of things entering into the situation down there that would not make it a wise thing to try to accomplish overnight." Five Vacancies Next Month Dr. Douglas explained there were five vacancies to occur on the board next month-the posts of the four re- signed members and that of Dr. Spencer, a white member. "We have been told on good au- thority that our good Governor has promised to reappoint Dr. Spencer and to replace the four colored men, who have labored faithfully and well, with four other colored men who shall be able to get things done at Cheltenhan in shorter order than we have been able to do; and, since he has promised our positions to these wonder workers, we folk who have been there all these years and have had every opportunity to do what they are now anxious to do, we thought it might be a good idea to let Governor Nice have the pleasure of appointing them to the board at the earliest possible moment." Dr. Douglas added that "it must be remembered that Cheltenham has been under fire for years and that the con- ditions that obtain there are not of recent development, but the result of years of inactivity on the part of the colored people of the State and neglect on the part of the dominant group who largely, if not entirely, dictated the management of the in- stitution." Resignations Voluntary, Governor Nice Asserts Commenting on the statement of the Rev. Dr. Frederick Douglas on conditions prevailing at the Chelten- ham School for Boys, Governor Nice last night said: "The resignations of the four mem- bers that I have received came to me voluntarily, and I quite agree with the Rev. Dr. Douglas that six never can outvote nine. I know that the four who have resigned have done the best that they could under trying circum- stances and insurmountable handicaps. "I know that they resigned in order that their people might be furnished the opportunity of learning that their best efforts in the face of these handi- caps could not prevail. "I do not for a moment think that I can replace them with wonder work- ers. There can be no correction of the ! terrible conditions short of majority appointments to the board. I feel that the four have done to the limit the best they could under the handicap- ping circumstances." Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: CHELTENHAM ISSUE TO GET COURT TEST: BOARD ANNOUNCES PURPOSE AFTER PARLEY WITH JONES ON PERSONNEL COMMISSIONER HITS LACK OF PERSPECTIVE AND INITIATIVE
full_text: CHELTENHAM ISSUE TO GET COURT TEST Board Announces Purpose After Parley With Jones On Personnel Commissioner Hits Lack Of Perspective And Initiative Howard C. Hill, member of the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys, said last night the board would take its controversy with Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, over personnel issues into court. Hill said the decision was reached at a conference between a committee from the board and Jones. He an- nounced: "The seeming conflict between the merit system act and the act making Cheltenham a State institution will be taken to court for settlement. The procedure has not been finally de- cided." May Center On Pay Roll He indicated the court test possibly would be precipitated by submitting a pay roll to Jones, including the names of twenty-six employes Jones has ordered dismissed, then seeking a mandamus action when Jones refuses to sign it. At the start of the conference, Jones told the committee that the "lack of perspective and initiative" character- izing private management of the in- stitution could not continue under State direction. Jones, who has recommended dis- missal of half of Cheltenham's per- sonnel as "unfit for any State serv- ice," warned a committee of board members that the board must accept the State's plan for reorganizing the school or contest it in court. Clause In Act At Issue Cheltenham became a part of the State penal system last October 1, by an act of the 1937 Legislature. At issue yesterday was a section of the 1937 act requiring Cheltenham em- ployes to be blanketed into the State merit system without examination. "This is impossible," Jones told the committee, at a conference called to discuss "technicalitics" in a reor- ganization plan Jones offered the Cheltenham board last week. The board asked for the conference. He asserted that "whoever was re- sponsible" for drawing the legisla- tion transferring Cheltenham to the State was not "entirely candid." "They concealed from both the Gov- ernor and the Legislature what they must have known," he contended, re- ferring to the authors of the bill, "about the obvious unfitness of the employes an unfitness which caused them to reserve the sum of t $30,000 to take care of such of the (Continued on Page 4, Column 6) employes as might be rejected in a contingency such as now has arisen." Under private management, Jones said, the Southern Maryland reforma- tory, "like many other similar insti- tutions, has failed in its mission" chiefly because of lack of funds, lack of experienced technical direction and the "virtual admission by all con- cerned that the institution was a local project fostered by local interests and having little to do with the State as a whole." Cheltenham's development since its founding sixty-seven years ago has been retarded, Jones said, by divi- sion of responsibilities and "well- meaning but inadequate efforts." Its managers must "make a clean break" with past practices under the State's direction, he warned. Should the board contest his posi- tion in court, he added, "the Com- missioner doubts exceedingly whether, in the well-known state of public opinion as regards Cheltenham, any Maryland court will assume a respon- sibility which the State Employment Commissioner has definitely declined." He asserted the institution's future depends on its personnel as well as its management and he felt the con- struction he placed on the Chelten- ham legislation was "sensible and practicable." Urges Acceptance in Principle He said he "refused to believe" the Legislature "intended that Chelten ham should be continued as it is now being run for the next generatior under State auspices and at the State's expense." Jones advised the committee that, in his opinion, the board should ap- prove his recommendations in prin- ciple and appoint another committee to confer with him in connection with placing them in operation as "promptly as circumstances will permit." Jones said he wanted to "make one thing clear"-that "nothing in my survey or in this memorandum sanc- tions the continuance of the super- intendent, assistant superintendent, executive secretary, director and parole officer" of the institution in their present jobs. Considers Contributory State Retirement System Maryland is contemplating shifting some of the burden of its State em- ployes' retirement system onto the employes, Harry C. Jones, State Em- ployment Commissioner, disclosed yesterday. Jones, supervising head of the State's present pay-as-you-go retire- ment plan, said the system's board of trustees was investigating a "contribu- tory pension system set up on actuarial lines." Under the pay-as-you-go policy the State carries the entire pension load, appropriating fixed sums annually to care for the pension fund. Under the contributory system, the State would match contributions from employes, whose portion would be deducted from their salaries. Jones, ex-officio secretary of the board, said he and the chairman of The board, William S. Gordy, Jr., State Comptroller, had held a preliminary conference with George Buck, actuary of the State teachers' retirement sys- em and the Baltimore city employes' Dension system, on the contributory pian. Pending presentation of the new system to the Legislature, Jones said, the, pay-as-you-go system would "doubtless" be continued. The plan, marking the State's first retirement system for classified employes, was set up last year with a $40,000 appro- priation for 1938.

full_text: Pre-Views Arthur GuiteRMAN wrote the libretto for the new all-American opera, with music by Walter Damrosch, which was produced recently. It is the classic story of "The Man Without a Country." Guiterman is one of America's most popular writers of "light" verse, but underneath the rip- pling rhythms, the clever rhymes and the humor there is often a kindly but deep philosophy. Не likes especially to point a satiric finger at faddists, posers, snobs, and pretenders generally. His most famous poem, "Strictly Germ-Proof," was a rollicking bit about an "antisep- tic baby and a prophylactic pup." This poem has been read around the world and translated into Esperanto. Six people have liked it so well that they have claimed it as their own. One man sold it, as his work, to the "New York World" two years after it had appeared in "Woman's Home Compan- ion," and was so determined to prove that he was the author that he forged "affidavits." On page 12 of this issue you will find some delightful little verses written by Guiterman especially for THIS WEEK. ARTHUR GUITERMAN Ten years ago a novel called "The Hounds of Spring" was heading best sellers in the United States. It was written by a girl of 23 who had been expelled from Cheltenham for pawning a pair of stockings and invited to leave Oxford because she wouldn't study. Sylvia Thompson was gay, beautiful, feminine, with a taste for dancing, traveling, ice cream, seventeenth-century furniture and paintings by Whistler. Since this first successful novel she has written eight more, and become one of England's most distinguished women novelists. title: Cheltenham: Why It Is Proposed That The State Assume Ownership And Control Of This Much-Criticized Institution For Colored Boys
full_text: Cheltenham Why It Is Proposed That The State Assume Ownership And Control Of This Much-Criticized Institu- tion For Colored Boys It is now all but certain that delinquent, vagrant, feeble-minded, and otherwise un- fortunate colored boys will get something like a square deal from the State of Mary- land. At any rate, when the bill authorizing the State to take over and operate the House of Reformation for Colored Boys passes the Legislature and goes into effect, colored boys will no longer be sent to an institution outside the control of the State, miserably financed and ill-equipped to carry on passable work in this field. The board of trustees of the Cheltenham Reforma- tory has accepted the bill now before the Legislature, having waived all financial con- sideration, and the bill, which has been introduced by a legislative group including members of both political parties, ought to have clear sailing. The spade work for this encouraging step away from an antiquated and unenlightened policy of dealing with colored boys has been performed to a large extent by Enoch Har- lan and M. Hampton Magruder, representing the Cheltenham trustees, and Morris A. Rome, of the Board of State Aid and Chari- ties. Patience, fact and energy have been generously applied to this problem by all parties, with the result that a bill has been framed which in time will end forever the medieval policy which remote control and stingy appropriations have for so long im- posed upon Cheltenham. From now on colored boys will actually be wards of the State and not its neglected stepebitdren. -0- The Cheltenham bill begins with the state- ment that, "in consideration of the State of Maryland assuming its obligations to the colored mate minors under its care and custody," the Cheltenham trustees are an- thorized to transfer the physical property to the State, reserving from cash on hand the sum of $30.000 to be used in general for pensions and other adjustments in the com- pensation of present employés. The employés are placed under the civil- service regulations of the State. This should mean that better trained workers can be obtained for Cheltenham and, with the higher scale of salaries which will now be possible, the staff should soon round out into something like adequney. One of the principal weaknesses of Chel- tenham has been that until recently it has lacked funds to make possible the separa- tion of young colored criminals from col- ored boys who have been sent there merely for protection or shelter. Boys ill from tuberculosis have not been segregated or adequately treated. Feeble-minded boys re- ceive little special treatment. The broom factory where the older boys at. Cheltenham used to work under contract to a private corporation has been liquidated and other reforms have been inaugurated since the report made by the Child Welfare League of America on conditions in 1931. But much remains to be done which can- not be done until the State of Maryland has established the same control over the care and reformation of colored boys that it exercises over white boys, It should not be imagined that, when the Legislature has passed this bill, vali- dating the arrangement which the Chelten- ham trustees and the Board of State Aid and Charities have arrived at, Maryland's custodianship of colored boys will be per- fect. The physical plant at Cheltenham will have to be improved and perhaps enlarged, and there should be a greater amount of coöperation between the committing magis- trates and the school. Paroled boys and those discharged from the institution need more careful and sympathetic following-up. -o- State control and responsibility is obvi- ously the first step to permanent and assured improvement. It is hard to believe that the Legislature will look for reasous to upset the hard work and real sacrifice which have distinguished the activities of both the State officials and the Cheltenham trustees in this matter. The trustees are, after all, turning over property estimated as worth $400,000 to the State for no con- sideration whatever. The Board of State Aid and Charities is accepting new respon- sibilities and a tough assignment all round. Judges who have to commit delinquent colored boys to Cheltenham have for years been tossing and monning because there was no better place to, send them. One judge told me a few years ago that he sent as few colored boys as possible down there because it did them more harm than good. No reformatory is perfect, but a Legisla- ture which insisted that Maryland must commit boys to a private institution beyond its control where, in the past at any rate, they have been underſed and overreformed to no purpose, would have a lot of explain- ing to do.
