title: JONES ORDERS 26 OUSTED AT CHELTENHAM: DECLARES NEARLY HALF OF STAFF UNFIT FOR PRESENT DUTIES BARS THEM FROM MERIT SYSTEM UNLESS OVERRULED BY COURT
full_text: JONES ORDERS 26 OUSTED AT CHELTENHAM Declares Nearly Half Of Staff Unfit For Pres- ent Duties Bars Them From Merit System Unless Over- ruled By Court Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, yesterday ordered the board of the Cheltenham School for Boys to dismiss twenty-six of the fifty- seven members of its staff. Most of these twenty-six are "physi- cally or otherwise unfit" for any duty in the State service, and all are unfit for their present duties, Mr. Jones said. He served a point-blank ultimatum on the board that he would not accept these employes in the State merit system unless he is forced to do so by. a court order. Refuses To Approve Pay Rolls He added that unless the board promises to cooperate with him in a wholesale reorganization of the per- sonnel, he will not approve any pay roll for the institution subsequent to that of March 31. As an essential part of this reorgani- zation, he insisted that the board of managers immediately terminate the employment of four of its own mem- bers on the institution's staff, that it obtain an experienced executive for the post of superintendent, and that it cooperate in obtaining qualified per- sons for several other key positions.. These recommendations were con- tained in a report which the State Employment Commissioner delivered to board members and which will be considered by them at a meeting to be held at Cheltenham this afternoon. Follows 3-Month Inquiry This report was the result of a three-month investigation of the in- stitution's personnel which Mr. Jones conducted for the purpose of classify- ing employes preparatory to their in- corporation into the State merit system. Investigation of the fifty-seven em- ployes, case by case, convinced the State Employment Commissioner, he said, that he could not "assume the responsibility" of "blanketing" them into the classified service. The 1937 General Assembly, in the act which extended State control over the 67-year-old Negro reformatory, provided that the present personnel be accepted into the State service "without need of special examination as to fitness." : Interprets Language Of Act Mr. Jones told the board of man- agers that he construed this wording to "apply only to employes who are physically and otherwise fit to per- form the duties to which they are assigned." He added that he did not believe the General Assembly intended that the reorganization of Cheltenham as a State institution should be delayed "until after the death of practically one-half of the present employes." These employes, he said, the "em- ployment commissioner has found to be physically, mentally and otherwise unfit for present duties, and, in all but two or three cases, unfit for any duty. in the State service.". Finds 22 Classified Mr. Jones found twenty-two of the institution's employes qualified for classification in the State service and ordered nine others "not classified": pending efforts to find work they!! could do. The others, he said, should be dismissed. In a letter to Joseph H. Blandford, president of the board, he explained that all except the twenty-two em- ployes to whom classifications were granted should become temporary.em- ployes, and either must be trans- ferred to duties they can perform or must be released as rapidly as com- petent replacements can be made. In his report, Mr. Jones placed par- ticular cimphasis upon the division of responsibility in the management of the reform school which resulted from the superintendent having as salaried employes several members of his em- ploying board. Board Members Employed Those board members serving as employes, he said, are: MR. BLANDFORD. DR. WILLIAM H. GIBBONS. REV. FREDERICK DOUGLAS. JOHN E. McCORMACK.. "As board members, these employes are able to vote on their own com- pensation and duties, and are respon- sible to the board only for the manner in which their duties are performed," the employment commissioner said. "The superintendent . naturally is not in a position to issue orders to the members of his own board, who are in effect his employers, and, as he thus lacks any disciplinary or admin- istrative authority over thei: actions, it is impossible for him to maintain the standards necessary for the proper administrative conduct of the institu- tion." Would Demote Superintendent Mr. Jones recommended that the present acting superintendent of Chel- tenham School for Boys be relegated to a subordinate position and that a new superintendent "equipped with the necessary educational and techni-: (Continued on Page 20, Column 2) 1 1 cal qualifications" be employed, at a salary of $3,600 a year. Instead of having a member of the board serve as executive secretary, he urged that an administrative assistant be employed to serve under the super- intendent and be responsible, under him, for fiscal operation. A drastic revision of personnel in the supervision of inmates will be necessary, Mr. Jones said, finding thir- teen employes out of seventeen in this department incompetent. The depart- ment head, John S. Beckwith, he found "competent and satisfactory." Hits Education Facilities The employment commissioner said that Cheltenham was "totally unpre- pared" for its proper educational functions. There is no vocational instruction, he said, except in shoe cobbling. He recommended that the State Board of Education be asked to survey the situation and draw up plans for a proper course of academic and voca- tional studies. Medical duties, Mr. Jones said, at present are exercised by a member of the board who lives some distance from the institution. He recomanended that an institutional physician be employed who would give half his time daily to the school and would be on call at other times. The revision of the parole depart- ment, now headed by an aged Negro minister, also a member of the board, is badly needed, Mr. Jones found. He recommended that the parole work be centralized at the institution under the supervision of the superintendent, and that the Baltimore parole office be abolished. Demands Licensed Engineer Cheltenham's heating plant, now operated by unlicensed engineers, must be put in charge of at least a licensed shift engineer and a licensed steam fireman, he recommended, in order that there may be a licensed engineer on duty at all times. Mr. Jones said the board has an im- portant service to perform in the in- duction of Cheltenham into the ranks of accredited State institutions, and that "it will be most unfortunate and a great disappointment to the critics of Cheltenham as a private institution if any minor consideration, such as matters connected with unfit person- nel, should delay or impede its ac- complishment." He also called attention to tthe fact that there is a fund of $30,000 which may be used to aid those employes who are released from the institution's staff in the course of a reorganization of personnel

Finds 22 Classified Mr. Jones found twenty-two of the institution's employes qualified for classification in the State service and ordered nine others "not classified": pending efforts to find work they!! could do. The others, he said, should be dismissed. In a letter to Joseph H. Blandford, president of the board, he explained that all except the twenty-two em- ployes to whom classifications were granted should become temporary.em- ployes, and either must be trans- ferred to duties they can perform or must be released as rapidly as com- petent replacements can be made. In his report, Mr. Jones placed par- ticular cimphasis upon the division of responsibility in the management of the reform school which resulted from the superintendent having as salaried employes several members of his em- ploying board. Board Members Employed Those board members serving as employes, he said, are: MR. BLANDFORD. DR. WILLIAM H. GIBBONS. REV. FREDERICK DOUGLAS. JOHN E. McCORMACK.. "As board members, these employes are able to vote on their own com- pensation and duties, and are respon- sible to the board only for the manner in which their duties are performed," the employment commissioner said. "The superintendent . naturally is not in a position to issue orders to the members of his own board, who are in effect his employers, and, as he thus lacks any disciplinary or admin- istrative authority over thei: actions, it is impossible for him to maintain the standards necessary for the proper administrative conduct of the institu- tion." Would Demote Superintendent Mr. Jones recommended that the present acting superintendent of Chel- tenham School for Boys be relegated to a subordinate position and that a new superintendent "equipped with the necessary educational and techni-: (Continued on Page 20, Column 2) 1 1 cal qualifications" be employed, at a salary of $3,600 a year. Instead of having a member of the board serve as executive secretary, he urged that an administrative assistant be employed to serve under the super- intendent and be responsible, under him, for fiscal operation. A drastic revision of personnel in the supervision of inmates will be necessary, Mr. Jones said, finding thir- teen employes out of seventeen in this department incompetent. The depart- ment head, John S. Beckwith, he found "competent and satisfactory." Hits Education Facilities The employment commissioner said that Cheltenham was "totally unpre- pared" for its proper educational functions. There is no vocational instruction, he said, except in shoe cobbling. He recommended that the State Board of Education be asked to survey the situation and draw up plans for a proper course of academic and voca- tional studies. Medical duties, Mr. Jones said, at present are exercised by a member of the board who lives some distance from the institution. He recomanended that an institutional physician be employed who would give half his time daily to the school and would be on call at other times. The revision of the parole depart- ment, now headed by an aged Negro minister, also a member of the board, is badly needed, Mr. Jones found. He recommended that the parole work be centralized at the institution under the supervision of the superintendent, and that the Baltimore parole office be abolished. Demands Licensed Engineer Cheltenham's heating plant, now operated by unlicensed engineers, must be put in charge of at least a licensed shift engineer and a licensed steam fireman, he recommended, in order that there may be a licensed engineer on duty at all times. Mr. Jones said the board has an im- portant service to perform in the in- duction of Cheltenham into the ranks of accredited State institutions, and that "it will be most unfortunate and a great disappointment to the critics of Cheltenham as a private institution if any minor consideration, such as matters connected with unfit person- nel, should delay or impede its ac- complishment." He also called attention to tthe fact that there is a fund of $30,000 which may be used to aid those employes who are released from the institution's staff in the course of a reorganization of personnel

title: MARRIAGE LICENSE DELAY BILL URGED: CONFERENCE OF JEWS AND CHRISTIANS CALLS FOR MEASURE'S SUPPORT ALSO APPROVES REVISION OF LAW ON ILLEGITIMATE CHILDREN
full_text: MARRIAGE LICENSE DELAY BILL URGED Conference Of Jews And Christians Calls For Meas- ure's Support Also Approves Revision Of Law On Illegitimate Children Support of proposed legislation mak- ang illegitimate children eligible for State aid, and the marriage bill, re- quiring a lapse of three days between application and issuance of a license, has been urged in resolutions adopted by the executive committee of the Baltimore Round Table of the Na- tional Conference of Jews and Chris- tians. The resolutions, which have been made public, are signed by the Rev. Dr. Thomas Guthrie Speers, pastor of the Brown Memorial Presbyterian Church: the Rev. Dr. Edward L. Israel, rabbi of the Har Sinai Congregation; Vincent de Paul Fitzpatrick, editor of the Baltimore Catholic Review, and the Rev. A. W. Gottschall, secretary of the Baltimore Round Table. Social Legislation Studied The preface to the resolution says: "The Baltimore Round Table of the National Conference of Jews and Christians is deeply interested in everything that concerns the reli- gious and moral welfare of the citi. zens of our State. We take no part in partisan politics. But we have a very deep common interest in social con- ditions in our State because of the effect of those conditions upon the living standards, and the moral and spiritual life of our fellow-citizens. For this reason the executive commit- tee of the Baltimore Round Table has made a study of the social legislation to be submitted to the present session of the General Assembly. "After a careful scrutiny of the va- rious bills we find that while as indi- viduals or as separate religious groups, there are differences in our attitudes toward certain of them, we can unite whole-heartedly in recommending that the members of the Baltimore Round Table of Jews and Christians should actively support the following": 1. The marriage bill previously men- tioned. 2. Unemployment insurance, a bill to expand present legislation to cover all forms of business that ☐ employ four or more persons. We agree in principle with this bill, but state emphatically that we look forward to the time when there will be a complete coverage for every employed person. 3. The status of illegitimate children. For instance, making them eligible to receive State aid. 4. State program for delinquent col- ored boys, whereby the State ulti- mately takes over and expands Cheltenham. 5. Legislation for prison labor. State- use program. 6. More funds for Board of Mental Hygiene, 7. More funds for State tuberculosis program. 8. More funds for State penal pro- gram. 2. An appropriation of sufficient. funds to finance the public-assist- ance program. 10. In addition we suggest that, in view of the damage to health and morals caused by slums, the As- sembly pass an enabling act which would make it possible for the State to take advantage of the terms of a Federal housing law if it should be passed by Congress. "In our opinion these are the more pressing needs of our State at the pres- ent time. And we unite in urging the passing of such legislation at this ses- sion of the Assembly. Realizing the financial stringency of the budget wé believe it is the duty of the Assembly to find equable and morally reputable forms of taxation to make possible the carrying out of such social legislation.' title: Blandford Is New Head Of Cheltenham School
full_text: Blandford Is New Head Of Cheltenham School State Takes Over Reformatory For Boys As Board Agrees To Provisions Of Bill The board of managers of the House of Reformation at Cheltenham has ac- cepted the provisions of the Chelten- ham bill passed by the General As- sembly, it was disclosed yesterday. Joseph H. Blandford has been named president of the board of the new State-controlled organization, to be known as the Cheltenham School for Boys. Enoch Harlan, president of the board of managers of the old insti- tution, said the reformatory for Negro minors would become the property of the State on October 1. Since its foundation in 1870, the institution has been operated privately. In addition to Mr. Blandford, other officers of the new organization are: HAL B. CLACETT, vice-president. JOHN E. MCCORMACK, secretary-treas- urer. THE REV. FREDERICK DOUGLASS and WILLARD W. ALLEN, members of the executive committee. The board of managers of the old institution also remain as members of the new board. title: Fireworks
full_text: Fireworks Baltimore police last night were ordered by their commissioner, Wil- liam P. Lawson, to enforce the ban upon the shooting of fireworks within the city limits, and to see that children are not allowed to play slot and pin- ball machines. The order, in part, read: . "After numerous complaints, espe- cially from outlying sections at- tention is directed to the promiscuous discharge of firecrackers and other explosive preparations a prac- tice that is not only annoying but dangerous, and every member of the force is instructed to be particularly vigilant and suppress the nuisance." Cites 'Pinball Law And: "This office is reliably informed that the practice of children playing penny pinball machines is prevalent-a con- dition that demands immediate sup- pression." The order went on to quote the law that says the playing of pinball ma- chines-penny or 5 cents or a quar- ter-by anyone under the age of 18 is unlawful, and commanded the po- lice to see that any storekeeper who allows the youngsters to drop in their spare change be cited to court. Cheltenham Dispute Brought To City Court Jones Given Until Friday To Show Cause Why He Should Not Pay 23 Employes Legal controversy over the State's refusal to accept twenty-three em- ployes of the Cheltenham School for Boys into the State merit system was transferred to Baltimore yesterday when mandamus proceedings were in- stituted against Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commissioner, in Supe- rior Court. The suit was filed through Enoch Harlan and Charles C. Marbury, coun- sel for the board of managers of the House of Reformation. The petition states that the plaintiff has a money interest in the case, as well as a natural interest in the welfare of the affected employes. Judge Rowland K. Adams signed an order directing Mr. Jones to show cause why he should not approve pay rolls for these employes, giving him until Friday to file his answer. The case was set for hearing July 11. Passenger Reported Lost Off Bay Steamer Master Of Tolchester Boat Spends More Than An Hour On Fruitless Search Due to investigation of a report that someone had fallen off the steamer Tolchester last night while on her return trip from a moonlight, the steamer was more than an hour late, arriving at her pier about 1.30 о'стоск this morning. Searchlights were played on the water and a lifeboat was ordered lowered by Capt. Fred Kolb, but after a search of an hour could not locate anything. Woman Hurt By Truck Miss Louise Wagner, 67, of the 1000 block West Lombard street, suffered cuts and bruises of the face and body last night when she stepped into the side of a truck as she was crossing Howard street at Lombard. title: Conference Planned On Cheltenham School
full_text: Conference Planned On Cheltenham School Committee From Board Of Man- agers To Meet Employment Commissioner Monday A committee from the board of managers of the Cheltenham School for Boys will confer with Harry C. Jones, State Employment Commis- sioner, Monday afternoon, the com- missioner said yesterday. It will seek to clarify "certain legal technicalities" involved in Mr. Jones' order that the institution agree to dis- miss nearly half its staff as unfit for entrance into the classified service of the State. The committee, appointed by Joseph H. Blandford, president of the fifteen- man board, will report back to the board before any decision is reached on whether the institution will con- cur with the Employment Commis- sioner's order. State Income Tax Unit Working On Two Shifts Collections Thus Far Total $331,- 285, With Thousands Of Returns Untabulated Annapolis, March 18 (P)-Employes of the income tax division of the State Comptroller's office went on two shifts today to clean up the tax payments received before the dead line expired on Tuesday.midnight. One group worked from 9 A. M. to 4 P. M., and the other from 2 to 9 P. M. The fifty employes will follow this schedule until the mail is opened and returns tabulated. The first tabulation in a week to- day added $135,977.33 from 100 cor- porations and 2,700 individuals. This brought the total collections from the 1½ of 1 per cent. tax to $331,285.53 from 19,842 corporations, fiduciaries, non- residents and individuals. Thousands of tax returns remain to be tabulated. CHICKEN THEFTS ALLEGED Two Men Sentenced To Cut For Eighteen Months On Charges Thomas E. Nash, 52, of Woodensburg, and Frank Becraft, 36, of Reisters- town, were sentenced to eighteen months in the House of Correction last night by Magistrate J. E. Myers, of Reisterstown, for the larceny of thirteen chickens. Nash was found guilty of stealing six of the fowls from J. E. Pinkler, of Woodensburg, and Becraft was con- victed of the theft of seven from Mrs. Alice Turnbaugh, near Reisterstown. The men were arrested Wednesday night. Appeals To Tax Board Washington, March 18 (P) - Henry A. B. Dunning, of Baltimore, petitioned the Board of Tax Appeals for re- determination of an alleged 1934 in- come-tax deficiency of $37,530. He said the Internal Revenue Collector erred in treating income of his wife and of five trust estates he created as his own taxable income.

title: Suit For Cheltenham Wages Is Dismissed
full_text: Suit For Cheltenham Wages Is Dismissed Court At Upper Marlboro Says Ac tlon Should Have Been Filed In Baltimore Upper Marlboro, Md., June 20 (AP)- The Prince George's County Circuit Court dismissed without prejudice to- day proceedings to compel the Mary- land State Employment Commissioner to pay the salaries of twenty-four employes of the Cheltenham School for Boys. Presiding Judge Walter J. Mitchell said State officers should be sued in the jurisdiction in which their offices were located. He said the court's ac- tion was not based on the merits of the case. Attorneys for the plaintiff, Joseph K. Cox, an employe of the school, said a similar suit would be filed in Baltimore. title: Governor Signs 27 Measures Passed At Recent Session Of Legislature: Executive Changes Mind And Sanctions $9,052,000 Increase In Debt Bills Become Laws After Sasscer And Gorfine Also Affix Signatures
full_text: Governor Signs 27 Measures Passed At Recent Session Of Legislature APPROVES ACT PROVIDING FOR STATE BONDS Executive Changes Mind And Sanctions $9,052,000 Increase In Debt Bills Become Laws After Sasscer And Gorfine Also Affix Signatures [By the Associated Press] Annapolis, April 15-Governor Nice late today signed twenty-seven bills passed by the recent Legislature. They became law when the Gov- ernor, Senate President Lansdale G. Sasscer and Speaker Emanuel Gor- fine affixed their signatures. Among them was a measure author- izing issuance of $9.052.000 in State bonds. Earlier during the day, Gov- ernor Nice announced he would de- fer signing the bill. Less than half an hour later he changed his mind and signed it. The bond issue bill includes $3.300,000 in bonds for restoration to the State Roads Commission of highway reve- nue diverted to balance the general fund budget, of following the State's usual policy of borrowing money for current expenses. State Wide Bills Among State-wide bills signed today were: Setting the State property tax rate for 1935 at 28 cents per $100 and for 1989 at 2014. The current rate is 2214. Providing that in the future names of Presidential electors shall not appear on Maryland ballots. Voters will ballot directly for the candidates and a vote for a candidate will count as a vote for each of his eight electors. Authorizing establishment of non- profit hospital insurance associations. Providing that drug and grovers stores shall not sell goods at less than cost. Authorizing the State to take over Cheltenham Reformatory for Negro boys. Authorizing appointment of a com- missioner to regulate and inspeet small Joan companies. It is reported that the post has been offered to J. Wilson Ryon, former State's Attorney of Prince George's county. Authorizing State to use certain funds for matching any Federal funds which may be appropriated for aid to crippled children. Authorizing State Department of Health to administer services for aid to rippled children. Regulating weights of trucks and loads allowed on Maryland highways. and allowing solid-tire trucks to carry 42,000 pounds. Authorizing State Roads Commission to issue refund bonds. Authorizing appointment of cominis- sion to study need for bridge building in Maryland. Authorizing countles and cities to es- tablish reasonable facilities for public recreation. Other Bills Other bills signed included: 11. B. 273. By Abramson-Authorizing adoption of Audrey Ruth Leininger, of Baltimore. II. B. 545. By Barrick and Others- To authorize $45.000 sewer bond issue for Brunswick, Frederick county. Н. В. 431, By Garrett Delegation- Regarding issuance of beer licenses in Garrett county. Н. В. 202. By Prince George's Dele gation-Allowing three years in which to redeem property sold at Prince George's tax sales. H. B. 646. By Worcester Delegation- To set up Worcester county liquor dis- pensaries in wholesale beer and wine business. Н. В. 672. By Somerset Delegation- Authorizing $200,000 Somerset county school bond issue. S. B. 14. By Wilson-Authorizing $06,000 Centreville electric plant bond Issue. S. R. 262. By Latimer-Authorizing deputy treasurer for Calvert county. S. B. 206, By Latimer-Authorizing Calvert county to issue $45,000 in lateral road bonds. Another bill signed was one requir- ing that persons desiring to become undertakers must have a high school education and must serve an appren- ticeship. title: MISLAID?
full_text: MISLAID? Among the consequences of dilatory tactics at Annapolis in this legislative session one of the most tragic would be the failure of the - Legislature to act upon the bill, now pending, by which the Cheltenham reformatory for colored boys is to be taken over and admin- istered by the State of Maryland. The bill reposes in the Senate Committee of Finance, where it has been for several weeks, although no explanation has been advanced for the delay in reporting a bill upon which agree- ment has been reached between the State and the Cheltenham board of trustees. Experts in child welfare and criminology are all agreed upon the necessity of passing this bill. Chief Judge Samuel K. Dennis, of the Baltimore City Supreme Bench, has said that it is "a blot upon the State" that no • adequate institution has been made available - for colored boys who are either homeless or delinquent. Thomas J. S. Waxter, former judge of the Baltimore Juvenile Court, is equally emphatic in asserting the need of State control for Cheltenham. Committing magistrates and officials who are forced to send colored boys to an institution inadequate to care for them are overwhelmingly in favor . of this bill. • Nevertheless, it stays in committee for reasons unascertained, although there are _suspicions that the ancient prerogative of "back scratching" is being indulged in the legislative corridors: "You lick Bill X and *I'll lick Bill Y." Only it would be rather - shameful if colored boys, wards of the State of Maryland, should be the victims of this kind of "practical politics." Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Other Recommendations Other recommendations made by the jurors were, briefly: Limitation of the possible speed of automobiles. Creation of north and south bound arteries. Removal of pylons from York road and the replacing of street cars with busses which will discharge passengers at the curb. Move car tracks to center of Eastern avenue, between Savage street and Dundalk avenue, where there have been many accidents. Allow right-hand turns on red lights and have the street properly marked for the direction of traffic. Widen Calvert street from twenty- five to thirty feet between Lexing- ton street and North avenue. Traffic light at University Parkway and Forticth street. Eliminate parking on the main streets of the business district from early morning until late in the afternoon. Have police pay strict attention to taverns where dancing is permitted as minors frequent them un- chaperoned. Cheltenham Criticized The grand jury also reported it con- sidered as "inhuman" the manner in which the hospital at the Cheltenham School for Colored Boys is conducted and recommended that the State take over the institution. It asserted the men in charge are "most unsuited and incapable of managing this institution," and recom- mended that it be managed by cap- able Negroes who are available. After having watched at close range the work of J. Bernard Wells, State's Attorney, and his staff, the jury de- clared it "a very efficient organiza- tion to protect the interests of the people." It also praised the work of the Domestic Relations Department under Morgan M. Buchner. Would Cut Autos' Speed Citing the great number of acci- dents reported monthly, the jurors declared the automobile had become ... If we went back to the thirty-horse- power engine of 1926, we could go 'back to the low death rate of 1926 and save 10,000 people from death each year and 400,000 from injury. Discusses Voting Laws Concerning the voting laws, it was said: "We recommend the purchase of voting machines by the city. We are convinced that a permanent syster of registration of voters has merit, and therefore, recommend the adoption of the system. We suggest that when registration is made that a photograph be made of the applicant, which would be autographed by the voter and a permanent file be kept and used for identification when a voter casts his ballot." The grand jury would eliminate daytime parking on Charles street between Centre and Fayette streets and on Baltimore, Fayette, Redwood and Lombard streets between Falls place and Greene streets. full_text: Lothian Small To Address Open Forum Here Today Official of League Of Nations So- ciety Also Will Speak At Schools Tomorrow Lothian Small, of Scotland, assist- ant secretary-general of the Interna- tional Federation of League of Na- tions Societies, will speak on the League on Nations and labor at 3 P. M. today at the Baltimore Open Forum in the Auditorium Theater. Mr. Small, who will arrive in Bal- timore this morning, will be the guest of Theodore Marburg for a few days. He will be introduced this afternoon by Dr. John H. Latane, professor of American history and lecturer on in- ternational law at the Johns Hopkins University. At 9.45 A. M. tomorrow Mr. Small will address the Goucher College as- sembly in Catherine Hooper Hall and will speak at the State Normal School in Towson two hours later. His sub- ject on both occasions will be What the Youth of Europe is Intending. Negro Boy Makes Escape From Police Station Here Awaiting Transfer To House Of Reformation, Youth Kicks Hole In Wall A 12-year-old Negro boy yesterday escaped from the Northern District Police Station, where he was held awaiting transfer to the House of Reformation for Colored Children at Cheltenham, the police reported. The boy was sentenced Friday on a charge of incorrigibility and taken to the detention room of the police sta- tion, located on the second floor. Yesterday, after kicking a hole through the plaster and lathing of the room, he crawled out into the hall and mingled with a group of children lined up to receive food and clothing. He is believed to have escaped through a rear door. title: Boys Held For Arson In Reformatory Fire: Trio, Inmates At Cheltenham Institution, Said To Admit Causing Blaze
full_text: Boys Held For Arson In Reformatory Fire Trio, Inmates At Cheltenham In- stitution, Said To Admit Causing Blase Three inmates of the House of Ref- ormation for Colored Boys, at Chelten- ham, Md., have admitted starting a fire in the broom factory of the insti- tution March 10, the police said yester- day. 4 Joseph F. Dougherty, investigator for the State Insurance Department, said that he gained admissions from the boys, but that they denied causing another blaze in the broom factory several weeks previously. The last fire did considerable damage. The youths, George Johnson, 16, of Baltimore; Thomas Dashields, 17. of Somerset county, and Granville Has- kill, 17, of Kent county, were held at the Marlboro Jail charged with arson. title: WHY NOT CHELTENHAM?
full_text: WHY NOT CHELTENHAM? R Governor Ritchie, taking up the case of two Negro boys sentenced to the House of Correc-A tion from St. Mary's county last month, sug- gested either a parole or transfer to the Chelten- ham Reformatory. The fact that the Parole Com- missioner has recommended the former course does not answer the question why they were not v sent to Cheltenham in the first placc. The two boys, one 13 and the other 15 years of age, received sentences of eighteen months and a year, respectively, the younger for forging check for $14, the older under accusation of stealing an automobile. The sentences, imposed by Judge Loker, of the Seventh Judicial Circuit, were certainly drastic. And they were not ren- dered less so by the judge's selection of a penal institution. Cheltenham, adjacent to St Mary's county, would certainly seem a more logical as well as a preferable place of confinement for these and similar Negro juvenile offenders. It is true that the county committing prisoners to Cheltenham is responsible for a small contribution toward their expenses. But it is hard to believe that this was in Judge Loker's mind when he passed the sentences. A WRITER FOR ENJOYMENT Stanley J. Weyman was 35 and the "gay nineties" had just dawned when he modestly in- troduced "The House of the Wolf" to the Eng- lish-reading world. From then on, for a decade or more, no year seemed quite complete without its Weyman romance. T T V I ( f C li 0 ก t 1 Sometimes they tumbled out at almost six- month intervals. "Under the Red Robe" and "My Lady Rotha" both appeared in 189-4. The next year saw the "Memoirs of a Minister of France" and "The Red Cockade." It was just 1 about that time, if memory serves, that New England began to be popular as a summer resort. And years will pass before all the Weyman novels imported into its boarding houses by vacationists are finally rounded up. ( Weyman, as we look back upon him, seems to stand as lineal successor to Dumas and natural forerunner of Sabatini. Combining a comely style with vivid descriptive powers, a sound knowledge of history with a keen sense of the dramatic, his art was pre-eminently that of men- tal refreshment. Therefore, death will not end his appeal. Put a carefully selected volume of Stanley Weyman on the bookshelf in your guest room, and a year hence you will find it exhibit- ing many signs of wear. Or, if you want a sim- pler test, call up the library. full_text: ST. MARY'S LACKS FUNDS, IS DEFENSE Unable To Support Addi- tional Youtliful Law Break- ers, Secretary Cecil Says. FIVE AT CHELTENHAM Governor Considering Paroles For Two Negro Boys In House Of Correction. With tive juvenile prisoners in the Cheltenham Reformatory, each costing county $200 a year, St. Mary's coumy cannot afford to send more youthful) violators of the law to the institution, George B. Cecil, president of the Board of County Commissioners for St. Mary's, said yesterday. Instead, the juvenile offenders are sent to the Ilouse of Correction, where the county does not have to pay for their support. Paroles Under Consideration. Mr. Cecil made this statement after Howard C. Hill, executive secretary of the Prisoner's Aid Society, had charged that St. Mary's county does not care properly for its youthful transgressors. Mr. IMill recalled that a 14-year-old Negro boy last fall was sent to the Rouse of Correction for n criminal offense and that Governor Ritchie released the boy immediately after the case had been called to his attention.. At the present Governor Ritchie has recommendations of parole from Ed- ward M. Parrish, State Parole Com- missioner, under consideration for two Negro boys, one 33 and the other 15, who were sent to the House of Cor- rection from St. Mary's county. "About All" County Could Pay. Mr. Cecil said that allowance for the county prisoners in Cheltenham is made each year when the levy for the county is struck and that St. Mary's county cannot afford to send more youthful prisoners there. He added that $1,000 a year for the support of the five now in the reforma- tory was "about all" the county could pay. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. full_text: PAROLE OF 2 BOYS IN "CUT" IS URGED Parrish's Recommendations Result Of Probe Ordered By Ritchie. RELEASE NOW EXPECTED Negroes, 13 And 15, Given 18 Months And Year In Check Forgery And Auto Theft. [.Annapolis Bureast of The Sun.) Annapolis, April 10.-Recommenda tions for the parole of two Negro boys 13 and 15 years old. who were sen tenced to the House of Correction las March from St. Mary's county. have been received by Governor Ritchie from Edward M. Parrish, State Parol Commissioner. The recommendation followed an in vestigation by Mr. Parrish which Gov Fernor Ritchie ordered last week after be had been informed by Stuart S. Janney, Director of the Department of Welfare, that boys were sergin terms in the prison for larceny and forgery. To Rest With Ritente. Final disposition of the cases will depend on the Governor. In view of his action in starting the investiga- tion, however, it is expected he will favor release. The boys-Clarence Jones and Had- man.Holt-were sentenced to eighteen months and one year in the House of Correction, respectively, by Judge Wil- liam M. Loker, of the Seventh Judicial Circuit. Jones, 13, was convicted of forging a check for $14 while Holt was accused of stealing an automo bile. Judge Loker, when informed last weck that the Governor had initiated an investigation, remarked: "I have no comment to make on the subject. Governor Ritchie mas settle the questions he is concerned with and I will settle mine." "Apt Reproduction." Philip H. Dorsey, State's Attorney for St. Mary's county, said the forgery of which Jones was convicted was an "apt reproduction" of the signature of the man upon whom the check was drawn. In asking Mr. Parrish to investigate, Governor Ritchie pointed out that in view of the extreme, youth of the boys he did not believe they should have been sentenced to the House of Corree- tion. He suggested either a parole or their transfer to the Cheltenham Re- formatory. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: Negro Sentenced As Minor Taken From Cheltenham Accused, Sald To Be 21, Gave Age As 15-Convicted in At- tempted Robbery. The alleged deception of a 21-year- old Negro, who gave his age as 15 when arrested for attempted burglary, was discovered yesterday after he had been sentenced to the House of Reformation for Colored Boys at Chel- tenham. Richard L. Mitchell, the ac- cused, was removed to the Northwest- Tern Police Station for a new trial. ■ The accused, who gave an address in the first block East Belvedere ave- nue, was charged February 15 with breaking into the store of Joe Cohen, 1000 block North Stricker street. Magistrate T. J. C. Williams, in the Juvenile Court, sentenced Mitchell to Cheltenham, thinking him a minor. The police said they obtained his birth certificate from a Connecticut town. Magistrate Paul Johannsen committed him to Jail in default of $500 bail for grand jury action. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

full_text: ASKS NEGRO STAFF FOR CHELTENHAM City Council Adopts Resolu- tion On House Of Reformation. GONDITIONS ASSAILED Institution Said. To Be In Need Of New Buildings And Fire Escape. A resolution requesting the board of managers of the House of Reformation at Cheltenham to employ Negro super- visors and teachers exclusively was adopted by the City Council last night at the request of Walter S. Emerson, of the Fourth district. Conditions at the institution were criticized during the argument over the resolution, and some of the Coun- cilmen suggested that the city or state establish an institution for the care of Negro boys without homes. Favors New Buildings. Philander B. Briscoe, Second dis- trict, chairman of the Committee on Education, which considered the re- solution and visited the institution, refused to sign a favorable. report on the measure. He said, however, that he thought conditions should be im- proved by the erection of new build- ings, a fire escape and by providing the inmates, with better food and an education. J. Warren Burgess, Third district, a member of the Committee on Educa- tion, asserted that while at the insti. tution he asked what would happen to the 300 boys if a fire broke out on the first floor while they were on the third floor. "I was told that they could jump out of the windows," Mr. Burgess said. Attention was drawn to the report of the May term grand jury criticiz- ing conditions at the institution. "Treated As Criminals." "The boys are treated as criminals," Daniel Ellison, Fourth district, as- serted, "and the Committee on Edu- cation found conditions there that should not be allowed to exist. The committee felt that it should go deeper into the matter than by recommending a simple resolution requesting a change in the system of supervisors and teachers.. "The committee felt that it should call attention to the food that is served the boys and to the system of farming them out, as well as working them in the shop and the broom factory up to a late hour Saturday afternoon. There were other conditions we thought should be improved." Educational facilities were among the improvements urged by Council- men Emerson and Warner T. Me- Guinn. the Negro members of the Council. - Opposed By Harris. The resolution was opposed by Samuel Y. Harris, Sixth district, on the ground that it was "a matter over which the city has no control." Mr. Harris quoted Howard Bryant, presi- dent of the Council, as saying "it was a matter the Council should not take пр." The city appropriates about $35,000 a year toward the maintenance of the institution and has two representa- tives on the board of managers. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. The State and Baltimore use this institution for delinquent colored boys, and for this service the State appropriates only $15,000 a year. Is the Free State fully awake to the importance to the community of the Colored House of Reformation? Are public-spirited uplifters, the well wish- ers of youth, whether white or colored, doing their duty? Is it because the management of the Colored House of Reformation has been carrying a load for the city and state for years, striv- ing to balance a budget, working under disadvantages, lacking political environ- ment? title: STRUCK BY AUTO, WOMAN, 69, DIES
full_text: STRUCK BY AUTO, WOMAN, 69, DIES Mrs. Rachel Siscovich Suc- cumbs In Hospital-Driver Of Machine Held: Mrs. Rachel Siscovich, 00 years old, 2714 West Fayette street, died yester- day evening of injuries, received earlier in the day when she was' s'struck by an automobile, at Baltimore and Stricker streets. The driver, of the machine, Alfred Smith, colored, of Ellicott City, took her to the Franklin Square Hospital, where it was discovered that her skull and both legs were fractured and that she had received internal injuries. Smith, who was held by the South- western district police for the action of a coroner's inquest, said that Mrs. Sis- covich ran in front of his machine so suddenly he could not stop in time to prevent hitting her. Talkative Husband Tried On Non-Support Charge John Piscor Beconies So Loquacious Magistrate Has Him Locked In Cell. If money talks, it had said nothing to Mrs. John Piscor, she told Magistrate Joseph J. Rettalinta yesterday in the Eastern Police Court. It was her hus- band who did the talking. That was why she had him stummoned on a non- support.charge. Mr. Piscor denied some of his wife's statements, but unwittingly comfirmed to the magistrate's satisfaction what she said about his talking. He, talked so long and so rapidly that the magis trate inquired if it would be necessary to hit him over the head with a club to stop him. At that Mr. Piscor subsided. But not for long. After his second outburst the magistrate ordered him locked in a cell to ponder such proverbs as "talk is cheap" and "silence is golden." Finally he was brought back into court and dismissed. "But even if your wife hits you with a rolling, pin, for your own sake don't say a word," was the magisterini nd monition. Young Offenders Scarce : As Christmas Draws Near fudge Williams Finds Benches In Juvenile Court Almost Deserted. 8 It was "almost Christmas.". Judge T. J. C. Williams, of the Juve- mile Court, was reminded anew of this fact when he went to the courtroom Festerday. The benches were deserted, save four Negro boys, charged with stealing from a store in the 1100 block South Charles street • And the judge was glad, for he "never likes to punish boys around Christmas time," he said. Instead of sending the boys to the Cheltenham Reformatory, the judge paroled, them in the care of George Ralph, Negro probation officer of the court. Then he adjourned court until January 4. This en- lightenment could have been gleaned at the institution or from those officers in attendance in the grand jury rooms, But, save the assistant superintendent, who was appointed to that position sevs eral days previous to the investigation. none of the officials was called. Several inmates were interviewed, one of whom Was the cause of the inquiry. This boy is totally unreliable as to truth and ofttimes not amenable to dis- cipline. He has been transferred three times to other school cottage buildings during the past. 18 months for brutally attacking smaller boys and for other offenses not printable. The gist of the grand jury's report was lack of discipline, improper food and chastisements. A proper knowledge of the institution -the management, the inmates-would show that Mr. John B. Pyles is emi- nently fitted for the position of super- intendent. full_text: 13 MURDER CASES : ACTED ON BY JURY Retiring Grand Inquest Reports Smallest Number Since 1920. CITY IS DECLARED ORDERLY 34 Presentments Made For Alleged Criminal Assault. New Record Being Set. L Fewer cases of murder were reported to the January term grand jury than to any similar body since 1920, according to the grand jury's report submitted yes- terday to Judge Eli Frank. The report was one of the shortest on record and contained fe recom- mendations. Crime and disorder are at a minimum in Baltimore, the report asserted. According to the figures announced, 13 presentments of murder were made during the term which closed yester- day. The September term grand jury presented. 25 murder cases; the May term last year presented 15; the Janu- ary term 18. In 1922 70 cases were presented by the three grand juries. Sixty-four cases were presented in 1921. Only 35 cases were presented in 1920. Assault Cases Set Record. On the other hand, cases of criminal assault reported by the January term grand jury set a record for the city. Presentments were made in 34 cases. Comparative figures for the last 10 years show that such cases have been increasing steadily. Seventy-two cases were presented last year-a record num- ber up to that time. In its Penitentiary report. the grand jury said conditions there were satis- factory. Although no recommenda- tions were made, salaries of guards were called inadequate. The strongest language in the re- port was used by the committee that inspected Cheltenham Reformatory for Colored Boys. The institution con- tributed little to the moral uplift of the boys incarcerated there, it was de- clared, and "little hope for improve- ment in the boys at Cheltenham," was expressed. The committee suggested that the State assume control of the institution. State's Attorney Praised. The work of Herbert R. O'Conor, State's Attorney, was praised by the body, which reported that his office was "functioning capably and well." The Police Department and the Criminal Courts also were lauded for "estimable and commendable work." The attitude of the body toward crime and other evils in the city was indicated in one sentence of its report: "It is gratifying to the members of the grand jury to note the orderly con- dition of our community." This was in contrast with the report of the Sep- tember. 1923. term grand jury sub- nitted last January. which contained many radical reform recommendations striking at the root of the city's so- cial and economic life. In discharging the jury, Judge Frank commented on tlíe members "intelligent and diligent application to Guty." J. Arthur Nelson was foreman of the body and Moses Rothschild was assistant foreman. The May term grand jury will be sworn in Monday. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Further reproduction prohibited without permission.

On the other hand, cases of criminal assault reported by the January term grand jury set a record for the city. Presentments were made in 34 cases. Comparative figures for the last 10 years show that such cases have been increasing steadily. Seventy-two cases were presented last year-a record num- ber up to that time. The institution con- tributed little to the moral uplift of the boys incarcerated there, it was de- clared, and "little hope for improve- ment in the boys at Cheltenham," was expressed. O'Conor, State's Attorney, was praised by the body, which reported that his office was "functioning capably and well." full_text: The Trouble At Cheltenham. TO THE EDITOR OF THE SUN-Sir: In a particular form the Cheltenham institution is up for criticism before the public. I do not address myself to the present point of criticism, but to one of vastly more practical importance. believe I am the senior member of the board of managers of that institution, having been first elected by the sub- scribers in 1901 and subsequently re- elected each year since. I The institution should conform to the State policy of colored teachers for colored schools.. I pressed this point as soon as I became a member of the board, and have steadily advocated it ever since. In the light of all the ex- perience I have had with both races I can conceive of no good reason for excluding the colored race from teach- ing their own flesh and blood. Gen- eral Shryock was heartily with me in this matter, and in 1903 a beginning was made in this direction. Mrs. Mitchell, a well-qualified colored woman, taught one of the schools most accept- ably, while her husband rendered effi- cient work as the head of the chair- caning department. Both of them were most highly complimented by General Shryock, as well as by the superintend- ent of the institution. After some years of effort this couple, feeling heavily the isolation, re- signed. Not only would such isolation cease to exist where a number of colored persons are thus employed, but a new and helpful atmosphere would De created, and the boys living in that atmosphere, and reflecting the same, would more and more be transformed Into the likeness of the same. I have not one word of criticism of Mr. Pyles, the superintendent. During all these years I have come into close personal contact with him and believe that he bas honestly striven to do his whole duty. But in the language of Grover Cleveland, it is a condition and not a theory which confronts us. GEORGE F. BRAGG, JR. Baltimore July 6 Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: FIVE NEGRO BOYS FEAST AFTER LOOT
full_text: FIVE NEGRO BOYS- FEAST AFTER LOOT Tale Of Grandmammy's $180 Loss And Round-Up At Bridge Told In Court.- Five little negro boys sat in a row under the Stony Run bridge and ate and ate and ate and ate. One of the boys, it is alleged, stole $180.50 from his grandmother, Sarah Perkins Morris street, on April 23 last. A week later the boys were found under the bridge. Each is about 10 years old. Of the stolen money $150 had been spent for butter, bread, sausage and fruit, of which a liberal supply re mained. Each boy wore a khaki suit, three had rifles and there were boxes containing 3,000 cartridges. Only $12 of the stolen money was left. The story was told yesterday before Judge Robert F. Stanton, in Part 2, Criminal Court, when an unsuccessful effort was made to obtain the release of one of the boys, Louis Marshall, from the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham, to which he was sentenced in the Juvenile Court following the round-up under the bridge. Promised To Visit Judge; And He Did-With Officer Was All Right When He Tele- phoned, But When He Got There-How Different! -"Tom" Murray, well known in South Baltimore, felt that he should add his felicitations to those of friends of Mag- istrate John E. Potee, of the Southern police district. Magistrate Potee, Tom learned, has been mentioned for sheriff Yesterday Tom called up the magis- trate, saying: : "This is Tom Murray talking. I am coming up to see you in a minute. Wait for me." - The magistrate waited-5, 10 even 15 minutes. Still Tom failed to make his appearance. Just as he had begun to think himself hoaxed Tom made his appearance; but such an appearance! Escorted by Patrolman Joseph Rivers, Tom came reluctantly into the pres- ence of the man whom only shortly be- fore lie had called and told he was com- ing free and unescorted.. Tom explained volubly. He left the telephone booth and stepped into the street, he said, when he became in- volved in a street brawl. Then a police- man appeared and that was all. He was dismissed. full_text: : : N EYE FOR AN EYE" RE- A reads of the offer of a foreign journalist to give one of his good eyes to the French painter Lemordant who has become blind. There is, in fact, some virtue in the phrase if science is really ready to graft a new eye into a blinded socket and make it work. Mere revenge has no ethical foundation, but the trans- fer of an optic to an injured man to restore his sight would be a reasonable penalty to exact of the one who had maliciously caused the injury; and to give one's eye voluntarily would be self- denial of heroic type. BALTIMORE HOUSEWIVES WHO in the public markets have taken on a task that has never been completely carried through, but there is no reason for them to feel discouraged. Clean markets are possible, and the markets of Baltimore might as well be the ones which first get the prize for sanitary excellence. That they have missed it hitherto is not a thing to be proud of, for they are such an important element in Baltimore's domestic economy that one would expect them, above almost all else, to be kept in first-rate condi- tion. They are public institutions, so to speak, but the inspectors and the market men between them are respon- sible in many instances for a state of disorder that is a reproach to the com- munity. As the Baltimore Housewives' League, latest crusader for cleanliness, sets out to create sanitary order in place of the insanitary chaos which all too frequently reigns, it will have the best wishes of other marketers who know that food should be kept free from contamination. What is the use of keep- ing one's home' clean if the markets where one buys food are dirty? BOY OYS AT THE CHELTENHAM School in Prince George's county, a negro reformatory, are making brooms under conditions which have been criti- cized by President Broening of the Bal- timore Federation of Labor. But apart from his charges, which deal with the alleged unfairness of allowing the manu- facture of brooms with under-paid con- tract labor, one wonders why broom- making is fostered in a rural institution. Would agriculture not be a more use- ful and wholesome pursuit? Warden Sweezey wants to get his men on a farm, while a school that could farm is making brooms. No JOON DINNER DOES NOT MEET with the approval of Baltimore housewives whose views have been as- certained, and one doubts whether any large number could be found to support it on theoretical grounds. To se sure, a real meal is still being served at mid- day in many homes where circumstances are such as to permit the family to as- semble at that hour; but, generally speaking, "father" is at work some dis- tance from home when the noon whistle blows, and there is no sense in serving the chief meal of the day with him away. It would be interesting, perhaps, to trace the causes which have led to the abandonment of the noontide dinner, which only a generation ago was still popular and which is still customary on farms and in small towns. Has Amer- ica so speeded up as to be unable any more to spend an hour or more for Junch? Or has Baltimore grown so big that the average man is unable to find a job near home, with the result that the trip home is too long to squeeze into the noon hour? The latter seems quite probable; in which case the advocates of noon dinners and shorter hours for servants-are up against a large-sized obstacle. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. title: RITCHIE SEEKS DATA ON PEONGE CHARGE: GOVERNOR TO TAKE NO ACTION AT CHELTENHAM UNTIL REPORT IS FILED BROOM CONTRACTOR REPLIES E. N. RIPPLE SAYS COMPLAINT FOLLOWED FAILURE TO ORGANIZE UNION HERE
full_text: RITCHIE SEEKS DATA ON PEONAGE CHARGE Governor To Take No Action At Cheltenham Until Report Is Filed. BROOM CONTRACTOR REPLIES E. N. Ripple Says Complaint Fol- lowed Failure To Organize Union Here. Governor Ritchie will take no action( regarding the broom-making and other contracts at the Cheltenham Reform School for Colored Boys, in Prince George's county, until the Federation of Labor has supplied him with the information regarding the contracts and conditions at the school. This the of- ficials of the federation have promised to send him. The federation wants the contract abrogated, it now being en- gaged in organizing the broom-makers of the city into a union. The Governor said yesterday he was heartily in favor of the principle of not permitting prison labor to compete with free labor. Not State Institution. "Cheltenham School, however," he said, "is not a State institution. It re- ceives State aid and is entitled to its appropriation this year, contract or no contract, for the Legslature attached no strings to the appropriation. I shall be glad, however, to take the matter up with the Cheltenham authorities and find out if some arrangements cannot be made to put the school in line with the policy followed at the State institu- tions." Charges of alleged exploitation and peonage at the Cheltenham School made by officials of the Federation of Labor are due to disappointment on the part of organized labor over efforts to enlist Baltimore broom makers into its ranks, said E. N. Ripple, of the firm of S. A. Ripple & Bros., which has the contract at the reformatory. Mr. Ripple denied the Cheltenham situation had anything to do with al- leged cheap brooms on the general market. Boys Pald For Work.. "We have only about 40 of 300 boys at the institution working for us," he said, "and what they turn out is not more than one-quarter of our entire out- put. The institution receives 50 cents a day for each worker, and for this we require three dozen brooms as a day's work. All over that we pay for at reg- ular outside working rates, and in this way some of the more proficient boys make from $3 to $7 a week. "The entire trouble with the unions grew out of recent efforts to form a local here by Chicago organizers. They failed in this except that I understand they have secured about a dozen mem- bers." Edward Stabler, Jr., founder of the coal company which for many years bore his, name, and associated actively with many of Baltimore's cultural in- stitutions, died yesterday at his home, 610 Reservoir street. He had been in failing health for several months. Mr. Stabler was 88 years old. Born in Sandy Spring, Montgomery county, Mr. Stabler had lived here nearly 70 years. He was engaged in the retail coal trade for 50 years and took an active part in the Baltimore Coal Exchange. Mr. Stabler was a lifelong member of the Society of Friends and for years served as secretary of their annual meetings. He also acted as secretary of the Maryland Academy of Sciences and the House of Reformation (for negroes) at Cheltenham, Md. title: LABOR LEADERS ATTACK SYSTEM AT CHELTENHAM: CHARGE EXPLOITATION OF NEGRO BOYS AT PRIVATE REFORM SCHOOL SAY PEONAGE PLAN NOW EXISTS THERE PROTEST AGAINST CONTRACTS WILL BE FILED WITH GOVERNOR RITCHIE
full_text: LABOR LEADERS ATTACK SYSTEM AT CHELTENHAM Charge Exploitation Of Negro Boys At Private Reform School. SAY PEONAGE PLAN NOW EXISTS THERE Protest Against Contracts Will Be Filed With Gov- ernor Ritchie. Organized labor in Baltimore soon will file with Governor Ritchie charges of alleged exploitation, which they term a form of peonage, of the inmates of the Cheltenham School for Boys, in Prince George's county, according to Henry F. Broening, president of the Baltimore Federation of Labor. The Cheltenham school is a negro reformatory and is supported partly by the State. Broommakers Complain. According to Mr. Broening, outside contractors are allowed to make use of the boys in the manufacture of brooms and similar work, to the detriment of the trade in general. This. in turn, he said, has a depressing effect upon wages paid to skilled workers in the industry, members of which now are being organ- ized into a local, affiliated with the Federation of Labor. Mr. Broening, accompanied by Sam- uel Gompers, president of the American Federation of Labor; H. L. Eichel- berger, Maryland representative of the central body; Charles L. Wiegand, sec- retary of the Baltimore Federation of Labor, and several other labor leaders, called on Governor Ritchie at Annapolis Tuesday and explained their grievances. Governor Ritchie promised to investi- gate the complaints and asked Mr. Broening to file with him a brief of the charges. Given Small Pay. "Boys at the institution are paid from 16 to 18 cents a day for their work in broommaking," said Mr. Broen- ing, "with the result that contractors employing them can underbid outside concerns in the same line of business. Even the Maryland Workshop for the Blind is not able to compete with the cut rates of the product from the Chel- tenham institution. This sort of edu- cation is not doing the negroes any good either, because, from investigations we have made, not one in 100 who come from there follow the trade of broom- making when they are discharged. "Aside from this, however, is the ele- ment of unfairness all along the line, as we have been able to observe it. Some of the chain stores and cut-rate establishments in Baltimore and else- where are enabled, through their deal- ings with Cheltenham contractors, to offer the product of the shops at prices which the ordinary dealer, who buys in the open market, cannot possibly meet. Called Form Of Peonage. "We feel that no State-aided insti- tution should be used for exploitation in such manner. We understand that the main object of the Cheltenham school is to educate the boys to some useful occupation they will follow after leaving the school. Cheltenham, ap- parently, is not doing this but is being utilized to beat down legitimate labor values to the enrichment of a few indi- viduals or firms. This we regard as a form of peonage and exploitation' in its worst form." John B. Pyles, superintendent of Cheltenham, said that the institution receives 50 cents a day from the con- tractors. The boys, he said, make from $3 to $7 a week, depending on their agility and also on their ability to do overtime work. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Broening, president of the Baltimore Federation of Labor. The Cheltenham school is a negro reformatory and is supported partly by the State. Broommakers Complain. According to Mr. Broening, outside contractors are allowed to make use of the boys in the manufacture of brooms and similar work, to the detriment of the trade in general. This. in turn, he said, has a depressing effect upon wages paid to skilled workers in the industry, members of which now are being organ- ized into a local, affiliated with the Federation of Labor. Mr. Broening, accompanied by Sam- uel Gompers, president of the American Federation of Labor; H. L. Eichel- berger, Maryland representative of the central body; Charles L. Wiegand, sec- retary of the Baltimore Federation of Labor, and several other labor leaders, called on Governor Ritchie at Annapolis Tuesday and explained their grievances. Governor Ritchie promised to investi- gate the complaints and asked Mr. Broening to file with him a brief of the charges. Given Small Pay. "Boys at the institution are paid from 16 to 18 cents a day for their work in broommaking," said Mr. Broen- ing, "with the result that contractors employing them can underbid outside concerns in the same line of business. Even the Maryland Workshop for the Blind is not able to compete with the cut rates of the product from the Chel- tenham institution. This sort of edu- cation is not doing the negroes any good either, because, from investigations we have made, not one in 100 who come from there follow the trade of broom- making when they are discharged. "Aside from this, however, is the ele- ment of unfairness all along the line, as we have been able to observe it. Some of the chain stores and cut-rate establishments in Baltimore and else- where are enabled, through their deal- ings with Cheltenham contractors, to offer the product of the shops at prices which the ordinary dealer, who buys in the open market, cannot possibly meet. Called Form Of Peonage. "We feel that no State-aided insti- tution should be used for exploitation in such manner. We understand that the main object of the Cheltenham school is to educate the boys to some useful occupation they will follow after leaving the school. Cheltenham, ap- parently, is not doing this but is being utilized to beat down legitimate labor values to the enrichment of a few indi- viduals or firms. This we regard as a form of peonage and exploitation' in its worst form." John B. Pyles, superintendent of Cheltenham, said that the institution receives 50 cents a day from the con- tractors. The boys, he said, make from $3 to $7 a week, depending on their agility and also on their ability to do overtime work. . .

title: MORE FUNDS VOTED TO REFORMATORIES
full_text: MORE FUNDS VOTED TO REFORMATORIES Estimates Board Authorizes $30 Per Capita Increase For Institutions. MONEY NEEDED FOR SICK Situation Concerning Care Of In- sane Serious, N. G. Grasty Declares. The Board of Estimates yesterday au- | thorized the Supervisors of City Chari- ties to increase from $150 to $180 per capita the annual allowance for the maintenance of boys and girls com- mitted to reformatory institutions as city charges. ر If the increase dates from January 1 last it will amount to $22,800 for 1923. It will be taken from the Board of Estimates' contingent fund. Institutions affected are St. Mary's Industrial School, House of Good Shep- herd, Mount street; House of Good Shepherd for Colored Girls, Calverton road; Industrial School for Colored Girls, Melvale, and the House of Refor- mation for Colored Boys, Cheltenham, Prince George's county. There are 760 city boys and girls in these institutions. Appeal For St. Mary's. • The increase of $30 is a result of an appeal from St. Mary's Industrial School for more money for the care of 323 city boys in that institution. St. Mary's requested $200 per boy, but T. Foley Hisky, representative of the school, said it could get along with $180, the allowance to the Maryland School for Boys, Loch Raven, and the Mary- land Training School for Girls, fixed by the Legislature. All institutions should be treated alike, the board said. Albert G. Towers, president of the Board of Supervisors, said he would favor the increase, and it is expected | to be approved at a meeting of the board next Friday. In their budget for 1923 the super- visors requested $200 per capita for the city boys and girls in reformatories. The Board of Estimates cut it to $150. More Funds Needed For Sick. N. G. Grasty, secretary of the super- visors, called the attention of the Board of Estimates to the fact that the year's appropriation for the care of sick in hospitals under contract with the super- visors would be spent by October. ! He said an additional appropriation of $36,000 would be needed to take care. of the patients until December 31. The- situation, Mr. Grasty said, was the re- sult of a cut of $36,000 by the Board of Estimates last fall in the allowance for hospital patients. It will be necessary to make the additional appropriation out of the contingent fund. Care Of Insane. Mr. Grasty also said the Supervisors faced a serious situation in the care of the insane. The hospital for the insane at Bay View is overcrowded, he de- clared, and the Supervisors are con- sidering the building of a barracks for the overflow at a cost of approximately $25,000. The insane who are city and state charges are increasing at the rate of 100 a year, Mr. Grasty said. The city has 960 beds at Springfield, 560 at Spring Grove and 270 at Mount Hope. All are filled. There are 94 on the Springfield wait- ing list. The city pays these institu- tions $125 a year per capita. A sim- ilar payment is made by the State to provide sufficient money for the proper care of the patients. Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner. Thomas Compher, 13 years old, 1026 West Saratoga street, one of the four, will be committed to Cheltenham an- less he is sent out of the city by to- morrow. title: LEAVES ALL TO DESCENDANTS
full_text: LEAVES ALL TO DESCENDANTS Will of Hrs. Louisa Wallace Gill Admitted To Probate. In her will probated in the Orphans' Court yesterday. and bequeathing the halk of her estate to her children and grandchildren. the late Mrs. Louisa Wal- lace Gill stated that her jewelry, house- hold furniture and personal effects in her home would not form part of her estate, as she had given them to her children. Louise Wallace Hazlehurst, Olivia Louise. Thompson. Louise Wallace Macy and Louise Levering, namesakes of Mrs. Gill, are left $1,000 each. William Clark, if in Mrs. Gill's e- ploy at the time of her death, and her godchild, Charlotte Blanchard, if living, are also to get $1.000 each. Each servant other than Clark in Mrs. Gill's employ two years or more when sbe died is to receieve $100. Any inheritance tax on the specific legacies is to be paid out of the estate. The residue, including any property left in trust by Mrs. Gill's father, the late William Wallace Spence, of which she had the disposition. is left in trust to The Mercantile Trust and Deposit Com- pany. The entire trust estate is to be livided into four equal shares for Mrs. Gill's three daughters and the children of her deceased daughter, Mary Esther Масу. Letters on the estate were granted to the Mercantile Trust and Deposit Com- pany, which bonded for $500,000. SENTENCE DELAYS TRIAL Man: Must Serve 30 Days Before Facing Liquor Charges. When, John Lennert, 5 Elm avenue, Curtis Bay, finishes a sentence of 30 lays imposed by Magistrate Potee in the Southern Police Court on a charge of beating his wife, he will have to face Judge Rose, in the United States Dis- trict Court, to answer charges of manu Cacture and possession of illicit whisky. Before being taken to jail yesterday Lennert was arraigned before United States Commissioner Supplee. Police of the Curtis Bay section testified that when they went to Lennert's home to arrest him on complaint of his wife they found a still in operation, 20 gal- lons, of mash and the liquor. Lennert admitted making the whisky and claimed he used it for tubercular infection. The Commissioner glanced at Lennert's 240- pound bulk and rugged complexion and shook his head. "I am going to place a detainer against you for your appearance in court when your time expires," said Commissioner Supplée, "and you can tell your story to the judge." After Robert Preston, colored, 12 years old. 045 Sarah Ann street, had been committed yesterday to the Colored House of Reformation at Cheltenham by Judge Williams, in the Juvenile Court, it was learned that the boy was suffer- ing from a mild.case of scarlet fever. The sentence was stricken out and he was turned over to the Health Com- missioner. The boy was before the court on a charge of disorderly conduct, but was sentenced as a minor without prop- er care.
